alert tcp $HOME_NET any -> 35.198.166.240 any (msg:"LOCAL C2 connection attempt to known C2 IP 35.198.166.240"; flags:S; classtype:trojan-activity; sid:1000205; rev:1;)
alert tcp $HOME_NET any -> $EXTERNAL_NET $HTTP_PORTS (msg:"LOCAL C2 HTTP request Host amellet.bit"; flow:established,to_server; content:"Host|3a| amellet.bit"; http_header; nocase; classtype:trojan-activity; sid:1000206; rev:1;)
alert tcp $HOME_NET any -> $EXTERNAL_NET $HTTP_PORTS (msg:"LOCAL Chthonic-like C2 POST - HTTP/1.0 to /a/ or /html/ without User-Agent"; flow:established,to_server; content:"POST /"; depth:6; content:" HTTP/1.0|0d 0a|"; distance:0; within:20; content:"POST"; http_method; pcre:"/^\/(?:a|html)\/$/U"; content:!"User-Agent|3a|"; http_header; classtype:trojan-activity; sid:1000207; rev:1;)
  • sid 1000205 (IOC) — SYN only (flags:S) to the C2 IP. An IP-only rule without flags:S fires on every packet, thousands of times. Always narrow IP rules like this. Any port (any).
  • sid 1000206 (IOC) — Host: amellet.bit in the HTTP headers. |3a| = :. Fires even if the IP changes, as long as the domain is the same.
  • sid 1000207 (behaviour) — looks only at the shape of the C2 request, not the domain or IP. All conditions must match:
    • content:"POST /"; depth:6; — the first 6 bytes of the packet are POST /. (The request line is not in the HTTP header buffer, so we look in the raw packet.)
    • content:" HTTP/1.0|0d 0a|"; distance:0; within:20; — HTTP/1.0 + line break within the next 20 bytes. So the request line is POST /short-path HTTP/1.0.
    • content:"POST"; http_method; — Snort's HTTP parsing also sees the method as POST.
    • pcre:"/^\/(?:a|html)\/$/U" — the URI is exactly /a/ or /html/. ^ = start, $ = end, (?:a|html) = a or html, U = in the URI.
    • content:!"User-Agent|3a|"; http_header; — no User-Agent: header.

docs.title: C. The first download — URL and "EXE without a User-Agent" (sid 1000208–1000210)
docs.text:
alert tcp $HOME_NET any -> $EXTERNAL_NET $HTTP_PORTS (msg:"LOCAL Malware download URL jgbennett.com 30_723bio_152.exe"; flow:established,to_server; content:"Host|3a| jgbennett.com"; http_header; nocase; content:"/30_723bio_152.exe"; http_uri; nocase; classtype:trojan-activity; sid:1000208; rev:1;)
alert tcp $HOME_NET any -> $EXTERNAL_NET $HTTP_PORTS (msg:"LOCAL EXE requested without User-Agent - set flowbit"; flow:established,to_server; content:"GET"; http_method; content:".exe"; http_uri; nocase; pcre:"/\.exe$/Ui"; content:!"User-Agent|3a|"; http_header; flowbits:set,exe.noua; flowbits:noalert; classtype:trojan-activity; sid:1000209; rev:1;)
alert tcp $EXTERNAL_NET $HTTP_PORTS -> $HOME_NET any (msg:"LOCAL Windows EXE downloaded by non-browser client (no User-Agent)"; flow:established,to_client; flowbits:isset,exe.noua; file_data; content:"MZ"; within:2; content:"This program cannot be run in DOS mode"; distance:0; within:200; classtype:trojan-activity; sid:1000210; rev:1;)
  • sid 1000208 (IOC) — the exact download URL. Two conditions: Host header and URI.
  • sid 1000209 + 1000210 (behaviour, a flowbits pair) — alert when "an .exe was requested without a User-Agent and the response really is a Windows executable".
    • 1000209 (request): GET + URI ending in .exe (pcre:"/\.exe$/Ui") + no User-Agent → flowbits:set,exe.noua marks this connection, and flowbits:noalert means no alert yet.
    • 1000210 (response): the reverse direction ($EXTERNAL_NET $HTTP_PORTS -> $HOME_NET any, to_client) = the server's response. flowbits:isset,exe.noua = only on marked connections. file_data; = in the response body, content:"MZ"; within:2; = the body's first 2 bytes are MZ (executable marker), and within 200 bytes after that This program cannot be run in DOS mode (in every Windows EXE).
    • Why two rules? The request alone could be a fake that is only named .exe; the response alone also catches legitimate update downloads. To see "something that is not a browser + received a real EXE" you have to tie request and response together, and that is what flowbits does.

docs.title: D. Tech support scam (sid 1000211–1000214)
docs.text:
alert tcp $HOME_NET any -> $EXTERNAL_NET $HTTP_PORTS (msg:"LOCAL Tech support scam domain helpcenterforall.bid or krep2010123.tk"; flow:established,to_server; pcre:"/^Host\x3a\s*(?:helpcenterforall\.bid|krep2010123\.tk)/Hmi"; classtype:bad-unknown; sid:1000211; rev:1;)
alert tcp $HOME_NET any -> $EXTERNAL_NET $HTTP_PORTS (msg:"LOCAL Tech support scam landing - phone number in URI"; flow:established,to_server; content:"number="; http_uri; pcre:"/[?&]number=\d{3}-\d{3}-\d{4}/U"; classtype:bad-unknown; sid:1000212; rev:1;)
alert tcp $EXTERNAL_NET $HTTP_PORTS -> $HOME_NET any (msg:"LOCAL Tech support scam page - fake Microsoft call-now text"; flow:established,to_client; threshold:type limit, track by_dst, count 1, seconds 60; file_data; content:"Call Microsoft"; nocase; content:"Toll Free"; nocase; distance:0; within:100; classtype:bad-unknown; sid:1000213; rev:1;)
alert tcp $EXTERNAL_NET $HTTP_PORTS -> $HOME_NET any (msg:"LOCAL Injected popunder script on website (popundr cookie)"; flow:established,to_client; file_data; content:"doOpen(|22|http"; content:"setCookie(|22|popundr|22|"; distance:0; within:100; classtype:web-application-activity; sid:1000214; rev:1;)
  • sid 1000211 (IOC) — either of the two scam domains. content cannot do "or", so use a regex: ^Host\x3a\s*(?:A|B). \x3a = :, \s* = zero or more spaces, H = in the HTTP headers, m = ^ matches at the start of each line (headers are multi-line), i = ignore case.
  • sid 1000212 (behaviour) — a phone number shaped number=000-000-0000 in the URI. This scam family changes domains often but tends to keep passing the phone number in the URL. content:"number="; http_uri; filters quickly first and the slower regex runs after (good practice).
  • sid 1000213 (behaviour) — Call Microsoft in the response body with Toll Free within 100 bytes after it. In the first test it fired twice on the same response, so threshold … track by_dst, count 1, seconds 60 (once per 60 s per PC) was added. This is why you test.
  • sid 1000214 (behaviour) — catches the hacked or malvertising website side. In the response body, doOpen("http and then setCookie("popundr" within 100 bytes. |22| = ". Even when the scam domain changes, it finds sites carrying the same pop-under code. file_data sees the body after gunzip and de-chunking, so it matches compressed pages too (this page was chunked).

docs.title: Step E3 — Testing against the PCAP
docs.text:
1. Paste the 14 lines into local.rules (e.g. sudo nano /etc/snort/rules/local.rules).
  2. Syntax check:
sudo snort -T -c /etc/snort/snort.conf
  • -T — validate the configuration and rules without running. On success the last line is Snort successfully validated the configuration!.

  • An error we actually hit: Unknown ClassType: social-engineering — a classification that does not exist in Snort 2.9's classification.config. List the valid ones with grep "config classification" /etc/snort/classification.config. That is why the scam rules use bad-unknown.

  • Run against the PCAP and count per rule:

mkdir -p /tmp/snorttest
sudo snort -c /etc/snort/snort.conf -r 2017-10-21-traffic-analysis-exercise.pcap -A console -q -k none -U -l /tmp/snorttest | grep -o "\[1:[0-9]*:[0-9]*\] [^[]*" | sort | uniq -c
  • -r file — read a PCAP file instead of a live interface.
  • -A console — print alerts to the screen.
  • -q — hide the start-up banner.
  • -k none — turn off checksum verification. Captures often contain packets with "wrong" checksums (NIC offloading); if Snort drops them, rules silently fail to fire. This PCAP gives the same result without -k none, but make it a habit.
  • -U — show times in UTC.
  • -l /tmp/snorttest — a test log folder, so the real alert.log stays clean.
  • grep -o "\[1:[0-9]*:[0-9]*\] [^[]*" — extract just [1:sid:rev] title from each alert line.
  • sort | uniq -c — group identical lines and count them.

docs.title: Step E4 — Actual results
docs.text:
Reading one alert line:

10/21-04:52:47.886843  [**] [1:1000210:1] LOCAL Windows EXE downloaded by non-browser client (no User-Agent) [**] [Classification: A Network Trojan was detected] [Priority: 1] {TCP} 107.180.41.148:80 -> 10.0.1.95:49691
  • 10/21-04:52:47.886843 — packet time (UTC because of -U).
  • [1:1000210:1] — [engine:sid:rev] — which rule fired.
  • {TCP} source -> destination — the matching packet. 1000210 is a response rule, so the direction is server → PC.

Results per rule (identical with HOME_NET 10.0.0.0/8 and HOME_NET any):

sid Rule Kind Expected Actual First – last (UTC) 1000201 TCP DNS amellet.bit IOC 37 (queries in D3) 37 ✅ 04:53:52 – 05:02:05 1000202 TCP DNS .bit Behaviour 37 37 ✅ 04:53:52 – 05:02:05 1000203 UDP DNS .bit Behaviour 0 (no UDP this time) 0 ✅ — 1000204 External TCP 53 SYN (once per 10 min) Behaviour 1 1 ✅ 04:53:52 1000205 C2 IP SYN IOC 34 (C2 connections) 34 ✅ 04:54:03 – 05:02:05 1000206 Host amellet.bit IOC 39 (POSTs) 39 ✅ 04:54:03 – 05:02:05 1000207 C2 POST shape Behaviour 39 39 ✅ 04:54:03 – 05:02:05 1000208 Download URL IOC 1 1 ✅ 04:52:47 1000209 (mark only, no alert) — 0 0 ✅ — 1000210 EXE received without User-Agent Behaviour 1 1 ✅ 04:52:47 1000211 Scam domains IOC 6 (requests) 6 ✅ 05:03:25 – 05:03:31 1000212 Phone number in URI Behaviour 1 1 ✅ 05:03:25 1000213 Scam page text Behaviour 1 1 ✅ (2 before threshold) 05:03:26 1000214 Pop-under script Behaviour 1 1 ✅ 05:02:27

Reading the result:

  1. Every rule fired the expected number of times. The expected counts came from the Zeek/Arkime counts in Part D. Writing the expected count before writing the rule lets you check the result immediately.
  2. 0 false positives. The capture also contains traffic to Microsoft, Google, Bing and dozens of ad networks, yet every alert IP belongs to the malicious chain (107.180.41.148, 35.198.166.240, the external DNS servers, 104.18.61.210, 162.244.35.33/36). In particular, 1000210 did not fire on the 63 other sessions without a User-Agent (C2, msftconnecttest, OCSP) — thanks to the .exe + MZ conditions.
  3. flowbits worked. 1000209 only set the mark, and 1000210 fired once on the response in the same connection.
  4. Testing showed where a threshold was needed. 1000213 initially fired twice on the same response.

Question: why is the output not in time order?

Snort checks HTTP rules after reassembling the TCP stream, so the alert is printed when reassembly finishes and can appear after other alerts. Each alert's time is still the real packet time. Sort the timeline by time, not by output order.

docs.title: Step E5 — If you use Snort 3
docs.text:
In Snort 3, buffers such as http_uri and http_header go before the content (sticky buffers). sid 1000206, for example, becomes:

alert http $HOME_NET any -> $EXTERNAL_NET any ( msg:"LOCAL C2 HTTP request Host amellet.bit"; flow:established,to_server; http_header; content:"Host|3a| amellet.bit",nocase; classtype:trojan-activity; sid:1000206; rev:2; )
  • alert http — Snort 3 accepts http as the protocol and recognises HTTP by content instead of by port.
  • http_header; — every content after this is searched in the headers.
  • content:"…",nocase — options attach with a comma.
  • file_data keeps the same name in Snort 3. The DNS rules (A) can be used as they are.
  • This Snort 3 example shows the syntax only; this time the rules were tested with Snort 2.9 only. On a Snort 3 sensor, run snort -T and the PCAP test again.

docs.title: Part F — Timeline, IOCs, host-operator leads
Timeline (UTC, 2017-10-21)

docs.title: Leads for the host operator
docs.text:
The network evidence translated into clues to look for inside the PC. Each event ID is explained.

  1. Isolate and capture memory first. Isolate DELOREAN-PC (10.0.1.95, MAC 60:a4:4c:6a:b2:1f) and capture memory before rebooting. Zeus-family malware hides inside other processes (injection) and leaves few disk traces.
  2. Time windows: 04:52:30 – 04:56:15 UTC (Office start → EXE → C2 modules), and 05:00:50 – 05:03:35 UTC.
  3. Find the Office document opened around 04:52:40:
    • Sysmon event ID 1 (process created, with command line and parent) / Security 4688 (a new process has been created): child processes of WINWORD.EXE or EXCEL.EXE (cmd.exe, powershell.exe, wscript.exe, or the EXE itself).
    • Recent-documents lists, Office's Trusted Records registry key (whether the user clicked "Enable Content"), documents in download or mail temp folders, Zone.Identifier (marks files downloaded from the internet).
  4. Find the EXE. 30_723bio_152.exe (SHA256 above) — it may have been renamed, so search by hash.
    • Sysmon event ID 11 (file created): executables created around 04:52:47. Check %TEMP% and %APPDATA%.
    • Prefetch, Amcache: execution traces and SHA1 (fe4116d0…529d).
  5. Processes that made network connections.
    • Sysmon event ID 3 (a process made a network connection): processes that connected to 107.180.41.148:80, 35.198.166.240:80 and TCP 53 on external IPs. Check whether the process that hit www.msftconnecttest.com without a User-Agent is the same one (verifies the D6 assessment).
    • Sysmon event ID 22 (DNS query, Sysmon 10+): the process that asked for amellet.bit. This malware asked directly over TCP, bypassing Windows DNS, so ID 22 may be empty — then ID 3 is the reference.
  6. Injection. Sysmon event ID 8 (CreateRemoteThread: one process creates a thread inside another), ID 10 (one process accesses another's memory). Public analyses report that the Chthonic loader runs inside legitimate processes such as msiexec.exe — check for a msiexec.exe running without its normal parent.
  7. Persistence. Sysmon event ID 13 (registry value set) — auto-run keys such as HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run. Security 4698 (a scheduled task was created), System 7045 (a new service was installed).
  8. The 04:53:08 DHCP re-request — the network reconnected 21 s after the download. Check the System log (network profile, adapter events) for an adapter restart, wake from sleep or user action.
  9. Banking details and passwords. Zeus-family malware steals browser input and saved passwords. Have the user change passwords (especially banking and email) from a different, clean device. About 23 KB left encrypted to the C2.
  10. Tech support scam. Ask the user whether, after 05:03:25, they called 888-779-0939 or installed/allowed a remote-access tool (TeamViewer, AnyDesk, LogMeIn …). If so, handle it as a separate incident. IE's popundr cookie (24 h) is also a trace.

docs.title: Copy-ready query sheet
docs.text:
Replace <…>. In Splunk use the All time range and ts for times.

Splunk — baselining

| tstats count where index=zeek by sourcetype

index=zeek sourcetype=zeek:conn
| stats count min(ts) AS first max(ts) AS last
| eval first=strftime(first, "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"), last=strftime(last, "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S")

index=zeek sourcetype=zeek:conn (id_orig_h=10.0.0.0/8 OR id_orig_h=172.16.0.0/12 OR id_orig_h=192.168.0.0/16)
| stats count dc(id_resp_h) AS unique_destinations BY id_orig_h
| sort - count

index=zeek sourcetype=zeek:dhcp
| table ts client_addr server_addr assigned_addr mac host_name domain lease_time msg_types

index=zeek sourcetype=zeek:conn (id_resp_h=10.0.0.0/8 OR id_resp_h=172.16.0.0/12 OR id_resp_h=192.168.0.0/16) id_resp_p<10000
| stats dc(id_orig_h) AS clients count values(id_resp_p) AS ports BY id_resp_h

index=zeek sourcetype=zeek:conn id_resp_p IN (88, 135, 139, 389, 445, 464, 636, 3268, 3389, 5985, 25, 110, 143, 465, 587, 993, 995)
| stats count BY id_resp_h id_resp_p

index=zeek sourcetype=zeek:dns
| stats count values(proto) AS proto BY id_resp_h
| sort - count

index=zeek sourcetype=zeek:conn
| stats count BY proto service

index=zeek sourcetype=zeek:http id_orig_h=<host-IP>
| fillnull value="(none)" user_agent
| stats count BY user_agent

index=zeek sourcetype=zeek:conn id_orig_h=<host-IP> NOT (id_resp_h=10.0.0.0/8 OR id_resp_h=172.16.0.0/12 OR id_resp_h=192.168.0.0/16 OR id_resp_h=224.0.0.0/4 OR id_resp_h=255.255.255.255)
| stats count sum(orig_bytes) AS bytes_out sum(resp_bytes) AS bytes_in values(id_resp_p) AS ports BY id_resp_h
| sort - count

Splunk — malicious activity

index=zeek sourcetype=zeek:http NOT user_agent=*
| fillnull value="-" host
| stats count dc(uid) AS connections values(method) AS method values(version) AS ver BY host id_resp_h

index=zeek sourcetype=zeek:files mime_type="application/x-dosexec"
| table ts tx_hosts rx_hosts seen_bytes total_bytes md5 sha1

index=zeek sourcetype=zeek:dns NOT id_resp_h=<internal-DNS-IP> NOT id_resp_h=224.0.0.0/4 NOT id_resp_h=<broadcast>
| stats count values(query) AS queries BY id_resp_h proto

index=zeek sourcetype=zeek:http host="<domain>"
| sort ts
| streamstats current=f last(ts) AS prev_ts
| eval t=strftime(ts, "%H:%M:%S"), gap=round(ts-prev_ts, 1)
| table t method uri version request_body_len response_body_len gap

index=zeek sourcetype=zeek:weird
| stats count BY name id_resp_h

Arkime

ip.src == 10.0.0.0/8 || ip.src == 172.16.0.0/12 || ip.src == 192.168.0.0/16
ip.src != 10.0.0.0/8
protocols == dhcp
ip.dst == 10.0.0.0/8
ip.src == <host-IP> && ip.dst != 10.0.0.0/8 && ip.dst != 224.0.0.0/4 && ip.dst != 255.255.255.255
protocols == http && http.user-agent != EXISTS!
port.dst == 53 && ip.protocol == tcp
host.dns == *.bit
host.http == <domain>
host.http == [<domain1>, <domain2>]
mac.src == <MAC>

Snort

sudo snort -T -c /etc/snort/snort.conf
sudo snort -c /etc/snort/snort.conf -r <file>.pcap -A console -q -k none -U -l /tmp/snorttest | grep -o "\[1:[0-9]*:[0-9]*\] [^[]*" | sort | uniq -c

Analysis VM

sha256sum <file>.pcap
tshark -r <file>.pcap -Y "dhcp.option.dhcp == 5" -V | grep -E "^ +(DHCP Server Identifier|Subnet Mask|Router|Domain Name Server|Domain Name|IP Address Lease Time):"
tshark -r <file>.pcap --export-objects http,http_objects

docs.title: Lessons learned
docs.text:
1. Baseline first. Because we knew "this PC asks the router DNS (10.0.1.1) over UDP", asking external DNS over TCP stood out immediately.
  2. Number of IPs ≠ number of devices. There were 3 IPs, but by MAC only 2 devices (the router has two IPs).
  3. "None" is also a result. Confirming and recording that there is no DC, file server, mail server, inbound connection or lateral movement saves the next person from searching again.
  4. The User-Agent tells you who made the request. Splitting browser (IE11), Windows components (CryptoAPI, WNS) and programs that send nothing gathered the malicious traffic together. But "none" also contains normal noise (408 responses, OCSP), so check each one.
  5. A few seconds before and after tell you the cause. Office queries 1–7 s before the EXE download pointed to the infection vector (document macro). It could not be confirmed, so it is written as "assessed" and passed on as a host lead.
  6. .bit and direct external DNS are strong signals. Company PCs almost never ask for Namecoin names, and even less often use TCP 53 that bypasses company DNS. Behaviour rules like these survive the attacker changing domains and IPs.
  7. One capture can hold two incidents. The malware C2 and the tech support scam pop-up are close in time but show no link. Do not merge them into one story; record them separately.
  8. Write the expected count before the rule, and test against the PCAP. Testing caught a classtype error (social-engineering) and a duplicate alert (sid 1000213).
  9. You can still reach conclusions on a closed network. Record hashes for others, judge by behaviour, and write families as "consistent with … – unconfirmed".

docs.title: BEGUILESOFT — Splunk-first baselining to HawkEye Keylogger stealing passwords, keylogs and screenshots over FTP
BEGUILESOFT — HawkEye Keylogger: stolen passwords, keylogs and screenshots over FTP
docs.text:
Case summary

The malware-traffic-analysis.net 2019-05-02 "BEGUILESOFT" PCAP, worked Splunk-first on the home-lab pcapbox VM, with Arkime only where the packet content is needed. One Windows 7 PC in an AD domain (Breaux-Win7-PC, user adriana.breaux) looks up its public IP, then logs in to the free hosting service files.000webhost[.]com over FTP with the account snifferzett and uploads five files in three sessions, 10–15 minutes apart: a "Stealer Records" file with saved passwords for Gmail, BB&T online banking and Outlook mail, two keylogs (payment data typed into Excel) and two screenshots — about 5 MB. File names say HawkEye Keylogger. The page ends with one very simple Snort rule and a short report.

Evidence 2019-05-02-traffic-analysis-exercise.pcap — 2019-05-02 21:35:18 – 22:05:23 UTC (about 30 min) Source malware-traffic-analysis.net 2019-05-02 "BEGUILESOFT" Environment Closed network. pcapbox VM: Splunk (index=zeek, case field pcap_case), Arkime (tag = case name), Snort 2.9.20. No Wireshark. Deliverables Analysis, one Snort rule Related pages Night Dew (pcapbox setup, Snort test guide) · SPL cheat sheet · Arkime search syntax · Zeek logs · Playbook: data exfiltration

How to read this page

The order is the order the case was worked: baselining → suspicious destinations → FTP detail → Arkime for content → Snort. Every SPL query is explained line by line, followed by what the result looked like and how to read it. The Question boxes are questions asked while working the case, with their answers.

The indicators on this page are real

Domains, IPs and account names come from real 2019 malware traffic. Prose and tables are defanged ([.]); code blocks keep values as typed. Do not visit them. The victim's real password is not shown on this page.

docs.title: Answers at a glance
docs.text: Item Answer Status Infected PC 10.0.0.227, Breaux-Win7-PC, MAC 84:8f:69:09:86:c0 (Dell) Confirmed User adriana.breaux (domain BEGUILESOFT) Confirmed DC 10.0.0.10, beguilesoft-dc.beguilesoft[.]com Confirmed First malicious event 21:36:14 UTC public IP lookup (whatismyipaddress[.]com), then 21:36:33 first FTP login Confirmed Exfil destination files.000webhost[.]com — 145.14.145.4, 145.14.144.10, 145.14.145.99 (one name, three IPs) Confirmed FTP account snifferzett (attacker's account, same in all three sessions) Confirmed Data stolen 5 files, ~5.06 MB: Stealer Records (Gmail, BB&T bank, Outlook POP3 — one password reused for all three), 2 keylogs (Excel payment data, Word typing), 2 screenshots Confirmed Upload result All 5 STOR commands got 226 File successfully transferred Confirmed Initial access Not in the capture — the PC was already infected Inferred Malware family HawkEye Keylogger — taken from the uploaded file names, not from a sample Inferred (strong)

docs.title: Step 0 — Before the first query
docs.text:
The PCAP was dropped into \\10.50.10.60\incoming as 20190502_BEGUILESOFT.pcap, so the case name is 20190502_BEGUILESOFT (Splunk field pcap_case, Arkime tag). Two things to check before any query:

  1. Splunk time range = All time. On pcapbox _time is the packet time (2019), so the default "Last 24 hours" returns nothing.
  2. Splunk account time zone = UTC (account menu → Preferences), because strftime prints in your Splunk time zone.

Setup and ingest are explained in Night Dew — Step 0.

docs.title: Step 1 — Baselining
docs.text: Goal: before looking for anything bad, learn the basics — when the capture runs, which logs exist, which internal PCs talk, and the host name, MAC, DC and user. None of this goes into the report except the host details.

docs.title: 1-1. Capture window and log types
docs.text:
index=zeek pcap_case="20190502_BEGUILESOFT"
| stats count AS events min(ts) AS first max(ts) AS last BY sourcetype
| eval first=strftime(first, "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"), last=strftime(last, "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S")
| sort - events
  • Line 1 takes every Zeek event of this case. pcap_case is the field pcapbox fills with the PCAP file name.
  • Line 2 stats works like a pivot table: "group, then calculate". BY sourcetype groups by log type (conn, dns, http…). For each group it counts events (count), finds the earliest time (min(ts)) and the latest (max(ts)). AS names the result column.
  • Line 3 eval calculates or overwrites a value. ts is an epoch number such as 1556832918; strftime turns it into a readable date.
  • Line 4 sort - events sorts by event count, largest first. - means descending.

Result (281 events, 15 log types):

sourcetype          events  first                last
zeek:conn           99      2019-05-02 21:35:18  2019-05-02 22:05:23
zeek:dns            49      2019-05-02 21:35:18  2019-05-02 22:01:33
zeek:kerberos       39      2019-05-02 21:35:18  2019-05-02 22:05:23
zeek:ldap_search    23      2019-05-02 21:35:18  2019-05-02 21:36:13
zeek:dce_rpc        15      2019-05-02 21:35:18  2019-05-02 21:36:57
zeek:ldap           15      2019-05-02 21:35:18  2019-05-02 21:36:13
zeek:ftp            10      2019-05-02 21:36:35  2019-05-02 22:01:34
zeek:files          9       2019-05-02 21:35:24  2019-05-02 22:01:35
zeek:smb_mapping    9       2019-05-02 21:35:18  2019-05-02 22:05:23
zeek:ntp            4       2019-05-02 21:35:23  2019-05-02 21:52:27
zeek:weird          3       2019-05-02 21:35:18  2019-05-02 21:36:57
zeek:http           2       2019-05-02 21:35:26  2019-05-02 21:36:14
zeek:smb_files      2       2019-05-02 21:35:24  2019-05-02 21:36:13
zeek:dhcp           1       2019-05-02 21:35:21  2019-05-02 21:35:21
zeek:software       1       2019-05-02 21:35:26  2019-05-02 21:35:26

Reading the result:

  • The zeek:conn first–last is the capture window: 21:35:18 – 22:05:23 UTC, about 30 minutes.
  • kerberos, ldap, dce_rpc and smb are normal Windows domain traffic.
  • zeek:ftp has 10 events (21:36:35 – 22:01:34), there is no zeek:ssl at all, and HTTP has only 2 events. An office PC rarely uses FTP, while info-stealer malware often sends stolen data over FTP. Not a conclusion yet — but the first place to look after baselining.

docs.title: 1-2. DHCP — host name, MAC, domain
docs.text:
index=zeek sourcetype=zeek:dhcp pcap_case="20190502_BEGUILESOFT"
| eval time=strftime(ts, "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S")
| table time assigned_addr mac host_name domain msg_types
  • sourcetype=zeek:dhcp takes DHCP logs only.
  • table shows only the columns you name, in that order.
  • assigned_addr = IP the DHCP server gave · mac = the PC's MAC · host_name = the name the PC announced (the report HOSTNAME) · domain = domain name from DHCP · msg_types = DHCP message types.
time                 assigned_addr  mac                host_name       domain           msg_types
2019-05-02 21:35:21                 84:8f:69:09:86:c0  Breaux-Win7-PC  beguilesoft.com  INFORM ACK

Why is assigned_addr empty?

msg_types is INFORM, not REQUEST. A PC that already has an IP (fixed address, or a lease from before) sends DHCPINFORM to ask only for settings such as the domain name. Nothing is "assigned", so the field is empty. The IP comes from the next query (10.0.0.227). Add client_addr to the table to see the IP the PC used to ask.

docs.title: 1-3. Which internal IPs start connections
docs.text:
index=zeek sourcetype=zeek:conn pcap_case="20190502_BEGUILESOFT"
| where cidrmatch("10.0.0.0/8", id_orig_h) OR cidrmatch("172.16.0.0/12", id_orig_h) OR cidrmatch("192.168.0.0/16", id_orig_h)
| stats count AS conns dc(id_resp_h) AS dests BY id_orig_h
| sort - conns
  • id_orig_h = the IP that started the connection.
  • where keeps only events where the condition is true. cidrmatch("10.0.0.0/8", id_orig_h) asks "is this IP inside 10.0.0.0/8?". With the three private ranges joined by OR, only internal IPs stay.
  • count = connections; dc(id_resp_h) = distinct count of destination IPs. BY id_orig_h gives one row per internal IP.
id_orig_h    conns  dests
10.0.0.227   99     10

Only one internal PC starts connections, to only 10 destinations. 10.0.0.227 is the suspect.

docs.title: 1-4. Kerberos — DC and user account
docs.text:
index=zeek sourcetype=zeek:kerberos pcap_case="20190502_BEGUILESOFT"
| stats count BY id_orig_h id_resp_h client

Kerberos (port 88) is the Windows domain logon. One log gives three facts: id_resp_h = the server that answers = the DC, and client = user/DOMAIN = the logged-on account.

id_orig_h    id_resp_h   client                            count
10.0.0.227   10.0.0.10   /BEGUILESOFT.COM                  15
10.0.0.227   10.0.0.10   BREAUX-WIN7-PC$/BEGUILESOFT.COM   12
10.0.0.227   10.0.0.10   adriana.breaux/BEGUILESOFT        2
10.0.0.227   10.0.0.10   adriana.breaux/BEGUILESOFT.COM    5
10.0.0.227   10.0.0.10   breaux-win7-pc$/BEGUILESOFT.COM   2
10.0.0.227   10.0.0.10   breaux-win7-pc$/beguilesoft.com   2

Reading the result:

  • DC = 10.0.0.10.
  • Names ending in $ are computer accounts (the PC itself logging on) — they confirm the host name, nothing more.
  • /BEGUILESOFT.COM with no name (15) are TGS requests (ticket for a service). A TGS request does not carry the user name in readable form, so Zeek leaves it empty.
  • What is left is the user: adriana.breaux.

If zeek:kerberos is missing, use sourcetype=zeek:ntlm with BY id_orig_h username hostname domainname.

Baseline summary: capture 21:35:18 – 22:05:23 UTC · one PC 10.0.0.227 Breaux-Win7-PC, MAC 84:8f:69:09:86:c0 · domain beguilesoft.com · DC 10.0.0.10 · user adriana.breaux. And FTP is unusual.

docs.title: Step 2 — Every destination, in time order
docs.text:
There are only 10 destinations, so look at all of them.

index=zeek sourcetype=zeek:conn pcap_case="20190502_BEGUILESOFT"
| stats count AS conns sum(orig_bytes) AS sent sum(resp_bytes) AS recv min(ts) AS first BY id_resp_h id_resp_p service
| eval first=strftime(first, "%H:%M:%S")
| sort first
  • sum() adds up the values in each group. orig_bytes = bytes the PC sent, resp_bytes = bytes it received. More sent than received points to data leaving (exfil).
  • BY id_resp_h id_resp_p service makes one row per destination IP + port + protocol that Zeek recognised (dns, http, ftp…).
  • sort first has no -, so it is ascending — first contact first, like a timeline.
id_resp_h        id_resp_p  service             conns  sent      recv    first
10.0.0.10        135        dce_rpc             1      496       548     21:35:18
10.0.0.10        389        ldap_tcp,krb,gssapi 4      11310     14015   21:35:18
10.0.0.10        445        gssapi,smb,krb      5      20962     7212    21:35:18
10.0.0.10        53         dns                 21     1307      2354    21:35:18
10.0.0.10        88         krb_tcp             24     28669     31383   21:35:18
...              (more DC, broadcast, LLMNR, DHCP, NTP rows)
204.2.193.137    80         http                1      97        179     21:35:26
104.16.154.36    80         http                1      71        564     21:36:14
145.14.145.4     21         ftp                 1      152       540     21:36:33
145.14.145.4     37280      ftp-data            1      2791      0       21:36:35
145.14.144.10    21         ftp                 1      205       747     21:46:27
145.14.144.10    40651      ftp-data            1      891       0       21:46:27
145.14.144.10    47434      ftp-data            1      2832685   0       21:46:28
145.14.145.99    21         ftp                 1      206       746     22:01:33
145.14.145.99    35396      ftp-data            1      2225681   0       22:01:34
145.14.145.99    36091      ftp-data            1      601       0       22:01:34

Reading the result:

  • Everything at 21:35 to 10.0.0.10 is the domain logon: DNS, Kerberos, LDAP, SMB, RPC. Normal.
  • Only three external groups: 204.2.193.137 (Windows connectivity check), 104.16.154.36 at 21:36:14, and three 145.14.x IPs on FTP.
  • ftp and ftp-data come in pairs. Port 21 carries only a few hundred bytes; the high-port ftp-data connections carry up to 2.8 MB — and received 0 bytes. That is the shape of an upload.
  • Three FTP sessions: 21:36, 21:46, 22:01 (10 and 15 minutes apart).

docs.title: 2-1. DNS — which names are behind those IPs
docs.text:
index=zeek sourcetype=zeek:dns pcap_case="20190502_BEGUILESOFT"
| stats count values(answers) AS answers min(ts) AS first BY query
| eval first=strftime(first, "%H:%M:%S")
| sort first
  • query = the name the PC asked about.
  • values(answers) collects every answer for that name without duplicates into one cell, so you can match "name → IP" with the conn result.

Key lines (domain lookups such as _ldap._tcp..., WPAD, isatap are normal Windows noise):

query                              count  answers                                              first
beguilesoft-dc.beguilesoft.com     2      10.0.0.10                                            21:35:18
breaux-win7-pc.beguilesoft.com     2      add: A breaux-win7-pc.beguilesoft.com 10.0.0.227 ... 21:35:26
www.msftncsi.com                   1      204.2.193.137 204.2.193.138 a1961.g2.akamai.net ...   21:35:26
whatismyipaddress.com              1      104.16.154.36 104.16.155.36                          21:36:14
files.000webhost.com               8      145.14.144.10 145.14.145.4 145.14.145.99 us-east-1.route-1000.000webhost.awex.io  21:36:33
dns.msftncsi.com                   2      131.107.255.255 fd3e:4f5a:5b81::1                    21:41:28

Reading the result:

  • breaux-win7-pc.beguilesoft.com with add: A ... 10.0.0.227 is the PC registering its own DNS name — another confirmation of IP + host name.
  • www.msftncsi.com / dns.msftncsi.com = Windows "am I online?" checks. Normal.
  • whatismyipaddress[.]com at 21:36:14 — a "what is my public IP?" service. People rarely visit it; malware uses it to learn where it runs. HawkEye is known for this lookup.
  • files.000webhost[.]com at 21:36:33, asked 8 times, answers three IPs — exactly the three FTP servers. 000webhost is a free hosting service: cheap and anonymous for an attacker to receive stolen data.

docs.title: Step 3 — What went over FTP
docs.text:
index=zeek sourcetype=zeek:ftp pcap_case="20190502_BEGUILESOFT"
| eval time=strftime(ts, "%H:%M:%S")
| table time id_resp_h user command arg reply_code reply_msg

zeek:ftp has one line per FTP command. user = login account · command = the FTP command (STOR = upload to the server, RETR = download) · arg = its argument (for STOR, the file name) · reply_code = server answer (226 = transfer complete).

time      id_resp_h      user         command  arg                                                                          reply_code  reply_msg
21:36:35  145.14.145.4   snifferzett  PASV                                                                                 227         Entering Passive Mode (145,14,145,4,145,160).
21:36:35  145.14.145.4   snifferzett  STOR     ftp://145.14.145.4/HawkEye_Keylogger_Stealer_Records_BREAUX-WIN7-PC 5.2.2019 9:36:28 PM.txt  421  Idle timeout (30 seconds): closing control connection
21:46:27  145.14.144.10  snifferzett  PASV                                                                                 227         Entering Passive Mode (145,14,144,10,158,203).
21:46:28  145.14.144.10  snifferzett  STOR     ftp://145.14.144.10/HawkEye_Keylogger_Keylog_Records_2_BREAUX-WIN7-PC 5.2.2019 9:46:22 PM.txt  226  0.068 seconds (measured here), 12.72 Kbytes per second
21:46:28  145.14.144.10  snifferzett  PASV                                                                                 227         Entering Passive Mode (145,14,144,10,185,74).
21:46:28  145.14.144.10  snifferzett  STOR     ftp://145.14.144.10/screenshot1_BREAUX-WIN7-PC.jpeg                         421         Idle timeout (30 seconds): closing control connection
22:01:34  145.14.145.99  snifferzett  PASV                                                                                 227         Entering Passive Mode (145,14,145,99,138,68).
22:01:34  145.14.145.99  snifferzett  STOR     ftp://145.14.145.99/HawkEye_Keylogger_Keylog_Records_3_BREAUX-WIN7-PC 5.2.2019 10:01:28 PM.txt  226  0.064 seconds (measured here), 9.12 Kbytes per second
22:01:34  145.14.145.99  snifferzett  PASV                                                                                 227         Entering Passive Mode (145,14,145,99,140,251).
22:01:34  145.14.145.99  snifferzett  STOR     ftp://145.14.145.99/screenshot2_BREAUX-WIN7-PC.jpeg                         421         Idle timeout (30 seconds): closing control connection

Reading the result:

  1. The file names give the malware away: HawkEye_Keylogger_Stealer_Records_..., HawkEye_Keylogger_Keylog_Records_2/3_..., screenshot1/2_.... HawkEye is a well-known info-stealer (keylogger).
  2. The first upload is "Stealer Records" — passwords saved in browsers and mail clients. The next two sessions each send one keylog (keystrokes) and one screenshot.
  3. Same account snifferzett every time, three different 000webhost IPs.
  4. The times in the file names (9:36:28 PM, 9:46:22 PM, 10:01:28 PM) match the UTC times in the capture: the PC clock is set to UTC.
  5. Why does Zeek show USER/PASS nowhere? Zeek's ftp.log does not log every command. By default (FTP::logged_commands) it keeps one line only for transfer-related commands (STOR, RETR, APPE, DELE, PASV, PORT, EPSV, EPRT…) and adds the login to the user and password columns of those lines. The password is <hidden> by default; the real value is visible in Arkime (Step 4).

docs.title: 3-1. Matching each file to its size (PASV port arithmetic)
docs.text:
zeek:ftp has no file sizes; the sizes are on the ftp-data lines of conn. Match them with the PASV reply: in (h1,h2,h3,h4,p1,p2) the first four numbers are the IP and the data port is p1 × 256 + p2.

(145,14,145,4,145,160)   → 145×256+160 = 37280 → 2,791 B     Stealer_Records
(145,14,144,10,158,203)  → 158×256+203 = 40651 → 891 B       Keylog_Records_2
(145,14,144,10,185,74)   → 185×256+74  = 47434 → 2,832,685 B screenshot1
(145,14,145,99,138,68)   → 138×256+68  = 35396 → 2,225,681 B screenshot2
(145,14,145,99,140,251)  → 140×256+251 = 36091 → 601 B       Keylog_Records_3

Total sent on the data channels: 5,062,649 B ≈ 5.06 MB, received 0. A second check: the 226 reply for Keylog_Records_3 says 0.064 s at 9.12 KB/s ≈ 584 B — close to the 601 bytes on the wire.

Question: please explain the FTP commands in more detail

FTP uses two connections. The control connection (port 21) carries only commands and answers ("log me in", "I am sending this file"). The file contents go over a separate data connection. That is why conn shows ftp (port 21, a few hundred bytes) next to ftp-data (high port, megabytes). Read the control connection for what and where, the data connection for how much and what content.

One upload in this PCAP, as Arkime shows it (C: = infected PC, S: = server):

S: 220 ProFTPD Server (000webhost.com) [::ffff:145.14.144.10]   ← server greeting
C: USER snifferzett                         ← account name
S: 331 User snifferzett OK. Password required
C: PASS ********                            ← password (clear text!)
S: 230 OK. Current restricted directory is /
C: OPTS utf8 on                             ← use UTF-8 for file names
S: 200 OK, UTF-8 enabled
C: PWD                                      ← which folder am I in?
S: 257 "/" is your current location
C: CWD /                                    ← go to the top folder
S: 250 OK. Current directory is /
C: TYPE I                                   ← binary mode
S: 200 TYPE is now 8-bit binary
C: PASV                                     ← open a data port for me
S: 227 Entering Passive Mode (145,14,144,10,158,203).
C: STOR HawkEye_Keylogger_Keylog_Records_2_BREAUX-WIN7-PC 5.2.2019 9:46:22 PM.txt
S: 150 Connecting to port 44294             ← send it on the data connection
   [data connection 10.0.0.227 → 145.14.144.10:40651, 891 B]
S: 226-File successfully transferred        ← received
C: TYPE I / PASV / STOR screenshot1_BREAUX-WIN7-PC.jpeg
   [data connection → :47434, 2,832,685 B]
S: 226-File successfully transferred
S: 421 Idle timeout (30 seconds): closing control connection

Command by command:

  • USER / PASS — login name and password. FTP has no encryption, so the password crosses the network in clear text. The attacker builds the FTP account into the malware, so the account is exposed — a good IOC.
  • OPTS utf8 on / PWD / CWD / — set UTF-8 file names, ask the current folder, move to the top folder. Normal FTP client libraries send these automatically.
  • TYPE — transfer mode: TYPE A = text (ASCII), TYPE I = binary (Image). JPEG files are sent with TYPE I.
  • PASV — "Passive mode, open a port for me". The reply 227 (h1,h2,h3,h4,p1,p2) gives the IP and the port p1×256+p2.
  • STOR — upload: the client stores a file on the server. An internal PC doing STOR to an external server means exfiltration. The key command of this case.
  • QUIT — end the session. Here the server closed it first with 421.

Other commands you will meet:

Command Meaning Why it matters RETR Download (server → client) Pulling a malicious file from outside APPE Append to an existing file Can be used for exfil like STOR PORT / EPRT Active mode (the server connects back to the client) Rare today because of NAT and firewalls EPSV Extended PASV (IPv6-ready, port only) Reply looks like 229 (\|\|\|port\|) LIST / NLST Folder listing Reconnaissance CWD / MKD / DELE Change folder, make folder, delete file DELE to clean up SYST / FEAT Ask server type / features Normal clients use them too

Why malware almost always uses PASV: the infected PC is usually behind NAT, so nothing outside can connect in. In passive mode the client connects out, which always works.

Reply codes — the first digit is enough: 1xx in progress (150 opening data connection), 2xx success (220 greeting, 227 passive mode, 230 logged in, 226 transfer complete), 3xx more information needed (331 password please), 4xx temporary failure (421 closing), 5xx permanent failure (530 login failed, 550 file not found / no permission).

Question: what are PASV and STOR?

Think of the FTP server as a parcel depot, and the infected PC as someone dropping off parcels (stolen files).

In FTP the counter where you talk (commands) and the door where parcels go in (files) are separate. The counter is always in the same place (port 21); the door is opened fresh each time. So the PC first says:

PC:      PASV
Server:  227 Entering Passive Mode (145,14,144,10,158,203)

"Please open a door for my parcel." — "Door 40651 at 145.14.144.10 is open, come there." The first four numbers are the IP; the door number is 158 × 256 + 203 = 40651. Passive means the server just opens the door and waits; the PC walks to it.

Then the PC says which parcel it is leaving:

PC:      STOR HawkEye_Keylogger_Keylog_Records_2_BREAUX-WIN7-PC ... .txt
Server:  150 ...                          ← "OK, put it through that door"
         [PC sends 891 bytes through door 40651]
Server:  226 File successfully transferred ← "Received"

STOR = Store = upload from the PC to the server. The opposite, download, is RETR (Retrieve).

Every upload is a PASV → STOR pair: open a door, drop the file, open another door for the next file. That is why PASV and STOR alternate in zeek:ftp. The one thing to remember: an internal PC doing STOR to an external server = our files left the network. Five STORs here = five stolen files.

docs.title: Step 4 — Arkime for the content
docs.text:
Splunk shows the shape; the packet content (password, file contents) needs Arkime. FTP is not encrypted, so everything is readable.

tags == 20190502_BEGUILESOFT && ip.src == 10.0.0.227 && port.dst == 21
tags == 20190502_BEGUILESOFT && ip.src == 10.0.0.227 && (ip.dst == 145.14.145.4 || ip.dst == 145.14.144.10 || ip.dst == 145.14.145.99)
tags == 20190502_BEGUILESOFT && ip.src == 10.0.0.227 && port.dst == 37280
tags == 20190502_BEGUILESOFT && ip.src == 10.0.0.227 && http.host == whatismyipaddress.com

  2. Everything to 000webhost → 8 sessions (3 control + 5 data).
  3. The data connection that carried Stealer Records.
  4. The public IP lookup.

tags == <case> keeps only this case's sessions on pcapbox. Leave it out on a live network.

docs.title: 4-1. The FTP login
docs.text:
Expand any of the three port 21 sessions and read the packet view. All three show the same login:

220 ProFTPD Server (000webhost.com) [::ffff:145.14.145.4]
USER snifferzett
331 User snifferzett OK. Password required
PASS trible22
230-Your bandwidth usage is restricted
230 OK. Current restricted directory is /

The attacker's FTP password is in clear text — record it as an IOC (it identifies the attacker's account; it is not the victim's password).

Correction: 421 did not mean the upload failed

In Splunk, Stealer Records and both screenshots seemed to get 421 Idle timeout instead of 226, which looked like "maybe not saved". Arkime shows the real sequence: every STOR got 226-File successfully transferred, and 421 came afterwards, when the control connection had been idle for 30 seconds. Zeek pairs each command with the last reply it saw, so the final 421 was attached to the last STOR. All five files reached the server. Lesson: do not decide from the Zeek summary alone — open the raw session.

About 150 Connecting to port 38174 in the 150 reply: that number does not match the PASV port (37280). It is internal to 000webhost; the real data port is the one calculated from 227, as Arkime's session list confirms.

Reading the result:

docs.text:
Expand the 40651 (Keylog_Records_2) and 36091 (Keylog_Records_3) sessions:

Summary of Steps 2–4: HawkEye on Breaux-Win7-PC sent a password report, keystrokes and screenshots to an attacker-controlled 000webhost FTP account, roughly every 10–15 minutes.

docs.title: 4-4. Initial access
docs.text:
Before 21:36 there is only domain logon traffic and the Windows connectivity check — no email, no web download, no file transfer from the internet. The malware was already on the PC and ran after logon. Report: "Initial access not in capture". Host check: Run keys, scheduled tasks, email attachments.

Question: please give the Arkime queries again with the tag added

On pcapbox, add tags == <case> && in front so only this case's sessions are searched:

tags == 20190502_BEGUILESOFT && ip.src == 10.0.0.227 && port.dst == 21
tags == 20190502_BEGUILESOFT && ip.src == 10.0.0.227 && (ip.dst == 145.14.145.4 || ip.dst == 145.14.144.10 || ip.dst == 145.14.145.99)
tags == 20190502_BEGUILESOFT && ip.src == 10.0.0.227 && port.dst == 37280
tags == 20190502_BEGUILESOFT && ip.src == 10.0.0.227 && ip.dst == 145.14.145.4 && port.dst == 21
tags == 20190502_BEGUILESOFT && ip.src == 10.0.0.227 && http.host == whatismyipaddress.com

The report keeps the untagged versions: tags only exists on pcapbox, not in the team environment.

Question: how do I search for HawkEye_Keylogger in Arkime?

Not from the Sessions search bar. Arkime does not store FTP file names as a field. To find any text inside packets, use Hunt:

  1. In Sessions, set the scope first: tags == 20190502_BEGUILESOFT && port.dst == 21. Hunt only searches the sessions in the current result — the narrower, the faster.
  2. Top menu Hunt → Create a packet search job.
  3. Fill in: Name hawkeye_ftp · Search HawkEye_Keylogger · Search type ascii (case insensitive) (like Snort's nocase) · Src/Dst tick Src only (the PC sends STOR) · Max packets per session default.
  4. Create. When it finishes it shows the number of matching sessions — here 3 (each control session has a HawkEye_Keylogger STOR).
  5. Open the results in Sessions with huntName == hawkeye_ftp. Matching sessions are labelled with the hunt name, so it works like a field.

Faster alternative: Arkime does store the FTP login as the Users field, so this works directly in the search bar:

tags == 20190502_BEGUILESOFT && user == snifferzett

Rule of thumb: any text inside packets → Hunt; values Arkime extracted as fields (IP, port, host, user…) → search bar. Hunt is like a string search run over many sessions at once.

docs.title: Step 5 — One Snort rule
docs.text:
The easiest version, with no depth/distance:

alert tcp $HOME_NET any -> $EXTERNAL_NET 21 (msg:"HawkEye Keylogger FTP upload - Sung"; content:"HawkEye_Keylogger"; nocase; sid:1000021; rev:1;)

Header (which packets to look at):

  • alert — raise an alert when it matches.
  • tcp — TCP only.
  • $HOME_NET any — from the internal network, any source port.
  • -> — direction: inside to outside.
  • $EXTERNAL_NET 21 — to an external host on port 21 (FTP control).

Options (what to find inside the packet):

  • msg — the text shown in the alert.
  • content:"HawkEye_Keylogger" — this text appears in the packet.
  • nocase — ignore case (hawkeye_keylogger matches too).
  • sid — rule number; own rules use 1000000+.
  • rev — rule version.

Question: can the rule be written without depth or distance?

Yes — the rule above. depth and distance say where in the packet the text must be, to cut false positives and speed things up. Here the text HawkEye_Keylogger is so unusual that normal FTP traffic will not contain it, so position does not matter. The STOR condition was dropped for the same reason: this file name going to port 21 is practically always an upload. flow and classtype were dropped too; the -> and port 21 in the header already fix the direction.

Expected result: put it in \\10.50.10.60\rules\local.rules and run snort-test 20190502_BEGUILESOFT → 3 alerts (the three STORs with HawkEye_Keylogger in the name: Stealer_Records, Keylog_Records_2, Keylog_Records_3). The two screenshot STORs do not contain the text. The full testing guide is in Night Dew — 8-3.

docs.title: Copy-ready queries
docs.text:
Replace <case> with your case name. Drop pcap_case/tags on a live network.

Splunk (Zeek)

index=zeek pcap_case="<case>" | stats count AS events min(ts) AS first max(ts) AS last BY sourcetype | eval first=strftime(first, "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"), last=strftime(last, "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S") | sort - events
index=zeek sourcetype=zeek:dhcp pcap_case="<case>" | eval time=strftime(ts, "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S") | table time client_addr assigned_addr mac host_name domain msg_types
index=zeek sourcetype=zeek:conn pcap_case="<case>" | where cidrmatch("10.0.0.0/8", id_orig_h) OR cidrmatch("172.16.0.0/12", id_orig_h) OR cidrmatch("192.168.0.0/16", id_orig_h) | stats count AS conns dc(id_resp_h) AS dests BY id_orig_h | sort - conns
index=zeek sourcetype=zeek:kerberos pcap_case="<case>" | stats count BY id_orig_h id_resp_h client
index=zeek sourcetype=zeek:conn pcap_case="<case>" | stats count AS conns sum(orig_bytes) AS sent sum(resp_bytes) AS recv min(ts) AS first BY id_resp_h id_resp_p service | eval first=strftime(first, "%H:%M:%S") | sort first
index=zeek sourcetype=zeek:dns pcap_case="<case>" | stats count values(answers) AS answers min(ts) AS first BY query | eval first=strftime(first, "%H:%M:%S") | sort first
index=zeek sourcetype=zeek:ftp pcap_case="<case>" | eval time=strftime(ts, "%H:%M:%S") | table time id_resp_h user command arg reply_code reply_msg
index=zeek sourcetype=zeek:ftp id_orig_h=10.0.0.227 command=STOR
index=zeek sourcetype=zeek:conn id_orig_h=10.0.0.227 id_resp_h IN (145.14.145.4, 145.14.144.10, 145.14.145.99)
  • command=STOR keeps uploads only. id_resp_h IN (a, b, c) matches any of the three — the same as three ORs.

Arkime

tags == <case> && ip.src == 10.0.0.227 && port.dst == 21
tags == <case> && ip.src == 10.0.0.227 && (ip.dst == 145.14.145.4 || ip.dst == 145.14.144.10 || ip.dst == 145.14.145.99)
tags == <case> && ip.src == 10.0.0.227 && port.dst == 37280
tags == <case> && user == snifferzett
huntName == hawkeye_ftp

Snort

alert tcp $HOME_NET any -> $EXTERNAL_NET 21 (msg:"HawkEye Keylogger FTP upload - Sung"; content:"HawkEye_Keylogger"; nocase; sid:1000021; rev:1;)

docs.title: Lessons
docs.text:
1. The log-type list is already a clue. FTP on an office PC with no TLS at all pointed straight at the exfil channel.
  2. DHCP INFORM has no assigned address. Take the IP from conn, the name and MAC from DHCP.
  3. Bytes sent vs received tell the direction. ftp-data with megabytes sent and 0 received = upload.
  4. PASV arithmetic links files to sizes. p1 × 256 + p2 = the ftp-data port.
  5. Zeek pairs a command with the last reply. Check the raw session before calling an upload failed.
  6. Clear-text protocols hand you the evidence. FTP showed the attacker's account and every stolen file.
  7. Name the family carefully. "HawkEye" comes from file names the malware itself wrote — strong, but still not a sample analysis.
  8. Keep victim passwords out of reports. Write "see evidence".

docs.title: IcedID (Cold as Ice) — from a redirect, Firebase and a fake gzip to an HTTPS beacon and BackConnect (Arkime analysis)
IcedID (Cold as Ice) — from a redirect, Firebase and a fake gzip to an HTTPS beacon and BackConnect
docs.text:
Case summary

One of three Windows PCs in the boogienights.live domain opened a link made of a bare IP address (80.77.25.175/main.php) in Edge. That server sent the PC on to Google Firebase Storage, where it downloaded Scan_Inv.zip. When the IcedID installer inside the archive ran, it sent details about the PC hidden in cookies and received a malicious file disguised as application/gzip. From then on the PC contacted an HTTPS C2 with a self-signed certificate every 5 minutes (for about 6 hours). About 5 hours after the infection a remote-control channel called BackConnect opened, and the attacker typed net group "Domain Computers" /domain and browsed the drives and folders by hand. Unlike the 36-second RedLine PCAP, this is a 6-hour PCAP, so the way you search is different.

Evidence Unit 42 Wireshark quiz April 2023 PCAP ("Cold as Ice"), 2023-04-19 15:26:28 – 21:22:36 UTC (about 5 h 56 min), about 1,640 sessions Environment Closed network assumed (no hash or reputation lookups). Order and queries for Arkime, decoding in CyberChef Output Answers to the 6 quiz questions Related pages Arkime-only analysis — Trickbot case · RedLine Stealer case · Arkime search syntax

Want to solve it yourself first?

The answers start below. If you want to try first, stop here and answer these 6 questions.

  1. Date and time (UTC) the infection started
  2. IP address of the infected Windows PC
  3. MAC address
  4. Hostname
  5. User account name
  6. Was there any follow-up malicious activity after the infection? If so, what?

About the numbers on this page

This page analysed the PCAP directly with Python to calculate the values Arkime would show (sessions, bytes, fields), and pairs them with the Arkime queries that find them. Some numbers such as session counts may differ slightly from your Arkime screen, so check them as you follow along. The results were compared with the official Unit 42 answers.

How to read this page

Same order as the two earlier cases. Each step: goal → query → query explained → actual result → reading the result. Copy queries with the copy button on the right of each code block. Basics such as the time range, time zone and SPI View are covered in detail in steps 0–1 of the Trickbot case.

docs.title: Answers at a glance
docs.text: # Question Answer Status 1 Infection start 2023-04-19 15:31 UTC (first malicious request: 15:31:07 GET /main.php) Confirmed 2 IP 10.4.19.136 Confirmed 3 MAC 14:58:d0:2e:c5:ae Confirmed 4 Hostname DESKTOP-SFF9LJF Confirmed 5 User csilva (LDAP full name Cornelius Silva) Confirmed 6 Follow-up Yes — BackConnect. From 20:48 UTC a remote shell and a file manager opened to 193.149.176.100:443 (not TLS). The attacker ran net group "Domain Computers" /domain and listed the drives and C:\ Confirmed Item Value Network 10.4.19.0/24, gateway 10.4.19.1, DC/DNS 10.4.19.19 (WIN-GP4JHCK2JMV), domain boogienights.live Clients 10.4.19.136 DESKTOP-SFF9LJF (infected), 10.4.19.138 DESKTOP-RETP4BU, 10.4.19.143 DESKTOP-JAL4D68 Starting link hxxp://80.77.25[.]175/main.php → 302 → Firebase Storage Scan_Inv.zip gzip loader hxxp://skigimeetroc[.]com/ (192.153.57.233), PC details in cookies, 520,803-byte response HTTPS C2 askamoshopsi[.]com · spakernakurs[.]com (104.168.53.18), skansnekssky[.]com (217.199.121.56, 5-minute beacon) BackConnect 193.149.176.100:443 (raw TCP) Extra 10.4.19.138 downloaded a zip (.wsf) resembling Qakbot distribution at 17:17 — step 11

docs.title: Step 0 — Data range and the big picture
docs.text:
Goal: Learn the start and end of the data, its size and the internal PCs first.

Query: Set the time range to All, leave the search bar empty and press Search. In Sessions, sort Start Time ascending / Stop Time descending to see the start and end (method in Trickbot case step 1).

Actual result:

Start  2023/04/19 15:26:28 UTC
End    2023/04/19 21:22:36 UTC   (duration 05:56:08)
Sessions about 1,640
Src IP 10.4.19.138 (833)   10.4.19.136 (718)   10.4.19.143 (85)   10.4.19.19 (4)

SPI View → General → Dst Port (session count, protocol/port):

udp 53 (586)   tcp 443 (483)   tcp 389 (114)   tcp 445 (85)   udp 389 (73)   tcp 135 (67)
tcp 49669 (63) tcp 88 (63)     tcp 80 (47)     tcp 49684 (12) tcp 139 (11)   udp 1900 (9)
tcp 53 (6)     udp 137 (5)     udp 138 (4)     udp 123 (3)    udp 111 (3)    udp 5353 (2)   udp 5355 (1)

Reading the result:

  • The capture is almost 6 hours long. You cannot just scan the session list by eye like in the RedLine case (36 seconds). This time we use a "filter out, then look at what is left" approach.
  • There are 4 internal IPs. 10.4.19.19 starts almost no sessions (4) and mostly receives them, so it is a server (confirmed as the DC later). The other 3 are client PCs. The quiz also says "3 clients, only one infected".
  • Grouping the ports by role:
Port Protocol Verdict 53, 88, 389, 445, 135, 139, 49669·49684 (dynamic RPC), 123 DNS, Kerberos, LDAP, SMB, RPC, NTP Normal AD traffic. Mostly to 10.4.19.19 137/138, 1900, 5353, 5355, 111 NetBIOS, SSDP, mDNS, LLMNR, RPC portmapper Local noise 443 (483) HTTPS Mostly Microsoft and Bing services. We have to find what is hiding inside 80 (47) HTTP Cleartext — we can read everything, so always look
  • Unlike RedLine, there is no "unknown port". That means the malicious traffic is hiding inside 80 and 443. So the order is: identify the 3 PCs → odd names in DNS → cleartext HTTP → HTTPS (certificates, intervals) → port 443 that is not TLS.

docs.title: Step 1 — IP, MAC and hostname of the 3 clients (Q2–Q4)
docs.text: Goal: We do not yet know which PC is infected, so we first record who all 3 are. When we later find "which PC went somewhere odd", we can name it straight away.

docs.title: Check DHCP first
docs.text:
protocols == dhcp

Actual result: 0 sessions

There is no DHCP in this PCAP. The capture started after the PCs already had their IPs. As the tip in the RedLine case says, we use Kerberos, NetBIOS and the Ethernet MAC instead.
