docs.title: Invoice email — Word macro to Hancitor-style C2
Invoice email — Word macro to Hancitor-style C2
docs.text:
Case summary

A Windows 7 client in the maricheika.net domain downloaded invoice_284615.doc with Internet Explorer. The document carried an auto-run VBA macro. About two minutes later the host checked its public IP with api.ipify.org, began POSTing to perranrowsin.com every two minutes, and downloaded three more files from a hijacked WordPress site. The traffic pattern matches Hancitor (inferred; no hash lookup was possible offline).

Evidence Phase1_PCAP_6.pcap, 2018-10-01 18:37:28 – 18:58:35 UTC (21 min) Environment Offline Linux analysis VM, Zeek 4.x, tshark, no internet Main tool Zeek logs + zeek-cut, awk, grep; tshark where it is simpler Lab guide Training → PCAP IR Labs → Lab 6

docs.title: The questions
docs.text:
1. Date and time (UTC) of the infection.
  2. IP address of the infected client.
  3. Hostname of the infected client.
  4. MAC address of the infected client.
  5. Windows user account name.
  6. Hash of the Word document, and how you handled it safely.
  7. Type of malware used in the initial infection.
  8. Public IP address of the infected client.
  9. Key network information (LAN range, gateway, domain, DC).
  10. Explanation of the compromise.

docs.title: Answers at a glance
docs.text: # Answer Status 1 2018-10-01 18:38:00 UTC (HTTP request for the document; file data first seen 18:38:01) Confirmed 2 172.16.1.125 Confirmed 3 Anatoliy-PC Confirmed 4 b8:97:fa:74:de:c0 Confirmed 5 anatoliy.demchuk Confirmed 6 SHA256 e2b0c9f57dcf08c0e14456f5cb54d8e50714c8e7a3a88cf818896dc8ba1dba51 (MD5/SHA1 in step 4) Confirmed 7 Malicious Word document with an auto-run VBA macro (downloader); traffic consistent with Hancitor Macro confirmed, family inferred 8 31.44.188.95 Confirmed 9 172.16.1.0/24, gateway 172.16.1.1, domain maricheika.net, DC 172.16.1.3 Maricheika-DC Confirmed 10 See the report —

docs.title: Step 0 — Set up and generate the Zeek logs
docs.text:
cd ~/Investigation_6
ls                                             # find the PCAP name
sha256sum Phase1_PCAP_6.pcap | tee pcap.sha256 # record the evidence hash first
mkdir zeek_full && cd zeek_full
zeek -C -r ../Phase1_PCAP_6.pcap local \
     frameworks/files/extract-all-files \
     policy/protocols/conn/mac-logging 2>/dev/null
ls
Part Why sha256sum ... | tee pcap.sha256 Proves later that the evidence did not change during analysis. tee prints the hash and saves it. mkdir zeek_full && cd zeek_full Zeek writes its logs into the current folder. A dedicated folder keeps them together and stops a later Zeek run from overwriting them. -C Ignore bad checksums. Captures taken on the sending host often have "wrong" checksums because the network card calculates them; without -C Zeek can drop those packets. -r ../Phase1_PCAP_6.pcap Read a file instead of a live interface. local Load the standard site policy (the same scripts a sensor would run). frameworks/files/extract-all-files Save every transferred file to extract_files/ so it can be hashed and inspected later. policy/protocols/conn/mac-logging Add MAC address columns (orig_l2_addr, resp_l2_addr) to conn.log. 2>/dev/null Hide warning messages.

ls should now show conn.log, dns.log, http.log, files.log, dhcp.log, kerberos.log, ssl.log and the extract_files/ folder.

docs.title: Capture window
docs.text:
zeek-cut -u ts < conn.log | sort | sed -n '1p;$p'

2018-10-01T18:37:28+0000
2018-10-01T18:58:35+0000
  • zeek-cut -u ts prints only the timestamp column, converted to UTC (-u).
  • sort puts the times in order; sed -n '1p;$p' prints just the first and the last line.
  • The capture covers 21 minutes. Every later event must fit inside this window.
tshark alternative 
TZ=UTC capinfos -a -e ../Phase1_PCAP_6.pcap

capinfos (installed with Wireshark) prints the first and last packet times directly. TZ=UTC forces UTC instead of the analysis machine's local time zone.

docs.title: Internal hosts
docs.text:
zeek-cut id.orig_h < conn.log | grep -E "^10\.|^172\.|^192\.168\." | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn

    160 172.16.1.125
  • id.orig_h is the host that started each connection.
  • The grep keeps private (RFC 1918) addresses only. Strictly, 172.16.0.0/12 is 172.16.–172.31.; ^172\. is a quick approximation that is fine here.
  • uniq -c counts each address; sort -rn puts the busiest first.
  • Only one internal host started connections. It is the only candidate for the infected client.

docs.title: Hostname and MAC from DHCP
docs.text:
zeek-cut -u ts client_addr mac host_name < dhcp.log

2018-10-01T18:37:28+0000   172.16.1.125   b8:97:fa:74:de:c0   Anatoliy-PC
2018-10-01T18:37:32+0000   172.16.1.125   b8:97:fa:74:de:c0   Anatoliy-PC
2018-10-01T18:40:20+0000   172.16.1.125   b8:97:fa:74:de:c0   Anatoliy-PC
2018-10-01T18:42:31+0000   172.16.1.125   b8:97:fa:74:de:c0   Anatoliy-PC
2018-10-01T18:45:48+0000   172.16.1.125   b8:97:fa:74:de:c0   Anatoliy-PC
2018-10-01T18:47:40+0000   172.16.1.125   b8:97:fa:74:de:c0   Anatoliy-PC
2018-10-01T18:52:29+0000   172.16.1.125   b8:97:fa:74:de:c0   Anatoliy-PC

A Windows client sends its own hostname (DHCP option 12) when it asks for an address, so dhcp.log ties IP, MAC and hostname together in one line. Every entry agrees: 172.16.1.125 · b8:97:fa:74:de:c0 · Anatoliy-PC (answers 2–4).

tshark alternative 
tshark -r ../Phase1_PCAP_6.pcap -Y "dhcp.option.hostname" \
       -T fields -e ip.src -e eth.src -e dhcp.option.hostname | sort -u

-Y filters for DHCP packets that carry a hostname; -T fields -e prints only the chosen fields. On Wireshark 2.x use bootp.option.hostname.

docs.title: User account and Domain Controller from Kerberos
docs.text:
zeek-cut client id.resp_h < kerberos.log | sort | uniq -c

      5 -                               172.16.1.3
      2 anatoliy.demchuk/MARICHEIKA     172.16.1.3
      5 anatoliy.demchuk/MARICHEIKA.NET 172.16.1.3
      2 anatoliy-pc$/maricheika.net     172.16.1.3
      2 anatoliy-pc$/MARICHEIKA.NET     172.16.1.3
     12 ANATOLIY-PC$/MARICHEIKA.NET     172.16.1.3
Value Meaning anatoliy.demchuk/... A user account: no $ at the end → answer 5 anatoliy-pc$/... The computer account. Machine accounts always end in $ and match the hostname text after / The Kerberos realm, i.e. the AD domain: MARICHEIKA.NET (short and long forms, any case, are the same domain) id.resp_h = 172.16.1.3 The server answering Kerberos (TCP/UDP 88) is the Domain Controller tshark alternative 
tshark -r ../Phase1_PCAP_6.pcap -Y "kerberos.CNameString" \
       -T fields -e ip.src -e ip.dst -e kerberos.CNameString -e kerberos.realm | sort | uniq -c

CNameString is the client name in Kerberos requests and replies; the source and destination columns show the client and the DC (172.16.1.3) talking.

docs.title: Step 2 — Find the suspicious file
docs.text:
zeek-cut -u ts tx_hosts rx_hosts source mime_type filename seen_bytes < files.log \
  | grep -i -E "msword|officedocument|ms-office|dosexec|zip"

2018-10-01T18:38:01+0000   47.88.158.115   172.16.1.125   HTTP   application/msword   invoice_284615.doc   225280
Column Value Meaning ts 18:38:01 When Zeek first saw the file data (the start of the response body) tx_hosts 47.88.158.115 Who sent the file (an external server) rx_hosts 172.16.1.125 Who received it, the infected client mime_type application/msword Zeek decides the type from the file's content (magic bytes), not its name filename invoice_284615.doc An "invoice" lure, a classic malspam theme

The grep searches for the type names Zeek gives Word documents (msword, officedocument, ms-office), executables (dosexec) and archives (zip). Only the Word document matched, and no EXE followed it. That matters later.

Pitfall: a misspelled field gives an empty column, not an error

The first run of this command used seen_types instead of seen_bytes. zeek-cut printed an empty last column and no error. If a column is unexpectedly empty, check the field name in the log header with head -8 files.log.

docs.title: The URL that served the document
docs.text:
zeek-cut -u ts id.resp_h host uri status_code resp_mime_types user_agent < http.log | grep -i msword

2018-10-01T18:38:00+0000   47.88.158.115   pitchbocaraton.com   /?82a1=APYBKsCs3LUw   200   application/msword
    Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 6.1; WOW64; Trident/7.0; rv:11.0) like Gecko
  • Full URL = host + uri → http://pitchbocaraton.com/?82a1=APYBKsCs3LUw.
  • status_code 200 + application/msword: the server really returned the document.
  • Trident/7.0; rv:11.0 is Internet Explorer 11; WOW64 means 32-bit IE on 64-bit Windows 7 (NT 6.1). The user fetched the file with the browser, most likely by clicking a link (in an email, inferred).
  • http.log records the time the request started (18:38:00); files.log records when the file data was first seen (18:38:01). Answer 1 = 18:38:00 UTC, noting the one-second difference.
tshark alternative 
tshark -r ../Phase1_PCAP_6.pcap -Y "http.request" -T fields \
       -e frame.time_utc -e ip.dst -e http.host -e http.request.uri -e http.user_agent

Lists every HTTP request with its UTC time. It is useful for reading the whole browsing sequence in one view.

docs.title: Step 3 — Was anything malicious before the document?
docs.text:
Before calling 18:38:00 the start of the infection, check that nothing suspicious happened earlier. The capture starts at 18:37:28, only 32 seconds before the document request, so there is little room for earlier activity, but confirm it:

zeek-cut -u ts query answers < dns.log | awk -F'\t' '$1 <= "2018-10-01T18:38:01+0000"'
zeek-cut -u ts host uri < http.log     | awk -F'\t' '$1 <  "2018-10-01T18:38:00+0000"'
  • awk -F'\t' splits on tabs (Zeek's separator); $1 is the first column, the time.
  • ISO timestamps can be compared as text: the biggest unit comes first (year → month → day → hour …), so alphabetical order equals time order.
  • What to expect: Windows start-up lookups (_ldap._tcp… SRV records for the DC, wpad, isatap, msftncsi) and the lookup for pitchbocaraton.com just before the download. Any other unknown domain would push the start of the incident earlier. With nothing else suspicious, the document download is the first malicious event.

Two ways to look at what came before an event

  • grep -B 15 "msword" shows the matching line and the 15 lines before it (-A = after, -C = both). It is fast for "what happened just before?".
  • awk -F'\t' '$1 <= "…"' cuts an exact time range. Use it for reports.

docs.title: Step 4 — Handle and hash the document safely (Q6)
Get the file ID and the hashes Zeek already calculated
docs.text:
zeek-cut fuid mime_type seen_bytes md5 sha1 < files.log | grep -i msword

F5VYtO3n6Uvp1v0TU1   application/msword   225280   41a3101af94fca79bbdb0db2a52994c0   103dc7e3100963f31c2280b129d8280b22194c72
  • fuid is Zeek's ID for the file. The extracted copy is named extract_files/extract-<time>-HTTP-<fuid>, so the fuid finds it.
  • Zeek calculates MD5 and SHA1 by default, but not SHA256.

docs.title: Safe copy, file type, SHA256
docs.text:
cp extract_files/*F5VYtO3n6Uvp1v0TU1 evidence.doc.bin   # .bin: will not open in Word on double-click
chmod a-x evidence.doc.bin                               # remove execute permission for everyone
file evidence.doc.bin                                    # identify by content, not extension
md5sum evidence.doc.bin; sha1sum evidence.doc.bin; sha256sum evidence.doc.bin

extract-1538419081.436962-HTTP-F5VYtO3n6Uvp1v0TU1: Composite Document File V2 Document, Little Endian,
Os: Windows, Version 6.1, Code page: 1252, Title: , Author: 444555, Template: Normal.dotm,
Last Saved By: win7home, Revision Number: 2, Name of Creating Application: Microsoft Office Word,
Create Time/Date: Mon Oct  1 12:17:00 2018, Last Saved Time/Date: Mon Oct  1 12:17:00 2018,
Number of Pages: 1, Number of Words: 3, Number of Characters: 20, Security: 0

e2b0c9f57dcf08c0e14456f5cb54d8e50714c8e7a3a88cf818896dc8ba1dba51
Hash Value Size 225,280 bytes (seen_bytes = size on disk → complete file) MD5 41a3101af94fca79bbdb0db2a52994c0 SHA1 103dc7e3100963f31c2280b129d8280b22194c72 SHA256 e2b0c9f57dcf08c0e14456f5cb54d8e50714c8e7a3a88cf818896dc8ba1dba51

What the file metadata says

Field Why it is suspicious Composite Document File V2 Legacy OLE .doc format, which can carry VBA macros Created and saved Oct 1 2018 The same date as the infection: a freshly built document Number of Words: 3, Characters: 20 A real invoice has content. Malicious documents usually hold only an image saying "Enable content" Author: 444555, Last Saved By: win7home Throw-away names

Why this is safe: the work happens in an isolated Linux VM with no network and no Microsoft Office, so the macro cannot run. The document is never opened, only read by file, strings and hash tools. The .bin name and chmod a-x protect against an accidental double-click. Only the hash would be looked up on VirusTotal (never upload the file). The sample is kept in a password zip (zip -P infected evidence.zip evidence.doc.bin).

tshark alternative 
mkdir objs && tshark -r ../Phase1_PCAP_6.pcap -q --export-objects http,objs
file objs/* | grep -i composite        # find which carved file is the Word document
sha256sum "objs/<name shown by file>"

--export-objects http,objs carves every HTTP object into objs/ (Wireshark's File → Export Objects → HTTP). File names come from the URI, so find the document by its type with file. The hash should equal Zeek's.

docs.title: Step 5 — Look for the macro without Office (Q7)
docs.text:
olevba (oletools) is the usual tool, but it was not installed and the VM had no internet (which olevba oleid returned nothing). strings still works:

strings -n 6 evidence.doc.bin | grep -i -E "vba|autoopen|document_open|shell|powershell|cmd|http|createobject"

http://ns.adobe.com/xap/1.0/  ... xmp:CreatorTool="Adobe Photoshop CC 2017 (Windows)" ...
<b:Sources ... xmlns:b="http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/officeDocument/2006/bibliography"> ...
1VBA.@Create
Document_Open
CreateObject
ShellV
  • strings -n 6 prints runs of 6 or more readable characters; grep -i -E keeps lines containing any keyword (case-insensitive).
  • The ns.adobe.com and schemas.openxmlformats.org lines are normal metadata. The Photoshop XMP block shows an embedded image, most likely the "enable content" lure (inferred).
String Meaning VBA A VBA project is present Document_Open The macro runs as soon as the document is opened (after "Enable content") CreateObject Loads Windows COM objects (file system, shell, HTTP) Shell Runs a program or command

That combination is a malicious auto-run macro. VBA source is compressed inside the file, so strings shows keywords and not the full code. No download URL appears, and no EXE was downloaded after the document. Hancitor-era macros often carried the payload inside the document and dropped it locally (inferred).

If oletools is available 

oleid evidence.doc.bin      # summary: VBA macros present? encrypted?
olevba -a evidence.doc.bin  # analysis table only: AutoExec / Suspicious / IOC
olevba --decode evidence.doc.bin  # also decode obfuscated strings
AutoExec + Suspicious (Shell, CreateObject) rows confirm the same thing, and IOC rows list any URLs.

docs.title: Step 6 — What happened after the document?
docs.text:
zeek-cut -u ts id.resp_h host method uri status_code resp_mime_types user_agent < http.log \
  | awk -F'\t' '$1 >= "2018-10-01T18:38:01+0000"'

18:40:20  54.243.179.137   api.ipify.org          GET   /                                          200  text/plain  Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 6.1; Win64; x64; Trident/7.0; rv:11.0) like Gecko
18:40:20  62.109.30.243    perranrowsin.com       POST  /4/forum.php                               200  text/plain  Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 6.1; Win64; x64; Trident/7.0; rv:11.0) like Gecko
18:40:21  205.186.179.236  stopfuckinaround.com   GET   /wp-content/plugins/google-sitemap-generator/1  200  -       Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 6.1; Win64; x64; ...)
18:40:27  62.109.30.243    perranrowsin.com       POST  /mlu/forum.php                             200  -           Mozilla/4.0 (compatible; MSIE 7.0; Windows NT 6.1; WOW64; Trident/7.0; SLCC2; .NET CLR ...)
18:40:29  205.186.179.236  stopfuckinaround.com   GET   /wp-content/plugins/google-sitemap-generator/2  200  -       Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 6.1; Win64; x64; ...)
18:40:29  205.186.179.236  stopfuckinaround.com   GET   /wp-content/plugins/google-sitemap-generator/3  200  -       Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 6.1; Win64; x64; ...)
18:40:30  62.109.30.243    perranrowsin.com       POST  /d2/about.php                              200  -           Mozilla/4.0 (compatible; MSIE 7.0; ...)
18:42:30  62.109.30.243    perranrowsin.com       POST  /4/forum.php                               200  text/plain  Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 6.1; Win64; x64; ...)
18:44:31  ... POST /4/forum.php
18:46:31  ... POST /4/forum.php
18:48:32  ... POST /4/forum.php
18:50:33  ... POST /4/forum.php
18:52:34  ... POST /4/forum.php
18:54:34  ... POST /4/forum.php
18:56:35  ... POST /4/forum.php

(Dates trimmed for width; all on 2018-10-01, UTC.)

docs.title: Reading it
docs.text: Time Event Meaning 18:38:00 Document downloaded Delivery 18:38–18:40 No HTTP for ~2 min 20 s The user opened the document and clicked "Enable content" (inferred) 18:40:20 GET api.ipify.org/ Malware asks "what is my public IP?" 18:40:20 POST /4/forum.php First C2 check-in, sending victim information 18:40:21–29 GET .../google-sitemap-generator/1, /2, /3 Three follow-up payloads from a compromised WordPress site. MIME type - means Zeek could not identify them, which is typical of encrypted payloads (inferred) 18:40:27, 18:40:30 POST /mlu/forum.php, /d2/about.php Check-ins from different malware: the follow-up payloads now running (inferred) 18:42:30 → 18:56:35 POST /4/forum.php every ~120 s Beaconing: the main implant calls home on a fixed timer

docs.title: The User-Agent tells you which program sent each request
docs.text:
Requests User-Agent Verdict Document download Windows NT 6.1; WOW64; Trident/7.0; rv:11.0 The user's real 32-bit IE 11 ipify, /4/forum.php, WordPress /1 /2 /3 Windows NT 6.1; Win64; x64; Trident/7.0; rv:11.0 Looks like IE but differs from the real browser: a different program (the first-stage malware) /mlu/forum.php, /d2/about.php Mozilla/4.0 (compatible; MSIE 7.0; …) IE 7 on a 2018 Windows 7 host is not plausible: a hard-coded string in another program

One host, one real browser, two malware User-Agents. Comparing User-Agents per destination is one of the fastest ways to separate user browsing from malware.

docs.title: Measure the beacon interval
docs.text:
zeek-cut ts uri < http.log | grep "/4/forum.php" | awk '{ if (prev) print $1 - prev; prev = $1 }'
  • Without -u, ts stays in epoch seconds, so awk can subtract.
  • The difference between consecutive POSTs is about 120 seconds each time (from the timestamps above: 18:42:30 → 18:44:31 → 18:46:31 …). Regular timing is a beacon; a human is never that regular.

docs.title: Why "Hancitor" (and why it stays inferred)
docs.text:
This sequence is a well-documented 2018 Hancitor pattern:

  1. Word document with a macro;
  2. api.ipify.org IP check;
  3. POST to /4/forum.php;
  4. GETs for numbered files under a hijacked WordPress path;
  5. Extra check-ins to /mlu/forum.php and /d2/about.php (follow-up stealer malware).

Confirmed: macro document → IP check → C2 POSTs → follow-up downloads → 2-minute beacon. Inferred: the family name. The lab was offline, so no hash lookup was possible. Write "consistent with Hancitor", not "Hancitor".

docs.title: Step 7 — Public IP of the client (Q8)
docs.text:
The client uses a private address, and NAT on the gateway swaps it for a public address on the way out. A capture taken inside the LAN never shows that public address in packet headers. The IP-check service's answer does: api.ipify.org replies with the caller's public IP as plain text.

zeek-cut host uri resp_fuids < http.log | grep ipify   # find the response's file ID
cat extract_files/*FGnsSi1OKpfguaYN9d; echo              # print the response body

31.44.188.95
  • resp_fuids is the ID of the response body. Zeek saved that body as a file, like any other download.
  • echo only adds the missing newline so the prompt does not join the IP.
tshark alternative (simpler) 
tshark -r ../Phase1_PCAP_6.pcap -Y 'http.response and http.response_for.uri contains "ipify"' \
       -T fields -e http.file_data

One command, no file ID needed: it prints the response body of the ipify request directly. If your tshark version prints hex, add | xxd -r -p. In Wireshark: right-click the request → Follow → HTTP Stream, and the IP is in the blue (server) text.

Answer 8: 31.44.188.95 (confirmed).

docs.title: Domain and DC hostname
docs.text:
zeek-cut service < kerberos.log | sort | uniq -c

      4 -
      1 anatoliy-pc$
      1 ANATOLIY-PC$
      2 anatoliy-pc$@MARICHEIKA.NET
      3 cifs/maricheika-dc.maricheika.net
      1 host/anatoliy-pc.maricheika.net
      1 krbtgt/MARICHEIKA
      1 krbtgt/maricheika.net
      9 krbtgt/MARICHEIKA.NET
      2 ldap/Maricheika-DC.maricheika.net
      1 ldap/Maricheika-DC.maricheika.net/maricheika.net
      2 LDAP/Maricheika-DC.maricheika.net/maricheika.net

service is the service a ticket was requested for. krbtgt/<REALM> is the domain's ticket service; ldap/… and cifs/… (file sharing) are services on the DC. The name after the / is the DC: Maricheika-DC.maricheika.net.

zeek-cut query answers < dns.log | grep -i -E "_ldap|_kerberos" | sort -u

_ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs.maricheika.net                                   maricheika-dc.maricheika.net
_ldap._tcp.default-first-site-name._sites.domaindnszones.maricheika.net  maricheika-dc.maricheika.net
_ldap._tcp.default-first-site-name._sites.forestdnszones.maricheika.net  maricheika-dc.maricheika.net
_ldap._tcp.default-first-site-name._sites.maricheika.net              maricheika-dc.maricheika.net
...

_ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs.<domain> is the DNS SRV question Windows asks to mean "who are the DCs of this domain?". The answer confirms the DC name.

tshark alternative 
tshark -r ../Phase1_PCAP_6.pcap -Y "dns.flags.response == 1 && dns.qry.type == 33" \
       -T fields -e dns.qry.name -e dns.srv.target | sort -u

dns.qry.type == 33 is SRV; dns.srv.target is the host the SRV record points to.

dhcp.log says localdomain, so why is the domain maricheika.net?

zeek-cut domain < dhcp.log returned localdomain. That is the DHCP server's default suffix (common on VMware NAT and home routers), not the Active Directory domain. The AD domain comes from Kerberos and DNS: maricheika.net. It also shows that the DHCP server is a separate device from the DC.

docs.title: Subnet mask and gateway
docs.text:
dhcp.log has no mask or gateway columns. A Zeek event script can print them, but tshark does it in one line, so tshark is the better tool here:

tshark -r ../Phase1_PCAP_6.pcap -Y dhcp -T fields \
       -e ip.src -e dhcp.option.subnet_mask -e dhcp.option.router | sort -u

0.0.0.0
172.16.1.125
172.16.1.254    255.255.255.0    172.16.1.1
Line Who sent it Why 0.0.0.0 Client without an address yet (Discover / Request) Clients have no mask or router to report → empty fields 172.16.1.125 Client renewing or informing after it has an address Still a client message → empty fields 172.16.1.254 255.255.255.0 172.16.1.1 DHCP server (Offer / ACK) Only the server hands out option 1 (mask) and option 3 (router)

sort -u collapses identical lines, which is why many DHCP packets become three. Mask 255.255.255.0 = /24. With client IP 172.16.1.125, the LAN is 172.16.1.0/24, the gateway is 172.16.1.1, and the DHCP server is 172.16.1.254.

Zeek-only ways to get the gateway

By MAC address (needs the mac-logging script used in step 0). Traffic to the internet is addressed to the gateway's MAC:

zeek-cut id.resp_h resp_l2_addr < conn.log | grep -v "^172\.16\." | awk '{print $2}' | sort | uniq -c
zeek-cut id.resp_h resp_l2_addr < conn.log | grep "^172\.16\." | grep <gateway-MAC> | sort -u

Event script (prints mask and router from server replies; run it in an empty folder so the existing logs are not overwritten):

zeek -C -r ../Phase1_PCAP_6.pcap -e 'event dhcp_message(c: connection, is_orig: bool, msg: DHCP::Msg, options: DHCP::Options) { if (!is_orig) print c$id$resp_h, options?$subnet_mask ? fmt("%s", options$subnet_mask) : "-", options?$routers ? fmt("%s", options$routers) : "-"; }'

docs.title: Report (Q10)
docs.text: At 18:38 UTC on 2018-10-01, user anatoliy.demchuk on Anatoliy-PC (172.16.1.125) used Internet Explorer to download a Word file, invoice_284615.doc, from pitchbocaraton.com. The file had an auto-run macro. About 2 minutes later, the PC checked its public IP (31.44.188.95) with api.ipify.org. It then sent C2 POSTs to perranrowsin.com every 2 minutes and downloaded 3 more files from another site. This matches Hancitor (not confirmed by hash). The PC should be isolated and rebuilt, and the user's password reset.

docs.title: Detection ideas
docs.text:
ZeekSnort 2Splunk 
# POSTs to forum.php / about.php gates
zeek-cut -u ts id.orig_h host uri method < http.log | awk -F'\t' '$5=="POST" && $4 ~ /(forum|about)\.php$/'
# Hosts that ask an IP-check service (worth a look, not proof)
zeek-cut -u ts id.orig_h host < http.log | grep -i -E "ipify|checkip|icanhazip|ip-api|myexternalip"
# Old-IE User-Agents from modern Windows
zeek-cut id.orig_h host user_agent < http.log | grep "MSIE 7.0" | sort | uniq -c

alert tcp $HOME_NET any -> $EXTERNAL_NET $HTTP_PORTS (msg:"LOCAL Hancitor-style gate POST forum.php"; flow:established,to_server; content:"POST"; http_method; content:"/forum.php"; http_uri; pcre:"/\/(4|mlu)\/forum\.php$/U"; classtype:trojan-activity; sid:1000601; rev:1;)
alert tcp $HOME_NET any -> $EXTERNAL_NET $HTTP_PORTS (msg:"LOCAL External IP lookup api.ipify.org"; flow:established,to_server; content:"Host: api.ipify.org"; http_header; nocase; classtype:policy-violation; sid:1000602; rev:1;)

index=zeek sourcetype=zeek:http method=POST uri IN ("*/forum.php", "*/about.php")
| stats count min(_time) as first max(_time) as last values(uri) as uris by id.orig_h host
| eval span_min=round((last-first)/60,1)

Index and sourcetype names depend on how Zeek logs are ingested; adjust them. See Beaconing & C2 for interval analysis with streamstats.

docs.title: Lessons learned
docs.text:
• One internal host makes triage fast, but still confirm IP, MAC and hostname from two sources (DHCP + Kerberos/conn).
  • "No EXE after the document" does not mean "no infection". The payload can be inside the document; watch the traffic that follows instead.
  • Compare User-Agents. A browser string that differs from the user's real browser, or an impossible one (IE 7 in 2018), points to malware.
  • Use the right tool for each question. Zeek is best for overview, files and HTTP; tshark is simpler for DHCP options and for reading a single response body.
  • Typo check. An empty zeek-cut column usually means a misspelled field name.
  • Separate confirmed from inferred, especially malware family names when no hash lookup is possible.

docs.title: Webmail to an AutoIt downloader and multi-C2 traffic
Webmail to an AutoIt downloader and multi-C2 traffic
docs.text:
Case summary

A stand-alone Windows 7 PC opened Yahoo Mail in Internet Explorer. About 45 seconds later a non-browser program downloaded jjjj.exe. Fourteen minutes later, an AutoIt-based program downloaded a second EXE, zugu.exe, checked the public IP and started talking to several C2 servers:

  • HTTP POSTs with the LokiBot-style User-Agent Charon; Inferno;
  • a config.jpg / gate.php panel;
  • HTTPS to a host with an expired certificate;
  • 232 rejected attempts to TCP port 5552.

It also sent about 4 KB over encrypted SMTP to AOL. The capture lost packets, so neither EXE can be hashed.

Evidence Phase1_PCAP_7.pcap, 2017-11-20 23:58:00 – 2017-11-21 00:16:33 UTC (18.5 min) Environment Offline Linux analysis VM, Zeek 4.x, tshark, no internet Main tool Zeek logs + zeek-cut, awk, grep; tshark for TTL and DHCP options Lab guide Training → PCAP IR Labs → Lab 7

docs.title: The questions
docs.text:
The host is not assumed to be Windows.

  1. IP address of the compromised host.
  2. MAC address.
  3. Hostname.
  4. Operating system.
  5. What was downloaded, and how many files.
  6. Where each file was downloaded from.
  7. Did the files come from an internal or an external source?
  8. Information that could help further investigation.
  9. Did anything else happen after the downloads?
  10. What started the downloads?
  11. Explanation of the compromise.

docs.title: Answers at a glance
docs.text: # Answer Status 1 10.192.1.157 Confirmed 2 50:46:5d:d5:24:3b Confirmed 3 WIN-D5243B Confirmed 4 Windows 7 (User-Agent Windows NT 6.1, DHCP MSFT 5.0, TTL 128) Confirmed 5 Two 32-bit Windows EXEs: jjjj.exe (3,061,200 bytes) and zugu.exe (5,895,226 bytes) Confirmed 6 http://lucrecianos.com.ar/imagen/1/2/jjjj.exe (170.231.127.136) and http://virtualsmsonline.site/zugu.exe (104.31.92.140) Confirmed 7 External: public IPs on the internet, fetched over HTTP Confirmed 8 URLs, IPs, sizes, compile time, C2 hosts, User-Agents, SMTP; no hashes (capture loss) See IOCs 9 Second download, public IP check, C2 to four destinations, ~4 KB over SMTPS Traffic confirmed; families and exfiltration inferred 10 Not the browser: first request had no User-Agent; second came from AutoIt Partly confirmed 11 See the report —

docs.title: Step 0 — Set up and generate the Zeek logs
docs.text:
cd ~/Investigation_7
sha256sum Phase1_PCAP_7.pcap | tee pcap.sha256
mkdir zeek_full && cd zeek_full
zeek -C -r ../Phase1_PCAP_7.pcap local \
     frameworks/files/extract-all-files \
     policy/protocols/conn/mac-logging 2>/dev/null
ll

The options are explained in Invoice email case, step 0. This time, the list of logs is already evidence:

capture_loss.log  conn.log  dhcp.log  dns.log  extract_files/  files.log  http.log
loaded_scripts.log  notice.log  packet_filter.log  pe.log  reporter.log  ssl.log
stats.log  x509.log
What you see What it tells you no kerberos.log, no smb_*.log No domain logons: a stand-alone PC, not part of Active Directory (inferred). There is no account question in this lab pe.log Zeek parsed at least one Windows executable in the traffic notice.log Zeek flagged something worth a look capture_loss.log Zeek keeps packet-loss statistics. It matters in step 5 no software.log This install's local policy does not log software versions (or found none). Read User-Agents from http.log instead

docs.title: Step 1 — The big picture
docs.text:
zeek-cut -u ts < conn.log | sort | sed -n '1p;$p'
zeek-cut id.orig_h < conn.log | grep -E "^10\.|^172\.|^192\.168\." | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
zeek-cut service < conn.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn

2017-11-20T23:58:00+0000
2017-11-21T00:16:33+0000

    575 10.192.1.157

    254 -
    163 dns
    119 ssl
     31 http
     10 dhcp
  • 18.5 minutes of traffic and one internal host, the only candidate.
  • service is the protocol Zeek recognised in each connection. Only DNS, TLS, HTTP and DHCP, so the downloads are not over FTP, SMB or TFTP.
  • 254 connections with service -: Zeek could not identify the protocol. That is usually because the connection never got far enough to show any content. They are examined in step 7.
tshark alternative 
tshark -r ../Phase1_PCAP_7.pcap -q -z io,phs

-z io,phs prints the Protocol Hierarchy (Wireshark Statistics → Protocol Hierarchy). It also lists protocols Zeek writes no log for, such as ARP, LLMNR, NBNS, mDNS and TFTP. That is useful when the download protocol is unknown.

docs.title: Step 2 — IP, MAC and hostname (Q1–3)
docs.text:
zeek-cut -u ts client_addr mac host_name < dhcp.log

2017-11-20T23:58:00+0000   10.192.1.157   50:46:5d:d5:24:3b   -
2017-11-20T23:58:04+0000   10.192.1.157   50:46:5d:d5:24:3b   WIN-D5243B
2017-11-21T00:08:27+0000   10.192.1.157   50:46:5d:d5:24:3b   WIN-D5243B
2017-11-21T00:13:01+0000   10.192.1.157   50:46:5d:d5:24:3b   WIN-D5243B
2017-11-21T00:13:28+0000   10.192.1.157   50:46:5d:d5:24:3b   WIN-D5243B
2017-11-21T00:14:46+0000   10.192.1.157   50:46:5d:d5:24:3b   WIN-D5243B
2017-11-21T00:15:48+0000   10.192.1.157   50:46:5d:d5:24:3b   WIN-D5243B
  • 10.192.1.157 · 50:46:5d:d5:24:3b · WIN-D5243B (Q1–3, confirmed).
  • The first line has no hostname: the very first DHCP message did not carry option 12. That is normal.
  • WIN- + six characters is the shape of the random name Windows gives itself at install time. It is a hint, not proof, of the OS.
tshark alternative (when DHCP has no name) 
tshark -r ../Phase1_PCAP_7.pcap -Y "nbns || llmnr || mdns" \
       -T fields -e ip.src -e eth.src -e nbns.name -e dns.qry.name | sort | uniq -c

Non-Windows hosts often send no DHCP hostname but announce themselves with NBNS, LLMNR or mDNS (name.local). Zeek writes no NBNS log, so tshark is the easy way here. In this capture DHCP already gave the name.

docs.title: User-Agents
docs.text:
zeek-cut user_agent < http.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn

     15 Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 6.1; Trident/7.0; rv:11.0) like Gecko
      8 Mozilla/4.0 (compatible; MSIE 7.0; Windows NT 6.1; Trident/7.0; SLCC2; .NET CLR 2.0.50727; .NET CLR 3.5.30729; .NET CLR 3.0.30729; Media Center PC 6.0; .NET4.0C; .NET4.0E)
      7 Mozilla/4.08 (Charon; Inferno)
      3 Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 6.3; Trident/7.0; rv:11.0) like Gecko/20100101 Firefox/12.0
      2 AutoIt
      1 Microsoft NCSI
      1 -
Count User-Agent Reading 15 IE 11, Windows NT 6.1 The user's real browser on Windows 7 1 Microsoft NCSI Windows' "am I online?" check, sent only by Windows 8 MSIE 7.0 … .NET CLR … IE 7 on a 2017 Windows 7 host is not plausible: a string hard-coded in a program 7 Mozilla/4.08 (Charon; Inferno) Not a browser. A hard-coded string widely associated with LokiBot 3 NT 6.3 … like Gecko/20100101 Firefox/12.0 A malformed mix of IE and Firefox. It only went to an ad network (step 4), so it is probably an ad script, not malware 2 AutoIt The default User-Agent of AutoIt, a Windows automation language often used to build malware 1 - A request with no User-Agent: not a browser

User-Agents need context

The malformed Firefox string looked malicious on its own. The destinations show it was advertising traffic. Always read a User-Agent together with where it went and when.

docs.title: TTL and DHCP vendor class (tshark)
docs.text:
Zeek records neither the IP TTL nor the DHCP vendor class. tshark reads both directly:

tshark -r ../Phase1_PCAP_7.pcap -Y "ip.src==10.192.1.157" -T fields -e ip.ttl | sort | uniq -c
tshark -r ../Phase1_PCAP_7.pcap -Y "dhcp.option.vendor_class_id" \
       -T fields -e eth.src -e dhcp.option.vendor_class_id | sort -u

     10 1
   6809 128

50:46:5d:d5:24:3b    MSFT 5.0
Evidence Meaning TTL 128 on 6,809 packets Windows' default initial TTL (Linux/macOS/Android use 64, network devices 255). Captured on the LAN, so the value is unchanged TTL 1 on 10 packets Link-local multicast such as LLMNR (224.0.0.252) or IGMP. TTL 1 keeps them inside the LAN; this says nothing about the OS MSFT 5.0 The DHCP vendor class sent by every Windows version since 2000 Which packets have TTL 1? 

tshark -r ../Phase1_PCAP_7.pcap -Y "ip.src==10.192.1.157 && ip.ttl==1" \
       -T fields -e ip.dst -e _ws.col.Protocol | sort | uniq -c
_ws.col.Protocol is Wireshark's Protocol column.

Answer 4: Windows 7. The browser User-Agent (NT 6.1), the DHCP vendor class (MSFT 5.0) and TTL 128 all agree, and NCSI plus the WIN- hostname fit as well. The lack of WOW64/Win64 in the IE string suggests 32-bit Windows 7 (inferred).

docs.title: Step 5 — The downloaded files (Q5–Q8) and why there are no hashes
docs.text:
zeek-cut -u ts tx_hosts rx_hosts source mime_type filename seen_bytes fuid < files.log \
  | grep -v -i -E "x509|pkix"

grep -v hides lines that match: every HTTPS session puts its certificates in files.log, and they are not downloads. Two lines are executables:

2017-11-20T23:59:36+0000  170.231.127.136  10.192.1.157  HTTP  application/x-dosexec  -  2870222  FwavXQ2AM4W84BhH44
2017-11-21T00:13:29+0000  104.31.92.140    10.192.1.157  HTTP  application/x-dosexec  -  5812128  FuT2N64AuTHxEdqVil

The rest are small web objects and the C2 exchanges. When tx_hosts is the infected PC, the "file" is a POST body the PC sent: 204 and 177 bytes to 185.118.166.155, 345 bytes to 37.48.82.212. One stands out: config.jpg, 81,393 bytes of image/jpeg from the C2 panel path. It may hide configuration or data inside an image (inferred).

docs.title: PE header details
docs.text:
zeek-cut -u ts id machine os compile_ts is_exe is_64bit < pe.log

2017-11-20T23:59:36+0000  FwavXQ2AM4W84BhH44  I386  Windows 95 or NT 4.0          2017-11-20T15:10:13+0000  T  F
2017-11-21T00:13:29+0000  FuT2N64AuTHxEdqVil  I386  Windows Vista or Server 2008  2017-07-31T15:19:47+0000  T  F
  • Both are 32-bit (I386) EXEs (is_exe T, is_64bit F).
  • os is the minimum Windows version the file declares, not the victim's OS.
  • jjjj.exe was compiled about 9 hours before it was downloaded, a freshly built sample. Compile times can be faked, so treat this as supporting detail.

docs.title: Why MD5 and SHA1 are empty: capture loss
docs.text:
zeek-cut fuid mime_type md5 sha1 < files.log | grep dosexec
zeek-cut < files.log | grep dosexec        # all columns

FwavXQ2AM4W84BhH44   application/x-dosexec   -   -
FuT2N64AuTHxEdqVil   application/x-dosexec   -   -

The full line for jjjj.exe, read against the Zeek 4 files.log column order:

Field Value Meaning conn_uids CJ9NTy1RmcRnZRVcma The connection that carried the file analyzers EXTRACT,MD5,SHA1,PE Hashing was attempted seen_bytes 2,870,222 Bytes present in the capture total_bytes 3,061,200 Real size announced by the server (Content-Length) missing_bytes 190,978 Bytes the capture never saw md5 / sha1 - Not calculated

zugu.exe: total 5,895,226, seen 5,812,128, missing 83,098.

A hash covers every byte, and one missing byte changes it completely. Zeek therefore refuses to produce a wrong hash. For the same reason, sha256sum on the extracted file, or on a tshark export, is not the real file's hash and must not be reported as one.

Report total_bytes, not seen_bytes

The file size is the declared size: 3,061,200 and 5,895,226 bytes. seen_bytes is only what the capture contained. This walkthrough first answered Q5 with seen_bytes and corrected it after checking missing_bytes.

Confirm the loss:

zeek-cut -u ts peer gaps acks percent_lost < capture_loss.log
zeek-cut uid id.resp_h missed_bytes history < conn.log | grep -E "CJ9NTy1RmcRnZRVcma|CtsW3u4avJGUQUma66"
zeek-cut fuid seen_bytes total_bytes missing_bytes < files.log | grep -E "FwavXQ2AM4W84BhH44|FuT2N64AuTHxEdqVil"
  • percent_lost above 0 means the sensor missed packets.
  • missed_bytes in conn.log should roughly match missing_bytes.
  • In history, a g/G marks a content gap.
tshark alternative 
tshark -r ../Phase1_PCAP_7.pcap -Y "tcp.analysis.lost_segment || tcp.analysis.ack_lost_segment" | wc -l
mkdir objs && tshark -r ../Phase1_PCAP_7.pcap -q --export-objects http,objs && ls -l objs/*.exe

The first line counts packets where Wireshark noticed a missing TCP segment. The export saves files under their URL names (jjjj.exe, zugu.exe), which is handy. With capture loss they are incomplete, though, so do not hash them for the report.

docs.title: Q7 — internal or external?
docs.text:
zeek-cut -u ts tx_hosts rx_hosts mime_type seen_bytes < files.log | grep dosexec
zeek-cut -u ts query answers < dns.log | grep -E "lucrecianos|virtualsmsonline"

tx_hosts (sender) is 170.231.127.136 and 104.31.92.140. Both are public addresses outside 10/8, 172.16/12 and 192.168/16, reached by internet domain names. rx_hosts is the victim, so the direction is external → internal. The stand-alone PC has no internal servers, and it was the only internal host starting connections.

docs.title: Step 6 — Zeek notices and HTTPS destinations
docs.text:
zeek-cut -u ts note msg src dst < notice.log
zeek-cut -u ts id.resp_h server_name < ssl.log | awk -F'\t' '$1 >= "2017-11-20T23:59:30+0000"'

notice.log: eleven SSL::Invalid_Server_Cert … unable to get local issuer certificate notices, mostly for large cloud and CDN providers such as Google (172.217.x) and Amazon (52.x, 34.x). That is noise: Zeek could not complete the chain for an old capture. The last one is different:

2017-11-21T00:13:39+0000  SSL::Invalid_Server_Cert  SSL certificate validation failed with (certificate has expired)  10.192.1.157  5.189.170.24

ssl.log (server_name is the SNI, the hostname the client sends in clear text even though the content is encrypted):

Time Server Reading 23:59:41 ieonline.microsoft.com IE housekeeping, benign 00:08:34 update.googleapis.com Google updater, benign 00:13:39 – 00:16:08 idea.bsit.pk (5.189.170.24), in bursts every 30–50 s Expired certificate, starts right after zugu.exe → HTTPS C2 #3 (inferred) 00:14:14 smtp.aol.com (152.163.0.69) Outbound mail submission from a PC whose user uses webmail

The 14-minute gap contains only benign HTTPS, so the first stage was waiting, or working without network traffic, until 00:13 (inferred).

docs.title: SMTP: how much was sent?
docs.text:
zeek-cut -u ts id.resp_h id.resp_p service duration orig_bytes resp_bytes < conn.log | grep 152.163.0.69

2017-11-21T00:14:14+0000  152.163.0.69  465  ssl  2.435390  4380  5804
2017-11-21T00:14:16+0000  152.163.0.69  465  -    3.016734  0     0
2017-11-21T00:14:25+0000  152.163.0.69  465  -    -         -     -
  • Port 465 is SMTPS (SMTP inside TLS from the start), so the content is not visible.
  • orig_bytes 4,380 is what the PC sent. The TLS handshake takes 1–2 KB, which leaves a few KB of mail, enough for a list of stolen credentials.
  • The user read mail in a browser, so a desktop-style SMTP session is out of place. Probable exfiltration of stolen data (inferred).

docs.title: Step 7 — Connections Zeek could not identify (Q9)
docs.text:
zeek-cut id.resp_h id.resp_p proto service conn_state < conn.log \
  | awk -F'\t' '$4=="-" {print $1, $2, $3, $5}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -20

    231 213.183.58.34 5552 tcp REJ
      6 64.94.116.170 443 tcp S0
      3 64.94.116.170 443 tcp RSTRH
      3 181.215.247.234 1031 tcp REJ
      2 64.12.88.133 465 tcp S0
      2 172.217.0.227 443 tcp OTH
      2 152.163.0.69 465 tcp S0
      1 213.183.58.34 5552 tcp S0
      1 131.253.33.200 80 tcp RSTR
      1 13.107.13.80 80 tcp RSTR
      1 10.192.1.157 49322 tcp OTH
      1 10.192.1.157 49304 tcp OTH
conn_state Meaning SF Normal open and close S0 SYN sent, no reply REJ Rejected (the server answered with RST) RSTR / RSTRH The responder reset the connection OTH Zeek did not see the start (mid-stream)
  • 213.183.58.34:5552, 232 attempts, all refused. A program retrying the same server and port again and again is malware trying to reach its C2. REJ means the port was closed, so the server was probably already down (inferred). TCP 5552 is njRAT's default port (weak inference from the port only).
  • 181.215.247.234:1031 (REJ ×3) and 64.94.116.170:443 (S0/RST): more failed outbound attempts to unknown hosts, worth listing as indicators.
  • 64.12.88.133:465: two more failed SMTPS attempts (an AOL-range address, inferred).
  • The OTH lines toward 10.192.1.157 are fragments of connections whose start was not captured. They are not inbound attacks.
  • Zeek shows service - because these connections never carried data it could recognise.

When did the 5552 attempts start?

zeek-cut -u ts id.resp_h id.resp_p conn_state < conn.log | awk -F'\t' '$3==5552' | sed -n '1p;$p'

awk -F'\t' '$3==5552' keeps rows whose third column (destination port) is 5552; sed -n '1p;$p' prints the first and the last.

docs.title: Step 8 — What started the downloads? (Q10)
docs.text:
Evidence Status jjjj.exe was requested with no User-Agent. Browsers always send one, so a script or program fetched it. PowerShell's Net.WebClient, for example, sends none by default Confirmed (no UA); tool inferred zugu.exe and the icanhazip.com check carry the User-Agent AutoIt Confirmed The user opened Yahoo Mail about 45 seconds before the first download Confirmed strings on jjjj.exe found no AutoIt / AU3! markers Not confirmed: the file may be packed, incomplete (capture loss), or may have dropped the AutoIt component 
strings -n 6 extract_files/*FwavXQ2AM4W84BhH44 | grep -i -E "autoit|AU3!" | sort | uniq -c | head

Conclusion: the browser did not download the executables. A non-browser program fetched the first one, and an AutoIt-based program fetched the second. A malicious email opened in Yahoo Mail is the likely starting point, but the mail is encrypted (HTTPS), so it cannot be confirmed from this capture.

docs.title: Timeline
docs.text: UTC Event Source 2017-11-20 23:58:00 Capture starts; DHCP for WIN-D5243B (10.192.1.157) dhcp.log 23:58:11 Windows NCSI check http.log 23:58:49–51 User types mail.yahoo.com in IE (Bing autosuggest) http.log 23:58:56 Yahoo page ad pixels (btrll.com) http.log 23:59:35 jjjj.exe downloaded from lucrecianos.com.ar, no User-Agent http.log, files.log, pe.log 23:59:41 – 00:08:34 Only benign HTTPS (Microsoft, Google) ssl.log 00:13:28 zugu.exe downloaded from virtualsmsonline.site, User-Agent AutoIt http.log, files.log, pe.log 00:13:38 Public IP check, icanhazip.com http.log 00:13:39 → HTTPS to idea.bsit.pk (expired certificate), in bursts ssl.log, notice.log 00:13:59 → POST fre.php to tcoolonline.mobi (Charon; Inferno), about every minute http.log 00:14:04 → config.jpg / gate.php on harddomainname.biz (MSIE 7 UA), every ~60 s http.log 00:14:14 SMTPS to smtp.aol.com, ~4.4 KB sent conn.log, ssl.log during capture 232 refused connections to 213.183.58.34:5552 conn.log 00:16:33 Capture ends conn.log

docs.title: ATT&CK mapping
docs.text: Technique Evidence T1566 Phishing Downloads began right after Yahoo Mail was opened (inferred) T1105 Ingress Tool Transfer jjjj.exe, zugu.exe T1059.010 Command and Scripting Interpreter: AutoHotKey & AutoIT AutoIt User-Agent T1016.001 Internet Connection Discovery icanhazip.com, yandex.ru checks T1071.001 Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols fre.php, gate.php, HTTPS C2 T1571 Non-Standard Port TCP 5552, 1031 T1048.002 Exfiltration Over Asymmetric Encrypted Non-C2 Protocol SMTPS to AOL (inferred)

docs.title: Report (Q11)
docs.text: On 2017-11-20 at 23:59 UTC, the Windows 7 host WIN-D5243B (10.192.1.157) downloaded jjjj.exe from lucrecianos.com.ar, shortly after the user opened Yahoo Mail. At 00:13, an AutoIt-based program downloaded a second EXE, zugu.exe. The host then checked its public IP and contacted several C2 servers. One pattern matches LokiBot (not confirmed). It sent about 4 KB over encrypted SMTP to AOL, likely stolen data. It also kept trying a possible njRAT server on port 5552. The host should be isolated and rebuilt, and all saved passwords changed.

docs.title: Detection ideas
docs.text:
ZeekSnort 2Splunk 
# Non-browser User-Agents that fetch executables
zeek-cut -u ts id.orig_h host uri user_agent resp_mime_types < http.log | grep dosexec
# Known-bad / impossible User-Agents
zeek-cut id.orig_h host user_agent < http.log | grep -E "AutoIt|Charon; Inferno|MSIE 7\.0" | sort | uniq -c
# Hosts hammering one closed port (many REJ to the same destination)
zeek-cut id.orig_h id.resp_h id.resp_p conn_state < conn.log | awk -F'\t' '$4=="REJ"' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head
# Workstations talking SMTP(S) directly
zeek-cut -u ts id.orig_h id.resp_h id.resp_p orig_bytes < conn.log | awk -F'\t' '$4==25 || $4==465 || $4==587'

alert tcp $HOME_NET any -> $EXTERNAL_NET $HTTP_PORTS (msg:"LOCAL LokiBot-style User-Agent Charon Inferno"; flow:established,to_server; content:"Charon|3B| Inferno"; http_header; classtype:trojan-activity; sid:1000701; rev:1;)
alert tcp $HOME_NET any -> $EXTERNAL_NET $HTTP_PORTS (msg:"LOCAL AutoIt User-Agent"; flow:established,to_server; content:"User-Agent|3A| AutoIt|0D 0A|"; http_header; classtype:policy-violation; sid:1000702; rev:1;)
alert tcp $HOME_NET any -> $EXTERNAL_NET 5552 (msg:"LOCAL Outbound TCP 5552 (njRAT default port)"; flags:S; threshold:type both, track by_src, count 10, seconds 60; classtype:trojan-activity; sid:1000703; rev:1;)

index=zeek sourcetype=zeek:http (user_agent="AutoIt" OR user_agent="*Charon; Inferno*" OR resp_mime_types="*dosexec*")
| table _time id.orig_h host uri user_agent resp_mime_types
| sort _time

Adjust index and sourcetype to your ingestion. |3B| and |3A| in the Snort rules are hex for ; and :.

docs.title: Lessons learned
docs.text:
• The log list is evidence. No kerberos.log means no domain; pe.log means executables crossed the wire.
  • Check missing_bytes before hashing. With capture loss, Zeek leaves md5/sha1 empty, and hashing a carved file gives a wrong answer. Report total_bytes as the size and state why there is no hash.
  • Read User-Agents with their destinations. The odd Firefox string was ad traffic; AutoIt and Charon; Inferno were malware.
  • service - hides the loudest signal. 232 refused connections to one port only showed up by summarising unknown-service connections.
  • An encrypted SMTP session from a webmail user is out of place and worth reporting as possible exfiltration, while saying the content cannot be seen.
  • tshark fills Zeek's gaps: TTL, DHCP vendor class, protocol hierarchy, NBNS names and lost-segment counts.

docs.title: Phishing Red Herring to Exploit-Kit Drive-by — Angler-like EK, Ursnif-like C2, CAB Exfil (Splunk + Arkime + Snort)
Phishing Red Herring to Exploit-Kit Drive-by — Angler-like EK, Ursnif-like C2, CAB Exfil
docs.text:
Case summary

An after-hours SOC analyst receives seven malicious emails that slipped past the spam filter, an employee list, and a 12-minute PCAP of a host that raised alerts. The emails are analysed first (headers, MIME, base64, zip internals) and look like the obvious cause. The traffic then shows something else: the host — Dekker-PC, the Finance Director's workstation — was infected by visiting a compromised website. A Flash-based gate sent the browser to an exploit kit (pattern consistent with Angler EK), which exploited an outdated Flash Player 15.0.0.189 and delivered an encrypted payload. Eight seconds later the host began C2 check-ins (pattern consistent with Ursnif / Gozi-ISFB), downloaded a further encrypted module and uploaded four CAB-compressed files to the C2. The emails were a red herring for this capture — and a separate lead for other hosts. The case ends with 11 Snort rules tested against the PCAP and a complete incident report.

Evidence 7 .eml files (dangerous attachments), an employee list (CSV), one PCAP: 2016-02-05 21:24:05 – 21:36:39 UTC (12 min 34 s), 321 Zeek connections Environment Closed network (no VirusTotal, no OSINT). Splunk with Zeek logs, Arkime v5.6.4 web UI, Snort 2.9 on the analyst workstation Deliverables Email IOC analysis, network analysis, Snort rules that find the traffic again, leads for the host operator Related pages Spotting exploit kits · Base64 · Arkime search syntax · Zeek logs · SPL cheat sheet · Beaconing & C2 · Snort rules (DC/SMB)

How to read this page

It is written so a complete beginner can follow it from the first click to the finished report. Every step uses the same order:

  1. Goal — what the step tries to find out
  2. Query / command — copy it with the copy button on the code block
  3. Explained — what each piece (each line, each option) means
  4. Actual result — what appeared on screen in this case
  5. Reading the result — what it means and why it matters

Question boxes are real questions asked during the analysis. Correction boxes are places where a first reading was wrong and later evidence fixed it — they are kept on purpose, because spotting and correcting your own mistakes is part of the job.

Indicators on this page are real

Domains, IPs and hashes come from real 2016 malware traffic and real spam. They are defanged (hxxp, [.]) in prose and tables; inside code blocks (queries, rules, raw output) they are left exactly as typed. Never browse to them. Never open the attachments outside an isolated analysis VM.

docs.title: Answers at a glance
docs.text: Item Answer Status Host in the PCAP 10.41.245.114 Dekker-PC, MAC 00:17:31:7d:52:ba (ASUSTek NIC), Windows 7 + IE11 — user Justini Dekker, Finance Director Confirmed (DHCP + employee list) Cause of infection Web drive-by: compromised site www.source-werbeartikel[.]com → gate lsbery[.]tk (85.93.0.32) → exploit kit bsbkxs.zdxwx3m[.]pw (86.106.93.167) Confirmed First malicious event 21:28:24 UTC — GET /shop.php?sid=<86 hex> to the gate, which returned a Flash file Confirmed Exploit and payload Flash exploit /charge.zhtml (38,557 bytes) against Flash 15.0.0.189; encrypted payload /today.jst (360,468 bytes) at 21:28:32 Confirmed C2 tplandthepropforcontent[.]com (round-robin 185.86.77.12, 192.210.137.123), /images/<base64>/*.gif\|jpeg\|bmp, from 21:28:41 Confirmed Exfiltration 4 POST uploads of CAB files (MSCF) named XXXX.bin (21:28:52, 21:30:54, 21:33:16, 21:35:15) Confirmed Phishing emails 7 emails, 3 campaigns, zipped .js downloaders to 5 users — no trace in this capture Confirmed (not related to this capture) EK family Angler-like (Flash gate, /index.php?PHPSESSID=…&action=… landing, random-English-word parameters, fake extensions) Inferred Malware family Ursnif / Gozi-ISFB-like (/images/ base64 path C2, upload_file CAB uploads) Inferred IDS coverage Existing Snort alert data contained nothing for this host — 11 new rules written, all fired as expected, 0 false positives in the capture Confirmed

docs.title: Part A — The scenario and the given items
What was given
docs.text:
The exercise brief, paraphrased:

  • You are the only analyst in a 24/7 SOC after hours, and alerts fire for suspicious activity.
  • You identified the IP and pulled the related traffic (the PCAP).
  • You were already examining malicious emails that got through the spam filter (7 .eml files, in a folder named ..._emails_DANGER).
  • You retrieved a list of people on the network during the alert window (employee CSV: name, login name, job title, work email, phone).
  • Leave leads for the host operator, and create Snort rules to find the traffic again.

docs.title: The plan
docs.text:
1. Analyse the emails (they are already on hand) and pull out IOCs.
  2. Use Splunk (Zeek logs) to understand the capture: who, when, what.
  3. Test whether the emails explain the traffic — and follow the evidence when they don't.
  4. Confirm everything at packet level in Arkime, save evidence, record hashes.
  5. Write Snort rules and test them against the PCAP.

docs.title: Step B0 — Safety first
docs.text:
The folder is called DANGER for a reason

  • Work only inside an isolated Linux analysis VM. On Windows, double-clicking a .js file runs it with wscript.exe.
  • Opening an .eml in a text editor is safe — it is just text.
  • Listing a zip (unzip -l), hashing (sha256sum) and decoding one line of base64 are safe — nothing executes.
  • Never upload samples to online services. Look up hashes only, and only where policy allows (here: closed network, no lookups at all).
  • Rename anything you extract with a .bin or .infected suffix.

docs.title: Step B1 — Read Received: headers bottom-up
docs.text:
Every mail server that handles a message adds one Received: line at the top. So:

  • the bottom Received: line = where the message started
  • the top line = the moment it reached our server (mx1)

Read them bottom to top to follow the path in time order. In each line:

Part Meaning from NAME (… [IP]) Who connected. The IP in square brackets is what our server saw on the wire — it cannot be forged by the sender. The name before it is only what the sender claimed by NAME The server that wrote this line with ESMTP / with ESMTPS SMTP without / with TLS encryption (the S) with local The message was created by a program on that same server (e.g. a PHP script), not received from another server for <address> The recipient date -0500, +0300 The server's local time and its offset from UTC. Convert to UTC: 09:25 -0800 = 17:25 UTC

Which IP is the IOC?

The bracketed IP in the top Received: line (the one that connected to our MX) is the most reliable IOC. But if that server is a legitimate ISP mail relay (Mediacom, Telstra …), do not block it — find the real origin further down instead.

docs.title: Step B2 — The other headers that matter
docs.text: Header What to look for From: Display name vs real address. Fully forgeable Sender: / X-Authenticated-Sender: / X-Authentication-Info: The account that actually sent it. If it differs from From:, someone sent on someone else's behalf — or an account was hijacked X-PHP-Originating-Script: / X-PHP-Script: Added by PHP/cPanel hosting: a PHP script sent this mail. Typical of mailers uploaded to hacked websites. X-PHP-Script: site/path.php for <IP> also reveals which IP called the script X-Mailer: The claimed mail client. A "Windows Live Mail" claim next to a PHP header is a forgery Date: Compare with the Received: times. Big differences or an impossible time zone = forged or queued Message-ID: Must be <unique@domain>. An empty domain (<…@>) is malformed Content-Type: multipart/mixed; boundary=… The message has several parts separated by the boundary string Content-Transfer-Encoding: How the part is encoded (see B4) Content-Disposition: attachment; filename=… This part is an attachment, and its name

docs.title: Step B3 — Getting the file name inside a zip attachment
docs.text:
Goal: know what is inside the attachment without running anything.

The attachment headers show only the zip name:

Content-Type: application/x-zip-compressed;
        name="invoice304-18.zip"
Content-Transfer-Encoding: base64
Content-Disposition: attachment;
        filename="invoice304-18.zip"
  • Content-Type: application/x-zip-compressed — the part claims to be a zip.
  • name= / filename= — the name the recipient sees.
  • Content-Transfer-Encoding: base64 — the binary zip was turned into text so it can travel in email.
  • Content-Disposition: attachment — a separate attachment, not inline content.

The name of the file inside the zip is hidden in the base64 block. Three ways to read it:

docs.title: Method 1 — decode only the first line of base64
docs.text:
echo 'UEsDBBQAAAAIAJFhRUhPkndCTgsAAGUdAAAQAAAAaW52b2ljZTMwNC0xOC5qc41ZW4+jyBV+718x' | base64 -d | xxd | head -4
  • echo '…' — print the first base64 line.
  • | base64 -d — decode base64 back to bytes (-d = decode).
  • | xxd — show the bytes as hex next to printable characters (if xxd is missing: od -A x -t x1z).
  • | head -4 — first 4 lines only.

Actual result:

00000000: 504b 0304 1400 0000 0800 9161 4548 4f92  PK.........aEHO.
00000010: 7742 4e0b 0000 651d 0000 1000 0000 696e  wBN...e.......in
00000020: 766f 6963 6533 3034 2d31 382e 6a73 8d59  voice304-18.js.Y

The right-hand column shows invoice304-18.js — a JavaScript file.

Why UEsDB means zip: every zip starts with the bytes PK (Phil Katz). PK\x03\x04 in base64 is always UEsDB. Memorise a few:

base64 starts with Real file type UEsDB ZIP (also .docx, .xlsx, .jar — they are zips) TVqQ Windows executable MZ (.exe/.dll) JVBERi PDF (%PDF) 0M8R4K Old Office (.doc/.xls, OLE) iVBORw0K PNG /9j/ JPEG

The zip local file header, byte by byte:

Bytes (hex) Meaning Value 50 4b 03 04 Zip signature PK.. 14 00 Version needed 2.0 00 00 Flags No encryption 08 00 Compression method 8 = Deflate 91 61 / 45 48 DOS time / date 2016-02-05 12:12:34 (local time of the PC that made it) 4f 92 77 42 CRC-32 — 4e 0b 00 00 Compressed size 0x0B4E = 2,894 bytes 65 1d 00 00 Uncompressed size 0x1D65 = 7,525 bytes (~7.5 KB) 10 00 File-name length 0x10 = 16 characters 00 00 Extra-field length 0 69 6e 76 … File name invoice304-18.js

Little-endian

Zip stores numbers backwards. 65 1d is read as 1d65 = 7,525. 10 00 is 0010 = 16, so the next 16 bytes are the name.

The last 2–3 lines of the base64 block hold the zip's central directory and end record. Decode them the same way to see the name again and the number of files in the zip.

docs.title: Method 2 — extract the attachment and list the zip
docs.text:
mkdir ~/email1_attach && cd ~/email1_attach
python3 -c "
import email, sys
msg = email.message_from_file(open(sys.argv[1]))
for part in msg.walk():
    name = part.get_filename()
    if name:
        open(name, 'wb').write(part.get_payload(decode=True))
        print('saved:', name)
" ~/PCAPS/.../Phase2_PCAP_1_email_092704UTC.eml
unzip -l invoice304-18.zip
sha256sum invoice304-18.zip
unzip -p invoice304-18.zip | sha256sum
  • email.message_from_file(...) — parses the .eml into its MIME parts.
  • msg.walk() — visits every part (text, HTML, attachments).
  • part.get_filename() — only attachments have a file name.
  • get_payload(decode=True) — base64-decodes the part back to the original zip bytes.
  • unzip -l — lists the zip without extracting (-l = list). Nothing is written to disk.
  • sha256sum — the hash for the report (look up hashes, never upload files).
  • unzip -p … | sha256sum — -p streams the inner file to the next command without writing it, so you can hash the .js itself.

Expected unzip -l output:

Archive:  invoice304-18.zip
  Length      Date    Time    Name
---------  ---------- -----   ----
     7525  2016-02-05 12:12   invoice304-18.js
---------                     -------
     7525                     1 file

The same name and size as Method 1. zipinfo -v shows more (compressed size, CRC, extra fields).

docs.title: Method 3 — other tools
docs.text:
• CyberChef (offline): paste the base64 → From Base64 → Unzip. Shows names and contents (nothing executes).
  • Arkime shows the attachment name (email.fn) for cleartext SMTP, but not what is inside the zip.
  • Zeek files.log shows the zip name, hash and MIME type, not the inner names.

docs.title: Step B4 — Is email always base64?
docs.text:
Question: Is email always sent as base64?

No. SMTP was built for 7-bit ASCII text with lines under 1,000 characters. MIME lets each part declare its encoding in Content-Transfer-Encoding. All five appear in these seven emails:

Encoding Meaning Typical use In this case 7bit Plain ASCII, unchanged English body Emails 3, 4 body 8bit Unchanged, may contain non-ASCII Body (when servers support 8BITMIME) Email 2 body quoted-printable Mostly unchanged, special bytes as =XX Mostly-English text with a few special characters Emails 1, 5, 6, 7 body base64 Everything turned into A–Z a–z 0–9 + / Attachments, images All 7 attachments binary Raw bytes Rare —

Reading quoted-printable (Email 1 body):

We=A0are sorry to=A0inform you,=A0but the item you have=A0purchased is=A0=
  • =A0 — byte 0xA0, a non-breaking space in windows-1251.
  • =20 — a normal space (written out so a trailing space is not lost).
  • = at the end of a line — soft line break: the sentence continues on the next line.
  • =3D — the = character itself (bgColor=3D#ffffff = bgColor=#ffffff).

Headers can be encoded too (encoded-words):

Subject: =?UTF-8?B?7ZmY67aI?=
Subject: =?UTF-8?Q?Refund_=E2=80=93_Order?=

?B? = base64, ?Q? = quoted-printable. Phishers sometimes encode subjects this way to slip past keyword filters — a header-based IDS rule will miss them.

Question: So base64 means there is an executable attachment?

No. base64 only means "content that could not travel as plain text". Normal mail is full of it: signature logos, PDFs, Office files, even whole bodies with non-English text. When you see base64, check three things:

  1. Attachment or inline? Content-Disposition: attachment = a file the user opens; inline or Content-ID: = an image shown in the body.
  2. What does it claim to be? Content-Type and filename= — written by the sender, so they can lie.
  3. What is it really? Decode the first line and read the magic bytes (table in B3). Only TVqQ (MZ) is a real Windows executable — and filters usually block those.

Dangerous attachments are wider than "executables": scripts (.js .vbs .wsf .hta .ps1 .bat), macro documents (.docm, .xlsm, macro .doc/.xls), shortcuts and disk images (.lnk, .iso, .img), HTML (fake login pages), PDF (links, JavaScript). A zip — or a zip inside a zip — around them is a common filter bypass. So when you see a zip, always read the name of the file inside.

docs.title: Step B6 — Email 2 (09:34:13 UTC, to jdekker) — a different campaign
docs.text:
Recipient: jdekker — Justini Dekker, Finance Director.

Path (bottom-up):

Received: from love2dat by server.hoast.com with local (Exim 4.86)
        (envelope-from <love2dat@server.hoast.com>)
        id 1aQpdL-0004cE-9d; Wed, 03 Feb 2016 00:05:39 -0500
Received: from server.hoast.com (server.hoast.com [67.222.128.148])
        by mx1.<customer-domain> with ESMTPS id u159YBT4009585
        (version=TLSv1.2 cipher=DHE-RSA-AES256-GCM-SHA384 bits=256 verify=NO)
        for <jdekker@<customer-domain>>; Fri, 5 Feb 2016 09:34:13 GMT
  • from love2dat + with local — created inside server.hoast[.]com by the local hosting account love2dat, not received from another server. Exim is the default MTA on cPanel hosting.
  • Created Wed 3 Feb 00:05:39 -0500 = 05:05:39 UTC; delivered Fri 5 Feb 09:34:13 UTC — about 52 hours later. Bulk spam sitting in a queue, or repeated retries. Either way the campaign started two days earlier, so other organisations may already have published IOCs.
  • verify=NO — mx1 did not verify the sender's certificate. Normal between mail servers; not suspicious by itself.

Who really sent it — five headers:

From: "Finance Department" <wgygbcgync@love2date.us>
Sender:  <love2dat@server.hoast.com>
X-Get-Message-Sender-Via: server.hoast.com: authenticated_id: love2dat/from_h
X-Authenticated-Sender: server.hoast.com: wgygbcgync@love2date.us
X-PHP-Script: love2date.us/headers/wrigs61.php for 185.60.133.27
  • From — "Finance Department", but the address is a random string at a dating-site domain.
  • Sender — the account that really sent it.
  • X-Get-Message-Sender-Via / X-Authenticated-Sender — cPanel adds these to trace spam to a hosting account: the hosting account love2dat sent it, taking the From address from the header (from_h).
  • X-PHP-Script: love2date.us/headers/wrigs61.php for 185.60.133.27 — the PHP file /headers/wrigs61.php on love2date[.]us sent it, and 185.60.133.27 called that script over the web. A dating site has no reason for a randomly named script under /headers/ → the site was hacked and a mailer uploaded. 185.60.133.27 is the closest IP to the attacker — record it as a threat-intel IOC (it never talked to our network).
185.60.133.27 --(web request)--> love2date.us/headers/wrigs61.php (on server.hoast.com)
   -> Exim creates the mail (Feb 3 05:05 UTC)
   -> 67.222.128.148 (server.hoast.com) --(SMTP over TLS)--> mx1 (Feb 5 09:34 UTC)
   -> jdekker mailbox

Other oddities:

  • To: appears twice — a sloppy mailer.
  • Message-ID: <211504694.20160203000538@> — empty domain, malformed. The number contains the creation time 2016-02-03 00:05:38.
  • Date: Wed, 3 Feb 2016 0:05:38 -0500 — matches the bottom Received: line, so this Date is genuine (unlike Email 1). Another sign of a different tool.
  • No X-Mailer at all.

Body (text/html, 8bit): "NOTICE! You have received a remittance … Money Order can be cashed at any branch or bank in Your city . … Division of Payments WU000076846645". Greed lure aimed at a finance director; capital Your mid-sentence; a space before the full stop; image alt="western unioun".

<IMG ... alt="western unioun" ... src="https://www.cehost.ro/templates/cehostv3/html/images/westernunion_logo_big.gif">

A remote image tells you who opened the email

The logo is loaded from another website instead of being embedded. When anyone opens the HTML, their PC makes a DNS query for www.cehost[.]ro and an HTTPS connection to it (the name is visible in the TLS SNI). Both appear in Zeek dns.log / ssl.log — so you can find who opened the email and when without reading the mail. cehost[.]ro looks like a Romanian hosting company being hot-linked; treat it as an "opened" indicator, not a block IOC.

Attachment — a zip inside a zip:

Content-Type: application/octet-stream;
 name="WU7328899085.zip"
Content-transfer-encoding: base64
Content-Disposition: attachment;
 filename="WU7328899085.zip"

application/octet-stream ("just bytes") hides the type, unlike Email 1. Decode the first two base64 lines together:

echo 'UEsDBAoAAAAAAIEoQ0gqQtZfwgYAAMIGAAAIABwAZmlsZS56aXBVVAkAA0GKsVZ9irFWdXgLAAEEAAAAAAQAAAAAUEsDBBQACAAIAPWiQkgAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAWAAAAaW52b2ljZV9zY2FuX0RneUVmbC5qc' | base64 -d | xxd

(The tail is cut mid-character, so base64 may warn invalid input — the start decodes fine.)

00000000: 504b 0304 0a00 0000 0000 8128 4348 2a42  PK.........(CH*B
00000010: d65f c206 0000 c206 0000 0800 1c00 6669  ._............fi
00000020: 6c65 2e7a 6970 5554 0900 0341 8ab1 567d  le.zipUT...A..V}
00000030: 8ab1 5675 780b 0001 0400 0000 0004 0000  ..Vux...........
00000040: 0000 504b 0304 1400 0800 0800 f5a2 4248  ..PK..........BH
00000050: 0000 0000 0000 0000 0000 0000 1600 0000  ................
00000060: 696e 766f 6963 655f 7363 616e 5f44 6779  invoice_scan_Dgy
00000070: 4566 6c2e 6a                             Efl.j

Two PK signatures = two zips.

Outer zip WU7328899085.zip:

Bytes Meaning Value 0a 00 Version 1.0 00 00 Compression 0 = stored (a zip is already compressed) 81 28 / 43 48 Time / date 2016-02-03 05:04:02 c2 06 00 00 ×2 Compressed = uncompressed size 1,730 bytes 08 00 / 1c 00 Name length / extra length 8 / 28 name file.zip UT … ux … Extra fields Unix timestamp + Unix UID → built with Linux zip. UT time = 2016-02-03 05:04:01 UTC, 1.5 min before the mail was created

Inner zip file.zip (starts at byte 0x42 = 66 = 30 + 8 + 28):

Bytes Meaning Value 08 00 (flags) Bit 3 set Sizes written after the data (streamed creation) — so CRC and sizes here are 0 08 00 Compression Deflate f5 a2 / 42 48 Time / date 2016-02-02 20:23:42 16 00 Name length 22 name invoice_scan_DgyEfl.js (random suffix per recipient)

The real sizes are in the central directory at the end (decode the last base64 lines): 1,572 bytes compressed, 4,500 bytes uncompressed — a different script from Email 1's 7,525 bytes.

Why two zips? Many mail gateways open only one layer. One layer shows just file.zip, so the .js inside slips through.

Confirming with the full file:

unzip -l WU7328899085.zip
unzip -p WU7328899085.zip file.zip > file.zip
unzip -l file.zip
sha256sum WU7328899085.zip file.zip

Archive:  WU7328899085.zip
     1730  2016-02-03 05:04   file.zip
Archive:  file.zip
     4500  2016-02-02 20:23   invoice_scan_DgyEfl.js

docs.title: Step B10 — Email 6 (18:23:42 UTC, to jdekker via mx2)
docs.text:
Received: by b106.mac7.ru (Postfix, from userid 48)
        id A96CC729DE6; Fri,  5 Feb 2016 18:07:01 +0300 (MSK)
Received: from b106.mac7.ru (b106.mac7.ru [212.232.52.106])
        by mx2.<customer-domain> with ESMTP id u15INfdw020639
        for <jdekker@<customer-domain>>; Fri, 5 Feb 2016 18:23:42 GMT
  • Same server, UID 48, configsese.php, subject Refund for the Order #284822.
  • From "Chaney Vinson" <vestibulum@ullamcorpermagnaSed[.]edu>; Date 15:06:34 -0800 (same mistake); X-Mailer WLM 16.4.3528.331.
  • Delivered by mx2 — the company has two MX servers. Any search filtered on mx1's IP misses this email.
  • Attachment: invoice304-25.zip → invoice304-25.js, 2,922 / 7,571 bytes.
  • jdekker is the second user targeted twice (Emails 2 and 6).

Correction — the attacker's clock

This zip also carried an NTFS extra field, whose times are always UTC. Its modification time was 08:12:38 UTC, while the DOS time was 12:12:38 — so the attacker's PC clock was UTC+4, not MSK (UTC+3) as first assumed. All four invoice304-N.js files (DOS 12:12:24, 12:12:34, 12:12:38, 12:12:40) were therefore created at ~08:12 UTC within 16 seconds, then sent from different servers at different times all day.

How the NTFS time was read: the extra field holds three little-endian 64-bit FILETIME values (100-ns ticks since 1601-01-01):

python3 -c "
import datetime, struct
v = struct.unpack('<Q', bytes.fromhex('005fe6f9ec5fd101'))[0]
print(datetime.datetime(1601,1,1) + datetime.timedelta(microseconds=v//10))"

2016-02-05 08:12:38

docs.text:
• Same server b106.mac7[.]ru, UID 48, configsese.php, subject Refund for the Order #284822, delivered by mx1.

Correction — why Emails 6 and 7 arrived three hours late

At first it looked like mx1 rejected Email 6 and it was retried to mx2. Email 7 disproves that: Emails 6 and 7 left the attacker's server 4 seconds apart (18:07:01 / 18:06:57 MSK) and arrived 1 second apart (mx2 18:23:42 / mx1 18:23:43), both ~3 h 17 min late. The delay was on the sender's queue, which then delivered to both MX servers at once.

docs.title: Step B13 — What a network sensor can see of these emails
docs.text:
STARTTLS hides the mail

with ESMTPS … TLSv1.2 in the top Received: line means the hop into our MX was encrypted. A sensor on that link sees only TLS — no subject, no attachment name.

  • Encrypted (ESMTPS): Emails 1, 2, 4
  • Cleartext (ESMTP): Emails 3, 5, 6, 7

So content-based Snort rules can only fire on 3, 5, 6, 7 (unless a later internal hop — MX to mail server, POP3/IMAP, webmail — is cleartext). IP-based rules still work, and Zeek ssl.log (port 25, matching time and cipher) still proves delivery.

Splunk check for encrypted delivery (in a capture that contains SMTP):

index=zeek sourcetype=zeek:ssl id_resp_p=25
| table _time id_orig_h id_resp_h version cipher server_name
  • id_resp_p=25 — TLS sessions whose server port is 25 (SMTP with STARTTLS).
  • If 213.133.123.17 appears at 09:27 with TLS_DHE_RSA_WITH_AES_256_GCM_SHA384, it matches Email 1's Received: header exactly.

docs.text:
