docs.title: rex, Field Extraction & eval
docs.text:
Category: Splunk · Last updated: 2026-09-17

In one sentence

When the field you need doesn't exist, make it: rex pulls values out of text with a regex named group, spath walks JSON/XML, eval reshapes what you have — and once a pattern is proven in a search, promote it to a permanent extraction so nobody has to type it again.

docs.title: rex essentials
docs.text:
| rex field=<source field> "<regex with (?<name>...) groups>"
  • Default field=_raw. Name each capture with (?<fieldname>…) — that becomes the new field.
  • Regex flavour is PCRE. Splunk double-parses backslashes inside "…": write \\d for \d when the pattern is in double quotes — or, simpler, keep patterns short and use \d, \s, \w which usually survive; test in the UI.
  • Add max_match=0 to capture all matches into a multivalue field (default 1).
  • (?i) at the start = case-insensitive.
  • mode=sed turns rex into search-and-replace: | rex field=x mode=sed "s/old/new/g".

docs.title: Worked examples
docs.text:
Base64-encoded PowerShell

index=botsv3 sourcetype="XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational" EventID=1 Image="*powershell.exe"
| rex field=CommandLine "(?i)-(?:e|en|enc|encodedcommand)\s+(?<b64>[A-Za-z0-9+/=]{20,})"
| where isnotnull(b64)
| eval decoded=replace(base64decode(b64),"\x00","")
| table _time, host, User, decoded

The regex matches any of -e, -en, -enc, -encodedcommand (case-insensitive), whitespace, then 20+ base64 characters captured as b64. where isnotnull(b64) keeps only rows where the capture succeeded. base64decode (Splunk 8+; older versions need a custom command) turns it back into text; the replace strips the UTF-16 null bytes PowerShell inserts between characters.

Username without domain

| rex field=User "^(?<domain>[^\\\\]+)\\\\(?<username>.+)$"

Captures CORP\jsmith into domain=CORP, username=jsmith. The four backslashes become a regex \\ (one literal backslash) after Splunk's quote-unescaping.

IP + port out of free text

| rex field=Message "Source Network Address:\s+(?<src_ip>\d{1,3}(?:\.\d{1,3}){3})\s+Source Port:\s+(?<src_port>\d+)"

Every IP in an event (multivalue)

| rex max_match=0 "(?<ips>\b(?:\d{1,3}\.){3}\d{1,3}\b)"
| mvexpand ips
| search ips!=127.0.0.1 ips!=0.0.0.0

max_match=0 collects all IPs into ips; mvexpand makes one row per IP so you can filter and count them.

File name and extension from a path

| rex field=TargetFilename "(?<fname>[^\\\\]+)$"
| rex field=fname "\.(?<ext>[^.]+)$"

Domain from a URL / SNI

| rex field=url "^(?:https?://)?(?<fqdn>[^/:]+)"
| eval domain=mvindex(split(fqdn,"."),-2).".".mvindex(split(fqdn,"."),-1)

split breaks the FQDN on dots into a multivalue list; mvindex(...,-2) and -1 pick the last two labels; . concatenates them (mail.evil-example.com → evil-example.com). Good enough for most TLDs; co.uk-style needs a lookup.

Sysmon XML without the add-on

| rex field=_raw "<Data Name='Image'>(?<Image>[^<]+)"
| rex field=_raw "<Data Name='CommandLine'>(?<CommandLine>[^<]+)"
| rex field=_raw "<Data Name='ParentImage'>(?<ParentImage>[^<]+)"
| rex field=_raw "<EventID>(?<EventID>\d+)</EventID>"

Each rex grabs one <Data Name='…'>value</Data> element. Better: spath below, or install the add-on.

docs.title: spath for JSON / XML
docs.text:
| spath                                            # auto-extract everything (JSON) — fine for small results
| spath path=userIdentity.arn output=who           # one path, renamed
| spath path=Event.EventData.Data{@Name}           # XML attributes → multivalue
| spath input=Message path=alert.signature         # spath on a field that contains JSON

For Sysmon XML you'll usually pair spath with mvzip/mvexpand or just install the add-on — the XML shape (<Data Name="X">value) makes rex simpler than spath here.

docs.title: Auto-extraction that already exists
docs.text: Before writing rex, check what Splunk already gives you: Interesting Fields panel; | fieldsummary; key=value pairs in raw text are extracted automatically (user=admin → user); the Field Extractor (Extract New Fields → highlight text → Splunk writes the regex) is the GUI way to build and save a rex.

docs.title: eval — the functions you actually use
docs.text: Need Function Conditional if(cond, a, b) · case(c1, v1, c2, v2, true(), default) · coalesce(a, b, c) · nullif(a, b) Strings lower, upper, len, substr(s, start, len), replace(s, regex, repl), trim, ltrim, rtrim, split(s, delim), . (concat), urldecode, md5, sha1, sha256 Tests like(s, "pat%"), match(s, "regex"), cidrmatch("10.0.0.0/8", ip), isnull, isnotnull, in(field, "a","b"), searchmatch("user=admin*") Numbers round(x, 2), floor, ceil, abs, pow, log, tonumber(s), tostring(n, "commas"), random() Time now(), strftime(t, fmt), strptime(s, fmt), relative_time(t, "-1d@d"), time() Multivalue mvcount, mvindex(mv, i), mvjoin(mv, ","), mvfilter(match(mv, "x")), mvdedup, mvappend, mvzip, split, mvsort Encoding base64decode / base64encode (8.1+), printf, tostring(x,"hex") Type typeof(x), tonumber, tostring

docs.title: Small eval recipes
docs.text:
| eval user=lower(coalesce(user, Account_Name, User))                       # normalise usernames across sourcetypes
| eval is_admin=if(match(user,"(?i)admin|adm_|svc_"),1,0)
| eval logon_type_name=case(Logon_Type==2,"Interactive",Logon_Type==3,"Network",Logon_Type==10,"RemoteInteractive",Logon_Type==9,"NewCredentials",true(),"Other")
| eval internal=if(cidrmatch("10.0.0.0/8",dest_ip) OR cidrmatch("192.168.0.0/16",dest_ip) OR cidrmatch("172.16.0.0/12",dest_ip),"int","ext")
| eval MB_out=round(bytes_out/1048576,2)
| eval cmd_len=len(CommandLine), has_b64=if(match(CommandLine,"[A-Za-z0-9+/]{50,}={0,2}"),1,0)
| eval entropy_hint=len(replace(lower(query),"[aeiou0-9.-]",""))/len(query)   # crude consonant ratio for DGA-ish names
| eval day=strftime(_time,"%Y-%m-%d"), hour=strftime(_time,"%H")
| eval hash_sha256=mvindex(split(mvindex(split(Hashes,"SHA256="),1),","),0)  # Sysmon Hashes field "MD5=…,SHA256=…,IMPHASH=…"

The last one: split(Hashes,"SHA256=") cuts the string at SHA256=; mvindex(...,1) takes what follows; splitting that on , and taking index 0 leaves just the hash.

docs.title: Lookups — enrich and allow-list
docs.text:
# CSV with columns ip,owner,criticality uploaded as lookup "assets"
| lookup assets ip as dest_ip OUTPUTNEW owner, criticality

# Allow-list: drop rows whose process is in known_good.csv (column: process)
| lookup known_good process as Image OUTPUT process as known
| where isnull(known)

# Build a baseline once, reuse it
index=botsv3 sourcetype=stream:http earliest=-30d@d latest=@d | stats count by http_user_agent | outputlookup baseline_ua.csv

OUTPUTNEW only fills fields that are empty; OUTPUT overwrites. The allow-list trick: join against the list and keep rows where the lookup failed (isnull) — i.e. not on the list.

docs.title: Promote a rex to a permanent extraction
docs.text:
Once a rex works, save it so it is applied automatically at search time: Settings → Fields → Field extractions → New, sourcetype + the same regex (drop field= unless it's not _raw), or in props.conf:

[XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational]
EXTRACT-sysmon_image = <Data Name='Image'>(?<Image>[^<]+)
EXTRACT-sysmon_cmd   = <Data Name='CommandLine'>(?<CommandLine>[^<]+)

Also useful: Field aliases (Account_Name → user), Calculated fields (eval stored once), Event types (a saved search condition, e.g. eventtype=win_failed_logon), Tags (tag=authentication). These are how add-ons make CIM fields appear.

docs.title: Debugging extraction
docs.text:
• Nothing extracted? Test the regex on one event: | head 1 | rex … | table b64 — then loosen it.
  • Backslash trouble? Put the pattern in the Field Extractor GUI, or use [\\\\] for a literal backslash class.
  • Wrong field name? Check spelling and case — field names are case-sensitive (EventCode ≠ eventcode), values usually aren't.
  • Field appears in the sidebar but stats says null? It may exist in only some events — | stats count(field) count shows coverage.
  • Multivalue surprises: stats by Account_Name splits on each value; use mvindex or mvjoin first.

docs.title: Security Searches by Question
docs.text:
Category: Splunk · Data: Windows Security, Sysmon, PowerShell, Zeek/Stream · Last updated: 2026-09-17

In one sentence

The searches you run during an incident, grouped by the question you are answering, each with a plain-English breakdown of what the SPL does and what the event codes mean — swap index=botsv3 and the sourcetype names for your environment's.

Conventions: SEC = index=botsv3 sourcetype=WinEventLog (Security log; use source="WinEventLog:Security" if System/Application share the sourcetype), SYSMON = index=botsv3 sourcetype="XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational", PS = index=botsv3 sourcetype="XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational". Event ID meanings: Windows Event IDs.

docs.title: Who logged on, from where?
docs.text:
Successful logons by type and source

index=botsv3 sourcetype=WinEventLog EventCode=4624
| eval user=mvindex(Account_Name,1)
| eval type=case(Logon_Type==2,"2 Interactive",Logon_Type==3,"3 Network",Logon_Type==4,"4 Batch",Logon_Type==5,"5 Service",Logon_Type==7,"7 Unlock",Logon_Type==9,"9 NewCredentials",Logon_Type==10,"10 RDP",Logon_Type==11,"11 Cached",true(),Logon_Type)
| stats count, earliest(_time) as first, latest(_time) as last by host, user, type, Source_Network_Address
| convert ctime(first) ctime(last)
| sort host, - count

4624 = a logon succeeded. Account_Name has two values (subject, target); mvindex(...,1) takes the account that logged on. case turns the numeric Logon_Type into a label — type 3 (network: SMB/WinRM/PsExec), 10 (RDP) and 9 (runas /netonly, pass-the-hash tooling) are the ones to read carefully. stats gives one row per host/user/type/source with first and last time.

Failed logons — brute force and spraying

index=botsv3 sourcetype=WinEventLog EventCode=4625
| bin _time span=10m
| stats count, dc(Account_Name) as users, values(Sub_Status) as substatus by _time, Source_Network_Address, host
| where count >= 10
| eval pattern=if(users >= 5, "spraying (many users)", "brute force (few users)")
| sort - count

4625 = logon failed. Bucketing to 10 minutes and counting per source IP finds bursts; dc(Account_Name) (distinct accounts) separates spraying (one password, many users) from brute force (one user, many passwords). Sub_Status explains why: 0xC000006A wrong password, 0xC0000064 user doesn't exist (spraying a wordlist), 0xC0000234 locked out, 0xC0000072 disabled account.

Explicit credentials / lateral movement source side

index=botsv3 sourcetype=WinEventLog EventCode=4648
| stats count, values(Target_Server_Name) as targets, values(Process_Name) as procs by host, Subject_Account_Name, Account_Name
| where mvcount(targets) > 3

4648 = a logon was attempted with explicit credentials (runas, scheduled task creds, tools that supply a username/password/hash). It's logged on the source machine, so host is where the attacker is, targets is where they went. One account reaching many servers in a short window is lateral movement.

RDP sessions with source IP

index=botsv3 sourcetype=WinEventLog (EventCode=4624 Logon_Type=10) OR EventCode=4778 OR EventCode=4779 OR (sourcetype="WinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-TerminalServices-LocalSessionManager/Operational" EventCode IN (21,24,25))
| eval src=coalesce(Source_Network_Address, Client_Address, Source_Network_Address)
| eval user=coalesce(mvindex(Account_Name,1), Account_Name, User)
| table _time, host, EventCode, user, src
| sort 0 _time

4624/10 = RDP logon; 4778/4779 = RDP session reconnected/disconnected (with client name/IP); LocalSessionManager 21 = session logon succeeded, 24 disconnect, 25 reconnect. coalesce merges the differently-named IP fields into one src column so the timeline reads cleanly.

Admin logons

index=botsv3 sourcetype=WinEventLog EventCode=4672
| stats count by host, Account_Name
| sort - count

4672 = special privileges assigned at logon — effectively "an admin-level account logged on". Pair it with the 4624 that has the same Logon_ID.

docs.title: What ran?
docs.text:
Process creation with command lines (Security 4688)

index=botsv3 sourcetype=WinEventLog EventCode=4688
| eval user=mvindex(Account_Name,0)
| stats count by host, user, New_Process_Name, Process_Command_Line, Creator_Process_Name
| sort - count

4688 = new process created. Process_Command_Line is only present if "Include command line in process creation events" is enabled by policy; Creator_Process_Name (parent) exists on Win10+/2016+.

Sysmon process tree — suspicious parents

index=botsv3 sourcetype="XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational" EventID=1
| eval parent=lower(replace(ParentImage,".*\\\\","")), child=lower(replace(Image,".*\\\\",""))
| search (parent IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","acrord32.exe","msedge.exe","chrome.exe") AND child IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","msiexec.exe"))
   OR (parent="wmiprvse.exe" AND child IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe"))
   OR (parent="services.exe" AND child IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe"))
   OR (parent IN ("w3wp.exe","httpd.exe","tomcat*.exe") AND child IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","whoami.exe"))
| table _time, host, User, parent, child, CommandLine

Sysmon 1 = process create with full parent/child and hashes. replace(ParentImage,".*\\\\","") strips the path, leaving the file name. The search lists classic bad parent→child pairs: Office spawning a shell (macro), WMI provider host spawning a shell (remote WMI exec), services.exe spawning a shell (PsExec-style service), a web server spawning a shell (web shell).

LOLBins & suspicious command lines

index=botsv3 sourcetype="XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational" EventID=1
| where match(CommandLine, "(?i)(-enc|-encodedcommand|frombase64string|iex\s*\(|invoke-expression|downloadstring|downloadfile|net\.webclient|invoke-webrequest|certutil.*-urlcache|certutil.*-decode|bitsadmin.*transfer|mshta.*http|regsvr32.*/i:http|rundll32.*javascript|vssadmin.*delete|wbadmin.*delete|bcdedit.*recoveryenabled|wevtutil\s+cl|schtasks.*/create|sc\s+create|reg\s+add.*\\run|whoami|net\s+(user|group|localgroup)|nltest|dsquery|adfind|mimikatz|sekurlsa|procdump.*lsass|comsvcs.*minidump|ntdsutil|esentutl.*ntds)")
| stats count, values(CommandLine) as cmds, earliest(_time) as first by host, User, Image
| convert ctime(first)
| sort first

One long case-insensitive regex covers download cradles, encoded PowerShell, LOLBin downloaders, shadow-copy/backup deletion (ransomware prep), log clearing, persistence commands, discovery commands and credential dumping. values(CommandLine) collects every matching command per host/user/binary so you read them in one row.

PowerShell script blocks

index=botsv3 sourcetype="XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational" EventCode=4104
| where len(ScriptBlockText) > 500 OR match(ScriptBlockText,"(?i)frombase64string|invoke-mimikatz|amsi|bypass|-nop|hidden|downloadstring|reflection\.assembly|virtualalloc|kernel32")
| stats count, min(_time) as first, values(Path) as paths by host, ScriptBlockText
| convert ctime(first)
| sort first

4104 = the actual decoded script text, even for -enc payloads — it's the single best PowerShell artifact. Long blocks and the keyword set (AMSI bypass, reflection, memory allocation, download cradles) surface offensive tooling.

Renamed / out-of-place binaries (Sysmon)

index=botsv3 sourcetype="XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational" EventID=1
| eval fname=lower(replace(Image,".*\\\\","")), orig=lower(OriginalFileName)
| where isnotnull(orig) AND orig!="?" AND fname!=orig AND NOT (fname="powershell.exe" AND orig="powershell.exe")
| stats count by host, Image, OriginalFileName, CommandLine

Sysmon records the PE header's OriginalFileName. If the file on disk is svchost.exe but the header says mimikatz.exe, the attacker renamed it. Also useful: Image under \Users\Public\, \ProgramData\, \Windows\Temp\, \AppData\Local\Temp\, \PerfLogs\.

docs.title: How do they persist?
docs.text:
New services

index=botsv3 sourcetype="WinEventLog:System" EventCode=7045
| table _time, host, Service_Name, Service_File_Name, Service_Type, Service_Start_Type, Account_Name
| sort 0 _time

System 7045 = a service was installed. PSEXESVC = PsExec; random 8-char names with %COMSPEC% /b /c start /b /min powershell -nop -w hidden -enc = Cobalt Strike/Metasploit service payloads; a service whose binary sits in a user folder is persistence.

Scheduled tasks

index=botsv3 sourcetype=WinEventLog EventCode IN (4698, 4702)
| rex field=Task_Content "<Command>(?<cmd>[^<]+)</Command>"
| rex field=Task_Content "<Arguments>(?<args>[^<]+)</Arguments>"
| table _time, host, Subject_Account_Name, Task_Name, cmd, args

4698 = task created, 4702 = task updated (requires audit policy). The task XML lives in Task_Content; rex pulls the command and arguments out of it.

Registry run keys & other ASEPs (Sysmon)

index=botsv3 sourcetype="XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational" EventID IN (12, 13, 14)
| where match(TargetObject, "(?i)\\\\CurrentVersion\\\\Run|\\\\RunOnce|\\\\Winlogon\\\\(Shell|Userinit)|\\\\Image File Execution Options|\\\\Services\\\\[^\\\\]+\\\\ImagePath|\\\\AppInit_DLLs|\\\\Command Processor\\\\AutoRun|\\\\Environment\\\\UserInitMprLogonScript|\\\\Classes\\\\CLSID\\\\[^\\\\]+\\\\InprocServer32|\\\\Policies\\\\Explorer\\\\Run|\\\\Active Setup")
| table _time, host, User, Image, EventID, TargetObject, Details

Sysmon 12 = key created/deleted, 13 = value set, 14 = key/value renamed. TargetObject is the registry path; Details the value written. The regex lists the autostart locations from the Registry keys page.

WMI persistence

index=botsv3 (sourcetype="XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational" EventID IN (19,20,21)) OR (sourcetype="WinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-WMI-Activity/Operational" EventCode=5861)
| table _time, host, sourcetype, EventID, EventCode, User, EventNamespace, Name, Query, Destination, Consumer, Filter, Message

Sysmon 19/20/21 = WMI event filter / consumer / binding created — all three together = persistence. WMI-Activity 5861 is the OS's own record of a new permanent consumer.

New local users and group changes

index=botsv3 sourcetype=WinEventLog EventCode IN (4720, 4722, 4724, 4728, 4732, 4756)
| eval action=case(EventCode==4720,"user created",EventCode==4722,"user enabled",EventCode==4724,"password reset",EventCode==4728,"added to global group",EventCode==4732,"added to local group",EventCode==4756,"added to universal group")
| table _time, host, Subject_Account_Name, action, Account_Name, Member_Name, Group_Name
| sort 0 _time

4720 create, 4722 enable, 4724 admin password reset, 4728/4732/4756 member added to a security group (global/local/universal). A 4720 followed within seconds by 4732 into Administrators is textbook backdoor account creation.

docs.title: Lateral movement (target side)
docs.text:
PsExec / SMB admin share pattern

index=botsv3 (sourcetype=WinEventLog EventCode IN (4624, 5140, 5145)) OR (sourcetype="WinEventLog:System" EventCode=7045)
| eval share=coalesce(Share_Name, Relative_Target_Name)
| where EventCode!=4624 OR Logon_Type=3
| eval src=coalesce(Source_Network_Address, Source_Address)
| stats values(EventCode) as codes, values(share) as shares, values(Service_Name) as services, values(Account_Name) as accounts, min(_time) as first, max(_time) as last by host, src
| where match(mvjoin(codes,","),"5140|5145") AND match(mvjoin(codes,","),"7045")
| convert ctime(first) ctime(last)

The PsExec chain on the target: 4624 type 3 (network logon) → 5140/5145 (share ADMIN$/IPC$ accessed, file PSEXESVC.exe written) → 7045 (service installed). Grouping everything by target host and source IP, then requiring both a share-access code and a service-install code in the same group, finds the chain even without knowing the tool's name.

WMI / WinRM remote execution

index=botsv3 sourcetype="XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational" EventID=1 (ParentImage="*\\wmiprvse.exe" OR ParentImage="*\\wsmprovhost.exe")
| table _time, host, User, ParentImage, Image, CommandLine

On the target, remote WMI runs children under wmiprvse.exe; PowerShell Remoting runs them under wsmprovhost.exe. Neither should normally spawn cmd/powershell.

Pass-the-hash indicators

index=botsv3 sourcetype=WinEventLog EventCode=4624 Logon_Type=9 Logon_Process=seclogo Authentication_Package=Negotiate
| table _time, host, Account_Name, Logon_ID, Process_Name

Mimikatz sekurlsa::pth and similar create a 4624 with Logon Type 9 (NewCredentials), logon process seclogo, package Negotiate on the attacker's machine. On the target, PtH looks like a normal type 3 NTLM logon — so also hunt 4624 Logon_Type=3 Authentication_Package=NTLM from workstation-to-workstation in a Kerberos domain.

Kerberoasting (on DCs)

index=botsv3 sourcetype=WinEventLog EventCode=4769 Ticket_Encryption_Type=0x17 Failure_Code=0x0
| where NOT match(Service_Name, "\\$$|krbtgt")
| bin _time span=10m
| stats dc(Service_Name) as spns, values(Service_Name) as services by _time, Account_Name, Client_Address
| where spns >= 5

4769 = service ticket requested. Encryption type 0x17 = RC4 — what cracking tools request. Excluding computer accounts ($) and krbtgt, one user requesting five or more distinct SPNs in ten minutes is Kerberoasting.

docs.title: Network side (Zeek / Stream in Splunk)
docs.text:
Beacon candidates — see Beaconing & C2 for the full streamstats version.

Rare user agents

index=botsv3 sourcetype=stream:http
| stats dc(src_ip) as hosts, count, values(site) as sites by http_user_agent
| where hosts <= 2
| sort count

dc(src_ip) = how many clients use each UA; one or two = bespoke tool or malware; values(site) shows where it goes.

Executable downloads

index=botsv3 sourcetype=stream:http (http_content_type="application/x-msdownload" OR http_content_type="application/x-dosexec" OR uri_path="*.exe" OR uri_path="*.dll" OR uri_path="*.ps1")
| table _time, src_ip, dest_ip, site, uri_path, http_user_agent, bytes_in

DNS oddities

index=botsv3 sourcetype=stream:dns record_type=A
| eval qlen=len(query), first=mvindex(split(query,"."),0)
| where qlen > 50 OR len(first) > 30 OR record_type IN ("TXT","NULL")
| stats count, dc(query) as uniq by src_ip, dest_ip
| sort - uniq

Large uploads

index=botsv3 sourcetype=stream:tcp
| stats sum(bytes_out) as out, sum(bytes_in) as in by src_ip, dest_ip, dest_port
| eval out_MB=round(out/1048576,1), ratio=round(out/(in+1),1)
| where out_MB > 50 AND ratio > 5
| sort - out_MB

ratio = bytes sent divided by bytes received; a client sending 5× more than it receives, in the tens of megabytes, is uploading.

docs.title: Log tampering
docs.text:
index=botsv3 (sourcetype=WinEventLog EventCode IN (1102, 4719, 4616)) OR (sourcetype="WinEventLog:System" EventCode=104)
| eval what=case(EventCode==1102,"Security log cleared",EventCode==104,"Event log cleared",EventCode==4719,"Audit policy changed",EventCode==4616,"System time changed")
| table _time, host, what, Account_Name, Subject_Account_Name, Message
| sort 0 _time

1102 = Security log cleared (records who), 104 = any other log cleared, 4719 = audit policy changed (logging turned off before the action), 4616 = system time changed (timeline confusion). Also check for hosts whose log volume drops to zero — Data discovery → log gap detection.

docs.title: Build a host timeline (everything about one machine)
docs.text:
index=botsv3 host=FYODOR-L earliest="08/20/2018:00:00:00" latest="08/21/2018:00:00:00"
  (sourcetype=WinEventLog EventCode IN (4624,4625,4648,4672,4688,4698,4720,4732,7045,1102))
  OR (sourcetype="XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational" EventID IN (1,3,11,12,13,22))
  OR (sourcetype="XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational" EventCode=4104)
| eval code=coalesce(EventCode, EventID)
| eval who=coalesce(User, mvindex(Account_Name,1), Account_Name)
| eval what=coalesce(CommandLine, Process_Command_Line, ScriptBlockText, TargetFilename, TargetObject, QueryName, DestinationIp." :".DestinationPort, Service_File_Name, Task_Name, Message)
| eval what=substr(what,1,300)
| table _time, sourcetype, code, who, what
| sort 0 _time

One search, three sourcetypes, a handful of event codes; coalesce picks the most descriptive field each event has and substr trims it so the table stays readable. This is the table you paste into a report timeline.

docs.title: SPL Cheat Sheet
docs.text:
Category: Splunk · Level: foundations → intermediate · Last updated: 2026-09-17

In one sentence

SPL is a pipeline: the first part finds events (index, sourcetype, keywords), every | after that transforms what came before — filter, compute, group, count, sort, present. Learn ~25 commands and you can do 95% of incident-response work.

docs.title: Anatomy of a search
docs.text:
index=botsv3 sourcetype=WinEventLog EventCode=4625 earliest=-24h latest=now
| eval user=lower(Account_Name)
| stats count by user, src_ip
| where count > 10
| sort - count
| head 20

Read it top to bottom: 1) get failed-logon events (4625) from the last 24 hours in the botsv3 index; 2) make a lowercase user field; 3) count events per user + source IP; 4) keep only pairs with more than 10; 5) biggest first; 6) top 20. Every line receives the rows the previous line produced.

Rules of thumb: always name the index (index=* is slow and often forbidden in production); put the most selective terms first (EventCode=4625 before free text); filter early with the search bar rather than late with where; use stats instead of table on large result sets.

docs.title: Search-time filtering (before the first |)
docs.text: Syntax Meaning index=botsv3 Which index sourcetype=WinEventLog · source="WinEventLog:Security" · host=FYODOR-L Metadata fields EventCode=4688 Field = value (case-insensitive value match for strings) EventCode IN (4624, 4625, 4648) Any of a list user=admin* Wildcard (at end is fast; leading *admin is slow) NOT user=SYSTEM · user!=SYSTEM Exclude (NOT field=x also keeps events without the field; field!=x drops them) "cmd.exe /c" Phrase (quotes) mimikatz OR procdump · A AND B (AND is implicit) Booleans earliest=-7d@d latest=@d Time modifiers — @d snaps to midnight; -7d@d = midnight seven days ago earliest="09/15/2026:00:00:00" Absolute time src_ip=10.0.0.0/24 CIDR works on IP fields TERM(10.0.0.5) Match a raw token exactly, fast, avoids segmentation surprises CASE(Mimikatz) Case-sensitive keyword

docs.title: Commands — the ones you use daily
docs.text: Each row: what it does, then a copy-ready example.

docs.title: Filter & shape rows
docs.text: Command Does Example search Filter again mid-pipeline (same syntax as the search bar) … | search count > 5 user!=svc* where Filter with an expression (functions, comparisons between fields) | where bytes_out > 10*bytes_in AND like(dest, "10.%") dedup Keep first event per unique value(s) | dedup user, host · | dedup 3 host sortby -_time head / tail First / last N rows | head 50 sort Order rows (- = descending; 0 = no 10k limit) | sort 0 - count, +user reverse Flip order fields Keep (or - remove) columns — speeds things up | fields _time, host, user, CommandLine · | fields - _raw table Show columns as a table (presentation only) | table _time host user CommandLine rename Rename fields (wildcards ok) | rename Account_Name as user, "Source Network Address" as src_ip regex Filter rows by regex on a field | regex CommandLine="(?i)-enc|-e\s+[A-Za-z0-9+/]{20,}"

docs.title: Compute new fields
docs.text: Command Does Example eval Create/modify a field with functions | eval MB=round(bytes/1024/1024,2), user=lower(user) eval + if / case Conditional values | eval type=case(Logon_Type10,"RDP", Logon_Type3,"Network", true(),"Other") eval + coalesce First non-null of several fields | eval user=coalesce(Account_Name, user, User) eval + string funcs len, upper, lower, substr, replace, split, mvindex, trim, urldecode | eval domain=mvindex(split(query,"."),-2) eval + time funcs strftime, strptime, relative_time, now() | eval day=strftime(_time,"%Y-%m-%d") eval + match / like / cidrmatch Pattern tests (return true/false) | eval internal=if(cidrmatch("10.0.0.0/8",dest_ip),"yes","no") rex Extract fields with regex named groups | rex field=CommandLine "-enc\s+(?<b64>[A-Za-z0-9+/=]+)" — see rex & fields rex mode=sed Find/replace in a field | rex field=user mode=sed "s/^CORP\\//" spath Pull fields out of JSON/XML | spath input=_raw path=Event.EventData.Data{@Name} lookup Enrich from a CSV/KV lookup | lookup asset_inventory ip as dest_ip OUTPUT owner, criticality iplocation GeoIP | iplocation src_ip fillnull Replace nulls | fillnull value="-" user, src_ip makemv / mvexpand Split a string into multivalue / one row per value | makemv delim="," answers | mvexpand answers convert Convert formats (epoch → readable etc.) | convert ctime(first) ctime(last)

docs.title: Group, count, summarise (the heart of SPL)
docs.text: Command Does Example stats Aggregate over all rows, optionally by group | stats count, dc(dest) as hosts, values(CommandLine) as cmds by user stats functions count, dc (distinct count), sum, avg, min, max, stdev, median, perc95, values (unique list), list (all, in order), first, last, earliest, latest, range | stats earliest(_time) as first, latest(_time) as last, count by host eventstats Same as stats but keeps every row and appends the result | eventstats avg(count) as avg_count by user streamstats Running/rolling calculations in row order | streamstats current=f last(_time) as prev by src, dest | eval gap=_time-prev timechart Aggregate into time buckets (for charts) | timechart span=1h count by EventCode bin (a.k.a. bucket) Round _time (or numbers) into buckets, then stats | bin _time span=10m | stats count by _time, src_ip chart 2-D pivot table | chart count over user by Logon_Type top / rare Most / least common values with count and percent | top limit=20 Image · | rare limit=20 parent_process tstats Fast stats on indexed fields / data models / accelerated data | tstats count where index=botsv3 sourcetype=WinEventLog by _time span=1h, host transaction Group events into sessions by a field + time gap (slow; prefer stats) | transaction Logon_ID maxspan=8h addtotals / addcoltotals Row/column totals

docs.title: Combine searches
docs.text: Command Does Example append Glue results of a subsearch below | append [search index=zeek sourcetype=zeek:conn …] join SQL-style join on a field (limits: 50k rows, slow) | join type=left uid [search index=zeek sourcetype=zeek:http | fields uid, host, uri] [ subsearch ] in the search bar Use one search's result as the filter for another (10k-row limit) index=botsv3 sourcetype=WinEventLog [search index=botsv3 EventCode=1102 | fields host] stats … by with OR The fast alternative to join: search both sourcetypes at once and stats values() by the shared key (sourcetype=zeek:conn OR sourcetype=zeek:http) | stats values(host) as http_host, sum(orig_bytes) as up by uid inputlookup / outputlookup Read / write a lookup table | inputlookup known_admins.csv · | outputlookup baseline_ua.csv map Run a search per result row (slow, niche)

docs.title: Presentation & housekeeping
docs.text: Command Does fieldsummary Per-field stats (count, distinct, top values) — first look at unknown data metadata type=sourcetypes index=botsv3 List sourcetypes with first/last time and counts (instant) | tstats count where index=botsv3 by sourcetype Same, faster and more flexible eventcount summarize=false index=* Event count per index (allowed use of * — metadata only) rest /services/data/indexes List indexes typeof, isnull, isnotnull Type/null checks inside eval/where format Turn subsearch rows into an (a OR b OR c) expression collect Write results into a summary index

docs.title: Patterns you will reuse
docs.text:
Baseline vs. today (find new things)

index=botsv3 sourcetype=WinEventLog EventCode=4688 earliest=-30d@d latest=@d
| stats count by New_Process_Name
| eval period="baseline"
| append [ search index=botsv3 sourcetype=WinEventLog EventCode=4688 earliest=@d
           | stats count by New_Process_Name | eval period="today" ]
| stats values(period) as seen by New_Process_Name
| where mvcount(seen)=1 AND seen="today"

The first search lists every process name seen in the 30 days before today, labelled baseline; append adds today's list labelled today; stats values(period) merges them into one row per process with the set of labels; a process whose only label is today never appeared in the baseline.

Rarity (long tail)

index=botsv3 sourcetype="XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational" EventID=1
| stats dc(host) as hosts, count by Image
| where hosts <= 2
| sort count

dc(host) counts how many distinct machines ran each binary; a program on one or two hosts out of the fleet is worth a look, and the rarest are at the top after sort count (ascending).

Time-bucketed spike

index=botsv3 sourcetype=WinEventLog EventCode=4625
| bin _time span=5m
| stats count, dc(Account_Name) as users by _time, Source_Network_Address
| where count > 20

bin rounds each event's time to the 5-minute bucket it falls in; stats then counts failures and distinct accounts per bucket per source; > 20 failures in 5 minutes from one IP is a brute force (many users = spraying).

First/last seen

index=botsv3 sourcetype=WinEventLog EventCode=4624 Logon_Type=10
| stats earliest(_time) as first, latest(_time) as last, count by Account_Name, Source_Network_Address, host
| convert ctime(first) ctime(last)
| sort first

earliest/latest return the first and last timestamp for each group; convert ctime() makes them readable; sorting by first shows when each RDP source/account pair appeared for the first time — new pairs during the incident window are the interesting rows.

docs.title: Speed & etiquette
docs.text:
• Name the index and sourcetype; narrow the time range; put keywords in the search bar not in where.
  • fields early, table late. stats beats transaction; stats … by key beats join.
  • tstats for counting on indexed fields (host, source, sourcetype, _time, and any field in an accelerated data model) — orders of magnitude faster.
  • Avoid leading wildcards (*admin) and index=*.
  • Save useful searches as Reports; put the pattern with a placeholder in this handbook.

docs.title: Traffic Analysis Dashboards (Zeek + Splunk)
docs.text:
Category: Splunk · Data: Zeek logs (index=zeek), Snort alerts (index=snort) · Last updated: 2026-11-26

In one sentence

Run a PCAP through Zeek into Splunk, and the two dashboards on this page take you from baselining (what normal looks like) to finding malicious activity for most traffic cases — one is a whole-traffic overview, the other is dedicated to SMB and the Windows domain. Written for beginners: installation, the SPL behind every panel, and how to read each result, line by line.

docs.title: What you get
docs.text:
Dashboard File Panels Questions it answers Zeek Traffic Analysis - Overview zeek_traffic_overview.xml 57, sections A–J When does the capture start and end? Which PCs and servers are there? Who talked to whom outside, how much? Suspicious DNS, HTTP, TLS, files, beacons, alerts? Everything one host did, in time order Zeek SMB and Windows Domain Analysis zeek_smb_ad.xml 66, sections A–I Who connected to which share on which host? Which files were opened, deleted, renamed? Which RPC functions were called (pipe, endpoint, operation)? NTLM and Kerberos successes and failures? Lateral movement traces such as PsExec, WMI, scheduled tasks, DCSync? 
flowchart LR
  P[PCAP] --> Z[Zeek] --> S[(Splunk<br/>index=zeek)]
  P --> N[Snort] --> S2[(Splunk<br/>index=snort)]
  S --> D1[Dashboard 1<br/>Traffic overview]
  S --> D2[Dashboard 2<br/>SMB · domain]
  S2 --> D1
  S2 --> D2
  D1 -->|suspicious IP, time| D2
  D1 & D2 -->|uid, time, IP| A[Check packets in Arkime]

docs.title: Pages in this section
docs.text:
• Dashboard basics — Simple XML skeleton, inputs and tokens, $$ and CDATA, base searches, click filters, colours, adding your own panel
  • Dashboard 1 — Traffic overview — every panel in sections A–J: query, line-by-line notes, example result, how to read it
  • Dashboard 2 — SMB and the Windows domain — SMB, DCE/RPC, NTLM and Kerberos basics, pie charts and timelines, lateral movement checklist, RPC risk rules
  • Analysing a PCAP with the dashboards — which panel in which order, where each attack type shows up, event IDs to hand to the host team

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
The dashboards match the Zeek data shape that the home-lab pcapbox VM loads into Splunk. If yours differs, see Adapting to another environment.

Item pcapbox value Used by Zeek index index=zeek Zeek index box at the top (default zeek) Snort index index=snort sourcetype=snort:alert (sid, msg, src_ip, dest_ip, dest_port) Snort index box (default snort) sourcetypes zeek:conn, zeek:dns, zeek:http, zeek:ssl, zeek:x509, zeek:files, zeek:smb_mapping, zeek:smb_files, zeek:dce_rpc, zeek:ntlm, zeek:kerberos, zeek:ldap_search … every panel Field names underscores instead of dots: id_orig_h, id_resp_p, times_created, certificate_subject every panel Time ts = UTC epoch seconds table times, timelines (eval _time=ts) Case pcap_case = PCAP file name Case dropdown files.log tx_hosts, rx_hosts, file_source (= Zeek's source), hashes md5/sha1/sha256 section H, D10

Set Splunk to UTC: your user name (top right) → Preferences → Time zone → (GMT) Coordinated Universal Time. The dashboards build times with strftime(ts, ...), which follows your user time zone. With UTC, Zeek, Arkime and Snort times all match.

docs.title: Step 0 — Check the data shape
docs.text:
Before installing, check three things in Search & Reporting.

① Which Zeek logs exist

| tstats count where index=zeek by sourcetype
| sort - count
  • Leading | — the search starts with a command, not an event search.
  • tstats count — counts from index metadata, very fast, without reading each event.
  • where index=zeek — only the zeek index. Per company guidance we never use index=*.
  • by sourcetype — one row per log type. sort - count — biggest first (- = descending).
sourcetype          count        ← example result
zeek:conn           12840
zeek:dns            5310
zeek:ssl            2207
zeek:http           1122
zeek:files          980
zeek:dce_rpc        411
zeek:smb_mapping    66
zeek:smb_files      58
zeek:ntlm           21
zeek:kerberos       145

Missing logs are fine — only the panels that use them say "No results found". No zeek:smb_*, for example, means the capture had no file sharing.

② Field name shape

index=zeek sourcetype=zeek:conn
| head 1
  • head 1 — the first event only. In the field list on the left, check id_orig_h (underscore) vs id.orig_h (dot). Underscores → use the dashboards as they are.

③ List of cases

index=zeek sourcetype=zeek:conn
| stats count min(ts) as first max(ts) as last by pcap_case
| eval first=strftime(first,"%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"), last=strftime(last,"%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S")
  • stats ... by pcap_case — connections and first/last time per case.
  • strftime(field, "format") — epoch number → readable date. %Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S = 2018-05-11 02:06:52.
pcap_case               count  first                last          ← example result
LAB_PSEXEC_EXAMPLE      1840   2026-01-20 01:00:03  2026-01-20 01:42:55
LAB_WEB_EXAMPLE         729    2026-01-21 09:10:15  2026-01-21 09:42:06

These names appear in the dashboards' Case dropdown.

docs.title: Option A — paste in the web UI (recommended)
docs.text:
1. Download zeek_traffic_overview.xml from Download the XML at the bottom of this page, open it in Notepad and copy all of it (Ctrl+A → Ctrl+C).
  2. In Splunk: Search & Reporting → Dashboards → Create New Dashboard.
  3. Dashboard Title: Zeek Traffic Analysis - Overview. Permissions: Private or Shared in App.
  4. Choose Classic Dashboards (not Dashboard Studio) → Create.
  5. In the empty dashboard, click Source (top of the edit view, </>).
  6. Delete everything in it, paste the XML → Save.
  7. Repeat for zeek_smb_ad.xml (title Zeek SMB and Windows Domain Analysis).

Can't see Source?

Dashboard → Edit (top right) → Source at the top of the edit view. In newer Splunk it may sit in the ... menu next to Edit.

Not Dashboard Studio

These files are Classic (Simple XML). Dashboard Studio uses JSON and will reject them. Why Classic: basics page.

docs.title: Option B — copy files into pcapbox
docs.text:
Put the files into a Splunk app's dashboard folder over SSH. Use scp — not \\10.50.10.60\incoming, which is for PCAPs.

# on the host PC (PowerShell)
scp zeek_traffic_overview.xml zeek_smb_ad.xml analyst@10.50.10.60:/tmp/

# on pcapbox
sudo mkdir -p /opt/splunk/etc/apps/pcapbox/local/data/ui/views
sudo cp /tmp/zeek_traffic_overview.xml /tmp/zeek_smb_ad.xml /opt/splunk/etc/apps/pcapbox/local/data/ui/views/
sudo chown -R splunk:splunk /opt/splunk/etc/apps/pcapbox/local/data
  • scp file user@host:folder — copy a file over SSH.
  • .../apps/pcapbox/local/data/ui/views/ — the app's dashboard folder. The file name (without .xml) becomes the dashboard's URL name.
  • chown splunk:splunk — let the Splunk process read the files.

Then open http://10.50.10.60:8000/en-US/debug/refresh and click Refresh (or sudo /opt/splunk/bin/splunk restart). Both dashboards appear under the pcapbox app's Dashboards.

docs.title: Step 2 — The input boxes
docs.text:
Both dashboards share the same boxes at the top. A box's value becomes a token ($name$) that goes into every panel's search. Tokens are explained on the basics page.

Box Token Default What it does Time range $tp.earliest$, $tp.latest$ All time Search time range. Keep All time for old PCAPs Zeek index $idx$ zeek Change only this if your index has another name Snort index $sidx$ snort Snort alert index Case (pcap_case) $case$ All data (*) Picking a case puts pcap_case="name" into the searches Host IP $ip$ * One IP (10.0.14.129) or a wildcard (10.0.14.*): every panel keeps only connections involving it Timeline bucket $span$ 1m Width of one bar in the time charts. 1m for a 30-minute PCAP, 5m–10m for a few hours

The SMB dashboard has six extra click-filter boxes — RPC named pipe, RPC endpoint, RPC operation, SMB file action, SMB share, NTLM user. Clicking a pie slice fills the box, and the timelines and detail tables then show only that value. Type * to clear.

docs.title: Step 3 — First run checks
docs.text:
1. Pick a Case; keep Time range = All time.
  2. If the numbers A1–A10 at the top of dashboard 1 appear, the data connection works. A1/A2 should match step 0 ③.
  3. A single panel with "No results found" usually means that log is not in this capture (e.g. section F in a capture with no HTTP). For red error icons see Troubleshooting.
  4. The magnifier (Open in Search) at the bottom right of a panel opens its search in the Search app — a good way to experiment.

docs.title: Adapting to another environment (team kit)
docs.text: Difference How to check Fix Different index name Settings → Indexes Type it into the Zeek index box Different sourcetypes (bro:conn:json, corelight_conn …) Step 0 ① In the Source editor find and replace sourcetype=zeek: with the local names Dotted fields (id.orig_h) Step 0 ② Find and replace id_orig_h → id.orig_h etc. Inside eval/where, wrap them in single quotes: 'id.orig_h' files.log uses source, not file_source sourcetype=zeek:files | head 1 Replace file_source with the local field _time is index time compare _time with ts The dashboards already use ts; just keep All time No pcap_case — The Case dropdown shows only All data; that's fine

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix Every panel says "Search is waiting for input…" A token is empty (a box was cleared) Put * in the empty box Every panel says "No results found" Narrow time range / wrong index All time, check Zeek index One panel says "No results found" That log isn't in the capture, or nothing matched Often normal; compare with B1 Error in 'eval' command Field names differ (dot/underscore) Adapting Times show 2026 The table used _time These dashboards use ts; for your own panels use strftime(ts, ...) Slow Lots of data Pick one case, narrow with Host IP XML error on save Paste was cut short Copy the whole file again

docs.title: Download the XML
docs.text:
• Download zeek_traffic_overview.xml — dashboard 1
  • Download zeek_smb_ad.xml — dashboard 2

To copy and paste: download the file, open it in Notepad (or VS Code) and press Ctrl+A → Ctrl+C. Or open it on GitHub and click Copy raw file at the top right — zeek_traffic_overview.xml · zeek_smb_ad.xml.

For a closed network, carry the two downloaded .xml files across and install them with Option A or Option B.

Next: Dashboard basics — once you know how the XML is built you can change and add panels yourself.

docs.title: Analysing a PCAP with the Dashboards
Analysing a PCAP with the Dashboards
docs.text:
Category: Splunk · Uses: Dashboard 1 (traffic overview), Dashboard 2 (SMB · domain), Arkime · Last updated: 2026-11-26

What this page does

A checklist of which panels to read, in which order, and what to note when a new PCAP arrives. Then a table of where each attack type shows up, one real lab scene (Night Dew) read through the dashboards, and the Windows event IDs to hand to the host team.

docs.title: The big picture
docs.text:
flowchart TD
  A[0. Load the PCAP<br/>check the case name] --> B[Part 1 Baselining<br/>Dashboard 1 A–C]
  B --> C[Part 2 Find what doesn't fit<br/>Dashboard 1 D–I]
  B --> D[Part 3 Domain · SMB<br/>Dashboard 2]
  C --> E[Part 4 One host in depth<br/>Dashboard 1 J, Dashboard 2 H4]
  D --> E
  E --> F[Confirm content in Arkime<br/>pages, POST bodies, files]
  F --> G[Conclusions and open questions<br/>for the host team]

Principle: don't hunt for bad things first. Draw normal first (baselining), then look for what doesn't fit it. In your notes, keep what you saw ([data]) apart from what you suspect ([guess]).

docs.title: Part 1 — Baselining (Dashboard 1, A–C)
docs.text:
• Pick the Case, Time range = All time, Host IP = *.
  • A1–A3 note capture start, end and length → set Timeline bucket to match (30 min → 1m, hours → 5m–10m).
  • A4–A8 connections, internal hosts, external destinations, bytes sent and received. Sent > received → note possible exfiltration.
  • B1 which logs exist and which don't. With kerberos/smb_*/dce_rpc, do Part 3. Without http, section F is empty.
  • B2–B4 services, connection states, protocols. Many (not recognised) or S0/REJ?
  • B6 note unfamiliar ports.
  • C1 internal hosts — who is the main character (most connections)?
  • C2 per IP: name, domain, users, MAC, OS.
  • C3 server roles — DC, DNS, DHCP, gateway, file/web/mail. Note any PC that looks like a server.
  • C4 with DHCP, check MAC vendors and names.

After baselining you should be able to write something like:

2026-01-20 01:00–01:43 UTC (43 min), 3 internal hosts (DC01 10.0.0.10, PC-01 10.0.0.101 alice, PC-02 10.0.0.102 bob), domain LAB. 41 external destinations, mostly HTTPS. The DC handles DNS, Kerberos, LDAP and SMB; gateway 10.0.0.1 does DHCP. PC-02 also appears as an SMB server (to check).

docs.title: Part 2 — Find what doesn't fit (Dashboard 1, D–I)
docs.text:
• D1 external destinations — no name, odd port, small repeated bytes.
  • D2 rare places visited once (in time order) — download server candidates.
  • D3 connections on ports other than 80/443/53/123, and their states.
  • D4 repeated connections with low jitter (< 0.2) — beacon candidates; check the names (D1, G2) for normal services.
  • D5 pairs that sent a lot — exfiltration candidates.
  • E5 read DNS names in first-asked order — the plot of the story.
  • E4, E6 rare names, long odd names, NXDOMAIN, TXT.
  • F5 rare User-Agents — a non-browser program?
  • F6 repeated POSTs — C2 check-ins?
  • F7 downloaded programs and documents, disguised EXEs (red).
  • F9 Referer chain — compromised site → redirect → payload.
  • G3, G4 TLS without SNI, TLS off 443, self-signed certificates.
  • H3, H4 file hashes and Windows program (PE) details.
  • I1–I4 Snort, Zeek weird, notice — line their times up with other panels.

docs.title: Part 3 — Windows domain and SMB (Dashboard 2)
docs.text:
• A numbers — any red cells (HIGH RPC, admin shares, NTLM failures, Kerberos errors)?
  • B1 SMB pairs — any PC → PC? Pairs with large sent bytes?
  • B4 445 scanning — one source failing against many IPs.
  • C1–C3 pipe, endpoint and operation pies. One slice filling the pie → C8 bursts.
  • C5 risky RPC calls (HIGH first).
  • D6, D7 programs on admin shares, PsExec/C2 pipe names.
  • D8, D9 mass deletes/renames (ransomware), sensitive file names.
  • E6, E8 admin shares, SMB to non-DC hosts.
  • F6, F7 guessing / spraying, accounts used in many places.
  • G3, G4 what the Kerberos errors mean, RC4 tickets (Kerberoasting).
  • H1 lateral movement checklist — a verdict per pair.
  • H4 domain story timeline — read row by row around the suspicious time.

docs.title: Part 4 — One host in depth, and Arkime
docs.text:
1. Type the suspicious IP into Host IP; every panel in both dashboards narrows to it.
  2. Read everything the host did in dashboard 1 J1; click the row at the suspicious time to open J2 (all records of that uid).
  3. What Splunk can't show — page content, POST bodies, file content — open in Arkime by time, IP and port: ip == 10.0.0.101 && port == 445. In pcapbox add tags == <case>.
  4. Write up what you found in time order (the H4 table is a ready-made start).

docs.title: Attack type → where it shows
docs.text: Attack / behaviour Dashboard 1 Dashboard 2 One-line clue Compromised site → exploit kit F9, F7, E5 — Flash/EXE/odd page at the end of a Referer chain Malicious document / script download F7, H3, F5 — No Referer + new User-Agent, disguised EXE HTTP C2 beacon D4, F6, F5 — Steady POSTs to one address, odd UA HTTPS C2 D4, G3, G4 — No SNI, non-443 port, self-signed certificate Dead / blocked C2 D3, B3 — Only S0/REJ at a steady interval DNS tunnel / DGA E6, E2 — Long random names, TXT, many NXDOMAIN Data exfiltration A7, D5 B3 Sent ≫ received SMB scan / worm (EternalBlue) B6 B4, I1 One source hitting many IPs on 445, mostly failing Password guessing (SMB/NTLM) — F6, A11 Many failures for one user Password guessing (via netlogon) — C8, C3 Hundreds of NetrLogonSamLogonWithFlags Password spraying — F6, G3 Many users, 1–2 failures each, PREAUTH_FAILED User name enumeration — G3 Many KDC_ERR_C_PRINCIPAL_UNKNOWN Kerberoasting — G4, G7 RC4 TGS for many services, SPN searches AD recon (BloodHound) — C5, C8, G7 samr listing, NetrSessionEnum, broad LDAP searches PsExec / smbexec C3 H1, D6, D7, C5 ADMIN$ + EXE + svcctl CreateServiceW + PSEXESVC pipe Remote scheduled task (atexec) — H1, C5 atsvc JobAdd, SchRpcRegisterTask WMI / DCOM remote execution — H1, H2, C5 135 then a high port, IWbemServices ExecMethod Pass-the-hash — F5, F7, H1 Admin account over NTLM PC → PC, many targets DCSync — H3, C5 DRSGetNCChanges from a PC Hive / NTDS theft — D9, H3 ntds.dit, sam/system copies, BaseRegSaveKey Coercion (PetitPotam, PrinterBug) — C5, H3 EfsRpc*, RpcRemoteFindFirstPrinterChangeNotificationEx Ransomware (share encryption) — D8, D4 Hundreds of FILE_RENAME in minutes, one new extension RDP / WinRM movement B6 H2 Internal → internal 3389, 5985

docs.title: Example: reading the Night Dew netlogon burst with the dashboards
docs.text:
Follow the values actually seen in the Night Dew case.

  1. Dashboard 1 C1 — the PC (10.0.14.129) sent about 948 KB, while A7 (sent to external) is far smaller: the rest went inside. B6 shows the DC's (10.0.14.3) high port 49158.
  2. Dashboard 2 A6 — a large DCE/RPC count; the C3 RPC Operations pie is almost one colour.

  3. C8 bursts:

    minute            id_orig_h     id_resp_h   endpoint  operation                    calls
2018-05-11 02:08  10.0.14.129   10.0.14.3   netlogon  NetrLogonSamLogonWithFlags   1522

  4. Click the C3 slice to put NetrLogonSamLogonWithFlags in the operation box. In C9 DCE_RPC Timeline only the 02:08 bucket towers; in C10 the first call is at 02:08:12.836.

  5. The pipe in C1 is 49158 — RPC straight over a high TCP port, not an SMB pipe.
  6. Earlier in H4 domain story: the normal logon cluster at 02:06:52 (ept_map, NetrServerReqChallenge, NetrServerAuthenticate3, DRSCrackNames); then the burst starts 0.6 s after the second malicious POST (02:08:12.248) seen in dashboard 1 F6.
  7. Conclusion — [data] the PC asked the DC to validate NTLM credentials 1,522 times in 32 seconds. [guess] malware trying a built-in password list against accounts. Which accounts and passwords, and whether any worked, is encrypted and not visible in traffic → ask the host team for DC event 4776.

docs.title: Event IDs to hand to the host team
docs.text:
Traffic tells you who, when, from where to where; host logs tell you what ran and whether it worked.

Seen in traffic Host to check Event ID (log) Meaning NTLM/Kerberos logon target PC 4624 (Security) Logon success; type 3 = network (SMB), 10 = RDP Logon failure target PC 4625 (Security) Logon failed; sub-status 0xC000006A wrong password, 0xC0000064 no such user NTLM validation burst DC 4776 (Security) DC validated NTLM credentials; result 0x0 = success Kerberos password error DC 4771 (Security) Kerberos pre-authentication failed RC4 service tickets DC 4769 (Security) Service ticket requested; encryption 0x17 = RC4 Account locked DC 4740 (Security) Account locked out Share mapping (ADMIN$, C$) target PC 5140 (Security) Network share accessed Files / pipes in a share target PC 5145 (Security) Access check on an object in a share (pipe names too) svcctl CreateServiceW target PC 7045 (System), 4697 (Security) New service installed — name and executable path Remote scheduled task target PC 4698 (Security), 106 (TaskScheduler) Scheduled task created Remote WMI execution target PC 4688 (Security) New process with parent WmiPrvSE.exe DCSync DC 4662 (Security) Directory object access with replication rights GUIDs Account created / group change DC 4720, 4728, 4732 User created, added to a global / local group Remote log clearing target PC 1102 (Security), 104 (System) Audit log / System log cleared

Related: Windows Event IDs · Lateral movement / domain playbook · PsExec & SMB

docs.title: Dashboard Basics (Simple XML)
docs.text:
Category: Splunk · For: first-time dashboard builders · Last updated: 2026-11-26

What you learn here

Starting from saving one search as a panel, you learn every Simple XML feature used in the two dashboards — inputs, tokens, $$, CDATA, base searches, click filters, colours, in-panel dropdowns — each with a small example. At the end you add a panel yourself.

docs.title: Why Classic (Simple XML)
docs.text:
Splunk has two dashboard types.

Classic (Simple XML) Dashboard Studio Format XML text JSON text Writing / copying by hand Easy; a panel is a few lines Long and nested Click filters, in-panel inputs, base searches All supported Supported (different syntax) Docs and examples Plenty Fewer

This guide uses Classic because it is easy to paste and easy to read line by line. Later you can move a dashboard with Dashboard Studio's Import → Classic dashboard.

docs.title: What a dashboard is made of
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  I[Input boxes<br/>Case, Host IP] -->|value| T["Tokens<br/>$case$, $ip$"]
  T --> S[SPL search]
  S --> V[Visualisation<br/>pie, table, chart]
  V -->|click| T
  • search — each panel has one SPL search.
  • visualisation — draws the result as a number, pie, bars or a table.
  • input — puts the user's choice into a token.
  • token — a placeholder like $name$. $case$ in a search is replaced with the box value before the search runs.
  • drilldown — what happens on click; usually puts the clicked value into a token.

docs.title: 1. Your first panel — from the Search app
docs.text:
1. Run this in Search & Reporting with time range All time.

    index=zeek sourcetype=zeek:conn
| fillnull value="(not recognised)" service
| stats count by service
| sort - count
    • Line 1: Zeek connection logs only.
    • Line 2 fillnull value="..." service — writes (not recognised) into events whose service is empty (Zeek did not recognise the protocol). Without it the next line stats ... by service drops those events (an empty by-field removes the row).
    • Line 3 stats count by service — count per service.
    • Line 4 sort - count — biggest first.
    service            count     ← example result
dns                5310
ssl                2190
(not recognised)   1874
http               1120
krb_tcp            61
smb,gssapi,krb     18

  2. Visualization tab above the results → chart type Pie Chart.

  3. Save As → Existing Dashboard (or New Dashboard; for new, enter a title and choose Classic Dashboards). Panel Title: Connections by service → Save.
  4. View Dashboard shows a one-pie dashboard.

Now look at what it is underneath.

docs.title: 2. View the Source — the XML skeleton
docs.text:
Dashboard → Edit → Source shows something like:

<dashboard version="1.1" theme="dark">
  <label>My first dashboard</label>
  <row>
    <panel>
      <title>Connections by service</title>
      <chart>
        <search>
          <query>index=zeek sourcetype=zeek:conn | fillnull value="(not recognised)" service | stats count by service | sort - count</query>
          <earliest>0</earliest>
          <latest></latest>
        </search>
        <option name="charting.chart">pie</option>
      </chart>
    </panel>
  </row>
</dashboard>
Line Meaning <dashboard version="1.1" theme="dark"> Start. version="1.1" = current Classic format, theme="dark" = dark background <label> Dashboard title <row> One horizontal row; several panels in it share the width equally <panel> One box <title> Panel title <chart> Visualisation type. Pie, bar and line are all <chart> with the charting.chart option; a single number is <single>, a table <table> <search> / <query> The panel's SPL <earliest>0</earliest><latest></latest> Time range. 0 = from 1970 = All time; empty latest = now <option name=".."> Display settings

Two XML rules: every <x> needs its </x>, and <, >, & cannot appear as plain text — the fix is in section 4.

docs.title: 3. Inputs and tokens
docs.text:
For inputs, change the outer <dashboard> to <form> and put the inputs inside <fieldset>.

<form version="1.1" theme="dark">
  <label>Token practice</label>
  <fieldset submitButton="false" autoRun="true">
    <input type="time" token="tp" searchWhenChanged="true">
      <label>Time range</label>
      <default>
        <earliest>0</earliest>
        <latest></latest>
      </default>
    </input>
    <input type="text" token="idx" searchWhenChanged="true">
      <label>Zeek index</label>
      <default>zeek</default>
    </input>
    <input type="text" token="ip" searchWhenChanged="true">
      <label>Host IP</label>
      <default>*</default>
    </input>
  </fieldset>
  <row>
    <panel>
      <title>Connections by service</title>
      <chart>
        <search>
          <query>index=$idx$ sourcetype=zeek:conn (id_orig_h="$ip$" OR id_resp_h="$ip$") | fillnull value="(not recognised)" service | stats count by service</query>
          <earliest>$tp.earliest$</earliest>
          <latest>$tp.latest$</latest>
        </search>
        <option name="charting.chart">pie</option>
      </chart>
    </panel>
  </row>
</form>
  • <fieldset submitButton="false" autoRun="true"> — the input group. No Submit button (search as soon as a value changes); run on first load.
  • <input type="time" token="tp"> — time picker; the range becomes $tp.earliest$ and $tp.latest$.
  • <input type="text" token="idx"> — text box; its text becomes $idx$. <default>zeek</default> = initial value.
  • searchWhenChanged="true" — rerun searches using this token when it changes.
  • index=$idx$ becomes index=zeek before the search runs.
  • (id_orig_h="$ip$" OR id_resp_h="$ip$") — with *, id_orig_h="*" matches any value, i.e. no filter. With 10.0.14.129, the IP matches as source or destination.

Never leave a box empty

An empty token freezes every panel that uses it at "Search is waiting for input…". To see everything, type *, don't clear it.

docs.title: 4. A literal $, and CDATA
docs.text:
① $$ — Simple XML reads every $...$ as a token. SMB is full of names with $ (IPC$, ADMIN$, C$), and computer accounts end with $ (PC-01$). Inside a dashboard, write a literal $ as $$.

Goal Search app Dashboard XML ADMIN$ share share="ADMIN$" share="ADMIN$$" Names ending in $ like(share,"%$") like(share,"%$$") Regex end anchor match(f,"\.exe$") match(f,"\.exe$$")

When you copy a dashboard query into the Search app, change $$ back to $. Queries printed in this guide already use a single $.

② CDATA — SPL often has < and > (e.g. where count>=50), which XML reads as tags. Text between <![CDATA[ and ]]> is treated as plain text.

<query><![CDATA[
index=$idx$ sourcetype=zeek:dce_rpc
| stats count by operation
| where count>=50
]]></query>
  • Tokens are still replaced inside CDATA ($idx$ → zeek); the $$ rule still applies.
  • Every query in both dashboards sits in CDATA, so they can span lines and use <, > freely.

docs.title: 5. Dropdowns — static and search-filled
docs.text:
The Case dropdown fills itself from the case names in Splunk.

<input type="dropdown" token="case" searchWhenChanged="true">
  <label>Case (pcap_case)</label>
  <choice value="*">All data</choice>
  <default>*</default>
  <fieldForLabel>pcap_case</fieldForLabel>
  <fieldForValue>filter</fieldForValue>
  <search>
    <query><![CDATA[
index=$idx$ sourcetype=zeek:conn
| stats count by pcap_case
| eval filter="pcap_case=\"".pcap_case."\""
| sort pcap_case
]]></query>
    <earliest>0</earliest>
    <latest>now</latest>
  </search>
</input>
  • <choice value="*">All data</choice> — a static choice that is always there; picking it sets $case$ = *.
  • <search> — fills the other choices: one result row = one choice.
  • <fieldForLabel>pcap_case</fieldForLabel> — the text shown comes from pcap_case.
  • <fieldForValue>filter</fieldForValue> — the value put into the token comes from filter.
  • eval filter="pcap_case=\"".pcap_case."\"" — builds the whole condition, e.g. pcap_case="20180511_NIGHT_DEW". . joins strings; \" is a literal double quote.

Why put the whole pcap_case="..." into the token? If the search said pcap_case="$case$" with All = *, then pcap_case="*" would match only events that have a pcap_case field — nothing at all in a team environment without that field. Writing just $case$ in the search, with a bare * for All (= every event) and pcap_case="name" for a case, works in both environments.

docs.title: 6. Visualisation types and common options
docs.text:
Visualisation Tag Result shape Common options Single number <single> 1 row × 1 column (stats count as v) underLabel, colorMode (none/block), rangeValues, rangeColors Pie <chart> + charting.chart=pie 2 columns: name, number charting.chart.showPercent, charting.chart.sliceCollapsingThreshold (when small slices fold into "other") Column <chart> + column timechart output, or name + numbers charting.chart.stackMode=stacked, charting.legend.placement=bottom Bar <chart> + bar name + numbers charting.legend.placement Table <table> anything count (rows per page), wrap, drilldown (none/row/cell)

Any visualisation takes <option name="height">300</option>.

docs.title: 7. Time charts — eval _time=ts + timechart
docs.text:
index=zeek sourcetype=zeek:dce_rpc
| eval _time=ts
| timechart span=1m limit=12 useother=t count by endpoint
  • eval _time=ts — overwrite Splunk's time field _time with Zeek's own timestamp ts. Some environments stamp _time with the load date (2026), so charts always use ts. Where _time is already right (pcapbox), nothing changes.
  • timechart — cuts _time into equal buckets and calculates per bucket.
  • span=1m — one bucket = 1 minute. In the dashboards: span=$span$ (Timeline bucket box).
  • count by endpoint — count per bucket per endpoint; each value becomes one colour.
  • limit=12 useother=t — draw the top 12 separately, fold the rest into OTHER.
_time               epmapper  lsarpc  netlogon  drsuapi    ← Night Dew lab values (as a table)
2018-05-11 02:06    4         0       4         8
2018-05-11 02:07    0         0       0         0
2018-05-11 02:08    0         1       1522      0

Drawn as column + stacked, each bucket is a stacked bar. A sudden tall bar is the time to check in the detail table.

docs.title: 8. Base searches and post-processing
docs.text:
If three pies (pipe, endpoint, operation) all count dce_rpc, there is no need to read the data three times. Run one base search, and each panel adds a post-process to its result.

<search id="b_dce">
  <query><![CDATA[
index=$idx$ sourcetype=zeek:dce_rpc $case$
| eval pipe=lower(mvindex(split(named_pipe,"\\"),-1))
| fillnull value="-" pipe endpoint operation
| stats count by id_orig_h id_resp_h pipe endpoint operation
]]></query>
  <earliest>$tp.earliest$</earliest>
  <latest>$tp.latest$</latest>
</search>
...
<chart>
  <search base="b_dce">
    <query><![CDATA[
| stats sum(count) as calls by endpoint
]]></query>
  </search>
  <option name="charting.chart">pie</option>
</chart>
  • <search id="b_dce"> — a named search placed directly inside <form> (before the first <row>). It draws nothing by itself.
  • <search base="b_dce"> — "take b_dce's result and continue". The query starts with |; the time range comes from the base.
  • Post-process stats sum(count) as calls by endpoint — the base already counted (count), so only add (sum). Using count again would count rows and give wrong numbers.

Base search rules

  1. End the base with an aggregating command such as stats. Passing raw events on is capped at 500,000 events and the rest is dropped silently.
  2. Before stats ... by, fillnull the by-fields, or rows with empty values vanish.
  3. Fields the post-process needs must be in the base's by clause or results.

docs.title: 9. Click filters (drilldown)
docs.text:
① Pie slice → input box

<input type="text" token="ep" searchWhenChanged="true">
  <label>RPC endpoint</label>
  <default>*</default>
</input>
...
<chart>
  <search base="b_dce"><query>| stats sum(count) as calls by endpoint</query></search>
  <option name="charting.chart">pie</option>
  <drilldown>
    <set token="form.ep">$click.value$</set>
  </drilldown>
</chart>
...
<query><![CDATA[
index=$idx$ sourcetype=zeek:dce_rpc
| search endpoint="$ep$"
| table ts endpoint operation
]]></query>
  • $click.value$ — the name of the clicked slice (e.g. netlogon).
  • <set token="form.ep"> — with form., the visible input box changes too, so you can see which filter is on and clear it with *.
  • Other panels' search endpoint="$ep$" become endpoint="netlogon".

Clicking the other slice

other groups small slices and is not a real value, so clicking it empties the results. Type * in the box to clear.

② Table row → token, reveal a hidden panel

<table>
  <search>...| table time id_orig_h id_resp_h operation uid</search>
  <option name="drilldown">row</option>
  <drilldown>
    <set token="sel_uid">$row.uid$</set>
  </drilldown>
</table>
...
<panel depends="$sel_uid$">
  <title>Every Zeek log for the clicked connection (uid)</title>
  ...
</panel>
  • $row.uid$ — the clicked row's uid column, so the table must include uid.
  • <panel depends="$sel_uid$"> — hidden until sel_uid exists; it appears after a click.
  • uid is Zeek's per-connection tag. conn, smb_files, dce_rpc and ntlm records of one connection share it, so one uid collects the whole connection.

docs.title: 10. In-panel "Split by" dropdowns
docs.text:
Inputs can also sit inside a panel, as choices for that panel only.

<panel>
  <title>DCE_RPC Timeline</title>
  <input type="dropdown" token="dce_split" searchWhenChanged="true">
    <label>Split by</label>
    <choice value="endpoint">Endpoint</choice>
    <choice value="operation">Operation</choice>
    <choice value="id_orig_h">Client</choice>
    <default>endpoint</default>
  </input>
  <chart>
    <search>
      <query>index=$idx$ sourcetype=zeek:dce_rpc | eval _time=ts | timechart span=$span$ count by $dce_split$</query>
      ...
  • The token holds a field name and changes by $dce_split$, so the same data can be viewed per service or per PC.
  • Inside a panel, <input> must come before the visualisation tag.

docs.title: 11. Colours
docs.text:
Table column — colour per value

<format type="color" field="sev">
  <colorPalette type="map">{"HIGH":#DC4E41,"MEDIUM":#F1813F,"LOW":#F8BE34,"INFO":#708794}</colorPalette>
</format>
  • field="sev" — the column. type="map" — {"value":colour} pairs for exact values.

Single value — green at 0, red at 1 or more

<option name="useColors">1</option>
<option name="colorBy">value</option>
<option name="colorMode">block</option>
<option name="rangeValues">[0]</option>
<option name="rangeColors">["0x53a051","0xdc4e41"]</option>
  • rangeValues [0] — one threshold → two ranges (≤ 0, > 0). rangeColors — one colour each.
  • Both dashboards use this for numbers that should turn red only when something is wrong (HIGH RPC calls, admin shares, NTLM failures, Snort alerts).

Pie / bars — colour per series name

<option name="charting.fieldColors">{"FAILED":0xDC4E41,"success":0x53A051}</option>

docs.title: 12. Exercise — add a panel yourself
docs.text:
Goal: add a table of RDP (3389) connections between internal hosts to dashboard 1.

① Build it in the Search app first

index=zeek sourcetype=zeek:conn pcap_case="<case>" id_resp_p=3389
| stats count as conns sum(orig_bytes) as sent sum(resp_bytes) as received min(ts) as first max(ts) as last values(conn_state) as states by id_orig_h id_resp_h
| eval first=strftime(first,"%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"), last=strftime(last,"%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S")
| sort - conns
  • id_resp_p=3389 — destination port RDP only.
  • values(conn_state) as states — all connection states; only S0/REJ means attempts that failed.

② Swap in tokens — zeek → $idx$, pcap_case="<case>" → $case$, and add the IP filter (id_orig_h="$ip$" OR id_resp_h="$ip$").

③ Paste into Source — Dashboard → Edit → Source → after the last </row>, just before </form>.

<row>
  <panel>
    <title>X1. RDP connections (port 3389)</title>
    <table>
      <search>
        <query><![CDATA[
index=$idx$ sourcetype=zeek:conn $case$ (id_orig_h="$ip$" OR id_resp_h="$ip$") id_resp_p=3389
| stats count as conns sum(orig_bytes) as sent sum(resp_bytes) as received min(ts) as first max(ts) as last values(conn_state) as states by id_orig_h id_resp_h
| eval first=strftime(first,"%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"), last=strftime(last,"%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S")
| sort - conns
]]></query>
        <earliest>$tp.earliest$</earliest>
        <latest>$tp.latest$</latest>
      </search>
      <option name="count">10</option>
      <option name="drilldown">none</option>
    </table>
  </panel>
</row>

④ Save → the new panel appears at the bottom. For errors see below.

docs.title: Common errors
docs.text:
Message / symptom Cause Fix XML Syntax Error on save Missing closing tag, < or & outside CDATA Check tag pairs at the line number; wrap the query in CDATA "Search is waiting for input…" A token used in the search has no value Fill boxes with *; check token spelling $ disappears from a panel title Titles are token-parsed too Use $$ in titles as well Panel says "No results" but Search finds data Dashboard time range or token values differ Use the panel's magnifier (Open in Search) to see the query that actually ran Pie numbers too small Post-process counted again Use sum(count) Numbers too low Events with empty stats by fields dropped fillnull value="-" fields... Clicking does nothing charting.drilldown is none, or no <drilldown> <option name="charting.drilldown">all</option> plus <drilldown>

Next: Dashboard 1 — Traffic overview

docs.title: Dashboard 1 — Traffic Overview and Baselining
docs.text:
Category: Splunk · Dashboard: zeek_traffic_overview.xml (57 panels) · Last updated: 2026-11-26

What this dashboard does

Sections A–C are baselining — capture window, log types, internal PCs and servers, names, users and OS first. Sections D–I look for what does not fit — external traffic, beacons, DNS, HTTP, TLS certificates, files, alerts. Section J lists everything one host did in time order; click a row to open every Zeek record of that connection (uid).

How to read this page

Each panel follows purpose → query → line-by-line notes → example result → how to read it. Queries are written to paste straight into the Search app with index=zeek and pcap_case="<case>" (replace <case>). Inside the dashboard those parts are tokens ($idx$, $case$, the Host IP filter). Example results are made-up illustration values (lab range 10.0.0.0/24, external addresses from the documentation ranges 198.51.100.x and 203.0.113.x).

docs.title: Section map
docs.text: Section Question Panels A Capture at a glance When, and how big? 10 numbers B What is in it Which logs, services, ports, connection states? log types, 3 pies, time chart, port table C Who is who Internal PCs, names, users, MACs, OS, server roles 4 tables D External traffic With whom, how much, odd ports, beacons, exfiltration 5 tables, bar, time chart E DNS Names looked up, rare names, odd names 2 pies, 4 tables F HTTP Hosts, User-Agents, POSTs, downloaded programs, redirect chain 3 pies, 6 tables G TLS SNI, versions, odd ports, self-signed certificates pie, 3 tables H Files Which files moved, hashes, Windows programs 2 pies, 2 tables I Alerts and oddities Snort, Zeek weird, Zeek notice bar, 3 tables J Activity timeline Everything a host did; every record of one connection 2 tables

docs.title: Dashboard queries vs queries on this page
docs.text: This page In the dashboard Meaning index=zeek index=$idx$ Zeek index box pcap_case="<case>" $case$ Case dropdown (* for All) (none) (id_orig_h="$ip$" OR id_resp_h="$ip$") Host IP box (default * = all) span=1m span=$span$ Timeline bucket box IPC$, "%$" IPC$$, "%$$" A literal $ inside XML (basics 4)

docs.title: Internal vs external
docs.text:
Many panels decide whether an IP is internal or external with one line:

| eval dst_scope=case(match(id_resp_h,"^(22[4-9]|23[0-9]|255)\.|\.255$|^ff"),"multicast/broadcast", match(id_resp_h,"^(10\.|192\.168\.|172\.(1[6-9]|2[0-9]|3[01])\.|127\.|169\.254\.|0\.0\.0\.0$|fe80:|fc|fd)"),"internal", true(),"external")
  • eval new=case(cond1,val1, cond2,val2, true(),default) — the value of the first condition that matches; true() = everything else.
  • match(field,"regex") — true when the field matches.
  • First condition — 224–239.x (multicast), 255.x, ending in .255 (broadcast), ff.. (IPv6 multicast): addresses that go to many hosts.
  • Second — private ranges 10., 192.168., 172.16–31., plus 127. (self), 169.254. (auto address after DHCP failure), 0.0.0.0 (DHCP request), fe80:/fc/fd (internal IPv6).
  • \. — in regex . means "any character", so a real dot is \.. ^ = start, $ = end.
  • The sender side (id_orig_h) gets src_scope the same way.

docs.title: Zeek conn.log fields
docs.text: Field Meaning id_orig_h / id_orig_p IP / port of the side that started the connection (originator) id_resp_h / id_resp_p IP / port of the side that answered (responder) proto tcp, udp, icmp service Protocol Zeek recognised (dns, http, ssl, smb …); empty = not recognised orig_bytes / resp_bytes Payload bytes each side sent duration Seconds conn_state How the connection ended (B3) uid Connection tag that links to other logs

docs.title: A. Capture at a glance
docs.text:
Purpose: know the size and time window before anything else; every conclusion is about this window.

A1–A8 share one base search, b_kpi.

index=zeek sourcetype=zeek:conn pcap_case="<case>"
| eval src_scope=case(match(id_orig_h,"^(22[4-9]|23[0-9]|255)\.|\.255$|^ff"),"multicast/broadcast", match(id_orig_h,"^(10\.|192\.168\.|172\.(1[6-9]|2[0-9]|3[01])\.|127\.|169\.254\.|0\.0\.0\.0$|fe80:|fc|fd)"),"internal", true(),"external")
| eval dst_scope=case(match(id_resp_h,"^(22[4-9]|23[0-9]|255)\.|\.255$|^ff"),"multicast/broadcast", match(id_resp_h,"^(10\.|192\.168\.|172\.(1[6-9]|2[0-9]|3[01])\.|127\.|169\.254\.|0\.0\.0\.0$|fe80:|fc|fd)"),"internal", true(),"external")
| stats min(ts) as first max(ts) as last count as conns dc(eval(if(src_scope="internal",id_orig_h,null()))) as int_hosts dc(eval(if(dst_scope="external",id_resp_h,null()))) as ext_ips sum(eval(if(dst_scope="external",orig_bytes,0))) as ext_out sum(eval(if(dst_scope="external",resp_bytes,0))) as ext_in
  • Line 1: connection logs only; the dashboard adds the Case and Host IP filters.
  • Lines 2–3: internal/external — src_scope for the sender, dst_scope for the receiver.
  • Line 4 stats (one summary row):
    • min(ts) as first, max(ts) as last — earliest and latest time.
    • count as conns — connections.
    • dc(eval(if(src_scope="internal",id_orig_h,null()))) as int_hosts — dc() = distinct count; eval(if(cond,value,null())) yields a value only when the condition holds → internal IPs that started connections.
    • sum(eval(if(dst_scope="external",orig_bytes,0))) as ext_out — bytes sent outside; received bytes are ext_in.
first        last         conns  int_hosts  ext_ips  ext_out   ext_in       ← example result
1768870803   1768873375   1840   3          41       918233    22610004

Each number panel adds a post-process that picks one cell.

Panel Post-process How to read it A1 First event | eval v=strftime(first,"%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S") | fields v Capture start; compare with Snort/Arkime A2 Last event same with last Capture end; nothing later is visible A3 Duration | eval v=round((last-first)/60,1) Minutes. 30 min → Timeline bucket 1m; hours → 5m+ A4 Connections | fields conns Total connections A5 Internal hosts | fields int_hosts Internal IPs that started connections; 1 = a one-PC capture A6 External IPs | fields ext_ips Browsing gives tens to hundreds; beacon-only traffic a handful A7 MB sent | eval v=round(ext_out/1024/1024,2) Sent outside. More than received = possible exfiltration A8 MB received same with ext_in Usually 10× or more what was sent A9 Distinct names | stats count as v on base b_dnsq Names looked up in DNS (E) A10 Snort alerts own search (below) Turns red when not 0
  • fields v — keep only v; a number panel shows the first cell large.
  • round(x,1) — one decimal. /1024/1024 — bytes → MB.
index=snort sourcetype=snort:alert pcap_case="<case>"
| stats count as v
  • sourcetype=snort:alert — where pcapbox puts Snort alerts. The dashboard adds (src_ip="$ip$" OR dest_ip="$ip$").

docs.title: B. What is in the capture
B1. Zeek log types
docs.text:
index=zeek pcap_case="<case>"
| stats count by sourcetype
| sort - count
  • No sourcetype → every log type of the case. IP field names differ per log, so the Host IP filter is not applied.
sourcetype          count      ← example result
zeek:conn           1840
zeek:dns            702
zeek:ssl            311
zeek:http           188
zeek:files          160
zeek:dce_rpc        96
zeek:kerberos       44
zeek:smb_mapping    12
zeek:smb_files      9
zeek:ntlm           3

How to read it — logs present and absent are both clues.

If you see Meaning kerberos, ldap, dce_rpc, smb_*, ntlm Windows domain (AD) PCs; user and computer names are findable → Dashboard 2 dhcp A PC got its IP during the capture; name and MAC directly (C4) pe Zeek saw a Windows program (EXE/DLL) in the traffic (H4) smtp, ftp Mail / FTP — clear text, content visible weird, notice Rule-breaking traffic / Zeek warnings (section I) no http All web is HTTPS; judge by SNI and certificates

docs.title: B2. Connections by service
docs.text:
index=zeek sourcetype=zeek:conn pcap_case="<case>"
| fillnull value="(not recognised)" service
| stats count by service
| sort - count
