docs.title: Zeek files.log & pe.log
docs.text:
Category: Network · Source: Zeek · Last updated: 2026-09-16

In one sentence

Every file Zeek sees moving through any protocol it understands (HTTP, SMTP, FTP, SMB, IRC, TLS certs…) gets a row here with its sniffed type, size, hashes and the connection(s) it rode in on; pe.log adds Windows-executable header details — so this is where "what was downloaded/uploaded/copied over the network, and is it malicious" gets answered without touching a pcap.

docs.title: files.log fields
docs.text: Field Meaning Analyst notes ts When the file was first seen fuid File unique ID Join key: http.log resp_fuids/orig_fuids, smtp.log fuids, ssl.log cert_chain_fuids, smb_files.log fuid, pe.log id uid (Zeek 6+) / conn_uids (older) Connection(s) that carried it → conn.log id.orig_h, id.resp_h (6+) / tx_hosts, rx_hosts (older) Sender / receiver For HTTP download: tx = server, rx = client source Protocol: HTTP, SMTP, FTP_DATA, SMB, SSL (certs), IRC_DATA, KRB depth Nesting depth (e.g. inside MIME) analyzers Analyzers attached: MD5, SHA1, SHA256, PE, EXTRACT, X509 If hashes are blank, the analyzer wasn't loaded mime_type Sniffed type by magic bytes Trust this over the HTTP header / filename filename From Content-Disposition, URI, SMB path, MIME Often blank for HTTP duration Transfer time local_orig Whether the sender is local is_orig File sent by connection originator? T = upload from client, F = download seen_bytes / total_bytes Bytes Zeek saw / declared size Different → truncated (missing_bytes, overflow_bytes) missing_bytes, overflow_bytes, timedout Gaps / oversize / timeout Hash is unreliable if any are non-zero parent_fuid Container file e.g. attachment inside an email md5, sha1, sha256 Hashes (if analyzers on) Search threat intel with these extracted Path of extracted copy (if EXTRACT on) extract_files/HTTP-FdvK1A3z4tPEujBU9c.exe extracted_cutoff, extracted_size Truncation info for extraction

docs.title: pe.log fields (Windows PE files only)
docs.text: Field Meaning Analyst notes id = fuid machine I386, AMD64, ARM64 compile_ts PE header timestamp Future / very old / matches other samples → forged or family marker os, subsystem Windows XP+, WINDOWS_GUI / WINDOWS_CUI (console) A "GUI" app that is actually a console loader; NATIVE = driver is_exe, is_64bit is_exe=F = DLL/driver uses_aslr, uses_dep, uses_code_integrity, uses_seh Security mitigations Malware & old tools often lack ASLR/DEP has_import_table, has_export_table, has_cert_table, has_debug_data Presence of tables No import table → packed; has_cert_table=T → signed (check the sig on host) section_names Section names .text .rdata .data .rsrc .reloc normal; UPX0, .vmp0, .themida, random names → packed

docs.title: Enabling hashes and extraction
docs.text:
By default only MD5 runs (sometimes nothing, depending on distro). In local.zeek or on the command line:

@load policy/frameworks/files/hash-all-files      # md5 + sha1 + sha256 for every file
@load policy/frameworks/files/extract-all-files   # write every file to extract_files/ (disk!)
# Or extract only executables:
event file_sniff(f: fa_file, meta: fa_metadata) {
    if ( meta?$mime_type && meta$mime_type == "application/x-dosexec" )
        Files::add_analyzer(f, Files::ANALYZER_EXTRACT);
}
redef FileExtract::prefix = "/data/zeek/extract/";
redef FileExtract::default_limit = 50000000;      # 50 MB cap per file

zeek -C -r capture.pcap local policy/frameworks/files/hash-all-files policy/frameworks/files/extract-all-files
ls extract_files/            # HTTP-F..., SMTP-F..., SMB-F...  (named by source + fuid)

docs.title: Quick queries
docs.text:
zeek-cut / shellSplunk 
# All executables, scripts, archives and Office docs that crossed the wire
zeek-cut -d ts fuid source id.orig_h id.resp_h mime_type filename total_bytes sha256 < files.log \
  | grep -E 'x-dosexec|x-msdownload|x-executable|zip|x-rar|x-7z|msword|officedocument|vnd.ms-|x-shellscript|hta|javascript|x-powershell'

# Uploads (is_orig = T) leaving the network — exfil / web-shell uploads
zeek-cut -d ts source id.orig_h id.resp_h mime_type total_bytes filename < files.log | awk -F'\t' '$0 ~ /\tT\t/'   # (add is_orig to the cut)

# SMB file copies between internal hosts (lateral movement, staging)
zeek-cut -d ts id.orig_h id.resp_h filename mime_type total_bytes < files.log | awk -F'\t' '$1 ~ /SMB/ || 1' | grep -F 'SMB'
# better: smb_files.log
zeek-cut -d ts id.orig_h id.resp_h action path name size < smb_files.log | grep -E 'WRITE|OPEN' | grep -iE '\.(exe|dll|ps1|bat|vbs|sys)\b'

# Hash list for VT / intel lookup
zeek-cut sha256 mime_type < files.log | awk '$2 ~ /dosexec|zip|msword|officedocument/ && $1!="-" {print $1}' | sort -u > hashes.txt

# PE: unusual sections / no ASLR / console apps downloaded via HTTP
zeek-cut id machine compile_ts subsystem uses_aslr has_import_table section_names < pe.log \
  | awk -F'\t' '$5=="F" || $6=="F" || $7 !~ /\.text/'

# From a file back to the URL that served it
grep -F 'FdvK1A3z4tPEujBU9c' http.log | zeek-cut -d ts id.orig_h host uri user_agent

index=zeek sourcetype=zeek:files mime_type IN ("application/x-dosexec","application/x-msdownload","application/zip","application/x-rar","application/msword","application/vnd.openxmlformats-officedocument.wordprocessingml.document")
| stats values(filename) as names values(source) as proto dc(id.resp_h) as receivers count by sha256, mime_type, total_bytes
| sort - count

Groups every risky file type by its hash, listing the filenames it travelled under (values(filename)) and how many machines received it (dc(id.resp_h)). One hash arriving at many hosts under different names is a worm or a tool being pushed around during lateral movement.

index=zeek sourcetype=zeek:files is_orig=true local_orig=true
| eval MB=round(total_bytes/1024/1024,2)
| stats sum(MB) as total_MB count by id.orig_h, id.resp_h, source
| where total_MB > 50

is_orig=true means the client sent the file (an upload); local_orig=true means that client is inside your network. Summing uploaded megabytes per internal→external pair and keeping those over 50 MB is a simple exfiltration hunt.

docs.title: Analysis tips
docs.text:
Hash → intel → host, in that order

Pull sha256 for every executable/archive/Office file in the window, check them against VirusTotal/MISP/your EDR, then take each bad hash to Amcache (same SHA-1 — use sha1 from files.log) and Prefetch on the receiving host to prove it landed and ran. That is a complete download→execution chain without opening a pcap.

  • Sniffed MIME is the truth; the filename and HTTP Content-Type are attacker-controlled. mime_type=application/x-dosexec with filename=invoice.pdf is the finding.
  • Partial files: if missing_bytes > 0 or timedout = T, the hash will not match VT — the sensor dropped packets. Say so instead of claiming "unknown file".
  • SMB copies show up twice: files.log (source=SMB, if the file analyzer fires) and smb_files.log (action=SMB::FILE_WRITE/OPEN/CLOSE, path=\\host\C$, name). A WRITE of *.exe to ADMIN$ followed by dce_rpc.log CreateServiceW / StartServiceW = PsExec-style lateral movement (see Adversary section).
  • Email attachments: source=SMTP, parent_fuid set, filename from MIME; join to smtp.log (mailfrom, rcptto, subject, fuids) to get sender → recipient → attachment → hash in one line.
  • Certificates are files too (source=SSL, mime_type=application/x-x509-user-cert) — that's why x509.log joins on fuid. Filter them out when counting "real" files.
  • pe.log fast red flags: compile_ts within hours of ts (freshly built), section names not in the standard set, has_import_table=F, uses_aslr=F on a 64-bit binary, subsystem=WINDOWS_CUI for something that claimed to be an installer.
  • Extraction hygiene: extracted malware is live malware — extract to an isolated analysis box, and remember extract_files/ can fill a disk fast on a busy sensor; prefer the MIME-filtered extraction script above in production.
  • Missing everything? Check analyzers — if it only says X509 or is blank, the hash policies weren't loaded when the logs were generated. Re-run Zeek on the pcap with them.

docs.title: Correlation
docs.text: Question Then look at Where did it come from / go to? uid → conn.log; fuid → http.log (host, uri), smtp.log, smb_files.log, ftp.log Did it execute on the receiving host? Prefetch, Amcache (SHA-1), 4688/Sysmon 1; Zone.Identifier in $MFT carries the download URL Is it known-bad? VirusTotal, MalwareBazaar, MISP; Suricata file rules (fileinfo events in eve.json share md5/sha256) Did it spread? stats … by sha256 across id.resp_h; SMB writes to ADMIN$/C$ in smb_files.log What does it do? Static/dynamic analysis of extract_files/<fuid>; pe.log for a first look

docs.title: Zeek http.log
docs.text:
Category: Network · Source: Zeek · Last updated: 2026-09-16

In one sentence

One row per HTTP request/response pair in cleartext HTTP (and TLS-decrypted traffic if you have a decrypting proxy feeding Zeek) — method, host, URI, user agent, status, sizes, and the fuids of any files that moved, which makes it the fastest place to spot payload downloads, web-shell traffic and HTTP-based C2.

docs.title: Fields
docs.text: Field Meaning Analyst notes ts, uid, id.* As in conn.log One TCP uid can carry many requests (keep-alive) trans_depth Request number within the connection (1, 2, 3…) Pipelining / keep-alive count method GET, POST, HEAD, PUT, OPTIONS, PROPFIND, CONNECT… PUT/PROPFIND = WebDAV (payload staging), CONNECT = proxy tunnelling, weird casing/methods = tooling host Host: header Compare to id.resp_h reverse/dns.log; raw IP as Host = suspicious; mismatch with SNI-style expectations = domain fronting uri Path + query string Short random paths, .php?cmd=, base64 params, /api/v1/ on odd hosts referrer Referer: header Missing on direct malware requests; present on drive-by chains version 1.0 / 1.1 / 2 1.0 from a modern host = scripted client user_agent User-Agent: header Golden field — see below origin Origin: header request_body_len / response_body_len Bytes POST with large body to unknown host = exfil; tiny periodic GETs = beacon status_code / status_msg Response code See HTTP status codes info_code / info_msg 1xx interim tags Zeek's own flags (e.g. URI_SQLI) username / password From Authorization: Basic Cleartext creds proxied Headers that suggest a proxy (X-Forwarded-For, Via) Real client IP behind a proxy orig_fuids / resp_fuids File IDs uploaded / downloaded → files.log orig_filenames / resp_filenames From Content-Disposition / URI orig_mime_types / resp_mime_types Sniffed MIME types (by content, not header) application/x-dosexec behind image/png = disguised EXE client_header_names / server_header_names (optional policy) Header names in order Order & set of headers fingerprints tools (e.g. missing Accept-Language) cookie_vars, uri_vars (optional) Parsed variables

docs.title: Quick queries
docs.text:
zeek-cut / shellSplunk 
# Rare user agents (count of distinct hosts using each UA — malware UAs are used by 1 host)
zeek-cut id.orig_h user_agent < http.log | sort -u | awk -F'\t' '{print $2}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -n | head -30

# Executables downloaded (by sniffed MIME type), with where from
zeek-cut -d ts id.orig_h host uri resp_mime_types resp_fuids < http.log | grep -E 'x-dosexec|x-msdownload|x-executable|x-msdos' 

# POSTs to raw-IP hosts or to hosts never seen before (exfil / C2 check-ins)
zeek-cut -d ts id.orig_h host uri method request_body_len < http.log | awk '$5=="POST"' | grep -E '\t[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\t'

# Beacon-like: same host+uri hit repeatedly by one client with small responses
zeek-cut id.orig_h host uri response_body_len < http.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | awk '$1>50' | head

# Web shell hunting on your own web server (internal resp_h): POSTs to .php/.aspx/.jsp with 200
zeek-cut -d ts id.orig_h uri method status_code < http.log | grep -E '\.(php|aspx?|jsp|jspx)\b' | awk '$4=="POST" && $5==200'

# Directory brute force: one source, hundreds of 404s
zeek-cut id.orig_h status_code < http.log | awk '$2==404' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head

# Cleartext credentials
zeek-cut -d ts id.orig_h host username password < http.log | awk '$4!="-"'

# Everything one connection said (pivot from conn.log uid)
grep -F 'CHhAvVGS1DHFjwGM9' http.log | zeek-cut -d ts method host uri status_code user_agent

index=zeek sourcetype=zeek:http
| stats dc(id.orig_h) as hosts count by user_agent
| where hosts <= 2
| sort count

Counts how many different clients (dc(id.orig_h)) use each user agent. A UA used by one or two machines in the whole company is either a bespoke tool or malware — legitimate browsers are used by hundreds.

index=zeek sourcetype=zeek:http resp_mime_types="application/x-dosexec"
| table _time, id.orig_h, host, uri, response_body_len, resp_fuids
| join type=left resp_fuids [ search index=zeek sourcetype=zeek:files | rename fuid as resp_fuids | fields resp_fuids, sha256, md5 ]

table picks the columns to show. join type=left resp_fuids [ … ] runs a second search on files.log, renames its fuid to match, and glues the hashes onto each download row — so you go from "an EXE was downloaded" to "here is its SHA-256" in one query. (join is slow on big data; for large ranges use stats … by fuid after an OR search instead.)

docs.title: Analysis tips
docs.text:
User-Agent triage in three buckets

  1. Real browsers — long UA, many hosts use it, consistent with the OS fleet.
  2. Legit tools/updaters — Microsoft-CryptoAPI/10.0, Windows-Update-Agent, Microsoft BITS/7.8, Microsoft-Delivery-Optimization, Google Update, Mozilla/4.0 (compatible; MSIE 7.0; Windows NT 6.1; …) used by Office/WinHTTP. Learn these so they stop scaring you.
  3. Everything else — python-requests/2.x, curl/…, Go-http-client/1.1, PowerShell/WindowsPowerShell/5.1, Wget, Java/1.8, empty UA, UA with typos (Mozila), a default Cobalt Strike-style UA that is a real-looking IE string but pinned to MSIE 9.0; Windows NT 6.1 on Win11 hosts. Rare + on a workstation + to an unknown host = pull the thread.
  • Host ≠ IP: Zeek logs host from the header. host = cdn.example.com while id.resp_h belongs to a random VPS, or host blank / raw IP, is worth a look. Malware often hard-codes the IP and omits or fakes Host.
  • Sniffed MIME beats declared: resp_mime_types is what the bytes are. uri ends in .jpg, resp_mime_types is application/x-dosexec → stage-2 payload disguised as an image. Also watch text/plain bodies that are actually PowerShell.
  • Beacon pattern: GET to a fixed or rotating short uri every N seconds/minutes, response_body_len tiny (0–200) when idle, occasionally larger when tasked; POST with request_body_len growing when results are sent back. Cobalt Strike defaults: GET /ca, /dpixel, /__utm.gif, /pixel.gif, /activity, /submit.php?id=… — customised in malleable profiles but often left default in lab/cheap ops.
  • Web-shell traffic on your servers: POST to a single script, 200, referrer -, odd UA, request bodies of varying length, response bodies containing command output sizes. Check files.log for the upload that created the shell (a PUT/POST with orig_fuids).
  • HTTP on non-80 ports still lands here (service=http by DPD). Filter id.resp_p!=80 to find proxies, C2 on 8080/8443-plaintext, and internal tools.
  • HTTP/2 and HTTPS are not here — ssl.log for the handshake, and for content you need decryption at a proxy or EDR-level visibility.
  • Chunked / compressed bodies: response_body_len is the decompressed length Zeek saw; resp_bytes in conn.log is on-the-wire.

docs.title: Correlation
docs.text: Question Then look at What was the downloaded file? resp_fuids → files.log (sha256, mime_type, total_bytes) → pe.log, extract_files/<fuid> Did it get executed? Host: Prefetch, Amcache, Zone.Identifier HostUrl in $MFT will contain this URL Which process made the request? Sysmon 3 matching uid 5-tuple/time; proxy logs with username What did the name resolve from? dns.log query=host just before ts Alerts? Suricata HTTP rules (eve.json http.hostname, http.url), notice.log Full request/response bodies pcap: tshark -Y "http.request && ip.addr==…" -T fields -e http.file_data; Arkime session view

docs.title: Zeek ssl.log & x509.log
docs.text:
Category: Network · Source: Zeek · Last updated: 2026-09-16

In one sentence

You can't read encrypted traffic, but the handshake is cleartext: ssl.log gives you the server name the client asked for (SNI), the TLS version and cipher, a JA3/JA4 fingerprint of the client software, and pointers to the certificate chain in x509.log — which is enough to identify C2 by its self-signed or default certificate, spot tools by their fingerprint, and separate real browsing from scripted traffic.

docs.title: ssl.log fields
docs.text: Field Meaning Analyst notes ts, uid, id.* As in conn.log version TLSv10, TLSv12, TLSv13, SSLv3, DTLSv12 TLS 1.3 encrypts the server cert → x509.log may be empty for it cipher Negotiated cipher suite Ancient/weak suites from a modern host = old tooling curve Key-exchange curve server_name SNI — hostname the client asked for The "what did they connect to" field. Blank SNI = direct-to-IP or old tooling resumed Session resumption used Beacons often resume; many full handshakes to one host is also odd last_alert TLS alert if any handshake_failure, unknown_ca… next_protocol ALPN (h2, http/1.1) Missing ALPN from a "browser" = not a browser established Handshake completed F with many attempts = probing / failing C2 ssl_history (Zeek 5+) Letter history of the handshake Like conn.log history, for TLS cert_chain_fuids / client_cert_chain_fuids File IDs of server / client cert chain → x509.log First element = leaf cert subject / issuer Leaf cert subject / issuer (if seen) Self-signed when equal client_subject / client_issuer Client cert (mutual TLS) Rare — VPNs, some C2 validation_status ok, self signed certificate, unable to get local issuer certificate, certificate has expired… Requires the validate-certs policy ja3 / ja3s (policy) Client / server TLS fingerprint (MD5) Client software fingerprint ja4 / ja4s (policy, Zeek 6+) Newer, sortable fingerprint e.g. t13d1516h2_8daaf6152771_02713d6af862 sni_matches_cert (policy) Does SNI match the cert's names? F = domain fronting, misconfig, or fake cert

docs.title: x509.log fields
docs.text: Field Meaning Analyst notes ts, id / fingerprint File ID (fuid) of the cert; SHA-1/256 fingerprint Join to ssl.log cert_chain_fuids certificate.version 3 usually certificate.serial Serial number Default tool certs have known serials certificate.subject CN=…,O=…,C=… Empty/garbage/CN=localhost → suspicious certificate.issuer Who signed it = subject → self-signed certificate.not_valid_before / not_valid_after Validity window Cert created minutes before first use, or valid for 1 or 100 years → generated by a tool certificate.key_alg, sig_alg, key_type, key_length, exponent, curve Key details 1024-bit RSA / sha1WithRSA = old/lazy san.dns, san.uri, san.email, san.ip Subject Alternative Names Real sites list many; C2 certs list none or one basic_constraints.ca, path_len CA flag Leaf with ca=T is odd host_cert, client_cert (Zeek 5+) Where the cert was seen

docs.title: Quick queries
docs.text:
zeek-cut / shellSplunk 
# Top SNIs from internal hosts — long tail again
zeek-cut server_name < ssl.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -n | head -40

# TLS to raw IP (no SNI) — legit CDNs rarely, C2 often
zeek-cut -d ts id.orig_h id.resp_h id.resp_p server_name version ja3 < ssl.log | awk '$5=="-"'

# Self-signed / invalid certs
zeek-cut -d ts id.orig_h id.resp_h server_name validation_status subject issuer < ssl.log | grep -v -P '\tok\t'

# Rare JA3 hashes (few clients use them) and where they go
zeek-cut id.orig_h ja3 < ssl.log | sort -u | awk '{print $2}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -n | head
zeek-cut -d ts id.orig_h id.resp_h server_name < ssl.log | grep -F '<ja3 hash>'

# Certificates valid for suspiciously short/long periods, or created just before use
zeek-cut -d ts certificate.subject certificate.issuer certificate.not_valid_before certificate.not_valid_after < x509.log \
  | awk -F'\t' '{print}' | sort -u | head

# Certs with no SAN (real sites almost always have one)
zeek-cut fingerprint certificate.subject san.dns < x509.log | awk -F'\t' '$3=="-"' | sort -u

# Pivot: one connection's cert chain
grep -F 'CHhAvVGS1DHFjwGM9' ssl.log | zeek-cut cert_chain_fuids | tr ',' '\n' | while read f; do grep -F "$f" x509.log; done | zeek-cut certificate.subject certificate.issuer certificate.not_valid_before

# Known-bad default certificates
# Cobalt Strike default: CN=Major Cobalt Strike, serial 146473198 ; Metasploit: random CNs but 'O=…' patterns; Sliver: random 'O=' words
grep -iE 'Major Cobalt Strike|146473198' x509.log

index=zeek sourcetype=zeek:ssl
| stats dc(id.orig_h) as clients dc(id.resp_h) as servers values(server_name) as sni count by ja3
| where clients <= 3
| sort - count

Groups all TLS handshakes by the client fingerprint ja3. values(server_name) lists every SNI seen with that fingerprint (deduplicated). A fingerprint used by ≤ 3 machines that talks to one or two servers thousands of times is a beacon; browsers produce fingerprints shared by the whole fleet.

index=zeek sourcetype=zeek:ssl validation_status!="ok" validation_status!="-"
| stats count min(_time) as first max(_time) as last by id.orig_h, id.resp_h, server_name, validation_status, subject
| convert ctime(first) ctime(last)

min(_time)/max(_time) give first and last time each internal host hit each untrusted certificate; convert ctime() turns the epoch numbers into readable dates. Sort by count to see which self-signed cert is being visited on a schedule.

docs.title: Analysis tips
docs.text:
The cheap C2 checklist for one ssl.log row

No SNI or SNI is a raw IP · validation_status ≠ ok · subject = issuer · cert valid from today · no SAN · next_protocol blank · JA3 unique to this host · id.resp_p 443 on a bare VPS IP · connection repeats at a fixed interval. Three or more ticks → treat as C2 until proven otherwise.

  • TLS 1.3 hides the server certificate. For 1.3 you keep SNI, JA3/JA4, ALPN and timing, but x509.log won't have the server cert (unless a decrypting proxy). Encrypted SNI/ECH removes even the name — then you're down to JA4, destination IP reputation and behaviour.
  • JA3 collisions: many tools share fingerprints (Go's TLS stack, .NET, Python requests). Use JA3 to cluster and rare-list, not as a signature by itself; JA4 splits better (t13d… shows version, ALPN, cipher count). Also fingerprint the server (ja3s/ja4s) — a C2 framework's listener answers the same way to every implant.
  • Domain fronting: SNI says a.legit-cdn.com, the inner Host (invisible) says otherwise. Signs: sni_matches_cert = F, SNI on a CDN with unusually regular traffic, resp_h in a CDN range hit by exactly one host on a schedule.
  • Let's Encrypt is not a green flag: modern C2 (Sliver, Mythic, Havoc, redirectors) uses valid LE certs. Then fall back to behaviour: interval, byte sizes, destination age, JA3 rarity.
  • Legit self-signed: printers, IoT, internal admin panels, dev boxes. Filter local_resp = T first, then look at what's left going to the internet.
  • Client certs (client_subject) in outbound traffic from a workstation → VPN, corporate proxy, or a C2 using mutual TLS (rare, but Sliver mTLS mode exists).
  • Version/cipher outliers: a single host negotiating TLSv10 with TLS_RSA_WITH_RC4_128_SHA in 2026 is running something very old — or a deliberately downgraded tool.
  • Certificate reuse across IPs: the same x509 fingerprint appearing on several id.resp_h over time = the actor moves infrastructure but keeps the cert. Great pivot for threat-intel and for retro-hunting.

docs.title: Correlation
docs.text: Question Then look at How much moved, how often? conn.log uid → bytes, duration; interval analysis (Beaconing & C2) What did the name resolve from? dns.log query = server_name moments earlier Which process? Sysmon 3 (with DestinationPort 443) on the host; EDR network telemetry Was the cert used elsewhere? x509.log fingerprint across time; Censys / Shodan / crt.sh for the same fingerprint or serial Alerts? Suricata tls.sni, JA3 rules (ja3.hash), notice.log SSL::Invalid_Server_Cert Payload Not available without decryption — pivot to host artefacts (Prefetch, SRUM, memory)

docs.title: Pentesting
docs.text: Offensive-side notes from studying for HTB CPTS. The reason they live in a DFIR handbook: every technique here leaves something behind, and knowing the attacker's next move makes the detection better. Each page keeps a defender view next to the pentester view.

docs.text:

Adding a page here

Then add the section to this folder's .pages if it should sit before the ... catch-all. Remember: the page must exist in both docs/ and docs-ko/.

docs.title: Recon
docs.text: Active reconnaissance: finding live hosts, open ports and the services behind them. It is the first thing run in an assessment and the first thing a defender can see.

docs.title: Pages
docs.text:
• Nmap

    Scan types, port states, service detection, NSE, output formats, performance tuning.

    Nmap

docs.title: Nmap
docs.text:
MITRE ATT&CK: T1595 Active Scanning · T1046 Network Service Discovery · T1018 Remote System Discovery · Tactic: Reconnaissance / Discovery · Last updated: 2026-10-13

What it does

Nmap sends crafted packets and classifies the replies (or the silence) into port states and service identities. Everything it reports is an inference from how the target answered, so the same output can mean different things depending on a firewall in between.

docs.title: Pages in this section
docs.text:
• Host discovery & port scanning — ARP/ICMP discovery, the six port states, SYN/Connect/ACK/UDP scans, DROP vs REJECT.
  • Service enumeration & NSE — -sV, banners, script categories, -sC, -A, vuln.
  • Output & performance — -oA, XML to HTML, timing templates, rate limits.

docs.title: Cheat sheet
docs.text: Goal Command Live hosts on a subnet, no port scan sudo nmap 10.129.2.0/24 -sn -oA hosts All TCP ports, fast sudo nmap <ip> -p- --min-rate 1000 -oA full_tcp Versions on the open ports only sudo nmap <ip> -p 22,80,443 -sV -oA svc Default scripts + versions sudo nmap <ip> -sC -sV -oA default Top UDP ports sudo nmap <ip> -sU --top-ports 100 -oA udp See exactly what was sent/received sudo nmap <ip> -p 80 --packet-trace -Pn -n --disable-arp-ping Why does Nmap think the port is that state add --reason Scan progress press Space or --stats-every=5s

docs.title: Pentester view
docs.text:
• Scope first. Scan only what the rules of engagement list. Pass the scope file with -iL scope.txt.
  • The real risk is availability, not detection. In a pentest the client usually knows you are scanning. What can hurt is a fragile device (printers, PLCs, old appliances) falling over under aggressive timing, or an intrusive/dos script. Keep -T4 for labs; on client networks lower --max-rate and avoid dos, intrusive, brute and exploit scripts unless the scope explicitly allows them.
  • Save everything. -oA every time. Reports and re-checks come from the saved files, not from memory.
  • Two-stage workflow. A quick -p- to find ports, then -sV -sC only on those ports. Much less traffic than -sV over 65535 ports.

docs.title: Defender view
docs.text:
Where Artifact What to look for Zeek conn.log conn_state = S0 (SYN, no reply) or REJ (RST reply) One source touching many destination ports or hosts in a short window Zeek notice.log Scan::Port_Scan, Scan::Address_Scan Built-in scan detection Firewall logs Many denied connections from one source Count distinct dest_port per src_ip Windows Security log 5156 allowed / 5157 blocked (Filtering Platform) Only if audit policy enabled IDS Nmap default User-Agent Nmap Scripting Engine in HTTP NSE web scripts are easy to fingerprint 
index=firewall action=blocked
| bin _time span=5m
| stats dc(dest_port) AS ports dc(dest_ip) AS hosts count BY _time src_ip
| where ports > 50 OR hosts > 20

bin _time span=5m puts events in 5-minute buckets, stats dc() counts distinct values per source per bucket, and where keeps only sources that touched many ports or hosts.

CPTS exam notes

Always run a full -p- TCP scan, not just the top 1000. Run UDP top ports too (SNMP 161, DNS 53, TFTP 69 are common finds). Keep every scan's -oA output for the report's evidence section.

docs.title: Output & performance
docs.text:
MITRE ATT&CK: T1595 Active Scanning · Tactic: Reconnaissance · Last updated: 2026-10-13

Summary

Save every scan in all formats, turn the XML into an HTML report, and tune speed to the network you are on rather than always going as fast as possible.

docs.title: Saving results
docs.text:
sudo nmap 10.129.2.28 -p- -oA target
xsltproc target.xml -o target.html
Flag File Use -oN .nmap Human-readable copy of the terminal output -oG .gnmap Greppable, one host per line (grep "/open/") -oX .xml Parsed by tools; convert to HTML with xsltproc -oA name all three Use this by default --resume file Continue an interrupted scan --append-output Append instead of overwrite

docs.title: Timing & rate
docs.text:
Template Name Typical use -T0 paranoid Extremely slow, rarely practical -T1 sneaky Very slow -T2 polite Lower load on fragile hosts -T3 normal Default -T4 aggressive Labs, reliable fast links -T5 insane Fast and error-prone; can miss open ports

Finer control: --min-rate, --max-rate (packets/s), --max-retries, --host-timeout, --initial-rtt-timeout. A high --min-rate with --max-retries 0 is fast but may drop answers, so a port reported closed might actually be open.

sudo nmap 10.129.2.0/24 -F --max-retries 0 --initial-rtt-timeout 50ms   # fast, may miss hosts
sudo nmap 10.129.2.0/24 -F -T2                                          # gentle

Check speed by comparing the "scanned in N seconds" line and the number of hosts/ports found between runs; if the faster run found fewer, it was too aggressive.

docs.title: Pentester view
docs.text:
• Pick the profile by the target: -T4 or --min-rate in labs, -T2/--max-rate on production or old gear.
  • If results differ between two runs, trust neither: rerun the slower one on the disputed ports.
  • Keep the .xml as evidence; the HTML report is quick to show a client.

docs.title: Defender view
docs.text:
• High-rate scans appear as bursts in firewall logs and in conn.log connection counts per second per source.
  • Slow scans (-T1) spread over hours slip under short-window thresholds, so aggregate over a long window (24h unique ports per source).

CPTS exam notes

Time is limited: run -p- with a sensible --min-rate in the background, work other targets while it runs, and always keep the -oA files.

docs.title: Host discovery & port scanning
docs.text:
MITRE ATT&CK: T1018 Remote System Discovery · T1046 Network Service Discovery · Tactic: Discovery · Last updated: 2026-10-13

Summary

Find which hosts are alive (-sn), then which ports answer (-sS, -sT, -sU). The skill is reading the state Nmap assigns and knowing what each state says about the network in between.

docs.title: Host discovery
docs.text:
sudo nmap 10.129.2.0/24 -sn -oA tnet | grep for | cut -d" " -f5
sudo nmap 10.129.2.18 -sn -PE --packet-trace --reason
Flag Meaning -sn Host discovery only, skip the port scan -PE Use ICMP Echo requests -PS/-PA/-PU TCP SYN / TCP ACK / UDP discovery probes -Pn Skip discovery, treat every host as up (use when ICMP is blocked) -n No DNS resolution (faster, quieter in DNS logs) --disable-arp-ping On a local segment Nmap uses ARP by default; this forces ICMP --packet-trace Show each packet --reason Show why a state was assigned (e.g. arp-response, syn-ack)

On the same Layer-2 segment Nmap prefers ARP, which cannot be filtered by host firewalls. reason: arp-response in the output tells you that is what answered. Across routers it falls back to ICMP echo, so a host that drops ICMP looks dead; rerun with -Pn.

TTL is a rough OS hint: ~64 is typically Linux/Unix, ~128 Windows, ~255 network gear.

docs.title: Port states
docs.text: State Meaning open A service accepted the connection (SYN-ACK) closed Host replied RST — reachable but nothing listening filtered No reply, or an ICMP error — a firewall is hiding the answer unfiltered Reachable, but can't tell open vs closed (ACK scan only) open|filtered No response; open or dropped (UDP, FIN/NULL/Xmas) closed|filtered Can't tell closed from filtered (idle scan only)

docs.title: DROP vs REJECT
docs.text: A firewall that DROPs silently gives Nmap nothing back, so the port shows filtered after retries (slow). A firewall that REJECTs sends an ICMP error such as type 3 code 3 (port unreachable) or an RST, which is fast and also shows filtered/closed. With --packet-trace --reason you can tell them apart: no-response means DROP, port-unreach or reset means REJECT. That tells you where the filtering sits and how fast the target can be scanned.

docs.title: Scan types
docs.text:
Scan Flag What happens Notes SYN ("half-open") -sS SYN → SYN-ACK → RST Default as root. Never completes the handshake TCP Connect -sT Full 3-way handshake Default without root; ends up in application logs ACK -sA ACK only Maps firewall rules (filtered vs unfiltered), cannot find open ports UDP -sU Empty or protocol-specific datagram ICMP type 3 code 3 = closed; reply = open; silence = open|filtered. Slow 
$ sudo nmap 10.129.2.28 -p 80 -sS --packet-trace -Pn -n --disable-arp-ping
SENT (0.0429s) TCP 10.10.14.2:63090 > 10.129.2.28:80 S ttl=56 ...
RCVD (0.0573s) TCP 10.129.2.28:80 > 10.10.14.2:63090 SA ttl=64 ...
PORT   STATE SERVICE
80/tcp open  http

S is the SYN we sent, SA is SYN-ACK so the port is open. An RA reply would mean closed.

UDP needs patience: -sU --top-ports 100 first, then target specific ports with -sV, because a version probe is often the only way to get a UDP service to answer.

docs.title: Pentester view
docs.text:
• Full TCP first (-p-), top UDP ports second, run in the background.
  • On a lab, --min-rate 1000 is fine. On a client production network stay conservative and agree on a rate.
  • A port that stays filtered isn't "closed": note it and retry from another source host or path if scope allows.

docs.title: Defender view
docs.text:
• SYN scan leaves S0/REJ in Zeek conn_state and never reaches the application log, so firewall and network sensors catch it where host logs do not.
  • Connect scan (-sT) shows up in service logs (e.g. SSH "connection closed by ... [preauth]", web access logs).
  • A flood of ICMP type 3 from one host is often the target answering a UDP scan.

docs.title: Service enumeration & NSE
docs.text:
MITRE ATT&CK: T1046 Network Service Discovery · T1595.002 Vulnerability Scanning · Tactic: Reconnaissance / Discovery · Last updated: 2026-10-13

Summary

An open port is only a number. -sV turns it into a product and version, and NSE scripts query the service for more. The version is what you search for CVEs with.

docs.title: Version detection
docs.text:
sudo nmap 10.129.2.28 -p- -sV --stats-every=5s -v
Flag Meaning -sV Probe open ports to identify service and version -v Print open ports as soon as they are found --stats-every=5s Progress line every 5 seconds --version-trace Show the probes and matches -sV used

Nmap first reads the banner the server volunteers after the handshake, then falls back to sending signature probes (slower). Nmap prints only the parsed part of the banner, so something useful can be hidden. Compare:

sudo nmap 10.129.2.28 -p 25 -sV -Pn -n --disable-arp-ping --packet-trace
nc -nv 10.129.2.28 25

Nmap showed Postfix smtpd; nc returned 220 inlane ESMTP Postfix (Ubuntu) — the OS family was in the raw banner. Use --packet-trace/--version-trace to see it inside Nmap, or nc when you want the raw conversation. Either works; banners can also be removed or faked by the admin, so treat them as hints.

docs.title: NSE categories
docs.text:
Scripts are written in Lua. 14 categories: auth, broadcast, brute, default, discovery, dos, exploit, external, fuzzer, intrusive, malware, safe, version, vuln.

sudo nmap <ip> -sC                                  # default category
sudo nmap <ip> --script vuln                        # a category
sudo nmap <ip> -p 25 --script banner,smtp-commands  # named scripts
sudo nmap <ip> -p 80 -A                             # -sV -O --traceroute -sC
sudo nmap <ip> -p 80 -sV --script vuln              # vuln needs -sV for useful matches

How to read it: http-enum listing /wp-login.php and a WordPress version tells you the CMS and exact version to look up; smtp-commands showing VRFY means user enumeration is possible; vulners prints CVE IDs with CVSS scores for the detected CPE.

Remember that vulners/vuln results are version matches, not confirmed exploitability. Verify manually before putting a finding in the report.

docs.title: Pentester view
docs.text:
• -sC -sV on discovered ports is the standard second pass.
  • Be careful with intrusive, dos, brute, exploit and fuzzer: they can lock accounts or crash services. Do not run them on production unless scope allows.
  • -A also runs OS detection and traceroute; fine in a lab, think twice on fragile networks.

docs.title: Defender view
docs.text:
• NSE HTTP scripts send a recognizable User-Agent unless changed (look for Nmap Scripting Engine in http.log / proxy logs).
  • -sV produces many short connections with odd probe strings; services see malformed requests. Web servers log 400/404 bursts, SMTP logs unknown commands.
  • Reducing banner detail (ServerTokens Prod, reverse proxy) slows version-based CVE lookup but isn't a fix on its own.

CPTS exam notes

CTF-style flags often sit in a banner or in NSE output (banner, http-title, smtp-commands). If a flag is not in -sV, rerun with --script banner or connect manually.
