A colleague says: "This phishing email's From: is notice@bank.example, so it really came from that bank's server." Using the structure of an SMTP conversation, explain why you can't say that, and say what you should look at instead.

Answer and explanation

Why: From: is a header the sender writes inside the message body, after the SMTP DATA command. Servers deliver using only the envelope addresses (MAIL FROM, RCPT TO), and original SMTP has no mechanism to verify that From: is genuine. Anyone can write From: notice@bank.example and send it — like writing "From the Bank" on a letter.

What to look at:

  1. The connecting IP recorded by our border MTA — the IP of the server that actually handed the message over. Is it that bank's mail server (ASN, reverse DNS, reputation)?
  2. The envelope sender (Return-Path) — is its domain the same as From:?
  3. The authentication results (Authentication-Results header) — did SPF, DKIM and DMARC pass, and does the domain that passed align with the From: domain? (Covered in detail on later pages)
  4. Where links and attachments point, and their reputation

docs.title: DMARC and the Email Wrap-up — How Many From Addresses, Alignment, Policy and Reports, What Authentication Proves
DMARC and the Email Wrap-up — How Many From Addresses, Alignment, Policy and Reports, What Authentication Proves
docs.text:
What this page covers

The last gap left by SPF and DKIM: a message carries more than one "from" address, and the one the checks look at is not the one the user sees. A spoofed conversation that passes SPF and DKIM for the wrong domain, line by line. Then DMARC: what a domain owner publishes, what alignment means (SPF-aligned, DKIM-aligned, relaxed vs strict), the _dmarc record tag by tag (including the tags the 2026 revision added and removed), how a receiver evaluates it step by step, what the results look like in Authentication-Results:, and how to read an aggregate report. Then the traps DMARC does not close (look-alike domains, display names, Reply-To:, compromised accounts), and a wrap-up of the whole email section with a triage checklist. Practice questions with explanations at the end.

Labels

[Supplement] = practical material you need to know, [Correction] = a commonly repeated claim that is wrong or outdated, [Changed]/[Caution] = what has changed recently and what is risky to do the old way. All domains, IPs, keys and report values are invented for illustration. Continues from SPF Results and DKIM. This page closes the email section.

docs.title: The 8 key points
docs.text:
1. A message has (at least) two "from" addresses: the envelope sender MAIL FROM (RFC 5321, becomes Return-Path:) and the header From: (RFC 5322, the one the mail client displays). They can be completely different.
  2. SPF checks the envelope domain; DKIM checks the d= domain; the user sees the From: domain. Without something linking them, an attacker can pass both checks for their own domain while displaying yours.
  3. DMARC links them. A message passes DMARC if SPF passes and is aligned, or DKIM passes and is aligned — one of the two is enough.
  4. Aligned means the authenticated domain matches the From: domain. Relaxed (default) = same organisational domain (mail.victim.example ≈ victim.example); strict = exactly the same name.
  5. The domain owner publishes a TXT record at _dmarc.<domain> that says what to do on failure (p=none, quarantine or reject) and where to send reports (rua=).
  6. Aggregate reports are the big gift of DMARC: every major receiver tells the domain owner, daily, which IPs sent mail using its name and whether they passed. Before DMARC, a domain owner could not see who was spoofing them.
  7. Passing SPF, DKIM and DMARC proves "this really came from that domain." It does not prove the content is safe: a compromised account, a look-alike domain or a malicious Reply-To: all pass.
  8. Email wrap-up: SMTP is unauthenticated by design; trust headers only from your border MTA inward; publishing SPF/DKIM/DMARC protects others from mail forged in your name; checking them on incoming mail protects you; none of them vouches for the content.

docs.title: One last problem: how many "From" addresses?
docs.text:
Think of a paper letter. The envelope has a return address written on the outside; the post office uses it to send the letter back if it cannot be delivered. Inside, the letter itself is written on letterhead with a name and signature at the bottom. Nothing forces the two to match: you could post a letter in an envelope from "PO Box 12, Smalltown" whose letterhead says "Office of the Managing Director, Big Bank." The recipient opens it, throws the envelope away and reads only the letterhead.

Email is built exactly like that, because it grew out of two separate standards:

  • RFC 5321 describes the transport — the SMTP conversation between servers. The address typed after MAIL FROM: is the envelope sender, called RFC5321.MailFrom. The receiving server stores it at delivery time as the Return-Path: header, and that is where bounces go. (Envelope vs header addresses.)
  • RFC 5322 describes the message format — what is inside DATA. The From: header there is RFC5322.From. This is the one Outlook, Gmail or a phone app shows the user.

And SPF checks... the envelope (which "from" SPF checks). So the check and the display look at different places.

docs.title: A spoofed conversation that passes the checks
docs.text:
Here is an attacker who has learned that SPF and DKIM exist and decided to pass them instead of failing them. They registered a cheap domain, cheap-hosting.example, published an SPF record listing their own server 203.0.113.66, and set up a DKIM key for it. Then they connect to the victim's MX:

S: 220 mx1.victim.example ESMTP
C: EHLO mail.cheap-hosting.example
S: 250-mx1.victim.example Hello [203.0.113.66]
C: MAIL FROM:<bounce@cheap-hosting.example>
S: 250 2.1.0 Ok
C: RCPT TO:<accounts@victim.example>
S: 250 2.1.5 Ok
C: DATA
S: 354 End data with <CR><LF>.<CR><LF>
C: From: "Payroll Team" <payroll@victim.example>
C: To: accounts@victim.example
C: Subject: Updated bank details for November salary run
C: Date: Thu, 19 Nov 2026 08:12:40 +0000
C:
C: Please use the attached details from today.
C: .
S: 250 2.0.0 Ok: queued as 4QvX2m

Line by line, the parts that matter:

  • EHLO mail.cheap-hosting.example — the attacker's server names itself honestly. It has nothing to hide here.
  • MAIL FROM:<bounce@cheap-hosting.example> — the envelope uses the attacker's own domain. This is what SPF will check, and the attacker's SPF record does list 203.0.113.66, so SPF will pass.
  • From: "Payroll Team" <payroll@victim.example> — the header From:, typed by the attacker inside DATA. It claims to be the victim's own payroll team. Nobody checked this line.
  • The attacker's server also signs the message with d=cheap-hosting.example before sending (not shown in the conversation; it is a header inside DATA), so DKIM will pass too.

What the recipient's server writes, if it checks SPF and DKIM but not DMARC:

Return-Path: <bounce@cheap-hosting.example>
Authentication-Results: mx1.victim.example;
       spf=pass smtp.mailfrom=cheap-hosting.example;
       dkim=pass header.d=cheap-hosting.example header.s=k1 header.b=Qm7Lx2Ra
From: "Payroll Team" <payroll@victim.example>
Subject: Updated bank details for November salary run
  • Return-Path: — the envelope sender, recorded by our server. Attacker's domain.
  • spf=pass smtp.mailfrom=cheap-hosting.example — a genuine pass, for cheap-hosting.example.
  • dkim=pass header.d=cheap-hosting.example — a genuine pass, for cheap-hosting.example.
  • From: ... <payroll@victim.example> — what the user sees. Neither check said anything about this domain.

The user sees "Payroll Team, payroll@victim.example," and if their client shows a "verified" indicator based on SPF/DKIM alone, it may even look trustworthy. This is not a bug in SPF or DKIM; both did exactly their jobs. The missing piece is a rule saying "the domain you authenticated must be the domain you show."

[Supplement] There are more "from"-like fields than these two, and attackers use all of them:

Field Who sets it What it is for Checked by MAIL FROM → Return-Path: Sending server (envelope) Bounces SPF HELO/EHLO name Sending server Server's name SPF (HELO check) d= in DKIM-Signature: Signing server Who takes responsibility DKIM From: address Sender (header) What the user sees as the sender DMARC (alignment) From: display name ("Payroll Team") Sender Friendly name shown instead of the address Nothing Reply-To: Sender Where replies go Nothing Sender: Sender "Sent on behalf of" Nothing (rarely shown)

docs.title: DMARC: tying the checks to the visible From
docs.text:
DMARC (Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting and Conformance) builds on SPF and DKIM. It adds no new cryptography and no new path check. What it adds is three things a domain owner can say, published in DNS:

  1. "Judge mail claiming to be from my domain by alignment." Use SPF and DKIM results, but only count a pass that is for my domain — the one in From:.
  2. "Here is what to do when it fails." Nothing (none), put it in junk (quarantine), or refuse it (reject).
  3. "Send me reports." Tell me who is sending mail with my name and whether it passed.

Back to the letter analogy: DMARC is the bank publicly announcing "every genuine letter from us is either posted from our own mailroom or carries our own wax seal, and the letterhead says our name. If a letter's letterhead says our name but it has neither, bin it — and please send us a note about it."

docs.title: Alignment
docs.text:
To pass DMARC a message needs at least one of:

  • SPF aligned pass — SPF result is pass, and the domain SPF checked (RFC5321.MailFrom) matches the RFC5322.From domain.
  • DKIM aligned pass — a DKIM signature is pass, and its d= domain matches the RFC5322.From domain.

Why "or" and not "and"? Because each check breaks in different ordinary situations. SPF breaks when mail is forwarded (new IP); DKIM breaks when a list modifies the message. Requiring both would reject too much legitimate mail. Requiring one means a sender with a solid DKIM setup survives forwarding, and so on.

How exact must "matches" be? The owner chooses, separately for SPF (aspf=) and DKIM (adkim=):

  • Relaxed (r, the default): the two domains must share the same organisational domain — the registered domain, the part someone actually bought. bounce.mail.victim.example and victim.example have the same organisational domain, victim.example, so they align.
  • Strict (s): the names must be identical.
From: domain Authenticated domain Relaxed Strict victim.example victim.example aligned aligned victim.example bounce.victim.example (SPF) aligned not aligned news.victim.example victim.example (DKIM d=) aligned not aligned victim.example victim-example.example not aligned not aligned victim.example cheap-hosting.example not aligned not aligned

The fourth row is the important one for analysts: a look-alike name is a different organisational domain, so it never aligns with the real one. (That does not stop a look-alike from passing its own DMARC — see below.)

How does a receiver know where the organisational domain begins? Under the original DMARC it used the Public Suffix List (a community list of suffixes like .com, .co.uk, .gov.au under which people register names). [Changed] The 2026 revision replaced that with a DNS tree walk: the receiver walks up the name, label by label, looking for _dmarc records, and a domain can mark itself as a public suffix or an organisational domain with the new psd= tag. For an analyst, the answer is the same in almost every real case.

Now apply it to the spoofed conversation:

Check Result Domain checked From: domain Aligned? SPF pass cheap-hosting.example victim.example no DKIM pass cheap-hosting.example victim.example no DMARC fail neither pass is aligned

docs.title: The DMARC record
docs.text:
A domain owner publishes the policy as a TXT record at _dmarc. in front of the domain:

$ dig +short TXT _dmarc.victim.example
"v=DMARC1; p=quarantine; sp=reject; np=reject; adkim=r; aspf=r; rua=mailto:dmarc-agg@victim.example,mailto:victim@reports.dmarc-vendor.example; ruf=mailto:dmarc-forensic@victim.example; fo=1"
  • dig +short TXT _dmarc.victim.example — ask DNS for the TXT record at _dmarc.victim.example and print only the answer. If the answer is empty, the domain has no DMARC policy and receivers fall back to their own judgement.

Tag by tag:

Tag Example Meaning v= DMARC1 Version. Must come first. Still DMARC1 after the 2026 revision p= quarantine Policy for the domain itself when DMARC fails: none (monitor only), quarantine (treat as suspicious, usually junk folder), reject (refuse during SMTP) sp= reject Policy for subdomains (anything.victim.example) if they have no record of their own. Defaults to p= np= reject [Changed] New in the 2026 revision: policy for non-existent subdomains (names that do not exist in DNS at all, such as payroll-secure.victim.example). Attackers love inventing subdomains; this closes them off adkim= r DKIM alignment mode: r relaxed (default) or s strict aspf= r SPF alignment mode: r relaxed (default) or s strict rua= mailto:... Where to send aggregate reports (daily XML summaries). Several addresses allowed, separated by commas ruf= mailto:... Where to send failure reports (copies or extracts of individual failing messages). Few receivers send these today fo= 1 When to generate failure reports: 0 (default) only if everything failed, 1 if anything failed, d/s for DKIM/SPF failures pct= 50 [Changed] Removed in the 2026 revision. Used to mean "apply the policy to only N% of failing mail." Still seen in old records; ignored by updated receivers t= y [Changed] New in the 2026 revision: test mode. t=y means "do not apply my p=, just report"; t=n (default) means apply it. Replaces the common pct=0 trick psd= n [Changed] New in the 2026 revision: marks a domain as a public suffix (y) or as an organisational domain (n) for the tree walk. Default u (unspecified)

The rf= and ri= tags (report format and interval) were also removed in the revision; you will still see them in older records, and they are harmless.

[Supplement] Notice the second rua address is at a different domain (reports.dmarc-vendor.example, a reporting service). To stop anyone from directing reports at a stranger's mailbox, a receiver only sends there if that domain publishes permission:

$ dig +short TXT victim.example._report._dmarc.reports.dmarc-vendor.example
"v=DMARC1"
  • The name is built as <domain whose reports these are>._report._dmarc.<domain receiving the reports>.
  • "v=DMARC1" — "yes, we accept reports about victim.example." No answer means the receiver should not send there.

What a policy record tells you as an analyst, at a glance:

  • p=none — the owner is only watching. Spoofed mail using this domain is not blocked by DMARC anywhere. Very common: many domains add a p=none record to meet the big providers' sender rules and never go further.
  • p=quarantine — failing mail goes to junk. If a user found the spoof in their junk folder and moved it to the inbox, this is why it was there.
  • p=reject — failing mail is refused. A spoof of this exact domain reaching an inbox means either the receiver does not enforce DMARC, or the message passed (compromised account, legitimate platform abuse).
  • No record — the domain has no published policy. Its mail can be spoofed freely to receivers that do not apply their own rules.

docs.title: How a receiver evaluates DMARC, step by step
docs.text:
For each incoming message, the receiving border MTA:

  1. Extracts the From: domain. If there is no From:, or more than one From: header, or one header with several addresses from different domains, many receivers reject or treat the message as failing; a valid message has exactly one From: header.
  2. Looks up the policy. TXT at _dmarc.<From domain>. If none, walks up to the organisational domain's record (and uses sp=/np= from there).
  3. Takes the SPF result it already computed and checks whether the SPF domain is aligned.
  4. Takes each DKIM result and checks whether any passing signature's d= is aligned.
  5. Decides: at least one aligned pass → dmarc=pass. Otherwise → dmarc=fail.
  6. Applies the policy (none/quarantine/reject) — or its own local override — and records what it did.
  7. Logs a line for the daily aggregate report to rua=, and optionally sends a failure report to ruf=.

What it writes in the trace headers, for our spoofed message, with victim.example publishing p=quarantine:

Authentication-Results: mx1.victim.example;
       spf=pass smtp.mailfrom=cheap-hosting.example;
       dkim=pass header.d=cheap-hosting.example header.s=k1 header.b=Qm7Lx2Ra;
       dmarc=fail (p=quarantine dis=quarantine) header.from=victim.example
  • dmarc=fail — neither pass was aligned with victim.example.
  • p=quarantine — the policy the owner published.
  • dis=quarantine — the disposition, what the receiver actually did. It can differ from p=: a receiver may apply a local override (for example, a known forwarding source, or the old pct= sampling). If p=reject but dis=none, ask why.
  • header.from=victim.example — the domain DMARC protected.

If the policy had been p=reject, the message would not have been delivered at all. The attacker's server would have seen something like this at the end of DATA:

S: 550 5.7.1 Unauthenticated email from victim.example is not accepted due to domain's DMARC policy
  • 550 — permanent failure; do not retry.
  • 5.7.1 — the enhanced status code family for "delivery not authorised / security policy."
  • The text varies by provider, but this is what a sender sees in a bounce, and what you see in your own mail platform's logs as a rejected inbound attempt. Those logs are often the only trace of a blocked spoofing campaign against your users.

And for comparison, a genuine message from the real payroll system, which sends through a hosted platform but has DKIM set up for its own domain:

Authentication-Results: mx1.victim.example;
       spf=pass smtp.mailfrom=bounce.mailer-hub.example;
       dkim=pass header.d=victim.example header.s=hub2026 header.b=aR5tW0qL;
       dkim=pass header.d=mailer-hub.example header.s=k1 header.b=Zx81PqWe;
       dmarc=pass (p=quarantine dis=none) header.from=victim.example
  • SPF passed but for the platform's bounce domain → not aligned.
  • The first DKIM signature is by victim.example → aligned pass. That alone makes DMARC pass.
  • The second signature is the platform's own; it is fine but irrelevant to DMARC.
  • dis=none — passed, nothing done.

This "SPF not aligned, DKIM aligned" pattern is completely normal for mail sent through third-party platforms. That is the reason DMARC needs only one of the two.

docs.title: Aggregate reports: seeing who uses your name
docs.text:
Before DMARC, a domain owner had no way to learn that someone in another country was sending a million phishing messages in their name. With rua=, every participating receiver sends a daily aggregate report: an XML file (usually zipped or gzipped and attached to an email) summarising every source IP that sent mail with your domain in From:.

A shortened example:

<feedback>
  <report_metadata>
    <org_name>bigmail.example</org_name>
    <email>noreply-dmarc@bigmail.example</email>
    <report_id>8842137765</report_id>
    <date_range><begin>1795046400</begin><end>1795132799</end></date_range>
  </report_metadata>
  <policy_published>
    <domain>victim.example</domain>
    <adkim>r</adkim><aspf>r</aspf>
    <p>quarantine</p><sp>reject</sp>
  </policy_published>
  <record>
    <row>
      <source_ip>198.51.100.24</source_ip>
      <count>18233</count>
      <policy_evaluated>
        <disposition>none</disposition><dkim>pass</dkim><spf>fail</spf>
      </policy_evaluated>
    </row>
    <identifiers><header_from>victim.example</header_from></identifiers>
    <auth_results>
      <dkim><domain>victim.example</domain><selector>hub2026</selector><result>pass</result></dkim>
      <spf><domain>bounce.mailer-hub.example</domain><result>pass</result></spf>
    </auth_results>
  </record>
  <record>
    <row>
      <source_ip>203.0.113.66</source_ip>
      <count>412</count>
      <policy_evaluated>
        <disposition>quarantine</disposition><dkim>fail</dkim><spf>fail</spf>
      </policy_evaluated>
    </row>
    <identifiers><header_from>victim.example</header_from></identifiers>
    <auth_results>
      <dkim><domain>cheap-hosting.example</domain><selector>k1</selector><result>pass</result></dkim>
      <spf><domain>cheap-hosting.example</domain><result>pass</result></spf>
    </auth_results>
  </record>
</feedback>

Reading it:

  • <org_name>bigmail.example</org_name> — who wrote the report: the receiving provider.
  • <date_range> — the period, in Unix seconds: 1795046400 → 2026-11-19 00:00:00 UTC, 1795132799 → 23:59:59 the same day. Convert with date -u -d @1795046400.
  • <policy_published> — the policy the receiver found for us when it checked. Useful for spotting a DNS change that did not take effect.
  • First <record>: 198.51.100.24 sent 18,233 messages. policy_evaluated shows the DMARC-level results: dkim>pass means aligned DKIM passed; spf>fail means SPF was not aligned (even though raw SPF passed — see auth_results). Disposition none. This is our legitimate hosted platform.
  • Second <record>: 203.0.113.66 sent 412 messages claiming victim.example. Raw SPF and DKIM both passed for cheap-hosting.example, so at the DMARC level both are fail. Disposition quarantine. This is the spoofing campaign.

The trap to avoid: policy_evaluated and auth_results use the same words with different meanings. policy_evaluated = aligned results (what DMARC decided); auth_results = raw SPF/DKIM results for whatever domain was checked. A "pass" in auth_results next to a "fail" in policy_evaluated is the signature of an alignment failure.

Nobody reads hundreds of these XML files by hand; organisations send rua= to a reporting service or parse them into their SIEM. For a SOC, the useful questions are:

  • Unknown sources with high counts claiming our domain → active spoofing, or a department using a new mail service nobody told IT about ("shadow" senders).
  • Known sources suddenly failing → a broken DKIM key or SPF change, which will put our real mail in junk.
  • Failure reports (ruf=) can contain message headers or content, so they are personal data; many large receivers do not send them for privacy reasons. Do not count on them.

docs.title: Rolling out DMARC on your own domain
docs.text:
The normal path, and why each step exists:

  1. p=none with rua= — collect reports for some weeks. You will discover every service sending in your name (payroll, marketing, ticketing, the CEO's newsletter tool).
  2. Fix each legitimate source so it passes aligned — usually by having it DKIM-sign with your domain, or by using a bounce subdomain of yours for SPF.
  3. p=quarantine, optionally first with t=y (test mode: reports show what would happen) — then without.
  4. p=reject, plus sp=reject and np=reject once subdomains are covered.
  5. Domains that never send mail (parked or defensive registrations) should publish v=spf1 -all and v=DMARC1; p=reject; straight away. They are favourite spoofing targets precisely because nobody watches them.

docs.title: Forwarding, mailing lists and ARC
docs.text:
DMARC inherits the weaknesses of its parts. A plain forward (an alias that resends unchanged) breaks SPF but keeps DKIM → still passes if DKIM was aligned. A mailing list that adds a subject tag or footer breaks DKIM as well → DMARC fails for a genuine message, and with p=reject it may be refused.

Two fixes are in use today:

  • From rewriting. Many list servers rewrite From: to the list's own address, for example From: "Kim Lee via Staff List" <staff-list@lists.victim.example>. Then DMARC is evaluated for the list's domain, which the list can pass. When you see "via" in a display name, this is usually why.
  • ARC (Authenticated Received Chain, introduced on the previous page). The list seals "DKIM and DMARC passed when I received it," and the final receiver may choose to honour that if it trusts the list. A receiver that honoured ARC may note it in its results (for example dmarc=fail ... arc=pass with a local override in dis=).

docs.title: What DMARC does not stop
docs.text:
DMARC closes exactly one door: using a domain you do not control in the From: address. Every other door stays open, and attackers moved through them long ago.

  • Look-alike (cousin) domains. victim-payroll.example, vict1m.example, or an internationalised look-alike. The attacker owns it, so they can publish perfect SPF, DKIM and p=reject DMARC — and pass all three. DMARC proves "from that domain"; it does not tell the user it is the wrong domain.
  • Display-name spoofing. From: "Payroll Team - victim.example" <payroll.team.4471@freemail.example>. DMARC checks only the address domain (freemail.example), which passes. Most phone mail apps show only the display name.
  • Reply-To: redirection. From: is genuine or a look-alike, Reply-To: <payroll@victim-payroll.example>. The user replies to the attacker. No authentication standard checks Reply-To:. This is a core move in business email compromise (BEC).
  • Compromised accounts. If an attacker logs into a real employee's or supplier's mailbox, every message they send passes SPF, DKIM and DMARC perfectly, because it is genuine mail from that domain. The same goes for abuse of legitimate cloud platforms and file-sharing notifications.
  • Domains without a strict policy. Any domain at p=none or with no record can still be spoofed outright.

So the rule is: authentication tells you who sent it; it never tells you whether to trust what it says.

docs.title: Email wrap-up
docs.text:
Pulling the whole section together:

  • A message may be traceable to its source through its headers — but there is no guarantee. Webmail and cloud apps usually leave no client IP at all, and every Received: line written before your border MTA was written by someone you do not control and may be false (trust boundary). The one solid fact is the connecting IP your border server recorded.
  • SMTP is unauthenticated by nature. It was designed for a small trusted network; security was bolted on later, and most of it works only for domains that opt in.
  • Without SPF, DKIM and DMARC, email is trivially spoofed — envelope, header, display name, all of it (spoofing).
  • Do not trust headers beyond your border MTA. This applies to Received: and to Authentication-Results: (forged results).
  • Publishing SPF, DKIM and DMARC for your domains stops attackers sending mail labelled as you — to your partners, your customers, and to yourself. It is mostly a favour to others; it does little against spam arriving at you from other domains. The important exception is internal spoofing: mail from outside pretending to be from your own domain, which your own p=reject (enforced by your own receiving server) blocks.
  • Checking SPF, DKIM and DMARC on incoming mail is what protects your users from people spoofing other domains to them — but only as far as those domains have published policies.
  • None of them guarantees the content is good.

docs.title: A triage checklist for a reported message
docs.text: Step Look at Question 1 Our top Authentication-Results: (authserv-id = our server) What are spf=, dkim=, dmarc=? 2 smtp.mailfrom, header.d, header.from Are the three domains the same organisation? Which one aligned? 3 header.from domain itself Is it our domain, a partner's real domain, or a look-alike? Recently registered? 4 From: display name vs address, Reply-To: Does the name match the address? Do replies go somewhere else? 5 Our border Received: line Connecting IP and its reputation; does it match client-ip in Received-SPF:? 6 DMARC policy of the From: domain (dig TXT _dmarc.<domain>) none, quarantine, reject? Did dis= match it? 7 Content: links, attachments, request Even if everything passed: is the request unusual (bank change, credentials, urgency)? 8 Scope Same sender IP/subject/URL in other mailboxes? Mail platform logs for rejected attempts?

docs.title: How the SOC uses DMARC
docs.text:
• Read dmarc= first, then explain it. dmarc=pass + unfamiliar domain → look-alike or compromised sender; dmarc=fail + our own domain in From: → someone spoofing us (check dis= and why it was delivered).
  • Know your own domains' policies. Keep a list of every domain the organisation owns, its p=, and whether it sends mail. Parked domains at p=none are open spoofing targets.
  • Feed aggregate reports into monitoring. New high-volume sources claiming your domain deserve an alert; known sources suddenly failing deserve a ticket to the mail team.
  • Check your receiving side enforces DMARC. Publishing p=reject does nothing for inbound spoofs of your domain if your own gateway ignores DMARC or has an allow-list rule that bypasses it.
  • Do not stop at authentication. For BEC-style messages the decisive evidence is usually the Reply-To:, the look-alike domain's registration date, and the request itself.

docs.title: The 2026 view
docs.text:
[2026 Current] Still valid

The two-"from"-addresses problem is unchanged: SPF still checks the envelope, the user still sees the header From:. DMARC's core idea — pass SPF or DKIM, aligned with From: — is unchanged, records still start v=DMARC1, p=none/quarantine/reject still mean the same, relaxed/strict alignment still work the same, and aggregate reports are still the main way a domain owner sees abuse of its name. "Authentication proves origin, not safety" is truer than ever.

[Changed] What has changed

  • DMARC became a standard. In 2026 the IETF published the DMARC revision as RFC 9989 (core), RFC 9990 (aggregate reports) and RFC 9991 (failure reports), making the old informational RFC 7489 obsolete and moving DMARC onto the standards track. Existing records keep working.
  • Tags changed. pct=, rf= and ri= were removed; np= (non-existent subdomains), t= (test mode, replacing pct=0 tricks) and psd= were added. The Public Suffix List was replaced by a DNS tree walk to find the organisational domain.
  • The big mailbox providers made DMARC mandatory for bulk mail. Gmail and Yahoo since February 2024 (SPF, DKIM, a DMARC record of at least p=none, aligned From:), with Gmail moving from warnings to temporary and permanent rejections of non-compliant bulk traffic from November 2025. Microsoft's Outlook.com consumer service has rejected non-compliant high-volume senders (over about 5,000 messages a day) since May 2025. As a result DMARC records are now extremely common — but a large share are still p=none, which protects nobody.
  • Old adoption figures are meaningless now. Statistics from the early 2020s about how few top sites had SPF or DMARC are out of date (and the "top sites" list they used was itself discontinued in 2022). Exact current figures vary by survey; check a current source if you need one.
  • BIMI (brand logos shown next to authenticated mail in some clients) requires an enforcing DMARC policy (quarantine or reject) and gave companies a marketing reason to move beyond p=none. Treat the logo as a sign of authentication only, not of safe content.
  • Attacks moved around DMARC. Phishing in 2026 leans on look-alike domains, compromised supplier accounts, legitimate cloud and e-signature platforms, and Reply-To: tricks — all of which pass authentication. AI-written lures remove the spelling mistakes analysts once relied on, which makes header and domain checks more important, not less.

[Caution] Wrong or risky to do the old way

  • Do not use pct= in new records. It has been removed; updated receivers ignore it. Use t=y for testing.
  • Do not leave domains at p=none forever. It was meant as a monitoring phase. A p=none domain is as spoofable as one with no record.
  • Do not forget parked and non-sending domains, and set sp=/np= so attackers cannot invent subdomains.
  • Do not read dmarc=pass as "safe." It means the From: domain is genuine — which could be a look-alike the attacker owns, or a real account they compromised.
  • Do not read auth_results pass in an aggregate report as "aligned." Only policy_evaluated shows the DMARC-level result.
  • Do not jump straight to p=reject without reports. You will block your own payroll, ticketing or marketing mail.

docs.title: Question 1
docs.text:
A user forwards a message as an attachment. Our border server wrote this. The user insists "it says payroll@victim.example, so it must be internal." What happened, and why was it delivered?

Return-Path: <bounce@cheap-hosting.example>
Authentication-Results: mx1.victim.example;
       spf=pass smtp.mailfrom=cheap-hosting.example;
       dkim=pass header.d=cheap-hosting.example header.s=k1 header.b=Qm7Lx2Ra;
       dmarc=fail (p=none dis=none) header.from=victim.example
From: "Payroll Team" <payroll@victim.example>
Reply-To: <payroll-updates@cheap-hosting.example>
Subject: Updated bank details for November salary run
Answer and explanation

It is an outside sender impersonating our own domain. SPF and DKIM both genuinely passed, but for cheap-hosting.example (smtp.mailfrom, header.d). The visible From: domain is victim.example, and neither pass is aligned with it, so dmarc=fail. The user is looking at the RFC 5322 From:, which the sender can type freely; the envelope (Return-Path:) shows the real origin domain.

It was delivered because our own domain's DMARC policy is p=none (dis=none): we told every receiver, including ourselves, to take no action on failures. Also note the Reply-To: pointing to the attacker's domain — any reply goes to them.

Actions: block the sending IP/domain, search other mailboxes for the same Return-Path domain and subject, warn payroll, and raise the case for moving victim.example to p=quarantine then p=reject (after checking aggregate reports that all legitimate senders pass aligned). Also consider a gateway rule flagging external mail that uses our own domain in From:.

docs.title: Question 2
docs.text:
Read this DMARC record and answer: (a) what happens to a message failing DMARC that claims to be from victim.example; (b) from hr.victim.example (which exists, with no record of its own); (c) from payroll-secure.victim.example (which does not exist in DNS); (d) is anything in it outdated?

"v=DMARC1; p=quarantine; sp=none; np=reject; pct=25; adkim=s; rua=mailto:dmarc-agg@victim.example"
Answer and explanation
  • (a) p=quarantine → goes to junk. (Under the old rules pct=25 would have meant only a quarter of failures were quarantined; see (d).)
  • (b) sp=none → no action for existing subdomains. An attacker can spoof hr.victim.example freely — a weak spot, and HR is a believable sender.
  • (c) np=reject → refused, because the subdomain does not exist. Receivers that do not yet support the 2026 revision will ignore np= and fall back to sp=none, so this protection is not universal yet.
  • (d) pct= was removed in the 2026 revision; updated receivers ignore it and apply the policy to all failing mail (equivalent to 100). Older receivers may still sample 25%. Remove it, and use t=y if a test phase is wanted. Also note adkim=s (strict DKIM alignment): mail signed d=mail.victim.example with From: victim.example will not DKIM-align — make sure every sender signs with the exact From: domain, or use relaxed. aspf is not set, so it defaults to relaxed.

docs.title: Question 3
docs.text:
An aggregate report for victim.example contains this record. What is this source, what is wrong, and what should the mail team do?

<row>
  <source_ip>192.0.2.40</source_ip>
  <count>2950</count>
  <policy_evaluated><disposition>quarantine</disposition><dkim>fail</dkim><spf>fail</spf></policy_evaluated>
</row>
<identifiers><header_from>victim.example</header_from></identifiers>
<auth_results>
  <dkim><domain>ticketdesk.example</domain><selector>td1</selector><result>pass</result></dkim>
  <spf><domain>mail.ticketdesk.example</domain><result>pass</result></spf>
</auth_results>
Answer and explanation

Raw SPF and DKIM both passed, but for the vendor's own domains (ticketdesk.example, mail.ticketdesk.example). At the DMARC level both are fail because neither is aligned with victim.example. Nearly 3,000 messages in a day from a ticketing vendor's IP, with a passing vendor signature, looks like a legitimate service our organisation uses (for example the IT help desk's ticket notifications) that was never configured to authenticate as our domain — not an attacker. The consequence is real, though: our own p=quarantine is sending those notifications to users' junk folders.

Fix: configure the vendor to DKIM-sign with d=victim.example (publish the vendor's public key under a selector like td1._domainkey.victim.example), and/or use a bounce subdomain of ours (tickets.victim.example) as the envelope sender with the vendor in its SPF. Either one gives an aligned pass. Before declaring it benign, confirm with the business that this vendor is actually in use — an unknown source with this pattern could also be someone abusing the vendor's platform.

docs.title: Reading Email Headers — Trace Headers, Message Headers, Body, Interpreting Received Lines
Reading Email Headers — Trace Headers, Message Headers, Body, Interpreting Received Lines
docs.text:
What this page covers

The three parts of a received message's source (trace headers, message headers, body), who writes each part, and therefore how far each can be trusted. How to pull the source and headers out of each mail client, and how to handle them safely. Then reading Received headers from bottom to top to retrace the message's route, interpreting a single Received line field by field, and finding the line written by our border server to draw the trust boundary. Practice questions with explanations at the end.

Labels

[Supplement] = practical material you need to know, [Correction] = a commonly repeated claim that is wrong or outdated, [Changed]/[Caution] = what has changed recently and what is risky to do the old way. All domains and IPs are invented for illustration. Continues from Email Delivery and SMTP.

docs.title: The 8 key points
docs.text:
1. A message's source runs, from the top: trace headers → message headers → body.
  2. Trace headers (Received and others) are added one at a time, on top, by each server that handles the message. Message headers and body are written by the sender's mail program (or submission server).
  3. Received lines have the newest at the top. To follow the route, read from bottom to top.
  4. One Received line = from <EHLO name> (<PTR name> [<connecting IP>]) by <server that wrote this line> with <protocol> id <ID> for <recipient>; <date>.
  5. The IP in brackets is what the receiving server saw itself, so it is real as long as you trust that server. The EHLO name is written by the sender.
  6. The Received line written by our border MTA is the trust boundary. Trust up to that line's from IP; lines below it can be fabricated by the sender.
  7. A legitimate message forms a chain from bottom to top where each by becomes the next line's from. Breaks, time going backwards and unexpected servers are clues.
  8. To receive a suspicious message for analysis, get it forwarded as an attachment (.eml/.msg) so the headers survive. A normal forward loses them.

docs.title: Why read headers
docs.text:
What a user sees in their mail client is the sender's name, subject and body. But as the previous page showed, all of those can be written however the sender likes. To judge "where did this message really come from?", you have to open the source behind the screen and read what the servers recorded.

Think of parcel tracking history. Anyone can write the "sender" sticker on the box, but each "arrived at depot X, 14:02" entry was recorded by that depot. An email's Received headers are those depot entries. There is one trap, though: entries from before the parcel reached our depot could have been pre-written on the label by the sender. So the core of this page is how to draw the line for what to trust.

docs.title: The three parts of a message source
docs.text:
Below is the source of a message received by an employee of the invented organisation victim.example. Clicking "Show original" produces text like this.

Return-Path: <user1@freemail.example>
Received: from mx1.victim.example (10.0.5.20) by mbx01.victim.example with ESMTPS
        id 7Hq2; Wed, 18 Nov 2026 22:41:07 +0000
Received: from out-7.freemail.example (out-7.freemail.example [198.51.100.71])
        by mx1.victim.example with ESMTPS id 4QzK7m1abc
        for <jsmith@victim.example>; Wed, 18 Nov 2026 22:41:05 +0000
Received: from LAPTOP-7Q2 (static-25-113-0-203.isp.example [203.0.113.25])
        by smtp.freemail.example with ESMTPSA id e5so1909
        for <jsmith@victim.example>
        (version=TLS1_3 cipher=TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384);
        Wed, 18 Nov 2026 14:41:02 -0800 (PST)
Authentication-Results: mx1.victim.example; spf=pass smtp.mailfrom=freemail.example;
        dkim=pass header.d=freemail.example; dmarc=pass header.from=freemail.example
From: "Kim User" <user1@freemail.example>
To: <jsmith@victim.example>
Subject: Meeting notes
Date: Wed, 18 Nov 2026 17:41:00 -0500
Message-ID: <013501d48651$07300ed0$15902c70$@freemail.example>
MIME-Version: 1.0
Content-Type: multipart/mixed; boundary="----=_Part_8812"
X-Mailer: Microsoft Outlook 16.0

------=_Part_8812
Content-Type: text/plain; charset="utf-8"
Content-Transfer-Encoding: 7bit

Notes from today attached.

------=_Part_8812
Content-Type: application/pdf; name="notes.pdf"
Content-Disposition: attachment; filename="notes.pdf"
Content-Transfer-Encoding: base64

JVBERi0xLjcKJeLjz9MKMSAwIG9iago8PC9UeXBlL0NhdGFsb2cvUGFnZXMgMiAwIFI+Pgpl
------=_Part_8812--
Part Where Who writes it What's in it Trace headers Top Each server the message passes through, adding its own line on top Received:, Return-Path:, authentication results (Authentication-Results:), X-... headers added by servers and security products Message headers Below that The sender's mail program (MUA) or submission server From:, To:, Subject:, Date:, Message-ID:, MIME-Version:, Content-Type:, X-Mailer: Body After a blank line, at the bottom The sender Text, HTML, images, attachments (usually Base64)

The "who writes it" column is the same as "how far you can trust it." Message headers and body were written by the sender and can be false; trace headers were written by servers and can be trusted only as far as you trust that server.

docs.title: Trace headers line by line
docs.text:
• Return-Path: <user1@freemail.example> — the envelope sender (MAIL FROM) from the previous page, written in by the final delivering server. Take note if its domain differs from From:
  • Top Received: from mx1.victim.example (10.0.5.20) by mbx01.victim.example — the most recent entry: the internal hop where our MX handed the message to our mailbox server (MDA)
  • Middle Received: from out-7.freemail.example (...[198.51.100.71]) by mx1.victim.example — the line written by our border MTA (mx1): a record that external server 198.51.100.71 connected to us. This line is the trust boundary (more below)
  • Bottom Received: from LAPTOP-7Q2 (...[203.0.113.25]) by smtp.freemail.example with ESMTPSA — the oldest entry: the sender's PC (LAPTOP-7Q2, IP 203.0.113.25) logged in to the mail service's submission server and sent the message. This line was written by freemail.example, so we can trust it only as far as we trust freemail.example
  • Authentication-Results: — the results of our mx1 checking SPF, DKIM and DMARC (covered in detail on later pages)

docs.title: Message headers line by line
docs.text:
• From: / To: / Subject: — the values shown on screen, written by the sender
  • Date: Wed, 18 Nov 2026 17:41:00 -0500 — the time according to the sender's PC clock and time zone. -0500 is five hours behind UTC. It can hint at where the sender is, but it's just a PC setting and can be changed
  • Message-ID: — a unique ID attached to each message. The domain after @ and the shape of the first part follow each mail program's habits (the $...$...$@ shape here is an Outlook habit). If From: says Gmail but the Message-ID looks like a completely different program's, that's a clue
  • MIME-Version: 1.0 — the body uses the MIME format, which carries several kinds of content (text, HTML, attachments)
  • Content-Type: multipart/mixed; boundary="----=_Part_8812" — "the body has several parts, separated by ------=_Part_8812 lines"
  • X-Mailer: Microsoft Outlook 16.0 — the sending mail program. Headers starting with X- are non-standard extras. Phishing kits and bulk-sending scripts often leave unusual values here, or omit it entirely

docs.title: Body and attachments
docs.text:
• Blank line — end of headers, start of body
  • ------=_Part_8812 — start of the first part. Content-Type: text/plain = a plain-text part
  • Second part Content-Type: application/pdf; name="notes.pdf" with Content-Disposition: attachment — this is an attachment
  • Content-Transfer-Encoding: base64 — the file is carried converted to Base64 text. SMTP was designed to carry only text, so binary data such as files is converted to Base64 for transport
  • JVBERi0x... — the Base64 data. The leading JVBERi0 decodes to %PDF-, so you can tell it really is a PDF (guessing file types from Base64 prefixes)
  • ------=_Part_8812-- — a trailing -- marks the end of the last part

[Supplement] If the body says Content-Transfer-Encoding: quoted-printable, you'll see transformed characters such as =3D (the = sign) and =20 (a space). Phishing messages sometimes wrap their HTML in this encoding or in Base64 to dodge simple keyword checks. If an HTML body arrives alongside text/plain as multipart/alternative, check whether the two versions differ (an innocent sentence in plain text, a phishing link in the HTML).

docs.title: How to view the source and headers
docs.text:
Environment How Outlook (classic desktop) Open the message in its own window → File → Properties → the "Internet headers" box. The box is small, so Ctrl+A, copy, and paste into an editor New Outlook / Outlook on the web The message's ... → View → View message details Gmail ⋮ at the top right of the message → Show original. The full headers and body appear as plain text, along with an SPF/DKIM/DMARC summary. "Download original" saves an .eml Thunderbird and others View → Message Source (Ctrl+U) Header analysis tools Microsoft Message Header Analyzer (MHA), Google Admin Toolbox Messageheader — paste the headers and they lay out the Received order and delays as a table

[Caution] Handling it safely.

  • Ask users to "forward as attachment", not to forward normally. A normal forward strips the original message's trace headers and turns it into a new message sent by the person forwarding. Use Outlook's "Forward as Attachment", Gmail's "Forward as attachment", or receive it as an .eml/.msg file. In many organisations a "Report phishing" button does this for you
  • Viewing the plain-text source is relatively safe, but rendering the HTML can load remote images (tracking pixels), signalling to the attacker that "this address is live and the message was opened." Turn off remote content loading in your analysis environment
  • Don't click links; defang them when recording (hxxps, [.]). Open attachments only in an isolated environment or sandbox
  • A message source contains the recipient's personal information, so check your organisation's rules before pasting it into a public analysis site

docs.title: Retracing a message's route with Received headers
Read from bottom to top
docs.text:
Each time a server receives a message, it adds its own entry on top. So Received lines are in reverse order: newest at the top, oldest at the bottom. To follow the route in the order the message actually travelled, start at the bottom and move up.

Below are only the Received lines of a message sent by a user of an external mail service to an organisation on Microsoft 365 (shortened for illustration). They're numbered from the bottom.

[6] Received: from AM9PR01MB7421.eurprd01.prod.outlook.example by AM9PR01MB7421.eurprd01.prod.outlook.example; Wed, 18 Nov 2026 22:41:09 +0000
[5] Received: from DB8PR04CA0012.eurprd04.prod.outlook.example (2603:10a6:10:12a::22) by AM9PR01MB7421.eurprd01.prod.outlook.example; Wed, 18 Nov 2026 22:41:08 +0000
[4] Received: from DB1EUR03FT041.eop-EUR03.prod.protection.outlook.example (2603:10a6:10:12a:cafe::5) by DB8PR04CA0012.outlook.office365.example; Wed, 18 Nov 2026 22:41:07 +0000
[3] Received: from out-7.freemail.example (out-7.freemail.example [198.51.100.71]) by DB1EUR03FT041.mail.protection.outlook.example; Wed, 18 Nov 2026 22:41:06 +0000
[2] Received: by out-7.freemail.example with SMTP id e5so1909 for <jsmith@victim.example>; Wed, 18 Nov 2026 14:41:05 -0800 (PST)
[1] Received: from LAPTOP-7Q2 (static-25-113-0-203.isp.example [203.0.113.25]) by smtp.freemail.example with ESMTPSA; Wed, 18 Nov 2026 14:41:03 -0800 (PST)

Building the story from bottom to top:

  • [1] The sender's laptop LAPTOP-7Q2 (IP 203.0.113.25, whose reverse DNS shows a static IP from some ISP) logged in (the A in ESMTPSA) to the mail service's submission server smtp.freemail.example and submitted the message. Because it was sent from a mail program (Outlook, Thunderbird and the like), the PC name and IP were recorded. Had it been sent from webmail, this line would usually show only the mail service's own servers, without the user's IP
  • [2] Another server inside freemail.example, out-7, received it. This line has no from; that sometimes happens between servers inside the same organisation and isn't a concern
  • [3] This is where it crosses the organisational border. freemail.example's border server out-7 (IP 198.51.100.71) connected to the receiving organisation's Microsoft 365 entry point (...mail.protection.outlook..., the receiving organisation's MX). This line was written by the receiving side (Microsoft 365), so you can trust that 198.51.100.71 really connected
  • [4]–[6] Microsoft 365 internal servers hand it along until the final mailbox server (internal hops commonly use IPv6 addresses)

Checking the chain: [3]'s by DB1EUR03FT041 continues as [4]'s from DB1EUR03FT041, and [4]'s by DB8PR04CA0012 continues as [5]'s from. When each line's by becomes the from of the line above it, the route is natural.

Checking the times: convert the time at the end of each line to UTC and compare. [1] 14:41:03 -0800 = UTC 22:41:03, [2] = 22:41:05, [3] 22:41:06, … [6] 22:41:09. Normally time increases from bottom to top. Take note if time goes backwards, if one hop is delayed by hours (it could be queueing or greylisting), or if the time zone notation looks odd. Servers use different time zones, so comparing without converting to UTC is an easy way to fool yourself.

docs.title: How far can you trust it: the trust boundary
docs.text:
This is the most important part of this page.

  • SMTP is TCP, so the IP a server records as "who connected to me" is real if that server is honest
  • We trust our own border MTA (or the entry point of the cloud mail service we use) to be honest. So the from IP on the line our border MTA wrote is real — [3] in the example above
  • But [1] and [2] are lines written by the sending side's servers. If the sender is a legitimate large mail service, those entries are generally reliable too, but if the sender is an attacker, they can fabricate lines like [1] and [2] wholesale and include them in the message in advance. Our server only adds its own line on top of the message it receives; it doesn't check the lines below
  ┌──────────── written by our side: trust ────────────┐
  [6] [5] [4]   internal hops (our servers / our cloud tenant)
  [3]  from ... [198.51.100.71]  by OUR border MTA   ← trust boundary: this IP is real
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  [2] [1]       written by the sender's side: claims only

So the analysis order is:

  1. Know the name of our MX (border) — the MX lookup from the previous page, or the name of the mail service or security gateway the organisation uses
  2. Work down from the top and find "the last line with one of our servers in by" — that line is the boundary
  3. Investigate that line's from IP — this is the message's real origin (at least, the server that handed it to us). Check its ASN, reverse DNS, reputation, and whether it is a legitimate sending server for the From: domain (checked with SPF, next page)
  4. Treat the lines below as "claims" only — use them as reference if the sender is a legitimate large service; be suspicious if the servers look odd

[Supplement] An example of forged Received lines. If an attacker sends something like the following, a quick read tells a story of "it started from inside the bank".

Received: from mail.bank.example (unknown [203.0.113.77]) by mx1.victim.example with ESMTP; Wed, 18 Nov 2026 22:50:12 +0000
Received: from internal-relay.bank.example ([10.40.1.12]) by mail.bank.example with ESMTP; Wed, 18 Nov 2026 22:50:10 +0000
Received: from ops-pc17.bank.example ([10.40.8.33]) by internal-relay.bank.example; Wed, 18 Nov 2026 22:50:09 +0000

But look at the top line — the line our mx1 wrote: the connecting IP 203.0.113.77 has no reverse DNS (unknown), and only the EHLO claims to be mail.bank.example. Check whether 203.0.113.77 is really bank.example's mail server (is it in that domain's MX or SPF, is the ASN the bank's?) and the lie shows. The two lines below may be decoration the attacker wrote in advance.

docs.title: Reading one Received line field by field
docs.text:
Here's one line written by our server at the border, broken into fields.

Received: from mailer.promo-deals.example (unknown [203.0.113.149])
        by mx1.victim.example with ESMTP id 922034ljg
        for <jsmith@victim.example>; Wed, 18 Nov 2026 22:26:53 +0000
Field Value Set by Meaning Right after from mailer.promo-deals.example The sender (the name announced in EHLO/HELO) May be false First item in parentheses unknown The receiving server (result of a PTR lookup on the connecting IP) Reverse DNS result; unknown if none. May or may not match the EHLO name [ ] in parentheses 203.0.113.149 The receiving server (seen directly on the TCP connection) The unspoofable connecting IP by mx1.victim.example The receiving server The server that wrote this line — the one that just received the message with ESMTP The receiving server The protocol used (table below) id 922034ljg The receiving server That server's queue ID — the key for matching against server logs for <jsmith@victim.example> The receiving server The envelope recipient (RCPT TO). Optional After ; Date and time The receiving server When it was received

Reading this example: IP 203.0.113.149, calling itself mailer.promo-deals.example, with no reverse DNS, connected to our mx1 without encryption (ESMTP, no S) and handed over the message. An EHLO name that doesn't match the PTR (here, there's no PTR at all) is common for spam and malicious senders, so it's a weak signal.

The protocol notation in the with field reads like this (RFC 3848):

Notation Meaning SMTP Old SMTP without extensions (HELO) ESMTP Extended SMTP (EHLO), no encryption ESMTPS ESMTP + TLS encryption (STARTTLS) ESMTPA ESMTP + login authentication (the user logged in to the submission server) ESMTPSA TLS + login authentication. Common when a user sends from a mail program LMTP Internal delivery to a mailbox server

[Supplement] Trace headers worth checking besides Received.

  • X-Originating-IP: — "the IP the user connected from", once added by some webmail services. Many large services no longer include it, for privacy reasons
  • Microsoft 365's X-Forefront-Antispam-Report: — contains CIP: (connecting IP), SFV: (spam verdict), SCL: (spam confidence level) and more; handy for quickly finding the border IP. X-MS-Exchange-Organization-AuthAs: Anonymous means the message came in from outside without authentication; Internal means it was authenticated inside the organisation
  • ARC-Seal:, ARC-Message-Signature:, ARC-Authentication-Results: — when forwarding or a mailing list breaks the original authentication results, an intermediate server signs a record saying "authentication passed when I received it" (ARC, explained on a later page)

docs.title: Viewing it in Zeek and on the command line
docs.text:
Zeek smtp.log pulls out some Received lines separately.

first_received=from LAPTOP-7Q2 (static-25-113-0-203.isp.example [203.0.113.25]) by smtp.freemail.example ...
second_received=by out-7.freemail.example with SMTP id e5so1909 ...
path=203.0.113.10,198.51.100.71,203.0.113.25
  • first_received / second_received — the top two Received lines in the header (the most recent at the point Zeek sees it)
  • path — the IP path extracted from the Received lines, most recent first

If you have the .eml file, Python's standard library can print the Received lines in the order the message actually travelled.

$ python3 -c '
import email, sys
msg = email.message_from_binary_file(open(sys.argv[1], "rb"))
for n, h in enumerate(reversed(msg.get_all("Received", [])), 1):
    print(n, " ".join(h.split()))
' suspicious.eml
  • import email, sys — the standard module for parsing mail, and the module for command-line arguments
  • email.message_from_binary_file(open(..., "rb")) — opens the .eml file in binary mode and parses it into a message object
  • msg.get_all("Received", []) — gets every Received header in source order (newest first); an empty list if there are none
  • reversed(...) — flips the order to oldest first
  • " ".join(h.split()) — unfolds headers that wrap across lines into one line for printing
  • suspicious.eml — the file to analyse (passed as sys.argv[1])

The output looks like this:

1 from LAPTOP-7Q2 (static-25-113-0-203.isp.example [203.0.113.25]) by smtp.freemail.example with ESMTPSA id e5so1909 for <jsmith@victim.example> (version=TLS1_3 cipher=TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384); Wed, 18 Nov 2026 14:41:02 -0800 (PST)
2 from out-7.freemail.example (out-7.freemail.example [198.51.100.71]) by mx1.victim.example with ESMTPS id 4QzK7m1abc for <jsmith@victim.example>; Wed, 18 Nov 2026 22:41:05 +0000
3 from mx1.victim.example (10.0.5.20) by mbx01.victim.example with ESMTPS id 7Hq2; Wed, 18 Nov 2026 22:41:07 +0000

Line 1 is the start, line 2 is our border (the line mx1 wrote), line 3 is our internal hop. The [198.51.100.71] in line 2 is the IP to investigate.

docs.title: The 2026 view
docs.text:
[2026 Current] Still valid

The three parts (trace headers, message headers, body), Received lines in reverse order read from bottom to top, the from EHLO (PTR [IP]) by ... format, the connecting IP being what the receiving server saw itself, and the principle that the line written by our border MTA is the trust boundary all still hold.

[Changed] What has changed

  • Cloud mail makes headers long. Passing through Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace adds many internal Received lines (internal IPv6 addresses are common) and dozens of service-specific X- headers (X-Forefront-Antispam-Report, X-MS-Exchange-*, X-Google-*). Rather than reading every line by hand, lay out the Received order with a tool such as MHA and focus on the border line and the authentication results.
  • Less and less of the sender's IP is left. Large webmail services don't put the user's IP in headers, and some strip it from the first Received line even when the message was sent from a mail program. Relay-address services such as Apple's "Hide My Email" have also grown. Expecting "the sender's IP is in the first Received line" now often fails.
  • Email security products rewrite links. Because of Microsoft Defender Safe Links and URL rewriting in other security gateways, links in the body look like https://...safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=<encoded original URL>&.... When analysing, URL-decode what follows url= to recover the original address.
  • Header analysis has been automated. A common flow: the user's "Report phishing" button → the mail platform (Defender for Office 365, Google Workspace) preserves the original → SOAR extracts headers, links and attachments and checks their reputation automatically. Even so, when the automated result is ambiguous, the judgement comes down to the reading skills on this page.
  • Generative AI has made message bodies more natural. Spotting phishing through spelling mistakes or awkward translation has become less reliable. That raises the weight of technical records in the header that a person can't edit (the border IP, authentication results, the consistency of the chain).

[Caution] Wrong or risky to do the old way

  • Don't assume the bottom Received line (the oldest) is "the real origin". An attacker can write it. The anchor is the line written by our border MTA.
  • Don't trust the EHLO name as the origin. Look at the [IP] in brackets.
  • Don't receive suspicious mail by normal forward. The headers disappear. Get it forwarded as an attachment, or pull the original from the mail platform.
  • Don't compare times without aligning time zones. Convert everything to UTC.
  • Don't open an HTML body with remote content enabled. Tracking pixels signal the attacker.

docs.title: Question 1
docs.text:
The MX for victim.example is mx1.victim.example. In the following Received lines (in source order), which line is the trust boundary, and which IP should you investigate? How should you treat the lines below it?

Received: from mx1.victim.example (10.0.5.20) by mbx01.victim.example with ESMTPS; Wed, 18 Nov 2026 23:05:44 +0000
Received: from relay.payroll-portal.example (unknown [203.0.113.201]) by mx1.victim.example with ESMTP; Wed, 18 Nov 2026 23:05:42 +0000
Received: from hr-gw.victim.example ([10.0.9.4]) by relay.payroll-portal.example with ESMTP; Wed, 18 Nov 2026 23:05:40 +0000
Received: from HR-PC03.victim.example ([10.0.9.77]) by hr-gw.victim.example with ESMTPSA; Wed, 18 Nov 2026 23:05:39 +0000
Answer and explanation

The boundary is the second line. Working down from the top for the last line with one of our servers in by: the first line (by mbx01, our internal server) and the second line (by mx1, our border MTA). From the third line on it's by relay.payroll-portal.example — lines written by an external server.

IP to investigate: 203.0.113.201. It's the connecting IP our mx1 saw itself, with no reverse DNS (unknown) and no encryption (ESMTP).

The two lines below make it look as though the message started from a PC in our own HR team (HR-PC03) and our internal gateway (hr-gw.victim.example). But those lines were written on the external relay.payroll-portal.example side, and there's no reason for our internal server to send mail back to us through an external relay. They're most likely forged lines dressed up to look internal. To confirm, check whether our hr-gw server logs have a record of that message at that time (if not, the forgery is confirmed).

docs.title: Question 2
docs.text:
Interpret the following Received line field by field and say what's suspicious.

Received: from mail.securebank.example (static-77-113-0-203.cheap-vps.example [203.0.113.77])
        by mx1.victim.example with ESMTP id 8Kd2Q
        for <finance@victim.example>; Wed, 18 Nov 2026 01:14:09 +0000
Answer and explanation
  • from mail.securebank.example — the name the sender announced for itself in EHLO, claiming to be a bank mail server
  • static-77-113-0-203.cheap-vps.example — the reverse DNS (PTR) our mx1 looked up for the connecting IP: the name of a cheap VPS provider
  • [203.0.113.77] — the connecting IP our mx1 saw itself (cannot be spoofed)
  • by mx1.victim.example — the server that wrote this line = our border MTA, so this line is the trust boundary
  • with ESMTP — connected without encryption (no S) and without login
  • id 8Kd2Q — mx1's queue ID, the key to finding this message in mx1's logs
  • for <finance@victim.example> — the envelope recipient: the finance team
  • Time — 01:14 UTC

What's suspicious: the name claiming to be a bank (EHLO) doesn't match the reverse DNS of the actual connecting IP (a cheap VPS). A real bank would normally send from its own or a large mail service's IPs and use encryption (ESMTPS). The recipient is the finance team, so this may be BEC impersonation. Next steps: look up the ASN and reputation of 203.0.113.77, check whether this IP is in the bank domain's SPF, check Authentication-Results, and find other messages from the same IP.

docs.title: Question 3
docs.text:
An employee says they received a suspicious message and sends it to the SOC mailbox using a normal "Forward". Opening the headers, you find the Received lines are all internal company servers and the sender is the employee. Why did this happen, and what do you need to do to analyse the original message?

Answer and explanation

Why: a normal forward copies the original content into a new message that the employee sends again. The new message's trace headers record only "employee PC → company mail server → SOC mailbox", and the original message's Received lines, Return-Path and Authentication-Results are gone. The mail program may also have altered links in the body.

Fix:

  1. Ask the employee to "Forward as attachment" or save it as an .eml/.msg file and send that (or point them to the organisation's "Report phishing" button)
  2. With admin rights, pull the original directly from the mail platform — for example, download it from Microsoft 365 message trace or Defender's Explorer, or use Google Workspace's investigation tool
  3. In the original's Received lines, find the line written by our border MTA, investigate its from IP, and search for whether the same message reached other employees
  4. Advise the employee to use the report button or forward as attachment, rather than a normal forward, in future

docs.title: SPF Results and DKIM — Result Values, Reading Authentication-Results and Received-SPF, How DKIM Signatures Work
SPF Results and DKIM — Result Values, Reading Authentication-Results and Received-SPF, How DKIM Signatures Work
docs.text:
What this page covers

What the receiving server writes down after an SPF check: the seven possible results (pass, fail, softfail, neutral, none, temperror, permerror), what each really means and how a receiver and an analyst should treat it. Where those results appear in the trace headers — the short Authentication-Results: summary and the detailed Received-SPF: line — read field by field, including a cloud-mail-platform style header and a forged header planted by an attacker. Then DKIM: why a signature-based check was needed on top of SPF, how signing and verification actually work step by step, the DKIM-Signature: header tag by tag, the public key record at selector._domainkey, the DKIM result values, and what a DKIM pass does not prove. Practice questions with explanations at the end.

Labels

[Supplement] = practical material you need to know, [Correction] = a commonly repeated claim that is wrong or outdated, [Changed]/[Caution] = what has changed recently and what is risky to do the old way. All domains, IPs, keys and signatures are invented for illustration. Continues from Email Spoofing and SPF.

docs.title: The 8 key points
docs.text:
1. An SPF check always ends in one of seven results: pass, fail, softfail, neutral, none, temperror, permerror. The domain owner chooses which one a non-listed sender gets (-all, ~all, ?all); the last three come from missing or broken records and DNS problems.
  2. neutral must be treated exactly like none; softfail should not cause a rejection on its own but justifies extra suspicion; what to do with fail is the receiver's local policy.
  3. Results appear in two headers: Authentication-Results: (a short summary of SPF, DKIM, DMARC and more, defined today by RFC 8601) and Received-SPF: (the full SPF detail — client IP, envelope sender, HELO, the reason — defined in RFC 7208).
  4. Only trust the results header written by your own border server. It is identified by the name at its start (the authserv-id). An attacker can put fake Authentication-Results: ... pass lines in the message they send.
  5. DKIM is signature-based: the sending organisation's mail server signs chosen headers and the body with a private key, and publishes the public key in DNS so any receiver can verify the signature.
  6. [Correction] The selector is not "the part of the message that gets signed." It is the name of the key (s=), used to find the public key at <selector>._domainkey.<domain>. What gets signed is listed in h= (headers) and covered by bh= (body hash).
  7. In an analyst's eyes the three DKIM outcomes that matter are dkim=pass (signed and verified), dkim=none (not signed — no proof either way) and dkim=fail (signed but did not verify — altered in transit or forged).
  8. A DKIM pass proves "the domain in d= signed this, and the signed parts did not change." It does not prove that d= is the domain the user sees in From:, nor that the message is safe. Linking the two is DMARC's job.

docs.title: SPF results: what the receiver concludes
docs.text:
On the previous page we walked through how the receiving border MTA evaluates an SPF record. Once it has finished, it has to write down a conclusion, and the SPF standard (RFC 7208, section 2.6 and 8) gives it a fixed vocabulary of seven words. Think of a bouncer with a guest list at a company event:

  • Your name is on the list → come in (pass).
  • The company told the bouncer "nobody except people on this list" and you are not on it → you are not allowed (fail).
  • The company said "probably only people on the list, but don't make a scene" → let them in, but keep an eye on them (softfail).
  • The company handed over a list but said "we're not saying anything about people who aren't on it" → no opinion (neutral).
  • The company never gave the bouncer a list at all → no information (none).
  • The bouncer's phone to head office is down right now → try again later (temperror).
  • The list is unreadable — torn, two contradictory lists, too long to check → the list itself is broken (permerror).

Now the technical reality, one result at a time.

Result When it happens What it means What a receiver should do Analyst reading pass A mechanism with + (or no qualifier) matched the connecting IP The IP is authorised to send for the envelope domain Accept; the domain can now be held responsible for the message (reputation) Path is fine for that domain — now check whether it is the domain the user sees fail A - mechanism matched, usually -all The domain explicitly says this IP may not send for it Local policy: reject, junk or mark. Often left to DMARC Strong spoofing signal — unless it is forwarded mail softfail A ~ mechanism matched, usually ~all "Probably not authorised," but the owner will not make a strong statement Should not reject on this alone; may look harder at the message Suspicious; very common for real domains still tuning their records neutral A ? mechanism matched, usually ?all A record exists but says nothing definite about this IP Must treat exactly like none No evidence either way none No SPF record at all, or the domain could not be determined (e.g. empty HELO) The receiver has no information Nothing to act on from SPF In 2026 a legitimate company domain without SPF is rare — a look-alike or throwaway domain is more likely temperror A DNS timeout or server failure during the lookup A temporary problem; the answer is unknown Usually defer with a 4xx code so the sender retries Rarely meaningful on its own; check whether it repeats permerror Syntax error, two v=spf1 records, more than 10 lookups, more than 2 void lookups The record itself is broken; it cannot be evaluated Treated as unauthenticated by most receivers Usually the sender's own mistake, not an attack — but the domain is now easy to spoof

Why does the standard bother to separate neutral from none if they must be handled the same way? Purely for information: neutral tells you the domain has an SPF record but chose ?all, which is useful when you are diagnosing why a partner's mail keeps landing in junk. For a filtering decision the two are identical.

Why should softfail not cause a rejection on its own? Because ~all is the domain owner saying "I'm not completely sure my list is complete." Many organisations use ~all while they are still discovering every service that sends mail for them. If receivers rejected softfail outright, those organisations would lose real mail. So the RFC lets the receiver look more closely (raise a spam score, apply stricter content scanning) but not block on that basis alone.

Why is fail "a matter of local policy"? The SPF standard deliberately does not order receivers to reject. Each receiving organisation decides, because they know their own situation — for example, how much forwarded mail they accept (forwarded mail fails SPF legitimately, because the forwarder's IP is not on the original domain's list). Today most large receivers let the DMARC result make the final call, which can rely on DKIM instead when SPF breaks.

[Supplement] Introductory material often lists only the first five results. temperror and permerror matter in practice: a permerror on your own domain means every receiver is treating your mail as unauthenticated, and it shows up only on the receiving side.

docs.title: Where the results appear in the headers
docs.text: The receiving server records its conclusions as trace headers it adds to the top of the message, just like its Received: line (trace headers). Two headers carry SPF results.

docs.title: Authentication-Results: the short summary
docs.text:
Authentication-Results: is a single header that summarises every authentication check the receiver ran: SPF, DKIM, DMARC, and sometimes others (ARC, reverse DNS, the provider's own composite verdict). It is defined by RFC 8601 (the version referenced in older material, RFC 7001, has been replaced twice since). It gives the answers, not the reasoning.

Here is a typical one written by a self-hosted border server:

Authentication-Results: mx1.victim.example;
       spf=pass smtp.mailfrom=billing.partner.example;
       dkim=pass header.d=partner.example header.s=s2026 header.b=Kp3vT9xQ;
       dmarc=pass (p=quarantine dis=none) header.from=partner.example

Line by line:

  • Authentication-Results: mx1.victim.example; — the first value is the authserv-id: the name of the server that did the checks. This is how you know who wrote this line. It should be your own border server (or your cloud mail provider).
  • spf=pass — the SPF result, one of the seven words above.
  • smtp.mailfrom=billing.partner.example — which identity SPF checked: the domain from the envelope MAIL FROM. (If SPF had checked the HELO name instead, you would see smtp.helo=.) Note it is a subdomain used for bounces — common for billing and marketing systems.
  • dkim=pass — the DKIM result (explained below).
  • header.d=partner.example — the domain that signed the message (d= in the signature).
  • header.s=s2026 — the selector of the key used.
  • header.b=Kp3vT9xQ — the first few characters of the signature value, so you can tell which signature this result refers to when a message has several.
  • dmarc=pass (p=quarantine dis=none) — the DMARC result; the comment says the domain's policy is quarantine and the disposition applied was none (nothing, because it passed). Covered on the next page.
  • header.from=partner.example — the domain in the visible From: header, which DMARC compared against.

Cloud mail platforms add their own fields. A message received by a large hosted mail platform might carry something like this (the structure is realistic; the names are invented):

Authentication-Results: spf=pass (sender IP is 198.51.100.24)
 smtp.mailfrom=newsletter.shop.example; dkim=none (message not signed)
 header.d=none;dmarc=bestguesspass action=none
 header.from=newsletter.shop.example;compauth=pass reason=109
  • spf=pass (sender IP is 198.51.100.24) — the comment in brackets adds the connecting IP. Here there is no authserv-id at the start; on this kind of platform you identify it by its position (it is the top-most results header, added inside the provider's own network) and by the Received: lines around it.
  • dkim=none (message not signed) header.d=none — no DKIM signature at all. Not a failure; simply no evidence.
  • dmarc=bestguesspass action=none — a provider-specific value. The From: domain has no DMARC record, so the platform guessed what the result would have been if it had one. It is not a real DMARC pass.
  • compauth=pass reason=109 — the provider's own composite authentication verdict, combining SPF, DKIM, DMARC and its own reputation signals. The reason codes are documented by the provider; treat them as hints, not as standards.

docs.title: Received-SPF: the full detail
docs.text:
If you need to know why SPF reached its conclusion, look for Received-SPF:. Its format is defined in RFC 7208 section 9.1, and it carries every piece of the evaluation.

Received-SPF: Pass (mx1.victim.example: domain of billing.partner.example
    designates 198.51.100.24 as permitted sender)
    receiver=mx1.victim.example; client-ip=198.51.100.24;
    envelope-from="invoices@billing.partner.example";
    helo=out2.partner.example; identity=mailfrom;
    mechanism="ip4:198.51.100.0/27";
  • Pass — the result.
  • ( ... designates 198.51.100.24 as permitted sender) — a human-readable comment explaining the result.
  • receiver=mx1.victim.example — the server that ran the check.
  • client-ip=198.51.100.24 — the connecting IP: the one fact the sender cannot fake (why). It should match the bracketed IP in your border Received: line.
  • envelope-from="invoices@billing.partner.example" — the MAIL FROM address.
  • helo=out2.partner.example — what the sending server called itself in HELO/EHLO.
  • identity=mailfrom — which identity was checked (mailfrom or helo).
  • mechanism="ip4:198.51.100.0/27" — which part of the record matched. Very useful: it tells you exactly which authorised range or include the IP came from.

Not every server writes every optional field, but client-ip, envelope-from and helo are almost always there. Compare three real-world-shaped variants:

Received-SPF: Softfail (mx1.victim.example: domain of transitioning
    partner.example does not designate 203.0.113.66 as permitted sender)
    client-ip=203.0.113.66; envelope-from="ceo@partner.example";
    helo=mail.partner.example;

Received-SPF: PermError (mx1.victim.example: permanent error in processing
    domain of growing-co.example: too many DNS lookups)
    client-ip=192.0.2.17; envelope-from="hello@growing-co.example";

Received-SPF: None (mx1.victim.example: domain of fresh-login.example
    does not designate permitted sender hosts)
    client-ip=203.0.113.200; envelope-from="security@fresh-login.example";
  • The first: the IP 203.0.113.66 is not in partner.example's list, the record ends ~all → Softfail. Combined with a From: claiming the partner's CEO, this deserves a close look.
  • The second: the record is broken (too many DNS lookups, the 10-lookup limit from the previous page). Probably the sender's misconfiguration, not an attack.
  • The third: fresh-login.example publishes no SPF at all. Combined with a "security alert" subject, that is typical of a throwaway phishing domain.

docs.title: Pulling the results out on the command line
docs.text:
