When you have a saved message (.eml file, collected safely), you can pull out just these headers. Headers can be folded over several lines (continuation lines start with whitespace), so a plain grep only shows the first line. This short awk unfolds them first:

$ awk '/^$/{exit} /^[ \t]/{h=h" "$0; next} {if(h)print h; h=$0} END{if(h)print h}' suspicious.eml \
    | grep -iE '^(Authentication-Results|Received-SPF|DKIM-Signature|Return-Path|From):'
  • /^$/{exit} — stop at the first empty line: that is where the headers end and the body begins.
  • /^[ \t]/{h=h" "$0; next} — a line starting with a space or tab is a continuation; glue it onto the current header h.
  • {if(h)print h; h=$0} — a new header starts: print the previous one (now complete), start collecting this one.
  • END{if(h)print h} — print the last header.
  • grep -iE '^(...):' — keep only the headers we care about, case-insensitively.

Output (one header per line):

Return-Path: <invoices@billing.partner.example>
Authentication-Results: mx1.victim.example; spf=pass smtp.mailfrom=billing.partner.example; dkim=pass header.d=partner.example header.s=s2026 header.b=Kp3vT9xQ; dmarc=pass (p=quarantine dis=none) header.from=partner.example
Received-SPF: Pass (mx1.victim.example: domain of billing.partner.example designates 198.51.100.24 as permitted sender) receiver=mx1.victim.example; client-ip=198.51.100.24; envelope-from="invoices@billing.partner.example"; helo=out2.partner.example; identity=mailfrom; mechanism="ip4:198.51.100.0/27";
DKIM-Signature: v=1; a=rsa-sha256; c=relaxed/relaxed; d=partner.example; s=s2026; ...
From: "Partner Billing" <billing@partner.example>

docs.title: [Supplement] Forged results headers
docs.text:
An attacker controls everything in the message they hand over, including headers that look like authentication results. They can simply write:

Authentication-Results: mx1.victim.example;
       spf=pass smtp.mailfrom=victim.example;
       dkim=pass header.d=victim.example;
       dmarc=pass header.from=victim.example

and put it in the message before sending. It looks perfect — it even uses your server's name. This is the same problem as forged Received: lines on the headers page, and the defence is the same idea:

  1. Find the results header your own border server added. It is the one at the top, directly above or next to your border Received: line. Anything below your border Received: line arrived with the message from outside and was written by someone else.
  2. RFC 8601 tells receivers to remove any incoming Authentication-Results: that carries their own authserv-id, precisely to stop this trick. Most modern servers do; older or misconfigured ones may not. If you see two results headers with your server's name, the lower one is a fake that slipped through.
  3. Results headers from other organisations (for example a partner's server that handled the message earlier) are only as trustworthy as that organisation. Use them as context, not as proof.

docs.title: Why a second check was needed
docs.text:
SPF looks only at the path: which IP handed the message over. That has two big weaknesses:

  • Forwarding breaks it. When a university alias or a mailing list forwards a message, it arrives from the forwarder's IP, which is not on the original domain's list → SPF fails even though the message is genuine.
  • It says nothing about the content. A message could pass SPF and still have been changed along the way.

DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail, RFC 6376) solves both by attaching proof to the message itself instead of relying on where it came from. Analogy: SPF is checking which post office van delivered the parcel. DKIM is a tamper-evident wax seal stamped with the company's crest. Whoever carries the parcel, and however many vans it changes, the recipient can look at the seal: if it is intact and matches the crest the company published, the parcel came from that company and has not been opened.

The technical reality behind the "seal" is a digital signature using public-key cryptography (RSA, or the newer Ed25519). The sending organisation keeps a private key secret on its mail servers and publishes the matching public key in DNS. Only the private key can create a valid signature; anyone with the public key can check one.

docs.title: How signing works, step by step
docs.text:
Setup, done once by the domain owner:

  1. Generate a key pair.
  2. Pick a selector — just a label for this key, such as s2026, mail1 or a vendor's name. Different services can have different keys, each with its own selector.
  3. Publish the public key as a TXT record at <selector>._domainkey.<domain>, e.g. s2026._domainkey.partner.example.
  4. Install the private key on the outbound mail server or gateway (or let the cloud mail provider hold it).

For every message sent:

  1. The sending mail server — not the user's mail client — prepares to sign. The user never sees or holds the key; signing is done centrally for all outgoing mail of that stream.
  2. It canonicalises the message: normalises things that harmless relays commonly change, such as extra whitespace or header capitalisation (c=relaxed), or changes nothing (c=simple, strict).
  3. It hashes the body (SHA-256) and stores the result in bh= (body hash).
  4. It takes the headers it has chosen to protect — listed in h=, for example From, To, Subject, Date, Message-ID — plus the new DKIM-Signature: header itself (with b= still empty), hashes them, and signs that hash with the private key. The result goes into b=.
  5. It adds the finished DKIM-Signature: header to the top of the message and sends it.

For every message received, the verifier:

  1. Reads d= and s= from the DKIM-Signature: header.
  2. Fetches the public key from DNS: TXT s= + ._domainkey. + d=.
  3. Canonicalises and hashes the body itself and compares it with bh=. If they differ, the body was changed → fail.
  4. Canonicalises and hashes the headers listed in h= and checks the signature in b= with the public key. If it does not verify, the headers were changed or the signature is not from that key → fail.
  5. Both succeed → pass.

[Correction] You will often read two simplifications. First, that the selector "chooses which parts of the email are signed." It does not; the selector only names the key. Which parts are covered is set by h= (headers) and the body hash bh= (always the body, optionally limited by l=). Second, that "the hash is encrypted with the private key." That is a loose description of RSA signing; it is better to think of it as a signature that only the private key can produce and anyone with the public key can verify. With Ed25519 there is no "encryption" involved at all.

docs.title: The DKIM-Signature header tag by tag
docs.text:
DKIM-Signature: v=1; a=rsa-sha256; c=relaxed/relaxed; d=partner.example;
        s=s2026; t=1795047600; x=1795652400;
        h=from:from:to:subject:date:message-id:mime-version:content-type;
        bh=lNXsHoS7vr6QrKDmysIJdvi6qfRmHA6shFtOVsiEKWc=;
        b=Kp3vT9xQm1Lr8bW0zYc4H6s2nDqPfE7uJ0aVxR5tKyM9...(about 340 characters)...
Tag Example Meaning v= 1 Version. Always 1 a= rsa-sha256 Algorithm: RSA signature over a SHA-256 hash. Also seen: ed25519-sha256. rsa-sha1 is obsolete and must no longer be used for signing c= relaxed/relaxed Canonicalisation for headers/body. relaxed tolerates whitespace and case changes; simple tolerates nothing d= partner.example The signing domain — the domain taking responsibility. The most important tag for an analyst s= s2026 Selector — the name of the key. Public key is at s2026._domainkey.partner.example t= 1795047600 Signing time, Unix seconds (here 2026-11-19 00:20 UTC) x= 1795652400 Expiry; after this the signature should not be accepted (here 7 days later) h= from:from:to:... Which headers are signed, in order. from appears twice on purpose — see below bh= lNXs...KWc= Base64 of the SHA-256 hash of the canonicalised body b= Kp3v... Base64 of the signature itself i= @partner.example Optional: the identity (user or subdomain) on whose behalf it was signed l= 1250 Optional: only the first N bytes of the body are covered. Dangerous: anything appended after them is not protected

The t= value converted: date -u -d @1795047600 prints Thu Nov 19 00:20:00 UTC 2026.

Why is from listed twice in h=? It is called over-signing. A verifier processes h= from the bottom of the header block upwards; listing from twice means "there is exactly one From:, and also sign the absence of a second one." Without it, an attacker could add a second From: header to a validly signed message, and some mail clients would display the added one while the signature still verified. Over-signing makes any added From: break the signature.

You can see how sensitive the body hash is with a one-line demonstration. Here are two bodies that differ by one character:

$ printf 'Please find the March invoice attached.\r\n' | openssl dgst -sha256 -binary | base64
lNXsHoS7vr6QrKDmysIJdvi6qfRmHA6shFtOVsiEKWc=

$ printf 'Please find the March invoice attached!\r\n' | openssl dgst -sha256 -binary | base64
dkZtOlxcLddR9/RIEYqlxeE/GcjT4zZZlrPMk+zMuss=
  • printf '...\r\n' — the body, with the line ending email uses (CR LF).
  • openssl dgst -sha256 -binary — compute the SHA-256 hash as raw bytes.
  • base64 — encode it the way DKIM writes it in bh= (Base64).
  • Changing . to ! produces a completely different hash. If an attacker (or a mailing list adding a footer) changes a single character of the body, bh= no longer matches and DKIM fails with a message such as "body hash did not verify."

(A real signer first applies canonicalisation to the whole body; for a one-line body with no trailing spaces, simple and relaxed give the same bytes as above.)

docs.title: The public key in DNS
docs.text:
$ dig +short TXT s2026._domainkey.partner.example
"v=DKIM1; k=rsa; " "p=MIIBIjANBgkqhkiG9w0BAQEFAAOCAQ8AMIIBCgKCAQEAx4Lr2Vq9...(about 390 characters)...IDAQAB"
  • s2026._domainkey.partner.example — selector + the fixed label _domainkey + the signing domain.
  • The answer comes back as two quoted strings. A single TXT string may be at most 255 characters, and a 2048-bit RSA key is longer, so it is split; the receiver joins the pieces.
  • v=DKIM1 — version of the key record.
  • k=rsa — key type (ed25519 for Ed25519 keys).
  • p=MIIB...IDAQAB — the public key in Base64. MIIB... is the usual start of a 2048-bit RSA public key; IDAQAB is the usual end.
  • Optional: t=y means "testing mode — don't treat failures harshly"; t=s means i= must not use a subdomain; h=sha256 restricts hash algorithms.
  • p= empty ("v=DKIM1; p=") means the key has been revoked. Any signature using that selector fails. Domains do this when they retire a key.

Selectors are also a small source of recon: common selector names reveal which mail and marketing services a company uses, in the same way SPF includes do.

docs.title: DKIM result values
docs.text:
Authentication-Results: reports one DKIM result per signature. A message may carry several signatures (for example one by the company, one by its mail provider), and each gets its own result.

Result Meaning Analyst reading pass Signed, key found, body hash and signature both verified The d= domain signed it and the signed parts are unchanged fail Signed, but verification failed (body changed, header changed, wrong key) Altered in transit (often a mailing list or security gateway rewriting content) or forged none No signature at all No evidence. Not proof of spoofing, but legitimate bulk senders are now required to sign neutral Signature present but could not be processed (e.g. a syntax problem) Treat like none policy Signature valid, but the receiver will not accept it (e.g. l= used, or a weak key) Look at why — sometimes a sign of a poor signer temperror Key lookup failed temporarily (DNS timeout) Retry later permerror Key record missing or broken, or key revoked (p= empty) Signer's configuration problem — or a signature naming a selector that never existed

Typical result lines and how to read them:

dkim=pass header.d=partner.example header.s=s2026 header.b=Kp3vT9xQ
dkim=fail (body hash did not verify) header.d=partner.example header.s=s2026 header.b=Kp3vT9xQ
dkim=none (message not signed)
dkim=permerror (no key for signature) header.d=partner.example header.s=old2019
  • The second line: the signature itself is fine but the body changed — classic after a list server adds a footer or a gateway rewrites links.
  • The fourth: the message names a selector old2019 that has no key in DNS. Either the company deleted an old key while something still uses it, or someone copied a signature header without understanding it.

docs.title: What DKIM does not prove
docs.text:
• d= does not have to match From:. Any domain can sign any message. An attacker can register lookalike-pay.example, sign perfectly with d=lookalike-pay.example, and write From: <ceo@victim.example>. The result is a genuine dkim=pass — for the wrong domain. DMARC alignment (next page) is what requires the d= domain to match the visible From: domain.
  • A pass does not mean the content is safe. A compromised account on a legitimate platform sends perfectly signed phishing.
  • Replay. Because a signature stays valid until it expires, an attacker who gets one genuinely signed message from a reputable domain (for example by signing up for its service and receiving a message whose signed headers and body they can use) can resend that exact message to thousands of other recipients. Each copy verifies. Unsigned headers such as To: (if not in h=) can be changed without breaking it. This is why short x= expiry and signing To: matter.
  • It does not encrypt anything. The message is still readable by every server it passes; DKIM only proves origin and integrity.

[Supplement] Forwarding that changes the message (mailing lists adding subject tags or footers, gateways rewriting URLs) breaks DKIM as well as SPF. The answer to that is ARC (Authenticated Received Chain, RFC 8617): each intermediary records the results it saw and seals them, so the final receiver can choose to trust "it passed when the list received it." You will see ARC-Authentication-Results:, ARC-Message-Signature: and ARC-Seal: headers on such messages.

docs.title: How the SOC uses SPF results and DKIM
docs.text:
• Start every phishing triage at your own results header. Find the top Authentication-Results: written by your border/cloud mail service. Read spf=, dkim= and dmarc= together, and note smtp.mailfrom, header.d and header.from. If the three domains differ from each other, ask why.
  • Use Received-SPF: to explain. client-ip + mechanism tell you which authorised range or vendor include the IP came from. A pass via a big shared platform's include only proves "sent through that platform."
  • Treat dkim=fail with context. A body hash failure on a message that went through a mailing list is normal; a failure on a direct message from a bank is not.
  • Ignore results headers below your border. Any Authentication-Results: that came in with the message is attacker-controllable.
  • For your own domains: monitor that every sending service signs with your domain (not just the vendor's), that keys are 2048-bit RSA or Ed25519, that old selectors are revoked, and that your SPF stays under 10 lookups. DMARC aggregate reports (next page) are the tool for this.

docs.title: The 2026 view
docs.text:
[2026 Current] Still valid

The seven SPF results and how receivers treat them are unchanged; RFC 7208 is still the SPF standard and Received-SPF: still has the same format. DKIM is still RFC 6376 with the same tags, the same selector._domainkey key lookup and the same pass/fail/none outcomes, and "look for dkim=pass, then check which domain passed" is still the right habit. Reading your own border server's Authentication-Results: first is still the core of email triage.

[Changed] What has changed

  • Authentication-Results: is now defined by RFC 8601, which replaced RFC 7001 (via RFC 7601). The header looks the same to an analyst.
  • DKIM became mandatory for bulk mail. Since 2024 Gmail and Yahoo require bulk senders to have SPF, DKIM and DMARC with an aligned From: domain, and Microsoft applied similar rules for high-volume senders to Outlook.com from May 2025. dkim=none on mail from a large, legitimate sender is therefore now unusual.
  • Stronger keys and a new algorithm. RFC 8301 (2018) says rsa-sha1 must not be used for signing and keys must be at least 1024 bits, with 2048 recommended. RFC 8463 added ed25519-sha256. In practice 2048-bit RSA is the norm and Ed25519 is usually published alongside RSA rather than instead of it, because not every verifier supports it.
  • DMARC is now a Proposed Standard (RFC 9989–9991, replacing RFC 7489), which changes how SPF and DKIM results are combined — covered on the next page.
  • DKIM replay became a mainstream problem, and the IETF is working on a redesigned "DKIM2" to resist replay and survive forwarding. As of late 2026 it is still a draft, not a standard; do not expect to see it in production headers yet.
  • Cloud platforms dominate. Most organisations' mail is signed by a hosted mail provider, and providers add their own composite verdicts (like compauth) alongside the standard results.

[Caution] Wrong or risky to do the old way

  • Do not trust dkim=pass or spf=pass on its own. Always check which domain passed (header.d, smtp.mailfrom) against the visible From:. A pass for the attacker's own domain is worthless.
  • Do not trust an Authentication-Results: you did not verify the author of. Use only the header written by your own border or cloud mail service.
  • Do not treat dkim=none as proof of spoofing, or dkim=fail always as an attack. Context (mailing lists, gateways rewriting links) matters.
  • Do not keep 1024-bit or rsa-sha1 keys, never use l=, and revoke old selectors (publish an empty p=) instead of leaving keys in DNS forever. A leaked or crackable old key lets anyone sign as you.
  • Do not describe the selector as "the part of the email that is signed." It is the key's name; the signed parts are in h= and bh=.

docs.title: Question 1
docs.text:
A user reports a message that "passed all checks". The top of its header block looks like this (oldest lines are lower). What is wrong, and what is the real authentication result?

Authentication-Results: mx1.victim.example;
       spf=softfail smtp.mailfrom=victim.example;
       dkim=none;
       dmarc=fail (p=none dis=none) header.from=victim.example
Received: from mail.victim.example (unknown [203.0.113.66])
        by mx1.victim.example (Postfix) with ESMTP id 7HnQ2c; Thu, 19 Nov 2026 03:05:11 +0000
Authentication-Results: mx1.victim.example;
       spf=pass smtp.mailfrom=victim.example;
       dkim=pass header.d=victim.example;
       dmarc=pass header.from=victim.example
From: "IT Service Desk" <it-support@victim.example>
Subject: Password expires today - confirm here
Answer and explanation

There are two results headers with our own authserv-id mx1.victim.example. The one below our border Received: line (the "everything passed" one) arrived inside the message from 203.0.113.66 — the attacker wrote it. Our server should have removed it (RFC 8601 says to strip incoming results headers carrying our own name), so this also points to a configuration gap worth fixing.

The real result is the top one, added by mx1 after the border Received: line: spf=softfail (the IP 203.0.113.66 is not in victim.example's list, which ends ~all), dkim=none (not signed), dmarc=fail. Our own domain's DMARC policy is only p=none, so nothing blocked it. Conclusion: an outside server impersonating our IT desk. Next steps: block the IP, search other mailboxes for the same subject/IP, and consider moving our DMARC policy beyond p=none.

docs.title: Question 2
docs.text:
A message shows From: "Partner Billing" <billing@partner.example> and this result. DKIM passed. Is the message proven to come from partner.example?

Authentication-Results: mx1.victim.example;
       spf=pass smtp.mailfrom=bounce.mailer-hub.example;
       dkim=pass header.d=mailer-hub.example header.s=k1 header.b=Zx81PqWe
Answer and explanation

No. Both checks passed, but for mailer-hub.example, not for partner.example:

  • smtp.mailfrom=bounce.mailer-hub.example — SPF only proved the bulk-mail platform's server was allowed to send for the platform's own bounce domain.
  • header.d=mailer-hub.example — the signature was made by the platform's key, not the partner's.
  • The visible From: domain partner.example was checked by neither.

This could be a legitimate partner who uses that platform but never set up DKIM for its own domain — or anyone else with an account on that platform pretending to be the partner. DKIM proves "the d= domain signed this"; whether d= matches From: is DMARC alignment, which this message would fail. Treat it as unverified: compare with earlier genuine mail from the partner (did it carry header.d=partner.example?), and confirm any payment change by phone using a known number.

docs.title: Question 3
docs.text:
Two copies of a newsletter from shop.example arrive: one directly, one via an internal mailing list that adds [staff-list] to the subject and a footer to the body. Results:

Direct:     dkim=pass header.d=shop.example header.s=s1
Via list:   dkim=fail (body hash did not verify) header.d=shop.example header.s=s1

The DKIM-Signature has h=from:to:subject:date:message-id. Why did the list copy fail, and which change alone would already have been enough to break it? Is this an attack?

Answer and explanation

"Body hash did not verify" means the verifier's hash of the body no longer matches bh=. The list added a footer to the body, so the body changed → hash mismatch. That alone is enough to fail.

The subject tag would also have broken it on its own, because subject is listed in h=: changing a signed header makes the signature in b= fail. (Here the verifier reported the body hash first.)

This is not an attack. It is the normal side effect of a mailing list modifying messages, and it is exactly why ARC exists: the list server can record "DKIM passed when I received it" in ARC headers, and the final receiver can choose to trust that chain. As an analyst, the clue is the context: the same d= and selector pass on the direct copy, and the list copy shows the list's own Received: line and modifications.

docs.title: Email Spoofing and SPF — Why SMTP Trusts Anyone, Spoofed Injection, the Three Defences, How SPF Works
Email Spoofing and SPF — Why SMTP Trusts Anyone, Spoofed Injection, the Three Defences, How SPF Works
docs.text:
What this page covers

Why the original SMTP design accepts any sender address without question, and what a spoofed message looks like at the SMTP level. How an attacker skips the login step that normal users go through by talking straight to the recipient's border MTA (spoofed email injection). The three standards built to close the gap — SPF, DKIM and DMARC — and which identity each one checks. Then SPF in detail: what the receiving server compares, why the connecting IP is the anchor, how to read an SPF record mechanism by mechanism with dig, how an evaluation is walked through, the 10-DNS-lookup and void-lookup limits, and what SPF does not protect. Practice questions with explanations at the end.

Labels

[Supplement] = practical material you need to know, [Correction] = a commonly repeated claim that is wrong or outdated, [Changed]/[Caution] = what has changed recently and what is risky to do the old way. All domains and IPs are invented for illustration. Continues from Reading Email Headers.

docs.title: The 8 key points
docs.text:
1. SMTP was designed in an era when nobody expected abuse. It does not check whether the sender is who they claim to be. Any server can write any address in MAIL FROM and From:.
  2. Normal users must log in (SMTP AUTH) to their own submission server before sending. An attacker simply skips that step and connects straight to the recipient's border MTA on port 25, which has to accept mail from the whole internet without a login.
  3. Three standards fill the gap: SPF (was this sent from a server the domain authorised?), DKIM (was the message signed by the domain, and is it unchanged?), DMARC (does the visible From: domain match a domain that passed SPF or DKIM, and what should happen if not?).
  4. SPF is path-based: the receiving MTA compares the connecting IP with a list of allowed senders that the domain publishes in a DNS TXT record.
  5. The connecting IP is the anchor because a TCP connection cannot be completed from a forged IP — the handshake reply would go to the real owner of that address.
  6. [Correction] SPF checks the envelope sender (MAIL FROM / Return-Path) and the HELO name, not the From: header the user sees. That gap is exactly what DMARC closes.
  7. An SPF record is read left to right; the first mechanism that matches decides the result, and the qualifier in front (+ - ~ ?) says pass, fail, softfail or neutral. all at the end catches everything else.
  8. One SPF evaluation may cause at most 10 DNS lookups (include, a, mx, ptr, exists, redirect) and at most 2 void lookups. Exceed either and the result is permerror — SPF silently stops working.

docs.title: Why SMTP is so easy to spoof
docs.text:
The first SMTP specification dates from 1982. The internet then was a small network of universities and research labs whose administrators largely knew each other. Nobody designed for an attacker who would lie about who they are, so the protocol has no step where the receiving server asks "prove that you are allowed to send for this address." The server simply records what it is told.

Think of the old postal system. You can write any return address you like on the back of an envelope, and the post office will still deliver it. Nobody at the post office checks whether you really live at the address you wrote. SMTP works the same way: the "return address" (MAIL FROM) and the "letterhead" (From: in the header) are both just text the sender types.

Here is what that looks like in practice. An attacker on a rented server at 203.0.113.66 connects to the mail server of victim.example and claims to be the company's own CEO.

$ nc mx1.victim.example 25
220 mx1.victim.example ESMTP Postfix
EHLO mail.victim.example
250-mx1.victim.example
250-PIPELINING
250-SIZE 52428800
250-STARTTLS
250 8BITMIME
MAIL FROM:<ceo@victim.example>
250 2.1.0 Ok
RCPT TO:<finance@victim.example>
250 2.1.5 Ok
DATA
354 End data with <CR><LF>.<CR><LF>
From: "Jane Park (CEO)" <ceo@victim.example>
To: finance@victim.example
Subject: Urgent - payment needed today

Please process the vendor payment I sent earlier before 3pm. I'm in meetings, reply by email only.
.
250 2.0.0 Ok: queued as 4QzK7m2XyZ
QUIT
221 2.0.0 Bye

Line by line:

  • nc mx1.victim.example 25 — open a raw TCP connection to the recipient's MX on the server-to-server SMTP port. No mail client is needed; SMTP is plain text.
  • 220 ... ESMTP Postfix — the server greets and announces its software.
  • EHLO mail.victim.example — the attacker introduces itself as the victim's own mail server. This is just a string; nothing checks it.
  • 250-... lines — the server lists its extensions. Notice there is no AUTH offered here — a receiving MX does not ask outside servers to log in.
  • MAIL FROM:<ceo@victim.example> — the envelope sender, set to the CEO. The server answers 250 Ok: accepted without question.
  • RCPT TO:<finance@victim.example> — the envelope recipient, the finance team. Accepted.
  • DATA / 354 — the server is ready for the message itself.
  • From: "Jane Park (CEO)" <ceo@victim.example> — the header From, the address the user will actually see. Also just text.
  • The line containing only . ends the message. 250 2.0.0 Ok: queued as 4QzK7m2XyZ means the message has been accepted and queued for delivery.

The only honest piece of information in this whole exchange is something the attacker never typed: the IP address the TCP connection came from, which mx1 records in its Received line.

Received: from mail.victim.example (unknown [203.0.113.66])
        by mx1.victim.example (Postfix) with ESMTP id 4QzK7m2XyZ
        for <finance@victim.example>; Thu, 19 Nov 2026 01:12:40 +0000 (UTC)

As on the previous page: the EHLO name says mail.victim.example, but the reverse DNS is unknown and the bracketed IP is an outside address. Without an extra check, though, the finance team's mail client just shows "Jane Park (CEO)".

[Supplement] Many modern mail servers and cloud mail platforms add their own rule on top — "reject or quarantine mail from the internet that claims to be from our own domain" — precisely because this attack is so cheap. That rule exists because SMTP itself never had one.

docs.title: Spoofed email injection: skipping the login
docs.text:
How does an honest employee send mail? Their mail client (MUA) talks to the company's submission server on port 587, and that server requires a login before it will accept anything.

$ openssl s_client -starttls smtp -connect smtp.victim.example:587 -quiet
250 smtp.victim.example
EHLO laptop-7q2
250-smtp.victim.example
250-AUTH LOGIN PLAIN
250-SIZE 52428800
250 8BITMIME
AUTH LOGIN
334 VXNlcm5hbWU6
amFuZUB2aWN0aW0uZXhhbXBsZQ==
334 UGFzc3dvcmQ6
************************
235 2.7.0 Authentication successful
MAIL FROM:<jane@victim.example>
250 2.1.0 Ok
  • openssl s_client -starttls smtp -connect ...:587 — connect to the submission port and upgrade to TLS with STARTTLS (so the login below is encrypted on the wire). -quiet hides the certificate dump.
  • 250-AUTH LOGIN PLAIN — this server offers authentication (the ESMTP AUTH extension). On a submission server, it is mandatory.
  • AUTH LOGIN — the client starts a login.
  • 334 VXNlcm5hbWU6 — the server's prompt in Base64. Decoded it is Username: (Base64). Base64 is encoding, not encryption — that is why TLS must already be on.
  • amFuZUB2aWN0aW0uZXhhbXBsZQ== — the username in Base64 (jane@victim.example).
  • 334 UGFzc3dvcmQ6 — Password:; the client then sends the Base64 password (masked here).
  • 235 2.7.0 Authentication successful — logged in. Only now will the server accept MAIL FROM, and a well-configured server will also check that Jane is allowed to use that sender address.

So the sending side does verify its own users. The problem is the receiving side:

 Normal path                                           Attacker's path
┌───────────┐ login (AUTH) ┌───────────────┐          ┌───────────────┐
│ Jane's MUA│─────────────▶│ victim.example│          │ Attacker's    │
└───────────┘   port 587   │ submission/MTA│          │ server        │
                           └──────┬────────┘          │ 203.0.113.66  │
                                  │ SMTP 25            └──────┬────────┘
                                  ▼ (no login)                │ SMTP 25 (no login)
                           ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
                           │  Recipient's border MTA (MX)           │
                           │  "Anyone may hand me mail for my users" │
                           └─────────────────────────────────────────┘

The recipient's border MTA must accept mail from any server on the internet without a login — otherwise nobody could email that organisation. So it cannot tell the difference between "a message that went through the sender's login check" and "a message an attacker handed over directly." Both arrive the same way, on port 25, from some IP, with a claimed sender. If the receiving MTA has no way to verify the claim, it believes what the headers say. For many years, that was simply how email worked.

The analogy: the honest letter goes through the sender's local post office, where the clerk checks ID. The forged letter is walked straight to the recipient's local post office and dropped in the slot — that office never sees the sender's ID check and has no idea it was skipped.

docs.title: Three ways to verify the source
docs.text:
The ideas for closing the gap are simple, and each became a standard:

  1. Check that the sending server was pre-authorised by the domain → SPF (Sender Policy Framework).
  2. Have the sending gateway sign the message with a private key, and publish the public key so anyone can verify → DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail).
  3. Make sure the address the user sees is not a trick — tie the visible From: domain to a domain that actually passed a check, and let the domain owner say what to do on failure → DMARC (Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting and Conformance).
SPF DKIM DMARC Type Path-based (where did it come from?) Signature-based (who signed it, is it intact?) Policy + alignment (does it match what the user sees?) What is checked Connecting IP vs allowed list Signature over chosen headers and body That SPF or DKIM passed for the same domain as From: Identity checked Envelope MAIL FROM (and HELO) The d= domain in the signature The header From: domain Published where TXT record on the domain TXT record at selector._domainkey.domain TXT record at _dmarc.domain Survives forwarding? Usually breaks (new IP) Usually survives if the message is not altered Depends on which of the two survives Covered on This page Next page Later page

The receiving server writes the outcome of all three into an Authentication-Results: trace header. The format was first standardised in 2009 (RFC 5451), revised several times, and the current version is RFC 8601. A typical line looks like this — the next pages take it apart field by field:

Authentication-Results: mx1.victim.example;
       spf=fail smtp.mailfrom=victim.example;
       dkim=none;
       dmarc=fail (p=reject) header.from=victim.example

docs.title: What the receiving MTA compares
docs.text:
For every incoming connection the receiving border MTA has two things:

  • A claimed domain — taken from the envelope MAIL FROM (for ceo@victim.example, the domain victim.example), or from the HELO/EHLO name.
  • A real connecting IP — the address at the other end of the TCP connection.

It then asks DNS: "What does victim.example say about which servers may send its mail?" and compares the answer with the connecting IP.

 Attacker 203.0.113.66 ──┐                      ┌── DNS TXT for victim.example:
                         │                      │   "v=spf1 ip4:198.51.100.0/28 ... -all"
 victim.example's MTA ───┼──▶ Recipient's MX ───┤
 198.51.100.5            │     1. Who is calling? (IP)
                         │     2. Who do they claim to be? (MAIL FROM domain)
                         │     3. Is that IP on the domain's list?
                         └──▶  198.51.100.5 → listed     → spf=pass
                               203.0.113.66 → not listed → spf=fail

Analogy: the receiving post office now has a register of approved sorting offices for each company, published by the company itself. A letter claiming to be from victim.example that arrives from an office not on the list is flagged.

docs.title: Why the connecting IP can be trusted
docs.text:
Everything else in the SMTP exchange is text the sender chooses. The connecting IP is different because SMTP runs over TCP, and TCP will not let a connection open without a three-way handshake:

Attacker (real IP 203.0.113.66, pretending to be 198.51.100.5)
  1. SYN      src=198.51.100.5  →  mx1
  2. SYN-ACK  mx1  →  dst=198.51.100.5     ← goes to the REAL 198.51.100.5, not the attacker
  3. ACK      (attacker never saw step 2's sequence number, so cannot answer correctly)
  → No connection, so no SMTP conversation

The attacker can put a fake source address on a single packet, but the reply goes to the real owner of that address. Without the reply, the attacker cannot complete the handshake, so it can never get as far as MAIL FROM. That is why the IP that mx1 records is real.

[Supplement] "Real" is not the same as "innocent." The IP is genuinely the machine that delivered the message — but that machine might be a cheap VPS the attacker rented, or a legitimate server the attacker has compromised, or a legitimate mail platform the attacker has an account on. In the last two cases SPF will happily pass. SPF answers "did an authorised server deliver this?", not "is this message safe?"

docs.title: [Correction] Which "from" SPF actually checks
docs.text:
It is common to read that SPF "looks at the From line." It does not look at the header From: the user sees. RFC 7208 defines two identities SPF checks:

Identity Where it comes from When it is used MAIL FROM The envelope sender in the SMTP conversation; later copied into Return-Path: Always, for normal mail HELO The name in HELO/EHLO Recommended as well; and the only identity when MAIL FROM:<> is empty (bounce messages)

This matters enormously. An attacker can do this:

MAIL FROM:<bounce@mailer.lookalike-pay.example>     ← attacker's own domain, with a valid SPF record
...
From: "Jane Park (CEO)" <ceo@victim.example>        ← what the user sees

SPF checks lookalike-pay.example, finds the attacker's IP on the attacker's own list, and returns pass. The user still sees ceo@victim.example. SPF alone does nothing about the address on screen. DMARC's "alignment" requirement — the SPF-passing domain must match the From: domain — is what closes this.

docs.title: Looking it up with dig
docs.text:
An SPF record is an ordinary DNS TXT record on the domain itself, starting with v=spf1 (DNS records).

$ dig +short TXT victim.example
"site-verification=Xa91kPq2v0m"
"v=spf1 ip4:198.51.100.0/28 ip6:2001:db8:25::/48 a:mail.victim.example mx include:_spf.mailvendor.example include:spf.crm-cloud.example -all"
  • dig — the DNS lookup tool.
  • +short — print only the answer data.
  • TXT victim.example — ask for all TXT records of the domain. A domain often has several (site ownership proofs and so on). Only the one starting with v=spf1 is SPF, and there must be exactly one — two v=spf1 records give a permerror.

docs.title: The record piece by piece
docs.text:
Part Meaning DNS lookups it costs v=spf1 Version tag. Must be first; it is what marks the TXT record as SPF — ip4:198.51.100.0/28 Any IPv4 address in this range (198.51.100.0–15) matches 0 ip6:2001:db8:25::/48 Any IPv6 address in this range matches 0 a:mail.victim.example Look up the A/AAAA records of that host; match if the connecting IP is one of them. Plain a means "the domain's own A record" 1 mx Look up the domain's MX hosts, then their addresses; match if the IP is one of the mail servers 1 (+ address lookups of up to 10 MX hosts) include:_spf.mailvendor.example Evaluate another domain's SPF record; if that evaluation passes, this mechanism matches. This is how you authorise a mail provider 1 + whatever the included record costs include:spf.crm-cloud.example Same, for a second service (a CRM platform that sends mail on the company's behalf) 1 + its cost -all all matches everything. With - in front, anything not matched earlier fails 0

Other parts you will meet:

  • exists:<domain> — match if the domain has any A record; used with macros for advanced setups. Costs 1 lookup.
  • ptr — match on reverse DNS. Deprecated in RFC 7208 (slow and unreliable); do not use it and treat its presence as a sign of an old record.
  • redirect=<domain> — a modifier, not a mechanism: "if nothing here matched, use that domain's record instead." Common for organisations that manage many domains centrally. Costs 1.
  • exp=<domain> — modifier pointing to an explanation text for rejections. Rarely seen.

docs.title: Qualifiers: what a match means
docs.text:
Each mechanism can have a prefix. If you write none, + is assumed.

Qualifier Result on match Meaning to the receiver + (default) pass Authorised - fail Explicitly not authorised — "hard fail" ~ softfail Probably not authorised; accept but treat as suspicious ? neutral The domain makes no statement

So the end of the record expresses the domain owner's confidence: -all ("anything else is definitely not us"), ~all ("anything else is probably not us"), ?all ("we're not saying"), or the dangerous +all ("anyone in the world may send as us" — effectively no SPF at all, and sometimes a sign of a misconfiguration or a tampered record).

docs.title: Following an include
docs.text:
include is a pointer to another list, so the receiver fetches that too.

$ dig +short TXT _spf.mailvendor.example
"v=spf1 ip4:192.0.2.0/25 include:_spf2.mailvendor.example ~all"

$ dig +short TXT _spf2.mailvendor.example
"v=spf1 ip6:2001:db8:ee::/48 ~all"

$ dig +short TXT spf.crm-cloud.example
"v=spf1 ip4:198.51.100.128/25 -all"
  • The mail vendor's list has an IPv4 range and includes yet another list — includes can nest.
  • An important subtlety: inside an include, the included record's own ~all/-all only means "no match here"; it does not end the outer evaluation. The outer record carries on to its next mechanism.

docs.title: Walking through an evaluation
docs.text:
Take the spoofed message from the top of the page: MAIL FROM:<ceo@victim.example>, connecting IP 203.0.113.66.

v=spf1                                   start
ip4:198.51.100.0/28           203.0.113.66 in 198.51.100.0-15?            no
ip6:2001:db8:25::/48          IPv4 address, IPv6 range                    no
a:mail.victim.example         mail.victim.example → 198.51.100.5          no   (lookup 1)
mx                            MX → mx1, mx2 → 198.51.100.2, .3            no   (lookup 2)
include:_spf.mailvendor...    192.0.2.0/25?                               no   (lookup 3)
   include:_spf2.mailvendor   2001:db8:ee::/48?                           no   (lookup 4)
   ~all                       → inner "no match", go back out
include:spf.crm-cloud...      198.51.100.128/25?                          no   (lookup 5)
-all                          matches everything                          → FAIL

Result: spf=fail. The receiver now knows that victim.example has stated this IP is not one of its senders. What it does with that — reject, send to junk, or just note it — is its own policy decision, and later DMARC lets the domain owner express a preference.

Now the honest message from Jane, sent via the company's server at 198.51.100.5: the very first mechanism ip4:198.51.100.0/28 matches with the default +, evaluation stops immediately, and the result is spf=pass. Order matters: the first match wins, so nothing after it is even looked up.

docs.title: The 10-lookup limit and void lookups
docs.text:
Each SPF check could cause the receiver to make many DNS queries, which could be abused to make mail servers attack DNS servers. So RFC 7208 sets hard limits:

  • At most 10 DNS-querying terms per evaluation: include, a, mx, ptr, exists and redirect each count 1, including those inside nested includes. ip4, ip6 and all cost nothing.
  • At most 2 void lookups — queries that come back with no answer or NXDOMAIN (for example an include pointing to a domain that no longer exists).
  • Exceeding either gives permerror ("the record is broken").

Count the example: a(1) + mx(1) + include mailvendor(1) + its nested include(1) + include crm-cloud(1) = 5 of 10. Fine. But a growing company that keeps adding services — mail suite, marketing platform, CRM, ticketing, HR system — each with its own nested includes, can quietly pass 10. Then every receiver gets permerror and, depending on its policy, treats the domain's mail as unauthenticated. This is one of the most common real-world SPF failures, and it often appears after a perfectly innocent change.

[Supplement] Other common record faults: two v=spf1 records (permerror), a typo such as ip4:198.51.100.0/33 or inculde: (permerror), a record longer than 255 characters not split into quoted strings, and an include of a service the company stopped using years ago (its domain may lapse and be registered by someone else — who could then authorise their own servers).

docs.title: How the SOC uses SPF
docs.text:
• Checking a suspicious message. From the border Received line take the connecting IP; from the envelope (Return-Path:) take the domain. Read the receiver's Received-SPF:/Authentication-Results: result, and if needed run dig TXT yourself to see why. A message claiming to be from a bank but delivered from a VPS IP not in the bank's record is a strong signal.
  • "Partners say they got mail from us that we didn't send." First check our own record: is there one, does it end in -all or ~all, is it under 10 lookups? Without SPF (and DKIM/DMARC), other organisations have no way to tell our mail from forgeries.
  • Comparing Return-Path with From. SPF pass on a Return-Path domain that has nothing to do with the From: domain is the classic sign that SPF alone was satisfied while the user was deceived.
  • [Supplement] Recon goes both ways. An SPF record lists every service allowed to send for a company — mail suite, marketing tool, CRM. Attackers read it to learn which platforms to imitate or abuse; defenders should review it for forgotten services.
  • Watch for record changes. A sudden change to your SPF record (especially a new include or +all) is worth an alert — it can mean DNS account compromise.

docs.title: The 2026 view
docs.text:
[2026 Current] Still valid

SMTP itself still has no built-in sender authentication, and anyone can still connect to an MX on port 25 and type any MAIL FROM and From:. The three-layer answer (SPF for the path, DKIM for the signature, DMARC for alignment and policy) is still the model. SPF is still defined by RFC 7208, with the same mechanisms, qualifiers, 10-lookup limit and 2-void-lookup limit. The connecting IP is still the one fact the sender cannot fake.

[Changed] What has changed

  • Big mailbox providers made authentication mandatory. Since February 2024, Gmail and Yahoo require every sender to have SPF or DKIM, and bulk senders (roughly 5,000+ messages a day to their users) to have SPF and DKIM and a DMARC record, with the From: domain aligned. Microsoft applied similar rules to Outlook.com, Hotmail and Live addresses for high-volume senders from May 2025, rejecting non-compliant mail with 550 5.7.515. In practice, legitimate senders without SPF have become rare, so "no SPF at all" is now a stronger warning sign than it used to be.
  • The Authentication-Results: standard moved on. The version first referenced in older material has been replaced; RFC 8601 is the current definition. The header looks the same to an analyst.
  • DMARC is now a Proposed Standard. The long-running "DMARCbis" revision was published in 2026 as RFC 9989–9991, replacing the old informational RFC 7489. SPF itself is unchanged, but some DMARC tags and behaviours changed — covered on the DMARC page.
  • Shared cloud platforms changed what "pass" means. Most organisations now include a large provider's whole range (include: of a cloud mail suite or marketing platform). An SPF pass therefore often only proves "it came from that platform," and abuse of legitimate platforms and compromised accounts has become a major source of phishing that passes SPF.

[Caution] Wrong or risky to do the old way

  • Do not read SPF pass as "the message is genuine." It only means the envelope domain authorised that IP. Attackers register look-alike domains with perfect SPF, or send from compromised accounts. Always check alignment with the visible From: (DMARC).
  • Do not believe SPF checks the From: header. It checks MAIL FROM/HELO.
  • Do not publish +all or use ptr. +all authorises the whole internet; ptr is deprecated.
  • Do not let your record exceed 10 lookups. It fails as permerror without any obvious error on your side. Check after every new service is added.
  • Do not reject mail on SPF fail alone without thinking about forwarding. Forwarded mail arrives from the forwarder's IP and fails SPF legitimately. Modern practice is to let DMARC (which can rely on DKIM) make the decision.

docs.title: Question 1
docs.text:
payroll-portal.example publishes this record. A message with MAIL FROM:<notify@payroll-portal.example> arrives from 192.0.2.140. What is the SPF result, and at which mechanism does evaluation stop? What if it had come from 198.51.100.9?

"v=spf1 ip4:192.0.2.128/26 include:_spf.sendgrid-like.example ~all"

(_spf.sendgrid-like.example contains "v=spf1 ip4:203.0.113.0/24 -all".)

Answer and explanation

From 192.0.2.140: pass, stopping at the first mechanism. 192.0.2.128/26 covers 192.0.2.128–191, so .140 matches. There is no qualifier, so + (pass) applies, and evaluation ends right there — the include is never looked up.

From 198.51.100.9: softfail. It is not in 192.0.2.128/26. The include is evaluated: not in 203.0.113.0/24, so the included record's -all matches — but inside an include that only means "no match here", not fail for the whole record. Back in the outer record, ~all matches everything → softfail ("probably not authorised"). Note how the included record's -all did not turn the result into a hard fail.

docs.title: Question 2
docs.text:
Count the DNS lookups for this record. What result will every receiver get, and why might the company not notice?

"v=spf1 a mx include:_spf.mailsuite.example include:mkt.example include:crm.example include:helpdesk.example include:hr-system.example include:billing.example ~all"

Assume _spf.mailsuite.example contains 3 nested includes, and the others contain none.

Answer and explanation

a = 1, mx = 1, six includes = 6, plus the 3 nested includes inside the mail suite's record = 3. Total 11 — over the limit of 10.

Result: permerror for everyone, on every message, regardless of which IP sent it. Receivers treat the domain as having a broken SPF record; with DMARC in place, mail will then rely entirely on DKIM, and any stream without DKIM may be junked or rejected.

Why nobody notices: the company's own outgoing mail still leaves without errors — the failure only shows on the receiving side (in their Authentication-Results, or in DMARC aggregate reports if the company reads them). The usual cause is an innocent addition of one more service. Fixes: remove services no longer used, replace a/mx with ip4/ip6 ranges where stable, or move some services to a subdomain with its own record.

docs.title: Question 3
docs.text:
A finance employee reports a message. Its headers show the following. SPF passed. Is the message from the company's real CEO? What does this tell you about the limits of SPF?

Return-Path: <bounce-7731@mail.lookalike-pay.example>
Received: from out-3.lookalike-pay.example (out-3.lookalike-pay.example [203.0.113.81])
        by mx1.victim.example with ESMTPS id 9Rt2Lq; Thu, 19 Nov 2026 02:41:10 +0000
Authentication-Results: mx1.victim.example;
       spf=pass smtp.mailfrom=mail.lookalike-pay.example
From: "Jane Park (CEO)" <ceo@victim.example>
Subject: Confidential - change of supplier bank details
Answer and explanation

Almost certainly not. Read the evidence in order:

  • Received ... by mx1.victim.example — our border line. The message came from 203.0.113.81, which calls itself out-3.lookalike-pay.example, not from our own mail servers.
  • spf=pass smtp.mailfrom=mail.lookalike-pay.example — SPF passed for lookalike-pay.example, the domain in the envelope (Return-Path). The attacker owns that domain and listed their own server in its SPF record.
  • From: ... <ceo@victim.example> — the address the employee sees belongs to our company, a completely different domain. SPF never looked at it.

The lesson: SPF only authenticates the envelope domain. It cannot stop a message whose visible From: is someone else's domain. That is the job of DMARC alignment — victim.example publishing a DMARC policy means that a message showing From: ...@victim.example must pass SPF or DKIM for victim.example itself, which this one cannot. Also note the internal-impersonation angle: a message from "our CEO" arriving from outside our servers should be blocked or tagged by an internal-impersonation rule regardless. Next steps: block the domain and IP, search for the same Return-Path domain in other mailboxes, and warn finance not to change bank details.

docs.title: Endpoint Attacks
docs.text:
In one line

Once delivery succeeds, the attack moves onto the host. This section follows an intrusion on the endpoint step by step — initial exploitation (service-side and client-side), execution, persistence, discovery, privilege escalation, credential dumping, lateral movement, collection and exfiltration — with the process, logon and file evidence each step leaves and the ATT&CK technique it maps to.

docs.title: Reading order
docs.text:
# Page Key points 1 Initial Exploitation — Why the Endpoint Matters, Delivery, Service-Side and Client-Side Exploits What the endpoint sees that the network can't (Zeek conn.log vs Sysmon 3 for the same connection); attack stages → ATT&CK tactics → best evidence; where delivery ends; the three doors (exploit, social engineering, valid credentials); the attacker becomes the compromised process — "what was compromised and with what privileges?" (Get-Process -IncludeUserName, ps --forest); service-side exploits: listening ports with Get-NetTCPConnection/ss -tlnp, an IIS log line and a w3wp.exe → cmd.exe 4688 field by field; client-side exploits: Zone.Identifier (MotW) and a WINWORD.EXE → hidden PowerShell Sysmon 1; comparison table and triage checklist; edge-device exploitation, ClickFix (T1204.004), native Sysmon; practice questions 2 Execution, Persistence and Discovery — What the Attacker Does Right After the Exploit Post-exploitation and why clean-up cost climbs; ATT&CK tactics → techniques → sub-techniques (current tactic list incl. BYOVD; Administrator protection; practice questions 4 Credential Dumping and Mimikatz — From One Admin to Many Accounts Credential Access (TA0006) and T1003 sub-techniques (LSASS, SAM, LSA secrets, cached, NTDS, DCSync, Linux); the two ingredients (access: T1210/T1078, code: T1570) and tools staged in the Recycle Bin (Sysmon 11 by System); remote-admin protocols → ports → T1021.x/T1047 → target-side evidence; PsExec style field by field (4624 type 3 → 5145 ADMIN$ 0x2 → 7045 LocalSystem), WMI (WmiPrvSE.exe → cmd.exe /Q /c … ADMIN$\__…), WinRM (wsmprovhost.exe), RDP 1149 and type 10, SSH Accepted publickey; Section complete

The endpoint-attacks section is complete. Next: Endpoint Defense — defence in depth on the host (inventory, vulnerability management and patching, exploit protection, Credential Guard, host firewalls, antivirus, application control, file integrity monitoring, PAWs, EDR, DLP, UEBA and audit policies).

docs.title: Things to remember
docs.text:
1. The network says that something happened; the endpoint says which process, which user, what.
  2. The attacker becomes the compromised process or user — always ask what it was and what privileges it had.
  3. Least privilege for services and users is the cheapest way to shrink the damage of any exploit.
  4. Service-side: needs a reachable listening port, no user, repeatable — patch or firewall it. Client-side: needs a user, passes inbound firewalls, hard to repeat — expect persistence.
  5. A server process (w3wp.exe, java.exe) or Office application spawning a shell or script host is one of the most reliable exploitation signals.
  6. Lateral movement is proven on the target: network/RDP logon + a tell-tale parent (services.exe, WmiPrvSE.exe, wsmprovhost.exe) + new services.
  7. Exfiltration needs staging, an open path and slowness — watch outbound denies, upload volume/ratio over days, and archiver command lines.
