docs.title: Enrichment, Normalisation and Storage — Context, Common Information Models, Categorisation, Hot/Warm/Cold and the Log Life Cycle
Enrichment, Normalisation and Storage — Context, Common Information Models, Categorisation, Hot/Warm/Cold and the Log Life Cycle
docs.text:
What this page covers

What happens to a log after it has been parsed, and why each step changes what you see and what you can find. First enrichment: the SIEM uses fields already in the log to look up extra context (asset owner, user role, domain age, reputation, patch status) and attaches it, turning a bare DNS query into something you can triage in seconds — and the traps of stale or point-in-time context. Then correlation, joining one log to others (DHCP, logons) to answer "which machine, which person". Then field normalisation and common information models (Splunk CIM, Elastic ECS, OCSF, Microsoft ASIM, Google UDM): why src_ip, sourceIP and source.ip should be searchable as one field, the three ways it is done (rename, copy, alias at search time), and why a normalised name may not exist in the raw log. Then categorisation: finding "all logins by mike" without knowing 4624 or sshd wording. Finally storage: like-with-like indexes, per-type retention, hot/warm/cold/frozen tiers, the log life cycle, what that means for old investigations, a list of questions to ask your SIEM engineer, and a summary of the whole pipeline. Practice questions with explanations at the end.

Labels

[Supplement] = practical material you need to know, [Correction] = a commonly repeated claim that is wrong or outdated, [Changed]/[Caution] = what has changed recently and what is risky to do the old way. Hostnames, domains, accounts, IPs and file names are invented for illustration (.example, documentation and private IPs).

docs.title: The 8 key points
docs.text:
1. Enrichment adds information that was not in the original log, looked up from fields that were (IP → host and owner, domain → age and rank, user → role). It is one of the biggest time savers a SIEM offers, and it only works if parsing worked.
  2. Enrichment is a snapshot. Ingest-time enrichment records what was true when the log arrived; search-time enrichment shows what is true now. For IP-to-host and user-to-role questions in an investigation, the difference matters.
  3. Correlation joins a log to other logs (DHCP leases, logons, DNS answers) to answer questions the single log cannot, such as which person was behind an IP at 03:12.
  4. Different products name the same thing differently. Field normalisation maps them to one name so one search finds them all. A collection of standard names is a common information model (data model, schema).
  5. Normalisation can rename fields at ingest, add a normalised copy next to the original, or alias at search time. Know which your SIEM does — a normalised field name may not appear in the raw log.
  6. Normalisation also covers values (allow/accept/permit → allowed; CORP\mike/mike@corp.example → mike) and meaning; two fields with the same name can still mean different things across sources.
  7. Categorisation tags events by what kind of thing happened (authentication, process start, network connection), so analysts and rules can ask "all failed logins by mike" across every source. Sources that the parser does not categorise are invisible to such searches.
  8. Logs are stored like with like, each type with its own retention, and age through hot → warm → cold → archived/frozen → deleted. New data is fast; old data is slow, needs restoring, or is gone. Know the numbers before an incident, not during one.

docs.title: Where we are in the pipeline
docs.text:
On the collection page an event travelled from the host to the SIEM, and on the formats page it was cut into named fields. That cut is the foundation for everything on this page. Enrichment needs a clean query or src_ip field to look things up with; normalisation needs to know which field is the source IP before it can rename it; categorisation needs to know the event is a logon. If parsing failed, none of the later steps happen and the event sits in the SIEM as an un-enriched, un-normalised, uncategorised blob that most rules and dashboards never see.

A useful picture is a mail-sorting centre. Collection is the van that picks up letters. Parsing is reading the address block. Enrichment is the clerk stamping extra information on the envelope ("sender is a known business", "postcode is a new development"). Normalisation is rewriting every address in one standard style. Categorisation is putting a coloured sticker on it (bill, parcel, legal notice). Storage is which shelf it goes on and how long it stays before being moved to the basement or shredded. Each step makes later work faster, and each step can introduce a mistake you will only notice if you know the step exists.

docs.title: What it is and why it matters
docs.text:
Most log sources write the minimum needed to describe the event. A DNS server logs who asked, what they asked and what type of record. Here is a realistic query log line after parsing:

{
  "@timestamp": "2026-11-20T03:12:44.218Z",
  "event.dataset": "dns.query",
  "source.ip": "10.0.10.3",
  "dns.question.name": "invoice-portal-secure.example",
  "dns.question.type": "A",
  "dns.response_code": "NOERROR"
}

Line by line: the event time; which log type this is (a DNS query); the IP that asked; the name asked for; the record type (A = an IPv4 address); and the result code (NOERROR = the name resolved). Is this bad? You cannot tell. Every one of the questions you would ask next — what did it resolve to, has anyone here seen this domain before, how old is it, is it on any blocklist, which machine is 10.0.10.3, who uses it, does that matter — needs a lookup somewhere else. If an alert fires on this event, an analyst spends ten minutes doing those lookups by hand, and does it again for the next alert, and the next.

Now the same event after the SIEM has enriched it:

{
  "@timestamp": "2026-11-20T03:12:44.218Z",
  "event.dataset": "dns.query",
  "source.ip": "10.0.10.3",
  "dns.question.name": "invoice-portal-secure.example",
  "dns.question.type": "A",
  "dns.response_code": "NOERROR",
  "dns.resolved_ip": ["203.0.113.77"],
  "enrich.domain.first_seen_org": "2026-11-20T03:12:44Z",
  "enrich.domain.newly_observed": true,
  "enrich.domain.popularity_rank": null,
  "enrich.domain.registered": "2026-11-17",
  "enrich.domain.age_days": 3,
  "enrich.ti.match": false,
  "host.name": "fin-ws-014",
  "host.patch_status": "missing 2 critical updates",
  "user.name": "kyle.ward",
  "user.roles": ["Domain Admins"],
  "enrich.added_at": "2026-11-20T03:12:46Z"
}

The first six fields are unchanged; everything after them was added. Reading the additions:

  • dns.resolved_ip — the answer, pulled from the matching DNS response log. Now you have an IP to check against firewall and proxy logs.
  • first_seen_org / newly_observed: true — no machine in this organisation has queried this domain before this moment. Most legitimate domains are queried again and again; a first-ever query is a useful weak signal.
  • popularity_rank: null — the domain is not in a top-sites popularity list. Unranked does not mean bad (most of the internet is unranked), but big, legitimate services usually are ranked.
  • registered / age_days: 3 — the domain was registered three days ago. Phishing and malware domains are often used within days of registration (domain age); attackers buy domains as part of their preparation (MITRE ATT&CK T1583.001, Acquire Infrastructure: Domains).
  • ti.match: false — not on any threat-intelligence list the SIEM has. New domains are often not on lists yet, which is exactly why the other signals matter.
  • host.name and host.patch_status — 10.0.10.3 is fin-ws-014, a finance workstation missing two critical updates. From an asset inventory or vulnerability scanner.
  • user.name and user.roles — the person logged on there is kyle.ward, and he is a domain admin. From directory and logon data.
  • enrich.added_at — when the enrichment was attached. [Supplement] Good pipelines record this, so you know how fresh the context was.

Put together: a domain admin, on an unpatched finance workstation, at 03:12, was the first person in the organisation ever to look up a three-day-old, unranked domain with a finance-themed name. Nothing in the original six fields said any of that. That is the whole point of enrichment: it turns "a DNS query happened" into a decision you can make in seconds. It is also the reason parsing matters so much — the SIEM cannot look up dns.question.name if it never extracted it.

docs.title: Common enrichment sources
docs.text: Enrichment Looked up from Answers Typical source Asset / host IP, hostname Which machine, which owner, how critical, what OS CMDB, asset inventory, EDR Identity Username, IP + time Which person, department, role, privileged or not, account enabled Directory (AD, Entra ID), HR feed, logon events Network location IP Internal subnet name (DMZ, server VLAN, guest Wi-Fi), site IPAM, subnet list Geolocation and ASN External IP Country, network owner, hosting vs residential GeoIP / ASN database Threat intelligence IP, domain, URL, hash Known bad? Which campaign? How confident? TI platform, feeds Domain data Domain Age, registrar, popularity rank, first seen here WHOIS/RDAP, rank lists, own DNS history Vulnerability Host Missing patches, known vulnerable software Vulnerability scanner Prevalence Hash, process name, domain How many machines have seen this EDR, own log history

docs.title: Ingest time or search time?
docs.text:
There are two moments the SIEM can attach context, and they give different answers.

Ingest-time enrichment looks things up as the event arrives and writes the result into the stored event. Its strength is that it records what was true at that moment. If 10.0.10.3 belonged to fin-ws-014 at 03:12 and DHCP gives it to a laptop at 09:00, the stored event still says fin-ws-014. Its weaknesses are that it can never be corrected (if the asset list was wrong that day, the event is wrong forever) and it cannot benefit from later knowledge: a domain that was added to a blocklist at 10:00 still shows ti.match: false on the 03:12 event.

Search-time enrichment looks things up when you run the search. Its strength is that it uses current data, so the 03:12 domain now shows as malicious. Its weakness is the opposite: if you ask "which host is 10.0.10.3?" today you get today's answer, which may be a different machine. For user roles, a person who was added to Domain Admins last night will appear as a domain admin on last week's events.

A rule of thumb that holds in most SOCs:

  • Things that change over time and must be historically correct — IP-to-host, IP-to-user, user role at the time — are best done at ingest, or by correlating with time-stamped logs (DHCP, logon events) rather than with a current table.
  • Things where the latest knowledge is better — threat intelligence, reputation — are best done at search time, or by re-scanning past data when new intelligence arrives (many SIEMs do retro-hunting of new indicators over the last N days).

[Caution] Always check whether an enrichment field is point-in-time or current before writing it in a report. "The host was owned by finance" is a claim about the past; if the field came from today's CMDB, say so.

docs.title: A simple search-time lookup, explained
docs.text:
Many SIEMs let you enrich in the query itself. In Splunk this is done with a lookup: a table (often a CSV file) the SIEM can join against. Suppose there is a lookup called asset_inventory with columns ip, hostname, owner, criticality. A search for the DNS event above:

index=dns query="invoice-portal-secure.example"
| lookup asset_inventory ip AS src_ip OUTPUT hostname owner criticality
| table _time src_ip hostname owner criticality query

For a complete beginner, piece by piece:

  • index=dns — search only the index (storage area) that holds DNS logs. More on indexes below.
  • query="invoice-portal-secure.example" — keep only events whose query field is exactly that name. Field names are whatever your DNS parser creates; here the field is query.
  • | — the pipe. It passes the results on the left into the command on the right, like a production line.
  • lookup asset_inventory — the lookup command: for each event, look up a row in the table called asset_inventory.
  • ip AS src_ip — match the table's ip column against the event's src_ip field.
  • OUTPUT hostname owner criticality — copy those three columns from the matching row onto the event as new fields. If no row matches, the fields are simply empty.
  • table _time src_ip hostname owner criticality query — show the results as a table with those columns, in that order. _time is Splunk's event time.

What the screen shows:

_time                    src_ip      hostname     owner        criticality  query
2026-11-20 03:12:44.218  10.0.10.3   fin-ws-014   finance-ops  high         invoice-portal-secure.example

Remember: this lookup is search-time, so hostname is whatever the table says now. If that table is refreshed daily from DHCP, an event from three weeks ago may be matched to the wrong machine.

docs.title: Correlation: joining logs to answer "who"
docs.text:
Enrichment from tables is one half; the other half is correlation, using other logs. The DNS event knows only an IP. Three other logs, written by three other systems, can turn that into a person:

# DHCP server log (lease granted)
2026-11-19 18:02:10  ASSIGN  10.0.10.3  mac=00:1a:2b:3c:4d:5e  hostname=fin-ws-014  lease=86400

# Windows Security 4624 on fin-ws-014 (interactive logon)
2026-11-20 02:58:31  EventID=4624  LogonType=2  TargetUserName=kyle.ward  TargetDomainName=CORP  WorkstationName=FIN-WS-014

# DNS query log
2026-11-20 03:12:44  client=10.0.10.3  query=invoice-portal-secure.example  type=A

Reading them in order: the DHCP server gave 10.0.10.3 to fin-ws-014 at 18:02 the previous evening for 86,400 seconds (24 hours), so at 03:12 the lease is still valid. Event 4624 is Windows' "an account successfully logged on" event, written on the machine the account logged on to; LogonType 2 means someone typed credentials at the keyboard or console (see logons). So kyle.ward sat down at fin-ws-014 at 02:58. Fourteen minutes later that machine looked up the new domain. Attackers care about 4624 because it shows exactly which account was used where — and defenders care for the same reason.

Two cautions. First, correlation needs time windows: the right DHCP lease is the one that was valid at the event time, and the right logon is the latest one on that host before the event with no logoff in between. Second, an IP on a shared machine (terminal server, NAT gateway, proxy) maps to many users, so "the user" can be a guess. Say so in the report.

docs.title: Field normalisation and common information models
The problem
docs.text:
Every vendor names fields its own way. Here is the source IP of a connection, as five different sources write it:

Zeek conn.log (JSON):        "id.orig_h": "10.0.10.3"
Windows Firewall log (W3C):  src-ip 10.0.10.3
Palo Alto traffic (CSV):     ...,10.0.10.3,...          (column "Source address")
Sysmon Event ID 3:           <Data Name="SourceIp">10.0.10.3</Data>
Windows 4624:                <Data Name="IpAddress">10.0.10.3</Data>

All five mean "the machine where this started". To find every connection from 10.0.10.3 without normalisation you need to know all five names and write:

id.orig_h=10.0.10.3 OR src-ip=10.0.10.3 OR src_addr=10.0.10.3 OR SourceIp=10.0.10.3 OR IpAddress=10.0.10.3

That works until someone adds a sixth source and forgets to tell the analysts. Then the sixth source is silently missing from every search and every rule. That is the real cost: not typing, but gaps nobody notices.

Field normalisation solves this by mapping each source's field to one agreed name. The set of agreed names (and agreed meanings and value formats) is called a common information model, common event model, data model or schema depending on the product. After normalisation the search is just:

source.ip=10.0.10.3        (or src=10.0.10.3, src_endpoint.ip=..., depending on the model)

docs.title: The common models you will meet
docs.text:
Model Used by Source IP User Notes Splunk CIM (Common Information Model) Splunk, Splunk ES src user Organised as data models (Authentication, Network Traffic, Endpoint…), mostly applied at search time ECS (Elastic Common Schema) Elastic, many shippers source.ip user.name Dotted, nested names; being merged into OpenTelemetry semantic conventions OCSF (Open Cybersecurity Schema Framework) AWS Security Lake and many vendors src_endpoint.ip user.name / actor.user.name Vendor-neutral, organised by event class with numeric IDs ASIM (Advanced Security Information Model) Microsoft Sentinel SrcIpAddr TargetUsername / ActorUsername Mostly query-time parsers (functions like _Im_Authentication) UDM (Unified Data Model) Google Security Operations principal.ip principal.user.userid / target.user.userid Uses principal / target / src / observer nouns

You do not need to memorise all five. You need to know which one your SIEM uses, where its field list is documented, and that a field like src in your SIEM may have been id.orig_h in the raw log.

docs.title: Three ways it is done
docs.text:
1. Rename at ingest. The pipeline renames id.orig_h to source.ip before storing. Searches are simple and fast. The original name is gone, so people looking at raw Zeek documentation may be confused, and if the mapping was wrong, the stored data is wrong.

2. Copy at ingest. The pipeline keeps id.orig_h and adds source.ip with the same value. Both names work. Costs a little more storage. This is common in ECS-style pipelines that also keep the original event in a field such as event.original.

3. Alias at search time. Nothing is changed in storage. When you search, the SIEM translates src into id.orig_h for Zeek data, src-ip for firewall data, and so on. Splunk field aliases and Sentinel's ASIM parser functions work this way. The raw data stays untouched and mappings can be fixed later, but searches are a bit slower and depend on the mapping being installed for that source.

A Splunk example of option 3, so you can recognise it (this goes in a configuration file called props.conf, normally maintained by the SIEM engineer):

[zeek:conn]
FIELDALIAS-cim_src  = "id.orig_h" AS src
FIELDALIAS-cim_dest = "id.resp_h" AS dest
EVAL-action = if(conn_state IN ("REJ","S0"), "blocked", "allowed")

Line by line: [zeek:conn] — these settings apply to events whose source type (Splunk's label for a log format) is zeek:conn. FIELDALIAS-cim_src = "id.orig_h" AS src — whenever someone searches this data, also make the value of id.orig_h available as src. The text after FIELDALIAS- is just a name for the setting. The second line does the same for destination. EVAL-action = ... — compute a new field action at search time: if Zeek's connection state is REJ (rejected) or S0 (no reply), call it blocked, otherwise allowed. That is value normalisation, the next topic. (Real mappings are more careful than this; S0 can also mean a dropped packet rather than a block.)

docs.title: Values and meanings, not just names
docs.text:
[Supplement] Renaming fields is only half the job. The values also need a common form:

  • Firewall actions: allow, accept, permit, pass, ALLOWED, 1 → allowed.
  • Usernames: CORP\kyle.ward, kyle.ward@corp.example, KYLE.WARD → kyle.ward, with the domain kept in its own field.
  • Protocols: 6, tcp, TCP → tcp.
  • Times: local time strings, epoch seconds, ISO 8601 with zone → one standard (UTC, ISO 8601).

Without this, action=allowed finds one vendor's events and misses the rest, and user=kyle.ward misses every event that wrote CORP\kyle.ward.

And meanings can still differ under the same name. Behind a NAT gateway, the firewall's src is the gateway's address, not the workstation's. In event 4624, IpAddress is the machine the logon came from, but for a local console logon it is - or 127.0.0.1. An analyst who treats every source.ip as "the attacker's machine" will draw wrong conclusions. When something looks odd, open the raw event (event.original, _raw) and check what the source itself meant.

docs.title: The trap: a field that is not in the raw log
docs.text: You find source.ip in the SIEM, then go to the raw Zeek file on the sensor and search for source.ip. Nothing. The field never existed there; the SIEM made it. The same happens in reverse: a colleague tells you to search SourceIp because "that's what Sysmon calls it", and in your SIEM it returns nothing because it was renamed at ingest. When a field name seems to be missing, the first suspect is normalisation. Your SIEM's data-model documentation, or a side-by-side look at _raw/event.original and the parsed fields, settles it in a minute.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text:
You need every login attempt by mike across the organisation. Without categorisation, you need to know what a login looks like in every source:

# Windows: success and failure events
index=windows (EventCode=4624 OR EventCode=4625) TargetUserName=mike

# Linux sshd: two different sentences
index=linux process=sshd ("Accepted password for mike" OR "Failed password for mike" OR "Accepted publickey for mike")

# Cloud identity provider sign-in logs, VPN, web applications, network devices ... each with its own wording

4624 is a successful logon and 4625 a failed one; both are written by the machine that checked the password. Attackers generate floods of 4625 when guessing passwords (T1110, Brute Force) and a single quiet 4624 when they use stolen credentials (T1078, Valid Accounts). The Linux lines come from the SSH server's free-text messages. A junior analyst may know none of this, and even a senior one will forget the VPN.

docs.title: What categorisation does
docs.text:
The parser attaches a category to every event it understands, describing what kind of thing happened, plus a few standard fields for the outcome. After that, one search works:

tag=authentication user=mike

In Splunk CIM, tag=authentication marks events that belong to the Authentication data model, and action is normalised to success or failure. Here is how a single failed SSH login looks after categorisation in an ECS-style SIEM, next to the raw line it came from:

Nov 20 03:20:07 web-07 sshd[48211]: Failed password for mike from 198.51.100.23 port 51544 ssh2

{
  "event.original": "Nov 20 03:20:07 web-07 sshd[48211]: Failed password for mike from 198.51.100.23 port 51544 ssh2",
  "event.category": ["authentication"],
  "event.type": ["start"],
  "event.outcome": "failure",
  "user.name": "mike",
  "source.ip": "198.51.100.23",
  "source.port": 51544,
  "host.name": "web-07",
  "process.name": "sshd",
  "process.pid": 48211
}

Line by line: event.original keeps the raw line, so you can always check the source; event.category: authentication says what kind of event it is; event.type: start says it was an attempt to begin a session; event.outcome: failure is the result; the remaining fields are the normalised user, source, host and process. A Windows 4625 for mike would produce exactly the same event.category, event.type and event.outcome, with user.name: mike — so a search for event.category:authentication AND event.outcome:failure AND user.name:mike finds both, without anyone needing to know either format.

In OCSF the same idea uses numbered classes: the Authentication class (class_uid 3002, in the Identity & Access Management category) with an activity_id of 1 for logon and a status_id of 1 or 2 for success or failure. Sentinel's ASIM uses an _Im_Authentication parser with EventResult set to Success or Failure.

docs.title: When the SIEM cannot categorise: tags
docs.text:
Some SIEMs categorise little out of the box. The simple fallback is tagging: a rule in the pipeline (or a saved search definition) that adds the word login to every event matching known login patterns. As long as everyone knows the tag exists, tag=login user=mike does the job. The weakness is the same as with normalisation: the tag only covers the patterns someone wrote. A new VPN appliance whose logins nobody tagged is invisible to every tag-based search and rule.

[Caution] Before trusting a category-based search, ask: which sources feed this category? Splunk's CIM, for example, lets you check which source types populate the Authentication data model. If the VPN is not in the list, "no failed logins by mike" means "no failed logins by mike in the sources we categorised".

docs.title: Like with like
docs.text:
The last step is writing the event somewhere it can be found again. Whatever the database underneath, most SIEMs store similar logs together: one place for firewall logs, one for Windows, one for proxy, one for IDS. Splunk calls these places indexes, Elastic uses indices or data streams, Sentinel uses tables. Settings that apply to a whole log type — parsing, access control, retention — are often attached at this level.

For you as a searcher, this means you should name the storage area in your search: index=proxy, index=windows, a specific Sentinel table, an Elastic data view. You can leave it out, but then the SIEM searches every storage area, which is slow and returns noise from log types you did not want. (We saw the same idea from the field side on the formats page.)

docs.title: Retention: how long each type is kept
docs.text:
Storage is finite, so each log type gets a retention period. One organisation might keep firewall logs for 30 days (huge volume, moderate value), DNS and proxy for 90 days, Windows security and authentication logs for a year, and legal or audit trails for seven years. These numbers come from three pressures: compliance (some regulations and government policies specify minimums — for example, US federal agencies' logging policy M-21-31 sets 12 months in active storage and 18 more in cold storage for many log types), investigation needs, and cost.

[Supplement] The investigation need is easy to underestimate. Intrusions are often discovered weeks or months after they began. If proxy logs are kept for 30 days and the first beacon was 45 days ago, the start of the story is gone. When retention is set, ask "if we find a compromise today, how far back do we need to look?" — not just "how much disk do we have?".

docs.title: Hot, warm, cold, frozen
docs.text:
Most SIEMs move data through storage tiers as it ages, trading search speed for cost:

Tier Typical hardware Search speed Typical age Hot Fast SSD, being written to Fastest Hours to days Warm SSD or fast disk, read-only Fast Days to weeks Cold Cheaper disk or object storage Slower Weeks to months Frozen / archive Object storage, tape, offline Slow, or not searchable until restored Months to years Deleted — Gone After retention ends

Product names vary: Splunk moves data in "buckets" through hot → warm → cold → frozen, where frozen means deleted by default unless an archive location is configured (archived buckets must be "thawed" to search again); Elastic's index lifecycle management moves indices through hot → warm → cold → frozen → delete, with frozen data searched from snapshots in object storage; cloud SIEMs offer an analytics tier plus cheaper lake or archive tiers with longer retention and slower, more limited queries.

Here is a Splunk index definition, the kind of file your SIEM engineer maintains, so you can read it:

[proxy]
homePath   = $SPLUNK_DB/proxy/db
coldPath   = $SPLUNK_DB/proxy/colddb
thawedPath = $SPLUNK_DB/proxy/thaweddb
frozenTimePeriodInSecs = 7776000
maxTotalDataSizeMB = 500000
coldToFrozenDir = /archive/splunk/proxy
  • [proxy] — the index name. This is what index=proxy refers to.
  • homePath — where hot and warm data live (usually fast disk).
  • coldPath — where cold data lives (often slower, bigger disk).
  • thawedPath — where archived data is put back if someone restores it.
  • frozenTimePeriodInSecs = 7776000 — data older than 7,776,000 seconds leaves the index. 7,776,000 ÷ 86,400 seconds per day = 90 days.
  • maxTotalDataSizeMB = 500000 — the index may not grow beyond about 500 GB. If it does, the oldest data is frozen early, even if it is younger than 90 days.
  • coldToFrozenDir — instead of deleting frozen data, copy it to this archive directory. Without this line, frozen means deleted.

[Caution] The size limit is the one people forget. A noisy week — a scanning worm, a misconfigured application, or an attacker deliberately flooding logs — can push the index past its size cap and quietly evict data that the time-based policy promised to keep. "We keep 90 days" is only true if the size cap is large enough for the busiest 90 days.

docs.title: The log life cycle
docs.text:
Logs follow a natural life cycle, and storage tiers are built around it:

  1. Written — the event is created and ingested.
  2. New — fresh data, used every day for alerting, triage, hunting and incident response. Lives on hot storage.
  3. Ageing — days to months old; searched less and less. Moves to warm, then cold.
  4. Old — very unlikely to be needed except for compliance or a long-running investigation. Archived, possibly offline.
  5. Deleted — retention has ended.

What this means in practice:

  • Searches over the last day or week are fast. Searches that reach back months are slower, may time out, or may skip data that is in a tier your search does not cover.
  • Archived data often has to be restored (rehydrated, thawed, reloaded) before you can search it. That can take hours and sometimes needs a ticket to another team. If you will need old data in an incident, ask for the restore early.
  • "No results" for a period older than the hot/warm window may mean "not searched", not "did not happen". Check the time range your SIEM actually covered.

A worked example: you learn today (20 November) that a vendor's software update was trojanised from 2 August. With the policy above, proxy logs from August are frozen; if the archive directory exists, they can be thawed, otherwise they are gone. Windows security logs kept for a year are still searchable, though from cold storage and slowly. EDR telemetry kept for 30 days covers none of the start. That one sentence — "we need August" — is why knowing these numbers before an incident matters.

docs.title: Questions for your SIEM engineer
docs.text:
You may not choose these settings, but you live with their consequences. A missing log because the agent never collected it looks identical to an attack that never happened. Get answers to these and keep them in your team wiki.

Data collection

  • Which systems do we collect from: all servers and workstations, or only some? Which cloud services?
  • Which channels or files are collected from each type of system (Security only, or Sysmon, PowerShell, Defender, task scheduler too)?
  • What filters are applied, where, and where are those configurations kept?

Data use

  • Which common information model does our SIEM use, and where is its field list?
  • Which sources feed each category or data model (Authentication, Network Traffic, Endpoint)?
  • Which fields are indexed for fast search (product dependent)? Which enrichments exist, and are they ingest-time or search-time?

Data storage

  • What is the retention for each log type, and are there size caps that can cut it short?
  • How long is data hot/warm (fast) vs cold/archive (slow or needs restoring), and how do I request a restore?

[Supplement] You can answer some of these yourself. In Splunk, this search lists what is actually arriving:

| tstats count latest(_time) AS last_seen WHERE index=* BY index sourcetype
| eval last_seen=strftime(last_seen, "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M")
| sort index sourcetype
  • | tstats ... — a fast command that reads only index metadata instead of whole events. It must start with a pipe because it is a generating command (it creates results rather than filtering them).
  • count latest(_time) AS last_seen — for each group, count the events and find the newest event time, naming it last_seen.
  • WHERE index=* — across all indexes you are allowed to see (respecting the time picker).
  • BY index sourcetype — one row per index and source type.
  • eval last_seen=strftime(...) — eval creates or changes a field; strftime turns the epoch number into a readable date.
  • sort index sourcetype — order the rows.

Output:

index     sourcetype              count      last_seen
dns       zeek:dns                18233412   2026-11-20 09:41
linux     linux_secure              912337   2026-11-20 09:41
proxy     squid:access            40117200   2026-11-20 09:41
windows   XmlWinEventLog:Security 25441090   2026-11-20 09:40
windows   XmlWinEventLog:Sysmon      1842   2026-11-12 22:05

The last row is the kind of thing this check exists to find: run over the last 30 days, Sysmon has only a few thousand events and the newest is from eight days ago, while every other source is current. Sysmon data stopped arriving on 12 November, and every Sysmon-based rule has been blind since then. (tstats only returns rows for data that exists in the time range, so a source that stopped before the range starts simply disappears from the list — run it over a window long enough to include the last time each source was seen.)

docs.title: The whole pipeline in one view
docs.text:
Log generated → Collect → Parse → Normalise → Enrich → Index → Store → Search / Alert
Stage What you should know How it fails silently Collect Agent or agentless, which hosts, which channels, which filters Host or channel not collected; filter drops what you need; agent stopped Parse Format, parser, fields extracted Field not extracted; columns shifted after an upgrade Normalise Model in use, field names, value mapping, which sources are mapped New source not mapped; same name, different meaning Enrich What is added, from where, when (ingest/search time) Stale table; point-in-time vs current confusion Index Which fields are indexed, how to scope searches Slow or timed-out searches on non-indexed fields Store Retention and tiers per type, size caps, restore process Data aged out or frozen; search did not cover the tier

The goal is not to become the SIEM engineer. It is to be able to say, for any log you are chasing, what happened to it at each step — so that when it is not where you expect, you know where to look next rather than concluding nothing happened.

docs.title: Putting it to work in a SOC
docs.text:
When you triage an alert, hunt, or a search returns nothing:

  1. Raw vs added. Which fields came from the source and which were added by enrichment or normalisation? Open the raw event when it matters.
  2. Time of truth. Is each enrichment point-in-time or current? For IP-to-host and IP-to-user, confirm with DHCP and logon events from the time of the event.
  3. Model. Search with the normalised fields, but know the raw names for each source you rely on.
  4. Coverage. Does every relevant source feed the category or data model you are searching? If not, add a raw search for the missing ones.
  5. Storage. Name the index/table. Check that your time range is inside the searchable tiers; ask for restores early.
  6. Health. Check that each source is still arriving (latest event time per source) before trusting "no results".

docs.title: The 2026 view
docs.text:
[2026 Current] Still valid

Everything on this page still holds: enrichment is still one of the biggest value-adds of a SIEM, ingest-time vs search-time is still the key question for historical accuracy, normalisation and categorisation are still what let one search and one rule cover many sources, and hot/warm/cold tiers with per-type retention are still how SIEMs control cost. The questions for your SIEM engineer have not changed.

[Changed] What has changed

  • Open schemas. OCSF reached 1.0 in 2023 and joined the Linux Foundation in late 2024; it keeps publishing 1.x releases and is used natively by AWS Security Lake and supported by many security vendors. Elastic contributed ECS to OpenTelemetry in 2023 and the two are being converged into OpenTelemetry semantic conventions. Splunk CIM, Microsoft ASIM and Google UDM remain the product models. Expect to translate between at least two of these in your career.
  • Normalisation moved earlier in the pipeline. Security data pipeline products (and the SIEMs' own pipeline features) now commonly route, filter, enrich and convert to a schema such as OCSF or ECS before data reaches the SIEM, often sending full-fidelity copies to cheap storage and a reduced copy to the SIEM. That makes the "what happened to my log on the way" question even more important.
  • Cheap lake tiers. Cloud SIEMs now pair an expensive analytics tier with a much cheaper data-lake tier. Microsoft Sentinel's data lake became generally available in 2025 with long retention (up to 12 years); other vendors offer similar lake, federated-search or archive tiers. Data in these tiers is usually searchable without restoring, but with slower queries, fewer features and sometimes per-query cost — and detection rules may not run on it.
  • AI-assisted enrichment and summaries. Many SIEM and SOAR products now add AI-generated alert summaries and enrichment. Treat these like any other enrichment: know where the information came from, and verify it against the raw events before acting on it.

[Caution] Things that are wrong or risky to do the old way

  • Do not treat current lookup tables as history. Using today's DHCP or CMDB table to say which machine had an IP last month can name the wrong host — and the wrong person.
  • Do not assume a category search covers every source. Check which sources feed it; new and cloud sources are the usual gaps.
  • Do not drop low-value data at the pipeline to save SIEM cost without keeping it somewhere. Route it to a lake or archive tier instead; you cannot enrich or search what was thrown away.
  • Do not trust "we keep 90 days" without checking size caps and what happens at freeze (archive or delete).
  • Do not report "no activity" for a period you could not actually search (frozen, archived, or outside the lake query's range). Say what was searched.

docs.title: Question 1
docs.text:
An alert shows a connection from 10.0.10.3 to a known-bad IP on 3 November. Your SIEM's search-time lookup says 10.0.10.3 is hr-lt-201, owned by an HR employee. You are asked to quarantine that laptop. What should you check first, and why?

Answer and explanation

Check whether the IP-to-host mapping is point-in-time or current. A search-time lookup uses today's table, so it tells you who has 10.0.10.3 now, not on 3 November. DHCP leases change daily, so the machine that made the connection may be a completely different host.

Confirm with time-stamped evidence from 3 November: the DHCP server's lease log for 10.0.10.3 valid at the connection time (lease granted before it, not yet expired or released), and ideally a 4624 logon on that machine shortly before. If your pipeline does ingest-time host enrichment, the host.name stored on the original event is also good evidence. Only then quarantine — otherwise you might isolate an innocent HR laptop while the real infected machine keeps running. In the report, note where the mapping came from.

docs.title: Question 2
docs.text:
A colleague runs tag=authentication action=failure user=svc_backup over the last 7 days and finds nothing, so they write "no failed logins for the service account". The account is also used to log in to a new VPN appliance added last month and to Linux servers over SSH. What is wrong with the conclusion, and how do you check it?

Answer and explanation

The search only finds events from sources whose parsers categorise them as authentication and normalise action and user. A VPN appliance added last month may not be mapped to the Authentication model at all, so its failures are invisible to this search. The Linux sshd events are probably mapped, but only if the add-on/parser for that source is installed and the user value is normalised the same way.

Check coverage: list which source types feed the Authentication data model (or category) and see whether the VPN is there. Run a raw search on the VPN index for svc_backup and its failure wording, and confirm that sshd failures (Failed password for svc_backup / Invalid user) are categorised. The correct conclusion until then is "no failed logins in the categorised sources (list them)". Then ask the SIEM engineer to map the VPN source.

docs.title: Question 3
docs.text:
Your Splunk proxy index has frozenTimePeriodInSecs = 7776000, maxTotalDataSizeMB = 300000 and no coldToFrozenDir. Normal volume is 2.5 GB per day. Last month, a misconfigured application tripled proxy volume for 30 days. What retention do you really have, and what happens to the oldest data?

Answer and explanation

7776000 seconds = 90 days of intended retention. At normal volume, 90 days is about 225 GB, under the 300 GB cap, so normally you do have 90 days.

During the bad month, 30 days were about 7.5 GB per day = 225 GB. Add the other 60 days at normal volume (150 GB) and the 90-day window would need about 375 GB — over the 300 GB cap. Splunk freezes the oldest buckets to stay under the cap, so you lose roughly the oldest 75 GB, around 30 days of normal-volume data: effective retention drops to about 60 days (the exact figure depends on compression and bucket sizes).

Because there is no coldToFrozenDir, frozen means deleted — there is no archive to thaw. Fixes: raise the cap to fit the busiest 90 days, add an archive location, alert when an index nears its cap, and fix or filter the noisy source. And remember: an attacker who can generate log volume can use the same effect to push evidence out.

docs.title: Log Formats and Structure — Unstructured Logs, CSV, Key-Value, JSON, CEF/LEEF, and Why Your SIEM Is Not Google
Log Formats and Structure — Unstructured Logs, CSV, Key-Value, JSON, CEF/LEEF, and Why Your SIEM Is Not Google
docs.text:
What this page covers

Why the format of a log decides whether it can be used for detection at all. We start with the worst case, the unstructured "sentence" log behind a syslog header, and see why parsing it needs a regular expression for every possible message and breaks when programs share a file or developers change wording. Then the structured formats — CSV, key-value pairs, JSON (and XML) — compared on size, robustness and nesting, using the same record in each. Then the SIEM-centric formats CEF and LEEF, with every header field and the escaping rules read piece by piece. Finally, why structure matters inside the SIEM: parsing feeds indexing, indexing makes search fast, and failed parsing makes rules silently miss (false negatives). We close with how to scope a search — log type first, then field — and why a search box that looks like a web search engine does not behave like one. Practice questions with explanations at the end.

Labels

[Supplement] = practical material you need to know, [Correction] = a commonly repeated claim that is wrong or outdated, [Changed]/[Caution] = what has changed recently and what is risky to do the old way. Hostnames, domains, accounts, IPs and file names are invented for illustration (.example, documentation and private IPs).

docs.title: The 8 key points
docs.text:
1. A log is only useful for detection if the SIEM can reliably pull the key fields out of it. Format decides how hard that is.
  2. Unstructured logs have a predictable syslog header followed by a free-text sentence. Parsing them needs a regular expression for every message variant of every program, and those regexes break silently when wording changes.
  3. Mixing many programs into one file (for example /var/log/syslog) multiplies the problem: each line can come from a different program with a different sentence shape.
  4. CSV is the most compact, but the reader must already know the column names and order; add, remove or reorder a column and every field after it shifts.
  5. Key-value pairs carry their own field names, so fields can be added, removed or shuffled without breaking parsing — a good middle ground. Watch out for spaces and delimiter characters inside values.
  6. JSON is the most robust: named fields, data types, nesting and arrays. It is also the most verbose. XML has the same power and converts to JSON without losing the hierarchy. For detection data, prefer JSON when you have the choice.
  7. CEF and LEEF are SIEM-oriented formats: a syslog header, a pipe-delimited header that says which product created the event, then key-value extensions.
  8. Parsing feeds indexing; indexing makes searches fast. Scope every search by log type and by the field you expect the value in — sara alone is the slowest and least precise search you can run.

docs.title: Why format matters to an analyst
docs.text:
On the collection page we followed an event from host to SIEM. One of the boxes on that path was parsing: cutting a log line into named fields such as user, src_ip or url. Everything you do afterwards depends on that cut being right. A detection rule that says "alert when user is a service account logging in from a workstation" cannot fire if user was never extracted. A search for src_ip=10.20.30.41 returns nothing if the parser put the IP into a field called message. Neither failure produces an error. You just get no result, which looks exactly like "nothing happened".

Think of it like a filing room. If every letter arrives in a standard form with labelled boxes (Sender, Date, Subject), a clerk can file thousands per hour and find any of them in seconds. If letters arrive as handwritten notes in different styles, the clerk has to read each one and guess where the sender's name is. Some will be misfiled, and a search for "everything from sender X" will quietly miss them. Log formats are the difference between the form and the handwritten note.

docs.title: Unstructured logs
docs.text:
Most Linux and network-device logs start with a syslog header whose shape is known (timestamp, host, program and optional PID — see syslog format). After the colon comes the message, and the message is whatever sentence the developer chose to write. Here are three lines that could sit next to each other in the same /var/log/syslog (or auth.log) file:

Nov 20 07:23:51 web-07 dhclient[75879]: bound to 10.20.40.17 -- renewal in 703 seconds.
Nov 20 08:17:59 web-07 CRON[55171]: pam_unix(cron:session): session opened for user root(uid=0) by (uid=0)
Nov 20 09:08:01 web-07 sudo:    sara : TTY=pts/2 ; PWD=/var/log ; USER=root ; COMMAND=/usr/sbin/service ssh start

Reading them:

  • Line 1. Header: Nov 20 07:23:51 (no year, no time zone), host web-07, program dhclient, PID 75879. Message: the DHCP client received address 10.20.40.17 and will renew in 703 seconds. The IP and the number are buried in a sentence; nothing labels them.
  • Line 2. Program CRON, PID 55171. The message itself starts with another program's tag, pam_unix(cron:session), then a sentence: a session was opened for user root. The user name sits after the words "for user" and is glued to (uid=0).
  • Line 3. Program sudo, no PID. This message is half-structured: sara ran a command as root, with TTY, PWD, USER and COMMAND separated by ;. But the invoking user sara has no label at all — it is just the first word, padded with spaces.

Three programs, three completely different message shapes, in one file. To turn them into fields you need a separate regular expression (regex) per message type. For the sudo line it might look like this:

^(?<ts>\w{3}\s+\d+\s[\d:]{8})\s(?<host>\S+)\ssudo:\s+(?<user>\S+)\s:\sTTY=(?<tty>\S+)\s;\sPWD=(?<pwd>\S+)\s;\sUSER=(?<run_as>\S+)\s;\sCOMMAND=(?<command>.+)$

Piece by piece:

  • ^(?<ts>\w{3}\s+\d+\s[\d:]{8}) — from the start of the line, capture a timestamp: three letters (Nov), one or more spaces, the day, a space, and eight characters of digits and colons (09:08:01). (?<ts>…) names the capture ts.
  • \s(?<host>\S+) — a space, then the host name (any run of non-space characters).
  • \ssudo:\s+ — the literal program name sudo: followed by one or more spaces (sudo pads the user name).
  • (?<user>\S+)\s:\s — the invoking user, then :.
  • TTY=(?<tty>\S+)\s;\sPWD=(?<pwd>\S+)\s;\sUSER=(?<run_as>\S+)\s;\s — each labelled part with its ; separator.
  • COMMAND=(?<command>.+)$ — everything to the end of the line is the command.

Applied to line 3 the result is:

Field Value ts Nov 20 09:08:01 host web-07 user sara tty pts/2 pwd /var/log run_as root command /usr/sbin/service ssh start

Now look at how easily it breaks:

  1. Optional parts. If sudo is run from a cron job there is no terminal, and the line says TTY=unknown or drops parts; if the command was refused, the line is sara : 3 incorrect password attempts ; TTY=pts/2 ; ... — an extra chunk the regex does not expect, so the whole line fails to match.
  2. Spaces where you assumed none. PWD=(?<pwd>\S+) fails for a directory such as /home/sara/My Files.
  3. Every other message. The regex does nothing for dhclient or CRON lines. Each program — and each kind of message from each program — needs its own pattern. sshd alone writes dozens of different sentences.
  4. Version changes. When a developer rewords a message ("session opened for user root(uid=0)" became that form in newer PAM versions; older versions wrote "session opened for user root by (uid=0)"), the old regex quietly stops matching.

The dangerous part is that a failed regex does not stop the log from arriving. The event is stored with only the raw text, and every rule that relied on user or command simply never sees a value. That is a false negative — the worst kind of error, because nobody notices it.

[Supplement] Most SIEMs tag events that could not be parsed (a default source type, a tags: _grokparsefailure-style marker in Elastic/Logstash pipelines, or an "unparsed" category). A quick weekly check of "what share of each source failed to parse" catches broken parsers before an investigation does. On Linux, the systemd journal helps a little: it stores fields such as _PID, _UID, _COMM and SYSLOG_IDENTIFIER in a structured way, so collecting from the journal as JSON gives you the header fields for free — though the MESSAGE text is still a free sentence.

docs.title: Structured log formats
docs.text:
The fix is to log in a format with a predictable structure, so a generic parser can cut every line correctly without knowing anything about the program. Here is the same DNS connection record in the three common shapes:

CSV:        10.20.30.41,198.51.100.53,55001,53,udp
Key-value:  src_ip=10.20.30.41 dest_ip=198.51.100.53 src_port=55001 dest_port=53 proto=udp
JSON:       {"src_ip":"10.20.30.41","dest_ip":"198.51.100.53","src_port":55001,"dest_port":53,"proto":"udp"}

Those lines are 38, 78 and 96 bytes long. Multiply by a billion events a day and the difference is real money in storage and licensing — but as we will see, the cost of a broken parser is higher.

Format Field names travel with the data? Survives added/removed/reordered fields? Nesting and lists Size CSV / TSV No — reader must know names and order No — everything after the change shifts No Smallest Key-value Yes Yes No (flat only) Medium JSON Yes Yes Yes Largest XML Yes Yes Yes Largest (often larger than JSON)

docs.title: CSV (comma-separated values)
docs.text:
A CSV log is just values in a fixed order. To parse it, the SIEM needs to be told: column 1 is src_ip, column 2 is dest_ip, column 3 is src_port, and so on. That is very efficient, and it is fragile. Suppose a firewall upgrade inserts a new action column after dest_ip:

Before:  10.20.30.41,198.51.100.53,55001,53,udp
After:   10.20.30.41,198.51.100.53,allow,55001,53,udp

With the old column list, the SIEM now reads src_port=allow, dest_port=55001, proto=53, and the last value has no name at all. No error is raised. A rule on dest_port=53 stops firing; a dashboard of "top destination ports" fills with 55001. Two more CSV traps: a value that contains a comma (a URL query string, a user agent, a file path such as C:\Users\sara\Q1,Q2.xlsx) must be quoted, and not every producer quotes correctly; and empty values (10.20.30.41,,55001,...) are easy to misread.

[Supplement] A useful halfway house is a CSV/TSV file that describes itself in a header. Zeek logs do exactly this:

#separator \x09
#fields ts  uid id.orig_h   id.orig_p   id.resp_h   id.resp_p   proto   service
#types  time    string  addr    port    addr    port    enum    string
1795164723.436  CkV1aB3xYz9 10.20.30.41 55001   198.51.100.53   53  udp dns
  • #separator \x09 — fields are separated by a tab.
  • #fields — the column names, in order, written into the file itself.
  • #types — the data type of each column, so id.orig_p is read as a port, not text.
  • The data line is then unambiguous. If a Zeek upgrade adds a column, the #fields line changes too, and a parser that reads it adapts. (Zeek can also write JSON directly, which most SOCs now prefer.)

docs.title: Key-value pairs
docs.text:
Here every value carries its name: key=value. Because the parser looks for names rather than positions, fields can be added, removed or shuffled without breaking anything. If the firewall adds action=allow anywhere in the line, the old fields are still found under their names and the new one simply appears. That is why many firewalls and proxies log this way, and why most SIEMs auto-extract key=value text without any configuration.

The weak spots are the delimiters:

src_ip=10.20.30.41 user=sara msg=login failed for sara reason=bad password

Where does msg end? A naive parser splits on spaces and gets msg=login, then nonsense words, then reason=bad. Well-behaved producers quote values (msg="login failed for sara") or escape spaces; badly behaved ones do not. And if an attacker controls part of a value — say, a user name typed into a login form — they may be able to inject a fake field:

user=x src_ip=203.0.113.99 action=success

If that whole string is logged unescaped as the user name, a careless parser sees user=x, then a second src_ip and an action=success that the application never wrote. This is log injection (CWE-117, Improper Output Neutralization for Logs). It is one reason to prefer formats with strict quoting rules, such as JSON, for security-relevant data.

docs.title: JSON and XML
docs.text:
JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) has the benefits of key-value pairs and adds three more: strict quoting and escaping rules (so a parser always knows where a value ends), data types (55001 is a number, "udp" is a string, true is a boolean), and nesting — objects inside objects, and arrays (lists). Here is a short endpoint process event in JSON, written out over several lines for readability (in a log file it would be one line):

{
  "@timestamp": "2026-11-20T09:08:01.512Z",
  "host": { "name": "web-07", "ip": ["10.20.40.17", "fe80::a1b2:3c4d"] },
  "user": { "name": "sara", "effective": { "name": "root" } },
  "process": {
    "executable": "/usr/sbin/service",
    "args": ["service", "ssh", "start"],
    "parent": { "name": "sudo", "pid": 81244 }
  },
  "event": { "category": ["process"], "type": ["start"] }
}
  • @timestamp — full date, time, milliseconds and the Z (UTC) zone. Compare that with the syslog header's Nov 20 09:08:01.
  • host — an object with a name and an array of two IP addresses. CSV and key-value cannot express "this host has two IPs" without inventing ip1, ip2 columns.
  • user.name and user.effective.name — nesting shows clearly that sara ran the command and it ran as root. The flattened field names (user.effective.name) are how most SIEMs let you search nested data.
  • process.args — the command line as a list, so ssh is a separate element rather than part of a string you have to split.
  • event.category / event.type — classification fields (from a common schema; more on that on the next page).

JSON's cost is size — every field name is repeated in every event, plus quotes and braces — but parsing it is dependable and needs no custom regex. XML offers the same power (Windows event logs are XML — see event structure), and because both formats are hierarchical, XML converts to JSON without losing structure. That is why the collection page recommended shipping Windows events as XML or JSON rather than flattening them to syslog text.

The rule of thumb: for anything you want to detect on, ease and reliability of parsing beat compactness. Choose JSON (or the source's native structured format) whenever the producer offers it.

docs.title: SIEM-centric formats: CEF and LEEF
docs.text: Some SIEMs defined their own formats so that every incoming event carries the same basic structure plus a clear statement of which product produced it. The two best known are CEF (Common Event Format, created for ArcSight and widely supported, including by Microsoft Sentinel) and LEEF (Log Event Extended Format, used by IBM QRadar). Both look the same at a glance: a syslog header, then a pipe-delimited header describing the source, then key-value extensions.

docs.title: CEF
docs.text:
The CEF header is:

CEF:Version|Device Vendor|Device Product|Device Version|Signature ID|Name|Severity|Extension

An invented example from an email-security gateway:

<134>Nov 20 08:50:00 mailgw01.corp.example CEF:0|ExampleSec|MailShield|4.2.1|av-1007|Malicious attachment blocked|8|externalId=995 rt=Nov 20 2026 08:49:58 UTC src=203.0.113.45 dst=10.20.50.10 suser=billing@supplier.example duser=a.chen@corp.example fname=invoice_2026-11.zip fileHash=0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef01234567 act=blocked cs1Label=policy cs1=inbound-attachments

Field by field:

Part Value Meaning <134> PRI 134 facility 16 (local0), severity 6 (info): 16 × 8 + 6 = 134. This is the syslog transport's severity, not the event's. Nov 20 08:50:00 mailgw01.corp.example syslog header when and from which device the message was sent CEF:0 version CEF format version 0 (the common one; version 1 also exists) ExampleSec Device Vendor who made the product MailShield Device Product which product 4.2.1 Device Version product version — useful when a parser change coincides with an upgrade av-1007 Signature ID the vendor's ID for this type of event; the most useful field for grouping and rules Malicious attachment blocked Name human-readable description of the event type 8 Severity the vendor's severity, 0 (lowest) to 10 (highest); 7–8 is "high" everything after the last | Extension space-separated key=value pairs

The extension keys come from a fixed CEF dictionary, which is what makes CEF parse the same way for every vendor: rt (receipt time of the event), src/dst (source and destination IP), spt/dpt (ports), suser/duser (source and destination user), fname (file name), fileHash, act (action taken), externalId (the vendor's own event ID). Anything not in the dictionary goes into custom fields such as cs1 with a label in cs1Label — here, "the policy that matched was inbound-attachments". Watch for those: in many products the most interesting data lives in cs1–cs6, and the label tells you what each one means in this product.

Escaping rules: in the header a literal | must be written \| and a backslash \\; in the extension a literal = must be written \= and a backslash \\. Spaces are allowed inside extension values — the parser knows a value ends where the next key= begins — which is exactly why an unescaped = in a value (for example in a URL query string) breaks CEF parsing.

docs.title: LEEF
docs.text:
LEEF has the same idea with a slightly different header:

LEEF:2.0|Vendor|Product|Version|EventID|Delimiter|Extension

An invented example from a web proxy:

<13>Nov 20 08:52:04 proxy02.corp.example LEEF:2.0|ExampleNet|EdgeProxy|7.1|deny|^|devTime=Nov 20 2026 08:52:03^src=10.20.30.88^dst=198.51.100.80^usrName=sara^url=http://files.download.example/setup.exe^cat=Uncategorized^action=blocked
  • <13> — PRI 13: facility 1 (user), severity 5 (notice).
  • LEEF:2.0 — format version 2.0. Version 1.0 has no delimiter field and always uses a tab between attributes.
  • ExampleNet|EdgeProxy|7.1 — vendor, product, version, just like CEF.
  • deny — the EventID: the vendor's identifier for this event type. QRadar maps vendor + EventID to its own event categories.
  • ^ — the delimiter chosen for the attributes (a 2.0 feature). A caret is used here because it will not appear in URLs, so values never need escaping.
  • The attributes — devTime (event time on the device), src, dst, usrName, url, cat (category), action — use LEEF's predefined key names; vendors can add their own.

Why it matters to you: if your SIEM receives CEF or LEEF, the header fields (vendor, product, signature/event ID, severity) are always reliable, even when a vendor fills the extension sloppily. Rules keyed on Device Product + Signature ID survive message-text changes. And when an event looks wrong, the device version in the header is the first thing to compare against the last known-good event.

docs.title: Why structure is so important inside the SIEM
docs.text:
A SIEM does not answer searches by grep-ing every stored byte. It could — that is called a full-text search — but over months of data it is painfully slow. Instead, at ingest the SIEM parses each event, takes the most commonly searched fields — user names, IP addresses, host names, domains, event IDs — and writes them into an index: a lookup structure from value to "which events contain this", like the index at the back of a book. A search on an indexed field jumps straight to the matching events.

Take a native-format Squid proxy line:

1795164723.436     17 10.20.30.88 TCP_MISS/503 861 GET http://updates.vendor.example/check.aspx sara HIER_NONE/- text/html
Position Value Meaning 1 1795164723.436 time as Unix epoch seconds with milliseconds: 2026-11-20 08:52:03.436 UTC 2 17 elapsed time in milliseconds the proxy spent on the request 3 10.20.30.88 client IP 4 TCP_MISS/503 cache result (TCP_MISS = not served from cache) / HTTP status the client received (503) 5 861 bytes sent to the client 6 GET HTTP method 7 http://updates.vendor.example/check.aspx requested URL 8 sara authenticated user name (- when the proxy did not authenticate) 9 HIER_NONE/- how the proxy fetched it (no upstream peer here) 10 text/html content type of the response

This is a positional format, like CSV with spaces. With a correct parser, the SIEM writes 10.20.30.88 into a source-IP index, updates.vendor.example into a domain/URL index, sara into a user index, and the whole line into storage. A later question such as "which users visited this domain this month?" is answered from the indexes in seconds. If the parser is wrong by one position — a proxy configured to log a different format, say — the "user" index fills with HIER_NONE/- and the user question returns garbage or nothing.

Parsing matters for rules even more than for searches. A rule matching url against a threat-intelligence list cannot match a field that does not exist. The alert does not fire, and you get a false negative. So, unless bandwidth or licence cost truly forces your hand, when a source offers a choice of output formats, pick the more structured and robust one over the more compact one.

[Supplement] SIEMs differ in when they extract fields, and it is worth knowing which kind you have:

  • Schema-on-write (index-time extraction): fields are parsed as events arrive. Searches are fast, but a parser bug is baked into stored data and fixing it only helps new events. Elastic and most cloud SIEMs (Microsoft Sentinel tables, Chronicle UDM) work mostly this way.
  • Schema-on-read (search-time extraction): raw text is stored and indexed by its words; named fields are extracted when you search. Splunk works mostly this way. A parser fix applies to old data immediately, but filtering on a field still means reading the candidate events to extract it.

Either way the analyst's rule is the same: know which fields are actually extracted and indexed for each source, and check parse-failure rates.

docs.title: Your SIEM is not Google
docs.text:
A SIEM search bar looks like a web search engine, so people type into it the way they would into one. Suppose sara might be infected and you want her proxy logs. Three ways to ask:

  1. sara
  2. proxy logs that contain sara anywhere
  3. proxy logs where the user field is sara

In Splunk's search language (SPL) these could be written as follows. A quick primer for SPL beginners: a search is a list of conditions, separated by spaces, that an event must all meet (spaces mean AND); index= picks which storage bucket of data to search (SOCs usually keep one index per log type, such as proxy, wineventlog or firewall); field=value matches only when that named field has that value; and a bare word matches if it appears anywhere in the raw event text. The time range is set separately (the time picker, or earliest=).

sara
  • A bare word, no index. Splunk searches the default indexes for any event whose raw text contains the term sara — Windows logs, firewall logs, DNS, everything. This is the most work for the SIEM and also the least precise result: it returns the file share \\fs01\sara-backup, the email to sara@partner.example, the process sara_report.exe.
index=proxy sara
  • index=proxy limits the search to the proxy data. sara still matches any part of the event: the user field, but also URLs such as http://intranet.corp.example/team/sara/ or a referrer. Faster than #1, but still searching fields where a user name makes no sense, and still giving you other people's traffic.
index=proxy user=sara
  • index=proxy again limits the data; user=sara matches only events whose extracted user field is exactly sara. Smallest scope, and the answer is exactly what you meant. Results might look like:
_time                   src_ip        user  method  url                                             status
2026-11-20 08:52:03.436 10.20.30.88   sara  GET     http://updates.vendor.example/check.aspx        503
2026-11-20 08:52:09.102 10.20.30.88   sara  GET     http://files.download.example/setup.exe         200

The same principle in other SIEMs: in Microsoft Sentinel's KQL, the table plays the role of the index, so CommonSecurityLog | where SourceUserName == "sara" (one log type, one field) beats search "sara" (every table, every column). In Elastic, user.name: "sara" with the right data view beats a free-text sara.

[Correction] How much faster #3 is depends on the SIEM's architecture. In schema-on-write SIEMs, a field-scoped search uses the field's own index and the speed gain is large. In Splunk, the raw-text index finds events containing the term sara first and then checks the user field, so the big speed gain comes from index= (and a tight time range), while user=sara mostly buys precision. In every SIEM, the order of importance is the same: time range, then log type, then field.

Two more habits that follow from how indexes work:

  • Avoid leading wildcards. user=*sara cannot use an index (an index is sorted by the start of each value) and forces a scan. user=sara* is usually fine.
  • Know which fields are indexed. Some SIEM architectures cannot index every field of every log — the index would be larger than the data. In those systems, make sure the frequently searched fields (IPs, user names, host names, domains, hashes, event IDs) are indexed, and build searches from indexed fields first; adding a non-indexed field as the only filter sends the SIEM back to reading events one by one.

docs.title: Putting it to work in a SOC
docs.text:
When you take on a new log source, or a search "should have" found something and did not:

  1. Format. Is the source unstructured text, CSV, key-value, JSON, CEF/LEEF or XML? Can it be switched to a more structured output?
  2. Parser. Which parser handles it, and what share of its events fail to parse? Look at a few raw events next to their extracted fields.
  3. Upgrades. Did the device version (CEF/LEEF header, agent version) change around the time results changed? Did a CSV column move?
  4. Fields. Which fields are extracted and which are indexed? Are the ones your rules depend on present in every event?
  5. Search scope. Time range, then log type (index=, table, data view), then field. Bare words only for exploration.
  6. Injection. For fields an outsider can influence (user names, URLs, user agents), does the format escape delimiters?

docs.title: The 2026 view
docs.text:
[2026 Current] Still valid

The ranking of formats (unstructured < CSV < key-value < JSON/XML for robustness, the reverse for size), the danger of regex-parsing free text, the fragility of positional formats, the way parsing feeds indexing and rules, and "scope by time, log type, then field" are all unchanged. CEF remains a common way for network and security appliances to send events to SIEMs, and LEEF is still QRadar's native format.

[Changed] What has changed

  • JSON is now the default transport. Agents, cloud services and EDR products overwhelmingly emit JSON, usually over HTTPS (vendor HTTP collectors, OpenTelemetry). Syslog text and CEF are now mostly for appliances and older products.
  • Common schemas moved into the pipeline. Elastic contributed ECS to OpenTelemetry in 2023, and the two are converging into OpenTelemetry's semantic conventions. OCSF (Open Cybersecurity Schema Framework), backed by AWS, Splunk and many others, reached 1.0 in 2023 and joined the Linux Foundation in 2024; AWS Security Lake stores data in OCSF. Microsoft Sentinel normalises with ASIM, Google SecOps with UDM. Covered on the next page.
  • Collector changes. In Microsoft Sentinel the old CEF/syslog connectors that relied on the retired Log Analytics agent (MMA) are deprecated; CEF and syslog now arrive through the Azure Monitor Agent on a Linux forwarder ("CEF via AMA"). ArcSight, where CEF was born, now belongs to OpenText; QRadar's SaaS business moved to Palo Alto Networks in 2024, while QRadar software (and LEEF) continues at IBM.
  • Cheap tiers change search habits. Data lakes and low-cost tiers (for example Microsoft Sentinel's data lake, generally available since 2025, and similar tiers from other vendors) store huge volumes cheaply but search more slowly and with fewer indexed fields. Scoping by time and log type matters even more there.
  • AI-assisted parsing. Several SIEMs and pipeline tools now offer AI-generated parsers and natural-language search. They speed up onboarding, but a generated parser is still a parser: check its extracted fields against raw events before writing rules on them.

[Caution] Wrong or risky to do the old way

  • Do not choose CSV or unstructured output just to save bytes for security-relevant data. A shifted column is a silent false negative.
  • Do not trust a parser after an upgrade without checking a few raw events. Vendors change formats in minor versions.
  • Do not treat "no results" as "it did not happen" until you have checked the field actually exists and is populated for that source.
  • Do not type bare words into the SIEM for real investigations — they are slow and pull in unrelated events. Scope by time, log type, then field.
  • Do not assume key-value or CEF values are safe when outsiders can influence them; check how the format escapes =, spaces and |.

docs.title: Question 1
docs.text:
Your firewall logs arrive as CSV: src_ip,dest_ip,src_port,dest_port,proto. After a weekend upgrade, the rule "alert on outbound connections to dest_port=4444" has not fired once, the "top destination ports" dashboard shows mostly five-digit numbers, and a new value allow appears in src_port. What happened, how do you confirm it, and what is the lasting fix?

Answer and explanation

What happened: the upgrade inserted a new column (an action field such as allow) after dest_ip. CSV has no field names in the data, so the SIEM still applies the old column list: allow is read as src_port, the real source port is read as dest_port (hence five-digit "destination ports" such as 55001), and the real destination port lands in proto. Nothing errored; the rule on dest_port=4444 simply never sees 4444 in that field — a false negative.

Confirm it: look at a few raw events from before and after the upgrade side by side and count the commas; check the device version in the device's own logs or release notes; check whether the parse-failure or "extra field" count for this source jumped at the upgrade time.

Lasting fix: switch the firewall to a self-describing format if it offers one — key-value, JSON or CEF — so added or reordered fields cannot shift the others. If CSV is the only option, update the column list, add a monitor that alerts when the number of columns or the share of non-numeric ports changes, and re-check the parser after every upgrade. Then re-run the dest_port=4444 hunt over the affected period using the corrected fields.

docs.title: Question 2
docs.text:
A gateway sends this event:

<134>Nov 20 10:02:11 mailgw01.corp.example CEF:0|ExampleSec|MailShield|4.2.1|av-1007|Malicious attachment blocked|8|src=203.0.113.45 duser=r.kim@corp.example fname=po_7781.docm act=blocked cs1Label=policy cs1=inbound-attachments

Name the vendor, product, event type ID, the vendor's severity and what PRI 134 tells you. Which header fields would you build a rule on, and why those rather than the Name text?

Answer and explanation
  • Vendor ExampleSec, product MailShield, version 4.2.1.
  • Event type (Signature ID) av-1007; Name "Malicious attachment blocked".
  • Vendor severity 8 on the 0–10 scale — high.
  • PRI 134 = facility 16 (local0) × 8 + severity 6 (info). That is the syslog transport priority, chosen by the sender's configuration; it does not describe how serious the event is. The CEF severity field does.
  • Extension: source IP 203.0.113.45, recipient r.kim@corp.example, file po_7781.docm, action blocked, and a custom field whose label says it is the matching policy, inbound-attachments.

Rule on: Device Vendor + Device Product + Signature ID (and possibly act). Those are fixed identifiers that every CEF parser extracts the same way. The Name is human-readable text the vendor can reword or translate in any release, which would silently break a rule matching on it — the same problem as regex-parsing free text.

docs.title: Question 3
docs.text:
During an incident a colleague runs the single word 10.20.30.88 over 90 days of all data. The search runs for many minutes and returns 2.4 million events across a dozen source types. You need the proxy requests made from that workstation in the last 24 hours. Write a better search, explain each part, and say why it is faster and more accurate.

Answer and explanation

A better search (in SPL, with the time picker set to the last 24 hours, or written inline):

index=proxy src_ip=10.20.30.88 earliest=-24h
  • index=proxy — only proxy data, instead of every index. This is the biggest saving in data the SIEM has to touch.
  • src_ip=10.20.30.88 — only events where the address is in the source field. The bare value also matched events where the workstation was a destination, appeared in a DHCP message, a Windows event, a firewall log, or any URL or text containing the string.
  • earliest=-24h — only the last 24 hours instead of 90 days; time is the first thing every SIEM uses to narrow the search.

It is faster because each condition shrinks the data the SIEM has to read, and the field condition can use (or quickly check) an extracted, indexed field instead of scanning raw text. It is more accurate because it returns exactly what was asked: requests from that host, in the proxy log, in the incident window. Check first that the proxy parser really extracts src_ip for this source; if the field name differs (c_ip, client_ip), use the one your parser produces.

docs.title: Mental Models
docs.text:
In one line

The previous section said the defence against perception and memory errors is many accurate mental models. This section is that toolbox: the standard models for attack, defence and threat intelligence — encapsulation and the OODA loop, the Cyber Kill Chain and campaign analysis, defence in depth, the NIST Cybersecurity Framework and the incident response cycle, threat-intelligence levels, the intelligence cycle and F3EAD, the Diamond Model, attack trees and graph thinking, threat modelling, the Pyramid of Pain and MITRE ATT&CK — with what each one is for, how it looks on real alerts and logs, and when to reach for which.

docs.title: Reading order
docs.text:
# Page Key points 1 Mental Models for Security, Encapsulation and the OODA Loop — Peeling Layers and Out-Cycling the Attacker Map of the standard models (general, offensive, defensive, threat intel) and the question each answers; encapsulation — evil on layers 2–7 (T1557.002, T1571), a cloud-hosted phishing download followed through Zeek conn/ssl/http/files (T1566.002, T1608.001, T1204.002), a nested attachment peeled with unzip, file, oleobj (email → ZIP → DOCX → OLE → EXE, T1566.001, T1027); go-to-the-bottom checklist; John Boyd's OODA loop, its two goals and ambiguity; the four stages in SOC terms and why Orient matters most; ops tempo and getting inside the attacker's loop; a slow vs fast defender loop against an attacker loop (beaconing T1071.001/T1036.005, 4624 type 10 RDP T1021.001); OODA in daily SOC work; practice questions

Coming next

The Cyber Kill Chain and campaign analysis, defence in depth, the NIST Cybersecurity Framework and the incident response cycle.

docs.title: Things to remember
docs.text:
1. Collect several models; each shows some aspects of a situation and hides others.
  2. Evil can sit on any layer from 2 to 7; many modern attacks only show at layer 7.
  3. Clear only the layers you actually inspected — and say which you couldn't see.
  4. Files are layered too: keep unpacking until you reach something that isn't a container.
  5. OODA: Observe, Orient, Decide, Act — a loop for acting under uncertainty against an opponent.
  6. Orient is where models and context meet data; a wrong model makes speed useless.
  7. Tempo wins: pre-approved playbooks shorten Decide, good context shortens Orient.
  8. Fast isn't hasty — acting before you know the scope teaches the attacker.
