docs.title: How Windows Event Logging Works — Providers, Channels, the Log Path, Audit Settings and the Three Views of One Event
How Windows Event Logging Works — Providers, Channels, the Log Path, Audit Settings and the Three Views of One Event
docs.text:
What this page covers

Why an analyst should understand log collection even when "someone else" runs it, and then how Windows actually produces the events you search every day. The path a log takes — program (provider) → Windows Event Log service → channel → .evtx file → Event Viewer, Get-WinEvent, wevtutil or a collection agent — and what each step means for you. Why .evtx files can't be read in a text editor, where they live and why the file names contain %4. Channel types (Admin, Operational, Analytic, Debug). What decides which security events exist in the first place: audit policies (legacy vs advanced, success vs failure, SACLs), add-ons such as Sysmon, custom channels written by scripts, and applications that keep their own text logs. The metadata every event carries — level, provider (source), event ID, task category, keywords — and the important correction that an event ID only means something together with its provider. Finally the same event in three views (General, Friendly, XML), how the "message" text is built from a template, and why the SIEM should receive the structured fields. Practice questions with explanations at the end.

Labels

[Supplement] = practical material you need to know, [Correction] = a commonly repeated claim that is wrong or outdated, [Changed]/[Caution] = what has changed recently and what is risky to do the old way. Hostnames, domains, accounts, IPs, file names and hashes are invented for illustration (.example, documentation and private IPs).

docs.title: The 8 key points
docs.text:
1. Log collection is not "someone else's job" for an analyst. If you don't know where a log comes from, what it can contain and what gets lost on the way, you can't tell "the attacker didn't do it" from "we never recorded it".
  2. Windows programs don't write log files themselves. They hand events to the Windows Event Log service, which sorts each event into a channel (Security, System, Application, and hundreds more) and stores every channel in its own .evtx file under C:\Windows\System32\winevt\Logs.
  3. .evtx is a binary-encoded XML format. You need a tool to read it — Event Viewer, Get-WinEvent, wevtutil, a forensic parser or a log agent — never Notepad.
  4. Which security events exist at all is decided before anything happens, by the audit policy (what to record, on success and/or failure), plus add-ons such as Sysmon, plus custom channels. If the audit setting was off, there is no event to find later.
  5. Not everything goes to the event log. Many applications and network services (web servers, DNS servers, databases) write their own text logs — or log nothing useful — so you configure them separately or capture that activity from the network with sensors such as Zeek or Suricata.
  6. Every event carries metadata: level (how serious), provider / source (which program wrote it), event ID (what kind of event), task category and keywords (for Security: Audit Success / Audit Failure).
  7. [Correction] An event ID is only unique per provider, not globally — and one channel can contain several providers. "Event ID 1" means different things from different providers, even in the same channel. Always filter on provider (or channel and provider) plus ID.
  8. One event, three views: the readable General (message) view, the Friendly details view and the raw XML view. The message is built by pouring the XML fields into a text template. Send the structured XML fields to your SIEM — the message text is for humans, is localised, and is hard to parse.

docs.title: Why an analyst must understand log collection
"Isn't that someone else's job?"
docs.text:
In many organisations a separate team installs the log agents, builds the SIEM and decides what gets forwarded. It is tempting to treat logs like tap water: you open the SIEM and data comes out. The problem appears the first time you search for something and get zero results. Zero results can mean three very different things:

  1. The activity really didn't happen.
  2. It happened, but Windows was never configured to record it (audit policy off, Sysmon not installed, command-line logging disabled).
  3. It was recorded on the host but never reached the SIEM (the channel isn't collected, the agent was down, the local log rolled over before collection, a parser dropped the field).

Only the first is a real "no". An analyst who doesn't know the pipeline will report case 2 or 3 as "no evidence of compromise" — which is one of the most expensive mistakes in a SOC.

Think of logs as a security camera system. If you don't know which corridors have cameras, whether they record at night, and how long footage is kept, an empty recording proves nothing. Knowing the camera map is part of the investigator's job, not just the installer's.

docs.title: What you need to know about every log source
docs.text:
For every log source you rely on, you should be able to answer three questions:

  • Format — how is it stored and structured? (binary XML for Windows, text lines for classic Linux syslog, JSON for many cloud and EDR sources). This decides how it can be parsed and what can go wrong.
  • Content — which fields exist and what do they really mean? (Does this 4688 include the command line? Is that IP the client or the proxy?)
  • Collection — how does it get from the host to you, how fast, and what gets dropped or changed along the way?

Reading logs is a daily task for an analyst. Understanding the pipeline turns that from "staring at whatever arrives" into knowing what you should be seeing — and asking for improvements when it's missing. The rest of this page answers the three questions for Windows.

docs.title: Why Windows is different from Linux
docs.text:
On a classic Linux system, logs are mostly plain text: a daemon sends a line to syslog, and syslog appends it to a file such as /var/log/auth.log. You can cat or grep it immediately (the next section, Linux Logging, covers this and the systemd journal).

Windows takes a more structured — and more complex — route:

  • The operating system and applications write events to log channels.
  • Each channel is stored in an .evtx file, which contains XML records in a binary-encoded form.
  • So a .evtx file can't simply be opened in a text editor. It must be interpreted by a tool that understands the format.
  • The most familiar tool is Event Viewer (eventvwr.msc). Its left pane lists the channels.

The analogy: a Linux text log is a notebook you can read by opening it. A Windows .evtx file is closer to a database file — the data is all there and well structured, but you need the right program to open it. The pay-off for the complexity is that every Windows event has named fields, which makes it far easier to parse reliably than free-form text.

docs.title: Opening Event Viewer: the channels you see
docs.text:
Open Event Viewer and you see two groups on the left:

  • Windows Logs — the classic channels everybody knows: Application, Security, Setup, System and Forwarded Events (the destination for Windows Event Forwarding).
  • Applications and Services Logs — hundreds of more specific channels, mostly under Microsoft → Windows → <component> → <type>, for example Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational, Microsoft-Windows-TaskScheduler/Operational, Microsoft-Windows-TerminalServices-LocalSessionManager/Operational or, once installed, Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational.

Many people stop at Application, Security and System. That's a mistake: several of the most useful sources for detecting attacks (PowerShell script blocks, scheduled-task changes, RDP session history, Defender detections, Sysmon) live in the second group. Many of the rest are noise. Which channels a SOC should actually collect is covered on the next page of this section.

[Supplement] Channel types. Each channel has a type that tells you its purpose:

Type Meant for Enabled by default? Example Admin Administrators — events that usually need action Yes Microsoft-Windows-PrintService/Admin and other …/Admin channels Operational Analysis and troubleshooting of a component Usually yes Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational Analytic High-volume, detailed tracing No (hidden) various …/Analytic channels Debug Developers No (hidden) various …/Debug channels

Analytic and Debug channels only appear after View → Show Analytic and Debug Logs, and must be enabled before they record anything. They are rarely worth collecting centrally because of the volume.

[Supplement] The Security channel is special. Only the Local Security Authority (LSA) can write to it, through the auditing subsystem. Normal programs can't add events to Security, which is part of why it is trusted. (Reading it also needs administrative rights or the "Manage auditing and security log" privilege.)

docs.title: The log path, step by step
docs.text:
Here is the journey of one event, from the moment something happens to the moment you read it:

[program / OS component]           e.g. LSA, Service Control Manager, PowerShell, Sysmon
        |  "provider" writes an event (ID + fields) via the Event Log / ETW API
        v
[Windows Event Log service]        svchost.exe hosting the "EventLog" service
        |  uses the provider's metadata (manifest) to pick the channel
        v
[log channels]                     Security, System, Application, …/Operational
        |  each channel = one file
        v
C:\Windows\System32\winevt\Logs\*.evtx
        |
        +--> Event Viewer (eventvwr.msc)
        +--> PowerShell Get-WinEvent / wevtutil.exe
        +--> forensic parsers (EvtxECmd, Hayabusa, Chainsaw, …)
        +--> collection agents / Windows Event Forwarding --> SIEM

Step by step:

  1. The provider writes the event. A provider is the software component that defines and emits events — for example Microsoft-Windows-Security-Auditing (LSA auditing), Service Control Manager, Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell or Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon. The provider supplies an event ID and the values for that event's fields.
  2. The Windows Event Log service receives it. This service (EventLog, running inside a svchost.exe) is the single post office for events. Using the provider's registered metadata (its manifest), it knows which channel the event belongs to.
  3. The event is written to a channel. Each channel is its own .evtx file. Each channel also has a maximum size and a retention behaviour (by default, overwrite the oldest events when full).
  4. Something reads the file. Event Viewer is the usual GUI, but PowerShell, wevtutil, forensic tools and log agents all read the same files through the same Windows API (or, for offline forensic parsers, by decoding the binary format directly).

Let's look at the files themselves:

PS C:\> Get-ChildItem C:\Windows\System32\winevt\Logs |
>>   Sort-Object Length -Descending | Select-Object -First 6 Name, @{n='MB';e={[math]::Round($_.Length/1MB,1)}}

Name                                                        MB
----                                                        --
Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon%4Operational.evtx                64.1
Security.evtx                                             20.1
System.evtx                                               20.1
Application.evtx                                          20.1
Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell%4Operational.evtx            15.1
Microsoft-Windows-TaskScheduler%4Operational.evtx         10.1
  • Get-ChildItem C:\Windows\System32\winevt\Logs — lists the folder where every channel's .evtx file lives.
  • Sort-Object Length -Descending | Select-Object -First 6 … — shows the six largest files with their size in MB (@{n='MB';e={…}} is a calculated column).
  • Security.evtx 20.1 — the Security channel. About 20 MB is the long-standing default maximum on many Windows versions. On a busy server that may hold only hours of events, which is why security baselines raise it a lot and why central collection must be quick.
  • Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon%4Operational.evtx — the channel Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational. A / can't appear in a file name, so Windows writes it as %4. When you search a forensic image for a channel's file, swap / for %4.
  • Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon%4Operational.evtx 64.1 — Sysmon is noisy, so its channel is usually given a larger maximum size than the default.

Why attackers care about this path. Every step is a place to blind the defender: stop or crash the EventLog service, turn auditing off with auditpol, shrink a channel so it rolls over fast, delete or corrupt .evtx files, or clear a channel (MITRE ATT&CK T1070.001 Clear Windows Event Logs, T1562.002 Disable Windows Event Logging). Clearing the Security log itself leaves Security 1102 ("The audit log was cleared"), and clearing other channels leaves System 104. That is exactly why logs must leave the host quickly — a copy in the SIEM survives what happens on the endpoint. See Impair Defenses & Log Clearing.

docs.title: Reading events from the command line
docs.text:
Event Viewer is fine for one event; for triage and hunting you'll use PowerShell. First, which channels exist and how full are they?

PS C:\> Get-WinEvent -ListLog Security, System, 'Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational' |
>>   Format-Table LogName, RecordCount, MaximumSizeInBytes, LogMode -AutoSize

LogName                                  RecordCount MaximumSizeInBytes   LogMode
-------                                  ----------- ------------------   -------
Security                                       41873           20971520  Circular
System                                         18240           20971520  Circular
Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational        9311           15728640  Circular
  • Get-WinEvent -ListLog … — returns the configuration of the named channels, not their events. -ListLog * lists every channel on the machine (several hundred).
  • RecordCount — how many events the channel currently holds.
  • MaximumSizeInBytes 20971520 — 20 MB. When full, LogMode Circular means the oldest events are overwritten. So "the earliest event in Security" tells you how far back the local evidence reaches.

Now the events themselves — the last three failed logons:

PS C:\> Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security'; Id=4625} -MaxEvents 3

   ProviderName: Microsoft-Windows-Security-Auditing

TimeCreated                     Id LevelDisplayName Message
-----------                     -- ---------------- -------
20/11/2026 02:14:09 AM        4625 Information      An account failed to log on....
20/11/2026 02:14:07 AM        4625 Information      An account failed to log on....
20/11/2026 02:14:05 AM        4625 Information      An account failed to log on....
  • -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security'; Id=4625} — the filter is handed to the Event Log service, so only matching events are returned. This is far faster than fetching everything and filtering with Where-Object.
  • -MaxEvents 3 — newest first, stop after three.
  • ProviderName: Microsoft-Windows-Security-Auditing — the provider that wrote these events (the LSA auditing provider).
  • Id 4625 — 4625 = "An account failed to log on". It is written on the machine where the logon was attempted, whenever a logon fails (bad password, unknown user, disabled account, logon type not allowed). Attackers generate it when guessing or spraying passwords (T1110), so bursts of 4625 — three in four seconds here — are a classic detection.
  • LevelDisplayName Information — note that a failed logon still shows as "Information". For Security audit events, success or failure is carried in the keywords (Audit Success / Audit Failure), not in the level. More on this below.
  • Message — the rendered description, truncated here. That's the "General" view you'll meet shortly.

wevtutil is the built-in command-line equivalent and is handy for quick XML output:

C:\> wevtutil qe Security /q:"*[System[(EventID=4625)]]" /c:1 /rd:true /f:xml
  • qe Security — query events from the Security channel.
  • /q:"*[System[(EventID=4625)]]" — an XPath filter on the System part of the event (the same filter language Event Viewer uses in "Filter Current Log → XML").
  • /c:1 — return one event. /rd:true — reverse direction, i.e. newest first. /f:xml — output the raw XML (/f:text gives the message view).

The XML it returns is shown in the three views section below.

[Supplement] Not every program uses the event log. Some applications write their own logs in text or other formats in their own folders: IIS writes W3C logs under C:\inetpub\logs\LogFiles, the Windows DNS server can write a text debug log, many third-party products keep logs under C:\ProgramData\<vendor>. These never appear in Event Viewer, so a "collect all event channels" policy silently misses them.

docs.title: Deciding which security events get created
docs.text: A camera that was never switched on doesn't record. In Windows logging terms, events only exist if something was configured to produce them before the activity. There are three sources of control.

docs.title: 1. Built-in: Windows audit policies
docs.text:
The main switch for operating-system security events is the audit policy. It is a set of fine-grained settings — "subcategories" — each of which can be set to record on Success, Failure, both or neither. Examples: Logon, Logoff, Process Creation, User Account Management, Security Group Management, File System, Registry, Kerberos Authentication Service.

C:\> auditpol /get /subcategory:"Logon","Process Creation","File System"
System audit policy
Category/Subcategory                      Setting
Logon/Logoff
  Logon                                   Success and Failure
Detailed Tracking
  Process Creation                        Success
Object Access
  File System                             No Auditing
  • auditpol /get /subcategory:… — shows the effective advanced audit policy for the named subcategories (/category:* shows them all). Run it as administrator.
  • Logon … Success and Failure — successful logons produce 4624, failed ones 4625. Turning on only Success would make password-guessing invisible.
  • Process Creation … Success — produces 4688 ("A new process has been created") each time a program starts. Failure has little meaning here, so Success is the usual setting. Remember the separate policy "Include command line in process creation events", or 4688 won't show arguments.
  • File System … No Auditing — no file-access events (4663). Note that for object access, turning the subcategory on is only half the job: you must also put an audit entry (a SACL, system access control list) on the specific folders or registry keys you care about. Auditing every file on the disk would bury you.

[Supplement] Legacy vs advanced audit policy. Windows has two layers: nine old "basic" categories (Local Policies → Audit Policy) and the newer ~60 "advanced" subcategories (Advanced Audit Policy Configuration). If both are configured through Group Policy, they can overwrite each other in confusing ways. The rule of thumb is to use only the advanced policy and enable "Audit: Force audit policy subcategory settings … to override audit policy category settings" (the SCENoApplyLegacyAuditPolicy setting). Always verify the result on a real host with auditpol rather than trusting what the GPO says.

Why attackers care: auditpol /clear or auditpol /set /subcategory:"Logon" /success:disable turns recording off without clearing anything — quieter than wiping a log. Changes to the audit policy are themselves recorded as 4719 ("System audit policy was changed"), which is worth an alert. (Audit policy design was also covered on PAWs, Permissions and Privileges, EDR, DLP, UEBA and Audit Logging.)

docs.title: 2. Add-ons: Sysmon and custom scripts
docs.text:
The built-in audit policy has gaps: it doesn't record outbound network connections per process with full detail, image hashes, DLL loads, named pipes, or DNS queries per process. Many organisations add Sysmon (System Monitor), a free Microsoft Sysinternals tool that installs a driver and service and writes rich events into its own channel, Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational: process creation with hashes and parent command line (Sysmon 1), network connections (3), driver and image loads (6, 7), process access such as opening LSASS (10), file creation (11), registry changes (12–14), DNS queries (22) and more. Because it writes to a normal event channel, the same agent that collects Security can collect it. Its value depends almost entirely on its configuration file — what to include and exclude.

You can also create your own channel. A short PowerShell script can register a new log and write any text into it — for example, the result of a nightly check of local administrators — so the log agent ships it with everything else:

PS C:\> New-EventLog -LogName 'SOC-Checks' -Source 'LocalAdminAudit'
PS C:\> Write-EventLog -LogName 'SOC-Checks' -Source 'LocalAdminAudit' -EventId 100 `
>>   -EntryType Information -Message 'Local Administrators: CORP\Domain Admins, CORP\ws-admins, WS-FIN-0217\Administrator'
  • New-EventLog -LogName 'SOC-Checks' -Source 'LocalAdminAudit' — registers a new classic channel called SOC-Checks and a source (provider) name allowed to write to it. Needs administrator rights, once per machine.
  • Write-EventLog … -EventId 100 -EntryType Information -Message '…' — writes one event. You choose the ID scheme (here 100 = "local admin snapshot"), so document it.
  • In the SIEM you can now alert when the member list changes. [Caution] these two cmdlets exist only in Windows PowerShell 5.1; they were removed from PowerShell 7. In PowerShell 7 use eventcreate.exe, a small .NET call, or run the script under powershell.exe 5.1.

docs.title: 3. Applications that log for themselves
docs.text:
For applications that do not use the Windows event log, what gets recorded depends entirely on the application's own settings and abilities. For network services — web servers, DNS servers, proxies — there are two good options:

  • Configure the service's logging so it includes every field security needs (for IIS: client IP, X-Forwarded-For, user agent, URI query, status, bytes; for DNS: queries and responses), and collect those files with the agent.
  • Capture the activity from the wire with a network sensor such as Zeek or Suricata, which writes consistent http.log, dns.log and similar records no matter how the server itself is configured. Earlier network pages, such as SMB, show what those records look like.

Often you'll want both: the server log shows what the application decided; the network log shows what actually crossed the wire.

docs.title: What every Windows event carries: the metadata
docs.text: Within a channel, each event is written with a set of metadata fields. You can see them at the bottom of Event Viewer's General tab, and they are the first things you filter on.

docs.title: Level — how serious?
docs.text:
The level describes the importance of the message. In the XML it's a number; Event Viewer shows a word:

XML Level Shown as Meaning 0 Information (LogAlways) Always logged; Security audit events use this 1 Critical Severe failure, e.g. unexpected reboot (Kernel-Power 41) 2 Error A problem, e.g. a service failed to start 3 Warning Possible problem worth noticing 4 Information Normal operation 5 Verbose Detailed tracing

Most events are informational. When hunting for crashes or failures (a security product crashing after tampering, a service that won't start because its binary was replaced), filtering for levels 1–3 is useful. But for Security events, level tells you nothing — successes and failures are both level 0. What separates them is the keywords field: Audit Success (0x8020000000000000) or Audit Failure (0x8010000000000000). Event Viewer shows this in the "Keywords" column of the Security log.

docs.title: Source (provider) — who wrote it?
docs.text: Some channels have a single writer. Others, like Application and System, have many programs writing into them. The Source field (in XML, Provider Name) is how you tell which program generated a given event. In System, for example, you'll see Service Control Manager (service installs and state changes), Microsoft-Windows-Kernel-General (time changes, boot), Microsoft-Windows-Eventlog (log cleared, 104) and many more side by side.

docs.title: Event ID — what kind of event?
docs.text:
The event ID is the most important field for Windows logs. Each provider defines a fixed set of event IDs so that the same kind of event always has the same number and is easy to find: in Security, every successful logon is 4624 and every failed logon is 4625, whichever machine you're on.

[Correction] Event IDs are unique per provider, not per channel and not globally. A common simplification is "event IDs are unique within a channel". Strictly, the ID is defined by the provider, and because one channel can contain several providers, the same number can mean different things even inside one channel. A real-world example from the System channel:

PS C:\> Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='System'; Id=1} -MaxEvents 4 |
>>   Format-Table TimeCreated, Id, ProviderName -AutoSize

TimeCreated            Id ProviderName
-----------            -- ------------
19/11/2026 07:58:31     1 Microsoft-Windows-Power-Troubleshooter
19/11/2026 07:58:30     1 Microsoft-Windows-Kernel-General
18/11/2026 23:10:02     1 Microsoft-Windows-Kernel-General
18/11/2026 17:42:55     1 Microsoft-Windows-Power-Troubleshooter
  • Both rows say Id 1 and both are in System.
  • From Microsoft-Windows-Power-Troubleshooter, ID 1 means "the system has resumed from a low-power state" (woke from sleep).
  • From Microsoft-Windows-Kernel-General, ID 1 means "the system time has changed". Changing the clock is an anti-forensic trick (it confuses timelines), so this one can matter.
  • And in the Sysmon channel, ID 1 means "process created". A detection written as just EventID=1 would mix all three.

So the reliable key is provider + event ID (and channel, to make collection filters explicit). Across channels, the well-known security IDs (4624, 4688, 7045 …) are effectively unique, which is why people get away with the shortcut — until they don't.

docs.title: Task category — a little more description
docs.text:
The task category is another metadata field. Each provider can define its own numbered categories with a text label. In Security they group events by audit subcategory: 4624 and 4625 have the task category Logon (in XML, <Task>12544</Task>), 4688 has Process Creation (13312), 4720 has User Account Management (13824). It's useful for broad filtering ("show me everything in Logon"), but the event ID is more precise.

[Supplement] The other System fields you'll meet — Opcode, Version, EventRecordID, Execution ProcessID/ThreadID, Correlation, Computer, TimeCreated — are taken apart field by field on the next page. One quick tip now: EventRecordID is a sequence number per channel. A jump in it (record 51203 followed by 51890 with nothing in between) on an exported log can show that events were removed.

docs.title: Same log, different views
docs.text: Windows logs are XML underneath, but Event Viewer can show them three ways, from easiest-to-read-but-least-structured to the raw XML. Let's take one failed logon on WS-FIN-0217.

docs.title: View 1: General (the "message")
docs.text:
This is what you see when you click on an event. It's the most human-readable and what analysts usually read:

An account failed to log on.

Subject:
    Security ID:        NULL SID
    Account Name:       -
    Account Domain:     -
    Logon ID:       0x0

Logon Type:         3

Account For Which Logon Failed:
    Security ID:        NULL SID
    Account Name:       svc-sql
    Account Domain:     CORP

Failure Information:
    Failure Reason:     Unknown user name or bad password.
    Status:         0xC000006D
    Sub Status:     0xC000006A

Process Information:
    Caller Process ID:  0x0
    Caller Process Name:    -

Network Information:
    Workstation Name:   WS-MKT-0088
    Source Network Address: 10.20.7.54
    Source Port:        0

Detailed Authentication Information:
    Logon Process:      NtLmSsp 
    Authentication Package: NTLM
    ...

It reads like a letter: an NTLM network logon (type 3) from WS-MKT-0088 at 10.20.7.54 for CORP\svc-sql failed because of a wrong password (0xC000006A = bad password for an existing account; 0xC0000064 would mean the user doesn't exist). The tabs and spacing are inconsistent, labels repeat ("Security ID" appears twice with different meanings), and the text is translated into the operating system's display language — on a Korean Windows install the same event reads "계정에 로그온하지 못했습니다." Lovely for a person, painful for a parser.

docs.title: View 2: Details → Friendly View
docs.text:
Click the Details tab and choose Friendly View. You now see the actual data the event was built from, as a tree with the XML tags hidden:

- System
    - Provider  [ Name]  Microsoft-Windows-Security-Auditing
                [ Guid]  {54849625-5478-4994-a5ba-3e3b0328c30d}
      EventID   4625
      Level     0
      Task      12544
      Keywords  0x8010000000000000
    - TimeCreated [ SystemTime] 2026-11-20T02:14:09.4371152Z
      EventRecordID 51207
      Channel   Security
      Computer  WS-FIN-0217.corp.example
- EventData
      TargetUserName      svc-sql
      TargetDomainName    CORP
      Status              0xc000006d
      SubStatus           0xc000006a
      LogonType           3
      LogonProcessName    NtLmSsp
      AuthenticationPackageName NTLM
      WorkstationName     WS-MKT-0088
      IpAddress           10.20.7.54
      IpPort              0

docs.title: View 3: Details → XML View
docs.text:
And the full XML — the true form in which the event is stored:

<Event xmlns="http://schemas.microsoft.com/win/2004/08/events/event">
  <System>
    <Provider Name="Microsoft-Windows-Security-Auditing" Guid="{54849625-5478-4994-a5ba-3e3b0328c30d}" />
    <EventID>4625</EventID>
    <Version>0</Version>
    <Level>0</Level>
    <Task>12544</Task>
    <Opcode>0</Opcode>
    <Keywords>0x8010000000000000</Keywords>
    <TimeCreated SystemTime="2026-11-20T02:14:09.4371152Z" />
    <EventRecordID>51207</EventRecordID>
    <Channel>Security</Channel>
    <Computer>WS-FIN-0217.corp.example</Computer>
  </System>
  <EventData>
    <Data Name="SubjectUserSid">S-1-0-0</Data>
    <Data Name="TargetUserName">svc-sql</Data>
    <Data Name="TargetDomainName">CORP</Data>
    <Data Name="Status">0xc000006d</Data>
    <Data Name="FailureReason">%%2313</Data>
    <Data Name="SubStatus">0xc000006a</Data>
    <Data Name="LogonType">3</Data>
    <Data Name="LogonProcessName">NtLmSsp </Data>
    <Data Name="AuthenticationPackageName">NTLM</Data>
    <Data Name="WorkstationName">WS-MKT-0088</Data>
    <Data Name="IpAddress">10.20.7.54</Data>
    <Data Name="IpPort">0</Data>
  </EventData>
</Event>

Reading the parts that matter now (the full field-by-field walk-through of System and EventData is on the next page):

  • <Provider Name="Microsoft-Windows-Security-Auditing" …/> and <EventID>4625</EventID> — the provider + ID pair that identifies the event type.
  • <Level>0</Level> with <Keywords>0x8010000000000000</Keywords> — level 0 as for all audit events; the keyword value is Audit Failure.
  • <Task>12544</Task> — task category Logon.
  • <TimeCreated SystemTime="…Z" /> — always stored in UTC (the Z). Event Viewer's General tab converts to the viewer's local time, which is a classic source of timeline mistakes. In the SIEM, keep UTC.
  • <Computer>WS-FIN-0217.corp.example</Computer> — the machine that recorded the event: the target of the logon attempt, not the source.
  • TargetUserName / TargetDomainName — the account someone tried to use.
  • FailureReason %%2313 — not text but a message-string placeholder. %%2313 is looked up in a message table and rendered as "Unknown user name or bad password." in the General view. That's why some XML values look cryptic.
  • LogonType 3, IpAddress 10.20.7.54, WorkstationName WS-MKT-0088 — where the attempt came from. A burst of these across many usernames from one IP is password spraying (T1110.003).

docs.title: How the message is built — and why it matters for the SIEM
docs.text:
The General view is not stored in the file. Each provider ships a message template for each event ID, with numbered slots, roughly:

An account failed to log on.
...
Account For Which Logon Failed:
    Account Name:       %6
    Account Domain:     %7
...
Network Information:
    Workstation Name:   %14
    Source Network Address: %20

When you open the event, Windows takes the EventData values in order and fills them into the slots (%6 ← TargetUserName, %7 ← TargetDomainName …), resolves %% placeholders, and shows the result. Windows and most log agents call this rendered text the Message field. A good analogy is a mail-merge letter: the XML is the spreadsheet row, the template is the letter, and the General view is the printed letter.

Three practical consequences:

  1. Rendering needs the provider's template on the reading machine. If you open an exported .evtx on a machine that doesn't have that provider installed (say a Sysmon or vendor log on your analysis laptop), Event Viewer shows "The description for Event ID … from source … cannot be found". The data isn't lost — it's still in the XML/Details view.
  2. The template decides what is shown. The log's author chooses which fields appear in the message. Some EventData values never appear in the General view at all, so reading only the message can make you miss fields.
  3. For the SIEM, send the structured fields. When logs are collected and shipped, the agent may send the XML data, the rendered message, or both, and that choice decides how the data is parsed on the other side:
    • The XML / EventData fields are well formatted, named, language-independent and easy for a SIEM to extract reliably (TargetUserName, IpAddress, LogonType …). These should always be sent.
    • The message is easier for a person to read and helpful for events whose XML uses generic field names (some providers only give param1, param2 …). But it is free text with inconsistent tabs and spaces, localised, and makes every event several times larger. Many teams drop it at ingestion or keep it only for selected events.

[Supplement] A real failure seen in multinational environments: a SIEM parser extracts the user name with a regular expression on Account Name: in the message. It works on English hosts and silently returns nothing for hosts installed in Korean, Japanese or German. Parsing EventData fields avoids this completely.

docs.title: The 2026 view
docs.text:
[2026 Current] Still valid

The architecture is unchanged: providers write events, the Windows Event Log service sorts them into channels, channels live as binary-XML .evtx files in C:\Windows\System32\winevt\Logs, and Event Viewer, Get-WinEvent and wevtutil read them. Audit policies still decide which Security events exist; the General/Friendly/XML views, the message-template mechanism and "provider + event ID" identity are the same. Event IDs 4624, 4625, 4688, 4719 and 1102 have not changed, and the advice to collect structured fields rather than message text is, if anything, stronger now that SIEMs normalise into common schemas.

[Changed] What has changed

  • Sysmon is now part of Windows. Since the February 2026 optional update for Windows 11 (KB5077241), Sysmon functionality ships as a built-in optional feature. It is off by default: you enable the feature and still supply a configuration, and the events still need to be collected. Server support and exact behaviour are rolling out over time — check the current Microsoft documentation for your build rather than assuming.
  • Agents changed. Microsoft's legacy Log Analytics agent (MMA) was retired in 2024; Azure Monitor Agent with data collection rules replaced it for Microsoft Sentinel. Elastic, Splunk and others have also moved to unified agents. Windows Event Forwarding (WEF/WEC) is still built in and still widely used as a free collection layer.
  • More of the important signal is no longer in local channels. Cloud sign-ins (Entra ID), Microsoft 365 audit data and EDR telemetry are collected through APIs, not .evtx files. Endpoint event logs remain essential, but they are one source among several.
  • Offline triage tools matured. Parsers such as EvtxECmd and rule-based scanners such as Hayabusa and Chainsaw (running Sigma rules directly over .evtx) are now standard in DFIR kits and are useful when a host was never collected into the SIEM.
  • Microsoft's documentation moved from docs.microsoft.com to learn.microsoft.com; the event-schema pages referenced by older material are still there under the new address.

[Caution] Wrong or risky to do the old way

  • Don't assume default log sizes are enough. With roughly 20 MB per channel a busy server can overwrite Security in hours. Raise sizes (baselines commonly call for hundreds of MB for Security) and forward events off the host quickly.
  • Don't write detections as bare EventID = N. Always pin the provider (or channel) too, or you'll mix unrelated events with the same number.
  • Don't parse the Message field with regex in a multi-language or multi-version estate. Use EventData fields.
  • Don't read zero results as "didn't happen" until you've checked the audit policy, the channel's collection and its retention for that time.
  • Don't rely on New-EventLog/Write-EventLog in PowerShell 7 — they don't exist there.
  • Don't trust a GPO screen for audit settings; verify the effective policy with auditpol on real hosts, and alert on 4719 and 1102/104.

docs.title: Question 1
docs.text:
A colleague builds a SIEM dashboard "process creations per host" by counting events with EventID = 1. Laptops that don't have Sysmon installed still show a few "process creations" every morning, all with an empty process name. What is going on, and how should the query be written?

Answer and explanation

What's going on: event IDs are only unique per provider. On laptops without Sysmon, events with ID 1 still exist — for example in the System channel from Microsoft-Windows-Power-Troubleshooter (resume from sleep, every morning) or Microsoft-Windows-Kernel-General (time changed). The query matches the number, not the event type, and those events have no process-name field — hence the empty values.

Fix: pin the source as well as the ID — channel Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational and provider Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon and EventID = 1 — then count. If you also want coverage where Sysmon is absent, add a second branch on Security 4688 from Microsoft-Windows-Security-Auditing (with command-line logging enabled).

docs.title: Question 2
docs.text:
Your SIEM extracts the user name from failed logons by matching Account Name: in the message text. After an acquisition, the new subsidiary's servers (installed in Korean) show 4625 events with an empty user field. Separately, when you open an exported Sysmon .evtx on your analysis laptop, Event Viewer says "The description for Event ID 1 from source Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon cannot be found". Explain both problems with one idea, and give the fix.

Answer and explanation

One idea: the readable message is not stored in the event. It is built when displayed (or when the agent renders it) by filling the EventData values into the provider's message template — and that template is localised and has to be present on the machine doing the rendering.

  • On Korean-language servers the template is Korean, so the text no longer contains Account Name: and the regex finds nothing.
  • On the analysis laptop the Sysmon provider (and its templates) isn't installed, so Event Viewer can't build the message. The data is still there in Details → XML.

Fix: parse the structured EventData fields (TargetUserName, IpAddress, LogonType …), which have the same names in every language, and make sure the agent ships them. Keep the message only as a human convenience (or drop it to save volume). For offline work, use a parser that reads the XML fields (or install the provider) instead of relying on Event Viewer's rendering.

docs.title: Question 3
docs.text:
During an incident you search the SIEM for 4625 events on file server FS-02 during a suspected password-spraying window two weeks ago and get zero results. Your manager wants to write "no failed logons observed". What would you check before agreeing, and in what order?

Answer and explanation

Zero results can mean "didn't happen", "never recorded" or "recorded but not collected". Check, roughly in this order:

  1. Was it recorded? Run auditpol /get /subcategory:"Logon" on FS-02 (and check the GPO history). If Failure wasn't enabled at the time, no 4625 could exist. Look for 4719 audit-policy changes around the window — an attacker might have turned it off.
  2. Is the local evidence still there? Get-WinEvent -ListLog Security → MaximumSizeInBytes, LogMode, and the oldest event's time. With a small circular log, two-week-old events are probably overwritten. Look for 1102 (Security log cleared) or 104 (another log cleared).
  3. Was it collected? Is the Security channel in the agent's configuration for FS-02? Was the agent healthy and sending during that window (heartbeat or gap in any event types from that host)? Did a filter or parser drop 4625 or the fields you searched on?
  4. Did you search correctly? Right host name format (short name vs FQDN in Computer), right time zone (events are UTC), right index/provider.
  5. Is FS-02 the right place to look? 4625 is written on the machine where the logon was attempted. Domain-account failures may also show on domain controllers as Kerberos (4771) or NTLM credential validation (4776) failures.

Only after these checks can you write "no failed logons observed"; otherwise write "no data available for that period", and record the logging gap as a finding.

docs.title: Network Forensics — Lecture Series
docs.text:
What this series is

Even when you can't image the disk, when there are thousands of systems to look at, or when the attacker has wiped their tracks, the network still keeps a record. This series explains, step by step from the beginning, how to collect, read and interpret that record — proxy logs, packets, flows and device logs. It is written Korean-first (this is the English translation). Each lesson moves through "why we need it → how it works → a small example → an example with extra conditions → how to interpret it in a real investigation", and ends with review questions and answers.

docs.title: How to read this series
docs.text:
If you're new, read from Part 1 in order. Later lessons assume the concepts from earlier ones (pcap, BPF, display filters, converting log timestamps and so on). If you already know a topic, jump straight to the lesson you need from the reading-order table on each part's first page.

flowchart TD
    P1["Part 1 · Foundations<br/>proxy logs · pcap · collection"] --> P2["Part 2 · Core protocols & logs<br/>HTTP · DNS · log aggregation"]
    P2 --> P3["Part 3 · NetFlow & file access<br/>flow analysis · SMB etc."]
    P3 --> P4["Part 4 · Tools · wireless · hunting<br/>auto extraction · CLI · Arkime"]
    P4 --> P5["Part 5 · Encryption · reversing · OPSEC<br/>TLS · undocumented protocols · capstone"]

The diagram shows the flow of the series. Going down, it moves from "how to get hold of the evidence" to "how to read evidence that is hidden". The capstone in Part 5 uses the methods from Parts 1–4 on a single case.

docs.text:

docs.title: Part 1 — Foundations of Network Evidence
docs.text:
What Part 1 covers

It starts with what the network leaves behind when you can't look at the disk. Then, in order: web proxy logs and caches, pcap files with tcpdump and BPF, Wireshark and tshark, where and with what equipment evidence is collected, and what makes network investigations hard.

docs.title: Lessons
docs.text:
All 13 lessons of Part 1 are published. Reading them in order is recommended, but the lab guides (lessons 1.10 and 1.13) can be tried right after skimming the lessons before them.

Lesson Topic Status 1.1 Evidence beyond the disk: why network forensics, and the investigator's mindset Published 1.2 Web proxies: how they work, the main products, why the config file is evidence Published 1.3 Reading proxy logs: default and custom formats, Unix time Published 1.4 Reconstructing an incident from proxy logs alone (investigation walkthrough) Published 1.5 Commercial proxy logs, and pulling responses out of the proxy cache Published 1.6 libpcap, tcpdump, and the pcap/pcapng file format Published 1.7 Selecting only the packets you need with BPF Published 1.8 Practical tcpdump options and reading the Wireshark window Published 1.9 Wireshark display filters and following streams Published 1.10 Lab guide: getting hands-on with tcpdump and Wireshark Published 1.11 Evidence acquisition: where, and with what equipment, to collect packets Published 1.12 Challenges and opportunities in network investigations Published 1.13 Lab guide: carving exfiltrated data Published

docs.title: Wrapping up Part 1
docs.text:
After Part 1 you should be able to:

  • Build and test hypotheses from evidence along the path the communication took (full packets, flows, logs), even when you can't see the disk (lessons 1.1 and 1.11).
  • Read proxy log fields, reconstruct the course of an incident from logs alone, and extract responses from the cache (lessons 1.2–1.5).
  • Understand pcap structure, capture and reduce with tcpdump and BPF, and dissect and tabulate with Wireshark and tshark (lessons 1.6–1.10).
  • Plan where and with what to acquire evidence, and find the clues that remain despite NAT, encryption and tunnels (lessons 1.11–1.12).
  • Carve an uploaded file out of a plaintext stream in several steps, show reproducibility with hashes, and report facts separately from interpretation (lesson 1.13).

Each lesson's outputs were produced with the tool versions stated in that lesson; changes are marked [Changed] and corrections [Correction].

docs.title: Lesson 1.7 — Selecting Only the Packets You Need with BPF
Lesson 1.7 — Selecting Only the Packets You Need with BPF
docs.text:
Scope of this lesson

The 'host ... and port 80' at the end of the tcpdump command in lesson 1.6 is a BPF filter. This lesson covers that filter language from the ground up.

  • What BPF is, and why it's the means of filtering "earliest and cheapest"
  • Protocol, address and port primitives, and the src and dst direction qualifiers
  • and, or, not and parentheses, and the commonly mistaken operator precedence
  • vlan, portrange, gateway, and byte- and bit-level conditions
  • What filters silently miss with IPv6, VLANs and fragmented packets
  • Reducing a large pcap with BPF, and testing and recording filters

Lab material and notation

(Actual output) in this lesson was produced with tcpdump 4.99.4 (libpcap 1.10.4) in this work environment. IPv6 is disabled in this environment, so IPv6 traffic couldn't be generated for real; instead the filter practice pcap (lab.pcap, 13 packets) was assembled by hand in Python. Only private and documentation ranges are used (10.10.0.0/16, 198.51.100.0/24, 203.0.113.0/24, 2001:db8::/32). Each packet's makeup is in the table in section 2.

docs.title: 1. One PC's traffic on a 1 Gbps link
docs.text:
(Hypothetical) Right after lesson 1.4's incident, it's decided to watch whether suspicious traffic recurs from research-segment PC 10.10.6.14. The tapped link carries an average of several hundred Mbps. Storing it all piles up several TB a day, but all that's needed is that one PC's traffic.

"Store everything and filter later" isn't the answer. The disk runs short, and if the capture machine's CPU and storage can't keep up, as in lesson 1.6, you may miss even the packets you need. You must take only what you need from the start. That's the job of BPF (Berkeley Packet Filter).

BPF decides "is this packet of interest?" at a very low level, as packets enter the OS kernel. Uninteresting packets are never even passed up to the user program (tcpdump, etc.), so every later step, whether on screen, to disk or handed to another tool, gets lighter. And almost every libpcap-based tool uses BPF, so once learned it applies everywhere: tcpdump, tshark's capture filters, Zeek, Arkime and more.

docs.title: 2. An analogy: the airport's first X-ray
docs.text:
Picture bags going through the X-ray machine at airport security. The screener judges each bag quickly against very simple rules ("pull out anything with liquids"). Only bags that pass on go to detailed inspection.

BPF is exactly this first X-ray: simple rules, but very fast, applied to every packet. But the analogy hides one of BPF's most important properties. The screener judges each bag on its own, without remembering "that passenger's other bag". BPF is the same: after judging one packet it forgets everything it saw and judges the next packet from scratch. So BPF can't express connection-level conditions such as "the rest of the packets of connections that started with a SYN", and this property also explains why src host, which we'll see later, catches only one side of a conversation.

The 13 practice packets in this lesson look like this:

# Content Notes 1–4 10.10.6.14 ↔ 203.0.113.50 port 80 HTTP: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK, GET IPv4 5 10.10.6.14 → 10.10.4.53 UDP 53 DNS query IPv4 6 10.10.6.14 → 10.10.4.53 TCP 53 SYN DNS over TCP 7 10.10.6.14 → 198.51.100.7 ICMP echo ping 8 2001:db8:6::14 → 2001:db8:ff::50 TCP 80 SYN IPv6 9 2001:db8:6::14 → 2001:db8:4::53 UDP 53 IPv6 10 10.10.6.14 → 203.0.113.60 TCP 443 SYN IPv4 11 10.10.6.14 → 224.0.0.251 UDP 5353 Multicast 12 10.10.6.14 → 203.0.113.50 TCP 80 SYN 802.1Q VLAN 20 tag 13 203.0.113.60 → 10.10.6.14 TCP 443 RST+ACK Reply from a closed port

docs.title: 3. How it works: BPF is a tiny program
docs.text:
The filter text we write is for people; the kernel turns it into a very small machine-code program and runs it on every packet. tcpdump -d shows that program (actual output):

$ tcpdump -d -y EN10MB 'udp port 53'
(000) ldh      [12]
(001) jeq      #0x86dd          jt 2    jf 8
(002) ldb      [20]
(003) jeq      #0x11            jt 4    jf 19
(004) ldh      [54]
(005) jeq      #0x35            jt 18   jf 6
(006) ldh      [56]
(007) jeq      #0x35            jt 18   jf 19
(008) jeq      #0x800           jt 9    jf 19
(009) ldb      [23]
(010) jeq      #0x11            jt 11   jf 19
(011) ldh      [20]
(012) jset     #0x1fff          jt 19   jf 13
(013) ldxb     4*([14]&0xf)
(014) ldh      [x + 14]
(015) jeq      #0x35            jt 18   jf 16
(016) ldh      [x + 16]
(017) jeq      #0x35            jt 18   jf 19
(018) ret      #262144
(019) ret      #0

-d means "don't apply the filter, show the compiled result", and -y EN10MB means "assume an Ethernet link". It looks like code at first, but reading a few lines reveals the principle.

  • ldh [12]: load 2 bytes from byte 12 of the packet (load half-word). In the Ethernet header, that's the EtherType field.
  • jeq #0x86dd jt 2 jf 8: if that value is 0x86dd (IPv6), go to line 2, otherwise line 8 (jump if equal; jt if true, jf if false).
  • The IPv6 side (lines 2–7): ldb [20] is the IPv6 header's "next header" field, 0x11 (17) is UDP, [54] and [56] are the UDP source and destination ports, and 0x35 is 53.
  • The IPv4 side (lines 8–17): 0x800 means IPv4, [23] is IPv4's protocol field, jset #0x1fff is the line that rejects the packet if the fragment offset is non-zero, and ldxb 4*([14]&0xf) computes the IPv4 header length to skip over it.
  • ret #262144: accept (pass up to 262,144 bytes). ret #0: reject.

This short program already shows two important facts. First, udp port 53 checks both IPv4 and IPv6. Second, because of line 12, IPv4 fragments other than the first never match a port condition. When a large UDP packet is split into several fragments, the second fragment onwards has no UDP header, so the port can't be known. Section 7 comes back to this.

docs.title: 4. Primitives: the basic units of a filter
docs.text: BPF expressions are built from small conditions called primitives. For each packet, each primitive is judged true or false.

docs.title: 4.1 Protocols
docs.text:
The simplest are protocol names: ip, ip6, tcp, udp, icmp and others. If the packet is that protocol it's "of interest" and evaluation continues; if not, libpcap stops processing that packet and waits for the next. The packet itself carries on its way; BPF isn't a blocking device, it selects copies.

Results against the practice file (actual output):

Filter Packets matched Interpretation (no filter) 13 Everything ip 10 IPv4 only. The two IPv6 packets (8, 9) and the VLAN-tagged packet (12) are excluded ip6 2 IPv6 only (8, 9) ip or ip6 12 Both IPv4 and IPv6. The VLAN-tagged packet (12) is still excluded tcp 8 Both IPv4 TCP and IPv6 TCP (8). The VLAN-tagged packet is excluded udp 3 5, 9, 11 icmp 1 7

Here's the first trap. ip means IPv4 only. If you wanted "all IP traffic", write ip or ip6. With IPv6 increasingly common, writing just ip and missing all IPv6 traffic happens more often than you'd think. The second trap (VLANs) is in section 6.1.

docs.title: 4.2 Addresses and ports
docs.text:
Primitive Meaning Example ether host Packets where the layer 2 MAC address is the source or destination ether host 00:50:56:0a:04:53 host Packets where the layer 3 IP address is the source or destination host 10.10.4.53 net Packets where an IP address is in that network range (CIDR) net 203.0.113.0/24 port Packets where the layer 4 port is the source or destination (TCP and UDP alike) port 53

The results (actual output):

Filter Matched Interpretation host 10.10.4.53 2 5, 6 (the DNS server's IPv4 address) net 203.0.113.0/24 6 1–4, 10, 13. The VLAN-tagged packet (12) is excluded ether host 00:50:56:0a:04:53 3 5, 6, 9 sent to the DNS server's MAC (including IPv6) port 53 3 UDP 5, TCP 6, IPv6 UDP 9 udp port 53 2 5, 9 tcp port 53 1 6

port ignores protocol. port 53 catches both UDP 53 and TCP 53. DNS is usually UDP, but uses TCP for large responses or zone transfers. To see all DNS, port 53 is right; for UDP only, put the protocol in front, as in udp port 53.

Note also that the IPv6 packet (9) appears in the ether host result. A MAC address is layer 2, so it doesn't matter whether IPv4 or IPv6 sits above it. You can use it to catch the same device's IPv4 and IPv6 traffic together. But MAC addresses only mean something within one segment. They change across a router, so depending on the tap position (lesson 1.1 section 10), what you see may be "the router's MAC" rather than "that device's MAC".

docs.title: 4.3 Direction: src and dst
docs.text:
All the primitives above ignore direction. host 10.10.4.53 matches whether that address is source or destination. To set a direction, put a direction qualifier, src (source) or dst (destination), in front (actual output):

Filter Matched Interpretation src host 10.10.6.14 8 Only IPv4 packets that PC sent dst host 10.10.6.14 2 Only IPv4 packets that PC received (2, 13)

To see both sides of the conversations that PC is part of, just use host 10.10.6.14. Remember section 2's analogy: BPF judges each packet separately, so src host looks only at that packet's source field and has no idea a reply to it comes separately.

Oddly, only MAC addresses use different syntax. For IP the qualifier comes before, as in src host, src net, src port, but for MAC it comes after ether and host is dropped, as in ether src and ether dst. Both directions is ether host. Annoying to memorise, but getting it wrong is a syntax error, so you'll soon get used to it.

docs.title: 5. Combining with logic
docs.text:
Primitives are simple, but combining them with and (or &&), or (||) and not (!) builds elaborate conditions, and parentheses set the order.

'tcp and (port 80 or port 443 or port 8080) and (not dst host 203.0.113.1)'

That means "TCP packets on one of ports 80, 443 or 8080, whose destination isn't 203.0.113.1". As lesson 1.6 said, parentheses and spaces are special to the shell, so wrapping the whole filter in quotes is essential.

docs.title: 5.1 [Caution] and and or have equal precedence
docs.text:
Many people get this wrong. In maths and most programming languages, "and" is evaluated before "or". BPF is different. Per the libpcap documentation, not comes first, and and and or have equal precedence and associate left to right. Compare directly (actual output):

Filter Matched tcp port 80 or udp port 53 and host 10.10.4.53 1 tcp port 80 or (udp port 53 and host 10.10.4.53) 6

If you wrote the first line meaning "all HTTP, or UDP DNS to the DNS server", you're in trouble. BPF groups it from the left as (tcp port 80 or udp port 53) and host 10.10.4.53, leaving only the one packet involving the DNS server (5). All five HTTP packets are dropped. As a capture filter, the HTTP would never have been stored. So when mixing and and or, always state your intent with parentheses.

One more: libpcap has a rule that "if a keyword is omitted, the most recent keyword is assumed". not host 10.10.4.53 and 10.10.4.54 is read as not host 10.10.4.53 and host 10.10.4.54, which means something completely different from not (host 10.10.4.53 or host 10.10.4.54). It's safer not to abbreviate and to write the keyword for every primitive.

docs.title: 5.2 Identical to the computer, different to people
docs.text:
Look at these two filters:

'ip and (tcp port 80 or udp port 53)'
'(ip and tcp port 80) or (ip and udp port 53)'

Drawn as a picture, one packet passes through the first filter in this order:

flowchart TD
    P["One packet arrives"] --> A{"IPv4?"}
    A -->|"no"| R["Reject"]
    A -->|"yes"| B{"TCP 80?"}
    B -->|"yes"| K["Accept (store · show)"]
    B -->|"no"| C{"UDP 53?"}
    C -->|"yes"| K
    C -->|"no"| R

How to read the diagram: each diamond is one decision, asked in turn from top to bottom. Once a decision reaches a conclusion (accept or reject), that packet's evaluation ends, and the next packet starts again from the top. Section 2's "each bag on its own" property is right there in the picture.

They mean the same. Both matched 5 packets in the practice file, and comparing the compiled output from tcpdump -d showed exactly the same 21-line program (actual output):

$ tcpdump -d -y EN10MB 'ip and (tcp port 80 or udp port 53)' > a.bpf
$ tcpdump -d -y EN10MB '(ip and tcp port 80) or (ip and udp port 53)' > b.bpf
$ cmp -s a.bpf b.bpf && echo "IDENTICAL compiled code"
IDENTICAL compiled code

Tools like tcpdump optimise filters before running them, so expressions with the same meaning often become the same program however a person wrote them. But the logical flow a person reads differs. The first reads "among IPv4, HTTP or DNS"; the second "IPv4 HTTP, or IPv4 DNS".

As the source material stresses, whether a person can understand and explain the filter matters as much as computational efficiency, perhaps more. Filters get written into reports, reused by colleagues, and become the answer in court to "under what conditions was this evidence collected?" The more complex a filter, the more room for syntax mistakes and the harder to explain, so pick the most readable form.

docs.title: 6.1 vlan: tagged traffic
docs.text:
A VLAN (virtual LAN) logically splits one switch into several segments, and when switches carry several VLANs over one link, a 4-byte 802.1Q tag is inserted into the Ethernet header. Such a link is called a trunk. If a tap or mirror is on a trunk, captured packets carry this tag.

The problem is that the 4-byte tag shifts every later position by 4 bytes. Fixed positions like [12] and [23] in section 3's compiled output no longer line up. So the practice file's VLAN-tagged packet (12, a TCP 80 SYN on VLAN 20) did this (actual output):

Filter Matched Interpretation tcp port 80 5 1–4 and the IPv6 packet 8. The VLAN-tagged packet 12 is excluded vlan and tcp port 80 1 Only 12 vlan 20 1 Packets with VLAN number 20

With the vlan keyword, libpcap computes the conditions after it at positions shifted by the tag. So for a file captured on a trunk, write vlan and tcp port 80. If tagged and untagged packets are mixed, write both, as in tcp port 80 or (vlan and tcp port 80) (6 matches, actual output). Order matters: putting vlan first and the untagged condition after can make the later condition use shifted positions too, contrary to intent. As the source material puts it, this "can get tricky", so always test filters for trunk links against real files.

The lesson for investigations: when a filter returns "nothing matched", first check whether the capture point was a trunk. The tags may have made the filter silently miss.

docs.title: 6.2 portrange
docs.text: Matches a contiguous range of ports rather than one port. portrange 50000-50002 matched 5 in the practice file (port 50000 in 1–4 and port 50002 in 8; actual output). Direction qualifiers work too, as in src portrange and dst portrange. It's handy for services using dynamic ports, or malware using source ports in a particular range.

docs.title: 6.3 gateway
docs.text:
gateway host matches packets whose layer 2 MAC address is that host's but whose layer 3 IP address is not that host's, i.e. packets that passed through that host. The libpcap documentation describes it as equivalent to ether host <MAC> and not host <IP>. Normally the default gateway (router) plays this role, so if a device that isn't the gateway matches, you might suspect a fake gateway intercepting traffic in the middle (a man-in-the-middle, MITM).

But per the documentation, gateway must be followed by a name, and that name must resolve on the analysis machine both to an IP address (hosts file, DNS, etc.) and to a MAC address (/etc/ethers, etc.). In practice it's simpler to write the equivalent ether host ... and not host ... directly, which also avoids creating OPSEC problems through name lookups.

docs.title: 6.4 Byte- and bit-level conditions
docs.text:
The most cryptic but most powerful feature. The form is protocol[offset:size], with size 1, 2 or 4 bytes (1 if omitted). You can use comparisons (=, !=, >, <) and bitwise operations (& and, | or).

[Correction] Offsets count from the start of that protocol's header. The source material says "the offset is zero-based and calculated from the first byte of the IP header", which is true for ip[...]. Per the libpcap documentation, tcp[...] counts from the start of the TCP header and ether[...] from the start of the Ethernet header.

Some examples (actual output):

Filter Meaning Matched ip[9] == 6 Byte 9 of the IPv4 header (protocol field) is 6 (TCP) 7 tcp[13] & 0x02 != 0 In byte 13 of the TCP header (flags), the SYN bit (0x02) is set 4 tcp[tcpflags] & tcp-syn != 0 The same meaning, written with names 4 tcp[tcpflags] == tcp-syn Only SYN is set in the flags 3

Unpacking tcp[13] & 0x02 != 0: bitwise-AND byte 13 with 0x02 (binary 00000010); if the result isn't 0, i.e. the SYN bit is set, it matches. libpcap provides names for these positions such as tcpflags, tcp-syn, tcp-ack, tcp-rst and tcp-fin, which read more easily than numbers.

The difference between the last two lines matters. & tcp-syn != 0 means "if SYN is set (even with other flags)", catching both SYN and SYN-ACK (1, 2, 6, 10), while == tcp-syn means "exactly SYN", catching only the first packets of new connections (1, 6, 10). To see "who started the connection", the latter is right.

Now we can unpack the puzzling filter from lesson 1.6:

'tcp[((tcp[12]&0xf0)>>2):4] = 0x47455420'
  • tcp[12]: byte 12 of the TCP header. Its upper 4 bits are the TCP header length (in 4-byte units).
  • & 0xf0: keep only those upper 4 bits.
  • >> 2: shift right 2 bits. The upper-4-bit value sits at 16× its value, so dividing by 4 (>>2) gives "header length × 4", i.e. the header length in bytes. A header length field of 5 is 0x50 → 0x14 = 20 bytes.
  • tcp[that value:4]: the 4 bytes right after the TCP header, i.e. the first 4 bytes of data.
  • = 0x47455420: are those 4 bytes G (0x47) E (0x45) T (0x54) space (0x20), i.e. GET?

In the practice file only packet 4 matched. It finds HTTP GET requests on any port, so you can use it to find lesson 1.2's "HTTP bypassing the proxy out on an odd port".

These conditions look complex but run very fast, close to the kernel. If this is the surest way to pick out the traffic of interest, filtering with BPF before handing it to CPU-heavy back-end processing is the right call.

docs.title: 7. [Caution] What filters silently miss
docs.text:
Here are the traps seen so far. None produces an error; they just silently catch less, which makes them more dangerous.

Byte conditions don't match IPv6. Packet 8 in the practice file is an IPv6 TCP SYN, yet none of section 6.4's SYN filters caught it. Checking (actual output):

Filter Matched ip6 and tcp[13] & 0x02 != 0 0 ip6 and ip6[6] == 6 1

The libpcap documentation still states (both the 1.10 branch and the current development documentation) that byte access for upper-layer protocols such as tcp[...] and udp[...] doesn't match IPv6 packets (checked 2026-11-05). For IPv6, count directly from the IPv6 header with ip6[...]. ip6[6] == 6 checks whether byte 6 of the IPv6 header (the next header field) is 6 (TCP). But this too only works when there are no extension headers, because extension headers push the TCP header further back. If you use byte-level filters in an environment with a lot of IPv6, always test against real files and record the limits. Distinguish this from named primitives like tcp and tcp port 80, which did catch IPv6 (section 4).

VLAN tags throw off fixed positions, as section 6.1 showed.

IPv4 fragments from the second onwards don't match port conditions, because of the jset #0x1fff in section 3's compiled output. If an attacker deliberately splits packets into small fragments, the later fragments can be missing from a capture using a port filter. To be sure of seeing fragmented traffic, capture on address conditions (host) only and judge ports later, after reassembly.

ip is IPv4 only, the trap from section 4.1.

docs.title: 8. Reducing large files
docs.text:
Another key use of tcpdump is reducing an existing pcap with BPF. Leave the original untouched, and make a new file by extracting what's relevant or removing what isn't (actual output):

$ cat reduce.bpf
not port 443
and not net 224.0.0.0/4
and not port 53
$ tcpdump -n -r lab.pcap -F reduce.bpf -w reduced.pcap
reading from file lab.pcap, link-type EN10MB (Ethernet), snapshot length 262144
$ capinfos -c -s lab.pcap reduced.pcap
File name:           lab.pcap
Number of packets:   13
File size:           1078 bytes
File name:           reduced.pcap
Number of packets:   7
File size:           587 bytes

It reads the original with -r, uses a filter written in a file with -F, and writes a new file with -w. -F lets you manage complex filters as files, so a team can keep its filters in a git repository and everyone uses the same ones. Inside a filter file you can split lines, and there are no shell quoting issues.

This filter removed port 443 (usually HTTPS, content not visible), 224.0.0.0/4 (multicast, usually noise) and port 53 (DNS, assumed to be in other logs already). 13 packets became 7, and 1,078 bytes became 587. On real large files you can cut size substantially this way too. Wireshark takes a long time to open large pcaps and may not open files beyond several hundred MB at all, so reducing before opening is especially important.

[Caution] Check the "it's elsewhere" assumption. If DNS was removed "because it's in the DNS server logs", confirm those logs really exist and cover the incident window. And because you're making a new file, not editing the original, you can always go back to the original to look at what was removed. Always keep the original.

docs.title: 9. How to interpret it in a real investigation
docs.text:
Capture filters are permanent. Packets dropped by a BPF applied at capture time can never be seen again. Wireshark's display filters, covered in lesson 1.9, only choose which already-stored packets to show, so they can always be undone. Hence the principle: keep capture filters conservative, i.e. generous, and do fine selection after storing. For section 1's case, it's safer to apply just host 10.10.6.14 and not filter by port or protocol, which is less exposed to section 7's traps (fragments, VLANs, IPv6).

Test filters and record them. The more elaborate a filter, the more chance of a syntax mistake. Before using one in operations, ① count matches against known traffic in the lab, ② check it compiles with tcpdump -d, and ③ confirm it doesn't drop packets under real load. And in reports, write the filter used verbatim. With pcapng, as lesson 1.6 showed, it's also kept in the file.

Don't read "the filter caught nothing" as "there was nothing". This is the BPF version of the principle repeated since lesson 1.1. If the result is 0, first check for IPv6, a VLAN trunk, fragments, or a precedence mistake.

docs.title: 10. Summary
docs.text:
• BPF is a filter language that judges "is this of interest?" for each packet close to the kernel, and almost every libpcap-based tool uses it. Filtering at capture reduces load and storage.
  • BPF judges each packet separately and doesn't remember earlier packets. So src host catches only one side of a conversation.
  • The basic primitives are protocols (ip, ip6, tcp, udp, icmp), addresses (ether host, host, net), port, and direction (src, dst, and for MAC ether src/ether dst). ip is IPv4 only, and port doesn't distinguish TCP from UDP.
  • and and or have equal precedence and group from the left. Always use parentheses when mixing them. Computers optimise equivalent meanings into the same code, but choosing a form people can read matters.
  • vlan, portrange, gateway and byte/bit conditions (ip[9], tcp[tcpflags]) are powerful, but offsets count from each protocol header's start, and they can silently miss VLAN-tagged packets, IPv6, and later IPv4 fragments.
  • Reduce large files with tcpdump -r original -F filterfile -w newfile, and keep the original.
  • Capture filters can't be undone, so keep them generous, and test and record the filters you use verbatim.

In the next lesson (1.8) we cover tcpdump's practical options (splitting, rotating and limiting files) and reading the Wireshark window.

docs.title: Review questions
docs.text:
Question 1. To capture "all IP traffic that PC exchanged", you wrote ip and host 10.10.6.14. The PC has both IPv4 and IPv6 addresses. What do you miss, and how should you fix it?

Answer and explanation

ip means IPv4 only, and host 10.10.6.14 is an IPv4 address too. So you miss all of the PC's IPv6 traffic. Writing the PC's IPv6 address (e.g. 2001:db8:6::14) as well, as host 10.10.6.14 or host 2001:db8:6::14, is right; you can drop ip and entirely. You could exploit both addresses being the same device and write ether host 00:50:56:0a:06:14, but MAC addresses only mean something within one segment, so if the tap is across a router, the PC's MAC won't be visible. Choose according to the capture point.

Question 2. (Precedence) How many packets does this filter match in the practice file? Explain why, and rewrite it to mean what the author probably wanted.

'host 203.0.113.50 or host 203.0.113.60 and tcp port 443'
Answer and explanation

BPF groups and and or at equal precedence from the left, so this filter is (host 203.0.113.50 or host 203.0.113.60) and tcp port 443. In the practice file, only packets 10 (SYN to 203.0.113.60) and 13 (RST from 203.0.113.60) involve port 443, both involving .60, so 2 match. The HTTP packets with 203.0.113.50 (1–4) are on port 80 and all drop out. If the author wanted "all traffic with 203.0.113.50, plus HTTPS with 203.0.113.60", write host 203.0.113.50 or (host 203.0.113.60 and tcp port 443). That matches 6: 1–4, 10 and 13 (the VLAN-tagged packet 12 still drops out). The results of 2 and 6 for the two filters were confirmed by running them against the practice file.

Question 3. Explain the difference between tcp[tcpflags] & tcp-syn != 0 and tcp[tcpflags] == tcp-syn, and say which is right for building "a list of internal PCs that started new connections outward".

Answer and explanation

The former means "if the SYN bit is set, even with other bits", catching both connection requests (SYN) and their replies (SYN-ACK). The latter catches only packets where SYN alone is set, i.e. the first packet that starts a connection. To find who started connections, == tcp-syn is right; with the former, external servers that sent SYN-ACKs get mixed into the list. Adding and src net 10.10.0.0/16 makes it "first SYNs sent by internal addresses". And this condition doesn't match IPv6 packets (section 7), so in an environment using IPv6, look at the IPv6 side separately by other means (ip6[...], or Wireshark filters after storage).

Question 4. (Common misconception) A colleague applied tcp port 80 to a pcap captured from a tap on a trunk link, got 0 results, and says "there was no HTTP on this segment". How would you check?

Answer and explanation

On a trunk link every packet carries an 802.1Q VLAN tag, shifting later positions by its 4 bytes. tcp port 80 then silently misses tagged packets (confirmed directly in section 6.1). First check with tcpdump -n -e -r file -c 5 whether packets show vlan, and if so, count again with vlan and tcp port 80 or tcp port 80 or (vlan and tcp port 80). If it's still 0, then you can say "within this file's scope, no HTTP on port 80 is visible", and check HTTP on other ports separately by a port-independent method such as section 6.4's GET byte condition.

Question 5. (Byte calculation) Byte 12 of a TCP header is 0x80. How many bytes is the TCP header, and where does section 6.4's GET filter look for the start of data in this packet?

Answer and explanation

0x80 & 0xf0 = 0x80, 0x80 >> 2 = 0x20 = 32, so the TCP header is 32 bytes, the same as the upper-4-bit value 8 times 4 (8 × 4 = 32). That's the common case of the basic 20-byte header plus 12 bytes of options (e.g. the timestamp option). So the filter compares tcp[32:4], the 4 bytes 32 bytes after the start of the TCP header, with 0x47455420. Had you assumed a fixed header length of 20 and written tcp[20:4], it would miss on most real packets with options. That's why the expression computes the length per packet.

Question 6. (IPv6) On an IPv6-only segment you want to capture "new TCP connection requests (packets with only SYN set)" with BPF. What happens with tcp[tcpflags] == tcp-syn, and what's the alternative?

Answer and explanation

Per the libpcap documentation, tcp[...] byte access doesn't match IPv6 packets, so nothing is captured (the same reason the IPv6 SYN got 0 in section 7). The alternative is to count directly from the IPv6 header. The basic IPv6 header is 40 bytes, and with no extension headers the TCP header follows immediately, so the TCP flags byte is ip6[40+13] = ip6[53]. You can write ip6 and ip6[6] == 6 and ip6[53] == 0x02 (or the expression form ip6[40+13]); in the practice file both forms matched only packet 8, the IPv6 SYN (actual output). ip6[6] == 6 checks "next header is TCP". But this approach misses when there are extension headers. So rather than a capture filter with such limits, it's safer to capture generously with something like ip6 and tcp and pick out SYNs afterwards with Wireshark or tshark display filters (lesson 1.9).

Question 7. (Data reduction) Before viewing a 5 GB pcap in Wireshark, you reduced it with not port 53 and not port 443 to 800 MB. What goes in the report, and what do you do if the hypothesis "C2 over DNS" comes up later?

Answer and explanation

The report gives the original file and its hash, the command and filter used to reduce it verbatim (tcpdump -n -r original.pcap -w reduced.pcap 'not port 53 and not port 443'), the reduced file's hash and packet count, and the limitation "this analysis used a file with ports 53 and 443 removed". If a DNS C2 hypothesis comes up later, the reduced file has no port 53, so go back to the original and extract with port 53 this time to analyse separately. That's possible because you kept the original. Had you written "no DNS anomalies" from the reduced file alone, you'd have said something wasn't there that you could never have seen.

Question 8. (Design) In section 1's case, a colleague proposes the capture filter host 10.10.6.14 and (tcp port 80 or tcp port 443) and not ip6. Give at least three risks of this filter, and propose a better capture filter.

Answer and explanation
  1. It permanently misses traffic outside 80 and 443. Attackers can run C2 on other ports (53, 8080, arbitrary high ports).
  2. It misses UDP. DNS tunnels and QUIC (UDP 443) traffic drop out.
  3. It explicitly excludes IPv6. If the PC has an IPv6 address, all that traffic drops out; and host 10.10.6.14 is an IPv4 address, so IPv6 was excluded anyway.
  4. It can miss later IPv4 fragments and VLAN-tagged packets. The port conditions drop fragments from the second onwards, and on a trunk, tagged packets drop out.

A better proposal: apply only the PC's addresses, as in host 10.10.6.14 or host 2001:db8:6::14 (considering vlan if it's a trunk), and do port and protocol selection with display filters after storage. The principle: capture filters generous, analysis filters fine-grained. If storage is a concern, manage it with lesson 1.8's file rotation options rather than narrowing the filter.

docs.text:
• The Tcpdump Group, libpcap 1.10 branch pcap-filter documentation source (checked 2026-11-05). Primitives and qualifiers; the rule that not comes first and and/or have equal precedence grouping from the left; the omitted-keyword rule; the definition of gateway and its name resolution requirement; offsets in proto[expr:size] being relative to that protocol layer; names such as tcpflags.
  • The Tcpdump Group, libpcap development branch pcap-filter documentation source (checked 2026-11-05). The current statement that upper-layer byte access doesn't match IPv6 packets.
  • IEEE 802.1Q (VLAN tags), RFC 8200 (IPv6 header and extension headers) and RFC 791 (the IPv4 fragment offset) are the basis for the header structures used in this lesson's offset calculations.

docs.title: 1.12 — Challenges and Opportunities in Network Investigations
1.12 — Challenges and Opportunities in Network Investigations
docs.text:
Scope of this lesson

  • Change is inevitable: a network diagram starts going stale the moment it's drawn
  • NAT: mapping one "address and port" reported from outside back to an inside PC (a correlation done by hand)
  • Encryption: [Changed] TLS you can decrypt with the server's private key has become rare (tested directly: only TLS 1.2 RSA decrypted)
  • Tunnels: BPF can't see traffic inside GRE and 6in4 (tested directly), DoH, and [Changed] ECH (RFC 9849)
  • VPNs, WAN optimisation, wireless, cloud: the challenges and opportunities of each
  • Traffic volumes grow, and malware still depends on the network

Lab environment and notation

(Actual output) comes from this environment's tshark 4.2.2, tcpdump 4.99.4 and OpenSSL 3.0.13. The TLS experiment captured real connections made on loopback with openssl s_server and s_client, using a self-signed certificate I created (files.lab.example). The pcaps for the NAT and tunnel experiments were assembled in Python (private and documentation addresses only).
