Assembled pcaps are for showing the principle, and may differ in detail from traffic produced by real equipment.

docs.title: 1. Change: inevitable, and usually hard
docs.text:
(Hypothetical) In an incident response meeting, the network engineer puts up the diagram. "The lab is behind this firewall, and all web traffic goes to the proxy." But when you actually capture packets, some traffic is leaving by a completely different path because of a device installed three months ago. It isn't on the diagram.

Network investigation is a field of constant change. Every new technology, every new design approach (sometimes just a buzzword) brings something to add to analysis toolkits and response plans. Nobody wants to tell the executives that "a device installed a few months ago made the whole response procedure useless". If the security team is involved from the moment a new technology is adopted, though, you can make use of the opportunities it brings.

This isn't only about new technology. Most organisations have detailed diagrams and operating documents, but they're never 100% accurate; they start going stale as soon as they're written. In the end, success depends less on pressing a fixed sequence of buttons than on adapting to the unexpected and seizing unexpected opportunities.

This lesson goes through the structures that most often trouble investigators, and for each one sums up the challenge it brings and, at the same time, the opportunity.

docs.title: 2. NAT: who on the inside is that one outside address?
2.1 What NAT is
docs.text:
When RFC 760 (later superseded by RFC 791) set IP addresses at 32 bits in 1980, hardly anyone imagined more than four billion devices on the Internet. Today IPv4 exhaustion is real, and one response is NAT (Network Address Translation). A NAT device maps one or more inside addresses to one or more outside addresses, remembers the mapping per connection, and rewrites the addresses on returning packets. Each end sees only addresses consistent with its own place on the network.

NAT is commonly used between private ranges (RFC 1918) and public addresses, but also between private and private, or public and public. A typical case is after one company acquires another and the two networks' addresses overlap. NAT is often inserted as a workaround instead of proper network integration.

What matters to the investigator is the observation point. The same connection appears as 10.10.6.14:51000 inside the NAT and 203.0.113.5:61022 outside. Depending on which side a pcap was captured or a log was written, the "source" differs.

docs.title: 2.2 Opportunity: devices that record both, and correlation
docs.text:
Some enterprise devices record NAT translations. Many flow deployments store both the pre- and post-translation addresses for each connection (the nfdump 1.7.3 used in lesson 1.11's lab also showed translated-address columns such as X-Src IP Addr the first time it printed in its default format; they were empty as 0.0.0.0 because softflowd doesn't do NAT). Then, when an outside party reports "your public address talked to a known C2 server", finding the connection in the flows gives you the inside address immediately.

Without such records, all is not lost. You can correlate several pieces of evidence; it just takes longer. I tried it.

(Hypothetical) The outside party's notification: "Around 2026-11-02 09:02:00 UTC, there was a connection from your 203.0.113.5, source port 61022, to 198.51.100.66:443." We have inside.pcap captured inside the NAT and outside.pcap captured outside.

① Inside, find every connection start (SYN) to that destination at that time

tshark -n -r inside.pcap -Y 'ip.dst == 198.51.100.66 && tcp.flags.syn == 1 && tcp.flags.ack == 0' \
  -T fields -e frame.time_utc -e ip.src -e tcp.srcport -e tcp.seq_raw

(Actual output)

Nov  2, 2026 09:02:00.200000000 UTC 10.10.7.11  50110   3492838502
Nov  2, 2026 09:02:00.900000000 UTC 10.10.6.14  51000   3340291515
Nov  2, 2026 09:02:01.300000000 UTC 10.10.7.15  49822   1388325221
Nov  2, 2026 09:02:01.600000000 UTC 10.10.6.11  53001   3794726010
Nov  2, 2026 09:02:02.400000000 UTC 10.10.6.14  51001   1337529987

Five connections to the same C2 within three seconds, from four PCs. "Around 09:02:00" alone can't pick one, and the outside party's clock may be a few seconds off. The inside port was changed by NAT, so you can't search for 61022 either.

② Outside, find the connection on the reported port and look at its TCP sequence number

tshark -n -r outside.pcap -Y 'tcp.srcport == 61022 && tcp.flags.syn == 1 && tcp.flags.ack == 0' \
  -T fields -e frame.time_utc -e ip.src -e tcp.srcport -e tcp.seq_raw

(Actual output)

Nov  2, 2026 09:02:00.900000000 UTC 203.0.113.5 61022   3340291515

tcp.seq_raw is the sequence number actually written in the packet, not the relative number Wireshark renumbers from 0 for readability. Ordinary NAT changes addresses and ports and leaves this value alone.

③ Search for that sequence number inside

tshark -n -r inside.pcap -Y 'tcp.seq_raw == 3340291515' -T fields -e ip.src -e tcp.srcport

(Actual output) 10.10.6.14 51000. The time (09:02:00.9) matches exactly too. When time, destination and sequence number all line up, that's fairly strong support.

[Caution] When this method fails

  • Devices that rewrite sequence numbers: some firewalls randomise the TCP initial sequence number for security (e.g. Cisco ASA's sequence number randomisation). Step ③ then fails, and you must match on other characteristics such as time, packet sizes and connection duration.
  • No outside capture: the time and source port in the notification alone can be matched against the NAT device's translation log. If even that is missing, narrow the candidates as in step ① and choose with other evidence.
  • Proxy logs: if the C2 used HTTP or HTTPS, the proxy logs (lesson 1.3) contain the inside address, host name and URL. If the connection seen from outside belongs to the proxy, the proxy log points directly to the inside PC.
  • The two pcaps in this lab were assembled to show the principle and assume a NAT that leaves sequence numbers unchanged.

docs.title: 3. Encryption: the biggest wall, and what remains
3.1 The challenge
docs.text:
The biggest wall in network investigation is encryption. There's no easy way to "crack" strong, properly deployed encryption, and plaintext services are disappearing fast. If your analytic methods are built on being able to see the content, their effectiveness drops immediately.

Still, encryption ultimately rests on trust, and trust is complicated. In enterprise environments, the TLS interception from lesson 1.2 (the proxy re-issues certificates from the organisation's CA) lets you inspect and capture most TLS in plaintext.

docs.title: 3.2 [Changed] "Capture now, decrypt later with the key" rarely works any more
docs.text:
The source material explains, from a law enforcement perspective, that "if you might acquire the private key later (e.g. by a search warrant), capturing the encrypted traffic now is useful, and with the key, tools like Wireshark can decrypt it". I tested how true this is for today's TLS.

With the same server certificate and private key, I made three kinds of connection and sent a GET /secret-report.txt request in each. Then I gave tshark ① no key, ② the server's private key, and ③ a key log of session secrets written by the client, and checked whether the request path became visible.

# ② decrypt with the server private key
tshark -n -r t13.pcap -d tcp.port==8444,tls -o 'uat:rsa_keys:"srv.key",""' -Y http.request -T fields -e http.request.uri
# ③ decrypt with the key log
tshark -n -r t13.pcap -d tcp.port==8444,tls -o 'tls.keylog_file:t13.keys' -Y http.request -T fields -e http.request.uri
  • -d tcp.port==8444,tls: "Decode As": dissect this port as TLS (lesson 1.9).
  • -o 'uat:rsa_keys:...': puts the server's private key file in Wireshark's RSA keys list.
  • -o 'tls.keylog_file:...': points to the file recording the keys created for each session. Browsers, curl and OpenSSL can write this file via the SSLKEYLOGFILE environment variable or the -keylogfile option.

(Actual output)

Connection Key exchange No key Server private key Key log TLS 1.2, AES128-GCM-SHA256 RSA not visible visible visible TLS 1.2, ECDHE-RSA-AES128-GCM-SHA256 ECDHE not visible not visible visible TLS 1.3, TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384 (EC)DHE not visible not visible visible

Why the difference? In RSA key exchange, the client sends the material for the session key encrypted with the server's public key. So with the server's private key you can recover that material, even later, and rebuild the session key. (EC)DHE key exchange such as ECDHE builds the session key from temporary keys that both sides use for that connection only and then discard. The server's private key is used only to sign "this server is genuine", not to build the session key. So obtaining the private key later doesn't decrypt past connections. This property is called forward secrecy.

And TLS 1.3 (RFC 8446) removed RSA key exchange altogether; every key exchange is designed to provide forward secrecy. Most TLS connections today are TLS 1.3 or TLS 1.2 with ECDHE, so assume that seizing the server's private key will almost never decrypt traffic you've already captured.

So what does work?

  • Key logs. All three connections in the table decrypted. That's possible if you prepared endpoints or proxies to write key logs in advance. But obtaining such a log after the fact for an attacker's connections is hard.
  • Devices that are one end of the connection. TLS-intercepting proxies and decryption appliances can see or record plaintext (lessons 1.2 and 1.11).
  • So a "capture now, decrypt later" plan is only possible after checking which key exchange the connections use. You can see it in the pcap from the Server Hello's tls.handshake.ciphersuite: in the experiment above, 0x009c (RSA), 0xc02f (ECDHE) and 0x1302 (TLS 1.3).

[Supplement] SSH and other protocols

The source material notes that decrypted SSHv2 content isn't accessible at this time. SSHv2's key exchange is also Diffie-Hellman based, so after-the-fact decryption is effectively hard for the same reason. There is research and tooling for extracting keys from endpoints, but that belongs to endpoint forensics.

docs.title: 3.3 Opportunity: flow analysis works the same on encrypted traffic
docs.text: If you can't see the content, do analysis that doesn't need content: flow analysis. Addresses and ports, and also packet sizes and timing, are enough to generate leads and build hypotheses, just as lesson 1.11 found five-minute-interval connections of identical size (717 bytes) and a 20 MB upload without any content. And even with TLS 1.3, the Client Hello is still mostly plaintext, so unless ECH is used, the server name being contacted (SNI) is visible (lesson 1.2).

docs.title: 4.1 What a tunnel is
docs.text:
In a tunnel, one stream of traffic becomes the payload of another. Some protocols are designed for tunnelling, such as GRE (IP protocol 47); others, such as HTTP, DNS and ICMP, are repurposed as tunnels. There's also 6in4 (IP protocol 41), joining two IPv6 enclaves across an IPv4 network, SOCKS, somewhere between a proxy and a tunnel, and SSH tunnels.

The challenge: many tools aren't tunnel-aware, and there are so many tunnel types that detecting, let alone managing, them is hard. Investigators must first notice that a tunnel exists and decide how to strip it before content analysis can begin.

docs.title: 4.2 Tested: BPF can't see inside a tunnel
docs.text:
I built a pcap containing the same HTTP request in three shapes: ① plain TCP 80 over IPv4, ② IPv4 TCP 80 inside GRE, ③ IPv6 TCP 80 inside 6in4.

(Actual output)

Filter Tool Matching packets tcp port 80 tcpdump (BPF) 1 ip proto 47 tcpdump (BPF) 1 (the GRE packet) ip proto 41 tcpdump (BPF) 1 (the 6in4 packet) host 10.20.1.5 (inner GRE address) tcpdump (BPF) 0 tcp.port == 80 tshark (display filter) 3 ip.addr == 10.20.1.5 tshark (display filter) 1 http.request tshark (display filter) 3

BPF's tcp port 80 looks only at the outer header (lesson 1.7). The GRE packet's outside is "IP protocol 47" and the 6in4 packet's outside is "IP protocol 41", so neither looks like TCP. Had tcp port 80 been the capture filter, the web traffic inside the tunnels wouldn't even have been saved. Wireshark's dissectors, on the other hand, strip tunnels and dissect what's inside, so the display filter found all three.

One more thing: printing ip.src for the GRE packet gave two values, 192.0.2.1,10.20.1.5 (actual output), because both the outer and inner IP headers are present. The "multi-value fields" of lesson 1.9 appear in tunnels even for an ordinary field like ip.src. A filter like ip.src != 10.20.1.5 may behave unexpectedly on such packets.

The opportunity: for engineered tunnels such as GRE or 6in4, the points of encapsulation and decapsulation are fixed. Identify them and place the capture platform after decapsulation, and you receive traffic in its original shape without messy preprocessing.

docs.title: 4.3 Everything over HTTPS: DoH and ECH
docs.text:
There's a strong recent trend towards repurposing HTTPS for all sorts of new uses. Visibility into network behaviour falls, and the importance of intercepting encrypted communication rises.

  • DoH (DNS over HTTPS, RFC 8484) puts DNS queries inside HTTPS. From outside it's an ordinary web connection on 443, so the premise from lesson 1.11, "force every endpoint to use the internal DNS servers and you see all DNS in one place", breaks down. There's also DoT (DNS over TLS, RFC 7858, usually port 853) and DoQ (DNS over QUIC, RFC 9250) for the same purpose. DoT uses a dedicated port, so it's easy to block or spot; DoH blends in with normal web traffic. Organisations therefore usually disable DoH or allow only an internal DoH server through endpoint and browser policy, and check proxies and firewalls for connections to known public DoH servers.
  • [Changed] ECH (Encrypted Client Hello) encrypts even the server name in the Client Hello. When lesson 1.2 was written it was treated mainly as a technology trend, but it was published as RFC 9849 in March 2026. As ECH spreads, the "server name from SNI" mentioned in section 3.3 also disappears from packet sensors. That's why records kept at one end of the connection, such as an explicit proxy's CONNECT log, matter even more.

docs.title: 5. VPNs: an opportunity, if placement is right
docs.text:
A VPN is a special case of tunnelling, used in nearly every network. Remote users send all their traffic into the corporate network inside an encrypted tunnel.

The challenge: place the capture platform outside the VPN endpoint and you see only the encrypted tunnel. That shows who connected, when and how much, so it isn't useless, but most investigations need the traffic after decryption, flowing "natively" inside the network. So understand the VPN architecture fully before choosing a capture location.

The opportunity: clear that small hurdle, and a VPN lets you watch and capture most of your scattered remote users' traffic in one place. Cross-check with the VPN authentication logs, and it becomes easy to tie traffic of interest to a source device, a user account, and sometimes a location.

[Supplement] Not all traffic may go through the VPN

Modern VPNs commonly use split tunnelling: only corporate destinations go through the tunnel, and other Internet traffic goes straight out over the user's own connection. In that case remote users' web activity won't appear in the corporate proxy or in capture behind the VPN. Check first whether the VPN is full tunnel or split tunnel.

docs.title: 6. WAN optimisation: flows that don't match the diagram
docs.text:
Devices that improve network speed and efficiency also change the flow. The most common is the web proxy: identical content is fetched from the remote server once and served to many inside users over the fast LAN (the cache in lessons 1.2 and 1.5). Extending that idea beyond HTTP gives WAN optimisation appliances. The source material cites commercial products such as Riverbed SteelHead and F5 BIG-IP, which act transparently like proxies for email, web applications, file sharing, video and more.

The challenge: the client thinks it connected to the remote server, but the optimiser in the middle may answer from its own cache. The remote server (and every segment outside the optimiser) may not even know the request happened, or who made it. From outside, every connection appears to come from the optimiser. In short, the actual flows differ from what the diagram leads you to expect. "Not in the outside pcap" doesn't mean no request was made inside.

The opportunity: these devices generally log very well, which is valuable for correlating activity seen on either side of the optimiser. And since they usually sit at the edge of large networks, that position itself may be a good place for capture or monitoring.

docs.title: 7. Wireless: it doesn't stop at the wall
docs.text:
Wireless is now a major part of networks. Not long ago many enterprises refused to deploy it, but user demand, mobile devices, security-conscious deployment options and convenience made it spread fast.

The challenges:

  • The network is everywhere. A wireless network's reach depends not only on the infrastructure but also on the client's equipment. Transmit power is regulated, but people with bad intent aren't guaranteed to comply, and large or highly directional receive antennas often aren't regulated. So even physically "controlled" wireless networks reach well beyond their designed area. As the source slide's picture shows, the perceived coverage (inside the office) and the actual coverage differ.
  • Legal requirements change a lot. Laws on capturing wireless signals vary by jurisdiction and are often stricter than for wired networks. Always get legal advice first. The source material cites, as a warning, the case of a mapping service's street-imagery vehicles collecting wireless data, which caused major trouble.

The opportunities:

  • One big shared medium. Unlike wired networks, where switches separate traffic per port, radio is shared by every device on that channel, so the capture constraints of lesson 1.11's mirror ports don't apply.
  • Location can be estimated. Commercial and free tools use signal strength and known location data (GPS, or points on a map) to find the approximate physical location of a device of interest.
  • Good logs. Large wireless deployments usually have controllers that record associations, authentication and roaming well.

[Caution] What's different in today's wireless networks

  • A shared medium, but the content is encrypted. Even capturing frames in monitor mode (lesson 1.11, section 3.1), data frames encrypted with WPA2 or WPA3 can't be read without keys. WPA2-Personal can be decrypted if you have the passphrase and also capture the 4-way handshake at connection start, but WPA3-Personal (SAE) is designed so that knowing the password doesn't let you passively decrypt traffic already captured. So controller logs and capture on the wired side have become more important in wireless investigations too.
  • MAC addresses change. Today's phone and laptop operating systems use randomised MAC addresses by default, per network (or periodically). Lesson 1.11 called DHCP logs "the key for mapping an IP back to a device", but with random MACs that key may not point to a single device. Look at it together with the wireless controller's user authentication records (802.1X accounts and so on).

docs.title: 8. The cloud: activity beyond the perimeter
docs.text:
"Cloud" became a buzzword quickly, but the shift back to centralised, remote computing is real: hosted applications, remote storage, elastic compute. The enterprise no longer ends at its traditional perimeter, and since these services' core functions depend on network connectivity, investigations must cover them.

The challenges:

  • Lack of visibility and control. For example: "How many failed logins came before the successful one that exported the whole customer database? From which IPs?" Depending on the service, that record may not exist at all, and if it does, the provider may not hand it over without legal process.
  • New and changing fast. Each service can be completely different, so be ready to "start from zero" when a new service comes into scope. The Azure NSG flow log retirement seen in lesson 1.11 is a good example.

The opportunity: most cloud services expose data and functions through structured HTTP requests: APIs. HTTP(S) can be proxied, so requests and responses can be intercepted and logged, and since providers publish their API documentation, you can use it to interpret, or reconstruct as a transcript, what happened in the service.

[Supplement] Check the cloud-side records first

Major cloud and SaaS providers today offer audit logs recording administrative actions and logins. But what's on by default, how long it's kept, and which items are recorded at which subscription tier varies by service and changes often. For any incident involving the cloud, check whether that service's audit logs were enabled and how long they're kept first, alongside the network evidence.

docs.title: 9. Trend 1: everything over the network
docs.text:
The once underused office LAN is now a high-speed switched fabric divided into VLANs, and it still never seems fast enough. Voice (VoIP), storage (SAN, iSCSI), backups, remote synchronisation, video and security cameras have all moved onto the network.

The challenge: new data brings new analytic challenges, and the volume is enormous. Links of tens of Gbps carrying several GB per second are common, so separating out the relevant data takes a lot of work. That's why this course spends so much time on flow analysis and data reduction: use flows to characterise large volumes of traffic quickly and find the time windows worth a deep look, then use data reduction (tcpdump and BPF from lesson 1.10, section 8) to pull out just that window's traffic and dig in.

The opportunity: as the source material jokes, more work means job security.

docs.title: 10. Trend 2: malware depends on the network
docs.text:
Malware's basic nature is to take commands from its master and return something. Spy films aside, malware almost always communicates over the network. There are clever ways to "hide" from host-based detection tools, but the network path involves many devices and fairly strict protocols, so hiding there is much harder. That's why finding and analysing malware from the network is sometimes faster and more fruitful than starting from the host and working up.

Attackers use encryption, obfuscation and more to make discovery and analysis harder, but the data is on the wire and can be found in a properly instrumented environment. This work is always an arms race: when we gain a new capability, attackers find a way around it, and round it goes.

Right now, the network is malware's weakness: malware relies on the network for its core functions, but can't control or manipulate the network extensively. We should seize on that weakness while it lasts.

[Supplement] Today's C2 tries to look ordinary

Recent malware often uses legitimate services everyone uses (cloud storage, collaboration tools, well-known CDNs) as its command channel instead of unfamiliar attacker-owned servers. Destination addresses or names alone make it hard to tell apart from normal traffic. That makes the size and timing patterns this course keeps stressing (the 900-second interval in lesson 1.10, the repeated identical sizes in lesson 1.11) and deviation from normal, such as "does that PC normally use that service?", even more important.

docs.title: 11. How to use this in real investigations
docs.text:
1. Trust the diagram, but verify. Check it against the actual paths in captured traffic (which device's address appears as the source, what tunnels exist).
  2. At every NAT boundary, note "which side's address is this?" When you get an outside notification, always obtain the time, public address and source port, then correlate in the order: translation logs, captures on both sides, proxy logs.
  3. For encrypted traffic, look at the key exchange first. Judge whether after-the-fact decryption is possible from the Server Hello's cipher suite; if not, turn to flow analysis and records from devices at the connection's ends.
  4. Make capture filters tunnel-aware. BPF like tcp port 80 can't see inside tunnels. On segments with tunnels, keep capture filters generous, or capture after decapsulation.
  5. State the scope of "nothing". Check for paths that bypass your observation (DoH, split tunnels, WAN optimisation, QUIC) and qualify conclusions with "from this observation point".

docs.title: 12. Summary
docs.text:
• Networks keep changing and diagrams are always out of date. Adapting and seizing opportunities decides the outcome more than fixed procedures.
  • NAT makes the source depend on the observation point. Flows or translation logs recording both sides are easiest; otherwise you can match on time, port and TCP sequence number (done by hand here; fails on devices that rewrite sequence numbers).
  • [Changed] The only TLS the server's private key decrypted was TLS 1.2 with RSA key exchange. ECDHE and TLS 1.3 needed a key log (tested directly). "Capture now, decrypt later with the key" rarely works now.
  • When content can't be seen, flow analysis (addresses, ports, sizes, timing) works regardless of encryption.
  • BPF can't see traffic inside tunnels (tcp port 80 caught 1 of 3). Display filters see inside, but fields like ip.src become multi-valued.
  • DoH undermines visibility centred on internal DNS servers, and [Changed] ECH, published as RFC 9849 (March 2026), hides even SNI. Records from devices at the connection's ends matter more.
  • With the right capture placement, a VPN lets you see remote users' traffic in one place, and authentication logs tie it to people. Watch out for split tunnelling.
  • WAN optimisers change flows but offer good logs and good capture positions.
  • Wireless doesn't stop at the wall and has heavy legal constraints, but offers a shared medium, location estimation and controller logs. Today, factor in encryption and random MACs too.
  • The cloud lacks visibility and changes fast, but APIs and audit logs are opportunities.
  • Traffic keeps growing, and malware still depends on the network. Exploiting that weakness is the job of this field.

docs.title: Review questions
docs.text:
Question 1. (Application) An outside party reports only "around 2026-11-02 09:02:02 UTC there was a connection from your 203.0.113.5 to 198.51.100.66:443". No port number. Can you tell which PC it was from the inside.pcap results in section 2.2 alone? What would you ask for?

Answer and explanation

No. Between 09:02:00 and 09:02:03 there were five connections to the same destination from four PCs, and around 09:02:02 both 10.10.6.11 (09:02:01.6) and 10.10.6.14 (09:02:02.4) are candidates. The outside party's clock may be a few seconds off too. Ask the outside party for the source port, and if possible the exact time (milliseconds) and packet sizes or byte counts; on your side, look for the NAT device's translation logs, outside captures or flows, and proxy logs. Until then, the report says "two candidates".

Question 2. (Changed conditions) In the situation of section 2.2, if the NAT firewall had TCP initial sequence number randomisation enabled, what happens to steps ②–③, and what could you match on instead?

Answer and explanation

The outside SYN's sequence number differs from the inside one, so the tcp.seq_raw search in step ③ finds nothing. Don't read "not found" as "not inside". Instead, match on ① time (down to milliseconds, if both capture boxes' clocks are right), ② the size of the first data packet and the sequence of subsequent packet sizes, ③ connection duration and bytes exchanged, and ④ the NAT device's translation logs. In this lab, four of the five candidates had the same size (517 bytes), so one size alone isn't enough; use several characteristics together. Whether both capture boxes' clocks are synchronised by NTP is decisive (lesson 1.11, section 10.2).

Question 3. (Common misconception) "We've secured the incident server's TLS private key, so we can decrypt all of that server's HTTPS traffic we captured last month." What condition must hold for this to be true?

Answer and explanation

Those connections must be TLS 1.2 or earlier using RSA key exchange. In section 3.2's experiment, only the AES128-GCM-SHA256 (RSA key exchange) connection decrypted with the server's private key; ECDHE-RSA-... and TLS 1.3 did not. Those build session keys from per-connection temporary keys (forward secrecy), so the server's private key isn't used in computing them. Most servers today use TLS 1.3 or ECDHE, so first check the cipher suite in the Server Hello in the pcap. The alternatives are key logs, or records from the proxy or load balancer that terminates TLS.

Question 4. (Interpretation) After seeing section 4.2's experiment, a colleague says, "Then it's better never to use capture filters at all." How would you respond?

Answer and explanation

The direction is right, but the conclusion goes too far. The experiment showed that BPF conditions that look only at the outer header (tcp port 80, the inner address) miss what's inside tunnels. Capture filters are still often needed for storage and throughput reasons (lessons 1.7 and 1.11). The realistic answer is: ① first find out what tunnels exist on that segment; ② set filters generously so tunnel protocols (ip proto 47, ip proto 41, etc.) aren't excluded; ③ where possible, capture after decapsulation; ④ record the capture filter used in the capture notes.

Question 5. (Changed conditions) Lesson 1.11 said "force every endpoint to use only the internal DNS servers and you can see DNS in one place". Give three cases where this premise breaks, and how you'd check each.

Answer and explanation

① DoH: a browser or malware puts DNS inside HTTPS and sends it to a public DoH server. Check proxy logs or firewalls for port 443 connections to known DoH servers, and the browser and endpoint policy settings. ② DoT: goes directly to an external DNS server on port 853. Look for outbound port 853 connections at the firewall. ③ Direct port 53 queries: an endpoint asks an external DNS server on 53 directly instead of the internal one. Look in firewall or flow records for outbound port 53 from sources other than the internal DNS servers. Others include DoQ (QUIC) and queries that leave directly over the user's own connection through a VPN split tunnel. Qualify conclusions with "based on internal DNS logs".

Question 6. (Calculation) In section 2.2's inside.pcap, the five SYNs were at 09:02:00.2, 00.9, 01.3, 01.6 and 02.4. If the outside party's clock may differ from ours by up to ±1 second and the reported time is 09:02:00.0, how many candidates are there? How many after finding the outside sequence number by port?

Answer and explanation

09:02:00.0 ± 1 s is 09:01:59.0 to 09:02:01.0. The SYNs in that range are 00.2 (10.10.7.11) and 00.9 (10.10.6.14): two. Finding the SYN on port 61022 outside and searching the inside for sequence number 3340291515 reduced it to one (10.10.6.14:51000). The calculation shows that time only narrows candidates; a value unique to each connection (port, sequence number) is what pins down one.

Question 7. (Application) A remote worker's laptop appears to be infected. There's a tap at the perimeter outside the VPN appliance, and no capture inside it. The VPN uses split tunnelling. What do you secure, and where?

Answer and explanation

① VPN authentication logs: when the user connected, from which public address, and which internal address they were given. ② The outside tap: the user's VPN tunnel is encrypted so the content isn't visible, but connection times and volumes are. ③ Traffic to and from that internal address inside the VPN appliance: internal server logs, firewalls, flows. If needed, place a temporary capture box behind the VPN (lesson 1.11's standby kit). ④ With split tunnelling, Internet traffic may have gone straight out over the user's own connection, so that part isn't in corporate records. Separately secure the endpoint's own records (browser, DNS cache, security product logs) or records from any cloud security service the endpoint uses.

Question 8. (Interpretation) At a branch office with a WAN optimiser, the head office file server's access log has no record of branch employee A opening a file. Yet the file was found on A's PC. What explanations are possible, and what should you check?

Answer and explanation

The most likely explanation is that the optimiser served the file from its own cache. If someone else had opened it first and it was cached, A's request may never have reached the head office server, and even if it did, the source would be recorded as the optimiser. So check ① the optimiser's logs (which client was served which object), ② capture or flows on the branch LAN (traffic between A's PC and the optimiser), and ③ head office server log entries recorded under the optimiser's address. Of course, keep other routes such as email or USB open as well.

Question 9. (Common misconception) "Wireless is one big shared medium, so one monitor-mode capture box lets you see all the communication content of everyone on that floor." Point out what's wrong.

Answer and explanation

① Monitor mode sees one channel at a time (lesson 1.11, section 3.1). If the APs use several channels and bands (2.4/5/6 GHz), you see only part. ② Data frames are encrypted with WPA2 or WPA3. WPA2-Personal needs the passphrase plus the 4-way handshake, and WPA3-Personal (SAE) is designed so that knowing the password still doesn't allow passive decryption. ③ The capture box's wireless chip must support the standard and channel width the network uses. ④ Wireless capture carries heavy legal constraints, so get legal advice first. In practice, wireless controller logs and capture on the wired side behind the APs are the more realistic evidence sources.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Tools used in this environment: tshark 4.2.2, tcpdump 4.99.4, OpenSSL 3.0.13 (s_server, s_client, -keylogfile). Outputs were obtained on 2026-11-05.
  • IETF, RFC 8446: TLS 1.3, section 1.2. Static RSA and static DH cipher suites removed; all public-key-based key exchange provides forward secrecy.
  • IETF, RFC 9849: TLS Encrypted Client Hello (published March 2026; checked through search results on 2026-11-05).
  • IETF, RFC 8484: DNS Queries over HTTPS, RFC 7858: DNS over TLS, RFC 9250: DNS over Dedicated QUIC Connections.
  • IETF, RFC 2784: GRE, RFC 4213: Basic Transition Mechanisms for IPv6 (IPv6 over IPv4 tunnels), RFC 1918: private addresses, RFC 791: IP.

About this page

A personal study note, rewritten in my own words from several learning resources. The experiment pcaps and certificate are my own, and the scenarios are hypothetical.

docs.title: 1.13 — Lab Guide: Carving Exfiltrated Data
docs.text:
Scope of this lesson

  • Find the relevant TCP stream in a full-packet pcap and isolate it
  • Extract the uploaded content (payload) from that stream, two different ways, and confirm with hashes that the results match
  • Unwrap the extracted data in several steps (multipart → Base64 → ZIP) back to the original files
  • Tell the "test upload" from the "real upload", and decide what you can state as fact about the recovered document
  • [Caution] if packets were retransmitted, simply concatenating packet contents produces the wrong file (tested directly)

Lab environment and notation

(Actual output) comes from this environment's tcpdump 4.99.4, tshark 4.2.2, GNU coreutils (base64, basenc, sha256sum) and Info-ZIP unzip. The lab pcap was captured from real uploads sent with curl to a practice paste server I ran on loopback (127.0.0.1). The example names drop.example and news.example were set with the Host header, and the times are the actual capture times (2026-11-05 UTC). The uploaded document and table were invented for the lab, and the whole case is (hypothetical). The "retransmission" file in section 8 is a variant deliberately made by duplicating one packet of the original pcap.

docs.title: 1. Logs only tell you "something was uploaded"
docs.text:
(Hypothetical) A case similar to lesson 1.4. Proxy logs show that an employee in the research segment uploaded something twice to the paste site drop.example. All that's left in the log is POST /post, a 302 response, and the response sizes. As lesson 1.4, section 8 showed, the uploaded content isn't in the log. Fortunately, this site accepted unencrypted HTTP, and full packet capture was running on that segment.

The question: what was uploaded? Finding the answer in the pcap and turning it back into the original file is called carving. The word originally meant cutting file fragments out of unallocated disk space; on the network, it means cutting out just the part of a stream's bytes that is the file.

As an analogy, the post office's counter log (the proxy log) tells you only "this person sent a parcel to this address at this time". To know what was in it, you have to open the parcel (extract it from the pcap). Where the analogy differs: the network's "parcel" is wrapped in several layers (three in this lab), and the same piece can be delivered twice in transit. So you need a procedure that unwraps the layers in order and filters out duplicates.

[Caution] If it had been encrypted

Had the site used HTTPS, as in lesson 1.4's case, the pcap would hold only encrypted bytes, and this lab's method couldn't extract the content. You'd need records from one end of the connection (a TLS-intercepting proxy) or session keys, as in lesson 1.12, section 3.2. Before you start carving, check that the stream is plaintext.

docs.title: 2. How this lab is organised
docs.text:
The same structure as lesson 1.10 (objectives, preparation, lab, takeaways).

Objectives

  1. Find and isolate the relevant TCP stream in a full-packet pcap.
  2. Extract the payload from that stream.
  3. Turn the extracted data back into the original files and judge their investigative value.

Preparation

  • tcpdump, tshark (Wireshark), base64, unzip (or Python's zipfile), sha256sum
  • The lab pcap exfil.pcap (60 packets). The starting lead: "there were two POSTs to drop.example".

To build the lab files yourself

In an empty folder: ① a tiny web server that answers POST /post with a 302 and a short Location (about 20 lines with Python's http.server); ② a file to upload (a few text files zipped and converted with base64); ③ capture with tcpdump -i lo -w exfil.pcap 'tcp port 8099' while sending requests such as curl -H "Host: drop.example" -F "content=<bundle.b64" http://127.0.0.1:8099/post. -F "content=<file" means "send the contents of the file as the value of the form field content". Run the practice server on your own loopback only.

Record a hash first, as soon as you receive it (lesson 1.11, section 4).

sha256sum exfil.pcap

(Actual output)

ea9b3939a8bc04cc66e70422cfa2db98f9ae3a5dc68294f098843df26bfc1fa3  exfil.pcap

docs.title: 3. Step 1: find the relevant stream
docs.text:
First, look at every HTTP request in the pcap as a table (lesson 1.10, section 6).

tshark -n -r exfil.pcap -Y http.request -T fields -E header=y \
  -e frame.number -e tcp.stream -e frame.time_utc -e http.request.method -e http.host \
  -e http.request.uri -e http.content_length -e http.content_type

(Actual output, date part of the time and part of the boundary values trimmed)

frame.number  tcp.stream  frame.time_utc   method  http.host     uri      content_length  content_type
4             0           03:53:13.774927  GET     news.example  /today
16            1           03:53:13.782464  GET     drop.example  /
30            2           03:53:14.792823  POST    drop.example  /post    268             multipart/form-data; boundary=------...ojmtmX...
42            3           03:53:16.806079  POST    drop.example  /post    5559            multipart/form-data; boundary=------...ijgAGQ...
52            4           03:53:17.816165  GET     news.example  /weather

Interpretation: two POSTs to drop.example, streams 2 and 3. Two seconds apart, but very different sizes: 268 bytes and 5,559 bytes. Both are multipart/form-data, i.e. data submitted through a web form. Look at the responses too.

tshark -n -r exfil.pcap -Y http.response -T fields -E header=y -e tcp.stream -e http.response.code -e http.location

(Actual output) Stream 2 got 302 with /j3XFdQ; stream 3 got 302 with /oC8GVg. Exactly the "after you post, the site redirects you to the new paste's short address" shape from lesson 1.4, section 8. This pcap has no GET actually opening those short addresses. That may mean the employee didn't check the paste after uploading, or checked it another way (this pcap alone can't tell).

tshark also dissects which fields the multipart contained.

tshark -n -r exfil.pcap -Y 'http.request.method == "POST"' -T fields -e tcp.stream -e mime_multipart.header.content-disposition

(Actual output)

2   form-data;name="content",form-data;name="expire"
3   form-data;name="content",form-data;name="expire"

Both requests sent two fields: content (the paste) and expire (expiry time). Stream 3 is now our focus.

[Supplement] With a big pcap, reduce first

This lab file is small, but in reality you may start from hundreds of GB for a day. As in lesson 1.10, section 8, first reduce with tcpdump to that PC's address and the relevant port (host address and tcp port 80), then run the tshark commands above on the reduced file. Stream numbers are reassigned per file, so when going back to the original, use addresses, ports and times (lesson 1.10, section 6.2).

docs.title: 4. Step 2: look into the stream
docs.text:
Look at only the packets in stream 3 that carry content.

tshark -n -r exfil.pcap -Y 'tcp.stream == 3 && tcp.len > 0' -T fields -e frame.number -e ip.src -e tcp.srcport -e tcp.len

(Actual output)

40  127.0.0.1   44158   254
42  127.0.0.1   44158   5559
44  127.0.0.1   8099    135

The request went in two packets: packet 40 (254 bytes) is the request header, packet 42 (5,559 bytes) the body, matching Content-Length: 5559 exactly. Packet 44 (135 bytes) is the server's 302 response. Wireshark marks packet 40 as "TCP segment of a reassembled PDU" and, at packet 42, joins the two pieces and dissects them as one HTTP request: the reassembly seen in lesson 1.10, section 8.3.

Now follow this stream in Wireshark (lesson 1.9, section 7). Select packet 42 and choose "Follow → TCP Stream", and the client's data looks like this. With tshark it's -z follow,tcp,ascii,3; below is the beginning, tidied.

(Actual output, beginning)

POST /post HTTP/1.1
Host: drop.example
User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 (X11; Linux x86_64; rv:140.0) Gecko/20100101 Firefox/140.0
Accept: */*
Content-Length: 5559
Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=------------------------ijgAGQGpxN7v6bpGEoTI7N

--------------------------ijgAGQGpxN7v6bpGEoTI7N
Content-Disposition: form-data; name="content"

UEsDBBQAAAAIAKAeZV1u0N79hQAAAKUAAAAIAAAAbWVtby50eHQVjrEOwjAMBfd+xRthoCsSIzDA
BOofmNQpkRy7ShxQ/p4y3Hp3j+lyu19BItaxFlsK5cw44EUe3jiicG3iFbtga98P59a5IJg6BT+h
...

Three things can be read here.

  • The multipart structure. The string after boundary= is the delimiter between fields. In the body it appears as a line prefixed with --, and the final delimiter has an extra -- at the end. Each field is a Content-Disposition header, a blank line, then the value.
  • The content field's value looks odd. It isn't human text but long lines of only upper- and lower-case letters, digits, + and /, broken every 76 characters. That's the classic shape of Base64, commonly used to turn a binary file into text for pasting into a text field.
  • The leading UEsDB. If Base64 data starts with UEsDB, the original data starts with PK\x03\x04, the ZIP file magic number. We haven't decoded it yet, but we can form the hypothesis that a ZIP was converted to Base64 and pasted.

[Supplement] The User-Agent is only a self-declared name

This request claims to be Firefox, but in this lab it was actually curl with a Firefox name supplied via -A. As lesson 1.3 showed, the sender sets the User-Agent freely. The absence of headers a browser commonly sends, such as Accept-Language or Accept-Encoding, can be a clue, but it too is only an observation, not grounds to identify the tool.

docs.title: 5. Step 3: extract the payload, two ways
5.1 Way 1: Export HTTP objects
docs.text:
mkdir obj && tshark -n -r exfil.pcap -q --export-objects http,obj
ls -l obj

(Actual output)

-rw-r--r-- 1 root root  126 Nov  5 03:54 %2f
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root  268 Nov  5 03:54 post
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root 5559 Nov  5 03:54 post(1)
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root  126 Nov  5 03:54 today
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root  126 Nov  5 03:54 weather

In lesson 1.10, section 6.3 we extracted response bodies; this time POST request bodies were extracted too. post (268 bytes) is stream 2 and post(1) (5,559 bytes) is stream 3; (1) is appended when names collide. %2f is the response for the / URL. As lesson 1.10 taught, the name only comes from the URL, so match files to streams by size and stream number.

docs.title: 5.2 Way 2: take the stream's raw bytes as-is
docs.text:
Many protocols have no export feature. For those cases, learn to take a stream's bytes directly too.

tshark -n -r exfil.pcap -q -z follow,tcp,raw,3 \
  | sed -n '7,$p' | grep -v '^=' | grep -v $'^\t' \
  | tr -d '\n' | tr 'a-f' 'A-F' | basenc --base16 -d > stream3-client.bin

Line by line:

  • -z follow,tcp,raw,3: follow stream 3 as hexadecimal text. The first six lines are a header (Follow: ..., Node 0: ... and so on).
  • sed -n '7,$p': keep from the seventh line to the end. grep -v '^=' drops the closing ==== line.
  • grep -v $'^\t': tshark indents the server-sent lines with a tab. Dropping them leaves only the client side.
  • tr -d '\n': remove newlines so the hex is one line.
  • tr 'a-f' 'A-F' | basenc --base16 -d: turn the hex text back into bytes. coreutils' basenc --base16 accepts only upper case, so convert first (this environment lacks the commonly used xxd; if you have it, xxd -r -p works too).

(Actual output) stream3-client.bin was 5,813 bytes, the sum of the two packets in section 4 (254 + 5,559). This is the whole request including headers, so cut off everything up to the blank line (\r\n\r\n) that ends the headers. In this lab a one-line Python snippet did it, splitting into 254 bytes of headers and 5,559 bytes of body.

Compare the two methods' results by hash.

(Actual output)

2135a02b95f648e6f5b50ed0570a616f7ebc26a38689a76da5218108d864b022  stream3-body.bin
2135a02b95f648e6f5b50ed0570a616f7ebc26a38689a76da5218108d864b022  obj/post(1)

They match. Two different methods produced the same bytes, so the extraction is more trustworthy. Record both methods and both hashes in the report.

docs.title: 6. Step 4: unwrap the layers
docs.text:
What we hold now is the multipart body. Three layers have to come off to reach the original files.

flowchart TD
    A["Stream 3 bytes<br/>5,813 bytes"] --> B["Strip HTTP headers<br/>body 5,559 bytes"]
    B --> C["Take only the<br/>content field"]
    C --> D["Decode Base64"]
    D --> E["Unzip"]
    E --> F["memo.txt<br/>orchid-b7-results.csv"]

How to read it: read top to bottom, one layer at a time. Each box is the output of that step; record a hash at every step and you can reproduce the same result from any point later.

docs.title: 6.1 Take only the content field from the multipart
docs.text:
awk 'BEGIN{RS="
"} /name="content"/{f=1;next} f==1&&/^$/{f=2;next} f==2&&/^--/{exit} f==2{print}' \
  "obj/post(1)" > content.b64
  • RS=" ": HTTP multipart lines end in , so use that as the record separator.
  • /name="content"/{f=1;next}: on finding the content field's header, set a flag (f=1) and move on.
  • f==1&&/^$/{f=2;next}: the next blank line ends the header; the value starts after it.
  • f==2&&/^--/{exit}: stop when, while reading the value, a delimiter line starting with -- appears.

(Actual output) content.b64 was 5,302 bytes, starting UEsDBBQAAAAI....

[Caution] This awk fits this file

This short command relies on this file's particulars: "there's one content field, and no line inside the value starts with --". Base64 contains no -, so it's safe here, but in plain-text or binary fields the value could contain such a line. To be exact, stop only at the line that matches the actual boundary string (-- plus the boundary= value from the header). Splitting fields like this is safer left to a tool that properly parses multipart, such as Python's email module. Whatever the method, record the result's size and hash.

docs.title: 6.2 Decode Base64, then check the file type
docs.text:
base64 -d content.b64 > recovered.bin
file recovered.bin
sha256sum recovered.bin

(Actual output)

recovered.bin: Zip archive data, at least v2.0 to extract, compression method=deflate
41d9c6322e7093ee9feae6e44ae6fe24f2f3adbb196ba0eba0d99db3a56eb747  recovered.bin

As hypothesised in section 4, it's a ZIP file. It matters that this was judged by the content's magic number, not by an extension (lessons 1.6 and 1.11, section 3.1).

In this lab we hold the uploader's original ZIP, so we could compare: its SHA-256 was also 41d9c632…b56eb747, not a single byte different. In real cases you often have nothing to compare against. Then you check integrity instead by whether it decompresses without error (section 6.3) and whether the format's own checks (ZIP CRCs) pass.

docs.title: 6.3 Unzip
docs.text:
Before unzipping, list the contents first. An archive may contain executables, or odd paths (../) that try to write into other folders as they extract.

unzip -l recovered.bin

(Actual output)

Archive:  recovered.bin
  Length      Date    Time    Name
---------  ---------- -----   ----
      165  2026-11-05 03:53   memo.txt
     9239  2026-11-05 03:53   orchid-b7-results.csv
---------                     -------
     9404                     2 files

Two text files, so the risk looks low. Extract into a separate folder (unzip -q recovered.bin -d unz). Running a CRC test with unzip -t too is a good idea.

(Actual output)

ORCHID alloy programme - batch 7 results (copy)
Buyer contact: see separate channel. Payment on delivery of full dataset.
Remaining files to follow after departure.

That's the content of memo.txt. orchid-b7-results.csv was a 401-line table: one header line and measurements for 400 samples (sample,temp_c,tensile_mpa,elong_pct).

[Caution] Opening extracted files

These were text files, so we read them directly, but extracted files may have been crafted by an attacker. For documents or executables, as in lesson 1.5, look first in an analysis environment cut off from the network, preferably with tools that don't execute the content (strings, format-specific analysers). If a document reaches out to an external address when opened, it can tip off the other side that you're investigating (the OPSEC point from lesson 1.4).

docs.title: 7.1 The test upload and the real one
docs.text:
Opening stream 2 (268 bytes) the same way, the content field's value was test 1 2 3 and the expire field was 10m (actual output). Side by side:

Stream 2 Stream 3 Time (UTC) 03:53:14.79 03:53:16.81 Body size 268 bytes 5,559 bytes content value test 1 2 3 ZIP converted to Base64 (5,302 bytes) Address returned /j3XFdQ /oC8GVg

It looks like a short text first, to test that the site works, then the real data two seconds later. This order is common in exfiltration cases, and it is circumstantial support weighing towards "prepared and uploaded" rather than "uploaded by mistake". Only circumstantial, of course.

docs.title: 7.2 How to write it up
docs.text:
• Observation (fact): at 2026-11-05 03:53:16 UTC, at this capture point, there was a POST /post request to drop.example (stream 3). Its body's content field held a Base64-encoded ZIP file (SHA-256 41d9c632…b56eb747) containing memo.txt (SHA-256 76d74957…6c22d006) and orchid-b7-results.csv (SHA-256 f2e19cc3…94345d8a482). Two seconds earlier there was a POST to the same site with the content test 1 2 3 (stream 2). The two extraction methods (HTTP object export, raw stream bytes) gave the same result hash.
  • Interpretation (hypothesis): the order is a short test upload followed by the real material, and the memo's content ("buyer contact via a separate channel", "payment on delivery of full dataset", "remaining files after departure") reads as showing intent to hand the material to an outside party.
  • Evidence still needed: the device and person using that source address at that time (DHCP, logon records, lesson 1.11, section 2.2); confirmation from the research department that the CSV matches actual internal research data; whether the pastes /j3XFdQ and /oC8GVg were actually published and who read them (may require legal process with the site operator); traces of the "separate channel" and "remaining files" the memo mentions (webmail, other uploads).
  • Limits of the observation: this pcap is a few seconds at one capture point. What left by other routes (HTTPS, other sites) before or after can't be known from this file. The modification times inside the ZIP (2026-11-05 03:53) follow the clock of the computer that made the ZIP; the ZIP format records them without a time zone and only in 2-second units. So use them only as a reference for "when the files were made".

Judging that "the intent is clear" is ultimately a human decision. The analyst shows reproducibly which bytes came from where, conveys what the document says accurately by quoting it, and draws conclusions together with other evidence.

docs.title: 8. [Caution] With retransmissions, simple concatenation is wrong
docs.text:
On real networks, packets are often lost or delayed and the same content is sent again (retransmitted). Depending on the capture point, both the original and the retransmission may be recorded. To test this, I made exfil-retrans.pcap by inserting packet 42 of exfil.pcap (the 5,559-byte body) once more, 0.2 seconds later.

(Actual output)

40  254     POST /post HTTP/1.1  [TCP segment of a reassembled PDU]
42  5559        POST /post HTTP/1.1
43  5559    1   [TCP Retransmission] 44158 → 8099 [PSH, ACK] Seq=255 Ack=1 Win=65536 Len=5559
45  135     HTTP/1.0 302 Found

Wireshark saw that packet 43's sequence numbers covered a range already received and flagged it tcp.analysis.retransmission. Now collect the client-side bytes three ways.

Method Result size Simply concatenating each packet's tcp.payload 11,372 bytes (254 + 5,559 × 2) Following the stream with -z follow,tcp,raw,3 5,813 bytes --export-objects http 5,559-byte body, hash 2135a02b… (same as the original)

(Actual output) Simple concatenation contains the body twice, 5,559 bytes larger than the original. Decode that as Base64 and you get a wrong file or an error. Stream following and object export filtered out the duplicate using TCP sequence numbers.

So carve with tools that reassemble streams by TCP sequence number, not tools that look at packets one at a time (tcpdump -A, per-packet tcp.payload). Conversely, packets can also arrive out of order or be missing from the capture (the "bytes missing" in lesson 1.9, question 7), so always check completeness: does the result's size match Content-Length, do compression and file-format checks pass?

docs.title: 9. How to use this in real investigations
docs.text:
1. Check that it's plaintext. If it's encrypted, look for connection-end records or keys instead of carving (lesson 1.12).
  2. Reduce, find, isolate. Reduce large originals with BPF (lesson 1.10), find candidate streams with tshark tables, and isolate them by connection.
  3. Extract two ways and compare hashes. Check that different methods, such as object export and raw stream bytes, give the same result.
  4. Unwrap one layer at a time, recording a hash at each step. Multipart, encodings (Base64, URL encoding), compression (gzip, ZIP) and other formats in turn. Record the commands so any step can be reproduced.
  5. Check completeness. Content-Length, archive checks, file-format checks. If bytes are missing, say so.
  6. Open extracted files safely. List first, in an isolated environment, with tools that don't execute content.
  7. Write up facts, interpretation, evidence needed and limits separately.

docs.title: 10. Summary
docs.text:
• Logs tell you "something was uploaded"; packets tell you "what was uploaded", but only when it's plaintext.
  • Tabulating http.request and looking at POST, size and Content-Type found the candidate streams. Of the two uploads, 268 and 5,559 bytes, the larger was our focus.
  • There were two ways to extract: HTTP object export (which also exports POST bodies) and raw stream bytes (-z follow,tcp,raw). Their results had the same hash.
  • There were three layers: multipart → Base64 → ZIP. UEsDB is the usual start of a Base64-encoded ZIP, and file types are judged by magic number, not extension. The recovered ZIP's hash matched the original.
  • A short test upload followed by the real one, plus the memo's content, is circumstantial evidence of intent; the device, the person and the authenticity of the data are confirmed with other evidence.
  • [Caution] With a retransmission present, simply concatenating packet contents bloated the result to 11,372 bytes. Carve with tools that reassemble streams by TCP sequence number, and check that the result is complete.

docs.title: Review questions
docs.text:
Question 1. (Reading a command) If you leave out grep -v $'^ ' from the command in section 5.2, what happens to stream3-client.bin?

Answer and explanation

In tshark's follow output, tab-indented lines are the server-sent side. Without removing them, the hex of the server's 302 response (135 bytes) is joined in too, giving a 5,948-byte file: the 5,813-byte client request followed by the server response. Cutting the body from after the headers to the end would then mix the HTTP response in after the Base64 field, and using it as-is gives a wrong result. When collecting one direction only, select that direction explicitly and compare the result size with Content-Length. (The 5,948 figure is calculated by adding this lab's two numbers.)

Question 2. (Changed conditions) If the same upload had arrived as application/x-www-form-urlencoded instead of multipart/form-data, which steps in sections 6.1–6.2 would change, and how?

Answer and explanation

A URL-encoded form body is one line like content=...&expire=10m, with & between fields and = between name and value. Special characters in values are percent-encoded, such as %2B (+), %2F (/) and %3D (=). So instead of section 6.1's delimiters, cut out the content value by & and =, and undo the percent-encoding before decoding Base64. There's also the rule that + turns into a space, so getting the order wrong breaks the Base64. Effectively there's one more layer. Recording size and hash at each step makes it easy to find where things went wrong.

Question 3. (Common misconception) "The post(1) extracted with --export-objects http is 5,559 bytes, so the file the employee exfiltrated is 5,559 bytes." What's wrong with this?

Answer and explanation

5,559 bytes is the size of the whole multipart body. It includes delimiters, field headers and the expire field, and the content value (5,302 bytes) is Base64 text, about four-thirds the size of the original data. The actual ZIP was 3,922 bytes, and the files inside were 165 and 9,239 bytes uncompressed. So when talking about "the exfiltrated file", say which layer's size you mean; usually you report the innermost original files and their hashes.

Question 4. (Interpretation) In section 3, this pcap had no GET opening the short addresses received with the 302s (/j3XFdQ, /oC8GVg). In lesson 1.4's case, that GET followed immediately. What can and can't you say from this difference?

Answer and explanation

You can say: at this capture point, no request opening the paste was seen right after the upload. If a browser had followed the redirect automatically, as in lesson 1.4, a GET would have followed, so the program that sent this request may not follow redirects (in this lab it was indeed curl without -L). You can't say: that nobody viewed the paste. It could have been opened from another device or by another route (a phone, HTTPS), and this pcap covers only a few seconds. Together with the User-Agent point in section 4, this difference is material for the hypothesis that "it may have been a tool, not a browser".

Question 5. (Calculation) The Base64 text in the content field was 5,302 bytes, with a newline ( ) every 76 characters. If the decoded ZIP is 3,922 bytes, roughly how many Base64 characters, excluding newlines, should there be? Does it match?

Answer and explanation

Base64 turns 3 bytes into 4 characters, so 3,922 bytes is 3,922 ÷ 3 = 1,307.33… → 1,308 groups, i.e. 1,308 × 4 = 5,232 characters (the last group padded with =). Split 76 per line, that's 69 lines (the last short), so 69 newlines, for a total of 5,232 + 69 = 5,301 bytes. The actual file was 5,302 bytes because awk added one more output newline after the extracted value, which already ended in a newline (the original bundle.b64 was 5,301 bytes). This habit of checking sizes by calculation is a good way to confirm that no bytes were lost or added in intermediate steps.

Question 6. (Changed conditions) If the same upload had used HTTP/1.1 Transfer-Encoding: chunked, what more would you need to do with section 5.2's "raw stream bytes" method? What about section 5.1's method?

Answer and explanation

With chunked transfer, the body arrives as a sequence of size (hex) data pieces, ending with 0 . Using the raw stream bytes as-is leaves those chunk-size lines interleaved with the data, breaking the multipart and Base64. So after removing the headers, you need one more step to de-chunk and join only the data. Wireshark's HTTP dissector, on the other hand, de-chunks and reassembles the body, so --export-objects normally exports the de-chunked body. This case wasn't tested directly in this lesson, though; if you meet it, compare both methods' results by hash on a small sample. If the response has Content-Encoding: gzip, a decompression step is added too.

Question 7. (Common misconception) A junior analyst reports: "I copied the output of tcpdump -A -r exfil-retrans.pcap, pasted just the Base64 part and decoded it, and the ZIP was broken. So this data is corrupted." What's wrong?

Answer and explanation

tcpdump -A just shows packets one at a time; it doesn't reassemble TCP streams. Section 8's file has the same body recorded twice due to retransmission, so joining that output puts the Base64 in twice and yields a broken ZIP. What's broken isn't the data but the extraction method. Extract again by stream following or object export and you get the same hash as the original. Also, tcpdump -A replaces unprintable bytes with ., so it should never be used for binary data in the first place. Before writing "corrupted" in a report, extract again by another method and compare.

Question 8. (Application) On hearing this lab's results, the legal counsel asks, "Is it certain that CSV is our research data?" Separate what you can answer as the network analyst from what needs someone else's confirmation.

Answer and explanation

What the analyst can answer: from which time, which stream and which bytes the CSV was extracted, by which steps; its hash; that two methods gave the same result; and its outward form (401 lines, column names, sample-number format B7-001). What needs other confirmation: whether its content matches actual internal research data must be judged by the research department against the original data. If the same file exists in an internal store, hash comparison is the strongest evidence; if not, an expert checks whether the values match. And who was using that address at that time is confirmed separately from DHCP and logon records (lesson 1.11).

Question 9. (Interpretation) Section 7.2 says to use the file modification times inside the ZIP "only as a reference". Why? Are there cases where this value helps?

Answer and explanation

The ZIP's basic time field is local time without time-zone information, recorded only in 2-second units, and simply follows the clock of the computer that made it. That clock may have been wrong or deliberately changed, and some archivers write different times. So it alone can't establish "when it was made". It can still help: for example, if it's a few minutes before the upload time observed on the network, that fits the interpretation that the files were bundled just before uploading, and matched with other evidence (the endpoint's file-system records) it helps judge whether the archive was made on that PC. In this lab the ZIP time (03:53) and upload time (03:53:16) fell in the same minute because the lab files were made and uploaded immediately.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Tools used in this environment: tcpdump 4.99.4, tshark 4.2.2 (--export-objects, -z follow), GNU coreutils base64, basenc, sha256sum, Info-ZIP unzip/zipinfo, the Python 3 standard library. Outputs were obtained on 2026-11-05.
  • Wireshark, tshark manual source (release-4.6) (checked 2026-11-05). --export-objects and the -z follow formats (ascii, raw, etc.).
  • IETF, RFC 7578: multipart/form-data and RFC 2046: MIME Media Types, section 5.1 (boundary syntax).
  • IETF, RFC 4648: The Base16, Base32, and Base64 Data Encodings.
  • IETF, RFC 9112: HTTP/1.1, section 7.1 (chunked transfer coding).
  • PKWARE, ZIP file format specification (APPNOTE.TXT). The local file header signature PK\x03\x04 and the MS-DOS date/time fields.

About this page

A personal study note, rewritten in my own words from several learning resources. The lab server, uploaded files and pcap are my own, and the scenario and document contents are hypothetical.

docs.title: 1.10 — Lab Guide: Getting Hands-On with tcpdump and Wireshark
1.10 — Lab Guide: Getting Hands-On with tcpdump and Wireshark
docs.text:
Scope of this lesson

  • Why tshark: explore small in the GUI, run big at the console
  • The options you'll use constantly: -r -w -n -Y -T -e -E -G, plus -2
  • [Changed] -G now requires a report type (4.6), and -e accepts field expressions (4.4)
  • Labs A–E: live capture → saving to a file and hashing it → basic display filters → turning packets into tables with -T fields → sweeping several files with a loop
  • Do data reduction with BPF: on the same job, tcpdump took 0.25 s and tshark took over 18 s (actual measurement)
  • [Caution] combining -Y with -w can drop the earlier packets of a reassembled message

Lab environment and notation

(Actual output) comes from this environment (Linux, 4 vCPUs) with tcpdump 4.99.4, libpcap 1.10.4 and tshark 4.2.2. Labs A–C use files actually captured on the loopback interface (lo), with a Python web server running and curl sending the requests. The DNS and large pcaps in Labs D and E were assembled in Python and use only private addresses, documentation addresses (RFC 5737) and example domains (.example). There is no GUI here, so the Wireshark steps are written as procedures only, and I checked the results by putting the same filters into tshark.

docs.title: 1. You found a method on screen and want to run it over 100 files
docs.text:
(Hypothetical) A colleague was looking through 30 minutes of pcap in Wireshark and found a suspicious name: sync.cdn-update.example. Now the question grows. "Did any other PC ask for this name in the past week?" A week of capture is 168 hourly files, hundreds of GB in total. Opening each one in Wireshark, typing the filter and counting by eye isn't realistic.

That's what tshark is for. tshark is the command-line version of Wireshark, using the same dissectors and the same display filters. With no screen to draw, it's lighter, and above all you can put it in a shell script. That gives you a natural order of work:

  1. Explore small. Open a small sample in Wireshark and settle on the field names and the filter. With a screen you find "ah, this is the field" much faster.
  2. Run big. Move that filter and those fields into a tshark command, and apply it identically to hundreds of files with a loop.
  3. Keep the record. You can paste the command line straight into a report and reuse it in the next case. It becomes a repeatable procedure: the same input gives the same output.

[Supplement] GUI-only features

Almost every Wireshark feature is in tshark too, but a few interactive ones exist only on screen. Following a stream and extracting files are not among them: tshark does both with -z follow and --export-objects, which we run in section 6.

docs.title: 2. Analogy: the test kitchen and the factory line
docs.text:
When a chef develops a new sauce, they taste from a small pot and adjust the proportions (the GUI). Once the recipe is fixed, it goes to the factory line, which makes a ton a day (tshark). Nobody on the line tastes and stirs by hand. The recipe, meaning the command line, is everything.

The analogy breaks in one place. The factory line isn't infinitely fast either. tshark dissects every layer of every packet just as Wireshark does, so feeding it a ton of raw material as-is is very slow. That's why we put a sieving step (tcpdump and BPF) in front of the line. That is section 8, the key measurement of this lesson.

flowchart TD
    S["Small sample pcap"] --> G["Explore in Wireshark"]
    G --> D["Fix filter and field names"]
    BIG[("Many large pcaps")] --> B["Reduce with tcpdump + BPF"]
    B --> R[("Reduced pcap")]
    D --> T["tshark -Y and -T fields"]
    R --> T
    T --> U["Count with sort, uniq"]
    U --> O["Tables and conclusions"]

How to read it: read top to bottom. The left branch (small sample → Wireshark) decides what to look at; the right branch (large pcaps → tcpdump) cuts down how much to look at. The two branches meet at tshark.

docs.title: 3. The tshark options you'll use most
docs.text:
Rather than memorising one line per option, group them by "what does this option decide?"

Input and output

  • -r file: read from a saved file instead of a network interface. In investigations you almost always use this.
  • -w file: write results to a file as packets, not text. Combined with a filter, this gives "a new pcap of only the matching packets". If you want to save the text you see on screen, use the shell's >, not -w.
  • [Changed] -F format: the format of the -w file. tshark's default is pcapng. The source material describes it as "writing a pcap file", but if the receiving tool can't read pcapng you need -F pcap. Run -F alone to see the list of formats.

Dissection and names

  • -n: disable all name resolution. As we confirmed in lesson 1.8, turning on network name resolution can make Wireshark-family tools send real DNS queries. Add it by habit when handling evidence.
  • -2: read the file twice. The first pass works out every forward/backward relationship ("the response to this request is packet N"), and the second pass prints. The input must be rewindable, so this can't be used on live capture or piped input.
  • -R filter: the filter for the first pass, used with -2. For single-pass reading, use -Y, not -R.

What to show

  • -Y 'filter': a display filter with the same syntax as Wireshark's filter bar (lesson 1.9). Wrap it in single quotes so the shell doesn't reinterpret parentheses, spaces or quotes. Inside the filter, strings use double quotes.
  • -T format: chooses the output shape. The default text is a one-line summary per packet like tcpdump. Others include pdml (XML), json, ek (line-delimited JSON for Elasticsearch), psml and tabs. The one investigators use most is fields.
  • -e field: with -T fields, chooses which fields to print. You can repeat it; columns appear in the order given. Use the "machine name" shown in Wireshark's status bar (such as dns.qry.name).
  • -E option=value: shapes the table for -T fields: header=y (field names as the first line), separator=, (column separator, tab by default), quote=d (wrap in double quotes), occurrence=f|l|a (first, last or all occurrences of a field that appears several times in one packet), aggregator=, (the separator between values when printing all), and others.

Looking things up

  • -G report: prints a list of things tshark knows and exits: fields (every field), protocols (every protocol), fieldcount (the counts) and more.

[Changed] -G now needs a report type

The source material says to use "-G ?" to see the available reports. In tshark 4.2.2, -G ? printed a usage text containing the list of reports (actual output). In the past, -G alone produced the fields report; that behaviour was deprecated in 4.4.0, and the 4.6 manual states that "the glossary type is now mandatory". The command the 4.6 manual gives for listing report types is -G help. If an old script contains tshark -G | grep ..., change it to tshark -G fields | grep ....

[Changed] What -e accepts has grown

  • Since 4.2.0 you can pull on-screen column text out as fields, such as _ws.col.info and _ws.col.protocol. The old way of using the column title (Info) remains only for the default columns, for backward compatibility.
  • Since 4.4.0 -e accepts not just a single field name but a field expression (display filter functions, slices, arithmetic and so on), for example -e 'len(dns.qry.name)'. This environment has 4.2.2, so I could not run this feature; it's based on the 4.4.0 release notes.

docs.title: 4. How this lab is organised
docs.text:
From this lesson on, lab guides have four parts. Knowing the purpose of each helps you decide where to pause and what to check.

  • Objectives: what you should be able to do at the end.
  • Preparation: the tools and files you need, and the lead you start from.
  • Lab: each step is "command → output → interpretation". Every part of each command is explained, so predict the result before you look, then compare.
  • Takeaways: what to carry away from the lab.

You can type the commands exactly as given, but there are many routes to the same answer. After one guided run, cover the explanations and try it alone; your skills grow much faster that way. Parts marked "Going further" aren't required for the objectives, so leave them for last.

Objectives

  1. Watch live traffic on screen with tcpdump, and save it to a file.
  2. Open the saved pcap in Wireshark (or tshark) and use basic display filters.
  3. Turn packets into tables with tshark's -T fields and count them with shell tools.
  4. Confirm by measurement that "reduce with BPF, dissect with display filters".

Preparation

  • tcpdump, Wireshark (with tshark, 4.x), curl, Python 3
  • Labs A–C: a practice web server. Make a few text files in an empty folder and run python3 -m http.server 8082 --bind 127.0.0.1 in that folder.
  • Lab D: three DNS pcaps cut into hourly files (dns-00.pcap, dns-01.pcap, dns-02.pcap). The internal DNS server is 10.10.4.53. The starting lead is "sync.cdn-update.example looks suspicious".

[Caution] Practise on your own equipment and your own traffic

Capture only on networks and equipment you're authorised for. This guide uses only the loopback interface (lo), so you see only traffic inside your own computer. If you want to practise on a company network, get permission first.

docs.title: 5. Labs A and B: watch live, save to a file
5.1 Lab A: watch packets go by on screen
docs.text:
sudo tcpdump -i lo -nn -c 12 'tcp port 8082'
  • -i lo: capture on the loopback interface.
  • -nn: don't turn addresses or port numbers into names (lesson 1.8).
  • -c 12: stop after 12 packets, so the screen doesn't scroll forever while practising.
  • 'tcp port 8082': a BPF selecting only the web server port (lesson 1.7), in single quotes.

Run curl -s -o /dev/null http://127.0.0.1:8082/report.txt in another terminal and you get this.

(Actual output, some options trimmed)

03:20:39.926766 IP 127.0.0.1.58600 > 127.0.0.1.8082: Flags [S], seq 3814503150, win 65495, ... length 0
03:20:39.926778 IP 127.0.0.1.8082 > 127.0.0.1.58600: Flags [S.], seq 1889376451, ack 3814503151, ... length 0
03:20:39.926794 IP 127.0.0.1.58600 > 127.0.0.1.8082: Flags [.], ack 1, win 64, ... length 0
03:20:39.926875 IP 127.0.0.1.58600 > 127.0.0.1.8082: Flags [P.], seq 1:88, ack 1, ... length 87
03:20:39.926880 IP 127.0.0.1.8082 > 127.0.0.1.58600: Flags [.], ack 88, ... length 0
03:20:39.927687 IP 127.0.0.1.8082 > 127.0.0.1.58600: Flags [P.], seq 1:190, ack 88, ... length 189
03:20:39.927704 IP 127.0.0.1.58600 > 127.0.0.1.8082: Flags [.], ack 190, ... length 0
03:20:39.927941 IP 127.0.0.1.8082 > 127.0.0.1.58600: Flags [P.], seq 190:5590, ack 88, ... length 5400
03:20:39.927954 IP 127.0.0.1.58600 > 127.0.0.1.8082: Flags [.], ack 5590, ... length 0
03:20:39.927990 IP 127.0.0.1.8082 > 127.0.0.1.58600: Flags [F.], seq 5590, ack 88, ... length 0
03:20:39.928023 IP 127.0.0.1.58600 > 127.0.0.1.8082: Flags [F.], seq 88, ack 5591, ... length 0
03:20:39.928052 IP 127.0.0.1.8082 > 127.0.0.1.58600: Flags [.], ack 89, ... length 0
12 packets captured
24 packets received by filter
0 packets dropped by kernel

Interpretation: one HTTP request became 12 packets. The first three lines set up the connection (S, S., .). The 87-byte packet is the request, 189 bytes is the response header, 5400 bytes is the body (the same size as report.txt), and the last three lines close the connection (F.). It's exactly the structure from lesson 1.6.

You also need to read the last three lines.

  • captured is how many were actually printed or saved; dropped by kernel is how many were missed because a buffer overflowed (lesson 1.6, section 7.1). Always record these numbers when collecting evidence. If drops aren't 0, the report must say "the capture is incomplete".
  • received by filter is exactly double captured (24) because of how loopback works. Lesson 1.6, section 7.1 said I hadn't determined the cause; here it is. Linux shows each loopback packet twice, once "outgoing" and once "incoming", and libpcap discards the outgoing copy so it doesn't record the same packet twice (as explained in libpcap 1.10.4's pcap-linux.c). The filter counts both, but only one is recorded. On an ordinary Ethernet interface the numbers won't be an exact double like this. Before being surprised by this number, check which interface it was.

docs.title: 5.2 Lab B: save to a file and record a hash
docs.text:
sudo tcpdump -i lo -nn -w lab11.pcap 'tcp port 8082'

With -w lab11.pcap, packets aren't printed; they're saved to the file. While it runs, send three requests from another terminal: a normal one, one with a changed User-Agent, and one for a file that doesn't exist.

curl -s -o /dev/null http://127.0.0.1:8082/index.html
curl -s -o /dev/null -A "lab-agent/1.0" http://127.0.0.1:8082/report.txt
curl -s -o /dev/null http://127.0.0.1:8082/nope.txt

After stopping with Ctrl+C it reported 36 packets captured (actual output): 12 for each of three requests. Now, before any analysis, record a hash.

sha256sum lab11.pcap

(Actual output)

c96571436262a2e4349875121d42d625f180f544d25ee7b664f17bfcb4a01254  lab11.pcap

Recomputing it after finishing all of Lab C gave the same value. This is how you confirm that read-only tools (tshark -r, tcpdump -r, editcap input) don't change the original. Results always go to new files.

[Supplement] Why -Z root was needed for saving

In this environment tcpdump drops privileges after capture starts, and then couldn't write the -w file, so I added -Z root (lesson 1.6, section 7). You may not need it.
