docs.text:
• Squid project, Squid 7 branch src/cf.data.pre (checked 2026-11-05). Definitions of the built-in squid, common, combined, referrer and useragent log formats, meanings of format codes, and the recommended access_log syntax (logformat= option and ACLs).
  • Squid project, Squid 7 src/LogTags.cc and src/format/Format.cc (checked 2026-11-05). The list of cache status names; %ts comes from the current time when the log line is written, and %tr is request processing time.
  • Squid project, Squid 7 release notes source (checked 2026-11-05). Ident support removed, configurations with %ui fail to start, and that field in common/combined is always -.
  • MDN Web Docs, Referrer-Policy (checked in the source repository 2026-11-05). With no policy specified, strict-origin-when-cross-origin is the default; before the November 2020 Fetch standard revision (whatwg/fetch#1066) it was no-referrer-when-downgrade.

About this page

Personal study notes rewritten in my own words from a range of study material. The sample log and configuration were made up for explanation.

docs.title: Lesson 1.8 — Practical tcpdump Options and Reading the Wireshark Window
Lesson 1.8 — Practical tcpdump Options and Reading the Wireshark Window
docs.text:
Scope of this lesson

  • tcpdump options for long captures: splitting files by size and time (-C, -G), limiting their number (-W), filter files (-F), and post-rotation processing (-z)
  • Reading four common capture and conversion commands piece by piece
  • The five parts of the Wireshark window (filter bar, packet list, packet details, packet bytes, status bar) and how they relate
  • Name resolution settings and OPSEC: what's safe to turn on and what to turn off
  • Adding columns and time display formats

Display filter syntax and following streams are the next lesson (1.9).

Lab environment and notation

(Actual output) was produced with tcpdump 4.99.4 and tshark 4.2.2 in this work environment. This environment has no display (GUI), so the Wireshark window itself couldn't be opened. The window is therefore described by its menu names and structure, and the same features (detail view, byte view, name resolution, time formats, custom columns) were actually run with tshark, which uses the same engine. Wireshark menu names may vary slightly between versions.

docs.title: 1. Capturing only DNS for two weeks
docs.text:
(Hypothetical) After lesson 1.4's incident, the security team decides "let's capture all of the organisation's DNS traffic for the next two weeks". As lesson 1.7 taught, port 53 will do for the capture filter, but problems remain.

  • Two weeks in one file is too big to open, and if the file gets corrupted midway you lose everything.
  • When the disk fills, capture may stop or the system may stall.
  • Later, when you want only "the afternoon of 20 October", you need to find that part straight away.

That's why tcpdump has options to split files, name them and limit their number. And the captured files eventually get opened in Wireshark, which has a setting you mustn't leave as it is. This lesson covers both.

docs.title: 2. tcpdump options for long captures
docs.text:
On top of lesson 1.6's basic options (-r, -w, -i, -n, -s), these are commonly used in practice:

Option Meaning Remember -r file Read from a pcap file instead of the network -w file Write to a pcap file instead of the screen -i interface Interface to capture on On Linux and others, any captures all interfaces at once -n No name lookups Almost always add it. Prevents slowdowns and OPSEC problems -C size Start a new file when the file exceeds that size Unit is 1,000,000 bytes (a million bytes, not MiB) -G seconds Start a new file every that many seconds The file name must include a time format -W count With -C, rotate through that many files; with -G, create that many and exit -F file Read the filter from a file instead of the command line For a team to share filters (lesson 1.7) -z command Run a command on each file as it's closed e.g. -z gzip to compress -c count Capture that many packets and exit -A Show content as text Lesson 1.6

Now the results of testing each option. Tests ran on the loopback interface while sending continuous requests to the test web server.

docs.title: 2.1 -G: splitting by time
docs.text:
$ tcpdump -n -i lo -G 2 -W 3 -w 'dns-%F_%H%M%S.pcap' 'tcp port 8082'
$ echo $?
0
$ ls -1 dns-*
dns-2026-11-05_025710.pcap
dns-2026-11-05_025712.pcap
dns-2026-11-05_025714.pcap

(Actual output. In reality -Z root was also added; see lesson 1.6 section 7.) -G 2 means a new file every 2 seconds and -W 3 means make three and exit; it really made three files and exited normally (0). The %F (year-month-day) and %H%M%S (hours, minutes, seconds) in the file name are strftime, the standard time format syntax, the same one you saw in lesson 1.3's awk. So you can tell from the file name alone when each file is from.

Testing revealed three things.

① Without a time format in the name, files keep getting overwritten. Capturing for 5 seconds with -G 1 -w same.pcap left only one file, same.pcap (actual output). The tcpdump documentation also warns that "if no time format is specified, each new file will overwrite the previous". Each new file made every second has the same name, so only the last second survives. For the same reason, a time format coarser than the rotation interval (e.g. rotating every second with only minutes in the name) also overwrites.

② The time in the file name is the capture machine's local time zone. Capturing with the time zone set to Sydney, a file made at 02:58 UTC was named tz-2026-11-05_135818.pcap, i.e. 13:58 (actual output). The times inside the packets are UTC (lesson 1.6) but the file names are local time, so looking for "the files from the 03:00 UTC hour" later, you might open the wrong file. Running capture scripts in UTC, as in TZ=UTC tcpdump ..., removes this confusion.

③ New files are only created when packets arrive. On the first test the traffic stopped partway, and even after waiting 20 seconds there were only two files and tcpdump hadn't exited (actual output). tcpdump checks "is it time to rotate?" when it receives a packet, so on a quiet link a file may not change even after the set time has passed. So don't assume "rotated every 2 hours, so each file is exactly 2 hours"; check each file's first and last packet times with capinfos.

docs.title: 2.2 -C and -W: splitting by size and rotating
docs.text:
$ tcpdump -n -i lo -C 1 -W 3 -w ring.pcap 'tcp port 8082'
$ ls -l ring.pcap*
1000021 ring.pcap0
1000021 ring.pcap1
589919 ring.pcap2

(Actual output, sizes and names only.) -C 1 means a new file every 1,000,000 bytes and -W 3 means rotate through three files (a ring buffer). The file names got 0, 1 and 2 appended. Per the documentation, with -W it pads names with leading zeros to fit the file count (e.g. from 00 for a count of 100) so they sort in order, and once the set number is used it overwrites from the first file. This test only filled up to the third file, so I didn't observe the overwriting itself.

The file size being 1,000,021 bytes rather than exactly 1,000,000 has a reason too. tcpdump checks "is the file now bigger than this size?" before writing each packet, so it overshoots by the last packet. And the documentation states that the unit is 1,000,000 bytes, not 1,048,576 (MiB).

[Changed] Unit suffixes depend on the version. The latest tcpdump documentation says you can add k, m or g suffixes, as in -C 20k or -C 500m, to change the unit. But -C 20k on this work environment's 4.99.4 gave the error tcpdump: invalid file size 20k (actual output). The repository's documentation and change log show this feature arrived in 4.99.6 (checked 2026-11-05). Distribution packages often lag the latest, so test on the capture device's tcpdump version first.

A ring buffer with -C and -W keeps the disk from overflowing, but old data silently disappears. Lesson 1.1 section 8.1's "retention" calculation applies directly. Work out in advance how many hours one ring buffer holds, and when an incident occurs, copy the files you need before they're overwritten.

docs.title: 2.3 -z: processing each file as it's closed
docs.text:
-z gzip runs gzip on each file as it's closed, compressing it. Put a small script that records a hash there instead of compressing, and you keep each file's hash from the moment it's created, which helps evidence management. In this lab environment no rotation happened within the test window, so I didn't directly confirm the -z result.

[Supplement] dumpcap's ring buffer. dumpcap, included with Wireshark, does the same job. It splits and rotates with -b duration:seconds, -b filesize:kilobytes and -b files:count, and its default save format is pcapng, so each file keeps the interface and filter information from lesson 1.6. Whichever you use, testing on the capture device under real load comes first.

docs.title: 2.4 Four common commands
docs.text:
The source material's examples, adapted to this series' hypothetical organisation and read piece by piece.

① A quick look on screen

sudo tcpdump -n -s 100 -A -i ens33 -c 1000

Captures the first 1,000 packets (-c 1000) on interface ens33, shows the first 100 bytes of each (-s 100) including content as text (-A), and exits. Good for getting a feel for what's on a link. Without -n it looks up a name for every IP and is much slower.

② Extracting one host from a large file

tcpdump -n -r input.pcap -w output.pcap 'host 10.10.6.14'

Reads input.pcap and writes only packets involving 10.10.6.14 to output.pcap: lesson 1.7's "data reduction". It only reads a file, so no administrator rights are needed.

③ 14 days of DNS, one file per day

sudo TZ=UTC tcpdump -n -i ens33 -w 'dns-%F_%H%M%S.pcap' -G 86400 -W 14 'port 53'

A new file every 86,400 seconds (24 hours × 60 minutes × 60 seconds), exiting after 14 files. The source material writes the filter as '(tcp or udp) and port 53', but as lesson 1.7 showed, port already catches both TCP and UDP, so it's effectively the same as 'port 53' (the original form is better if you need to exclude other transports such as SCTP precisely). TZ=UTC in front makes the file names UTC too (section 2.1 ②). But as in section 2.1 ③, files only change when packets arrive, so don't assume each file breaks exactly at midnight.

④ A suspicious host, 100 MB at a time, indefinitely

sudo tcpdump -n -i ens33 -w suspect.pcap -C 100 'host 203.0.113.77'

Writes traffic with 203.0.113.77 to a new file (suspect.pcap, suspect.pcap1, suspect.pcap2 …) every 100,000,000 bytes (100 × 1,000,000), without end. With no -W it doesn't rotate and just keeps growing, so watch the disk. This shape is for when you expect little volume, since it's just one suspicious host.

docs.title: 3. Reading the Wireshark window
docs.text:
Now open the captured files in Wireshark, the window you'll stare at longest in this series. From top to bottom it has five parts.

flowchart TD
    F["① Display filter bar<br/>choose packets to show"]
    L["② Packet list<br/>one row per packet · configurable columns"]
    D["③ Packet details<br/>frame → Ethernet → IP → TCP → HTTP"]
    B["④ Packet bytes<br/>hex + text"]
    S["⑤ Status bar<br/>field name · length · packet counts"]
    F --> L
    L -->|"select a row"| D
    D <-->|"highlight each other"| B
    B ~~~ S
    D -.->|"selected field name"| S

How to read the diagram: top to bottom is the actual layout of the window. Selecting a row in the packet list shows that packet in the details and bytes panes, and fields in the details pane and bytes in the bytes pane highlight each other (two-way arrow). Selecting a field in the details pane shows its name in the status bar (dotted line).

② Packet list. One row per packet, with configurable columns. The default "Time" column is seconds since the capture started, handy for intervals between packets but not the actual time. As lesson 1.6 showed, pcap has a UTC time for each packet, so you can switch to a human-readable time (section 5). The "Info" column is the dissector's one-line summary of the packet, good for scanning many packets for interesting ones.

③ Packet details. Where the dissectors show their real power. It unfolds every field in the packet by layer, from the IP, TCP and UDP headers up to the application data at the top. Even unfamiliar protocols are shown with human-readable field names and values, so start here when exploring a protocol you don't know. tshark's -V shows the same content as text (actual output, partial):

$ tshark -r nameres.pcap -n -Y 'frame.number==6' -V
Frame 6: 201 bytes on wire (1608 bits), 201 bytes captured (1608 bits)
    Arrival Time: Oct 14, 2026 17:46:40.600000000 UTC
    ...
Ethernet II, Src: 00:50:56:0a:06:14, Dst: 00:50:56:0a:00:01
    ...
Internet Protocol Version 4, Src: 10.10.6.14, Dst: 203.0.113.50
    ...
    Time to Live: 64
    Protocol: TCP (6)
    ...
Transmission Control Protocol, Src Port: 50010, Dst Port: 80, Seq: 1, Ack: 1, Len: 147

"Frame" at the top isn't data from the wire but metadata Wireshark attaches (capture time, stored length, etc.: lesson 1.6's record header). Below it are the real headers stacked as Ethernet, IP, TCP.

④ Packet bytes. A hex dump of every byte of the packet as stored in the pcap file (= as it crossed the wire). tshark's -x gives the same shape (actual output, partial):

$ tshark -r nameres.pcap -n -Y 'frame.number==6' -x
0000  00 50 56 0a 00 01 00 50 56 0a 06 14 08 00 45 00   .PV....PV.....E.
0010  00 bb 12 34 40 00 40 06 db be 0a 0a 06 0e cb 00   ...4@.@.........
0020  71 32 c3 5a 00 50 00 00 03 e9 00 00 1b 59 50 18   q2.Z.P.......YP.
0030  fa f0 00 00 00 00 47 45 54 20 2f 75 70 64 61 74   ......GET /updat

At first it seems unnecessary next to the details pane, but the raw bytes often reveal interesting parts the details pane passed over. So Wireshark links the two panes. Click a byte in the bytes pane and the field that byte decodes into is highlighted in the details pane; click a field in the details pane and its bytes are highlighted. For example, clicking the 06 at offset 0x17 in the dump above highlights "Protocol: TCP (6)" in the details pane. It does the byte-offset arithmetic you did by hand in lessons 1.6 and 1.7, and understanding this link is critical for an analyst.

① Display filter bar. At the top of the window, where you choose which packets to show. Lesson 1.9 covers it in detail.

⑤ Status bar. At the bottom, giving a quick frame of reference. On the left it shows the dissector field name and byte length of the field selected in the details pane (e.g. ip.proto), which is essential information for building display filters. In the middle it shows the total packet count and how many packets the current filter displays. If capturing with Wireshark directly, it also shows values such as how many packets libpcap dropped for lack of resources.

Changing the layout. Under Edit → Preferences → Appearance → Layout you can pick one of six pane layouts and what each pane shows. Only cosmetic, but on an odd screen ratio or a large shared screen it can make a big difference to usability.

docs.title: 4. Name resolution and OPSEC
docs.text:
Wireshark has several name resolution settings that show addresses and numbers as human-readable names (Edit → Preferences → Name Resolution). Some are safe to turn on; some can ruin an investigation.

Setting What it changes Where it looks OPSEC MAC address resolution First 3 bytes of a MAC → vendor name Wireshark's built-in vendor table Safe (no outbound traffic) Transport name resolution Port number → service name (80 → http) Wireshark's built-in service table Safe Network address resolution IP address → hostname The two methods below Depends on the method ├ Use captured DNS packets Name addresses from DNS responses in the file The pcap you opened Safe, and the name as of that time └ Use an external name resolver The analysis PC really asks a DNS server Today's DNS Dangerous

docs.title: 4.1 Testing it
docs.text:
I built a test pcap with a DNS query and response plus an HTTP request to that address, and ran it through tshark (actual output, partial):

$ tshark -r nameres.pcap -n
    2   0.120000   10.10.4.53 → 10.10.6.14   DNS 93 Standard query response 0xabcd A files.example.net A 203.0.113.50
    3   0.240000   10.10.6.14 → 203.0.113.50 TCP 54 50010 → 80 [SYN] Seq=0 Win=64240 Len=0
$ tshark -r nameres.pcap -N dn
    3   0.240000   10.10.6.14 → files.example.net TCP 54 50010 → 80 [SYN] Seq=0 Win=64240 Len=0
$ tshark -r nameres.pcap -N mt -T fields -e eth.src_resolved -e _ws.col.Info
VMware_0a:06:14 50010 → 80 [SYN] Seq=0 Win=64240 Len=0
VMware_0a:00:01 http(80) → 50010 [SYN, ACK] Seq=0 Ack=1 Win=64240 Len=0

-n turns off all name resolution. The letters after -N are the kinds of resolution to turn on; per the tshark documentation, d is use captured DNS packets, n network address resolution, N use external resolvers, m MAC, and t transport (ports). With -N dn, 203.0.113.50 became files.example.net based on the DNS response in the file; with -N mt, the MAC prefix 00:50:56 showed as VMware and port 80 as http(80).

So did the analysis PC send anything out? I ran it again watching the network operations tshark requested from the OS with a tool called strace (actual output):

tshark option Times the analysis PC tried to connect to a DNS server (port 53) -N dn (captured DNS + network address resolution) 0 -N dnN (plus external resolver) 2 (to the system DNS server 8.8.8.8) -o nameres.network_name:TRUE (only the setting equivalent to ticking "Resolve network addresses" in the GUI) 2

The third row is the key. In this version's (4.2.2) default preferences, the external resolver is already on and only network address resolution is off (checked with tshark -G defaultprefs). So the moment you tick "Resolve network addresses" in the GUI, the analysis PC starts sending real DNS queries for every IP in the pcap. The latest documentation (as of 4.6) also gives the default with no settings as -N dmN, i.e. with the external resolver on.

docs.title: 4.2 Why external resolution is dangerous
docs.text:
The source material gives three reasons.

  1. OPSEC. Attackers who run their own DNS servers often watch queries for their IPs and domains. A query from an unfamiliar source can tell them "someone has found my infrastructure". It sounds paranoid, but it has happened in the wild, and attackers react fast. And if the query goes out through the organisation's DNS server, the investigator's queries get mixed into the DNS logs from lesson 1.3, causing confusion later.
  2. Time differs. DNS records change often. The answer you get now may differ from the answer when the evidence was collected weeks ago. If the attacker changed the domain's address, you'll see the wrong name on screen.
  3. Location differs. DNS responses can vary with the network location of the querier (regional responses, internal-only names, etc.). The answer at the analysis PC may differ from the one the victim PC got.

So the rule is to almost never turn this setting on. Instead, the use captured DNS packets feature the Wireshark team added is a good alternative. It names addresses only from DNS responses inside the packets, so there's no outbound traffic and, above all, it shows the names as of when the evidence was collected: a kind of passive DNS. But remember that addresses with no DNS response in the file get no name (e.g. a capture filter that excluded DNS, lesson 1.7), and that the DNS response itself may have been forged.

MAC and transport name resolution are a matter of personal preference and create no outbound traffic, so there's no OPSEC worry. But transport names are a convenience feature attached from the port number alone, so http(80) doesn't mean the connection really is HTTP. Don't miss cases where an attacker uses a different protocol on port 80.

[Changed] Where the vendor and service tables live. The source material says these tables are in the files /usr/share/wireshark/manuf and services. Since Wireshark 4.2.0, these files (manuf, services, enterprises) were compiled into the program for faster start-up and are no longer shipped as separate files. You can dump the built-in content with commands like tshark -G manuf, and a manuf file in the personal configuration folder is read as well (checked 2026-11-05 in the Wireshark 4.2.0 release notes). Indeed, this environment's 4.2.2 had no /usr/share/wireshark/manuf, and 00:50:56 VMware could be found in tshark -G manuf (actual output). The latest documentation also adds an s option that names addresses from the server name (SNI) in TLS handshakes; this too uses only information in the file.

docs.title: 5.1 Any field as a column
docs.text:
The packet list's default columns are usually enough, but you can add, remove and reorder them. Besides the standard columns, any field Wireshark dissects can be a column. For example, right-click the User-Agent field in the details pane and choose "Apply as Column" to get an http.user_agent column; packets without that field show a blank. In tshark, -T fields -e field plays the same role (actual output):

$ tshark -r nameres.pcap -n -Y http.request -T fields -e frame.time_epoch -e ip.src -e http.host -e http.user_agent
1792000000.600000000    10.10.6.14  files.example.net   Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64; rv:144.0) Gecko/20100101 Firefox/144.0

Just as you handled proxy log fields in the shell in lesson 1.3, tab-separated output like this can be counted with sort and uniq straight away. The workflow of defining an analysis approach with columns in the GUI and then applying it to many files with tshark starts here.

docs.title: 5.2 Time display formats
docs.text:
View → Time Display Format changes the shape and precision of the Time column. I tried the same formats with tshark's -t (actual output, the time part of packet 2):

-t Meaning Result r Time since the first packet (default) 0.120000 d Time since the previous packet 0.120000 e Unix time 1792000000.120000 ad Date and time, analysis PC's local time 2026-10-14 17:46:40.120000 ud Date and time, UTC 2026-10-14 17:46:40.120000

ad and ud match only because this work environment's time zone is UTC. Rerunning with the time zone set to Sydney, ad came out as 2026-10-15 04:46:40.120000, even the date changed, while ud stayed the same (actual output). The same packet can appear on a different date depending on the analysis PC's time zone. So for investigations, the UTC date and time format ("UTC Date and Time of Day" in the GUI) is the best default, as it lines up directly with reports and other evidence (such as lesson 1.3's proxy logs).

[Caution] Packet times and times inside packets are different. A pcap's packet times are UTC (lesson 1.6). But times inside packets, such as an HTTP response's Date header, an email's date, or the time in a log string an application sent, follow whatever format and time zone that program chose. Don't treat the two as the same, and be especially careful with times that carry no time zone. This comes up again in later lessons.

docs.title: 6. How to use this in a real investigation
docs.text:
On the capture side:

  • For long captures, split with -G (time) or -C (size), put a time format like %F_%H%M%S in the name, and run with TZ=UTC.
  • With a ring buffer (-C + -W), calculate how many hours one cycle holds, and when an incident occurs, copy files before they're overwritten.
  • Confirm a split file's real range from capinfos's first and last packet times, not from its name.
  • Test options on the device's tcpdump version first (e.g. -C unit suffixes).

On the analysis side, before opening a pcap in Wireshark:

  1. Make sure network address resolution is off, or the external resolver is off. If you need names, turn on only "Use captured DNS packet data".
  2. Switch time display to UTC date and time.
  3. Add the fields the investigation needs (User-Agent, Host, etc.) as columns.
  4. If the file is large, open a reduced copy first, as in lesson 1.7.

Save these settings as a Wireshark profile and you don't have to redo them each time. Making one investigation profile for the team to share is also a good idea.

docs.title: 7. Summary
docs.text:
• -G seconds splits files by time and -C millions-of-bytes by size; -W with -C makes a ring buffer, and with -G creates that many files and exits. -F is a filter file, and -z runs a command on each file as it's closed.
  • -G file names must include a time format (or they're overwritten), and that time is the capture machine's local time zone. New files are created only when packets arrive.
  • -C's unit is 1,000,000 bytes, and the k, m, g suffixes arrived in tcpdump 4.99.6.
  • The Wireshark window consists of the display filter bar, packet list, packet details, packet bytes and status bar, with the details and bytes panes linked by highlighting. The field name in the status bar is the raw material for display filters.
  • MAC and transport name resolution are safe, but using an external resolver for network address resolution makes the analysis PC send real DNS queries. The external resolver is on by default, so if you need names, use only "Use captured DNS packet data".
  • Since Wireshark 4.2.0, the manuf and services tables are built into the program.
  • Any field can be a column, and viewing time as UTC date and time is the default to use. Times inside packets differ from packet times.

In the next lesson (1.9) we cover Wireshark display filter syntax, the syntax checker's three colours, the != trap, and following TCP streams.

docs.title: Review questions
docs.text:
Question 1. After a week of capturing with the command below, there's only one file, and it holds only the last hour. What went wrong and how should it be fixed?

sudo tcpdump -n -i ens33 -G 3600 -w capture.pcap 'host 10.10.6.14'
Answer and explanation

-G 3600 made a new file every hour, but the file name capture.pcap has no time format, so each new file was created with the same name, overwriting the previous one. Only the last hour survived; the tcpdump documentation warns about exactly this. Fixed: sudo TZ=UTC tcpdump -n -i ens33 -G 3600 -w 'capture-%F_%H%M%S.pcap' 'host 10.10.6.14'. The time format must be finer than the rotation interval (one hour), so it includes hours, minutes and seconds, and TZ=UTC keeps the names in UTC.

Question 2. (Calculation) On a segment that accumulates 40 GB a day on average, you set up a ring buffer with -C 1000 -W 48. Roughly how many hours does it hold? If incidents take a day on average to discover, what's the problem?

Answer and explanation

-C 1000 makes each file 1,000 × 1,000,000 = about 1 GB (a billion bytes), and -W 48 rotates 48 of them, so about 48 GB total. At 40 GB a day, that's about 1.67 GB an hour, so 48 ÷ 1.67 ≈ about 29 hours of retention. If discovery takes a day (24 hours) on average, there are only a few hours of margin, and on busier days or later-discovered incidents, the packets from the incident are likely already overwritten. It's the same problem as lesson 1.1 section 8.1's calculation. Add disk, adjust the capture filter, or set up in advance a procedure to copy the ring buffer files as soon as an incident is suspected.

Question 3. (Common misconception) Looking at dns-2026-10-20_020000.pcap, captured with -G 7200 (rotate every 2 hours), a colleague wrote in the report "this file is exactly two hours, from 02:00 to 04:00". What needs checking?

Answer and explanation

Three things. ① Time zone: the file name's time is the capture machine's local time zone, so unless capture ran with TZ=UTC, 02:00 may not be UTC. ② Actual range: tcpdump changes files only when packets arrive, so in a quiet period a file may run longer than two hours or its boundaries may miss the hour. ③ Gaps: capture may have stopped partway. So check the first and last packet times with capinfos and put those values in the report. The file name is a convenience label, not a guarantee of the evidence's range.

Question 4. (OPSEC) A colleague wanted to see names instead of IP addresses in Wireshark and ticked "Resolve network addresses" in the preferences. Everything else is at its default. What can happen, and what's the right setting?

Answer and explanation

In this version's defaults, "Use an external network name resolver" is already on, so the moment network address resolution is ticked, the analysis PC sends real DNS queries for every IP address in the pcap. This lesson's test directly confirmed connection attempts to the system DNS server with only this setting on. As a result ① the attacker's DNS server may notice the investigation, ② names may differ from those at the time of the evidence because they're today's answers, ③ answers from the analysis PC's location may differ from those the victim PC got, and ④ the investigator's queries mix into the organisation's DNS logs. The right setting is to turn off "Use an external network name resolver" and turn on only "Use captured DNS packet data". In tshark, leave out N, as in -N dn.

Question 5. The Protocol column in the packet list shows TCP rather than HTTP, yet the port in the Info column appears as http(80). Is this connection HTTP?

Answer and explanation

You can't tell. http(80) is a service label attached by transport name resolution from port number 80 alone; it doesn't mean the connection is really HTTP. If the Protocol column says TCP, Wireshark's dissector hasn't yet seen data it recognises as HTTP. It could be the SYN/ACK packets establishing the connection, or a non-HTTP protocol running over port 80. Look directly at the bytes of packets carrying data, or confirm the real content with lesson 1.9's stream following. Attackers using a different protocol over an easily allowed port like 80 is common.

Question 6. (Time) An analyst in Sydney and one in London open the same pcap in Wireshark, both with time display set to "Date and Time of Day". They report a packet's time differently. Why, and how do you align them?

Answer and explanation

"Date and Time of Day" converts to the analysis PC's local time zone (tshark's -t ad). In this lesson's test, changing the time zone made the same packet appear on a different date. The value in the pcap is the same UTC time, but Sydney and London have different time zones, so the displayed times differ. Switching both to UTC date and time ("UTC Date and Time of Day", tshark's -t ud) gives the same value. Putting this setting in a shared team investigation profile prevents this confusion.

Question 7. (Changes) You wanted to edit /usr/share/wireshark/manuf, as the source material describes, to name your organisation's device MAC prefixes, but a PC with Wireshark 4.6 installed has no such file. What should you do?

Answer and explanation

Since Wireshark 4.2.0, the manuf, services and enterprises tables are built into the program and not installed as separate files. You can view the built-in content with tshark -G manuf. Per the release notes, a manuf file is also read from the personal configuration folder (per profile), so put a manuf file with entries for your devices there. This kind of naming uses only files on the analysis PC, so there's no OPSEC issue. But remember that a MAC prefix's vendor name is only a clue for guessing the device, and MAC addresses can be changed.

Question 8. (Reading a command) Describe in one sentence what this command does, and name one problem it can cause.

sudo tcpdump -n -i any -w all.pcap -C 500
Answer and explanation

It saves traffic from all interfaces (-i any), unfiltered and without name lookups (-n), to a new file (all.pcap, all.pcap1, …) every 500,000,000 bytes (500 × 1,000,000), without end. The problem is that with no -W, files keep accumulating and the disk can fill up. When the disk fills, not only does capture stop, other functions of the system can stall too. Also, as lesson 1.6 showed, Linux's any interface doesn't use promiscuous mode, and its link type is a Linux-specific format rather than Ethernet, so layer 2 information such as MAC addresses is recorded differently from a normal Ethernet capture. For a long-running capture, limit the count with -W, or put disk monitoring in place alongside it.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• The Tcpdump Group, tcpdump 4.99 branch tcpdump.1 documentation source and change log CHANGES (checked 2026-11-05). -C's unit (1,000,000 bytes) and the pre-write size check, -G's time format and overwrite warning, -W's ring buffer and exit behaviour, and -z. That -C unit suffixes are a 4.99.6 change (confirmed by comparing documentation across tags).
  • Wireshark, tshark documentation source (release-4.6) (checked 2026-11-05). The meaning of the -N letters d, m, n, N, s, t and v, and the default -N dmN.
  • Wireshark, 4.2.0 release notes source (checked 2026-11-05). manuf, services and enterprises compiled into the program, viewable with tshark -G manuf|enterprises|services, and manuf also read from the personal configuration folder.

About this page

Personal study notes rewritten in my own words from a range of study material. The lab traffic and files were made in this work environment; the case is hypothetical.

docs.title: Lesson 1.2 — Web Proxies: How They Work, the Main Products, and Why the Config File Is Evidence
Lesson 1.2 — Web Proxies: How They Work, the Main Products, and Why the Config File Is Evidence
docs.text:
Scope of this lesson

The first part of the web proxy unit:

  • What a proxy is and why it exists (forward and reverse proxies)
  • How a performance device became a security and investigation device (blocking, logs, cache)
  • How TLS encryption blinds the proxy, and how TLS interception restores its view
  • Which products are in use, and what commercial vs open source means to an investigator
  • The three things to secure from a Squid proxy (config, logs, cache), and how to read the config file first

Reading each log field is the next lesson (1.3); pulling files out of the cache is lesson 1.5.

Notation

Same as lesson 1.1: (Hypothetical), (Illustrative output), [Changed], [Supplement], [Caution]. Configuration examples were written for this lesson, not taken from a real server.

docs.title: 1. Finding the PCs that reached the C2 among 30,000
docs.text:
Back to lesson 1.1's hypothetical organisation. (Hypothetical) An outside agency reports that the domain c2.example.net is an attack server. Management's first question: "How many of our PCs connected to it?"

Imaging PCs one by one would take weeks. But this organisation routes all web traffic through a web proxy. So a one-line search of the proxy log for that domain can give a first answer in minutes.

grep -F 'c2.example.net' /var/log/squid/access.log

grep is the Linux command that finds lines containing a given string in a file, and -F tells it to search for the text literally rather than as a regular expression. In a regular expression the dots in a domain mean "any single character", so without -F you could match odd lines like c2xexamplexnet. Each matching line contains the internal PC address that made the request, so collecting those addresses gives you "the list of PCs that connected".

Of course, as lesson 1.1 taught, "0 hits" doesn't mean nobody connected. Still, the fact that this one line can cut the scope from 30,000 machines to a handful is why this series turns to proxies straight away. So what exactly is a proxy, that it holds records like this?

docs.title: 2. An analogy: the company's purchasing desk
docs.text:
Picture a company where staff don't go out to shops themselves but ask the company's purchasing desk to buy things for them.

  • A staff member asks the desk: "Please buy this item from this shop."
  • The desk clerk goes to the shop, buys it and hands it over. From the shop's point of view it's always the clerk who comes in; it never sees the individual staff.
  • The clerk writes in a ledger: "at this time, this person asked for this item from this shop, and here's the result."
  • For frequently requested items, the clerk buys a spare and keeps it in the storeroom. When the next person asks for the same thing, the clerk hands it over from the storeroom without going to the shop.
  • If the company declares "no business with this shop", the clerk refuses those errands.

A web proxy is exactly this desk. Staff are internal PCs, shops are web servers on the Internet, the ledger is the proxy log, the storeroom is the proxy cache, and the banned-shop list is the block policy. The analogy also explains why, in lesson 1.1, the firewall showed the proxy's address rather than the PC's: the shop (external server) only ever sees the clerk (the proxy).

But there are differences between the analogy and reality. Remember three of them.

  1. The storeroom doesn't hold everything. A real proxy keeps only "responses that can be reused", and usually doesn't keep responses that differ per person, such as pages after login. So the cache is a "jackpot if it's there" source, not an "always there" one (lesson 1.5).
  2. It can't open sealed parcels. HTTPS is a sealed, encrypted parcel, so without extra configuration the clerk knows only "went to this shop", not what was bought (section 5).
  3. Some staff may skip the desk. Even with a rule in place, if there's a back door (a path that bypasses the proxy), it won't be in the ledger. Whether the ledger is complete can only be judged alongside the firewall rules.

docs.title: 3. How it works: how a proxy relays a request
3.1 Forward proxy
docs.text:
A proxy server is a server configured to broker traffic between a client and a server. It can be used for almost any protocol, but today "proxy" usually means a web proxy brokering HTTP and HTTPS. The proxy internal PCs pass through on the way out is a forward proxy.

sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Internal PC
    participant P as Proxy
    participant S as Web server
    C->>P: GET http://files.example.net/a.js
    alt HIT
        P-->>C: Cached response
    else MISS
        P->>S: GET /a.js + Host header
        S-->>P: 200 + content
        P-->>C: 200 + content (cached)
    end

How to read the diagram: the three vertical lines are three devices (internal PC 10.10.7.11, proxy 10.10.4.3:3128, web server 203.0.113.75:80), and time runs top to bottom. Solid arrows are requests, dashed arrows are responses. The "alt" box means only one of the two cases happens: the upper flow if it's in the cache (HIT), the lower flow if not (MISS).

There's a difference here that is very useful to an investigator. Compare the request lines of the first and third arrows.

Segment Request line Why it differs PC → proxy GET http://files.example.net/a.js HTTP/1.1 The proxy needs to know which server to go to, so the full URL is sent Proxy → server GET /a.js HTTP/1.1 + Host: files.example.net The server is itself, so it gets only the path, and the host comes in the Host header

The HTTP standard calls the first form absolute-form and the second origin-form. So if a request line in a packet capture starts with GET http://..., you know "this packet was captured on the way to a proxy". Conversely, if a PC that should use the proxy sends GET /path straight to an external server, it bypassed the proxy. That may be a policy violation or a sign of malware.

docs.title: 3.2 How does HTTPS get through? CONNECT
docs.text:
But what about HTTPS? The content is encrypted, so the proxy can't read the full URL. So the browser first asks the proxy:

CONNECT news.example:443 HTTP/1.1
Host: news.example:443

That means "open a tunnel to port 443 on news.example". Once the proxy answers 200 Connection established, it just relays the bytes in both directions without looking inside. So the log of a proxy without TLS interception keeps a single line like CONNECT news.example:443 per HTTPS connection, and not which pages were opened inside it or how many times. Section 5 shows how this limit is overcome.

[Supplement] Explicit vs transparent proxies. What we've described so far is an explicit proxy, where the PC's browser or OS is configured with "the proxy is 10.10.4.3:3128". The alternative, where the PC has no setting and network equipment quietly redirects port 80/443 traffic to the proxy, is a transparent (or intercepting) proxy. With a transparent proxy the PC doesn't know the proxy exists, so request lines are in origin-form (GET /path) and there's no CONNECT. The same "proxy log" looks different depending on the mode, so check the mode in the config first (section 7).

docs.title: 3.3 Reverse proxy
docs.text:
Proxies also sit the other way round. A proxy that stands in front of an organisation's few web servers and receives requests from the Internet's many visitors is a reverse proxy. It mostly handles performance features such as spreading requests across servers (load balancing) and compressing responses.

flowchart TD
    A1["Thousands of<br/>internal PCs"] --> FP["Forward proxy"] --> W1["Many servers<br/>on the Internet"]
    A2["Internet visitors"] --> RP["Reverse proxy"] --> W2["A few of our<br/>web servers"]

How to read the diagram: the left column is the forward proxy, the right column the reverse proxy, and in both the arrows are the request direction. A forward proxy stands in for "our people"; a reverse proxy stands in for "our servers".

Forward proxy Reverse proxy Stands in for Internal clients The organisation's web servers What its log answers Which internal PC requested which external URL Which outside visitor requested what from our servers Incidents it's used for Phishing clicks, malware downloads, C2, exfiltration Web server attacks, vulnerability scans, web shell access Watch out for Paths that bypass the proxy Server logs show the proxy's address instead of the visitor's → check headers like X-Forwarded-For

In lesson 1.1's organisation, the first clue was odd behaviour on the DMZ web server. In incidents like that, the logs of a reverse proxy in front of the web server (if there is one) are likely to hold the attacker's requests. This series mostly covers forward proxies, but the reading method is almost the same.

docs.title: 3.4 It started as a performance device
docs.text: Proxies weren't originally security devices. They were born to save slow Internet links. Hundreds of people used to share a single 1.544 Mbps T-1 line. With 200 users at once, each person's share is 1,544,000 ÷ 200 ≈ 7,700 bps, less than 1 KB per second. In that situation, 200 people each fetching the same news page is a huge waste. So the proxy kept a page it had fetched once (the cache) and handed it to the next person without using the link. Links are fast now, but the structure remains, and security people found new value in it.

docs.title: 4. A performance device becomes a security device
docs.text: Because it's "the gate every web request passes through", the proxy gained two security uses: preventing incidents (proactive) and investigating them (post-incident).

docs.title: 4.1 Proactive: blocking known bad things
docs.text:
Administrators can block requests to prohibited sites or known malicious domains at the proxy. This is very useful during incident response too. Blocking an attacker's C2 domain at the one proxy cuts that traffic across the whole organisation almost instantly, without touching tens of thousands of PCs.

[Caution] Choose the timing carefully, though. As lesson 1.1 showed, blocking C2 before the investigation finishes may tell the attacker they've been spotted, so they hide through another path or wipe their traces. On the other hand, if data is leaving right now, you must block immediately. So the incident lead decides the timing, weighing the risk of further damage against the need to investigate. And remember that blocked requests are still logged. A PC that keeps trying the domain after the block is likely still infected.

docs.title: 4.2 Post-incident: logs and cache
docs.text:
The log is the access roster of every HTTP(S) request the proxy handled. It usually holds the time, the requesting PC's IP address, the URL and the result status, plus the username where proxy authentication is used. So it can quickly answer "which internal systems tried to reach a known malicious site or file?" Whether it's a phishing incident or a botnet using HTTP for C2, it establishes scope far faster than analysing systems one by one.

The cache is copies of the responses the proxy fetched. Even if the malicious file has already been deleted from the infected PC, if it was stored in the proxy cache when first downloaded, you can pull it out and analyse it without touching the infected PC. If you've ever analysed an infected PC only to find the malicious file gone, you'll appreciate how welcome this is.

A small example. Here are some lines from the proxy log on one day (illustrative output, fields simplified):

2026-10-12 09:01:14 10.10.7.11  GET  http://parcel-redelivery.example/track?id=8812  200
2026-10-12 09:01:20 10.10.7.11  GET  http://parcel-redelivery.example/dl/label.zip   200
2026-10-12 09:03:51 10.10.6.14  GET  http://parcel-redelivery.example/track?id=1203  200
2026-10-12 09:40:02 10.10.7.15  GET  http://parcel-redelivery.example/track?id=5521  403

The facts these four lines show directly: three PCs (.7.11, .6.14, .7.15) connected to the same domain, only .7.11 also fetched a ZIP file, and .7.15's request ended with 403 (forbidden), probably because a block policy went in between. The hypothesis you can form is "the same phishing email went to several people". To conclude, check the mail server records (who received an email with that link) and each PC's execution records. And it's worth checking whether the ZIP .7.11 downloaded is still in the cache.

[Supplement] Conditions worth checking first in proxy logs. There are public cheat sheets listing suspicious conditions in proxy logs. The source material recommends a web proxy event analysis cheat sheet by security researcher Florian Roth; I couldn't confirm where that document is currently published. Here are representative conditions, listed in my own words. None of them is evidence of malice on its own; they're criteria for picking "candidates to look at first".

  • URLs that request an IP address directly instead of a domain
  • Executables, scripts or archives downloaded from never-before-seen domains
  • Rarely used top-level domains or free dynamic DNS domains
  • Very long or Base64-looking URLs, and same-size requests repeated at regular intervals
  • Odd or empty User-Agents (the browser identification string), and authentication failures (407) or blocks (403) piling up on one PC

These conditions are covered in more depth in the Blue Team Essentials HTTP(S) analysis lessons.

docs.title: 5. TLS blinds the proxy, and interception restores its view
5.1 The problem: sealed parcels
docs.text: As section 3.2 showed, TLS-encrypted HTTPS leaves a single CONNECT host:443 line in the proxy log. Most web traffic is now HTTPS, so an unconfigured proxy tells you little beyond "went to this site". If a C2 server uses the domain of a legitimate cloud service, that one line can't separate normal from malicious.

docs.title: 5.2 The fix: TLS interception
docs.text:
That's why many organisations turn on the proxy's TLS interception (also called TLS inspection, or "SSL inspection" in some products). The principle is that the proxy sets up two separate TLS connections in the middle.

sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Internal PC
    participant P as Proxy<br/>(holds internal CA)
    participant S as Real server<br/>news.example
    C->>P: CONNECT news.example:443
    P->>S: TLS connection ①
    S-->>P: Real certificate (signed by public CA)
    Note over P: Validate the real certificate, then<br/>generate a certificate with the same name<br/>(signed by internal CA)
    P-->>C: TLS connection ② + proxy-made certificate
    C->>P: Encrypted request
    Note over P: Decrypt → log · inspect → re-encrypt
    P->>S: Encrypted request

How to read the diagram: there are two TLS connections, one between the PC and the proxy (②) and one between the proxy and the server (①). The proxy decrypts the content in the middle, then re-encrypts it and passes it on. The PC receives a certificate the proxy made, signed by an internal certificate authority (a CA, the party that signs certificates to vouch that they're genuine).

For this to work, there are conditions:

  • Every PC must be preconfigured to trust the internal CA. Otherwise the browser shows a certificate warning on every HTTPS connection. So TLS interception only works on endpoints the organisation manages.
  • Programs that use certificate pinning break. Some apps hard-code "this server's certificate and no other". The proxy's certificate differs, so they refuse to connect. In practice, such apps and privacy-sensitive sites such as banking and healthcare go on an exception list and pass through uninspected.
  • Legal and privacy review is needed. You're decrypting employees' encrypted communications, so it's usually enabled after technical, legal and management teams review it together and staff are notified.

The most important result for the investigator: with interception on, the proxy logs HTTPS requests with the full URL too, like GET https://news.example/article/77. You'll see exactly this difference in lesson 1.4's investigation walkthrough. And remember that sites passed through on the exception list still leave only a CONNECT line. "That site's URL isn't in the log" may mean it was on the exception list, not that nobody visited.

docs.title: 5.3 [Supplement] What has changed in today's TLS landscape
docs.text:
Since the source material was written, TLS has seen several changes that affect investigators. Part 5 goes into detail; here are just the proxy-related ones.

  • In TLS 1.3 the server certificate travels encrypted. You used to see the server certificate just by looking at packets, but with TLS 1.3 a device watching in the middle (a packet sensor) can't see it. Only a device that is one end of the connection, like a proxy, can. That makes proxy records more valuable.
  • ECH (Encrypted Client Hello) hides even the server name (SNI). A device watching in the middle can't even see which site was visited. With an explicit proxy, however, the browser writes the destination directly in CONNECT host:443, so the proxy log still records the hostname.
  • HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP, not TCP. If UDP 443 is open on a path that doesn't go through the proxy, the browser may go out directly over QUIC and leave nothing in the proxy log. So organisations that want to funnel web traffic through a proxy block UDP 443 so browsers fall back to TCP, or turn QUIC off by browser policy. Chrome, for example, has a QuicAllowed policy; disabling it stops QUIC (checked 2026-11-05 in the policy definition file in the Chromium source). When investigating, check the firewall logs for UDP 443 traffic that bypassed the proxy before judging whether the proxy log is complete.
  • The interception device can itself become a risk. The US NSA issued an advisory on the risks of TLS interception in 2019, and CISA publicised it. It advises intercepting only once inside the organisation, protecting the internal CA key rigorously, and managing the interception device's logs carefully (checked 2026-11-05 via the CISA alert and secondary summaries; I couldn't read the original PDF this time). A proxy positioned to see all plaintext also means an attacker who controls the proxy sees all that plaintext. So when investigating, the proxy's own integrity is something to question as well.

docs.title: 6. Which products are in use
docs.text:
There are many proxies, both open source (FOSS) and commercial. These names come up often in investigations.

Product Form What the investigator should know Squid Open source, software The best-known open-source proxy. Plain-text logs and very detailed config documentation. This series' reference NGINX Open source (commercial edition exists), web server and proxy Usually deployed as a reverse proxy. Common in web server attack investigations Apache Traffic Server Open source Donated by Yahoo! to the Apache Foundation in 2009. Large-scale caching proxy Broadcom (formerly Symantec · Blue Coat) ProxySG / Edge SWG Commercial, appliance or virtual appliance Widely used in enterprises. Built-in TLS interception. Log fields configured in W3C extended format Forcepoint Web Security (formerly Websense) Commercial Used in large environments Zscaler Commercial, cloud service The proxy moved to the cloud. Logs live in the vendor's cloud

[Changed] The source material called Broadcom's product "Symantec WebFilter (formerly Blue Coat)". As of 2026-11-05, Broadcom's support documentation covers this proxy family as "Edge SWG (ProxySG)" (Broadcom knowledge article 240610: Edge SWG (ProxySG) access log fields). WebFilter is closer to the name of the URL categorisation database the proxy uses. Product names change often through acquisitions, so in reports it's better to confirm from the config and log headers "what device and version it actually was, whatever it's called".

[Supplement] How cloud proxies differ for investigation. Cloud proxies like Zscaler have the advantage of collecting home workers' traffic too. But the logs and config live in the vendor's cloud, so you can't get evidence by copying a server's disk. You have to get it via the admin console, an API or log forwarding (SIEM integration), and retention is set by contract. When writing an incident response plan, check in advance "who can get the logs, how fast, and in what format".

docs.title: 6.1 Commercial vs open source: what's different for an investigator
docs.text:
There's no right answer to "is commercial or open source better?" Each has pros and cons. For an investigator, though, the differences are clear.

  • Open source makes the data accessible. Logs are often plain text, and if you're unsure exactly what a field means, you can check the source code and documentation.
  • Commercial products can hinder access. Storage formats are often proprietary and need converting before analysis, and admin interfaces do a handful of set functions well but make other questions hard to ask. That doesn't make the data unusable; it means getting it out takes more effort (lesson 1.5 shows a commercial log example).

That's why this series uses Squid as its reference: it's open source, so it's good for understanding principles by looking inside, and it's widely used. But the goal isn't how to use Squid; it's investigation methods that work on any proxy. Major commercial proxies have the same or similar features and records, so ask them the same questions you learn here.

docs.title: 7. The three pieces of evidence to secure from Squid
docs.text:
Squid is free and ships as a standard package in most Linux distributions, so it's easy to install. But its simplicity hides powerful features. Skilled administrators run several Squid servers together, or set different cache retention policies per file type (e.g. keep .exe longer than .html), in hundreds of ways. That's why the first thing the investigator secures is the configuration file.

Evidence Common location (distribution packages) What it tells you Configuration file /etc/squid/squid.conf Where, in what format and under what conditions the other evidence is recorded Log files Under /var/log/squid/ (access.log, cache.log, etc.) The access roster of client requests Cache data Under /var/spool/squid/ Copies of responses the servers returned

[Caution] Locations differ per installation. The table above is for common distribution packages. Build from source and the defaults move under /usr/local/squid/, and administrators can change them freely in the config. So don't guess locations; follow the paths written in the config file. That's the first reason to secure the config first.

docs.title: 7.1 Why the config file comes first
docs.text:
This principle recurs throughout the series: once a device is judged relevant to the investigation, secure its configuration file quickly. Three reasons:

  1. It tells you where the other evidence is and what it means. Where the logs are, which fields are written in which order, whether query strings are stripped before logging, whether the cache is on disk: it's all in the config.
  2. Configs change. If an administrator adds a block rule or changes the log format during response, the config as it was at the time of the incident is gone. Without the incident-time config, you can misread the logs from that time. Evidence being altered or destroyed like this is called spoliation.
  3. It reveals evidence you'd otherwise miss. For example, if the config has a line splitting logs into two places, you only learn the second log file exists by reading the config.

When securing the config, follow lesson 1.1's principle: make a copy and record a hash (a unique fingerprint value computed from the file's content) (example commands):

sudo tar -czpf proxy-config-$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ).tgz /etc/squid/
sha256sum proxy-config-*.tgz | tee proxy-config.sha256

The first line's tar -czpf bundles the whole /etc/squid/ folder into one archive (c create, z compress, p preserve permissions, f set the file name). date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ puts the acquisition time in UTC into the file name, so "when was this config taken?" never gets confused later. The second line computes the archive's SHA-256 hash, showing it on screen and saving it to a file at the same time (tee). Recomputing the hash later and getting the same value is your basis for saying it hasn't changed since acquisition. The whole folder is bundled, not just the main config file, because the config may pull in other files via include directives, and the TLS interception certificates may sit in the same folder.

Squid also installs a default config file that explains every directive in great detail. Depending on the distribution it's called something like /etc/squid/squid.conf.default or squid.conf.documented. When a config line is confusing, this file is the primary reference. But use the documentation for the Squid version on the server under investigation, because config syntax changes between versions (section 8.2).

docs.title: 8. Reading a config file: a walkthrough
docs.text:
Let's actually read one. Below is the core of a config written for this lesson, assuming it's the proxy of lesson 1.1's hypothetical organisation. It follows Squid 7's documented syntax.

# --- Network presence ---
http_port 3128 ssl-bump tls-cert=/etc/squid/ca/proxy-ca.pem generate-host-certificates=on dynamic_cert_mem_cache_size=4MB

# --- Access control ---
acl localnet src 10.10.0.0/16
acl research src 10.10.6.0/24
acl SSL_ports port 443
acl CONNECT method CONNECT
http_access deny CONNECT !SSL_ports
http_access allow localnet
http_access deny all

# --- TLS interception rules ---
acl step1 at_step SslBump1
acl no_bump ssl::server_name .bank.example .health.example
ssl_bump peek step1
ssl_bump splice no_bump
ssl_bump bump all

# --- Logs and cache ---
access_log daemon:/var/log/squid/access.log squid
strip_query_terms off
cache_dir ufs /var/spool/squid 51200 16 256

Lines starting with # are comments, which Squid ignores. Let's read it a block at a time.

docs.title: 8.1 Line by line
docs.text:
Network presence: http_port 3128 ... Squid waits for requests on TCP port 3128. 3128 is Squid's conventional default, but administrators often change it to something like 8080. Knowing this value lets you read other evidence: in firewall logs, "PC → 10.10.4.3:3128" is normal proxy use, while "PC → Internet:443" is a direct connection bypassing the proxy. On the same line, ssl-bump marks this port for TLS interception, tls-cert= is the internal CA certificate file used for interception, and generate-host-certificates=on means generate a certificate on the fly for each site visited. dynamic_cert_mem_cache_size=4MB keeps up to 4 MB of generated certificates in memory for reuse.

Access control: acl and http_access. An acl (access control list) is a definition: "call requests matching this condition by this name". acl localnet src 10.10.0.0/16 means "call requests with a source address from 10.10.0.0 to 10.10.255.255 localnet". /16 is CIDR notation for an address range whose first 16 bits (10.10) are the same. http_access allows or denies using those conditions, and the first matching line from the top applies. So order matters. The config above ① denies CONNECT to any port other than 443 (stopping tunnels to arbitrary ports), ② allows internal addresses, ③ denies everything else. Besides addresses, conditions can use user authentication, User-Agent, day and time, URL regular expressions and more.

This matters to the investigator because it lets you understand which requests were denied and how denied requests appear in the log. And a separately defined group like research is a hint that different rules or a separate log may apply to just that group.

TLS interception rules: ssl_bump. Squid processes a TLS connection in several steps and decides at each step whether to look (peek), pass it through (splice) or intercept (bump). The config above ① peeks at the client's greeting (Client Hello) in the first step to learn the server name being requested (peek step1), ② passes through without interception if that name is one of the banking or healthcare example domains (splice no_bump), ③ intercepts everything else (bump all). If no rule matches, the default action is splice (pass through).

For the investigator, ② is the key. Records for .bank.example and .health.example appear in the log only as CONNECT lines. You're confirming in the config itself section 5.2's point that "no URL may be due to the exception list".

Logs and cache. access_log daemon:/var/log/squid/access.log squid means write the access log to /var/log/squid/access.log in Squid's native format (squid). The daemon: prefix has a separate helper process write the file. If the format name isn't squid but a self-defined name, there will be a logformat line somewhere in the same config; find it to confirm the field order (lesson 1.3). strip_query_terms off means log the query string after ? in URLs too. Squid's default is on, which strips query strings before logging. That default protects privacy, so switching it off needs agreement from the people with authority. cache_dir ufs /var/spool/squid 51200 16 256 means keep a ufs-type disk cache in /var/spool/squid of up to 51,200 MB (50 GB), split into 16 first-level folders each with 256 second-level folders. That's why cache files appear two numbered folder levels down, like /var/spool/squid/00/05/000005F4 (lesson 1.5).

docs.title: 8.2 [Changed] The source material's config vs today's syntax
docs.text:
The source material's example config uses Squid syntax from a few years ago, so it differs from the current version in places (as of 2026-11-05 the latest stable release is Squid 7.6, and Squid 6 is out of support). Checked against the Squid 7 branch's original config documentation (src/cf.data.pre) and config parsing code.

Line in the source material Current status What the investigator should know http_port ... cert=... key=... Documented names are tls-cert= and tls-key=. The parser still accepts cert= and key= Older servers may still use the old names, so recognise both ssl_bump server-first all server-first and client-first remain only as "backward compatibility actions". Today you combine peek, stare, splice and bump per step The old mode can't decide based on TLS greeting information, making fine-grained exception lists hard sslproxy_flags DONT_VERIFY_PEER This directive is obsolete. The same function is tls_outgoing_options flags=DONT_VERIFY_PEER [Caution] The proxy accepts even bogus server certificates and users never see a warning. It can hide connections to fake servers, so it's a dangerous setting; if found, report it as a risk sslcrtd_program /usr/lib64/squid/ssl_crtd ... The certificate generator helper was renamed security_file_certgen Check both names when searching by executable cache_dir ufs /var/spool/squid ... Same syntax. But with no cache_dir, there's no disk cache and caching is in memory only (Squid 7 documentation's default description) [Caution] Without a disk cache, the cache vanishes the moment Squid restarts. Don't restart before acquisition The store.log file cache_store_log defaults to none (not written) A missing store.log isn't strange; it exists only if enabled in the config

The most practical lesson in this table is the last two rows. Reading the config also tells you "this evidence never existed on this server". Without knowing that, reporting "the cache was wiped" or "someone deleted store.log" would be a wrong conclusion.

docs.title: 8.3 Changing the conditions
docs.text:
Even in the same organisation, a small config difference greatly changes what the log contains. Some cases compared:

Config difference Result in logs and cache Effect on the investigation No ssl-bump All HTTPS appears only as CONNECT host:443 The proxy can't tell you HTTPS paths or file names. Need packet or endpoint evidence strip_query_terms at default (on) Query strings like ?id=8812 are stripped Search terms, phishing link identifiers and C2 command parameters aren't in the log No cache_dir Cache in memory only Restart destroys cache evidence. Must acquire while running Two access_log lines Logged to two files by condition Looking at one file misses part http_port in transparent mode (intercept) Request lines in origin-form, no CONNECT Section 3.2's "find HTTPS via CONNECT lines" doesn't work

docs.title: 8.4 How to interpret it in a real investigation
docs.text:
After reading the config you can record the following in a report or case notes. Based on the example config above:

  • Observed facts (read directly from the config): the proxy uses port 3128, TLS interception is on, the banking and healthcare example domains are excepted, query strings are logged, and the disk cache is up to 50 GB.
  • What those facts support: HTTPS requests through this proxy should be in the log as full URLs, except for the excepted domains. Copies of responses may be in the cache.
  • What still needs checking: was the config the same at the time of the incident (change history, backups, file modification times, interviewing the administrator)? Did every PC actually use this proxy (were there direct 80, 443 or UDP 443 connections in the firewall rather than 3128)? Does the cache currently on disk cover the incident period (the cache deletes the oldest objects when full)?

The last point matters most. The config file shows the current state. That it matched the state at the time of the incident is a hypothesis to verify separately.

docs.title: 9. Summary
docs.text:
• A web proxy is a server that brokers HTTP(S) between clients and servers. A forward proxy stands in for internal PCs; a reverse proxy stands in for the organisation's servers.
  • It started as a performance device to save slow links, but because every web request passes through it, it gained security value: blocking (proactive) and logs and cache (post-incident).
  • Requests to a proxy start with the full URL (absolute-form), and HTTPS with CONNECT host:443. These shapes let you tell proxy use from proxy bypass.
  • TLS blinds the proxy, and TLS interception restores its view using an internal CA. It needs endpoint control, exceptions for certificate pinning and legal review, and excepted sites still leave only CONNECT.
  • With TLS 1.3 and ECH reducing what packets alone show, proxy records have become more valuable. QUIC (UDP 443), however, can slip past the proxy, so check the gap with firewall records.
  • Commercial or open source, the goal is method, not tool. Commercial and cloud proxies take more effort to get data out of.
  • Squid's evidence is config, logs and cache, and you secure the config file first. The config tells you where the other evidence is and what it means, and also tells you what evidence never existed.

In the next lesson (1.3) we read each field of the access.log this config produces, and cover custom log formats and Unix time conversion.

docs.title: Review questions
docs.text:
Question 1. In a packet capture, internal PC 10.10.7.11 sends the request line GET http://files.example.net/a.js HTTP/1.1. Another PC, 10.10.7.15, sends GET /a.js HTTP/1.1 to 203.0.113.75:80. The organisation is meant to use an explicit proxy. What can you tell from the two requests?

Answer and explanation

The first is absolute-form (full URL), so it's a request to the proxy: normal proxy use. The second is origin-form (path only) and the destination is an external server, so 10.10.7.15 requested the external server directly, without the proxy. In an organisation meant to use an explicit proxy, that's an observed anomaly. It doesn't prove malice by itself, though; it might be a PC missing the proxy setting or an updater that doesn't use the proxy. Check which process on that PC made the connection (endpoint records) and why the firewall allowed the direct connection. Also note that this request is absent from the proxy log. Looking at the proxy log alone, you'd have missed it.

Question 2. The proxy log has only CONNECT mail.example:443 and not a single https:// URL for that site. You were told this proxy does TLS interception. Give at least two possible explanations, and how you'd check each.

Answer and explanation
  1. It was on the exception list: if an ssl_bump splice rule includes that domain or its category, it passes through uninspected and only CONNECT is logged. Check the ssl_bump and related acl lines in the config.
  2. Interception was off at the time: it may have been enabled later or switched off for a while. Check the incident-time config via change history, backups and interviewing the administrator.
  3. The TLS connection failed midway: a program using certificate pinning rejects the proxy's certificate and the connection drops, so no requests follow. Check the error records in cache.log or on the endpoint.

Either way, the conclusion "interception is on, so no URL means no visit" is wrong. The CONNECT line itself is an observed fact that a tunnel to that host was opened.

Question 3. (Changed conditions) If you remove the strip_query_terms off line from section 8's example config, how do section 4.2's four example log lines change? What judgement becomes harder?

Answer and explanation

The default on applies, so query strings such as ?id=8812, ?id=1203 and ?id=5521 are stripped before logging. All three then look identical: http://parcel-redelivery.example/track. A phishing link's id value usually identifies "which email this was sent in", so with it you can match each recipient precisely against mail server records. With query strings stripped, that matching gets hard, and you also lose information such as search terms and C2 command parameters. That's why you read the config first: knowing "this log never had query strings" saves you time hunting for information that isn't there.

Question 4. (Common misconception) A colleague says: "The proxy server's /var/spool/squid/ is empty, so it looks like the attacker wiped the cache." How would you check?

Answer and explanation

First, see whether the config has a cache_dir. Per the Squid 7 documentation, with no cache_dir there's no disk cache at all, only memory. In that case an empty folder is normal. cache_dir may also point to another path, or be split across several paths with multiple lines, so check every path listed. Only if cache_dir is set to that path and it's still empty do you weigh the possibilities: was there recent admin work such as a reinstall or cache reset (interview the administrator, system logs), was the disk replaced, and are there real deletion traces (file system forensics)? "The attacker wiped it" is the last conclusion, and only with evidence.

Question 5. (Reading config) With the config below, what happens when user PC 10.10.7.11 sends CONNECT example.org:8443? Explain why.

acl localnet src 10.10.0.0/16
acl SSL_ports port 443
acl CONNECT method CONNECT
http_access allow localnet
http_access deny CONNECT !SSL_ports
http_access deny all
Answer and explanation

It's allowed. http_access applies the first matching line from the top. In the first line, allow localnet, the source 10.10.7.11 matches localnet (10.10.0.0/16), so it's allowed immediately and the lines below are never consulted. So the second line, meant to "deny CONNECT to ports other than 443", never applies to internal PCs. As in section 8's example, deny CONNECT !SSL_ports must come above allow localnet to work as intended. From an investigation standpoint, if this proxy's log shows internal PCs' non-standard-port CONNECTs being allowed, that may be a channel left open by a config mistake, and a handy one for an attacker's C2.

Question 6. (Calculation) In section 8's cache_dir ufs /var/spool/squid 51200 16 256, (a) what is the maximum cache size in GB, and (b) how many second-level folders can hold cache files in total?

Answer and explanation

(a) The third value, 51200, is in MB, so 51,200 ÷ 1,024 = 50 GB. (b) Each of the 16 first-level folders has 256 second-level folders, so 16 × 256 = 4,096. Knowing this, you can expect numbered folders from /var/spool/squid/00/00 to 0F/FF when acquiring the cache (16 first-level folders are hex 00–0F, 256 second-level are 00–FF). Copying only some folders misses part of the cache, so acquire the cache_dir path from the config in full. And once 50 GB fills, the oldest objects are deleted, so on a busy proxy the period the cache covers can be shorter than you'd think.

Question 7. (Today's environment) The proxy log shows a PC never connected to www.video.example. Yet the user says they watched videos there for hours. How could this be explained, and what should you check?

Answer and explanation

The most likely explanation is HTTP/3 (QUIC). Video services use QUIC heavily, and QUIC uses UDP 443, not TCP. If the firewall allowed UDP 443 on a path not going through the proxy, the browser may have gone direct, bypassing the proxy. Check the firewall logs for that PC's UDP 443 connections, and whether browser policy (e.g. Chrome's QuicAllowed) disabled it. Also check whether the PC was missing its proxy setting or went out by another path such as a VPN. The lesson: "not in the proxy log" doesn't mean "didn't connect", and whether the proxy log is complete can only be judged against firewall records.

Question 8. (Judgement) On day one of the response, as soon as the C2 domain is found, a colleague says "let's block it at the proxy right now". Give one argument for and one against, and if you do block, say how you can use the proxy log afterwards.

Answer and explanation
  • For: blocking at the one proxy cuts C2 traffic across the whole organisation almost instantly. If data is leaving right now, it's the fastest way to limit damage.
  • Against: the attacker may notice the C2 traffic stopping and realise they're being investigated. They may move to another C2 or wipe traces, and you lose them before scoping is complete (lesson 1.1's OPSEC and "remediate all at once").

The incident lead decides, weighing the risk of spread against the need to investigate. If you block, use the fact that blocked requests are logged too. PCs that keep requesting the domain after the block (recorded as 403 and so on) are likely still infected, so that list becomes your set for detailed analysis. And if the attacker moves to a new C2, look for requests to never-before-seen domains from the same PCs right after the block.

docs.text:
