About this page

A personal study note, rewritten in my own words from several learning resources. The experiment server and requests are my own, and the scenarios are hypothetical.

docs.title: 2.2 — Reading HTTP Responses: Status Codes, Response Headers and Investigative Use
2.2 — Reading HTTP Responses: Status Codes, Response Headers and Investigative Use
docs.text:
Scope of this lesson

  • The three parts of the status line: version, status code, reason phrase. One byte of reason phrase can fingerprint a server (tested directly)
  • The five families of status codes and the ones common in investigations. [Correction] the name of 400, and 302 versus 307/308
  • Reading attacker intent from the flow of status codes: a storm of 404s, a 200 after 500s
  • Response headers: Connection ([Correction] HTTP/1.1 keeps connections alive by default), Server, content information and compression, Date (measuring clock skew), cache directives, Location
  • Typical investigative uses of HTTP: paste sites, User-Agent profiles, Basic authentication, URI records

Lab environment and notation

(Actual output) was produced in this environment. Responses came from a practice server on loopback (written in Python for this lesson), deliberately built to run its clock 437 seconds slow and to return two redirects, a gzip-compressed body, and a response with one extra space after the reason phrase. Requests were sent with curl 8.5.0, captured with tcpdump 4.99.4 and read with tshark 4.2.2. Addresses and scenarios are hypothetical.

docs.title: 1. Responses tell you "what happened on the server side"
docs.text:
The requests of lesson 2.1 tell you what the client wanted. The response tells you how that request was actually handled. Writing "they accessed the admin page" from request logs alone is half the story. Whether the request got a 200 (success), a 403 (refused) or a 302 back to the login screen changes everything.

As an analogy, the request is an application form handed in at a service counter, and the response is the notice of outcome the counter returns. The notice carries a result number (the status code), a short description (the reason phrase), notes about the handling (response headers), and possibly an attached document (the body). Where the analogy differs: the server can write most of that description and those notes however it likes, just like request headers in lesson 2.1.

docs.title: 2. The status line: version, code, reason phrase
docs.text:
The first line of a response is the status line.

HTTP/1.1 301 Moved Permanently
  • Version (HTTP/1.1): usually matches the request's version.
  • Status code (301): a three-digit number. Programs decide what to do from this number alone.
  • Reason phrase (Moved Permanently): a short description for humans. The standard recommends phrases, but clients must ignore it and servers can write anything.

docs.title: 2.1 One byte of reason phrase becomes a fingerprint
docs.text:
The source material describes a researcher who found the servers of a popular attack and penetration-testing framework by a single space after the reason phrase. Those servers sent HTTP/1.1 200 OK with an extra space after OK, and scanning the Internet for this quirk turned up thousands of them (it has since been fixed). Clients ignore the reason phrase, so nothing breaks, but an implementation that deviates slightly from the standard becomes a fingerprint of that program.

I tested this principle. The practice server returns OK (with the space) only for /beacon requests.

tshark -n -r resp.pcap -Y 'http.response.phrase == "OK "' -T fields -e tcp.stream

(Actual output) 9. Of twelve responses, only the one with the space (stream 9) matched. The table below lists all responses; by eye, the difference between OK and OK is barely visible.

(Actual output, some columns trimmed)

tcp.stream  code  phrase             location            content_encoding  content_length
0           301   Moved Permanently  /promo                                0
0           302   Found              /landing?cid=8812                     0
0           200   OK                                     gzip              78
1           404   Not Found                                                12
...         ...   ...
8           404   Not Found                                                12
9           200   OK                                                       48

What it means for investigations: when threat intelligence reports "this C2 server sends this unusual response", one display filter can find the same server across all your past pcaps. Conversely, remember that such fingerprints vanish the moment the attacker fixes them. Don't conclude from one characteristic alone; use it alongside other evidence such as the destination, timing patterns and content.

[Changed] HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 have no reason phrase

HTTP/2 (RFC 9113) and HTTP/3 (RFC 9114) send only the status code, in the :status pseudo-header, and don't carry the version or reason phrase at all. So reason-phrase fingerprints work only on HTTP/1.x responses. If a logging tool shows a reason phrase for an HTTP/2 response, it's a standard phrase filled in by the tool to match the code.

docs.title: 3.1 The five families
docs.text:
Family Meaning One-line summary 1xx Informational still working, carry on 2xx Success the request was received and handled 3xx Redirection go elsewhere, or use what you already have 4xx Client error something is wrong with the request 5xx Server error the request was fine, but the server couldn't handle it

Even for an unfamiliar code, the first digit gives the broad meaning. The standard says to treat an unknown code as the x00 of its family.

docs.title: 3.2 Codes commonly seen in investigations
docs.text:
Code Standard name How to read it in investigations 100 Continue confirmation before sending a body (Expect: 100-continue). A precursor of large uploads 200 OK handled successfully. Read together with body size 204 No Content success, no body. Common as a beacon's "nothing to do" reply 206 Partial Content sent part only (Range request). The PDF fetched three times in the same second in lesson 1.4 301 Moved Permanently permanent move. Follow the Location header 302 Found temporary move. Return after login, the new post's address after an upload (lessons 1.4 and 1.13) 304 Not Modified use the copy you have. No body: no content was exchanged at that moment 307 · 308 Temporary · Permanent Redirect like 302 and 301, but resend without changing the method and body 400 Bad Request malformed request. Fuzzing, sloppy tools 401 Unauthorized authentication required. Look at subsequent Authorization attempts 403 Forbidden refused regardless of authentication 404 Not Found nonexistent resource. Many at once suggests reconnaissance (section 3.3) 405 Method Not Allowed that method isn't allowed. Traces of trying method after method 407 Proxy Authentication Required proxy authentication required (the proxy version of 401) 429 Too Many Requests requesting too often. Brute forcing or scraping hitting a limit 500 Internal Server Error internal server error. A web app falling over on strange input 502 · 504 Bad Gateway · Gateway Timeout front-end equipment got no answer from the back-end server 503 Service Unavailable overloaded or under maintenance 511 Network Authentication Required the login screen of places like public Wi-Fi (captive portals)

[Correction] The name of 400 and the meaning of 302

  • The source material calls 400 "Bad Syntax", but the standard name is Bad Request (RFC 9110 section 15.5.1).
  • The source material describes 302 as "in practice a temporary relocation, though not strictly in compliance with the standard". The background: 302 originally meant "repeat the request with the same method", but browsers turned a POST answered with 302 into a GET. Today's standard (RFC 9110 section 15.4.3) accepts that reality and allows the method to change to GET after a 302, and provides 307 (temporary) and 308 (permanent) for when the method must be kept. So in logs, POST → 302 → GET is a normal shape, while POST → 307 → POST means the same body was sent once more. It makes a difference when you count upload volume.

[Supplement] 304 means \"no content was exchanged\"

A 304 response has no body. It tells the client to use the copy it already has (the browser cache, lesson 1.5). So writing "they received that file at that time" from a 304 record is wrong. The file was received some time earlier; at that moment only the question "is it still valid?" was exchanged. To find when it was first received, search back for a 200 response to the same address.

docs.title: 3.3 Reading intent from the flow of codes
docs.text:
Status codes say more as a flow than one at a time. I requested common admin pages and config file names from the practice server one after another, like a reconnaissance tool.

(Actual output, requests joined with their response codes)

/phpmyadmin/      404   Mozilla/5.0 zgrab/0.x
/pma/             404   Mozilla/5.0 zgrab/0.x
/admin/setup.php  404   Mozilla/5.0 zgrab/0.x
/wp-login.php     404   Mozilla/5.0 zgrab/0.x
/.env             404   Mozilla/5.0 zgrab/0.x
/.git/config      404   Mozilla/5.0 zgrab/0.x
/backup.zip       404   Mozilla/5.0 zgrab/0.x
/server-status    404   Mozilla/5.0 zgrab/0.x

Eight requests all got 404 within 0.06 seconds; no person with a browser could do that. This is the source material's "long bout of 400-series codes from a single address", the classic shape of reconnaissance. The names requested also show what was being looked for (a database admin tool, WordPress login, config files holding passwords, source repositories, backups). Lesson 2.5 shows the same shape in real web server log formats.

Another flow the source material describes is 500-series codes against a search form, then a 200, followed by many POSTs. Input with broken SQL syntax causes an error between the web app and the database, so it usually comes back as a 500. If an attacker kept adjusting input and getting 500s and finally got a 200, that may be the moment the injection succeeded, and the POSTs after it may be post-compromise operations. The server's error log often holds database error messages in such cases, so secure it too.

[Caution] A pile of 404s doesn't mean \"it failed, so we're fine\"

If a reconnaissance run ended all in 404s, that only means nothing was found from that list. Check whether even one request from the same address got a 200, and whether that address came back days later in another way. Also, as lesson 1.10, section 6.3 showed, an exported file named backup.zip may contain a 404 page. In this lab too, the file exported under the name backup.zip was a 12-byte <h1>404</h1> (actual output).

docs.title: 4.1 Connection: [Correction] HTTP/1.1 keeps connections alive by default
docs.text:
The source material says HTTP/1.1 gained the ability to carry several request/response pairs over one TCP connection, and that when the client signals support with Connection: Keep-Alive, the server answers with the same header. More precisely, persistent connections are the default in HTTP/1.1 (RFC 9112 section 9.3). The connection stays open without any announcement, and the side wanting to close sends Connection: close. Stating Keep-Alive explicitly is the HTTP/1.0-era extension.

What it means for investigations: one TCP connection (one stream, as in lesson 1.9) can contain several requests. In this lab, the three requests curl -L made following redirects (/go, /promo, /landing) all travelled in stream 0 (actual output). So don't count "one stream = one request", and remember that one connection in flow records (lesson 1.11) can hold several requests. Zeek, covered in lesson 2.8, distinguishes them with trans_depth.

docs.title: 4.2 Server: the name the server declares for itself
docs.text: The server-side counterpart of lesson 2.1's User-Agent. Values like Apache/2.4.29 (Ubuntu), nginx and Microsoft-IIS/10.0 are common and useful for guessing the server type and version. But it can also be written freely. This lab's server was written in Python yet declared Server: Apache/2.4.29 (Ubuntu) (actual output), because I made it so. Many operators remove versions or write misleading names for security, and front-end CDNs or proxies may replace it with their own. Headers such as Via, X-Cache and X-Served-By are clues that a cache or CDN sits in between.

docs.title: 4.3 Content information: length, type, compression
docs.text:
• Content-Length: the number of bytes in the body. This is the size on the wire.
  • Content-Type: the body's type (MIME type) and character set. Only what the server claims; confirm the actual content by its magic number (lesson 1.13).
  • Content-Encoding: compression applied to the body: gzip, br (Brotli), and zstd seen in lesson 2.1, among others.

With compression, there are two "sizes". In this lab, the /landing response had Content-Length: 78, but the file tshark exported was 1,106 bytes of HTML (actual output), because Wireshark decompressed the gzip on export. The same response can appear in proxy logs with its on-the-wire size (around 78 bytes) and in Zeek's http.log with its decompressed size (response_body_len in lesson 2.8). When matching sizes across sources, first establish which size it is. And when carving directly from packets (lesson 1.13), decompression adds another layer.

docs.title: 4.4 Date: another clock
docs.text:
The time the server generated the response. Caches use it to calculate freshness (lesson 1.5), but for investigators it's another independent clock. Comparing the capture box's time (the packet time) with the server's Date shows whether one of the clocks is off.

(Actual output)

frame.time_epoch: 1793861118.334450000   → Thu Nov  5 06:45:18 UTC 2026
http.date:        Thu, 05 Nov 2026 06:38:01 GMT

date -u -d @1793861118

The capture time and the server's Date differed by 437 seconds (7 minutes 17 seconds), exactly as expected since I set the practice server's clock that far back. In a real case, a difference like this means checking ① the capture box's NTP status (lesson 1.11) and ② that server's clock, then correcting all of that server's log times by the same amount before matching them with other evidence. Conversely, in a pcap captured on a user's PC, if many servers' Date values are all off in the same direction, the PC's clock is likely wrong. The source material also mentions malware that used the Date value of an ordinary web request as the seed for its domain generation algorithm (lesson 2.7): a clock is useful to malware too.

docs.title: 4.5 Cache directives: Cache-Control, Expires, ETag, Vary
docs.text:
These are the headers seen with the proxy cache in lesson 1.5. Briefly:

  • Cache-Control: max-age=1800 means fresh for 30 minutes; no-store means don't store; private means don't store in a shared cache.
  • Expires is an absolute time when freshness ends (the older approach).
  • ETag is an identifier for that content. If the client sends it back in If-None-Match on the next request, the server answers 304 when it hasn't changed.
  • Vary: Accept-Encoding means "store separate copies by compression method".

ETag is surprisingly useful in investigations. The same ETag is the server's indication of the same content, so it can be used to compare whether requests at different times or from different PCs received the same file. But how ETags are generated varies by server (some build them from file size and modification time), and they can be faked, so they don't replace hashes.

docs.title: 4.6 Location: chains of redirects
docs.text:
3xx responses carry a Location header giving the next address. One request in this lab (/go) continued like this.

flowchart TD
    A["GET /go"] -->|"301 · Location: /promo"| B["GET /promo"]
    B -->|"302 · Location: /landing?cid=8812"| C["GET /landing?cid=8812"]
    C -->|"200 · gzip body"| D["Final page"]

How to read it: top to bottom, the order in which the browser (here curl -L) followed automatically. The text on each arrow is that step's response code and Location value.

The user clicked once, yet three requests went out. Such chains are very common, and mostly normal, with URL shorteners, ad tracking and login flows. But malicious delivery networks love chains too: multiple hops make it easier to hide the final server and evade blocking. In investigations, find both the start of the chain (the link the user actually clicked, and where it came from) and the end (the content actually received), and put the intermediate addresses into block lists and threat intelligence. The query in a Location (cid=8812) can, like a campaign identifier, tell you who sent the link.

docs.title: 5. Typical investigative uses of HTTP
docs.text:
The source material lists four. Tying them to earlier lessons:

  • Exfiltration to paste and file-sharing sites. Attackers open a browser on a remotely accessed PC and upload data to a paste site, or build the site's published API into malware to upload automatically. Lessons 1.4 (the shape seen in logs) and 1.13 (the content carved from packets) were this case. A 302 and short Location after a POST are the typical traces.
  • Profiles built from User-Agents. A well-managed organisation knows its permitted User-Agent values, so unfamiliar ones signal unauthorised software. Some malware puts its own version in the User-Agent, so collecting User-Agents at the perimeter quickly sketches the extent of an infection and its version distribution. Remember, as lesson 2.1 showed, that they can be faked.
  • Basic authentication. Every request carries the account in Base64 (lesson 2.1, section 6.5), so over plain HTTP the account can be obtained at any point while the subject uses the site. A strong identity clue, and sensitive information.
  • URI records. Search terms, clicked results, form submissions and API calls show up in URIs. For malware, a network analyst and a malware analyst working together can learn which commands were exchanged.

And the starting point of lesson 2.1 was that all of this remains on the wire and in logs even after private mode, portable apps and disk encryption have wiped it from the endpoint. The Date header becomes an independent clock for refining the sequence of events.

docs.title: 6. How to use this in real investigations
docs.text:
1. Pair every request with its response. Write not "they accessed it" but "they accessed it and got a 200 (or a 403)".
  2. Read status codes as a flow. Look for a storm of 404s from one address, a 200 after 500s, success after 401s.
  3. Read 304 and 206 carefully. 304 means no content was exchanged at that moment; 206 means only part was.
  4. State which layer a size belongs to. Compressed on-the-wire size, or decompressed size.
  5. Align clocks with Date. Measure the differences between the capture box, servers and endpoints, and record the corrected values and the method in the report.
  6. Find the start and end of redirect chains. Intermediate addresses are material for blocking and threat intelligence.
  7. Save unusual responses as fingerprints. Reason phrases, header order, unfamiliar X- headers. But don't conclude from one fingerprint alone.

docs.title: 7. Summary
docs.text:
• The response tells you how a request was actually handled. The status line is version, code and reason phrase.
  • The reason phrase is up to the server, so even one byte (a space after OK) becomes a fingerprint (tested: one display filter matched only that response). [Changed] HTTP/2 and 3 have no reason phrase.
  • Status codes come in five families. [Correction] 400 is Bad Request; after a 302 the method may change to GET, and 307/308 keep it. 304 means no content was exchanged at that moment.
  • A storm of 404s from one address suggests reconnaissance; a 200 after 500s can signal successful injection (a hand-made reconnaissance flow: eight 404s in 0.06 seconds).
  • [Correction] HTTP/1.1 keeps connections alive by default, so one stream can carry several requests (confirmed: three redirect requests in one stream).
  • Server is also a self-declared name. Content-Length is the on-the-wire size, so with compression it differs from the decompressed size (78 bytes versus 1,106).
  • Date is an independent clock; comparing it with packet times measured a 437-second skew.
  • Find both the start and the end of Location chains.

docs.title: Review questions
docs.text:
Question 1. (Status line) A response's first line is HTTP/1.1 200 Everything is fine, nothing to see here. How does a browser handle it, and what might an investigator consider?

Answer and explanation

The browser ignores the reason phrase and treats it as a normal response from the 200 alone. The standard says clients must ignore the reason phrase and servers can write anything, so nothing is formally wrong. For the investigator, the unusual reason phrase is the clue. Common web server software uses the standard phrase (OK), so this may be the trace of a hand-built server or a particular tool. Search past pcaps with a display filter (http.response.phrase contains "nothing to see") for other servers returning the same phrase, and look for what they have in common (address ranges, certificates, timing patterns).

Question 2. (Common misconception) A proxy log has GET /reports/q3-financials.xlsx 304 at 2026-11-03 14:10. Can you write "this employee downloaded this file at 14:10"?

Answer and explanation

No. A 304 (Not Modified) has no body. At 14:10 only "is my copy still valid?" was exchanged, and the server answered "it hasn't changed, use what you have". So the employee's browser had already received the file some time before 14:10 and held it in cache. To find when it was first received, search back for a 200 response to the same address, and check the endpoint's browser cache too. Use 14:10 only as grounds for "they probably reopened the file (from cache) at that time".

Question 3. (Corrected content) A web app log shows POST /upload 307 followed by POST /storage/upload 201. How many times did the client's uploaded file probably cross the wire, and how would it differ with a 302?

Answer and explanation

307 means "resend to another address keeping the method and body", so the client most likely sent the POST containing the same file to /storage/upload once more: the same body crossed the wire twice. Be careful not to double-count upload volume (the actual data is one copy). With a 302, most real browsers would change the method to GET and re-request without the body, so the second request wouldn't have carried the file. Clients can differ, though, so confirm from the second request's method and size.

Question 4. (Interpretation) In three minutes, one external address sent 1,200 GETs to the same web server: 1,196 got 404, 3 got 403 and 1 got 200. What do you check first?

Answer and explanation

The 1,196 404s are the classic shape of reconnaissance trying name after name (section 3.3). But the most important are the single 200 and the three 403s. ① The URI and response size of the request that got 200: did the attacker actually find what they were looking for (a config file, a backup, an admin screen)? ② The URIs of the 403s: resources that exist but are blocked, which told the attacker "there's something here". ③ Whether that address later came back and re-requested the resource that got 200, and whether other addresses requested the same resource. Use the 404 list itself as material showing what the attacker was after (which software, which files).

Question 5. (Calculation) In a pcap captured on a user's PC, the Date headers of three unrelated web servers are ahead of the packet times by exactly 3 min 2 s, 3 min 1 s and 3 min 3 s respectively. Which clock is probably wrong, and how should other evidence from this PC be handled?

Answer and explanation

If three unrelated servers are all consistently about three minutes ahead, the wrong clock is most likely not the servers but the PC that stamped the packet times: its clock is about 3 min 2 s slow (servers are usually NTP-synchronised). So when matching this PC's evidence (this pcap's times, its event logs, file times) with other evidence, correct by about +182 seconds. In the report, record the original times, the correction and its basis (the comparison with three servers' Date values). Differences of about a second are natural, given the gap between when the server generated the response and when the packet was stamped, and Date's one-second resolution.

Question 6. (Application) A proxy log records a response as 2,048 bytes, while Zeek's http.log records the same response's body as 15,320 bytes. Is one of them wrong?

Answer and explanation

Not necessarily. If the response was compressed (Content-Encoding: gzip etc.), the proxy log records the on-the-wire size sent to the client (possibly including headers, lesson 1.3), while Zeek's response_body_len records the decompressed body size (lesson 2.8). In this lab, a response with Content-Length: 78 was 1,106 bytes decompressed. Text compresses well, so a sevenfold difference isn't strange. First confirm the two records are the same response by time and URI, check the response's Content-Encoding header, and state in the report which layer's size you're quoting.

Question 7. (Interpretation) An employee's PC opened an unfamiliar short link, and at the end of a 301 → 302 → 302 → 200 chain an executable was downloaded. What goes on the block list, and what do you investigate further?

Answer and explanation

Record the hosts of every step of the chain, and put the intermediate steps and the final delivery server into block lists and threat intelligence. The URL-shortening service at the start may be a legitimate service, so block that short link, not the whole service. Investigate further: ① the start of the chain: where did the employee get the short link (email, messenger, another page's Referer)? ② query values in intermediate steps (like campaign identifiers, they may reveal who sent the link); ③ the final file's hash and content (the methods of lesson 1.13); ④ other PCs that opened addresses in the same chain (scoping, lesson 1.11).

Question 8. (Common misconception) "The response says Server: Microsoft-IIS/10.0, so this C2 server is a Windows server." Explain the problem with this judgement.

Answer and explanation

The Server header is a value the server declares for itself, and anything can be written there. This lab's server was written in Python but declared Apache/2.4.29 (Ubuntu). An attacker may imitate a common value to look like a normal server, or a front-end CDN or proxy may have changed it. To estimate the real server, look at several characteristics together: ① the order of its response headers and its combination of default headers, ② the look of its error pages, ③ its TLS certificate and TLS handshake fingerprints (Part 5), ④ other services at the same address. Even then, keep open the conclusion "it may be a server imitating IIS".

Question 9. (Changed conditions) You put the "reason-phrase fingerprint" detection rule from section 2.1 on the organisation's packet sensors, and it hasn't fired once in a year. Can you conclude the attacker is gone? Give possible reasons.

Answer and explanation

No. ① The attack tool may have fixed the quirk (the source material's example was fixed). ② If the traffic is HTTPS, sensors can't see the status line. ③ With HTTP/2 or HTTP/3, there's no reason phrase at all (the [Changed] box in section 2.1). ④ The sensors may not sit where that traffic passes (lesson 1.11). Fingerprint-based detection is "a strong clue when it fires, silent when it doesn't", so don't conclude absence from its silence. Record each detection rule's creation date, basis and applicable conditions (plain HTTP/1.x) alongside it.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Tools used in this environment: a practice server written in Python 3, curl 8.5.0, tcpdump 4.99.4, tshark 4.2.2. Outputs were obtained on 2026-11-05.
  • IETF, RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics. Section 15 (status codes; 15.4.3 for 302 and method change; 15.4.8–15.4.9 for 307 and 308; 15.5.1 for 400 Bad Request), section 6.6.1 (Date), section 8.8.3 (ETag), section 10.2.2 (Location), section 10.2.4 (Server).
  • IETF, RFC 9112: HTTP/1.1, section 4 (status line and reason phrase), section 9.3 (persistent connections by default).
  • IETF, RFC 9113: HTTP/2, section 8.3.2 (the :status response pseudo-header; no reason phrase).
  • IETF, RFC 6585: Additional HTTP Status Codes (429, 511, etc.), RFC 9111: HTTP Caching.

About this page

A personal study note, rewritten in my own words from several learning resources. The practice server and requests are my own, and the scenarios are hypothetical.

docs.title: 2.9 — Lab Guide: DNS Profiling, Anomalies and Scoping
2.9 — Lab Guide: DNS Profiling, Anomalies and Scoping
docs.text:
Scope of this lesson

  • Drawing a segment's "normal" from one day of Zeek dns.log: who asks which resolver, how much, and for which types
  • Finding anomalies: resolver bypass, NXDOMAIN surges and DGAs, TXT tunnelling, a C2 waking up from 127.0.0.1, look-alike domains
  • Separating them from everyday noise: the mail server's PTRs, typos, browsers' interception-detection queries
  • Scoping: starting from the names you found to locate other infected PCs and infection times
  • Writing results up as facts, hypotheses, evidence still needed and observation limits

Lab environment and notation

(Actual output) came from Zeek 9.0.1 (official Docker image), jq 1.7 and GNU coreutils in this environment. The lab pcap office-dns.pcap was assembled by me with dnspython to imitate one day (2026-11-03, UTC) of DNS in an office segment (94,324 packets). The collection point is between clients and the internal resolver (10.10.0.53) — lesson 2.6's "inside vantage point" — and the resolver's caching (TTLs counting down) is imitated too. Addresses are private and documentation addresses, domains are example domains, and all anomalous behaviour is invented for practice. Remember that assembled data is simpler and cleaner than the real thing.

docs.title: 1. The situation
docs.text:
(Hypothetical) A security appliance raised a vague alert: "a PC in the office segment is talking to an unknown outside address", without saying which PC or which address. A sensor in front of the internal resolver holds one day of pcap. Since DNS starts almost every connection (lesson 2.6), the goal is to profile that day through DNS, find what departs from normal, and from there scope the incident (which PCs, since when).

It's the same idea as lesson 2.4's HTTP profiling. Picture a local post office clerk. Knowing who usually sends letters where, they'd notice someone suddenly posting hundreds of letters a day to addresses that don't exist (a DGA), someone writing cipher-like text densely on the back of postcards (tunnelling), or someone skipping the post office to use another town's postbox (resolver bypass). Where it breaks: in DNS, "the letter's content" (the query name) can itself carry information, and when the post office answers from memory (the cache), nothing goes outside at all.

docs.title: 2. Lab guide
docs.text:
Objectives

  1. Summarise each host's "normal" from a day of DNS (resolver, volume, types, response codes).
  2. Find departures from normal and separate them from everyday noise.
  3. Scope from the names and addresses found (other PCs, start times).
  4. Report as facts, hypotheses, evidence still needed and limits.

Preparation

  • Zeek (or a ready-made dns.log), jq, sort, uniq
  • The lab pcap office-dns.pcap. The only lead is a vague alert that "some PC is odd".

Hash it on receipt and produce JSON logs with Zeek. The assembled pcap has correct checksums (no need for lesson 2.8's -C).

sha256sum office-dns.pcap
zeek -r office-dns.pcap LogAscii::use_json=T
jq -s 'map(.ts) | [min, max] | map(todate)' dns.log
jq -s 'length' dns.log

(Actual output)

9519a551b4fb32efb03b45894076df3b8ee97a28fce1cf943cda0821d047f2d0  office-dns.pcap
[
  "2026-11-03T00:00:01Z",
  "2026-11-04T00:00:25Z"
]
47162

A full day, 47,162 query/response records. -s (slurp) reads all lines into one array, used here for the overall min, max and count. It loads the whole file into memory, so be careful with big logs. I didn't record a hash of dns.log: as lesson 2.8 showed, uids change with every run, so the log file's hash differs even for the same pcap. As evidence, record the pcap's hash together with the processing conditions (Zeek 9.0.1, base scripts, JSON).

Figure 2-1. Order of this lab (top to bottom; each step looks again, from a different angle, at what the previous steps didn't filter out)

flowchart TD
    A["Step 1 · Who asks which resolver<br/>finding bypass"] --> B["Step 2 · Volume and types per host<br/>the normal shape"]
    B --> C["Step 3 · Response codes<br/>where NXDOMAINs pile up"]
    C --> D["Step 4 · Looking into the DGA<br/>rhythm and the single success"]
    D --> E["Step 5 · Distinct names and length<br/>tunnelling"]
    E --> F["Step 6 · A name's history<br/>the C2 waking up"]
    F --> G["Step 7 · Scoping<br/>from names to PCs"]
    G --> H["Step 8 · Look-alike domains"]
    H --> I["Facts · hypotheses · evidence needed · limits"]

docs.title: 3. Step 1: who asks which resolver
docs.text:
With the architecture from lesson 2.7, section 1, every PC should ask only the internal resolver 10.10.0.53. Count the responders (id.resp_h).

jq -r '."id.resp_h"' dns.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
jq -r 'select(."id.resp_h"!="10.10.0.53") | ."id.orig_h"' dns.log | sort | uniq -c
jq -r 'select(."id.resp_h"=="192.0.2.53") | .ts|todate' dns.log | sed -n '1p;$p'

(Actual output)

  47122 10.10.0.53
     40 192.0.2.53
     40 10.10.9.9
2026-11-03T19:00:02Z
2026-11-03T19:58:53Z

One PC, 10.10.9.9, asked the outside resolver 192.0.2.53 directly, 40 times between 19:00 and 19:59. That also means firewall policy didn't stop it. These queries don't appear in the internal resolver's records, so looking only at resolver logs would have missed them. They're visible because this sensor sits in front of the resolver.

Keep the interpretation open: a personal VPN, a hand-set DNS server, or malware evading internal controls. Look at what it asked too (select(."id.resp_h"=="192.0.2.53") | .query); in this data they were ordinary work site names. Record the bypass itself and revisit it during scoping in step 7.

docs.title: 4. Step 2: volume and type mix per host
docs.text:
Look at how many queries each host made and how the types mix. jq's group_by builds a per-host table in one go.

jq -s -r 'group_by(."id.orig_h")
  | map({h: .[0]."id.orig_h", n: length,
         t: (group_by(.qtype_name) | map({(.[0].qtype_name): length}) | add)})
  | sort_by(-.n) | .[:6][] | "\(.h)\t\(.n)\t\(.t)"' dns.log

Piece by piece:

  • -s reads everything as one array; group_by(."id.orig_h") makes groups per originating address (an array of arrays).
  • For each group, build {h: address, n: count, t: counts per type}. t regroups the group by qtype_name, makes {"A": count} pieces and merges them with add.
  • sort_by(-.n) sorts by count, descending; .[:6][] takes the first six one by one and prints them as strings.

(Actual output)

10.10.0.25  3436    {"MX":644,"PTR":2148,"TXT":644}
10.10.4.21  2381    {"A":1466,"AAAA":470,"HTTPS":445}
10.10.7.8   2001    {"A":779,"AAAA":473,"HTTPS":491,"TXT":258}
10.10.2.30  1970    {"A":967,"AAAA":506,"HTTPS":497}
10.10.1.26  1885    {"A":828,"AAAA":523,"HTTPS":534}
10.10.1.18  1856    {"A":823,"AAAA":501,"HTTPS":532}

How to read it:

  • 10.10.0.25: mostly PTR, with MX and TXT. That's lesson 2.6, section 3's mail server shape: a reverse lookup for each new connection, plus MX and SPF (TXT) checks for outgoing mail. In this segment that shape is normal (confirm it really is the mail server from the asset inventory).
  • User PCs (10.10.1.x and others): A, AAAA and HTTPS in similar proportions, lesson 2.6's user segment shape.
  • 10.10.4.21: noticeably more A than other PCs (1,466 versus the 800s), with similar AAAA and HTTPS. Something is asking for A records on its own; step 3 looks at it.
  • 10.10.7.8: a user PC with 258 TXT queries. No other user PC in the segment asks for TXT.

Counting only hosts that ask for TXT makes it clearer.

jq -r 'select(.qtype_name=="TXT") | ."id.orig_h"' dns.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn

(Actual output)

    644 10.10.0.25
    258 10.10.7.8

Only the mail server (SPF checks) and 10.10.7.8. A user PC asking for TXT already departs from this segment's normal. Step 5 looks at it.

docs.title: 5. Step 3: response codes, where NXDOMAINs pile up
docs.text:
jq -r 'select(.rcode_name=="NXDOMAIN") | ."id.orig_h"' dns.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -8

(Actual output)

    581 10.10.4.21
    429 10.10.0.25
    225 10.10.5.17
     17 10.10.1.12
     12 10.10.2.30
     12 10.10.1.15
     12 10.10.1.11
     11 10.10.1.29

Three hosts stand out; the rest have 10–20 or so. First set aside everyday NXDOMAINs.

  • The mail server's failed PTRs: of 10.10.0.25's 2,148 PTR queries, 1,719 were NOERROR and 429 NXDOMAIN (counted with select(."id.orig_h"=="10.10.0.25" and .qtype_name=="PTR") | .rcode_name). Many addresses have no reverse record, so a mail server's NXDOMAINs are usually normal.
  • Typos: docs.exmaple.com 66, exmaple.com 47 and wwww.example.com 45 times, from various user PCs. Noise made by human fingers.
  • Three dotless single-word names: 13 PCs each asked for exactly three, around the start of the working day.
jq -r 'select((.query|contains("."))|not) | [(.ts|strftime("%H:%M:%S")), ."id.orig_h", .query, .rcode_name] | @tsv' dns.log | head -6

(Actual output)

08:35:04    10.10.1.25  olwjlphi    NXDOMAIN
08:35:04    10.10.1.25  gcanpgsm    NXDOMAIN
08:35:04    10.10.1.25  imtqpbfbv   NXDOMAIN
08:35:46    10.10.1.11  bbbdldnwessgw   NXDOMAIN
08:35:46    10.10.1.11  pxfcnlkjycme    NXDOMAIN
08:35:46    10.10.1.11  poigwxrdl   NXDOMAIN

Three random names of 7–15 letters within the same second, just before that PC's first activity: lesson 2.7, section 4.3's browser interception-detection queries (assume these PCs have the check enabled by enterprise policy). They look random, but we don't classify them as DGA.

@tsv turns an array into one tab-separated line, and strftime("%H:%M:%S") converts Unix time to an hours:minutes:seconds string in UTC.

Setting those three aside leaves 10.10.4.21 (581) and 10.10.5.17 (225).

docs.title: 6. Step 4: looking into the DGA
docs.text:
Look at 10.10.4.21's NXDOMAIN names and times.

jq -r 'select(."id.orig_h"=="10.10.4.21" and .rcode_name=="NXDOMAIN") | .query' dns.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -5
jq -r 'select(."id.orig_h"=="10.10.4.21" and .rcode_name=="NXDOMAIN") | .ts | strftime("%M")' dns.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -3

(Actual output)

     24 zlonpnqfgvxwg.com
     24 zgijpsilzextwebb.com
     24 zehzobjyazd.com
     24 upgshfkgdnqje.com
     24 ugcuulcwzj.com
    576 07
      3 18
      1 49

Each name appears exactly 24 times a day, and 576 of the 581 NXDOMAINs fall at 7 minutes past every hour. Some program asks the same list of names in turn at :07 every hour. With the names' shape (10–16 random lowercase letters + .com), this fits lesson 2.7, section 4's DGA hypothesis well; people don't look up 24 nonexistent domains at :07 every hour.

If it's a DGA, one name on the list should succeed. Look at NOERROR answers the same PC got at the same minute (:07).

jq -r 'select(."id.orig_h"=="10.10.4.21" and .rcode_name=="NOERROR" and (.ts|strftime("%M"))=="07") | .query' dns.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -5

(Actual output)

     24 owxdarkhbvi.com
      9 news.example.net
      6 update.example.com
      6 telemetry.example.net
      5 time.example.org

Only owxdarkhbvi.com succeeded 24 times, once at :07 every hour; the rest are sites a person happened to open during that minute. The 09:07 batch shows the order.

jq -r 'select(."id.orig_h"=="10.10.4.21" and (.ts|strftime("%H:%M"))=="09:07") | [(.ts|strftime("%H:%M:%S")), .query, .rcode_name] | @tsv' dns.log | sed -n '15,20p'

(Actual output)

09:07:13    brugcsbfehzqw.com   NXDOMAIN
09:07:13    sdpdxazvjckhiq.com  NXDOMAIN
09:07:14    zgijpsilzextwebb.com    NXDOMAIN
09:07:15    owxdarkhbvi.com NOERROR
09:07:15    fljysaaludeuen.com  NXDOMAIN
09:07:16    szuvrwofhhw.com NXDOMAIN

One success sits among the NXDOMAINs. Its answer (select(.query=="owxdarkhbvi.com") | .answers) was 203.0.113.99. That address is likely the alert's "unknown outside address", which leads to the next evidence: 10.10.4.21 → 203.0.113.99 in firewall and NetFlow records.

Why does it keep asking after succeeding?

The program in this data asks the whole list every hour even after a success. Real DGA malware varies: it may stop on success, shuffle the order, or ask only part of a daily pool of thousands. Don't decide by a single number such as "more than N NXDOMAINs means DGA"; look at repetition of the same names, a fixed rhythm and the success among them together.

docs.title: 7. Step 5: distinct names and length — tunnelling
docs.text:
Now look at 10.10.7.8's TXT queries from step 2. DNS tunnelling (lesson 2.7) carries data in query names, so ① the number of distinct names under one domain grows sharply, and ② names get longer.

Distinct names per domain (treating a name's last two labels as the "domain")

jq -r '.query | split(".") | "\(.[-2:]|join("."))\t\(join("."))"' dns.log | sort -u | cut -f1 | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -6

split(".") breaks the name into labels, .[-2:] rejoins the last two as the "domain", and the "domain tab full name" pairs are deduplicated with sort -u and counted per domain.

(Actual output)

    503 in-addr.arpa
    262 example.net
     11 example.com
      3 example.org
      2 exmaple.com
      2 corp.example

in-addr.arpa is the mail server's reverse lookups, so high is normal. But 262 under example.net can't be explained by the usual handful (news, cdn, telemetry and so on).

[Caution] "The last two labels" is an approximation. For top-level domains where two labels form one unit, such as co.kr or co.uk, example.co.kr gets grouped as co.kr. In real investigations, use a tool that applies the Public Suffix List to get the "registrable domain".

Name length per host

jq -s -r 'group_by(."id.orig_h") | map({h: .[0]."id.orig_h", avg: ((map(.query|length)|add)/length), max: (map(.query|length)|max)}) | sort_by(-.max) | .[:4][] | "\(.h)\tavg=\(.avg|floor)\tmax=\(.max)"' dns.log
jq -r 'select(."id.orig_h"=="10.10.7.8" and .qtype_name=="TXT") | [(.ts|strftime("%H:%M:%S")), .query, (.answers|tostring)] | @tsv' dns.log | head -3

(Actual output)

10.10.7.8   avg=23  max=66
10.10.0.25  avg=20  max=27
10.10.1.11  avg=17  max=21
10.10.1.12  avg=17  max=21
13:20:00    jbhvgvb5izeu4lkqimwtaob3kvjukur5njvws3j3kezsaytv.0.t.example.net    ["TXT 8 rlrpw7ml"]
13:20:03    mrtwk5bamrzgcztuebzg653tebitgidcovsgozluebsheylg.1.t.example.net    ["TXT 8 7ak7gela"]
13:20:07    oqqhe33xomqfcmzamj2wiz3foqqgi4tbmz2ca4tpo5zsaujt.2.t.example.net    ["TXT 8 cayvlwnv"]

10.10.7.8 has the longest names, up to 66 characters. They look like [48 characters].[sequence].t.example.net, and the first label uses only a–z and 2–7, which looks like base32. A sequence number climbing 0, 1, 2… is the shape of chunked data sent in order. The TXT answers are short random strings, like acknowledgements. The 258 queries ran from 13:20:00 to 13:33:59.

I joined the first labels in sequence order and decoded them as base32.

jq -r 'select(."id.orig_h"=="10.10.7.8" and .qtype_name=="TXT") | .query | split(".") | "\(.[1])\t\(.[0])"' dns.log \
  | sort -n -u | head -43 | cut -f2 | tr -d '\n' > chunks.txt
python3 -c "import base64; s=open('chunks.txt').read().upper(); print(b''.join(base64.b32decode(c+'='*(-len(c)%8)) for c in [s[i:i+48] for i in range(0,len(s),48)])[:90])"

(Actual output)

b'HOST=FIN-PC-08;USER=jkim;Q3 budget draft rows Q3 budget draft rows Q3 budget draft rows Q3'

Out came a PC name, a username, and what looks like a "Q3 budget draft" (invented content). The sequence numbers went from 0 to 257, but every 43rd (0, 43, 86…) carried the identical chunk again: the same data sent six times over (the command above used head -43 to join only the first round). The decoded first round was 1,285 bytes. When you can decode it, you can show directly "what left"; real tunnelling tools often add encryption or compression, so it won't always decode. Then estimate the size from volume (distinct names × name length).

docs.title: 8. Step 6: a name's history — the C2 waking up
docs.text:
To find lesson 2.7, section 2.1's "parking" trick, check whether a name's answer changed. A quick way is to find names that had more than one answer during the day, one of them 127.0.0.1.

jq -r 'select(.answers != null and (.answers | index("127.0.0.1"))) | .query' dns.log | sort | uniq -c
jq -r 'select(.query=="sync.example.org") | .answers[]' dns.log | sort | uniq -c

(Actual output)

     30 sync.example.org
     19 198.51.100.7
     30 127.0.0.1

sync.example.org had two answers during the day: 127.0.0.1 and 198.51.100.7. In time order:

jq -r 'select(.query=="sync.example.org") | [(.ts|strftime("%H:%M:%S")), ."id.orig_h", (.answers|join(",")), (.TTLs|map(tostring)|join(","))] | @tsv' dns.log | sed -n '25,34p'

(Actual output)

12:00:11    10.10.2.30  127.0.0.1   1799.0
12:30:11    10.10.2.30  127.0.0.1   3600.0
13:00:12    10.10.2.30  127.0.0.1   1798.0
13:30:13    10.10.2.30  127.0.0.1   3600.0
14:00:12    10.10.2.30  127.0.0.1   1800.0
14:30:12    10.10.2.30  127.0.0.1   0.0
14:31:09    10.10.4.22  198.51.100.7    300.0
15:00:12    10.10.2.30  198.51.100.7    300.0
15:30:13    10.10.2.30  198.51.100.7    300.0
16:00:13    10.10.2.30  198.51.100.7    300.0

10.10.2.30 asked for this name every 30 minutes (48 times a day), and from 14:31 the answer changed to 198.51.100.7 (TTL 300). That's a parked C2 waking up.

Narrowing the change time with TTLs. TTL 3600 means the resolver freshly fetched the answer; 1799, 1800 and 0 mean answers from cache (lesson 2.6, section 9). So:

  • At 13:30:13 the resolver freshly fetched an answer that was still 127.0.0.1.
  • The 14:30:12 answer was an old one with 1 second left in cache, so it says nothing about whether the record had already changed by then.
  • At 14:31:09 another PC (10.10.4.22) asked, and the freshly fetched answer was 198.51.100.7.

So all you can say is that the record changed on the authoritative side after 13:30:13 and before 14:31:09. This inside vantage point can't narrow it further; you'd need captures outside the resolver, the resolver's own records, or an external passive DNS service. Also note that because of caching, 10.10.2.30 may have received the new address up to nearly an hour after the real change.

docs.title: 9. Step 7: scoping — from names to PCs
docs.text:
Starting from the "bad names" found so far, find other PCs that asked for the same names. This is what lesson 2.7, section 3.2 meant by "using DNS records to scope the infection and find newly infected hosts".

for n in owxdarkhbvi.com sync.example.org; do echo "$n:"; jq -r --arg n $n 'select(.query==$n) | ."id.orig_h"' dns.log | sort | uniq -c; done
jq -r 'select(.query|endswith(".t.example.net")) | ."id.orig_h"' dns.log | sort | uniq -c

(Actual output)

owxdarkhbvi.com:
     24 10.10.4.21
      9 10.10.5.17
sync.example.org:
     48 10.10.2.30
      1 10.10.4.22
    258 10.10.7.8
  • 10.10.5.17 also asked for the DGA's successful name, 9 times — the same PC that stood out in step 3 with 225 NXDOMAINs.
  • 10.10.4.22 asked for the woken C2 sync.example.org once, right after the change (14:31).
  • Only 10.10.7.8 used the tunnelling domain.

Search with the whole list, not just the successful name. A DGA's successful name changes daily, so put the full list 10.10.4.21 asked at :07 into a file and find PCs that asked for any name on it.

jq -r 'select(."id.orig_h"=="10.10.4.21" and .rcode_name=="NXDOMAIN" and (.ts|strftime("%M"))=="07") | .query' dns.log | sort -u > dga24.txt
jq -r --rawfile d dga24.txt '($d | split("\n") | map(select(length>0))) as $names
  | select(.query as $q | $names | index($q)) | ."id.orig_h"' dns.log | sort | uniq -c
jq -r --rawfile d dga24.txt '($d | split("\n") | map(select(length>0))) as $names
  | select(."id.orig_h"=="10.10.5.17" and (.query as $q | $names | index($q))) | .ts|todate' dns.log | head -1
  • --rawfile d dga24.txt: pass the whole file content as the string $d.
  • split("\n") | map(select(length>0)): turn it into an array of lines, dropping empty ones.
  • .query as $q | $names | index($q): the position if this record's name is on the list (truthy), null if not (falsy).

(Actual output)

    576 10.10.4.21
    216 10.10.5.17
2026-11-03T15:07:07Z

10.10.5.17 started asking for the same list at 15:07:07. Before that (09:00–15:05) it asked only for ordinary work sites. So this PC may have been infected around 15:05–15:07 (hypothesis: check web access, email and USB use just before then in endpoint records). Searching by the name list catches even freshly infected PCs that haven't yet asked for the successful name.

Figure 9-1. What this lab found and how it connects (four groups, top to bottom; arrows mean "asked for")

flowchart TD
    D1["DGA list of 24<br/>success: owxdarkhbvi.com<br/>→ 203.0.113.99"] --> P1["10.10.4.21<br/>all day, :07 every hour"]
    D1 --> P2["10.10.5.17<br/>from 15:07 (new infection?)"]
    P1 ~~~ D2["sync.example.org<br/>127.0.0.1 → 198.51.100.7<br/>(changed 13:30–14:31)"]
    D2 --> P3["10.10.2.30<br/>every 30 minutes"]
    D2 --> P4["10.10.4.22<br/>once at 14:31"]
    P3 ~~~ D3["*.t.example.net<br/>258 TXT queries, base32 data"]
    D3 --> P5["10.10.7.8<br/>13:20–13:34"]
    P5 ~~~ D4["outside resolver 192.0.2.53<br/>(bypass)"]
    D4 --> P6["10.10.9.9<br/>19:00–19:59"]

How to read it: four groups from top to bottom. The first box in each group is an odd name (or destination) found in this day; the boxes its arrows point to are the PCs that asked for it. Two arrows from one name mean the same thing happened on two PCs. There are no lines between groups: whether different names are related (the same attacker?) can't be told from this data alone.

docs.title: 10. Step 8: look-alike domains
docs.text:
Finally, find names starting with xn-- and decode them (lesson 2.7, section 7).

jq -r 'select(.query|startswith("xn--")) | [(.ts|todate), ."id.orig_h", .query, (.answers|join(","))] | @tsv' dns.log
python3 -c "n='xn--crp-sed.example'.encode().decode('idna'); print(n, [hex(ord(c)) for c in n[:4]])"

(Actual output)

2026-11-03T10:12:04Z    10.10.1.19  xn--crp-sed.example 203.0.113.140
cоrp.example ['0x63', '0x43e', '0x72', '0x70']

Decoded, it's cоrp.example, but the second letter is Cyrillic о (U+043E), not Latin o (0x6f). It's a look-alike that renders identically to our internal domain corp.example (seen in step 2's sites as intranet.corp.example and portal.corp.example). 10.10.1.19 asked once at 10:12:04 and got 203.0.113.140. Suspect a click on a phishing link, and check mail records just before that time and the HTTP/HTTPS connections afterwards (proxy logs). Include in scoping whether other PCs asked for the same name (none did in this data).

docs.title: 11. Writing it up
docs.text:
• Observations (facts):
    • On 2026-11-03, this collection point (in front of the internal resolver) saw 47,162 DNS query/response records.
    • All day, at :07 every hour, 10.10.4.21 asked in turn for 24 random-looking .com names; only owxdarkhbvi.com succeeded each time, answering 203.0.113.99 (576 NXDOMAINs).
    • From 15:07:07, 10.10.5.17 began asking for the same list on the same rhythm (216 NXDOMAINs, 9 successes).
    • 10.10.2.30 asked for sync.example.org every 30 minutes. Answers were 127.0.0.1 up to the one freshly fetched at 13:30:13, and 198.51.100.7 (TTL 300) from the one freshly fetched at 14:31:09. 10.10.4.22 also asked once at 14:31:09 and got the new address.
    • From 13:20:00 to 13:33:59, 10.10.7.8 sent 258 TXT queries to *.t.example.net. Joining the first labels in sequence and decoding as base32 yields a PC name, a username and what looks like document content.
    • From 19:00 to 19:59, 10.10.9.9 asked 192.0.2.53, not the internal resolver, directly, 40 times.
    • At 10:12:04, 10.10.1.19 asked for xn--crp-sed.example (Cyrillic о), resembling the internal domain, and got 203.0.113.140.
  • Interpretation (hypotheses):
    • 10.10.4.21 and 10.10.5.17 are infected with the same DGA-based malware, and the day's C2 is 203.0.113.99. 10.10.5.17 may have been newly infected around 15:05–15:07.
    • sync.example.org is a C2 normally parked on 127.0.0.1, woken between about 1:30 and 2:30 p.m. 10.10.2.30 and 10.10.4.22 may carry its implant.
    • Data left 10.10.7.8 through DNS tunnelling.
    • Whether these activities are one attack or separate events is not yet known.
  • Evidence still needed:
    • Connections to 203.0.113.99, 198.51.100.7 and 203.0.113.140 in firewall, NetFlow and proxy records (which PCs, when, how much).
    • Endpoint records on those PCs: the querying processes (Sysmon 22), 10.10.5.17's activity around 15:05, 10.10.1.19's mail around 10:12.
    • Records outside the resolver or external passive DNS (the exact time sync.example.org changed; its history on other days).
    • pcaps from other days (when the DGA and the 30-minute rhythm began).
    • The user and configuration of 10.10.9.9 (why it bypassed the resolver).
  • Observation limits:
    • One day, DNS at this collection point only. Encrypted DNS such as DoH (lesson 2.7, section 6) isn't visible.
    • Caching can make PCs receive answers later than the real change, and queries the resolver answered from cache never go outside.
    • "Domain" grouping approximated by the last two labels.
    • This data was assembled for practice.

docs.title: 12. Summary
docs.text:
• I summarised a day of dns.log with jq by resolver, host, type and response code to draw the segment's normal, building a per-host table in one go with -s and group_by.
  • I set aside everyday noise first: the mail server's PTRs and their NXDOMAINs, human typos, and browsers' three random single-word names at start-up.
  • Found directly: resolver bypass (10.10.9.9), a DGA (:07 every hour, one success in 24, 10.10.4.21), a new infection by the same DGA (10.10.5.17, from 15:07), TXT tunnelling (10.10.7.8, decoded from base32), a parked C2 waking up (sync.example.org, changed between 13:30 and 14:31), and a look-alike domain (10.10.1.19, Cyrillic о).
  • Scoping works backwards from names (or name lists) to PCs, and searching by the whole list catches even freshly infected PCs.
  • TTLs separate fresh answers (original value) from cached ones (counted down), which lets you state the window in which a record changed.
  • Results were written up as facts, hypotheses, evidence needed and limits.

docs.title: Review questions
docs.text:
Question 1. (Basics) In step 3, 10.10.0.25 had many NXDOMAINs (429). Why didn't we suspect a DGA? Under what conditions should we?

Answer and explanation

In step 2, 10.10.0.25 had the mail server shape (PTR, MX and TXT only), and all its NXDOMAINs came from PTRs (addresses without reverse records). Missing reverse records are common, so a mail server's PTR failures are usually normal. Conditions that should raise suspicion, for example: ① the mail server asking in bulk for random-looking names via A queries; ② its NXDOMAIN ratio rising well above its own normal (about 20% of PTRs in this data); ③ it repeatedly asking a particular domain for TXT or NULL records it doesn't usually request. Compare against "that host's normal".

Question 2. (Changed conditions) If this sensor had sat outside the resolver (on the Internet side) instead of in front of it, which of this lab's results would change or become impossible?

Answer and explanation

① You couldn't identify PCs. Outside, every query comes from the resolver (lesson 2.6, section 7.2), so conclusions such as "10.10.4.21 and 10.10.5.17" or "10.10.7.8" would be impossible. ② Caching reduces counts. The DGA's successful name has TTL 300, so it only goes outside when the cache expires, and two PCs asking may look like one lookup. ③ With QNAME minimisation, root and TLD servers see only part of the names. ④ Conversely, the resolver bypass (10.10.9.9 → 192.0.2.53) is visible to an outside sensor too, and stands out even more because the source is an internal PC rather than the resolver. ⑤ For sync.example.org's change time, the resolver's fresh lookups (13:30, 14:31) leave outside packets, so you could still state the same window.

Question 3. (Common misconception) "Step 5 found 262 distinct names under example.net, so block all of example.net." What's the problem?

Answer and explanation

example.net also covers names this segment uses legitimately (news.example.net, cdn.example.net, telemetry.example.net and others). The rise in distinct names came from t.example.net beneath it; blocking the whole domain would cut off work sites too. And "the last two labels" is an approximation that may not match the real registrable domain. Respond by ① narrowing to t.example.net (or the real registrable domain), ② sinkholing that zone at the resolver, and ③ finding other PCs that asked for it. In a real case where a tunnelling zone sits under a big service's domain like example.net, also check whether that service's free hosting or dynamic DNS was abused.

Question 4. (Interpretation) In step 6, the answer 10.10.2.30 received at 14:30:12 was 127.0.0.1 with TTL 0.0. What can and can't you tell from that line?

Answer and explanation

Can: with TTL 0, it's an old answer from the resolver's cache, about to expire (within a second). That cache entry was freshly fetched at 13:30:13 (TTL 3600 then). Can't: whether the authoritative record had already changed by 14:30:12, because the resolver answered from cache without asking outside. So the change can only be placed "after 13:30:13 and before 14:31:09 (when the new answer first appeared)". The interpretation should also account for this PC possibly getting the new address later than the real change (up to about an hour).

Question 5. (Application) You estimated 10.10.5.17's infection at "around 15:05–15:07". What would you look at to confirm or refute that?

Answer and explanation

① Endpoint records: process creation between 15:00 and 15:07 (new executables, scripts), new files in the downloads folder, mail attachments opened, USB connections, and the process that made the first DGA query at 15:07:07 (Sysmon 22). ② Network records: the PC's HTTP/HTTPS connections around 15:05 (proxy logs, downloads in Zeek's http.log and files.log) and the hashes of files received. ③ Possible refutation: the malware may have been present already and first started at 15:07 (PC boot time, a scheduled task, user logon). The PC was on, since its DNS activity began at 09:00, but the malware may have started on another condition (user action, a delay). So state the fact as "the time DGA activity began", not "the infection time", and fix the infection time from endpoint evidence.

Question 6. (Common misconception) "The amount tunnelled out is 258 TXT queries × name length (about 66 bytes) ≈ 17 KB." Explain the problem with this estimate using this lab's results.

Answer and explanation

① Not the whole name is data: the data is the first label (48 characters); .[sequence].t.example.net is framing. ② base32 turns 5 bytes into 8 characters, so 48 characters are 30 bytes originally. ③ In step 5, the sequence ran 0–257, but the content repeated every 43 chunks (six times). Since the same data was resent, the unique amount is 43 chunks × up to 30 bytes; decoded, it was 1,285 bytes (about 1.3 KB). "258 × 66" overstates it more than tenfold. Conversely, if the data was compressed, the original document could be larger. When estimating volume, account for encoding, framing and repetition, and decode to confirm when you can.

Question 7. (Interpretation) In step 2, 10.10.4.21 made more A queries than other PCs, but similar numbers of AAAA and HTTPS. How does this support the DGA hypothesis, and why isn't it enough on its own?

Answer and explanation

Human web use has browsers asking for A, AAAA and HTTPS together, so all three rise similarly. A rising on its own signals another program asking only for A, which turned out to be the DGA queries in step 4 (all A: 24 × 24 hours = 576). But that alone isn't enough: many legitimate programs ask only for A (update checks, time sync, mail clients), and it could be a heavy user. Only together with NXDOMAINs, the names' shape, the rhythm and the single success does it become a hypothesis.

Question 8. (Application) To monitor for this lab's findings automatically the next day, what rules (or queries) would you create? Propose at least three, with their false-positive risks.

Answer and explanation

For example: ① List monitoring: sinkhole today's DGA list (or tomorrow's, if you've recovered the algorithm), sync.example.org, t.example.net and xn--crp-sed.example at the resolver, and alert on PCs that ask. Few false positives, but DGA names change daily, so the list needs updating. ② NXDOMAIN rate: alert when a user PC gets 20 or more NXDOMAINs in an hour. False positives: typo-prone users, misconfigured programs, browser detection queries (exclude dotless names). ③ TXT/NULL from user PCs: alert when a non-mail host asks for TXT, or when one domain gets 50+ distinct names in an hour. False positives: some security products and cloud services fetch configuration via TXT; long CDN names. ④ Resolver bypass: port 53/853 queries whose id.resp_h isn't an internal resolver. False positives: approved exceptions, test equipment. ⑤ Outside names answered with 127.0.0.1 or private addresses changing: alert when an answer moves from loopback to a public address. False positives: some blocking services and ad-block lists. Give every rule a baseline and an exception list, and tune them regularly.

  • jq, manual (-s, group_by, --arg, --rawfile, strftime, @tsv, index).
