About this page

A personal study note, rewritten in my own words from several learning resources. The lab data and scenario are my own, and the scenarios are hypothetical.

docs.title: 2.4 — Lab Guide: HTTP Profiling
docs.text:
Scope of this lesson

  • Strategies for collecting useful HTTP artifacts: which fields, grouped by what
  • Finding what stands out (outliers): the User-Agent inventory, header counts, hours of activity
  • Forming hypotheses about human versus program: regularity of intervals, working hours, sub-resource requests
  • Seeing beyond the evidence with advertising cookies: finding a first visit seven months earlier in one day of pcap
  • Writing results up as facts, hypotheses and evidence still needed

Lab environment and notation

(Actual output) was produced with this environment's tshark 4.2.2 and GNU awk. The lab pcap day.pcap was assembled in Python to imitate one day (2026-11-02, UTC) of HTTP on an office segment (9,162 packets, private and documentation addresses and example domains only). It mixes human web use, a legitimate updater and a deliberately hidden automated channel. Being assembled, it shows a simplified version of human behaviour; real traffic is much messier.

docs.title: 1. When you must find "what's odd on this segment" with no leads
docs.text:
(Hypothetical) The day after lesson 1.11's "something seems off in the research lab" case. The capture box in front of the research segment holds a day of pcap, and there are proxy logs. But the proxy logs are in lesson 1.3's default format, with no User-Agent, only URLs and sizes. As the source material's lab takeaways put it, the data formats available are not always ideal. This time the pcap, with headers, is more flexible, so we build the profile from it.

Profiling means summarising "what normally travels on this segment" so you can find what deviates from it. Think of a door guard who knows the faces and arrival times of the staff, and so can spot a stranger or someone coming in at dawn. Where the analogy differs: we know even faces (User-Agents) can be forged (lesson 2.1). So we look not at one face but also at gait (header combinations), hours of movement (time of day) and rhythm of steps (intervals).

docs.title: 2. How this lab is organised
docs.text:
Objectives

  1. Form strategies for collecting useful HTTP artifacts (which fields, grouped by what).
  2. Identify outliers that warrant further investigation.
  3. Form hypotheses separating human activity from program activity.
  4. Use advertising cookies to see beyond the period of the evidence you have.

Preparation

  • tshark, awk, sort, uniq, date
  • The lab pcap day.pcap. There's no starting lead, only "the research segment seems odd".

Record a hash first, as soon as you receive it.

sha256sum day.pcap
capinfos -c -a -e day.pcap

(Actual output)

2cc699cf6bd7d49b69f8dd12b8589cbe052fc65255efcca74ebb69c58fc03bf6  day.pcap
Number of packets:   9162
First packet time:   2026-11-02 00:02:17.000000
Last packet time:    2026-11-02 23:55:02.382120

A full day. Note first that there are packets from just after midnight to just before midnight. If HTTP is moving on an office segment in the small hours, who (or what) is sending it?

flowchart TD
    A["User-Agent inventory<br/>faces"] --> B["Header counts<br/>gait"]
    B --> C["Hours of activity<br/>when they move"]
    C --> D["Intervals<br/>rhythm of steps"]
    D --> E["Cookies<br/>the past"]
    E --> F["Facts · hypotheses · evidence needed"]

How to read it: top to bottom, the order of this lab. Each step looks again, from another angle, at what the previous steps didn't filter out.

docs.title: 3. Step 1: the User-Agent inventory, this segment's "faces"
docs.text:
tshark -n -r day.pcap -Y http.request -T fields -e http.user_agent | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn

(Actual output)

   2823 Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/141.0.0.0 Safari/537.36
    951 Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64; rv:144.0) Gecko/20100101 Firefox/144.0
    777 Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/141.0.0.0 Safari/537.36 Edg/141.0.0.0
     30 VendorUpdate/5.3 (Windows)

As the source material's lab takeaways note, tshark's -T fields output makes such reports quick (lesson 1.10). There are only four faces: Chrome, Firefox, Edge, and an updater called VendorUpdate/5.3. No unfamiliar faces. By User-Agent alone, this segment looks clean. Stop here and the lab fails.

Whether VendorUpdate/5.3 really is that company's updater is checked against the administrators' allow list (lesson 2.2, section 5). In this lab we assume it's an allowed program.

docs.title: 4. Step 2: header counts, this segment's "gait"
docs.text:
Remember from lesson 2.1 that curl sent three headers and the browser fourteen? A User-Agent can be faked in one line, but not many programs imitate the whole combination of headers. Count the header lines per request, by source and site. The sub-resource host cdn.example.net is excluded because it's too numerous.

tshark -n -r day.pcap -Y 'http.request && http.host != "cdn.example.net"' -T fields -E aggregator='|' \
  -e ip.src -e http.host -e http.request.line \
  | awk -F'\t' '{n=split($3,a,"|"); print $1, $2, n}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -k2,2 -k3,3
  • -e http.request.line: the header lines after the request line. There are several, so one cell holds several values (lesson 1.10, section 7.2).
  • -E aggregator='|': joins those values with | instead of commas. Header values contain commas (like Accept's value), so joining with commas gives the wrong count. My first count with commas came out too high, which is why I switched.
  • awk ... split($3,a,"|"): the number of |-separated pieces is the number of header lines.

(Actual output, the 10.10.6.14 part and one other PC)

    144 10.10.6.14 cdn-sync.example 3
     31 10.10.6.14 docs.example.com 10
     24 10.10.6.14 intranet.lab.example 10
     19 10.10.6.14 jobs.rival.example 10
     18 10.10.6.14 mail.example.org 10
     26 10.10.6.14 news.example 10
      6 10.10.6.14 update.vendor.example 3
     ...
     36 10.10.7.11 docs.example.com 10
     29 10.10.7.11 intranet.lab.example 10
     30 10.10.7.11 mail.example.org 10
     31 10.10.7.11 news.example 10
      6 10.10.7.11 update.vendor.example 3

Two things show.

  • Browser requests from every PC have 10 header lines and the updater 3. That's this segment's "normal gait".
  • Only 10.10.6.14 (hq-rd-04) sent 3-line requests to cdn-sync.example, 144 times. No other PC has this site at all.

So what User-Agent did those 3-line requests use? Step 1's inventory had no unfamiliar faces, so it must have borrowed one of the existing ones.

tshark -n -r day.pcap -Y 'http.host == "cdn-sync.example"' -T fields -e http.user_agent | sort | uniq -c

(Actual output) 144 Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/141.0.0.0 Safari/537.36

A User-Agent identical, character for character, to the real Chrome. These 144 were hiding among the 2,823 Chrome requests of step 1. Same face, different gait: none of the Accept-Language, Accept-Encoding, Sec-Fetch-* or cookies Chrome sends when opening a page (lesson 2.1, section 6.2, question 5).

docs.title: 5. Step 3: hours of activity, when this segment "moves"
docs.text:
People arrive, work, eat lunch and go home. Look at the earliest and latest hour (UTC) at which requests appear, by source and site.

tshark -n -r day.pcap -Y 'http.request && http.host != "cdn.example.net"' -T fields -e ip.src -e http.host -e frame.time_epoch \
  | awk -F'\t' '{h=strftime("%H",$3,1); k=$1" "$2; c[k]++;
                 if(!(k in mn)||h<mn[k])mn[k]=h; if(!(k in mx)||h>mx[k])mx[k]=h}
                END{for(k in c) print k, c[k], mn[k]"-"mx[k]}' | sort
  • strftime("%H",$3,1): turns Unix time into the UTC hour; the final argument 1 means UTC (GNU awk). Fixed to UTC to avoid the time-zone trap from lesson 1.10.
  • mn[k], mx[k]: remember the earliest and latest hour for each group.

(Actual output, the 10.10.6.14 part)

10.10.6.14 cdn-sync.example 144 00-23
10.10.6.14 docs.example.com 31 08-17
10.10.6.14 intranet.lab.example 24 08-17
10.10.6.14 jobs.rival.example 19 09-17
10.10.6.14 mail.example.org 18 08-17
10.10.6.14 news.example 26 08-17
10.10.6.14 update.vendor.example 6 00-20

Browser requests from the other PCs were all between 08 and 17 as well (actual output). So human web use on this segment is concentrated in working hours, and only two things appear all day (00–23): update.vendor.example (every PC) and cdn-sync.example (10.10.6.14 only). The small-hours packets came from these two programs.

[Supplement] When there are no logon/logoff records

The source material's lab takeaways say "with no logon/logoff data, human activity is difficult to characterise, so we turn to other clues". This lab is exactly that case. With the endpoint's logon records (lesson 1.11, section 2.2) you could tell directly who was at the keyboard; without them you estimate from hours of activity, intervals, sub-resource requests and human irregularity. It's an estimate, so the report says so.

docs.title: 6. Step 4: intervals, this segment's "rhythm of steps"
docs.text:
Measure the intervals between requests from the same source to the same site, and compute the mean, standard deviation, minimum and maximum. Human browsing is irregular; programs are often regular (the 900 seconds of lesson 1.10, the five minutes of lesson 1.11).

for h in cdn-sync.example update.vendor.example jobs.rival.example; do
  tshark -n -r day.pcap -Y "http.request && http.host == \"$h\" && ip.src == 10.10.6.14" -T fields -e frame.time_epoch \
  | awk -v h=$h 'NR>1{d=$1-p; s+=d; ss+=d*d; n++; if(n==1||d<mn)mn=d; if(n==1||d>mx)mx=d} {p=$1}
                 END{m=s/n; printf "%-22s n=%d mean=%.1f sd=%.1f min=%.1f max=%.1f\n", h, n+1, m, sqrt(ss/n-m*m), mn, mx}'
done

(Actual output)

cdn-sync.example       n=144 mean=600.0 sd=2.5 min=594.3 max=605.7
update.vendor.example  n=6 mean=14400.0 sd=0.0 min=14400.0 max=14400.0
jobs.rival.example     n=19 mean=1601.6 sd=1663.5 min=4.8 max=5652.3
  • cdn-sync.example: mean 600 seconds (10 minutes), standard deviation 2.5 seconds, barely wavering between 594 and 606 seconds. 144 a day = 24 hours × 6. A machine's rhythm. The few seconds of wobble may be deliberate "jitter": many tools shake their intervals slightly to evade detection.
  • update.vendor.example: exactly every four hours (14,400 seconds). Also a machine's rhythm, but it appears identically on every PC and is an allowed program.
  • jobs.rival.example: intervals range wildly from 5 seconds to an hour and a half; the standard deviation is as large as the mean. Closer to a human rhythm. Looking at the request lines, each page carries Sec-Fetch-User: ?1, followed by a cluster of sub-resource requests (lesson 2.1, section 6.7).

By now cdn-sync.example has narrowed to "something pretending to be Chrome, sending requests every ten minutes all day that get no content back (204)". Look at the request paths too.

(Actual output, beginning)

1793577902.857440000    198.51.100.66   /api/ping?id=7f3a&n=0
1793578501.155126000    198.51.100.66   /api/ping?id=7f3a&n=1
1793579101.926539000    198.51.100.66   /api/ping?id=7f3a&n=2
1793579698.945641000    198.51.100.66   /api/ping?id=7f3a&n=3

id=7f3a looks like an identifier for the infected device, and n= like an incrementing counter. The response is a bodyless 204 No Content every time, the shape lesson 2.2's table described as "common as a beacon's nothing-to-do reply".

docs.title: 7. Step 5: seeing the past through cookies
docs.text:
Now to the human side. The user of 10.10.6.14 opened the competitor's recruitment site jobs.rival.example 19 times during working hours. Since when have they been looking at it? We have only one day of pcap, but we look at the cookies using lesson 2.3's method.

tshark -n -r day.pcap -Y 'http.request && ip.src == 10.10.6.14 && http.cookie && http.host != "cdn.example.net"' \
  -T fields -e http.host -e http.cookie | sort -u

(Actual output)

docs.example.com    _ga=GA1.1.16400249.1783036800
intranet.lab.example    _ga=GA1.1.19789581.1773446400
jobs.rival.example  _ga=GA1.1.18205781.1773792000
mail.example.org    _ga=GA1.1.16424006.1782777600
news.example    _ga=GA1.1.13668194.1785715200

There's one _ga value per site: the same browser store kept sending the cookie it received from each site. Convert the last number to a date.

date -u -d @1773792000 +%F

(Actual output)

Site Last number of _ga Date (UTC) jobs.rival.example 1773792000 2026-03-18 intranet.lab.example 1773446400 2026-03-14 mail.example.org 1782777600 2026-06-30 docs.example.com 1783036800 2026-07-03 news.example 1785715200 2026-08-03

Following lesson 2.3, section 3's interpretation (last number = the time the cookie was first created), this browser store first received the competitor's recruitment-site cookie on 18 March 2026. One day of pcap reached back seven and a half months. The internal intranet cookie dating from 14 March is interesting too. This browser store may have come into use in mid-March (a new PC, a new browser profile, cookies cleared). If so, 18 March is "four days after the store came into being", and the possibility remains that the site was visited before that from another store. That's what lesson 2.3, section 4's "a user is a store" means.

[Caution] The cookies in this lab are invented values

The _ga values in the lab pcap were made to show the structure. With real evidence, ① check the value format and the basis of the interpretation as lesson 2.3 cautions, ② bound it with browser cookie-lifetime caps (Chrome 400 days, Safari 7 days), and ③ check it against the endpoint's cookie database and past proxy-log records.

docs.title: 8. Writing it up
docs.text:
• Observations (facts):
    • On 2026-11-02, at this capture point, HTTP requests showed four User-Agent values.
    • Only 10.10.6.14 sent requests to cdn-sync.example (198.51.100.66): 144 of them, at a mean interval of 600 seconds (standard deviation 2.5 seconds), continuing from 00:00 to 23:00.
    • Those requests used the same User-Agent as genuine Chrome but carried three header lines (the same PC's browser requests carried ten). Every response was 204.
    • The same PC opened jobs.rival.example 19 times during working hours (09:00–17:00). The last value of the _ga cookie on requests to that site corresponds to 2026-03-18.
  • Interpretation (hypotheses):
    • The cdn-sync.example traffic appears to be periodic check-ins (beaconing) by an automated program imitating Chrome, not a person's browser.
    • The recruitment-site visits appear to be human browsing, and by this browser store may have continued since mid-March at the latest.
    • Whether the two activities are related isn't yet known.
  • Evidence still needed:
    • The process that opened the 198.51.100.66 connections on the endpoint.
    • DNS records for cdn-sync.example (lessons 2.6–2.7) and when it first appeared.
    • Pcaps and proxy logs from other days (when did the ten-minute rhythm start?).
    • Whether the same rhythm appears on PCs in other segments (scoping).
    • For the recruitment-site visits, whether HR or legal needs to make a judgement.
  • Limits of the observation:
    • One day, plain HTTP only. This method can't see headers of HTTPS traffic.
    • The cookie interpretation relies on a widely used interpretation, not official documentation.

As the last item suggests, the recruitment-site visits may be an HR matter, not a security incident. The investigator records the facts accurately and leaves it to the authorised departments to decide how to handle them.

docs.title: 9. Summary
docs.text:
• The data formats you have aren't always ideal. A pcap with headers is often more flexible for profiling than proxy logs without them.
  • The User-Agent inventory alone found nothing (no unfamiliar faces). Header counts (3 lines versus 10) found the 144 requests hiding inside the same User-Agent.
  • Human web use clustered in working hours (08–17), and only two programs appeared all day.
  • The standard deviation of intervals separated people from machines: 10 minutes ± 2.5 seconds (machine), exactly 4 hours (the allowed updater), 5 seconds to 1.5 hours (human).
  • Cookies let one day of pcap read a first visit seven and a half months earlier (2026-03-18), with the "store" caveat attached.
  • Write results up as facts, hypotheses, evidence needed and limits.

docs.title: Review questions
docs.text:
Question 1. (Strategy) In section 3 the User-Agent inventory looked clean, yet we didn't stop. Besides this lab's method, give at least two other ways to find a program hiding inside the same User-Agent.

Answer and explanation

① The number and order of headers (this lab); ② combinations of header values: for the same browser, the values of Accept, Accept-Language and Accept-Encoding are nearly identical across PCs; ③ presence of Client Hints and Sec-Fetch-* (lesson 2.1): claiming to be Chrome without sec-ch-ua is odd; ④ presence of cookies: browsers used by people send cookies for sites they visit often; ⑤ hours and intervals (sections 5–6); ⑥ for HTTPS, TLS handshake fingerprints (Part 5): the same User-Agent with a different TLS library gives a different fingerprint. Whatever the method, don't conclude from one alone; look at several characteristics together.

Question 2. (Reading a command) What goes wrong if you count section 4's command without -E aggregator='|', joining with commas?

Answer and explanation

-T fields joins several values in one cell with commas by default (lesson 1.10, section 7.2). But header lines themselves contain commas: Accept: text/html,application/xhtml+xml,... or Accept-Encoding: gzip, deflate, br, zstd is one line with several commas. So splitting on commas gives a count larger than the number of header lines, and the more commas a browser's values contain, the more wrong it is. In this lab too, my first comma-based count came out too high. Using a separator that doesn't appear in header values (|) gives the right count.

Question 3. (Calculation) In section 6, the 144 requests to cdn-sync.example spanned the day. If the interval were exactly 600 seconds, how many should there be in a day (86,400 seconds), and does it match?

Answer and explanation

86,400 ÷ 600 = 144, exactly matching the lab's 144. "Requests per day = day ÷ interval" fitting this neatly is itself a sign of a program that never stops: people sleep, turn PCs off and leave their desks. Conversely, if the number falls short, the PC was off, the network dropped, or capture missed a period, and looking for those gaps can reveal the PC's usage pattern (lesson 1.10, question 5).

Question 4. (Interpretation) update.vendor.example also appeared all day, exactly every four hours. Why didn't we suspect it like cdn-sync.example? What should still be checked?

Answer and explanation

① It appeared with the same rhythm on every PC (the shape of a program deployed organisation-wide). ② Its User-Agent is its own name, and its header combination is the same on every PC. ③ We assumed it's on the allow list. cdn-sync.example, by contrast, went from one PC only, under someone else's name (Chrome), to a destination not on the allow list. Still check that update.vendor.example's destination address (203.0.113.120) really belongs to that company, that response sizes are as usual, and the program file's signature: supply-chain attacks can abuse legitimate update paths.

Question 5. (Common misconception) "cdn-sync.example has CDN in its name and the responses were 204, so no content was exchanged and it's harmless." What's wrong?

Answer and explanation

① Anyone can choose a name; cdn and sync are common words used to look normal. ② 204 may mean the server had no command to send at that moment. A beacon gets "nothing to do" most of the time, then a different response (200 with a body) the moment the attacker queues a command. ③ The requests carry information too: id=7f3a looks like a device identifier, n= like a counter, and the request itself signals "this device is alive". ④ Above all, imitating Chrome is not how legitimate programs behave. So look in other days' records for non-204 responses, and at what happened on the PC right after them.

Question 6. (Changed conditions) You have to do the same investigation, but this time with no pcap, only Squid logs in lesson 1.3's default format (no User-Agent). Which steps of this lab can you do, and which can't you?

Answer and explanation

Can do: section 5's hours (the log's times and source addresses), section 6's intervals (time differences between the same address and destination), response codes and sizes (204 and 0 bytes), request URLs (/api/ping?id=7f3a&n=...). In fact, these alone are enough to expose the all-day ten-minute rhythm. Can't do: section 3's User-Agent inventory, section 4's header counts and section 7's cookies. So the fact that it "imitated Chrome" and the recruitment site's first-visit time can't be known. As the source material's lab takeaways suggest, when the available format isn't ideal, do what the fields you have allow first, and recommend adding User-Agent to the log format for the future (lesson 1.3).

Question 7. (Interpretation) In section 7, the intranet cookie dated from 14 March and the recruitment-site cookie from 18 March. Give two interpretations of these two dates, and say how you'd check each.

Answer and explanation

Interpretation ①: this browser store came into being around 14 March (a new PC, a new profile, all cookies cleared). Then the cookie for the intranet the employee uses daily was recreated that day, and the recruitment site may have been viewed earlier. Check: PC issue or reinstall records, the creation time of the endpoint's browser profile, and proxy logs before 14 March for the same PC's intranet and recruitment-site access. Interpretation ②: the store existed earlier and only the intranet cookie changed that day (e.g. a change to the intranet's analytics setup). Then 18 March is more likely the recruitment site's first visit. Check: whether other PCs' intranet cookie dates also cluster around 14 March. If they do, it's a change on the site's side.

Question 8. (Application) You want to turn this lab's method into organisation-wide continuous detection. What rules would you make, and what would you watch out for?

Answer and explanation

For example: ① "the same source requests the same destination more than 50 times a day with an interval standard deviation under 5% of the mean" (rhythm); ② "a browser User-Agent with far fewer headers than that browser normally sends" (gait); ③ "browser-shaped requests outside working hours" (hours); ④ "regular requests to a never-before-seen destination" (novelty). Watch out that ① legitimate programs (updaters, monitoring, messengers) are regular too, so maintain an allow list alongside; ② tools with large jitter can evade standard-deviation thresholds; ③ HTTPS hides headers, so flow- and TLS-fingerprint-based rules are needed. Record each rule's basis, creation date and false-positive cases.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Tools used in this environment: tshark 4.2.2, GNU awk (strftime with the UTC option), coreutils sort, uniq, date and sha256sum, capinfos. The lab pcap was assembled in Python, and outputs were obtained on 2026-11-05.
  • This lab uses lessons 2.1 (request headers), 2.2 (response codes), 2.3 (tracking cookies) and 1.10 (building tables with tshark). See each lesson's references too.
  • GNU, Gawk manual: time functions. strftime([format [, timestamp [, utc-flag]]]).

About this page

A personal study note, rewritten in my own words from several learning resources. The lab procedure and practice pcap are my own, and the scenarios are hypothetical.

docs.title: 2.14 — Lab Guide: Log Aggregation and Analysis
2.14 — Lab Guide: Log Aggregation and Analysis
docs.text:
Scope of this lesson

  • Gathering four different log sources (firewall syslog, Zeek dns.log and conn.log, and the central and local copies of a file server's auth.log) into one Elastic Stack and tying them into one incident
  • Counting that everything loaded arrived, and [Caution] aligning logs without a time zone with other logs
  • Pivoting on one suspicious address: DNS → connections → firewall → internal movement → server logs
  • Rhythm (beaconing), a large transfer, lateral movement, log tampering (central versus local copy), scoping
  • Writing results up as facts, hypotheses, evidence needed and limits

Lab environment and notation

(Actual output) came from the Elasticsearch, Logstash and Kibana 9.4.3 started in lesson 2.13. The lab data is five files I assembled in Python to imitate one day (2026-11-04, UTC) in an office segment. The firewall writes Korea Standard Time (UTC+9) without any time zone marker in RFC 3164 shape; Zeek logs are JSON in UTC; the file server's auth.log uses RFC 3339 timestamps in UTC. Addresses are private or documentation addresses, domains are example domains, and attacker behaviour and account names are invented. Instead of the SOF-ELK VM, I loaded the data with my own Logstash configuration into the same Elastic Stack version, so the lab uses Kibana Discover and ES|QL rather than SOF-ELK's dashboards.

docs.title: 1. The situation
docs.text:
(Hypothetical) The administrator of the finance team's file server fs-01 (10.10.0.30) says "the server was briefly slow yesterday afternoon, and there's nothing odd in the logs". But the security team saw the outside address 203.0.113.66 appear on a threat intelligence list the same day. Here's what's at hand:

Source File Format Time Perimeter firewall fw-edge-01 fw/2026/fw-edge-01.log syslog (RFC 3164), key=value Local time (UTC+9), no time zone marker Zeek on an internal sensor zeek/dns.log, zeek/conn.log JSON UTC (Unix time) fs-01's auth log as collected on the central log server auth/central/fs-01-auth.log syslog (RFC 3339 timestamps) UTC fs-01's auth log copied directly from the server auth/local/fs-01-auth.log same UTC

The goal, in lesson 2.12's words, is to put all the data in one place and follow the whole incident from a single suspicious address.

Figure 1-1. Order of this lab (top to bottom)

flowchart TD
    A["Step 1 · Load and count<br/>original lines = documents?"] --> B["Step 2 · Align time<br/>firewall logs without a time zone"]
    B --> C["Step 3 · Pivot on the suspicious address<br/>DNS → connections → firewall"]
    C --> D["Step 4 · Rhythm and a large transfer"]
    D --> E["Step 5 · Internal movement and server logs"]
    E --> F["Step 6 · Central copy versus local copy"]
    F --> G["Step 7 · Scoping"]
    G --> H["Facts · hypotheses · evidence needed · limits"]

How to read it: proceed top to bottom. Steps 1–2 check "are we ready to analyse?" Mistakes there undermine every later conclusion.

docs.title: 2. Step 1: load and count
docs.text:
Record the originals' hashes and line counts on receipt.

sha256sum fw/2026/*.log zeek/*.log auth/*/*.log
wc -l fw/2026/*.log zeek/*.log auth/*/*.log

(Actual output; first 16 hex digits of each hash)

6f9526a8acc2b08d  fw/2026/fw-edge-01.log       677 lines
fd21ddc200aa18a7  zeek/dns.log                 485 lines
1d448214ede60f8c  zeek/conn.log                678 lines
71e794f8ef083805  auth/central/fs-01-auth.log    9 lines
9689ab5a2d490055  auth/local/fs-01-auth.log      3 lines

The key points of the Logstash configuration (shaped like lesson 2.13's):

  • Firewall: strip the syslog prefix with grok, then split the remaining SRC=… DST=… DPT=… with the kv filter (key=value pairs into fields) into fields such as fw.SRC and fw.DST. Take the year from the path's 2026 (lesson 2.13, section 2.3).
  • Zeek: read with the json codec and turn ts (Unix time) into @timestamp.
  • auth.log: parse the timestamp with TIMESTAMP_ISO8601 and extract the user and source address from SSH login lines. The central and local copies go into different indices.

Compare document counts per index with the originals.

GET /_cat/indices/lab14-*?v&h=index,docs.count&s=index

(Actual output)

index                docs.count
lab14-auth-central            9
lab14-auth-local              3
lab14-fw                    677
lab14-fw-assumed-utc        677
lab14-zeek-conn             678
lab14-zeek-dns              485

All match the original line counts. Why there are two firewall indices is explained in the next step.

[Caution] Two things I ran into while loading

  • The clone filter's marker has changed. To load the firewall log under two time zone assumptions at once, I made copies with the clone filter and routed by [type], but at first all 1,354 events went into one index. In Logstash 9's ECS compatibility mode, clone marks copies in tags rather than type. Changing the condition to if "fw_kst" in [tags] fixed it. As in lesson 2.13, section 2.2, reusing old configuration examples can silently skew results like this; the habit of counting documents caught it.
  • You can't delete indices with a wildcard. Sending DELETE /lab14-* to reload returned Wildcard expressions or all indices are not allowed: since Elasticsearch 8 the default setting (action.destructive_requires_name) blocks accidental mass deletion. I deleted by naming each index. A welcome default for an evidence store.

docs.title: 3. Step 2: align time
docs.text:
One firewall line:

Nov  4 14:14:07 fw-edge-01 kernel: ACCEPT OUT IN=lan OUT=wan SRC=10.10.4.21 DST=203.0.113.66 PROTO=TCP SPT=… DPT=443

Neither year nor time zone. The path solved the year, but there's no way to tell the time zone from inside the log. So I loaded the same log under two assumptions: lab14-fw-assumed-utc ("assume UTC") and lab14-fw ("Korea Standard Time, Asia/Seoul, as the device documentation says"). Which is right is confirmed by comparing the same event from another source. I found the first 10.10.4.21 → 203.0.113.66 record in each.

FROM lab14-fw-assumed-utc, lab14-fw METADATA _index
| WHERE fw.SRC == "10.10.4.21" AND fw.DST == "203.0.113.66"
| STATS first_seen = MIN(@timestamp), n = COUNT(*) BY _index

(Actual output)

       first_seen       |       n       |       _index
2026-11-04T14:14:07.000Z|114            |lab14-fw-assumed-utc
2026-11-04T05:14:07.000Z|114            |lab14-fw

The same query against Zeek conn.log gives the first connection at 2026-11-04T05:14:07Z (step 3). The UTC assumption is off by exactly nine hours; the Asia/Seoul load matches to the second. The count (114) also equals Zeek's connection count. So the assumption that this firewall logs Korea Standard Time is supported by comparing two independent sources.

Reserved words in ES|QL

I first named the columns first and last and got a syntax error, no viable alternative at input 'first =' (actual output). In ES|QL, first and last are reserved, so use names such as first_seen.

What this means for investigations: for logs without a time zone, always determine the zone by comparison with another source, and state the grounds (which event, how many hours' difference) in the report. Loaded as UTC without comparison, this incident's firewall records would sit nine hours late — nothing like the "afternoon" the administrator described. If the difference is minutes rather than hours, it may be device clock error rather than a time zone, and should be recorded separately.

From here on, only lab14-fw (corrected to Korea Standard Time) is used.

docs.title: 4. Step 3: pivot on the suspicious address
docs.text:
Start from the threat intelligence address 203.0.113.66. First, who connected to it?

FROM lab14-zeek-conn | WHERE id.resp_h == "203.0.113.66"
| STATS conns = COUNT(*), first_seen = MIN(@timestamp), last_seen = MAX(@timestamp), max_out = MAX(orig_bytes) BY id.orig_h

(Actual output)

     conns     |       first_seen       |       last_seen        |    max_out    |   id.orig_h
114            |2026-11-04T05:14:07.000Z|2026-11-04T23:53:53.507Z|48211907       |10.10.4.21
98             |2026-11-04T07:40:02.000Z|2026-11-04T23:50:11.166Z|419            |10.10.5.17

Two PCs talked to it. How did they learn the address? DNS:

FROM lab14-zeek-dns | WHERE query == "beacon.example.org"
| STATS n = COUNT(*), first_seen = MIN(@timestamp) BY id.orig_h

(Beforehand I searched for queries whose answers contained 203.0.113.66; all 20 were for beacon.example.org.)

(Actual output)

       n       |       first_seen       |   id.orig_h
19             |2026-11-04T05:14:06.600Z|10.10.4.21
1              |2026-11-04T07:40:01.700Z|10.10.5.17

Both PCs looked up beacon.example.org 0.3–0.4 seconds before their first connection: name → address → connection, chained to the second. But 10.10.4.21 made 114 connections with only 19 lookups. With a 300-second TTL and a connection every ten minutes, it should have asked each time; it didn't, so the program seems to remember the answer longer itself (hypothesis). That's client-side behaviour, distinct from the resolver caching of lesson 2.6. Counting beacons from DNS records alone therefore undercounts.

I ran the same pivot in Kibana, with a data view on lab14-* (excluding the UTC-assumed firewall index) and one KQL query across the three sources' field names:

fw.SRC:"10.10.4.21" or id.orig_h:"10.10.4.21" or ssh_src_ip:"10.10.4.21"

Figure 4-1. Discover tying three sources together by one address (actual output). Time range 2026-11-04 04:00–09:00 UTC, oldest first. At the same 04:00:00 sit Zeek's DNS (answers 203.0.113.30), the firewall (a line whose event.original reads local time Nov 4 13:00:00) and Zeek's connection — possible only because the time zone was corrected. The tall histogram bar around 06:00 is step 5's SSH attempts and login.

What this means for investigations: the same meaning has different field names in each source (fw.SRC, id.orig_h, ssh_src_ip). Filter on one and the others drop out. In a real environment, normalising during parsing to common names such as ECS's source.ip makes pivots like this much easier (lesson 2.13, section 2.2).

docs.title: 5. Step 4: rhythm and a large transfer
docs.text:
I computed the intervals between 10.10.4.21's small connections (under 1,000 bytes) to 203.0.113.66 (timestamps from ES|QL, arithmetic in Python).

(Actual output)

n 113 mean 599.9 s, stdev 1.7 s, min 597.1, max 603.0

A mean of 600 seconds with a standard deviation of 1.7 seconds: as in lesson 2.4, a program's beacon rhythm, not a person's. And one connection was a different size.

FROM lab14-zeek-conn | WHERE id.orig_h == "10.10.4.21" AND id.resp_h == "203.0.113.66"
| SORT orig_bytes DESC | KEEP @timestamp, orig_bytes, resp_bytes, duration | LIMIT 3

(Actual output)

       @timestamp       |  orig_bytes   |  resp_bytes   |     duration
2026-11-04T06:47:31.000Z|48211907       |5120           |412.0
2026-11-04T09:24:04.259Z|420            |218            |0.3824181854724884
2026-11-04T15:44:14.688Z|420            |231            |0.4622810482978821

At 06:47:31 UTC, 10.10.4.21 sent about 46 MB and received only 5 KB in a connection lasting 412 seconds — utterly unlike the usual ~400-byte beacons, a large outbound shape (the same idea as lesson 2.8, review question 4). It's HTTPS (443), so the content isn't visible.

docs.title: 6. Step 5: internal movement and server logs
docs.text:
Where did 10.10.4.21 connect inside the network, besides outside?

FROM lab14-zeek-conn | WHERE id.orig_h == "10.10.4.21" AND id.resp_h != "203.0.113.66" AND id.resp_h LIKE "10.*"
| KEEP @timestamp, id.resp_h, id.resp_p, duration, orig_bytes, resp_bytes

(Actual output)

       @timestamp       |   id.resp_h   |   id.resp_p   |   duration    |  orig_bytes   |  resp_bytes
2026-11-04T06:02:12.000Z|10.10.0.30     |22             |1520.0         |5120           |90311

At 06:02:12 it connected to the file server 10.10.0.30 on SSH (22) and stayed 1,520 seconds (about 25 minutes). Now the file server's auth log (central copy):

FROM lab14-auth-central | KEEP @timestamp, syslog_msg | SORT @timestamp

(Actual output)

2026-11-04T01:05:02.000Z|Accepted publickey for admin_kim from 10.10.1.12 port 51022 ssh2
2026-11-04T02:30:40.000Z|Accepted publickey for admin_kim from 10.10.1.12 port 51190 ssh2
2026-11-04T06:01:50.000Z|Failed password for svc_backup from 10.10.4.21 port 52200 ssh2
2026-11-04T06:01:54.000Z|Failed password for svc_backup from 10.10.4.21 port 52201 ssh2
2026-11-04T06:01:59.000Z|Failed password for svc_backup from 10.10.4.21 port 52202 ssh2
2026-11-04T06:02:12.400Z|Accepted password for svc_backup from 10.10.4.21 port 52203 ssh2
2026-11-04T06:09:03.000Z|svc_backup : TTY=pts/2 ; PWD=/srv/finance ; USER=root ; COMMAND=/usr/bin/tar czf /tmp/.c.tgz /srv/finance
2026-11-04T06:27:40.000Z|Disconnected from user svc_backup 10.10.4.21 port 52203
2026-11-04T08:15:00.000Z|Accepted publickey for admin_kim from 10.10.1.12 port 52011 ssh2

Network records and server logs interlock.

  • 06:01:50–59: three failed passwords from 10.10.4.21 for the backup service account svc_backup, then success at 06:02:12.4, 0.4 seconds after Zeek's connection start (06:02:12.0).
  • 06:09:03: that account became root via sudo and archived /srv/finance into /tmp/.c.tgz (a hidden file name starting with a dot).
  • 06:27:40: disconnected. Zeek's start + 1,520 seconds = 06:27:32, within 8 seconds.
  • Twenty minutes later, at 06:47:31, 10.10.4.21 sent 46 MB outside (step 4).

Against the usual administrative access (admin_kim, public key, from 10.10.1.12), this login — by password, with a service account, from a never-seen PC — departs sharply from the baseline.

docs.title: 7. Step 6: central copy versus local copy
docs.text:
The server administrator said "nothing odd in the logs". What they looked at was the server's local auth.log. Count both copies.

FROM lab14-auth-central, lab14-auth-local METADATA _index | STATS n = COUNT(*) BY _index

(Actual output)

       n       |      _index
3              |lab14-auth-local
9              |lab14-auth-central

Three lines locally, nine centrally. The three local lines are just admin_kim's ordinary logins. Counting the lines missing from the local copy with KQL:

FROM lab14-auth-central | WHERE KQL("ssh_src_ip:10.10.4.21 or syslog_msg:*svc_backup*") | STATS n = COUNT(*)

(Actual output) 6

Exactly the six lines involving 10.10.4.21 and svc_backup are missing locally — the same pattern as lesson 2.12, section 3. That's why the administrator saw "nothing odd". The difference is itself evidence of what the attacker wanted to hide, and if the server is still running, the deleted original held open by the logging daemon (/proc/<PID>/fd, lesson 2.12, section 3.2) is worth checking too.

docs.title: 8. Step 7: scoping
docs.text:
Step 3 found two PCs talking to 203.0.113.66. Look at 10.10.5.17:

  • 07:40:01.7 lookup of beacon.example.org → 07:40:02 first connection → 98 connections every ten minutes afterwards (step 3).
  • Largest transfer 419 bytes: no large transfers.
  • Connections to 10.10.0.30 or any other internal address: zero (actual output, rerunning step 5's query with 10.10.5.17).

So 10.10.5.17 appears to be a second infected PC that started the same beacon at 07:40, with no sign of data leaving it within this data. It may still be in an "early stage", which makes it high priority: isolating it now might prevent what happened on 10.10.4.21 (internal movement, a large transfer).

docs.title: 9. Writing it up
docs.text:
• Observations (facts): all times UTC.
    • At 05:14:06.6, 10.10.4.21 looked up beacon.example.org and received 203.0.113.66, then connected to port 443 at that address 114 times from 05:14:07 to 23:53. Small connections were spaced at a mean of 599.9 s with a standard deviation of 1.7 s.
    • From 06:01:50 to 06:01:59, three failed passwords for the svc_backup account went from 10.10.4.21 to fs-01, followed by a successful login at 06:02:12 (central log and Zeek connection agree within 0.4 s). At 06:09:03 the account used sudo to archive /srv/finance into /tmp/.c.tgz; the connection ended at 06:27:40.
    • At 06:47:31, 10.10.4.21 had a 412-second connection to 203.0.113.66 sending 48,211,907 bytes and receiving 5,120.
    • fs-01's local auth.log lacks the six SSH/sudo lines above, which are present in the central log server's copy.
    • 10.10.5.17 looked up the same name at 07:40:01.7 and made 98 connections at ten-minute intervals to the same address from 07:40:02. No large transfers.
    • The firewall logs Korea Standard Time; this interpretation was confirmed by comparison with Zeek connections (first connection matching to the second, identical counts).
  • Interpretation (hypotheses):
    • 10.10.4.21 was infected around 05:14 with malware using 203.0.113.66 as C2.
    • Via 10.10.4.21, the attacker got svc_backup's password right (success after three failures: a guess, or a password obtained elsewhere), entered the file server, archived finance data, and may have taken it via 10.10.4.21 and sent it outside (the 46 MB at 06:47). How the archive reached 10.10.4.21, and whether the 46 MB is that archive, is not yet confirmed.
    • The attacker scrubbed their traces from fs-01's local log.
    • 10.10.5.17 is a second infection by the same malware.
  • Evidence still needed:
    • Whether /tmp/.c.tgz exists on fs-01, with size and hash; if the server is running, the logging daemon's open file handles (deleted original logs); shell history.
    • Endpoint evidence from 10.10.4.21 and 10.10.5.17: infection vector, the process that looked up beacon.example.org, files received from fs-01.
    • Where the svc_backup password is used and stored (other servers, scripts, configuration files).
    • Proxy and TLS negotiation records (server name and certificate for the 203.0.113.66 connections), and logs from the days before and after (when the infection began).
    • The firewall's time zone configuration documentation (to confirm the conclusion reached by comparison).
  • Observation limits:
    • Traffic was on 443, so contents weren't seen; "46 MB = finance data" is an inference from timing and size.
    • Apart from the sudo line in the server log, what happened inside the SSH session (06:02–06:27) is unknown.
    • fs-01's log source addresses and times are values as received by the central server; the reception time and sender address from lesson 2.10, section 3.4 aren't in this data.
    • This data was assembled for practice.

docs.title: 10. Summary
docs.text:
• I gathered four sources into one Elastic Stack and first checked that original line counts equal document counts; that habit caught the clone filter's ECS behaviour change.
  • The time-zone-less firewall log was loaded under two assumptions and compared with Zeek: UTC was off by exactly nine hours; Korea Standard Time matched to the second.
  • From one suspicious address I linked DNS (name) → Zeek (connections) → firewall (allowed) → internal movement (SSH) → server log (login, sudo tar) → large transfer (46 MB), putting each source's differently named fields into one KQL query.
  • I found a 600-second beacon, a password login with a service account from a never-seen PC, six lines missing only from the local copy, and a second infected PC starting at 07:40.
  • The results were written up as facts, hypotheses, evidence needed and limits.

docs.title: Review questions
docs.text:
Question 1. (Basics) What problem did step 1's check — "original lines equal documents?" — actually catch in this lab? And if you'd used SOF-ELK, what else should you suspect?

Answer and explanation

When splitting the firewall log across two time zone assumptions, counting revealed that all 1,354 events had gone into one index: in Logstash 9's ECS mode, the clone filter marks copies in tags rather than type (the [Caution] in section 2). Without counting, one index would have mixed the same records under two time zones and wrecked every time analysis. On SOF-ELK, also suspect Filebeat 9's rules (files under 1,024 bytes aren't read; files with identical first 1,024 bytes are skipped as duplicates; lesson 2.13, section 4.1). This lab's local auth.log (3 lines, 348 bytes), for example, might never have been loaded.

Question 2. (Changed conditions) If you had loaded the firewall log only under the UTC assumption (lab14-fw-assumed-utc) and analysed that, how would the incident timeline differ?

Answer and explanation

Firewall records would sit nine hours late. The first 10.10.4.21 → 203.0.113.66 record would show at 14:14 UTC rather than 05:14, out of line with Zeek (05:14) and DNS (05:14). That would ① invite wrong readings such as "the firewall only saw this traffic nine hours later" or "these are different communications"; ② place the firewall record for the 46 MB transfer (06:47) at 15:47, twisting its order relative to the SSH login (06:02); and ③ make every firewall-only event (periods without Zeek) wrong. Hence the need to determine the zone of time-zone-less sources by comparison, and record the grounds (section 3).

Question 3. (Interpretation) In step 3, 10.10.4.21 made 114 connections but only 19 DNS lookups. How do you interpret this, and how does it affect the investigation?

Answer and explanation

With a 300-second TTL and a connection every ten minutes, it didn't ask each time, so the program seems to remember the answer longer itself or use the address directly (hypothesis). Effects: ① counting beacons or activity periods from DNS alone underestimates them; ② if the attacker changes the name's address, this program may keep going to the old one for a while, so DNS sinkholing alone may not cut it off immediately; ③ so read DNS (names) and connection records (addresses) together, and block both names and addresses. Resolver caching (lesson 2.6) isn't the cause here, since this data observed traffic between client and resolver.

Question 4. (Common misconception) "There's nothing odd in fs-01's local auth.log, so the file server wasn't compromised." Refute this with this lab's results.

Answer and explanation

In step 6, the local copy had three lines and the central copy nine, and the six missing lines were exactly those involving 10.10.4.21 and svc_backup (three failures, the success, sudo tar, the disconnect). The local log is clean because someone scrubbed it, and the difference is itself evidence of compromise and concealment (lesson 2.12, section 3). Zeek's connection record (06:02:12, port 22, 1,520 seconds) is independent network evidence telling the same story. Don't conclude from one server log; read the central copy and network records together.

Question 5. (Application) To confirm whether step 4's 46 MB transfer really was the archive of /srv/finance, what do you need beyond this data, and in what order would you look?

Answer and explanation

① If /tmp/.c.tgz still exists on fs-01, its size and hash (around 46 MB?); if deleted, look for traces with disk forensics. ② How the file got from fs-01 to 10.10.4.21: the SSH connection's resp_bytes was only 90,311 bytes, so 46 MB didn't move over that session. Look for another path (another connection, SMB, SCP at another time) in Zeek conn.log between 10.10.0.30 and 10.10.4.21 from 06:09 to 06:47. In this data there were zero connections involving 10.10.0.30 in that window (actual output), so consider paths this sensor can't see (traffic within the same switch, another segment), or that the file may still be only on the server. ③ On 10.10.4.21's endpoint, the file or its traces and the process behind the 06:47 connection. ④ If proxy or TLS interception records exist, content or size information for the 06:47 connection. Until these pieces interlock, keep "46 MB = finance data" as a hypothesis.

Question 6. (Interpretation) If you had pivoted with only fw.SRC:"10.10.4.21" in KQL, what would be missing? How would you reduce this problem in a real environment?

Answer and explanation

Only firewall records would remain; the same PC's Zeek DNS and connections (id.orig_h) and the server log's source address (ssh_src_ip) would all drop out, because each source uses a different name for the same meaning (section 4). To reduce it: ① normalise during parsing (Logstash) to common field names such as ECS's source.ip, destination.ip, destination.port, user.name; ② failing that, OR all the fields when pivoting, or search by value without a field; ③ document which fields share meaning in each data view. As with lesson 2.13, review question 7's type conflict, also watch for fields with the same name but different meanings.

Question 7. (Application) The manager receiving this report asks, "Should we isolate both PCs now, or keep watching?" What decision grounds would you give from this lab's results?

Answer and explanation

Grounds: ① 10.10.4.21 talked to the C2 all day, entered the file server with a service account, archived data, and appears to have sent 46 MB outside — damage already in progress. ② 10.10.5.17 started the same beacon at 07:40 but shows no large transfers or internal movement in this data — early stage, so acting now may prevent greater damage. ③ The attacker knows the svc_backup account, so change its password and review where it's used. ④ But isolation may alert the attacker and lose endpoint memory evidence, so decide together whether to capture memory and disk evidence first and whether to isolate both at once (isolating one may warn the other). The decision is the manager's; the investigator's job is to convey the facts, hypotheses and risks clearly.

docs.title: References
docs.text:

  • Lab data: assembled by me. First 16 hex digits of SHA-256: fw-edge-01.log 6f9526a8acc2b08d, dns.log fd21ddc200aa18a7, conn.log 1d448214ede60f8c, central fs-01-auth.log 71e794f8ef083805, local fs-01-auth.log 9689ab5a2d490055.
  • Elastic, Logstash kv filter, clone filter (behaviour in ECS compatibility mode), ES|QL, action.destructive_requires_name.
  • This lab builds on lesson 2.4 (beacon rhythm), lessons 2.6–2.9 (DNS), lesson 2.8 (Zeek), lesson 2.10 (syslog timestamps), lesson 2.12 (central copies) and lesson 2.13 (the Elastic Stack).

About this page

A personal study note, rewritten in my own words from several learning resources. The lab data and scenario are my own, and the scenarios are hypothetical.

docs.title: 2.12 — Log Aggregation: Why Collect, How to Ship, What to Use
2.12 — Log Aggregation: Why Collect, How to Ship, What to Use
docs.text:
Scope of this lesson

  • Logs are the unsung heroes of network investigations, and they come with baggage (no standard, volume, dispersion)
  • Benefits of central aggregation: a second copy of what attackers delete, working in parallel, multiple vantage points
  • Confirmed directly: comparing a scrubbed local log with the central copy, and [Caution] the daemon that keeps writing to a file scrubbed with sed -i
  • Better transport: rsyslog and syslog-ng, queues, TLS, RELP, log shippers, message queues
  • Choosing an aggregation platform: file ingestion, parsing, custom formats; [Changed] what's changed since the book

Lab environment and notation

(Actual output) came from rsyslog 8.2312.0 (Ubuntu 24.04 packages, including rsyslog-gnutls) in this environment. A "server" rsyslog wrote to a local file while also forwarding over TCP and UDP to another rsyslog acting as the "central aggregator" (127.0.0.40). The log messages and the "attacker's log scrubbing" are invented for practice; addresses are private or documentation addresses.

docs.title: 1. Logs are the unsung heroes
docs.text:
Think how many systems a single network communication touches between source and destination. Each of those systems, and the software on them, may be recording valuable evidence of that packet's existence in some log.

That's great news for investigators. Logs are usually small and compress well. For compliance or ordinary record-keeping they're often retained for a long time, often in ways that can be considered forensically sound. If "long-term retention of forensically sound evidence" doesn't make your ears perk up, you might be in the wrong business. Even for incidents long past, logs are often the best material for recreating what happened.

But this gold mine comes with baggage.

  • There's no standard for "log data" in general. Specific formats have standards — syslog (lesson 2.10), HTTP's Common Log Format (lesson 2.5) — but there's no RFC or IEEE standard for all logs. Taking part in a TCP conversation requires following the protocol; logging can take any shape a software (or even hardware) developer dreams up.
  • There's no limit to the volume. Wading through overwhelming amounts in varied formats by hand will drive an investigator to the frayed edges of sanity.
  • Devices have no storage. Many network devices lack persistent storage and keep logs in memory. When the allocated memory fills, old entries roll out, lost forever, and a reboot starts with an empty buffer. Not conducive to forensics.
  • They're scattered. With thousands of systems each holding their own logs, remote collection to one place is the best plan, but in geographically dispersed or topologically complex environments it's never that simple. Even when feasible, it spends analysts' time on collecting, and correlating events across sources by hand degrades the analysis.
  • There's no common protocol. Every source has its own format needing its own parser, until you have an overflowing toolbox of Perl, Python, PowerShell and bash scripts.

In short, log analysis looks simple but is a very wide problem: vital evidence buried in voluminous free-form data — sometimes the only remaining evidence of an event.

docs.title: 2. Central aggregation: in one place, in real time
docs.text:
The answer is real-time, centralised, aggregated logging. Besides keeping the engagement manager happy, it brings the organisation many benefits.

A second copy. Most attackers know the systems they compromise log their activity, and actively scrub or remove logs. With aggregation, log entries are recorded in multiple places at once. Unless the attacker knows this and compromises the aggregator too, a secondary record survives. And the disparity between on-system and aggregated logs is itself a clear indication of what the attacker wanted to hide.

Divide and conquer. Several analysts can work on aggregated data at once, splitting a large task (many platforms offer web front ends). Some aggregation technologies send the same logs to multiple destinations simultaneously, so specialised analysis software and the long-term archive can receive the same source data.

Follow the whole incident from one place. The real power is having the entire environment's data in one place. Query by one infected PC and the malware download (proxy), execution and installation (endpoint) and C2 traffic (DNS, firewall) come together on one screen.

The same event from multiple vantage points. A perimeter IDS never sees activity between internal subnets, but an internal firewall or router may have logged events crucial to the incident timeline (the same idea as lesson 2.6's vantage points).

It's not a new idea. Some high-security environments used to connect badge readers to line printers in another room. A badge swipe was logged in the reader's memory and printed on paper at the same time, so an electronic compromise couldn't erase every record. With the printer under lock and key and fed tractor paper, a virtually indelible log was available. Central aggregation is that printer's modern form. Where the analogy breaks: printed records can't be altered later, but an aggregator's files can be altered by whoever compromises it. That's why the aggregator's own access control and integrity (separate privileges, append-only storage, hashes) matter.

Different roles, different needs. A network operations team may need only switches, routers, firewalls and proxies, for perhaps a month. A PCI compliance team at an organisation processing card payments needs real-time visibility of transaction-related records retained for the period PCI-DSS mandates, with stricter access controls for that sensitive data. Incident response and hunt teams want as much evidence as possible for as long as the lawyers allow (these figures are illustrations; organisations vary widely). Add multiple offices, jurisdictions, mergers and divestitures, and outside consultants, and today's network environment is too complex to run without some form of log aggregation.

Figure 2-1. The big picture of log aggregation (top to bottom: the direction logs flow)

flowchart TD
    S["Sources<br/>servers, network devices, endpoints, applications"] --> T["Shipping<br/>syslog (UDP, TCP, TLS, RELP), shipping agents"]
    T --> Q["Buffering<br/>sender-side disk queues, message queues (Kafka etc.)"]
    Q --> P["Receiving and parsing<br/>splitting fields, normalising time, enrichment"]
    P --> D["Storage and search<br/>aggregation platform, SIEM"]
    D --> A["Consumers<br/>operations, compliance, incident response"]
    S -.->|"originals stay at the source too"| L["The source's local logs<br/>(the baseline to compare with the second copy)"]

How to read it: solid lines are the path logs take to the centre; the dotted line is the original left at the source. Investigators compare the two streams (section 3). Remember that at each stage, logs can be lost (shipping), delayed (buffering) or reshaped (parsing).

docs.title: 3. Confirmed directly: a scrubbed local log and the central copy
3.1 Before and after
docs.text:
The "server" recorded six authentication events, writing them to a local auth.log while forwarding over TCP to the central aggregator. Then the "attacker" scrubbed their traces — lines containing the attacker's address 203.0.113.9 and the sudo line that archived /etc/shadow — with sed -i.

sed -i '/203\.0\.113\.9\|\/etc\/shadow/d' auth.log

(Actual output; the local file after scrubbing)

2026-11-05T08:17:44.716341+00:00 vm sshd: Accepted password for jkim from 10.10.1.19 port 50111 ssh2
2026-11-05T08:17:44.726769+00:00 vm sshd: Accepted password for mlee from 10.10.1.30 port 50190 ssh2

Two ordinary logins remain. Now compare just the message parts with the central copy.

diff <(sed -E 's/^\S+ \S+ //' auth.log) <(grep via=imtcp central.log | sed -E 's/^.* host=\S+ //')

sed -E 's/^\S+ \S+ //' strips the local lines' first two fields (timestamp and hostname), and the central sed strips everything up to the host= field, so diff compares only the message parts. <( … ) is a bash feature that hands a command's output to diff as if it were a file.

(Actual output)

1a2,5
> sshd: Failed password for root from 203.0.113.9 port 4444 ssh2
> sshd: Failed password for root from 203.0.113.9 port 4445 ssh2
> sshd: Accepted password for root from 203.0.113.9 port 4446 ssh2
> sudo: root : TTY=pts/1 ; PWD=/root ; USER=root ; COMMAND=/usr/bin/tar czf /tmp/x.tgz /etc/shadow

The four lines missing locally that diff shows are exactly what the attacker wanted to hide: two failed passwords → root login → archiving the password hash file. As the book says, the disparity between local and aggregated logs clearly showed "what they tried to hide".

A central line looked like this (the template records reception time, reported time, sender address and input path; lesson 2.10, section 3.4).

(Actual output, excerpt)

received=2026-11-05T08:17:44.719731+00:00 reported=2026-11-05T08:17:44+00:00 from=127.0.0.1 via=imtcp host=vm sshd: Failed password for root ...

[Caution] reported was cut to whole seconds, though the local file had microseconds, because the sender's forwarding action used the default template (the traditional, RFC 3164 shape). Configure forwarding with an RFC 5424 template too (such as rsyslog's RSYSLOG_SyslogProtocol23Format) so precision, year and time zone survive.

docs.title: 3.2 [Caution] The daemon keeps writing to a file scrubbed with sed -i
docs.text:
After the scrub, three new events occurred on the same server (the experiment in 3.3). But not one new line appeared in the local auth.log. I looked for the reason.

ls -l /proc/$(cat cli/pid)/fd | grep auth.log

(Actual output)

l-wx------ 1 root root 64 Nov  5 08:18 6 -> …/cli/auth.log (deleted)

sed -i doesn't edit a file "in place"; it writes a new file and renames it over the original name. rsyslog still held the original file (now nameless, deleted) open and kept writing to it. I read that deleted file through the open file handle.

(Actual output)

lines in deleted inode: 9; with 203.0.113.9: 3
visible file lines: 2
inode 829105 (the visible auth.log)   inode 829062 (the file rsyslog holds open)

The deleted original still held all six lines from before the scrub (including the three with the attacker's address) plus the three new ones: nine lines. The visible auth.log (a different inode) had two.

What this means for investigations:

  • On a live system, before restarting the logging daemon, look in /proc/<PID>/fd/ for log files marked (deleted) and copy them. The attacker's scrubbed original may be there. A restart, or rotation reopening files, closes that handle and returns the content to free disk space (then it's a disk forensics problem).
  • Conversely, scrubbing this way has a side effect: later local logs don't appear in the visible file. A log that "went quiet" at some point is a clue pointing to tampering like this.
  • And the central copy kept receiving regardless (next section).

docs.title: 3.3 When the aggregator goes down briefly: queues
docs.text:
I took the central aggregator down and sent the same events meanwhile over both TCP forwarding (with a disk-assisted queue) and UDP forwarding. The sender's TCP forwarding looked like this:

authpriv.* action(type="omfwd" target="127.0.0.40" port="10601" protocol="tcp"
                 queue.type="LinkedList" queue.filename="fwd_tcp" queue.saveOnShutdown="on"
                 action.resumeRetryCount="-1" action.resumeInterval="5")
  • queue.type="LinkedList" with queue.filename: an in-memory queue that spills to disk when full or at shutdown (disk-assisted).
  • action.resumeRetryCount="-1": retry forever until the destination returns.
  • action.resumeInterval="5": retry every 5 seconds.

I created three events at 08:18:02–04 and brought the aggregator back around 08:18:17.

(Actual output; the central copy)

received=2026-11-05T08:18:22.238783+00:00 reported=2026-11-05T08:18:02+00:00 from=127.0.0.1 via=imtcp … while-down 1 …
received=2026-11-05T08:18:22.238783+00:00 reported=2026-11-05T08:18:03+00:00 from=127.0.0.1 via=imtcp … while-down 2 …
received=2026-11-05T08:18:22.238783+00:00 reported=2026-11-05T08:18:04+00:00 from=127.0.0.1 via=imtcp … while-down 3 …
The same three events sent over UDP: 0

All three TCP events arrived once the aggregator was back, all received at 08:18:22 (the backlog delivered at once), with reported times 08:18:02–04 intact. None of the UDP copies survived, and neither side knew they were lost.

What this means for investigations: a cluster of identical reception times in the central copy may mean an outage of the aggregator or network just before. Re-sort that span by reported time, and note that sources received only over UDP may have gaps there. Queues have size limits too, so long outages can lose data even over TCP.

docs.title: 4. Better transport than plain syslog
docs.text: Lesson 2.10 showed syslog's two weaknesses: UDP's unreliability (fire-and-forget, so messages can be silently dropped or spoofed) and plaintext (sensitive logs, normally in root-only files, sent onto a wire where anyone can observe, intercept or alter them). Even if it's baked into most UNIX systems, weigh the risks before deploying a plaintext logging protocol. Fortunately, open source has produced improved implementations.

docs.title: 4.1 rsyslog and syslog-ng
docs.text:
• rsyslog: the default logging service in Red Hat-family distributions (Fedora, CentOS derivatives, etc.), Ubuntu and others, and buildable for other UNIXes such as BSD and Solaris. A big draw is that it can use the legacy syslog configuration format as is, easing migration (lesson 2.10, section 5's configuration worked unchanged).
  • syslog-ng: uses a different configuration format but offers much more granular filtering and parsing.

Both support TCP transport and encryption, and can queue messages generated while the server is unavailable, releasing them when it returns (confirmed in 3.3). They replace the aging syslog daemon with very little effort while adding many integrity and security features.

docs.title: 4.2 TLS: unreadable on the wire
docs.text:
I created a practice certificate authority, gave the aggregator a certificate (logs.example.net), and had the sender verify the certificate name (x509/name), sending on port 6514.

# sender
*.* action(type="omfwd" target="127.0.0.41" port="6514" protocol="tcp" StreamDriver="gtls"
           StreamDriverMode="1" StreamDriverAuthMode="x509/name" StreamDriverPermittedPeers="logs.example.net")

(Actual output)

== line stored on the aggregator
2026-11-05T08:18:59+00:00 vm sshd: TLS-TEST Failed password for root from 203.0.113.9
== packets on the wire
      6 TCP
      5 TLSv1.2
searching the pcap for plaintext "TLS-TEST": 0

The aggregator stored it normally, but the message text couldn't be found in the captured packets — the opposite of lesson 2.10's plaintext syslog. This rsyslog's TLS driver (GnuTLS) negotiated TLS 1.2.

From a network forensics perspective it cuts both ways. TLS stops logs being read or altered in transit, but, unlike lesson 2.10, section 6.2, pcaps no longer serve as a second copy. The more you use TLS, the more the aggregator's own retention and integrity matter.

docs.title: 4.3 RELP, log shippers, message queues
docs.text:
• RELP (Reliable Event Logging Protocol): built by the rsyslog team to confirm that each message reached its destination. With TCP alone, messages in a buffer can vanish the moment a connection drops; RELP prevents that with application-level acknowledgements. It has built-in TLS support. (The rsyslog-relp module is installed here, but I didn't run an experiment with it.)
  • Log shippers: small agents on each system watch data sources, normalise events and send them straight to storage or on to a parsing/enrichment stage. Elastic's Beats are the classic example: Filebeat for raw files, Winlogbeat for Windows event logs (lesson 2.11), Metricbeat for system status, and many (unsupported) community Beat modules.
  • Message queues: constructs originally for inter-process communication (IPC), but well suited by nature to exchanging log data between creator and recipient. Dozens are in use, including RabbitMQ, ZeroMQ and Apache Kafka, and most aggregation platforms can ingest some of them. They buffer when the aggregator slows or stops (Figure 2-1).

[Supplement] Shipping and collection tools that became common after the book (as of 2026-11-05)

Alongside Beats, Elastic Agent (lesson 2.11) and less vendor-tied tools such as Fluentd/Fluent Bit, Vector and the OpenTelemetry Collector (handling logs, metrics and traces together) are widely used. In cloud environments, each cloud's logging service can be both source and destination. Whatever the tool, the investigator's questions are the same: what does it drop, what does it change, and how much does it hold when the link breaks?

docs.title: 5. Choosing an aggregation platform
docs.text:
Many tools provide log aggregation and analysis. Most SIEMs use logs as core data; because of their scale and scope they tend to be commercial, but free (or free-ish) tools offer similar functions. Among general-purpose log aggregation tools, perhaps the most rapidly adopted is the Elastic Stack ("ELK": Elasticsearch for storage and search, Logstash for ingestion, parsing and enrichment, Kibana as the front end), and SOF-ELK, used in this course, is a free, full-stack community distribution of it (lesson 2.13). Others include ELSA (Enterprise Log Search and Archive) on the free side, and Splunk and LogRhythm on the commercial side.

The SIEM and aggregator market is crowded, with dozens of options. Evaluating with forensics, response and hunting in mind:

  1. How does data get in? Most log evidence comes as files; a platform that can't ingest them is unsuitable for most DFIR workflows. Being able to load both existing file evidence and live sources is a very powerful combination for ongoing incidents and hunting.
  2. How does it handle formats? A syslog message is just free text, each application choosing its own structure, which doesn't allow easy analysis. Most aggregators parse common formats automatically and let users define formats to split frequently met data into meaningful fields. Many recognise common data types such as IP addresses and dates and tokenise them for searching even without custom definitions.
  3. What's used for custom parsing? Custom parsing is almost always needed. Logstash uses a syntax called grok, for example, whereas ELSA used an XML-based structure. When evaluating, check that the language or framework suits your data.

[Changed] How the platform landscape has shifted since the book (as of 2026-11-05)

  • Elastic's licensing: the book presents the Elastic Stack as "free software". In 2021 Elastic relicensed Elasticsearch and Kibana from Apache 2.0 to the Elastic License and SSPL (free to use, but not OSI-approved open source licences), and AWS responded by forking 7.10.2 as OpenSearch (Apache 2.0). In August 2024 Elastic added AGPL as a third option, making it available under an open source licence again (checked via coverage). If your organisation is evaluating it, check the licence and the subscription terms for individual features.
  • ELSA: as far as searches show, ELSA is no longer actively developed, and Security Onion, which used ELSA, moved to an Elastic-based stack (Security Onion 2.x documentation doesn't mention ELSA). Unless old evidence lives in an ELSA instance, it isn't something to choose today.

docs.title: 6. How this is used in real investigations
docs.text:
1. Map where the copies are first. The source's local logs, the central aggregator, the queues in between, archival storage (Figure 2-1).
  2. Compare local with central. The differences are clues (section 3.1). Normalise the leading fields so you can diff the message parts.
  3. On live systems, secure open log handles first. (deleted) files under /proc/<PID>/fd (section 3.2). Restart daemons only afterwards.
  4. Look for clusters of reception times and gaps. Outages and losses from UDP sources (section 3.3).
  5. Check for changes in transit. Has precision, year or time zone been reduced (the whole-second timestamps in 3.1)? Have fields been dropped (lesson 2.11, section 5.1)?
  6. Treat the aggregator itself as evidence. Access records, integrity, configuration (which templates, from where it accepts).
  7. Know each role's retention. For old incidents, which team's store still covers that period?

docs.title: 7. Summary
docs.text:
• Logs are small, compress well and are often kept long, letting us recreate even old incidents. But there's no general standard, volumes are huge, some live only in device memory, they're scattered, and there's no common protocol.
  • Benefits of central aggregation: a second copy (what attackers delete survives, and the difference is a clue), working in parallel, following the whole incident from one place, multiple vantage points. It's the modern badge-reader line printer, but an aggregator can be altered if compromised, so integrity matters.
  • Confirmed directly: diff exposed the four scrubbed lines (two failures → root login → archiving /etc/shadow), and after sed -i, rsyslog kept writing to the deleted original, whose nine original lines were still reachable via /proc/<PID>/fd. The default forwarding template cut timestamps to whole seconds.
  • With the aggregator down, TCP (disk-assisted queue) events all arrived after it returned (reception times clustered), while none of the UDP copies survived. Logs sent over TLS couldn't be read from the pcap.
  • Better transport: rsyslog (legacy-config compatible), syslog-ng (granular parsing), TCP, TLS and queues, RELP, shippers such as Beats, message queues such as Kafka. [Supplement] Fluent Bit, Vector, OpenTelemetry Collector.
  • Platform evaluation: file and live ingestion, automatic parsing and custom formats (grok and others). [Changed] Elastic's licensing (SSPL/ELv2 in 2021, the OpenSearch fork, AGPL added in 2024) and ELSA's decline.

docs.title: Review questions
docs.text:
Question 1. (Basics) Give three benefits central aggregation brings to investigations, linking each to an experiment or example from this lesson.

Answer and explanation

For example: ① a second copy: if an attacker scrubs local logs, the central copy survives, and the difference shows what they hid (section 3.1: diff exposed the four scrubbed lines); ② following the whole incident from one place: query by one infected PC to link the proxy download, endpoint execution and DNS/firewall C2 on one screen (section 2); ③ multiple vantage points: internal firewall logs reveal activity between internal subnets that the perimeter IDS can't see. Parallel work by several analysts and sending the same logs to multiple destinations are benefits too.

Question 2. (Interpretation) Investigating a live Linux server, the last line of /var/log/auth.log is three days old and nothing follows, yet rsyslogd is running. What do you suspect, and what do you do first?

Answer and explanation

As in section 3.2, suspect that someone swapped the file with something like sed -i, so rsyslog keeps writing to the deleted original (no new lines in the visible file). First: don't restart rsyslog; look in ls -l /proc/$(pidof rsyslogd)/fd for log files marked (deleted), copy their content through the handle (cp /proc/<PID>/fd/<N> evidencefile) and hash it. It may hold the pre-scrub original plus everything since. Then compare the visible file's inode and modification time, shell history and the central copy. Also check other possibilities (rotation misconfiguration, a full disk, configuration changes).

Question 3. (Changed conditions) In section 3.3's experiment, suppose the sender had no queue (queue.type omitted) and default retry settings. How do you expect the result would differ, and how would you confirm it?

Answer and explanation

Expectation (hypothesis): events during the aggregator's downtime would likely be partly or wholly lost, even over TCP. With defaults, an action is suspended after a few failures, and there's no disk queue to hold messages meanwhile; in-memory capacity is limited, and restarting the sending rsyslog discards what's in memory. Confirm by repeating the experiment without a queue, counting lines in the central copy, and reading the sending rsyslog's internal messages (action suspended, messages discarded). This lesson didn't run that variant, so don't assert the result; confirm it experimentally.

Question 4. (Common misconception) "We have a central aggregator, so it doesn't matter if attackers delete logs." Give at least three holes in this claim.

Answer and explanation

① If the aggregator itself is compromised, the copy can be altered too (where section 2's analogy breaks); separate privileges, append-only storage and hashes are needed. ② Logs never sent don't exist: without configuration to ship every source and event, there's no copy (lesson 2.10's selectors). ③ Loss in transit: UDP drops silently (section 3.3), and even TCP can lose data during outages without a queue. ④ Delay: where events are batched, as with Windows Event Forwarding, deletion before sending leaves no copy (lesson 2.11, section 3.2). ⑤ Attackers can cut forwarding first: stopping the daemon or changing its configuration stops later events reaching the centre (though "it went quiet from this point" is itself a clue). ⑥ Alteration: a copy with reduced precision, missing fields or lost time zones may be less useful than the original (section 3.1).

Question 5. (Interpretation) In the central copy, 40 events from one server all have reception time 02:31:07.4, while their reported times spread from 02:12:00 to 02:30:55. What probably happened, and how do you handle it?

Answer and explanation

It's section 3.3's pattern. From around 02:12 until just before 02:31, transport between that server and the aggregator was interrupted (aggregator outage, network fault, firewall change, etc.), and events queued on the sender arrived all at once at 02:31:07. To handle it: ① build the timeline on reported time, remembering it's the sender's claim; ② note that other sources received only over UDP may have gaps during those 19 minutes; ③ find the cause of the interruption (aggregator logs, network device logs) — the attacker may have cut it deliberately; ④ check whether real-time alerting was delayed during the span.

Question 6. (Application) Your organisation is choosing a new aggregation platform. Write five evaluation questions from the incident response team's perspective.

Answer and explanation

For example: ① Can it easily ingest existing file evidence (Zeek logs from pcaps, log files from seized servers, CSV), alongside live inputs (section 5)? ② Does it parse common formats automatically, what language does custom parsing use (grok or similar), and does it keep the raw original when parsing fails? ③ Does it store reception time and original time, and sender address, separately (lesson 2.10, section 3.4)? How does it handle time zones? ④ Retention period and cost, search speed on old data, integrity (change and access records). ⑤ Export: can investigation results be extracted in original form or JSON for other tools and reports? ⑥ Licensing and cost structure (section 5's [Changed]), and degree of vendor lock-in. ⑦ Concurrent use by several analysts and separation of permissions.

Question 7. (Common misconception) "Sending logs over TLS is always better for investigations." Summarise the pros and cons using this lesson's experiment.

Answer and explanation

Pros: logs can't be read or altered on the wire (section 4.2: the message text couldn't be found in the pcap), and certificate name checks (x509/name) prevent sending to the wrong server. Cons (from an investigative view): as in lesson 2.10, section 6.2, pcaps stop serving as a second copy of the logs, so you rely more on the aggregator's own retention and integrity; and if forwarding stops because of an expired certificate or misconfiguration, logs pile up or vanish meanwhile (queue settings matter). In conclusion, use TLS in most environments, but pair it with measures that protect the aggregator as an evidence store and monitoring that notices forwarding failures.

Results obtained on 2026-11-05.
