About this page

A personal study note, rewritten in my own words from several learning resources. The log messages and tampering experiments are my own, and the scenarios are hypothetical.

docs.title: 2.10 — Syslog: Message Formats, Facility and Severity, Reading Configuration
2.10 — Syslog: Message Formats, Facility and Severity, Reading Configuration
docs.text:
Scope of this lesson

  • Syslog is both a daemon and a protocol, and why it's precious to investigators
  • Who sends syslog, and who receives it
  • Reading messages: the traditional format (RFC 3164) and the current standard (RFC 5424). [Caution] there's no year or time zone, and the timestamp and hostname are set by the sender
  • Facility, severity, and computing the PRI
  • Reading configuration files: selectors and actions. [Correction] a ! selector on its own selects nothing
  • Transport: UDP loss, TCP, and [Changed] syslog in the journald era

Lab environment and notation

(Actual output) came from rsyslog 8.2312.0, util-linux logger 2.39.3 and TShark 4.2.2 in this environment (Ubuntu 24.04). I ran a receiving rsyslog on 127.0.0.30, port 10514 (UDP and TCP), and a sending rsyslog that takes messages on its own socket, to watch the flow between the two instances. The container's hostname is vm, so messages carry vm. The year-rollover experiment used faketime to imitate only the receiving server's clock at 2027-01-01. Message contents (login failures, DHCP and so on) are invented for practice.

docs.title: 1. Syslog: a daemon and a protocol
docs.text:
As the name says, syslog handles system log events. But the word refers to two things.

  • The daemon: a long-standing UNIX program that receives log messages and delivers them to one or more destinations (files, other programs, other systems on the network) according to its configuration. rsyslog and syslog-ng are today's implementations.
  • The protocol: the agreement on what messages look like on the wire when sent over the network.

As an analogy, the syslog daemon is the company mail room and the protocol is the envelope format. Each department (program) hands a note to the mail room, which looks at the markings on the envelope (facility and severity, section 4) to decide which filing cabinet (file) it goes in, whether to send it to head office (a remote server), or, if urgent, to phone the boss (every user's screen). Where it breaks: a real mail room checks who sent something, but syslog trusts the sender and date written on the envelope (section 3.4). And an envelope sent by UDP can be lost without anyone knowing (section 6).

Syslog was built to help administrators with operations, but the security community soon saw its value. Logs are a partial transcript of past events. Used with an understanding of their limits, they greatly improve our picture of the past when added to the body of evidence, and point to further evidence to seek. Durable logs are therefore a critical part of security posture, and the book recommends every organisation keep at least a year of logs on hot standby. Storage keeps getting cheaper and logs compress well, so keeping more is advisable. Where regulations such as PCI-DSS, HIPAA, SOX or FISMA apply, the requirements are clear and inflexible, and some even mandate keeping logs in multiple locations via network aggregation (lesson 2.12).

docs.title: 2. Who sends, and who receives
docs.text:
Senders

  • UNIX, Linux and BSD: inherently syslog-aware, as are user programs whose developers include the feature.
  • Network equipment: most core devices — routers, switches, IDSes, firewalls, wireless access points — have long been able to send their log events to another host via the syslog protocol, even if they don't run a syslog daemon internally. Consumer gear increasingly can too.
  • Other devices: NAS heads, the drive sled banks of large storage area networks, surveillance cameras that log changes in their field of view, alarm systems logging door and window events, motion detectors. Many run embedded UNIX derivatives, so adding syslog is easy.
  • Windows: uses its own log format (lesson 2.11), but can "push" to a syslog destination with third-party service software.

What makes this convenient is that so many devices share a common logging mechanism. Instead of learning new tools or hand-parsing a sea of formats, mastering syslog gives you insight into the logs of thousands of kinds of devices. Forensic practitioners rarely get a break like this.

Receivers

  • The syslog daemon itself: easily configured to receive remote messages (like this lab's receiver).
  • NAS devices: embedded UNIX plus lots of storage, so many products include reception.
  • Log aggregation platforms: aggregators such as the free SOF-ELK (lesson 2.13) or commercial Splunk, and the SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) platforms investigators mostly meet, all receive syslog as a core feature. Tools built to vacuum up as many logs as possible would be remiss to ignore the most tried-and-true logging protocol.
  • Windows servers: can receive remote syslog with third-party software such as SolarWinds Kiwi Syslog Server or Snare Server.

docs.title: 3.1 On the wire: the traditional format (RFC 3164)
docs.text:
I sent one UDP message to the receiver with logger and captured the bytes on the wire.

logger --rfc3164 -n 127.0.0.30 -P 10514 -d -p local7.info -t dhcpd "DHCPACK on 10.10.1.19 to 02:00:00:00:01:19 via eth0"

-n is the server, -P the port, -d UDP, -p facility.severity (section 4) and -t the tag (program name).

(Actual output; UDP payload)

<190>Nov  5 07:59:40 vm dhcpd: DHCPACK on 10.10.1.19 to 02:00:00:00:01:19 via eth0
Part Value Meaning PRI <190> Facility and severity combined (section 4). 190 = local7.info Timestamp Nov 5 07:59:40 The sender's clock. No year or time zone Hostname vm The name the sender wrote Tag dhcpd: Usually program name and PID (like sshd[999]:), but a program can write any string Message DHCPACK on … Free text

This format is a later write-up (RFC 3164, 2001, informational) of practice on BSD systems, so it's convention rather than a strict standard, with many device-specific variants.

The receiver's traditional-format file (RSYSLOG_TraditionalFileFormat) stored it without the PRI.

(Actual output)

Nov  5 07:59:40 vm dhcpd: DHCPACK on 10.10.1.19 to 02:00:00:00:01:19 via eth0

docs.title: 3.2 The current standard: RFC 5424
docs.text:
logger --rfc5424 -n 127.0.0.30 -P 10514 -d -p authpriv.warning -t sshd "Failed password for invalid user admin from 198.51.100.23 port 51122 ssh2"

(Actual output; UDP payload)

<84>1 2026-11-05T07:59:40.968247+00:00 vm sshd - - [timeQuality tzKnown="1" isSynced="0"] Failed password for invalid user admin from 198.51.100.23 port 51122 ssh2

After <84> (the PRI) comes 1, the format version, then a timestamp with year and time zone (to microseconds), the hostname, the app name (sshd), the process ID (- = none), the message ID (-), structured data ([timeQuality …]) and the message.

[Supplement] RFC 5424 (2009) is the current standard

The book shows a default format and an "enhanced" one (with ISO 8601 timestamp and PRI). As a wire format, RFC 5424 (2009) is the standard that replaces RFC 3164. In the structured data timeQuality above, tzKnown="1" means "the time zone is known" and isSynced="0" means "the sender's clock is not synchronised (by NTP or similar)". The sender reports its own clock quality, a useful clue for investigators (this container really had no time-sync information). Many devices still send RFC 3164 shapes or variants, though.

docs.title: 3.3 [Caution] No year, no time zone
docs.text:
RFC 3164 timestamps have no year and no time zone. The receiver has to guess the year. I tested how rsyslog fills it in.

First, with the receiver's real clock (2026-11-05), I sent three messages with different timestamps.

(Actual output; the "reported time" as the receiver interpreted it, and the actual reception time)

<14> reported=2026-12-31T23:59:59+00:00 received=2026-11-05T07:59:53.993084+00:00
<14> reported=2026-11-30T12:00:00+00:00 received=2026-11-05T07:59:53.993084+00:00
<14> reported=2026-11-04T23:00:00+00:00 received=2026-11-05T07:59:53.993149+00:00

Next I used faketime to imitate the receiver's clock at 2027-01-01 00:00:30, simulating messages created just before year end arriving after the new year.

(Actual output)

<14> reported=2027-12-31T23:59:58+00:00 received=2027-01-01T00:00:32.516385+00:00
<14> reported=2027-01-01T00:00:29+00:00 received=2027-01-01T00:00:32.516385+00:00

The message created at Dec 31 23:59:58 was interpreted as 2027-12-31, nearly a year in the future relative to its reception. This rsyslog version attached the receiver's current year to year-less timestamps, even though the message was really from 2026-12-31.

What this means for investigations: in incidents spanning the new year, sorting RFC 3164-style logs chronologically can badly scramble the order. Confirm whether a Dec 31 line is really from last year using the file's last-modified time, log rotation dates and the surrounding lines. And with no time zone, check the device's configuration for whether it logs local time or UTC.

docs.title: 3.4 [Caution] The sender sets the timestamp and hostname
docs.text:
A message's timestamp and hostname are written by whoever created the message, and the receiver records them verbatim. A device with a bad clock is recorded with the bad time, and they can also be forged at will. I crafted a message with a different hostname and a timestamp from early this year.

printf '<38>Jan  2 03:04:05 fw-core-01 sshd[999]: Accepted password for root from 203.0.113.9 port 4444 ssh2' > /dev/udp/127.0.0.30/10514

/dev/udp/address/port is a bash feature that sends a UDP datagram to that address. You can "make up" syslog messages without any special program.

(Actual output)

Traditional-format file:
Jan  2 03:04:05 fw-core-01 sshd[999]: Accepted password for root from 203.0.113.9 port 4444 ssh2

File that also records receiver-side information:
<38> reported=2026-01-02T03:04:05+00:00 received=2026-11-05T07:59:40.970961+00:00 claimed_host=fw-core-01 from_ip=127.0.0.1 proto=imudp tag=sshd[999]: msg= Accepted password for root from 203.0.113.9 port 4444 ssh2

From the traditional file alone, it reads as "root logged in to the core firewall fw-core-01 in the early hours of 2 January". But the line with receiver-side information shows the actual reception time (5 November) and the address that actually sent it (127.0.0.1, not the firewall).

The second file comes from a template (output shape) defined on the receiver:

template(name="Forensic" type="string"
  string="<%PRI%> reported=%timereported:::date-rfc3339% received=%timegenerated:::date-rfc3339% claimed_host=%HOSTNAME% from_ip=%fromhost-ip% proto=%inputname% tag=%syslogtag% msg=%msg:::drop-last-lf%\n")
Property Meaning %timereported% The timestamp written in the message (set by the sender) %timegenerated% When the receiver received the message (receiver's clock) %HOSTNAME% The hostname written in the message %fromhost-ip% The network address that actually sent the message %inputname% The input module that received it (imudp, imtcp)

What this means for investigations: if you run a central collector, configure it to record reception time and sender address too, as here. If they aren't recorded, state in the report that logged hostnames and timestamps are claims, and confirm them with the device's own logs or network records (the real source of the syslog packets). The book's enhanced format (<%PRI%>%timegenerated:::date-rfc3339% …) uses timegenerated for the same reason; if you choose just one, understand what that choice means.

docs.title: 3.5 Message size
docs.text:
Maximum message length depends on the syslog implementation. Many older implementations cut messages at 1,024 bytes (the limit RFC 3164 describes). UDP has its own limit: over IPv4, a single UDP datagram can carry at most 65,507 bytes of data (65,535 − 20-byte IP header − 8-byte UDP header). The book's 65,527 doesn't subtract the IP header.

I sent this rsyslog UDP messages of various lengths.

(Actual output; start of each message and the length of the line stored)

LEN01000  1156
LEN02000  2156
LEN08000  8156
LEN09000  8210
LEN20000  8210

The 9,000- and 20,000-byte messages were both cut to the same 8,210-byte line (the line includes the template's prefix). This rsyslog's default maximum message size is 8 KB, and nothing in the line indicated truncation. For logs carrying long content — long command lines, entire web requests, stack traces — remember that the end may be missing. Check maxMessageSize on both sender and receiver if needed.

docs.title: 4. Facility, severity and the PRI
docs.text:
Every syslog message carries two values the daemon uses to decide how to process it and where to store it.

  • Facility: an identifier of the message's source. The daemon uses it to choose a file. There are eight local0–local7 facilities reserved for administrators, and de facto conventions have emerged (many Linux distributions use local7 for DHCP, for example). But assignment is arbitrary: nothing stops anyone tagging FTP messages as mail, and elaborate setups repurpose legacy facilities like news or uucp. That's why collecting the relevant services' configuration files is critical in an investigation.
  • Severity: importance. Its meaning is more straightforward, but it's also set arbitrarily by the sender, and the daemon uses it to decide what to do: drop debug, send info to a frequently truncated file, email administrators about errors, and send alert and emergency to every possible destination including local and remote terminals.

Facilities (RFC 5424)

No. Keyword Meaning No. Keyword Meaning 0 kern kernel 12 (none) NTP 1 user user-level 13 (none) log audit 2 mail mail 14 (none) log alert 3 daemon system daemons 15 cron scheduler (clock daemon) 4 auth security/authorisation 16 local0 local use 5 syslog syslogd itself 17 local1 local use 6 lpr line printer 18 local2 local use 7 news network news 19 local3 local use 8 uucp UUCP 20 local4 local use 9 (none) clock daemon 21 local5 local use 10 authpriv security/authorisation (private) 22 local6 local use 11 ftp FTP 23 local7 local use

Severities (RFC 5424)

No. Keyword Meaning 0 emerg (panic) System is unusable 1 alert Action must be taken immediately 2 crit Critical conditions 3 err (error) Error conditions 4 warning (warn) Warning conditions 5 notice Normal but significant condition 6 info Informational 7 debug Debug-level

The PRI combines the two into one number.

PRI = facility × 8 + severity
facility = PRI ÷ 8 (quotient),  severity = PRI ÷ 8 (remainder)

(Actual output; decoded with Python's divmod)

190 -> facility 23 severity 6     # local7.info  (the DHCP message in 3.1)
84 -> facility 10 severity 4      # authpriv.warning  (the sshd message in 3.2)
8 -> facility 1 severity 0        # user.emerg
38 -> facility 4 severity 6       # auth.info  (the forged message in 3.4)
13 -> facility 1 severity 5       # user.notice  (logger's default)
165 -> facility 20 severity 5     # local4.notice

TShark also splits the PRI into facility and level when it dissects syslog (this lab used port 10514, so I set the dissector with -d udp.port==10514,syslog). The default file format drops the PRI (the traditional file in 3.1), which makes it hard to tell a message's facility and severity from the log alone. That's why administrators often include the PRI in their configuration.

docs.title: 5. Reading the configuration: "where do this system's logs go?"
docs.text:
Here's the book's example adapted to this environment as the sender's configuration (only paths and addresses changed).

template(name="FullDateWithPRI" type="string" string="<%PRI%>%timegenerated:::date-rfc3339% %HOSTNAME% %syslogtag%%msg:::drop-last-lf%\n")
template(name="smsTemplate" type="string" string="%TIMESTAMP% %HOSTNAME% %syslogtag% %msg%\n")
$ActionFileDefaultTemplate FullDateWithPRI

*.info;mail.none;authpriv.none;cron.none     /…/log/messages
*.info;mail.none;authpriv.none;cron.none     @127.0.0.30:10514
authpriv.*                                   /…/log/secure
authpriv.=warning                            @@127.0.0.30:10514
mail.*                                       /…/log/maillog
local7.*                                     /…/log/dhcp.log
local3.*                                     /…/log/named.log
local6.!notice                               /…/log/clamd_debug.log
*.emerg                                      action(type="omprog" binary="/…/sms_send.sh" template="smsTemplate")

docs.title: 5.1 Selectors (left)
docs.text:
They take the form facility.severity, chain with semicolons (;) and allow wildcards (*).

  • Severity means "this or higher": *.info selects info and everything more important: notice, warning, err, crit, alert, emerg.
  • none: mail.none means "exclude mail".
  • =: exactly that severity. authpriv.=warning is warning only.
  • !: remove that severity and higher. See the [Correction] below.

docs.title: 5.2 Actions (right)
docs.text:
Form Meaning /path/file Write to that file @host:port Forward to a remote server over UDP @@host:port Forward over TCP ([Supplement]: the book's example has only @) ^/path/program;template Run a program for each message (legacy syntax) action(type="omprog" …) Keep a program running and pass messages on standard input (rsyslog's current way) :omusrmsg:* Show on every logged-in user's terminal (like wall)

$ActionFileDefaultTemplate sets the default template for file output. With several templates, remember that the same event can be stored in different shapes at different destinations.

docs.title: 5.3 Trying it
docs.text:
I fed eight messages into the sending rsyslog.

L="logger -u …/dev-log"                    # the sending rsyslog's socket
$L -p local7.info     -t dhcpd   "DHCPACK on 10.10.1.19"
$L -p authpriv.info   -t sshd    "Accepted publickey for jkim from 10.10.1.19"
$L -p authpriv.warning -t sshd   "Failed password for root from 198.51.100.23"
$L -p mail.err        -t postfix "connect to mx.example.net: Connection timed out"
$L -p local6.debug    -t clamd   "scan detail"
$L -p local6.warning  -t clamd   "Eicar-Test-Signature FOUND"
$L -p user.emerg      -t root    "LAB_EMERGENCY_TEST"
$L -p user.debug      -t app     "debug noise"

(Actual output; lines stored in each file)

== dhcp.log
<190>2026-11-05T08:00:28.816246+00:00 vm dhcpd: DHCPACK on 10.10.1.19
== maillog
<19>2026-11-05T08:00:28.821820+00:00 vm postfix: connect to mx.example.net: Connection timed out
== messages
<190>2026-11-05T08:00:28.816246+00:00 vm dhcpd: DHCPACK on 10.10.1.19
<180>2026-11-05T08:00:28.825199+00:00 vm clamd: Eicar-Test-Signature FOUND
<8>2026-11-05T08:00:28.826954+00:00 vm root: LAB_EMERGENCY_TEST
== secure
<86>2026-11-05T08:00:28.818307+00:00 vm sshd: Accepted publickey for jkim from 10.10.1.19
<84>2026-11-05T08:00:28.820128+00:00 vm sshd: Failed password for root from 198.51.100.23
== sms.out  (received by the script started via omprog)
SMS-GATEWAY got: Nov  5 08:00:28 vm root:  LAB_EMERGENCY_TEST
== receiver (127.0.0.30)
<190> … proto=imudp tag=dhcpd: …
<84>  … proto=imtcp tag=sshd: …
<180> … proto=imudp tag=clamd: …
<8>   … proto=imudp tag=root: …

How to read it:

  • The DHCP message (local7.info) went to two files, dhcp.log and messages, and to the receiver too (*.info also matches local7).
  • Authentication messages are absent from messages (authpriv.none) and present only in secure. Of those, only the warning-level failed login went to the receiver, over TCP (proto=imtcp, from authpriv.=warning → @@). The successful login isn't on the remote side.
  • The mail error is only in maillog, not on the receiver (mail.none).
  • The emergency message (user.emerg) went to messages, the receiver and the SMS script, which received it in smsTemplate shape (no PRI, year-less timestamp). The same event in three shapes.
  • user.debug is nowhere (below *.info).
  • clamd_debug.log, meant to receive local6.debug, was never even created. See the next box.

[Correction] kern.!notice on its own selects nothing

The book says "kern.!notice would match all kernel messages with a severity lower than notice". In rsyslog's rules (and sysklogd's, on which they're based), ! removes from what's already selected, so with nothing selected beforehand the result is empty. I checked directly.

(Actual output; sending local6 debug, info, notice, warning and err one each)

local6.!notice              → file never created (nothing matched)
local6.*;local6.!notice     → debug, info  (below notice)
local6.=warning             → warning

To select "below notice", select everything first, then remove: local6.*;local6.!notice. When reading someone else's configuration during an investigation, remember that a ! line may have logged nothing at all, contrary to its intent. Where you can, confirm with rsyslogd -N1 -f configfile (configuration check) and whether the files actually exist.

[Supplement] How ^ program execution actually behaves

The book's ^/usr/local/bin/sms_send.py;smsTemplate (legacy syntax) still worked in rsyslog 8.2312. Running it, a new program process was started for each message, with the message passed as a command-line argument (the script's arguments: CARET_TEST). Many messages mean as many processes, and message content lands on the command line verbatim, so rsyslog's documentation recommends omprog, which keeps the program running and passes messages on standard input.

Figure 5-1. Where logs go in this configuration (one group per selector, top to bottom: selector → destination)

flowchart TD
    A["*.info (except mail, authpriv, cron)"] --> F1["file: messages"]
    A --> N1["UDP @ receiver"]
    F1 ~~~ B["authpriv.*"]
    B --> F2["file: secure"]
    F2 ~~~ C["authpriv.=warning"]
    C --> N2["TCP @@ receiver"]
    N2 ~~~ D["mail.* / local7.* / local3.*"]
    D --> F3["files: maillog / dhcp.log / named.log"]
    F3 ~~~ E["*.emerg"]
    E --> P1["program: SMS script (omprog)"]
    E -.-> X["also matches *.info, so it also goes<br/>to messages and the UDP forward"]

How to read it: a message matching a selector goes to the destinations its arrows point to. A message matching several selectors goes to all their destinations (dotted line: an *.emerg message also matches *.info, so it also goes to messages and the UDP forward). The unlinked gaps between groups only stack them vertically and don't imply any order. As the book says, "where does this system's log data go?" is a deceptively complex question even for a basic configuration. During an investigation, collect the configuration (including included files such as /etc/rsyslog.d/*.conf) and draw a picture like this yourself.

docs.title: 6.1 UDP loses messages silently
docs.text:
On the same computer (loopback), I fired 200,000 short messages at the receiver over UDP and over TCP.

(Actual output)

UDP: sent 200000 in 0.63s   → received: 196760
TCP: sent 200000 over TCP in 0.19s → received: 200000

UDP lost 3,240 messages (about 1.6%), and neither sender nor receiver recorded the fact — on loopback, without even crossing a network. When the receive buffer overflows, the OS drops datagrams quietly. Every TCP message arrived.

What this means for investigations: a gap in the central syslog server's records doesn't mean nothing happened. Losses grow when logs surge, as during an incident. Where possible, compare against the original device's local logs, and for a UDP receiver check the OS's UDP receive error counters (such as receive buffer errors in netstat -su).

docs.title: 6.2 TCP, TLS, RELP
docs.text:
[Supplement] Transport options (as of 2026-11-05)

  • UDP 514 (RFC 5426): most common, most prone to loss, and plaintext.
  • TCP (port 514 by convention; RFC 6587 documents the framing): no loss while the connection holds, but if the receiver goes down, messages pile up in the sender's buffer and can overflow. The TCP messages in this lab were delimited by newlines (\n).
  • Syslog over TLS (RFC 5425, usually port 6514): encryption and peer authentication.
  • RELP (rsyslog's Reliable Event Logging Protocol): application-level acknowledgements prevent loss.

From a network forensics perspective: plaintext syslog (UDP/TCP 514) can be read straight from packet captures; this lab read the wire messages with TShark. If the central server's logs were deleted or tampered with, pcaps of the path in between can serve as a second copy. Conversely, it means sensitive information — failed authentications, usernames, internal addresses — flows in plaintext.

docs.title: 7. [Changed] Syslog in the journald era
docs.text:
[Changed] Modern Linux may have no /var/log/messages

On systemd-based Linux, systemd-journald receives logs first and stores them in its own binary format (the journal), read with journalctl. And some distributions no longer install a traditional syslog daemon by default. For example, Debian 12 (2023) dropped rsyslog from the default installation and made the journal persistent on disk (/var/log/journal) (checked via the Debian mailing-list discussion and related coverage; the official release notes couldn't be opened from this environment, 2026-11-05). Others, like this lab's Ubuntu 24.04, still ship rsyslog alongside.

What this means for investigations: ① When investigating a Linux server, don't conclude "there are no logs" because /var/log/messages or /var/log/syslog is missing. Collect the journal files under /var/log/journal/ and read them with journalctl --file. ② Unlike syslog, the journal records information about the sending process (PID, UID, executable path, systemd unit) for each entry as values verified by the kernel, making it more robust against section 3.4's "forged tag" problem. ③ To centralise, rsyslog or syslog-ng read from the journal and forward (imjournal), or tools such as systemd-journal-remote are used; on the wire it becomes syslog again.

docs.title: 8. How this is used in real investigations
docs.text:
1. Collect the configuration first. Use /etc/rsyslog.conf and /etc/rsyslog.d/*.conf (or syslog-ng's configuration) to map "what goes where" (section 5). Facility assignments are only convention.
  2. Separate sender-set values from receiver-verified ones. Timestamps and hostnames are claims; compare with reception time and sender address where recorded (section 3.4).
  3. Check year and time zone. In RFC 3164 shapes, the year is the receiver's guess and can go wrong across the new year (section 3.3). Check the device's time zone setting.
  4. Suspect gaps and truncation. UDP loss (section 6.1), maximum message size (section 3.5).
  5. Compare original and copies. The device's local logs, the central server's logs, and pcaps of the path between.
  6. Don't forget the journal. On systemd systems, /var/log/journal/ (section 7).

docs.title: 9. Summary
docs.text:
• Syslog is both a daemon that receives messages and routes them to destinations and a protocol on the wire, shared by UNIX, network equipment, all kinds of embedded devices and (via third parties) Windows. Receivers include syslog daemons, NAS devices, aggregation platforms and SIEMs.
  • The traditional format (RFC 3164) is PRI, timestamp, hostname, tag and message, with no year or time zone. In my test, rsyslog attached the receiver's year, so a Dec 31 message arriving after the new year was interpreted a year in the future. [Supplement] The current standard, RFC 5424, carries year, time zone and structured data (timeQuality isSynced).
  • The sender sets the timestamp and hostname, so they can be forged. My crafted message landed verbatim in the traditional file, while timegenerated and fromhost-ip showed the truth.
  • Message size: old implementations used 1,024 bytes; this rsyslog cut at its default 8 KB without any marker. IPv4 UDP carries at most 65,507 bytes of data.
  • PRI = facility × 8 + severity; 190 = local7.info. Facility assignment is arbitrary, so configuration files are needed.
  • Selectors: "this or higher", none, =, !. [Correction] ! alone selects nothing; write local6.*;local6.!notice for "below notice". Actions: file, @ UDP, @@ TCP, program (^ runs per message; omprog recommended), all user terminals.
  • UDP silently lost 3,240 of 200,000 messages even on loopback; TCP delivered all. [Supplement] TLS (RFC 5425), RELP. Plaintext syslog in pcaps is a second copy.
  • [Changed] More distributions default to journald; Debian 12 dropped rsyslog from the default installation.

docs.title: Review questions
docs.text:
Question 1. (Basics) Explain each part of this line, and name at least two things you can't tell from it alone.

<86>Mar  3 02:17:44 web-03 sshd[2231]: Accepted password for deploy from 203.0.113.50 port 50122 ssh2
Answer and explanation

<86>: the PRI. 86 = 10 × 8 + 6, so facility 10 (authpriv), severity 6 (info). Mar 3 02:17:44: time on the sender's clock. web-03: the hostname the sender wrote. sshd[2231]:: the tag (program name and PID). The rest is the message: the deploy account logged in successfully with a password from 203.0.113.50. Can't tell: ① the year (section 3.3); ② the time zone (is that server on UTC or local time?); ③ whether its clock was right; ④ whether web-03 really sent this message (section 3.4; needs the receiver's fromhost-ip); ⑤ whether this is the device's own log or a copy on a central server.

Question 2. (Changed conditions) An incident ran from the night of 31 December 2026 into the early hours of 1 January 2027. Sorting the central syslog server's file (received in RFC 3164 shape, stored with RFC 3339 timestamps) chronologically sends the lines that look like the start of the incident to the very end (2027-12-31). What happened, and how do you fix it?

Answer and explanation

RFC 3164-style messages have no year, so the receiver filled it in. As in section 3.3's experiment, this rsyslog attached the year at reception (2027), so messages created on 2026-12-31 were stored as 2027-12-31. To fix: ① if reception time (timegenerated) was stored too, compare and subtract a year from lines whose reported time is far in the future of their reception; ② if not, use line order in the file (written in reception order), log rotation times and comparison with other devices' logs; ③ document the method and grounds in the report. Going forward, have devices send RFC 5424 (with year and time zone) and have the receiver store reception time.

Question 3. (Common misconception) "The central syslog server holds a successful-login record from fw-core-01, so someone definitely logged in to that firewall." What else must you check?

Answer and explanation

A syslog message's hostname and timestamp are values written by the sender and can be forged (section 3.4: my crafted message landed verbatim in the traditional file). Check: ① the address that actually sent the line (whether fromhost-ip was stored; if not, pcaps of syslog packets for that period or the firewall's session records); ② whether the firewall's own local log has the same record; ③ the firewall's authentication server (RADIUS, TACACS+) records; ④ whether the message's format matches what that device normally sends (tag, field order, spacing). If the receiver accepts UDP 514 from any address, anyone on the same network can "plant" lines like this.

Question 4. (Reading configuration) In the configuration below, where do an authpriv.info message and an authpriv.err message go?

*.info;authpriv.none        /var/log/messages
authpriv.*                  /var/log/secure
authpriv.=err               @@198.51.100.5:514
*.err                       @198.51.100.6:514
Answer and explanation

authpriv.info: not to messages (authpriv.none), yes to secure (authpriv.*), not to 198.51.100.5 (not =err), and *.err means err or higher, so info doesn't match → secure only. authpriv.err: not to messages, yes to secure, to 198.51.100.5 over TCP (@@), and it matches *.err, so also to 198.51.100.6 over UDP (@) → three places. A message matching several lines goes to all their destinations, and the * in *.err includes authpriv (the first line's authpriv.none applies only to that line).

Question 5. (Corrected content) A colleague added kern.!info /var/log/kern-debug.log to collect only debug messages, but the file stays empty. Why, and how should it be fixed?

Answer and explanation

! removes from what's already selected, so with nothing selected first, nothing matches (section 5.3's [Correction]: local6.!notice alone didn't even create its file). To select "below info (= debug)", select everything and then remove — kern.*;kern.!info — or, for debug alone, use kern.=debug. After changing it, check the configuration with rsyslogd -N1. Since logger -p kern.debug from a user program can't easily produce kern-facility messages, testing the same syntax with another facility is safer.

Question 6. (Interpretation) On the day of the incident, one web server's logs on the central syslog server (UDP reception) are patchy from 14:02 to 14:09, exactly when the attacker's scan made the web server's logs surge. What possibilities do you consider, and how do you check?

Answer and explanation

Consider UDP loss first (section 6.1: even on loopback, 1.6% of 200,000 messages vanished silently). When logs surge, receive buffers overflow or the network in between drops datagrams. Other possibilities: rate limiting on the sender (rsyslog's rate limiting), or the attacker blocking log forwarding. Check: ① the web server's own local logs (are lines continuous for that period?); ② the receiving OS's UDP receive error counters and rsyslog's own statistics (if impstats was on); ③ pcaps for the period (did syslog packets actually arrive?); ④ internal messages from the sending rsyslog (such as "messages lost due to rate-limiting"). Don't read a gap as "nothing happened".

Question 7. (Changed conditions) You're investigating a Debian 12 server with neither /var/log/syslog nor /var/log/auth.log. Were the logs deleted?

Answer and explanation

Not necessarily. Debian 12 dropped rsyslog from the default installation and keeps the journal persistently in /var/log/journal/ (section 7). First collect the *.journal files under /var/log/journal/ (from an image, read them with journalctl --file or --directory), and check whether rsyslog was ever installed (package records, configuration files). If rsyslog was installed and the files are gone, then suspect deletion or rotation settings. The journal stores each entry's PID, UID, executable and unit, so it can actually tell you more. Also run an integrity check on the journal files (journalctl --verify).

Question 8. (Application) If you were designing a new central syslog server, what principles would you include to support investigations? Give at least four.

Answer and explanation

For example: ① store reception time and sender address too (timegenerated, fromhost-ip), kept separate from reported time and hostname (section 3.4); ② require devices to use RFC 5424 (year and time zone), UTC and time synchronisation (section 3.3); ③ receive important sources over TCP or TLS (RFC 5425), or RELP to reduce loss and eavesdropping (section 6); ④ restrict which addresses may send (firewall, rsyslog allow-lists) and alert on never-seen sources (against forged messages); ⑤ raise the maximum message size enough (section 3.5); ⑥ keep reception statistics (impstats) to measure loss; ⑦ retain a year or more, with copies elsewhere as regulations require (section 1); ⑧ keep the original devices' local logs for a period as well, so they can be compared.

docs.text:
• Tools used in this environment: rsyslog 8.2312.0 (Ubuntu 24.04 package; imudp, imtcp, imuxsock, omprog), util-linux logger 2.39.3, faketime (imitating the receiver's clock), TShark 4.2.2, tcpdump, bash's /dev/udp, Python 3.13. Results obtained on 2026-11-05.
  • IETF, RFC 3164 (the BSD syslog protocol, 2001, informational), RFC 5424 (the syslog protocol, 2009: facility and severity tables, PRI, format version, structured data, timeQuality), RFC 5426 (UDP transport), RFC 5425 (TLS transport), RFC 6587 (framing for TCP transport).
  • rsyslog, documentation (selector syntax; properties timereported, timegenerated, fromhost-ip; templates; omprog; maxMessageSize; RELP).
  • Debian 12 logging change: the Debian developers' mailing-list discussion of November 2021 and related coverage (checked via search results on 2026-11-05; the official release notes couldn't be opened from this environment).
  • systemd, journalctl manual.

About this page

A personal study note, rewritten in my own words from several learning resources. The configuration and messages are my own, and the scenarios are hypothetical.

docs.title: 2.3 — Seeing the Past Through Tracking Cookies, and HTTP/2 and HTTP/3
2.3 — Seeing the Past Through Tracking Cookies, and HTTP/2 and HTTP/3
docs.text:
Scope of this lesson

  • Why advertising and analytics cookies are useful to investigators: they contain times from a past you have no other evidence for
  • The structure and reading of the classic analytics cookies (__utma, __utmb, __utmz). [Changed] today it's _ga and _ga_<ID>
  • A "user" is not a person but a cookie store: browsers, private mode, deletion
  • Marketing cookies (__hstc, hubspotutk, hsfirstvisit) and millisecond timestamps
  • [Changed] Browsers cap cookie lifetimes: Chrome 400 days, Safari 7 days
  • HTTP/2: binary framing, header compression, multiplexing (confirmed by decrypting HTTP/2 traffic captured directly, using session keys). [Changed] server push has been removed from browsers
  • HTTP/3: HTTP over QUIC, and what changes for investigations

Lab environment and notation

(Actual output) was produced in this environment. HTTP/2 traffic came from nghttp2 1.59.0's nghttpd server on loopback, run both over TLS (with a self-signed certificate I created) and in cleartext (h2c), with requests sent by curl 8.5.0 (built with nghttp2) and captured with tcpdump. TLS session keys were written with SSLKEYLOGFILE and used to decrypt with tshark 4.2.2. All cookie values are invented for illustration, and time conversions were computed directly with date.

docs.title: 1. A window onto a past you have no evidence for
docs.text:
(Hypothetical) The pcap captured from the employee's PC under investigation covers only one week from 1 November 2026. But the question is "when did this employee first look at that competitor's recruitment site?" Even if the week's packets contain visits to the site, that only shows they visited that week, not when the first time was.

What unexpectedly helps here are advertising and analytics cookies. These companies make money by recording as precisely as possible when visitors first came, how often, and from where, so they often store that information inside the cookie value. The cookie travels in the Cookie header with every request (lesson 2.1, section 6.4), so a single line of today's packets can yield a first-visit time months ago.

As an analogy, it's a café loyalty card. Look at a customer's card today and you see the date it was issued, the date of the last visit and the number of stamps so far. The café's CCTV may hold only a week, but the card tells an older story. The analogy differs in two ways. First, the card belongs not to a person but to a wallet (the browser's cookie store). Second, the café (the company) designs the card format and often doesn't publish it, so interpretation always carries caveats.

docs.title: 2. The classic analytics cookies: __utma, __utmb, __utmz
docs.text:
The source material covers in detail three old cookies of what was long the most widely used web analytics service. They're no longer used (section 3), but you can still meet them in old evidence (pcaps from years ago, old cookie files on disk), and they're a good example for learning "how to read the numbers inside a cookie", so here is their structure. The utm in the names comes from Urchin Tracking Module, on which the service was based.

All are dot-separated (.), and the first value is a hash of the site (domain): it's the same across cookies of the same site.

Cookie Lifetime Composition of the value __utma 2 years domain hash . visitor identifier . first visit . previous visit . current visit . visit count __utmb 30 minutes domain hash . pages this session . outbound link countdown (from 10) . current visit time __utmz 6 months domain hash . time . visit count . source count . source information (utmcsr=source|utmccn=campaign|utmcmd=medium|utmctr=term)

(Hypothetical) Here's an __utma value invented for this lesson.

__utma=111872281.1938459823.1767225600.1793000000.1793512345.14

The time values are Unix time (seconds since 1970, lesson 1.3), so convert with date.

date -u -d @1767225600
date -u -d @1793000000
date -u -d @1793512345

(Actual output)

1767225600 → 2026-01-01 00:00:00 UTC   (first visit)
1793000000 → 2026-10-26 07:33:20 UTC   (previous visit)
1793512345 → 2026-11-01 05:52:25 UTC   (current visit)

The final 14 is the visit count. One line of packets from 1 November tells the story "this browser first came to this site on 1 January 2026, this is its 14th visit, and the previous visit was 26 October", a past a week of pcap could never show. This is exactly one of the objectives of the lab in lesson 2.4: using advertising cookies to see beyond the evidence you have.

__utmz's source information tells you how the visitor arrived at the site. utmcsr=search-engine|utmcmd=organic|utmctr=... means via search, utmcmd=referral via a link on another site, and utmcsr=(direct) via a typed address or bookmark. As lesson 2.1 showed, Referer now often gives only the origin, so such source information, where it survives, is valuable (especially in old evidence).

docs.title: 3. [Changed] Today's analytics cookies: _ga and _ga_<ID>
docs.text:
The old tracking code that set the __utm* cookies fell out of use long ago, and the generation that replaced it (Universal Analytics) stopped processing data for standard properties on 1 July 2023 (per Google's help centre). The official cookie documentation for the generation widely used today (GA4) lists these two:

Cookie Default lifetime Official description _ga 2 years used to distinguish users _ga_<container ID> 2 years used to persist session state

The official documentation doesn't describe the internal structure of the values. But a widely used interpretation is that _ga looks like GA1.1.<random number>.<Unix time>, with the last number being the time the cookie was first created. With the invented value placed in this lab's HTTP/2 requests:

_ga=GA1.1.1234567890.1793500000

date -u -d @1793500000

(Actual output) 2026-11-01 02:26:40 UTC. If the interpretation holds, that's "when this browser store first got that site's _ga cookie".

_ga_<ID> is known to hold values such as the session start time, session number and last activity time, and several sources reported around 2025 that its format changed from GS1.1.… to $-separated GS2.1.…. This change was confirmed from third-party analyses, not the vendor's official documentation, so when interpreting real evidence, look at the values as they were at the time, and open the same site in a test browser to see how the cookie changes before relying on it.

[Caution] Using undocumented values as evidence

Analytics vendors have no obligation to publish cookie formats, and change them without notice. So in the report, record ① on what basis you read a number as a time (official documentation, public analysis, or your own test), and ② whether it agrees with other evidence (as in the source material's example, compare with the browser history or the creation time in the cookie database). If there's only one interpretation, write "appears to be".

docs.title: 4. A "user" is a cookie store
docs.text:
The "user" a cookie identifies is not a person but one cookie store. Confusing the two badly skews conclusions.

  • Each browser is different. If one person uses Chrome and Firefox, there are two cookie stores and so two "users". The same goes for different profiles in the same browser.
  • Private mode is a new store each time. Every private window starts from an empty store, so by cookies it's a "new user arriving for the first time" every time. In private mode, __utma's first-visit time is just a time after that private window was opened.
  • Deleting starts over. If the user deleted cookies, the first-visit time resets to after that.
  • Several people can share one store. Shared PCs, shared accounts.

So read a cookie's first-visit time not as "when this person first visited" but as "when this store first received that site's cookie, and it hasn't been deleted since". Still, the same cookie value appearing on several days and from several addresses is a strong thread linking the same browser store, which other evidence (logon records, the endpoint) can tie to a person.

docs.title: 5. Marketing cookies: __hstc, hubspotutk, hsfirstvisit
docs.text:
Analytics services aren't the only ones using such cookies. Seeing cookies from several different trackers in one case is common, and each vendor's format has to be looked up and interpreted. The source material's example is a marketing automation service's cookies.

  • __hstc: the main visitor-tracking cookie. domain hash . visitor identifier . first visit . previous visit . current visit . visit count, almost the same structure as __utma, but with times in milliseconds (13 digits).
  • hubspotutk: the visitor identifier. The same as __hstc's second value, used to link the same person across several sites using that service.
  • hsfirstvisit: a cookie present in the source material's era that held the address through which the visitor first entered the domain and a millisecond time.

Convert millisecond times by dropping the last three digits or dividing by 1000.

date -u -d @1793512345    # first 10 digits of 1793512345678

(Actual output) 2026-11-01 05:52:25 UTC (the trailing 678 is 0.678 seconds).

[Changed] Lifetimes have changed, and official values need checking

The source material gives __hstc two years and hubspotutk and hsfirstvisit ten years. Many sites' published cookie lists now give __hstc and hubspotutk 13 months, but some say six months, so they disagree (search results, 2026-11-05). The vendor has changed lifetimes and its cookie list to meet privacy regulations. In real cases, check the vendor's current official documentation and the expiry of cookies actually received in a test browser.

docs.title: 6. [Changed] Browsers cap cookie lifetimes
docs.text:
Even if a vendor sets "two years" or "ten years", the browser may cut it shorter. GA4's official cookie documentation itself notes browser limits such as "a maximum of 400 days for Chrome and 7 days for Safari if a user doesn't return". Safari limits the lifetime of cookies set by script, and Chrome caps cookies at 400 days.

What it means for investigations: a first-visit time three weeks ago in a cookie doesn't mean "first came three weeks ago". A Safari user may have come earlier, with the cookie disappearing every seven days. Conversely, a first visit two years ago also means the browser didn't delete cookies in that time. You need the browser type and version (lesson 2.1's User-Agent and Client Hints) to know the upper bound of a cookie's times.

docs.title: 7. Where cookies are visible
docs.text:
• Plain HTTP packets: the Cookie header is visible as-is. Rare today.
  • HTTPS: not visible from packets alone. You need records from a TLS-intercepting proxy (lesson 1.2) or session keys (lesson 1.12, section 8).
  • Proxy logs: the default format doesn't record headers (lesson 1.3). They can be configured to record cookies, but session cookies are login keys in themselves, so store them with care.
  • The endpoint's cookie database: the domain of disk forensics. Not kept in private mode.

And today's analytics cookies mostly attach to the visited site's own domain (first party). So the _ga cookie appears in the Cookie header of requests to that site, not to the analytics vendor. In this lab too, the _ga value travelled on both requests to the site (127.0.0.1:8445) (actual output).

docs.title: 8. HTTP/2: a completely different shape, the same meaning
8.1 What changed
docs.text:
HTTP/2 (RFC 9113) keeps the meaning of methods, status codes and headers from HTTP/1.1, but its shape on the wire is completely different.

  • Binary framing: traffic moves in binary units called frames instead of text. Following the stream as in lesson 1.9 shows almost nothing readable.
  • Header compression (HPACK, RFC 7541): headers are compressed, and frequent ones are sent as index numbers. It's a stateful compression that remembers headers sent earlier in the same connection, so missing the beginning of a connection can make later headers undecodable.
  • Pseudo-headers: :method, :path, :authority (HTTP/1.1's Host) and :scheme replace the request line, and :status replaces the status line (lesson 2.2: no reason phrase).
  • Multiplexing: several streams (numbered request/response pairs) travel simultaneously in one TCP connection. Streams opened by the client have odd numbers (1, 3, 5, …).
  • TLS: not mandatory by the standard, but browsers use HTTP/2 only over TLS. Cleartext HTTP/2 (h2c) appears only between servers or in tools.

docs.title: 8.2 Seeing it: zero lines without keys, a table with them
docs.text:
I requested two files from nghttpd over HTTPS. curl put both requests on one TCP connection.

SSLKEYLOGFILE=$PWD/keys.log curl -s -k --http2 -A "Mozilla/5.0 (X11; Linux x86_64; rv:140.0) Gecko/20100101 Firefox/140.0" \
  -H "Cookie: _ga=GA1.1.1234567890.1793500000" https://127.0.0.1:8445/index.html https://127.0.0.1:8445/report.txt

Applying http2 in tshark without session keys gave zero lines: everything was encrypted with TLS. Given the keys written via SSLKEYLOGFILE:

tshark -n -r h2.pcap -o tls.keylog_file:keys.log -Y 'http2.type == 1' -T fields \
  -e tcp.stream -e http2.streamid -e http2.headers.method -e http2.headers.path \
  -e http2.headers.authority -e http2.headers.user_agent -e http2.headers.status

(Actual output, User-Agent column partly trimmed)

0   1   GET /index.html 127.0.0.1:8445  Mozilla/5.0 (X11; Linux x86_64; rv:140.0) ...
0   1,1                 200
0   3   GET /report.txt 127.0.0.1:8445  Mozilla/5.0 (X11; Linux x86_64; rv:140.0) ...
0   3,3                 200
  • http2.type == 1 selects only HEADERS frames (frames carrying headers).
  • The first column is 0 throughout: one TCP stream. Inside it, HTTP/2 streams 1 and 3 each carried one request. Lesson 1.9's "TCP stream" and HTTP/2's "stream" are different concepts; don't mix them.
  • Wireshark shows decompressed headers by name, as in http2.headers.user_agent and http2.headers.path. Only the field names differ from HTTP/1.1's http.user_agent; the meaning is the same, so the filters and tables of lessons 1.9 and 1.10 carry over directly.

Following the stream of a request sent in cleartext HTTP/2 (h2c), only the very beginning was text and the rest was binary.

(Actual output, beginning)

PRI * HTTP/2.0

SM

..............d.....................>...

PRI * HTTP/2.0\r\n\r\nSM\r\n\r\n is the fixed opening string (connection preface) with which a client starts HTTP/2. If you see it, it's a cleartext HTTP/2 connection, and the headers after it are HPACK-compressed and unreadable. To have Wireshark dissect it, designate the port as HTTP/2 (-d tcp.port==8446,http2); doing so immediately showed GET /index.html and 200 (actual output).

[Supplement] HTTP/2 in browser developer tools

The source material also shows viewing HTTP/2 requests in a browser's developer tools (network tab). The browser is the TLS endpoint, so it shows headers such as :authority and :path regardless of encryption, and marks h2 (HTTP/2) or h3 (HTTP/3) in the protocol column. In investigations, use it to learn by opening the same site in a test browser what requests go out and in what shape. It's rarely possible to do this on the subject's own browser.

docs.title: 8.3 [Changed] Server push is gone from browsers
docs.text: The source material warns about HTTP/2 server push, where a server pushes objects nobody requested into the browser cache. A file in the cache can't be told apart as user-requested or server-pushed, so endpoint cache analysis could be wrong. This feature was disabled by default in Chrome 106 (2022) for lack of real benefit, and Firefox announced in 2024 that it would disable it, then removed it. So in today's browser caches this concern has largely gone, but keep it in mind for evidence from before 2022. Its suggested replacement, the 103 Early Hints response, only sends a hint to preload a resource; the browser makes the actual request.

docs.title: 9. HTTP/3: HTTP over QUIC
docs.text:
HTTP/3 (RFC 9114, 2022) moves the ideas of HTTP/2 onto QUIC (RFC 9000). What changes for investigations:

  • It uses UDP 443. Not TCP, so as lesson 1.2 showed, it can bypass proxies that handle only TCP. That's why you need to look separately at UDP 443 in firewall records.
  • Almost everything is encrypted. QUIC builds in TLS 1.3 and encrypts not only HTTP headers but most of the transport-layer information that would be visible with TCP (sequence numbers, acknowledgements). From packets alone you can see little more than addresses, ports, sizes, timing and connection identifiers, plus the SNI in the Client Hello of the first Initial packet (unless ECH is used, lesson 1.12).
  • Header compression is QPACK (RFC 9204): a similar idea to HPACK, but a different mechanism.
  • Decrypting it still needs session keys. Wireshark documents decrypting QUIC with keys in SSLKEYLOGFILE format. The curl in this environment was built without HTTP/3 support, so I couldn't test HTTP/3 directly.

In the end, for both HTTP/2 and HTTP/3, investigators need records from one end of the connection (the browser, a TLS-intercepting proxy, server logs) or session keys to see content. With packets alone, turn to lesson 1.12's flow analysis (size and timing patterns).

docs.title: 10. How to use this in real investigations
docs.text:
1. Identify the vendor from the cookie name. Names like _ga, __utma and __hstc tell you the vendor and format. For unknown names, look for the vendor's public documentation and published cookie lists.
  2. Try converting numbers to times. Ten digits are often seconds, thirteen milliseconds. Check that the converted time falls in a plausible range (the last few years).
  3. Read the "user" as a store. Allow for browsers, profiles, private mode and deletion, and bound the times with the browser's cookie-lifetime caps.
  4. Record the level of documentation. Note whether the basis is official documentation, public analysis or your own test.
  5. For HTTP/2 and 3, look for keys or endpoint records first. Without them, use the TLS version, SNI, and size and timing patterns.
  6. Distinguish TCP streams from HTTP/2 streams. One TCP connection carries several requests simultaneously.

docs.title: 11. Summary
docs.text:
• Advertising and analytics cookies contain past information such as first visit, previous visit, visit count and traffic source, showing beyond the period of your evidence. From an invented __utma value we read the first visit (2026-01-01), the previous visit and the visit count (14).
  • [Changed] __utm* is an old generation, and the next one stopped processing on 2023-07-01. Today it's _ga and _ga_<ID> (official default lifetime two years); their structure isn't in official documentation, and the format has changed before.
  • A cookie's "user" is a cookie store, varying with browser, private mode and deletion.
  • Marketing cookies use millisecond times. [Changed] Lifetimes differ from the source material, and published lists disagree, so check.
  • [Changed] Browsers cap cookie lifetimes (Chrome 400 days, Safari 7 days). The upper bound on first-visit times depends on the browser.
  • HTTP/2 is binary framing, HPACK, pseudo-headers and multiplexing. Without keys, zero lines; with session keys, HTTP/2 streams 1 and 3 appeared inside one TCP connection. Cleartext starts with PRI * HTTP/2.0.
  • [Changed] Server push has been removed from Chrome 106 and Firefox.
  • HTTP/3 encrypts almost everything over QUIC on UDP 443. Content is visible only through endpoint records or session keys.

docs.title: Review questions
docs.text:
Question 1. (Calculation) A pcap from 4 November 2026 shows __utma=48210377.551902814.1735689600.1792800000.1793750400.37. Find the dates of the first, previous and current visits, and the visit count.

Answer and explanation

date -u -d @1735689600 is 2025-01-01 00:00:00 UTC, @1792800000 is 2026-10-24 00:00:00 UTC, and @1793750400 is 2026-11-04 00:00:00 UTC (you can verify by dividing the seconds by 86,400 per day). The visit count is the last value, 37. So this browser store first received this site's cookie on 1 January 2025, 4 November 2026 is the 37th visit, and the previous visit was 24 October. Note that the first visit means "this store first received it then and hasn't deleted it since" (section 4).

Question 2. (Common misconception) "The last number of the competitor site's _ga cookie on the employee's PC is three days ago, so the employee first visited that site three days ago." Give at least three cases where this conclusion could be wrong.

Answer and explanation

① In private mode, each window is a new store, so it's just a cookie first received in a private window opened three days ago. ② If cookies were deleted, it resets from then. ③ The employee may have visited earlier with another browser or profile. ④ A browser lifetime cap (e.g. Safari's short limit) may have removed an older cookie and created a new one. ⑤ Reading that number as "first creation time" is itself an interpretation not in official documentation. So the sentence you can write is "this browser store's _ga cookie for that site appears to have been created three days ago", and the first visit is traced back through other evidence (proxy logs, browser history).

Question 3. (Calculation) A marketing cookie contains the value 1793598745123. What time is it? What happens if you feed it as-is to date -u -d @1793598745123?

Answer and explanation

With 13 digits, treat it as milliseconds and convert the first 10 digits, 1793598745: 2026-11-02 05:52:25 UTC, with the trailing 123 being 0.123 seconds (1793512345 was 05:52:25 on 1 November; adding 86,400 seconds gives 1793598745, exactly one day later). Fed as-is, date takes the 13 digits as seconds and gives an absurd date tens of thousands of years in the future, or a range error. When an implausible year comes out, first suspect the unit (seconds, milliseconds, microseconds).

Question 4. (Interpretation) The same hubspotutk value appears in requests to three different companies' web sites. What can you tell, and what can't you?

Answer and explanation

What you can tell: the same browser store visited three sites that use that marketing service. The value is an identifier the service gave the visitor, so it links the same person (strictly, the same store) across different sites. What you can't: who the person using the store was (it may be a shared PC), and how the value was generated (the source material also says its composition is undocumented). How the value is shared across sites can also depend on the vendor and the browser's cookie policy (first-party, third-party restrictions), so confirm the behaviour at the time before writing it up.

Question 5. (Changed conditions) A procedure written in 2016 says "treat files in the endpoint's browser cache as requested by the user, but note the possibility of HTTP/2 server push". For a Chrome cache in a 2026 case, how should this caveat change?

Answer and explanation

Chrome disabled HTTP/2 server push by default from 106 (2022), so a cache from later Chrome versions is very unlikely to contain server-pushed objects. For a 2026 case, write "server push disabled since Chrome 106" with its basis, and instead note that files may be in the cache for other reasons the user didn't directly request: images and scripts the page loaded itself, prefetching, resources the browser fetched early due to 103 Early Hints. The principle of not reading a single cache file as "something the user chose to open" stays.

Question 6. (Structure) In section 8.2's results, tcp.stream is always 0 but http2.streamid is 1 and 3. Explain the difference, and say how the same requests would have looked over HTTP/1.1.

Answer and explanation

tcp.stream is the number Wireshark assigns per TCP connection; http2.streamid is the number HTTP/2 assigns per request/response pair within one connection. The two requests were multiplexed as HTTP/2 streams 1 and 3 inside one TCP connection (client-opened streams are odd). Over HTTP/1.1, persistent connections (lesson 2.2, section 4.1) could also put them on one TCP connection, but requests would go one after another (the next only after the previous response finished), with no stream numbers. Sending two requests at the same time often means opening two TCP connections. So in HTTP/2 environments there are fewer connections, and counting "one connection = one request" in flow records is even more wrong.

Question 7. (Application) UDP 443 traffic on the packet sensors has grown sharply, but the number of web requests in the proxy logs is unchanged. What has most likely happened, and what do you check?

Answer and explanation

Browsers or apps are most likely going out directly over HTTP/3 (QUIC), bypassing a proxy that handles only TCP (lesson 1.2). Check ① the sources and destinations of outbound UDP 443 at the firewall (which PCs, which services), ② browser policy (e.g. whether QUIC is allowed) and when it changed, ③ destination names from the SNI in QUIC Initial packets (unless ECH), ④ whether proxy-log requests from the same PCs to the same services decreased. Remedies include blocking UDP 443 so browsers fall back to TCP, or disabling QUIC by policy; record the decision and its basis.

Question 8. (Common misconception) "HTTP/2 headers are compressed, so with the session keys you can read all headers from any point in the pcap." What's missing?

Answer and explanation

HPACK is stateful compression: it remembers headers sent earlier in the same connection in a dynamic table and later refers to them by number. So if capture began in the middle of a connection, or early packets are missing, some later headers may point to entries you don't know and can't be fully decoded, even with session keys. The TLS session keys themselves also need to be matched with the handshake at the start of the connection. So analysing HTTP/2 needs a pcap captured from the start of the connection, and the capture notes should record the start time.

Question 9. (Interpretation) In an old pcap (2014), you find __utmz=...utmcsr=search-engine|utmccn=(organic)|utmcmd=organic|utmctr=orchid%20alloy%20formula. What can you tell?

Answer and explanation

__utmz records how the visitor arrived at the site. utmcmd=organic means they came by clicking a (non-advertising) search result, and decoding utmctr gives "orchid alloy formula", the search term used at the time. Back then, search terms were sometimes passed along when going from a search engine to another site, which is why such values survived. Today Referer passes only the origin (lesson 2.1) and search engines often don't pass search terms, so such information is especially valuable in old evidence. But note that the cookie records the store's most recent source (as of when the cookie was updated), and which visit it belonged to must be read together with the other values.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Tools used in this environment: nghttp2 1.59.0 (nghttpd), curl 8.5.0 (built with nghttp2, SSLKEYLOGFILE), tcpdump 4.99.4, tshark 4.2.2, GNU date. Outputs were obtained on 2026-11-05.
  • Google, GA4 cookie usage (checked through search results on 2026-11-05). _ga and _ga_<container-id> default two years; browser lifetime caps (Chrome 400 days, Safari 7 days).
  • Google, Universal Analytics shutdown notice (checked through search results on 2026-11-05). Standard properties stopped processing on 2023-07-01.
  • Chrome Developers blog, Removing HTTP/2 Server Push from Chrome (checked through search results on 2026-11-05). Disabled by default in Chrome 106; 103 Early Hints recommended.
  • IETF, RFC 9113: HTTP/2 (section 3.4 connection preface, section 5 streams), RFC 7541: HPACK, RFC 9114: HTTP/3, RFC 9204: QPACK, RFC 9000: QUIC, RFC 8297: 103 Early Hints.
  • Marketing cookie lifetimes disagreed between published cookie lists on several sites (13 months versus 6 months, search on 2026-11-05). Check the vendor's current official documentation.

About this page

A personal study note, rewritten in my own words from several learning resources. The cookie values and experiment traffic are my own, and the scenarios are hypothetical.

docs.title: 2.5 — Web Server Logs: Formats, Reading Them, Traces of Attacks
2.5 — Web Server Logs: Formats, Reading Them, Traces of Attacks
docs.text:
Scope of this lesson

  • Why web server logs are special in investigations: even for HTTPS, server logs are plaintext
  • Common formats: NCSA Common, Common+VHost, Combined, Apache mod_log_forensic, IIS's formats
  • Reading the fields one by one, and the pitfalls confirmed by running Apache 2.4.58: the time is when the request was received, so lines appear out of order; the size field means different things per distribution; the virtual-host field isn't the requested name; failed logins still record the username
  • [Correction] "W3C Extended" and "Combined" are different formats, and non-printable characters are written as \xhh, not +
  • Analysing with the shell: the source material's four commands run on real logs
  • Traces of attacks: reconnaissance, SQL injection attempts, remote administration tools

Lab environment and notation

(Actual output) came from Apache 2.4.58 (Ubuntu package) installed in this environment. I created a practice virtual host (www.lab.example, alias portal.lab.example) on port 8080 and configured it to write the same requests in several log formats at once. The search CGI is a practice script made to return 500 deliberately when it sees a quote; there's no real database. All requests were sent with curl from the same computer, so the source appears as 127.0.0.1. IIS couldn't be run here and was checked through documentation only.

docs.title: 1. Why web server logs are special
docs.text:
Web server logs are as old as web servers. Their original purpose is unchanged: usage reports (how much was transferred, how many pages served) and records for fixing server and content errors. Yet in incidents involving a web server, these logs often become the most important evidence, because they record line by line everything from automated and manual reconnaissance, to the attack itself, to the moment of compromise (SQL injection, say), to post-compromise operations. With attacks using remote administration tools (RATs), every one of the attacker's commands may be recorded as a request line.

Compared with lesson 1.3's proxy logs: proxy logs record our staff going out, and web server logs record outsiders coming in to our server. The same HTTP, seen from the other side.

And web server logs have one big advantage: HTTPS requests are recorded in plaintext too. The web server is the TLS endpoint, so it writes the log after decrypting the request and knows the result before encrypting the response ("one end of the connection" from lesson 1.12). Even when packet sensors saw only encrypted bytes, the server log has the method, path, query and status code. Such logs are often the investigator's only window onto web activity: logs from web servers, caching proxies, and network security monitoring tools like lesson 2.8's Zeek. Those logs are all created from network communication, so what lessons 2.1–2.4 taught with packets carries straight over to log analysis.

docs.title: 2. Common formats
docs.text:
There are many web server programs, but log formats converge on a few. Most servers offer standard formats as options, plus a way to define your own (templates).

Server Main formats Apache NCSA Common, Common+VHost, Combined, separate Referer and User-Agent logs, custom definitions via format strings, mod_log_forensic IIS W3C extended format (default), IIS format, NCSA Common, centralised binary logging (CBL), ODBC (database) nginx combined (a predefined format), custom definitions via log_format

nginx isn't in the source material, but it's very widely used today, so it's included. nginx's predefined combined format uses the same field order as Apache's Combined.

docs.title: 3. NCSA Common: the basic seven fields
docs.text:
The most basic format is Common, defined by NCSA (the US National Center for Supercomputing Applications), which created much of early web technology. As an Apache format string it's %h %l %u %t "%r" %>s %b. Here's a line written by the lab server.

(Actual output)

127.0.0.1 - jdoe [05/Nov/2026:07:03:23 +0000] "GET /admin/ HTTP/1.1" 200 11
Field Format string Value in this line Meaning 1 %h 127.0.0.1 the requester's address (or host name, depending on configuration) 2 %l - remote user name (identd). Almost always - today 3 %u jdoe user name from HTTP authentication (Basic etc.). Form logins don't count 4 %t [05/Nov/2026:07:03:23 +0000] the time the request was received, with time zone 5 "%r" "GET /admin/ HTTP/1.1" the request line as-is: method, request target (including query, no host name), version 6 %>s 200 the final status code (after internal redirects) 7 %b 11 bytes in the response body (excluding headers); - if zero

Missing values are filled with -. Like lesson 1.3's Squid logs, it can be read by field position, which suits awk. Now let's confirm the pitfalls hidden in these seven fields.

docs.title: 3.1 The time is "received", the lines are in "finished" order
docs.text:
In the lab I sent a request that takes three seconds (/cgi-bin/slow.cgi) first, then other requests in the meantime.

(Actual output, surrounding lines only)

127.0.0.1 - - [05/Nov/2026:07:03:22 +0000] "GET / HTTP/1.1" 200 29
127.0.0.1 - - [05/Nov/2026:07:03:23 +0000] "GET /index.html HTTP/1.1" 200 29
...
127.0.0.1 - - [05/Nov/2026:07:03:23 +0000] "GET /.git/config HTTP/1.1" 404 277
127.0.0.1 - - [05/Nov/2026:07:03:22 +0000] "GET /cgi-bin/slow.cgi HTTP/1.1" 200 17

The slow.cgi line is last, yet its time, 07:03:22, is earlier than the lines before it. %t is when the request was received, but the log line is written after the request finishes, exactly as the source material warns. Remember that lesson 1.3's Squid did the opposite and recorded the completion time (start = completion − elapsed). Even among "web logs", the meaning of the time differs.

What it means for investigations: building a timeline in line order is wrong. You must re-sort by the time field, and the longer a request took (large downloads, slow uploads, long-held connections), the further its line position strays from its time. Including %D (elapsed microseconds) in the format lets you calculate both start and end.

docs.title: 3.2 Size fields: %b and %O, and distribution defaults
docs.text:
I also recorded the same requests in a format writing both %b and %O.

(Actual output, some fields)

"GET / HTTP/1.1"            200  29      256
"GET /dataset.bin HTTP/1.1" 206  50000   50304
"GET /dataset.bin HTTP/1.1" 200  200000  200249
  • %b (middle column) is the size of the response body: 29 for a 29-byte page.
  • %O (right column) is the bytes actually sent, including headers, counted by mod_logio: 256 for the same page.
  • 206 (partial content): requesting only bytes from 150,000 onwards of a 200,000-byte file with curl -r 150000-, %b was 50,000. As the source material says, with resumed downloads this value is not "the file size" but the size of the part sent by that request. Be careful when matching it against file sizes on disk.

[Supplement] Ubuntu's combined uses %O, not %b

The Combined format in upstream Apache documentation uses %b as its size field, but the combined predefined by this environment's Ubuntu package is "%h %l %u %t \"%r\" %>s %O ...", using %O (confirmed directly in /etc/apache2/apache2.conf). So even logs called "combined" record the size as body only (29) or including headers (256) depending on the distribution. When you receive logs, check the server's LogFormat definitions in its configuration file before interpreting numbers. Lesson 1.2's "the configuration file is evidence" applies here too.

docs.title: 3.3 [Correction] Non-printable characters are written as \xhh
docs.text:
The source material says non-printable characters are in most cases replaced with +. Testing Apache 2.4 directly showed otherwise. I sent a User-Agent containing a tab, quotes and Korean text, and a request line containing a control character (\x01).

(Actual output)

"GET /index.html HTTP/1.1" 200 256 "-" "tab\there \"quoted\" \xed\x95\x9c\xea\xb8\x80"
"GET /a\x01b HTTP/1.1" 400 489 "-" "-"

The tab was escaped as \t, the quotes as \", the UTF-8 bytes of the Korean word "한글" as \xed\x95\x9c\xea\xb8\x80, and the control character as \x01. Apache's documentation also says non-printable characters in the request line and header values are written as \xhh, a safeguard against attackers injecting fake lines into logs. For investigations, remember two things. ① When searching logs for keywords, also search for the escaped form (a Korean User-Agent appears only as \xed...). ② A request line containing control characters is itself a sign it didn't come from a normal browser; this request got a 400.

docs.title: 4.1 [Caution] The virtual-host field is not "the requested name"
docs.text:
Common+VHost prefixes each line with the virtual host name, a format for environments running several sites on one IP (lesson 2.1, section 6.1). Ubuntu's vhost_combined starts with %v:%p. But a lab request sent with Host: portal.lab.example was recorded like this.

(Actual output)

www.lab.example:80 127.0.0.1 - - [05/Nov/2026:07:03:23 +0000] "GET /index.html HTTP/1.1" 200 256 "https://search.example/" "..."

The requested name was portal.lab.example, but the log shows www.lab.example:80. %v is the canonical name (ServerName) of the virtual host that handled the request, and %p is likewise the configured canonical port, not the 8080 actually used. If a virtual host has several aliases (ServerAlias), this field can't tell you which name was used. If you need the name the client actually sent, include %{Host}i (the value of the Host request header) in the format. The mod_log_forensic log in section 5 kept Host:portal.lab.example as-is.

docs.title: 4.2 Combined: Referer and User-Agent
docs.text:
Originally, Referer and User-Agent were written to separate files, so as not to break programs depending on the Common format. Later the Combined format, appending both to the end of the line, came into use as a de facto standard.

(Actual output)

127.0.0.1 - - [05/Nov/2026:07:03:23 +0000] "GET /index.html HTTP/1.1" 200 256 "https://search.example/" "Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/141.0.0.0 Safari/537.36"

In investigations the two values are used like this.

  • Looking at our server: Referer tells you where a click came from (a link posted on a suspicious forum, say), and the User-Agent tells you the tool that crawled the site (reconnaissance copying content to build a convincing phishing page, for example).
  • Looking at our staff (proxy side): Referer links movements within one browser tab, and the User-Agent gives the list of software actually in use in the organisation (lesson 2.4).

The source material also warns that the headers in logs are the values after modification inside the server by features like mod_headers. If the server configuration rewrites headers, the log may not hold the client's original values. And dropping these two values from logs loses valuable material for investigations.

[Correction] \"W3C Extended\" and \"Combined\" are not the same format

The source material calls this format "W3C Extended/Combined" and attributes it to W3C. But they're different. Combined is an NCSA-family format (Apache's and nginx's default): NCSA Common plus Referer and User-Agent. The W3C Extended Log File Format is, as seen in lesson 1.5, a different format that declares column names in a #Fields: line (IIS's default, some commercial proxies). Reading one with a parser for the other misaligns the fields, so first check whether the file starts with a #Fields: line.

docs.title: 4.3 [Caution] Failed logins still record the username
docs.text:
I requested the Basic-auth-protected /admin/ once with a valid account (jdoe) and once with a nonexistent one (admin:admin).

(Actual output)

127.0.0.1 - jdoe [05/Nov/2026:07:03:23 +0000] "GET /admin/ HTTP/1.1" 200 11
127.0.0.1 - admin [05/Nov/2026:07:03:23 +0000] "GET /admin/ HTTP/1.1" 401 462

In the second line %u is admin, but the status code is 401. So %u is not "the successfully authenticated user" but the username the client sent, recorded even on failure. The error log recorded AH01618: user admin not found: /admin/ at the same time (actual output). So don't read "%u says admin, so an administrator logged in"; always read it with the status code. Conversely, the list of %u values piling up with 401s is the list of account names used in a brute-force attempt.

docs.title: 5. Apache mod_log_forensic: recording every header
docs.text:
Despite its name, mod_log_forensic wasn't built for digital forensics, but it records every request header for each request. The server is the TLS endpoint, so HTTPS requests are recorded decrypted too. Here's what it produced when enabled.

(Actual output, the start line of one request)

+auwqO8D2TYfXTSURFaXOvAAAAAc|GET /index.html HTTP/1.1|Host:portal.lab.example|User-Agent:Mozilla/5.0 (...)|Accept:*/*|Referer:https%3a//search.example/
  • Lines look like +unique ID|request line|Header:value|Header:value|.... The unique ID is a per-request value added by mod_unique_id.
  • When processing finishes, a separate -unique ID line is written. In this lab there were 17 + lines and 17 - lines (actual output). A request during which the server crashed or was cut off has a + but no -, which helps find the request that brought the server down.
  • As section 4.1 noted, the Host actually requested (portal.lab.example) is recorded.
  • Special characters within header values are percent-encoded (the %3a in Referer:https%3a//...).

[Caution] The forensic log records passwords too

The line for the /admin/ request kept Authorization:Basic amRvZTpTcHJpbmcyMDI2IQ== verbatim (actual output). As lesson 2.1 showed, Base64 decodes instantly, so this log effectively contains a plaintext password (jdoe:Spring2026!). Session cookies likewise. It's valuable for investigations, but the log itself is a treasure trove for an attacker. When enabling it, narrow the scope to the virtual hosts or paths needed (which, as the source material suggests, also reduces the performance and disk burden), and set strict access permissions and retention.

docs.title: 6. IIS logs
docs.text:
IIS couldn't be run here; this is from documentation.

  • The W3C extended format is the default. A #Fields: line selects the fields to record (date time s-ip cs-method cs-uri-stem cs-uri-query s-port cs-username c-ip cs(User-Agent) sc-status sc-bytes cs-bytes time-taken, etc.), and according to Microsoft's IIS 6-era documentation, times are written in UTC. Read the #Fields: line and handle columns by name, the same way as lesson 1.5's ELFF.
  • The IIS format is a fixed, comma-separated format.
